**Source:** AHA/ASA 2019 Stroke Guidelines; Indian Stroke Care Pathway 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Bleeding proximal to ligament of Treitz, presenting as haematemesis (fresh red / coffee-ground), melaena (≥ 50 ml from upper GI), or occasionally haematochezia in massive bleeds (≥ 1 L) with rapid transit. Accounts for ~80% of acute GI bleeds; mortality 6–10%.

### Etiology

Peptic ulcer disease (35–50%) — duodenal > gastric; NSAIDs, H. pylori, stress.

Oesophagogastric varices (10–20%) — cirrhosis with portal HTN; high mortality.

Mallory-Weiss tear (5–10%) — vomiting/retching, longitudinal mucosal tear at GE junction.

Erosive oesophagitis / gastritis / duodenitis.

Dieulafoy lesion (submucosal artery, lesser curve).

Upper GI malignancy (gastric, oesophageal).

**Vascular:** angiodysplasia, GAVE (watermelon stomach), aortoenteric fistula.

Iatrogenic — post-endoscopy, post-sphincterotomy.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Symptoms: Haematemesis, melaena, syncope, weakness, epigastric pain (PUD), retching → haematemesis (Mallory-Weiss).

**Signs of shock:** Signs of shock: Tachycardia, hypotension, cool peripheries, delayed CRT, oliguria, altered sensorium.

**Stigmata of CLD:** Stigmata of CLD: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis → suggests variceal source.

**PR exam:** PR exam: Mandatory — melaena confirms upper GI source if not from iron/bismuth/spinach.

### Investigations

### Bedside

Vitals + GCS + capillary refill + tilt test (drop SBP > 20 mm = > 1 L loss).

ECG (rule out MI from anaemia/shock, especially elderly).

NG tube only if diagnostic doubt (not routine).

### Laboratory

CBC — Hb may be normal initially (haemoconcentration); reticulocyte for chronicity.

Urea/creatinine — disproportionate ↑ urea suggests UGI source (protein load).

LFT (cirrhosis screen), INR, APTT — coagulopathy correction.

Group & save, cross-match 4–6 units, blood gas (lactate, base deficit).

### Risk stratification

**GBS:** Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) — pre-endoscopy; GBS = 0–1 → outpatient endoscopy safe; ≥ 2 admit.

**Rockall:** Rockall score — post-endoscopy, mortality prediction (age, shock, comorbidity, endoscopic Dx, stigmata).

**AIMS65:** AIMS65 — albumin < 3, INR > 1.5, mental status, SBP ≤ 90, age > 65.

### Endoscopy (definitive)

Within 24 h of stabilisation; within 12 h if haemodynamic instability or known cirrhosis.

Diagnostic + therapeutic (injection, thermal, clips, banding).

**Forrest classification for PUD:** Ia spurting > Ib oozing > IIa visible vessel > IIb adherent clot > IIc flat pigment > III clean base.

### Management

### 1. Resuscitation (ABC)

2 large-bore (16-18G) IV cannulae; airway protection if encephalopathic / massive bleed.

Crystalloid bolus (Ringer's lactate / NS) 20 ml/kg; titrate to MAP ≥ 65, UO ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/h.

**Restrictive transfusion:** PRBC transfusion threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL (Hb < 8 if active cardiac disease).

**Correct coagulopathy:** FFP if INR > 1.5 + active bleed; platelets if < 50,000; reverse warfarin (4F-PCC + vit K); reverse DOAC (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet for FXa).

### 2. Pharmacotherapy

**PPI:** PPI: IV pantoprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/h infusion × 72 h (continue PO 40 mg BD after).

Vasoactive (if suspected variceal):Vasoactive (if suspected variceal): Terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h × 5 d (1st-line in India) OR octreotide 50 µg bolus → 50 µg/h × 5 d.

Prophylactic antibiotics (variceal/cirrhotic):Prophylactic antibiotics (variceal/cirrhotic): Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d (reduces SBP + rebleed; mortality benefit).

**Prokinetic before endoscopy:** Prokinetic before endoscopy: Erythromycin 250 mg IV 30–60 min before OGD (improves visualisation).

### 3. Endoscopic therapy

**PUD Forrest Ia–IIb:** dual therapy (adrenaline injection + thermal/clip).

**Oesophageal varices:** endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) — first-line.

**Gastric varices:** cyanoacrylate (N-butyl) glue injection.

**Mallory-Weiss:** usually self-limiting; if bleeding — clips, adrenaline.

### 4. Failed endoscopic Rx

Repeat endoscopy first (especially if rebleed within 24 h).

**Variceal:** Sengstaken-Blakemore (max 24 h) → early TIPS < 72 h (Child B/C).

**PUD:** angiographic embolisation (gastroduodenal artery for DU posterior bleed); surgery (over-sewing, antrectomy, oesophagogastrectomy) — last resort.

### 5. Post-bleed care

**PUD:** H. pylori test/treat; stop NSAIDs; long-term PPI if can't avoid NSAID.

**Variceal:** non-selective β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg BD titrate to HR 55) + repeat EVL every 2–4 wk till eradication.

**Cirrhotics:** surveillance OGD, MELD/Child-Pugh re-score, transplant evaluation.

### Complications

Shock, AKI, hypoxic encephalopathy.

Aspiration pneumonia (esp. variceal bleed + encephalopathy).

Transfusion reactions, TRALI, TACO.

Rebleed (15–20%), need for surgery (~5%).

**Cirrhotics:** decompensation, HE, HRS, SBP.

### Prognosis

Overall mortality 6–10%. Variceal bleed in Child C — 6-week mortality 30–40%. PUD bleed mortality < 5% with timely endoscopy. Restrictive transfusion (Villanueva) improves survival vs liberal.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.21; NICE NG12 (2016); Baveno VII (2022).

### Definition

Upper GI bleed (UGIB) = bleeding proximal to ligament of Treitz (haematemesis/melaena/coffee-ground). Lower GI bleed (LGIB) = bleeding distal to it (haematochezia, fresh PR bleed). Mid-GI bleed = small bowel between papilla and ileocaecal valve (obscure source — capsule/enteroscopy).

### Lower GI Bleed — Etiology

### Approach to Differentiation

### Investigations

**UGIB:** OGD first within 24 h.

**LGIB:** colonoscopy within 24 h after bowel prep (PEG); CT angiography first if haemodynamic instability or massive bleed (detects bleed rate ≥ 0.3 ml/min).

**Obscure / occult:** capsule endoscopy → balloon enteroscopy → CT/MR enterography → tagged RBC scan → angiography.

**Meckel's:** Children/young adults with painless massive PR bleed: technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel's scan).

### Management Principles

ABC resuscitation as in Q1.

**UGIB:** PPI ± vasoactive ± antibiotic (if variceal); endoscopic Rx.

**LGIB:** stabilise → colonoscopy with clips/cautery/EBL; angio-embolisation; surgery if uncontrolled.

**Haemorrhoids:** dietary fibre + sitz + topical → banding/sclerotherapy → haemorrhoidectomy.

### Definition

Bleeding from oesophageal or gastric varices in patients with portal hypertension. Defines decompensated cirrhosis; mortality 15–20% per episode (Child C up to 40%).

### Aetiology

**Portal HTN:** cirrhosis (commonest), schistosomiasis (Indian endemic in some regions), portal/splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN.

**Trigger threshold:** HVPG > 12 mm Hg → varices develop; HVPG > 20 mm Hg + active bleed → high failure / rebleed risk.

### Clinical Features

Sudden large-volume haematemesis (often bright red) ± melaena ± haematochezia (massive bleed).

Hypovolaemic shock — tachycardia, hypotension, cool peripheries.

Stigmata of CLD — jaundice, spider naevi, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis (precipitates HE).

Often painless (unlike PUD).

### Investigations

Urgent OGD within 12 h after stabilisation (definitive diagnostic + therapeutic).

**Bloods:** CBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, splenic sequestration), INR, LFT, urea/creatinine, blood gas, cross-match 4–6 units.

Child-Pugh + MELD scoring (prognosis, transplant listing).

USG abdomen + Doppler — portal vein patency, splenomegaly, ascites.

Calculate HVPG (transjugular) when planning TIPS.

### Management

### 1. Initial Resuscitation

ABC, 2 wide-bore cannulae, airway protection if encephalopathic.

Crystalloid + restrictive PRBC transfusion (target Hb 7 g/dL — over-transfusion ↑ portal pressure → rebleed; Villanueva 2013).

Correct coagulopathy carefully — INR target not too aggressive in cirrhotics (rebalanced haemostasis); platelets if < 50,000.

- Pharmacotherapy — START WITHIN 1 H, BEFORE OGD

**Vasoactive (1st-line in India):** Vasoactive (1st-line in India): Terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h × 5 d (2 mg q4h for 24 h → 1 mg q4h thereafter). MOA: V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure.

**Alternative:** Alternative: Octreotide 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d OR somatostatin 250 µg bolus → 250 µg/h.

**Antibiotic prophylaxis:** Antibiotic prophylaxis: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d (reduces SBP + early rebleed + mortality, Garcia-Tsao recommendation).

**PPI:** PPI: IV PPI till endoscopy (in case non-variceal lesion identified).

### 3. Endoscopic Therapy

**Oesophageal varices:** Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) — 1st-line (controls bleeding in ≥ 90%, lower rebleed than sclerotherapy).

Alternative if EVL not feasible: endoscopic sclerotherapy (ethanolamine oleate, polidocanol).

**Gastric varices:** cyanoacrylate (N-butyl) glue injection; BRTO (balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration) if available.

- Failure / Massive bleed

Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (oesophageal + gastric balloon) — bridging only, max 24 h, requires ICU + airway protection (risk of necrosis, aspiration, rupture).

Early TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) < 72 h — indicated in Child B with active bleed or Child C ≤ 13; reduces rebleed + mortality (Garcia-Pagán 2010).

Self-expanding metallic stent (Danis stent) — temporary tamponade alternative.

**Surgical:** emergency portocaval shunt / oesophagogastric devascularisation (rarely needed in TIPS era).

- Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

Non-selective β-blocker — propranolol 40 mg BD titrate to HR 55–60 or carvedilol 6.25 BD (preferred in compensated cirrhosis, also α-blockade).

EVL every 2–4 wk till varices obliterated; surveillance OGD 6-monthly.

Treat underlying liver disease (DAA for HCV, antivirals for HBV, abstinence for alcohol).

Liver transplant evaluation in selected cases.

Fig 4. Variceal bleed — Baveno VII pathway.

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (red wale marks, Child B/C) → NSBB.

Medium/large varices → NSBB OR EVL (patient choice/comorbidity).

**Cirrhosis without varices:** do NOT use NSBB for prevention; OGD surveillance.

### Complications

Rebleed (15–30%), aspiration, HE precipitation, SBP, HRS.

**Sengstaken-related:** oesophageal necrosis, perforation, aspiration.

**TIPS:** encephalopathy (20–30%), stent dysfunction, RV failure.

### Prognosis

6-week mortality after first variceal bleed: Child A 5%, Child B 20%, Child C 30–40%. Improved with vasoactive + endoscopic Rx + abx + early TIPS.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.541; Baveno VII (2022); AASLD 2017; ISG-Indian Society of Gastroenterology.

### Definition

Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) — visualisation of oesophagus, stomach and duodenum (up to D2) using a flexible fibre-optic endoscope. Allows biopsy, cytology, and therapeutic interventions. Should be performed by trained gastroenterologist with anaesthetic support / monitoring.

### Indications

### Diagnostic

Dyspepsia with alarm features ('ALARMS'): Age > 55 with new symptoms, Loss of weight, Anaemia, Recurrent vomiting, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty.

Persistent dyspepsia not responding to PPI / H. pylori eradication.

GORD with alarm features or atypical symptoms.

Dysphagia / odynophagia.

Suspected oesophageal varices in known CLD.

Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia (with colonoscopy).

Coeliac disease — duodenal biopsy.

Suspected upper GI cancer or post-resection surveillance.

Suspected peptic ulcer disease.

Persistent vomiting of unknown cause.

Caustic ingestion (within 12–48 h to assess injury).

**Surveillance:** Barrett's oesophagus, gastric premalignant conditions (atrophic gastritis, IM, dysplasia), post-gastric resection, post-EMR/ESD.

### Therapeutic

Variceal banding (EVL) / sclerotherapy.

Endoscopic haemostasis for ulcer bleed (adrenaline injection, thermal coagulation, mechanical clips, haemospray).

Foreign body removal.

Stricture dilatation (achalasia, peptic, malignant).

Stent placement (oesophageal Ca, GOO).

Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) / submucosal dissection (ESD) — early cancers, polyps.

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) — long-term feeding access.

**Achalasia:** balloon dilatation, botulinum injection, POEM.

ERCP — biliary/pancreatic interventions (separate procedure).

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Suspected perforated viscus.

Severe respiratory compromise (without intubation).

Uncooperative / unstable patient without sedation/anaesthesia support.

### Relative

Recent MI (within 30 days).

Severe coagulopathy (correct INR, platelets first).

Severe COPD, decompensated heart failure.

Suspected aneurysm of aortic arch.

### Pre-Procedure

NBM 6 h for solids, 2 h for clear fluids.

**Informed consent (risks:** perforation 0.05%, bleeding, aspiration, sedation complications).

Stop anticoagulants (per BSG/ESGE guidelines — warfarin INR ≤ 1.5 for high-risk procedures; DOACs hold 24–48 h).

Stop iron / bismuth (interfere with mucosal visualisation).

**Pre-procedure assessment:** vitals, BP, cardiac/respiratory status.

IV access, oxygen, suction.

Topical pharyngeal anaesthesia (lidocaine spray).

**Sedation:** midazolam 2–5 mg IV ± fentanyl 25–50 µg; or propofol (anaesthetist).

Antibiotic prophylaxis NOT routinely required (except cirrhotic + variceal bleed, post-PEG placement, PEH high risk).

### Procedure

Left lateral decubitus position, head tilted forward.

Mouth-guard, bite-block.

Pass endoscope under direct vision → oesophagus → stomach → D1, D2.

**Systematic inspection:** GE junction, fundus retroflexion, pylorus, duodenum.

**Biopsies:** gastric (2 antrum + 2 body + incisura — Sydney protocol), duodenum (4 from D2 if coeliac disease suspected), specific lesions.

Photographic documentation.

Total procedure time 5–15 min (diagnostic), longer for therapeutic.

### Post-Procedure

Monitor vitals 30–60 min in recovery.

Avoid food/fluids till gag reflex returns (60 min if pharyngeal lignocaine).

**Watch for complications:** persistent chest/abdominal pain, haematemesis, breathing difficulty.

Discharge with adult escort if sedated.

No driving 24 h post-sedation.

### Complications (overall 0.1–0.5%)

Perforation (0.03–0.05% diagnostic; higher for therapeutic).

Bleeding (0.03% diagnostic, up to 1% for therapeutic).

Aspiration pneumonia.

**Cardiopulmonary:** arrhythmia, hypoxia (sedation), MI (rare).

Sore throat (transient).

Infection (transient bacteraemia; rare endocarditis).

### Common Findings (Quick Reference)

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ASGE Guidelines 2020; BSG; ESGE; ISG India.

### Classification of helminths

- Nematodes (round worms)

Ascaris lumbricoides – round worm.

Enterobius vermicularis – pin/thread worm.

Trichuris trichiura – whip worm.

Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus – hook worm.

Strongyloides stercoralis – thread/dwarf worm.

Trichinella spiralis – muscle larva.

Filaria – Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Loa loa.

Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness).

Dracunculus medinensis (guinea worm).

- Cestodes (tape worms)

Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) — cysticercosis if eggs ingested.

Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm).

Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm).

Echinococcus granulosus (hydatid disease).

Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm).

### 3. Trematodes (flukes)

Schistosoma haematobium / mansoni / japonicum (schistosomiasis).

Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke).

Paragonimus westermani (lung fluke).

Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke).

Anti-helminthic drugs and dosage (adult, oral)

**Albendazole:** Broad-spectrum nematicide. Ascaris/hookworm/whipworm: 400 mg single dose; Enterobiasis: 400 mg, repeat at 2 weeks; Strongyloidiasis: 400 mg BD × 3 days; Hydatid: 400 mg BD × 28 days × 3 cycles; Cysticercosis: 15 mg/kg/day × 8–30 days. Pregnancy: avoid in 1st trimester.

**Mebendazole:** Ascaris/hookworm/whipworm: 100 mg BD × 3 days or 500 mg single dose. Enterobiasis: 100 mg single dose, repeat at 2 weeks.

**Ivermectin:** Strongyloides/scabies/filariasis: 200 µg/kg single dose, repeat in 2 weeks. Onchocerca: 150 µg/kg every 6–12 months.

**Praziquantel:** Cestodes (Taenia, hymenolepis): 10 mg/kg single dose. Cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis: 50 mg/kg/day × 14 days. Schistosomiasis: 40–60 mg/kg single dose. Clonorchis/paragonimus: 25 mg/kg TDS × 2 days.

**Diethylcarbamazine (DEC):** Filariasis (W. bancrofti): 6 mg/kg single dose × 12 days, or DEC + albendazole + ivermectin (triple) in mass drug administration (NVBDCP).

**Pyrantel pamoate:** Ascaris: 11 mg/kg single dose; safe in pregnancy. Hookworm and enterobiasis (3 days).

**Niclosamide:** Enterobiasis: 1 g daily × 7 days; tapeworm: 2 g single dose.

### Indian deworming policy

National Deworming Day (NDD) – February 10 and August 10. Albendazole 400 mg single dose for all children 1–19 years.

Mass Drug Administration for filariasis – DEC 6 mg/kg + albendazole 400 mg annually in endemic districts.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis. Commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide after polio eradication. Incidence 1-2/100,000/year.

### Aetiology / Triggers

Antecedent infection 1-3 weeks earlier in 2/3:

- Campylobacter jejuni (commonest, esp. AMAN variant) — molecular mimicry with GM1/GD1a gangliosides.

- CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV, hepatitis E.

- Zika, dengue, chikungunya (Indian relevance).

- SARS-CoV-2 (post-COVID-19).

Post-vaccination (rare — older 1976 swine flu, rabies, influenza).

Post-surgical (rare).

### Variants

AIDP (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy) — commonest in West.

AMAN (Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy) — common in India/Asia, post-Campylobacter, anti-GM1.

AMSAN (sensorimotor axonal) — severe, slower recovery.

**Miller-Fisher:** ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b in 90%.

Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis: + altered sensorium.

Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial.

### Clinical features

Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis (legs → arms → bulbar → respiratory) over hours-days.

Areflexia (or hyporeflexia) — cardinal.

**Sensory:** paraesthesias > objective sensory loss; back/limb pain common.

**Cranial:** bilateral VII (50%), bulbar palsy.

**Autonomic in 70%:** BP swings, arrhythmias, ileus, urinary retention.

Respiratory failure in 25-30% — needs ventilation.

Peak deficit by 2-4 weeks; plateau; then gradual recovery.

### Brighton diagnostic criteria

Bilateral flaccid limb weakness + reduced/absent reflexes + monophasic course (12 h - 28 days) + CSF and/or electrophysiology supportive + no alternative diagnosis.

### Investigations

### Bedside (essential)

Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) — q4h; intubate if < 20 mL/kg.

Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF) — intubate if > -30 cm H₂O.

**Single breath count:** < 19 → impending respiratory failure.

ECG, BP monitoring (autonomic).

### CSF

Albuminocytological dissociation — protein > 0.45 g/L with cells < 10/mm³.

Appears after day 7 (50% positive in first week, 75% by week 2).

Nerve conduction studies (most sensitive in week 1)

**AIDP:** prolonged distal latency, conduction block, slowed velocity, prolonged F-wave latency, abnormal H reflex.

**AMAN:** reduced CMAP amplitude with preserved velocity.

### Antibodies (optional)

Anti-GM1 (AMAN), anti-GQ1b (Miller-Fisher), anti-GD1a.

### Other

MRI spine with Gd — anterior nerve root enhancement.

Stool Campylobacter PCR; serology HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, Zika/dengue if febrile.

**Rule out:** porphyria, lead, botulism, MG, polio, tick paralysis, transverse myelitis.

### Management

- Supportive — most important

ICU admission if rapidly progressive, bulbar dysfunction, autonomic, or FVC < 20 mL/kg.

Mechanical ventilation if FVC < 15 mL/kg, NIF > -30, hypoxia, or aspiration.

**DVT prophylaxis:** LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg SC OD) + IPC.

NG feeds if bulbar; bladder care; physiotherapy from day 1; pressure-area care.

**Pain:** gabapentin 300-1200 mg/d or carbamazepine; opioids if severe.

**Autonomic:** avoid suctioning-induced bradycardia; atropine standby; cautious BP management.

- Disease-modifying (start within 4 weeks of onset)

IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Preferred — easier, equally effective.

OR Plasmapheresis 5 sessions over 1-2 weeks (200-250 mL/kg total).

Both equally effective; DO NOT combine (no added benefit, increased cost).

**Steroids:** NOT INDICATED — multiple RCTs show no benefit; may delay recovery.

### 3. Rehab

Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychological support.

### Prognosis

80% walk unaided at 6 months; 60% full recovery at 1 year.

Mortality 5-10% (resp failure, autonomic, PE, sepsis).

**Poor prognosticators:** rapid progression < 7 d, axonal pattern, age > 60, ventilation needed, severe distal CMAP reduction.

Fig 4. GBS work-up and management.

**Source:** EAN/PNS GBS Guidelines 2023; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.

### Definition

Alcohol Use Disorder (DSM-5) is a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment / distress, manifested by ≥2 of 11 criteria in a 12-month period (replacing DSM-IV abuse + dependence). ICD-10 retains alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria) and harmful use. India has the largest population of male alcohol users in Asia; NMHS 2016 estimates prevalence of any alcohol-use disorder at 4.6% in adults (9% in men).

Hazards of alcohol (Boloor A365)

### Neurological

Acute — intoxication, blackouts, traffic accidents, traumatic brain injury, alcohol-induced psychotic disorder.

Withdrawal — tremor, seizures, delirium tremens (see below).

Chronic — Wernicke encephalopathy / Korsakoff psychosis, cerebellar degeneration (truncal ataxia, gait), peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor, painful), optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia), central pontine myelinolysis (with rapid sodium correction), Marchiafava–Bignami disease (corpus callosum demyelination), alcohol-related dementia.

### Gastrointestinal / hepatic

Acute / chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome.

Pancreatitis — acute and chronic (alcohol is the #1 cause of chronic pancreatitis in India after gallstones).

Alcoholic liver disease — fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >32 → steroids/pentoxifylline) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Oesophageal varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal / hepatopulmonary syndromes.

Malabsorption — folate, thiamine, B6, B12, Mg, Zn.

### Cardiovascular

Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcoholic), holiday heart (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke, sudden cardiac death.

### Haematological

Macrocytic anaemia (folate deficiency, direct marrow toxicity), megaloblastic, sideroblastic, haemolysis (Zieve syndrome with hepatitis + hyperlipidaemia), thrombocytopenia, leucopenia.

### Endocrine / metabolic

Hypoglycaemia (gluconeogenesis blocked), ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia / gout, hyperlipidaemia, pseudo-Cushing's.

Hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, infertility, erectile dysfunction.

### Cancer (Group I carcinogen — IARC)

Oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver (HCC), breast, colorectum.

### Obstetric

Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder — microcephaly, growth retardation, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, intellectual disability.

Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm birth.

### Psychiatric

Depression, anxiety, suicide (alcohol present in ~40% of completed suicides in India), insomnia.

Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, pathological jealousy (Othello syndrome).

### Social

Domestic violence, marital breakdown, child neglect, occupational accidents, road traffic accidents, financial ruin, legal issues.

Diagnosis — DSM-5 AUD criteria (≥2 of 11 in 12 months)

**Severity:** 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥6 severe.

Larger amounts / longer than intended.

Persistent desire / unsuccessful attempts to cut down.

Great time spent obtaining / using / recovering.

Craving.

Failure to fulfil role obligations.

Continued use despite social / interpersonal problems.

Important activities given up.

Use in physically hazardous situations.

Continued use despite physical / psychological problems.

Tolerance.

Withdrawal.

ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria — ≥3 of 6 in past year)

Strong desire / compulsion to drink.

Impaired control over use (onset, level, termination).

Withdrawal state on abstinence.

Tolerance.

Neglect of alternative interests.

Persistence despite clearly harmful consequences.

### Screening

**CAGE:** Cut down, Annoyed by criticism, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 = significant.

**AUDIT (WHO, 10 items):** 0–7 low risk, 8–15 hazardous, 16–19 harmful, ≥20 dependence.

AUDIT-C — 3-item screening tool.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (Boloor A373 ★2026)

Figure 6. Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal triage by CIWA-Ar, thiamine-first inpatient protocol, methanol-poisoning pathway and maintenance pharmacotherapy.

Time course (after last drink)

**6–12 h:** Minor withdrawal — tremor, anxiety, nausea, sweating, palpitations, insomnia, headache.

**12–24 h:** Alcoholic hallucinosis — visual / tactile / auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium and orientation (key DDx from DT).

**24–48 h:** Withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic, brief, 1–6 episodes; usually self-limited; 3% progress to status.

**48–96 h (peak 72 h):** Delirium tremens (DT) — clouded sensorium, disorientation, agitation, fluctuating consciousness, fever, autonomic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis), vivid visual / tactile (formication — 'bugs crawling') hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% untreated; 1–2% with modern care.

Risk stratification — CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised)

10 items, scored 0–7 each (orientation 0–4); total 0–67.

<8 — mild, no intervention.

8–15 — moderate, BZD treatment.

16–20 — severe.

>20 — very severe, ICU.

Management of withdrawal — Indian protocol (NIMHANS / AIIMS de-addiction)

**Inpatient if:** CIWA-Ar ≥10, history of DT / withdrawal seizures, severe medical / psychiatric comorbidity, poor support.

Thiamine FIRST, before any glucose (Wernicke prevention) — 100 mg IV/IM TDS × 3 days, then 100 mg PO OD long-term.

Wernicke / Korsakoff treatment dose: thiamine 500 mg IV TDS × 2–3 days → 250 mg IV/IM daily × 3–5 days → 100 mg PO long-term. Also IV Mg replacement (thiamine requires Mg cofactor).

**Benzodiazepines — first-line:** chlordiazepoxide 25–50 mg PO q4–6h symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar guided), tapered over 5–7 days. Diazepam 10–20 mg PO/IV q1–2h for severe.

Lorazepam preferred in hepatic dysfunction, elderly (no active metabolites): 2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h.

Phenobarbital — for refractory / BZD-resistant DT.

IV fluids (NS + 5%D), electrolyte correction — Mg 1–2 g IV q12h, K, PO4.

Multivitamin, folate 5 mg/d.

AVOID antipsychotics as monotherapy (↓ seizure threshold); use only haloperidol low dose if psychosis / agitation persists despite adequate BZD.

AVOID alcohol substitution.

Monitor vital signs q1–2h initially; CIWA-Ar q1–4h.

Treat fever, sepsis, pneumonia (high risk in DT), dehydration, rhabdomyolysis.

### Withdrawal seizures

**Treat acute seizure:** IV lorazepam 2–4 mg or diazepam 10 mg.

**Prevention:** adequate BZD coverage during detox.

Long-term anti-epileptics not needed unless underlying epilepsy.

Maintenance — relapse prevention (anti-craving)

**Naltrexone:** 50 mg PO OD (or 380 mg IM monthly). μ-opioid antagonist; ↓ craving and pleasure of drinking (COMBINE trial). Avoid in liver failure, opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); LFT monitoring.

**Acamprosate:** 666 mg PO TDS (2 g/d in <60 kg). NMDA modulator; ↓ relapse rate (PROJECT MATCH). Safe in liver disease; needs adequate renal function.

**Disulfiram:** 250 mg PO OD (max 500 mg). Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor; causes aversive reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, hypotension) on alcohol ingestion. Supervised dosing (family member). Avoid in CAD, severe psychiatric illness, pregnancy, peripheral neuropathy. Warn re: hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrups, perfumes).

Baclofen (off-label, useful in liver disease): 10–30 mg TDS; GABA-B agonist; reduces craving especially in cirrhotics where naltrexone and disulfiram unsafe (ANRS-BACLOVILLE).

**Topiramate, gabapentin:** Off-label adjuncts.

Psychosocial interventions (cornerstone — often dominate outcome)

Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MI / MET) — stage-of-change-based.

CBT — relapse prevention, coping skills.

12-step facilitation / Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) — Indian chapters widespread.

Family therapy, community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT).

Residential rehabilitation for severe / relapsing.

Treat comorbid depression / anxiety / PTSD.

Indian de-addiction infrastructure: AIIMS NDDTC, NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine, Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP — MoHFW), state-level Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs).

Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning — Boloor A367

Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in adulterated illicit liquor ('hooch'), industrial solvents, anti-freeze, windshield-washer fluid and formalin. Toxic dose ~10 ml; fatal 30 ml.

### Toxicokinetics

Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → FORMALDEHYDE → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → FORMIC ACID — the principal toxin (causes optic neuritis, metabolic acidosis).

### Clinical features

Latent period 12–24 h (longer if co-ingested ethanol).

Phase 1 — CNS depression (mild intoxication / inebriation).

Phase 2 (12–24 h) — N/V, abdominal pain, headache, vertigo.

Phase 3 — visual disturbance ('snowstorm', blurring, blindness), optic disc hyperaemia / oedema → permanent blindness.

Phase 4 — severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) with ↑ osmolar gap, Kussmaul respiration, seizures, coma, parkinsonism (putaminal necrosis), death.

### Investigations

ABG — severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2, HCO3 <10).

Anion gap — high (>20).

Osmolar gap — high (>10 mOsm/kg) early, falls as methanol is metabolised.

Serum methanol level — confirmatory (toxic >20 mg/dL; severe >50).

Fundus — optic disc hyperaemia / oedema.

MRI brain — putaminal haemorrhage / necrosis (classic).

### Management

ABC, IV access, gastric lavage (if <1 h), activated charcoal NOT effective (poorly adsorbed).

Block ADH (prevent toxic metabolite formation):

- FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole) — drug of choice if available; 15 mg/kg IV load → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses → 15 mg/kg q12h thereafter (induces own metabolism). Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL + acidosis resolved + asymptomatic.

- ETHANOL (alternative if no fomepizole) — IV loading 10 ml/kg of 10% ethanol over 30 min → 1.5 ml/kg/h infusion. Target blood ethanol 100 mg/dL. Cheaper and widely available in India.

FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1 mg/kg IV q4–6h (max 50 mg) × 6 doses — accelerates formate metabolism. Folic acid acceptable if folinic unavailable.

Correct acidosis — IV sodium bicarbonate to keep pH >7.2.

HAEMODIALYSIS — definitive removal of methanol and formate. Indications: serum methanol ≥50 mg/dL, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), visual / mental status changes, electrolyte imbalance refractory, renal failure.

Supportive — ICU, mechanical ventilation, treat seizures.

Complications of alcohol use (summary)

Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis (irreversible amnesia, confabulation).

Delirium tremens — mortality 5–15% untreated.

Cirrhosis, HCC, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy.

Suicide, accidental injuries, road traffic accidents.

Family disruption, economic loss, occupational impairment.

### Prognosis

Without treatment — progressive decline, premature mortality.

With comprehensive treatment (pharmacotherapy + psychosocial) — 30–50% achieve sustained remission at 1 year.

Better with stable social support, employment, no comorbid psychiatric illness, motivation for change.

Worse with antisocial personality, depression / suicide history, polysubstance use.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18 + Ch.16 (toxicology); Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Alcohol Use Disorders; NIMHANS / AIIMS NDDTC protocols; COMBINE 2006; PROJECT MATCH; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology — methanol/fomepizole; DSM-5; ICD-10/11.

### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis) affecting skin, peripheral nerves, mucous membranes, eyes, testes, and reticulo-endothelial system. India carries ~60% of global new case burden; leprosy is a notifiable disease (NLEP).

### Classification (WHO operational)

Paucibacillary (PB) – 1–5 skin lesions, smear-negative.

Multibacillary (MB) – >5 lesions or smear-positive.

Single skin lesion – ROM regimen (Rifampicin + Ofloxacin + Minocycline single dose) – discontinued by NLEP 2022 in favour of standard MDT.

### Multi-Drug Therapy (NLEP / WHO 2018)

MB regimen (>5 lesions or smear+): 12 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily (self-administered).

Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered).

PB regimen (1–5 lesions, smear-negative): 6 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine added since 2018 — 300 mg monthly + 50 mg daily.

Dapsone 100 mg daily.

### Paediatric (10–14 yrs)

Rifampicin 450 mg monthly; Clofazimine 150 mg monthly + 50 mg alternate day; Dapsone 50 mg daily.

Children <10 yrs / <40 kg – body-weight-based dosing.

### Treatment of reactions

Type 1 (reversal reaction – upgrade or downgrade)

Continue MDT.

Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, taper over 12–20 weeks; treat neuritis aggressively (preserve nerve function).

Rest, splinting, analgesia.

Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL)

Continue MDT.

**Mild:** NSAIDs.

**Moderate-severe:** Prednisolone 40 mg/day, taper over 8–12 weeks.

Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (refractory ENL; contraindicated in women of childbearing age – teratogenic).

Clofazimine — high dose 300 mg/day × 12 weeks then taper.

Supportive care and rehabilitation

Education on disease, transmission, course.

Wound care, footwear, protective gloves to prevent injuries to insensate areas.

Physiotherapy, splinting for clawed hands, dropped foot.

Reconstructive surgery for established deformities (lagophthalmos, claw hand, foot drop, plantar ulcer).

Eye care – artificial tears, protective glasses, surgery for lagophthalmos.

Social rehabilitation – combating stigma, vocational training, monthly disability allowance for permanent disability ≥40% under NLEP.

Contact tracing and single-dose rifampicin chemoprophylaxis (SDR-PEP – NLEP 2017).

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Diastolic regurgitation of blood from aorta into LV due to incompetent aortic valve. Causes: bicuspid valve, rheumatic, IE, syphilitic aortitis, Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection.

### Symptoms

**Asymptomatic for years; later:** exertional dyspnoea, palpitations (forceful heartbeat), angina (nocturnal common), syncope, orthopnoea, PND.

Peripheral Signs (eponyms of free aortic regurgitation)

**Pulse pressure:** wide pulse pressure (>50% of systolic), low diastolic.

**Corrigan's pulse:** high-volume, collapsing, water-hammer (with raised arm).

**Corrigan's sign:** visible carotid pulsation.

**De Musset's:** head bobbing with each beat.

**Quincke's:** visible nail-bed capillary pulsation.

**Traube's:** pistol-shot femoral sounds.

**Duroziez's:** to-and-fro femoral murmur on light compression.

**Müller's:** pulsatile uvula.

**Hill's:** popliteal systolic BP >20 mmHg higher than brachial.

**Rosenbach's:** carotid systolic shudder.

**Becker's:** pulsation of liver.

**Landolfi's:** rhythmic pupillary fluctuation.

### Precordial Signs

Apex – hyperdynamic, displaced down and out (volume overload).

Soft S1, soft/absent A2; S3 if LV dysfunction.

**Early diastolic murmur (EDM):** Murmur: high-pitched, early-diastolic, decrescendo, best heard at 3rd–4th left sternal edge with patient leaning forward in expiration. Length correlates with severity.

**Austin Flint murmur:** Mid-diastolic rumble at apex from regurgitant jet hitting anterior MV leaflet – severe AR.

**Associated:** Aortic ejection systolic murmur (functional, due to large stroke volume) common.

### Definition

Narrowing of aortic valve area producing obstruction to LV outflow. Severe when valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4.0 m/s.

### Etiology

**Calcific (degenerative):** >70 yr, most common cause in developed countries.

**Bicuspid aortic valve:** presents 40–60 yr; commonest congenital cause.

**Rheumatic:** commonest cause in India in younger adults; usually with associated MS.

Subvalvular (HOCM, membrane) or supravalvular (Williams syndrome).

### Pathophysiology

Narrow valve → ↑ LV pressure to maintain stroke volume → concentric LV hypertrophy → compliance ↓ → diastolic dysfunction → ↑ LVEDP → pulmonary congestion. Hypertrophied myocardium also has ↑ O₂ demand and impaired subendocardial perfusion → angina. Fixed cardiac output during exertion + reflex vasodilation → syncope. Eventually LV decompensation → systolic failure.

### Clinical Features

Asymptomatic for decades; triad (SAD) of Syncope (exertional), Angina, Dyspnoea heralds critical AS – mean survival without surgery: 5/3/2 years respectively. Sudden cardiac death possible.

### Signs

**Pulse:** slow-rising, low-volume (pulsus parvus et tardus).

Narrow pulse pressure.

**Apex:** heaving, sustained, not displaced (pressure overload).

Systolic thrill at aortic area radiating to carotids.

**Auscultation:** ejection systolic murmur, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo, maximal at aortic area, radiating to carotids; in elderly, harsh murmur may radiate to apex (Gallavardin phenomenon).

S1 normal; S2 softens/absent (calcified valve); paradoxical splitting; S4 (LVH); ejection click in bicuspid valve.

**Severity pointers:** longer murmur peaking later, soft/absent A2, presence of S4, narrow pulse pressure, slow-rising pulse, signs of LVH.

### Investigations

**ECG:** LVH, strain pattern, LBBB late.

**Echocardiography (key):** valve morphology, AVA (planimetry/continuity equation), peak/mean gradient, LV function, LVH.

**CXR:** cardiomegaly, post-stenotic dilatation of aorta, calcified valve.

**Cardiac catheterisation:** gradient, coronary anatomy before surgery.

**Exercise testing:** only if asymptomatic to unmask symptoms.

**Cardiac CT:** TAVR work-up (annulus size, peripheral vascular access).

Natriuretic peptides (BNP) for risk stratification.

Pharmacotherapy does not alter prognosis; valve replacement is the only definitive treatment.

**Mild–moderate, asymptomatic:** review yearly with echo. Treat HTN cautiously (ACEi/ARB); avoid vasodilators (GTN) and aggressive diuresis in severe AS.

**Severe symptomatic AS:** aortic valve replacement (AVR). Indicated also if asymptomatic with LVEF <50% or undergoing other cardiac surgery.

SAVR (mechanical/bioprosthetic) for younger, lower-risk patients.

TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement) for elderly/high-surgical-risk patients; now extending into intermediate-risk groups.

**Balloon aortic valvuloplasty:** palliative or bridge to surgery, especially in children/young adults with congenital AS.

Endocarditis prophylaxis if history of IE or prosthetic valve.

Loud S1 (palpable as 'tapping' apex), reflects increased force of MV closure with elevated LA pressure.

**Opening snap (OS):** high-pitched, follows A2, best heard at apex, occurs 0.06–0.12 s after A2; shorter interval = more severe MS.

**Mid-diastolic murmur (MDM):** low-pitched rumble, best heard with bell at apex in left lateral decubitus position after exercise, in expiration; duration correlates with severity.

Pre-systolic accentuation (in sinus rhythm, due to atrial contraction) – absent in AF.

**Pulmonary hypertension signs:** loud P2, parasternal heave (RV hypertrophy), pansystolic murmur of TR.

**Associated:** Graham Steell murmur (early-diastolic murmur of functional PR), Carey-Coombs murmur of acute rheumatic mitral valvulitis (transient MDM, soft S1).

### Background

Zoonotic spirochaetal disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira (>250 serovars; L. interrogans most pathogenic). Reservoir – rodents (especially rats), dogs, cattle, pigs. Transmission – exposure to water/soil contaminated with urine of infected animals via abraded skin or mucosae. Endemic in tropical regions; epidemics after monsoon/floods. Common in India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha).

Anicteric leptospirosis (90%, mild biphasic)

Septicaemic phase (3–7 days) – abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia (especially calf muscles), conjunctival suffusion (near-pathognomonic), nausea, diarrhoea.

Immune phase (4–30 days) – aseptic meningitis, uveitis, purpuric rash; antibodies appear.

Severe leptospirosis (Weil's syndrome) – 5–10%

Jaundice (without hepatocellular failure – conjugated, with mild transaminase rise).

Acute kidney injury – interstitial nephritis, hypokalaemia.

Haemorrhagic manifestations – epistaxis, haemoptysis, haematemesis, melaena, purpura.

Pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome – ARDS-like; high mortality.

Myocarditis, arrhythmia.

Death from MOF, mortality 5–40%.

Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT) – serotype-specific, paired sera, gold standard.

IgM ELISA – rapid; positive from day 5–7.

Lepto rapid card test, IgM dipstick.

Blood/CSF culture (Fletcher's medium, weeks); urine culture from week 2.

PCR – early diagnosis, blood/urine.

CBC – leucocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia.

LFT (raised bilirubin > transaminases), renal function (hyperkalaemia, raised creatinine), CK (elevated), CXR (pulmonary haemorrhage).

### Mild (outpatient)

Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (drug of choice).

Amoxicillin 500 mg q6h × 7 days (children, pregnancy).

### Severe (admit)

Penicillin G 1.5 MU IV q6h × 7 days.

Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OD × 7 days (equivalent efficacy, more convenient).

Cefotaxime 1 g IV q6h is an alternative.

Fluids; vasopressors; haemodialysis for AKI; mechanical ventilation for pulmonary haemorrhage; transfusion; electrolyte correction (especially K).

Avoid contact with potentially contaminated water (flooded fields, sewage); protective clothing, boots, gloves for farmers, sewage workers.

Rodent control.

Animal vaccination (livestock, dogs).

### Definition

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetric, erosive, inflammatory polyarthritis predominantly affecting peripheral synovial joints, associated with systemic features and extra-articular manifestations. Prevalence ~0.75% in India; female:male ≈ 3:1; peak onset 30–55 yrs.

### Etiology / Risk factors

**Genetic:** HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (DR4, DR1) — strongest in seropositive RA; PTPN22, STAT4

### Female sex, postpartum

Smoking — major modifiable risk; interacts with shared epitope to drive anti-CCP production

Periodontal disease (Porphyromonas gingivalis citrullination)

Obesity, low birth weight

### Silica dust exposure

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Citrullination of self-proteins → anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) in genetically susceptible host

Synovial hyperplasia (pannus) infiltrated by T cells, B cells, plasma cells, macrophages

**Pro-inflammatory cytokines:** TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, IL-17

Osteoclast activation (RANKL) → bone erosion; matrix metalloproteinases → cartilage destruction

### Clinical features

### Articular

Insidious onset symmetric polyarthritis — MCPs, PIPs, MTPs, wrists, knees, ankles, cervical spine; DIPs and lumbar spine spared

Morning stiffness >30–60 min, improves with activity

Swelling, warmth, tenderness; reduced grip strength

**Late deformities:** ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, hammer toes, hallux valgus

Atlanto-axial subluxation — neck pain, neurological deficit (caution at intubation)

### Systemic

Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anorexia

Extra-articular manifestations (~40%; more in seropositive RA, high anti-CCP, smokers)

**Cutaneous:** rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces — olecranon, Achilles)

**Pulmonary:** ILD (UIP/NSIP), pleural effusion (exudative, low glucose, low pH), Caplan syndrome, bronchiectasis, rheumatoid lung nodules

**Cardiac:** pericarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis, ↑ MI risk (1.5×), cardiomyopathy

**Ocular:** keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren), episcleritis, scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, scleromalacia perforans

**Haematological:** anaemia of chronic disease, Felty's syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), large granular lymphocyte syndrome

**Neurological:** carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitic), atlanto-axial myelopathy

**Vasculitis:** small/medium vessel — digital gangrene, leg ulcers, mononeuritis

**Renal:** AA amyloidosis (long-standing disease), drug nephropathy

**Lymphoma:** 2–4× increased risk, especially DLBCL

**Bone:** peri-articular osteoporosis, systemic osteoporosis

Diagnostic criteria — ACR/EULAR 2010

Score ≥6/10 classifies as definite RA (in a patient with synovitis in ≥1 joint without alternative explanation):

### Investigations

### Inflammatory and serology

RF (IgM-RF) — sensitivity 60–80%, specificity 60–80%

Anti-CCP — sensitivity 60–70%, specificity >95%; prognostic for erosive disease

ESR, CRP — disease activity

### General workup

CBC (ACD, leukopenia in Felty), comprehensive metabolic, LFT, urinalysis

ANA — screen for overlap

HBsAg, anti-HCV, latent TB (Mantoux/IGRA) — pre-biologic

HIV (Indian context, before biologics)

### Imaging

X-ray hands and feet — soft-tissue swelling, juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, deformities, subluxation; cervical spine for atlanto-axial subluxation

Ultrasound joints — synovitis, power Doppler signal, erosions earlier than X-ray

MRI — most sensitive for early synovitis, erosions, bone marrow oedema

### Disease activity

DAS28-ESR or DAS28-CRP (tender + swollen joint count + global + ESR/CRP)

### CDAI, SDAI — alternatives

**Targets:** DAS28 <2.6 = remission; ≤3.2 low; 3.2–5.1 moderate; >5.1 high activity

### Management — treat-to-target

### General

Smoking cessation; weight reduction; physiotherapy and occupational therapy

Patient education; vaccination pre-immunosuppression (influenza, pneumococcal, HBV, HPV); avoid live vaccines on biologics

CV risk assessment and treatment (statin, BP control)

### Symptom relief

NSAIDs at lowest effective dose for short periods

Prednisolone 5–10 mg/d as 'bridge' until DMARD effective; intra-articular steroid for active joints

Avoid long-term steroids — osteoporosis, infection, diabetes

csDMARDs (conventional synthetic) — start within 3 months of diagnosis

**Methotrexate:** Anchor drug. Start 7.5–10 mg/week, titrate to 20–25 mg/week. Co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/wk (not on MTX day). AE: nausea, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, pneumonitis, teratogenicity. Stop 3 months before conception (M and F). Avoid alcohol. Reduce dose in CKD; contraindicated in eGFR <30.

**Sulfasalazine:** 1 g BD–TDS. AE: GI upset, rash, hepatitis, agranulocytosis, G6PD-related haemolysis, oligospermia.

**Hydroxychloroquine:** 200–400 mg/d (≤5 mg/kg). AE: retinal toxicity — eye check baseline + annual after 5 yrs.

**Leflunomide:** 10–20 mg/d (loading 100 mg × 3 days then maintenance — most centres skip loading). AE: hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, hypertension, teratogenicity (very long half-life; cholestyramine washout needed before pregnancy).

**Combination 'triple therapy':** MTX + SSZ + HCQ — Indian-favoured cost-effective combination, comparable efficacy to early biologic in many patients

Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) — after inadequate response to ≥2 csDMARDs

**TNF inhibitors:** etanercept (50 mg SC weekly), adalimumab (40 mg SC q2wk), infliximab (3–10 mg/kg IV q8wk + MTX), golimumab (50 mg SC monthly), certolizumab

**IL-6 inhibitor:** tocilizumab 162 mg SC weekly OR 4–8 mg/kg IV q4wk

**B-cell depletion:** rituximab 1 g IV × 2 (day 0 and 14), every 6 months — RF/anti-CCP-positive; safer in latent TB

**T-cell co-stimulation:** abatacept 125 mg SC weekly OR weight-based IV monthly

**IL-1 inhibitor:** anakinra (rarely used in RA)

Always combine with MTX where tolerated for synergy and reduced anti-drug antibodies

Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) — JAK inhibitors

Tofacitinib 5 mg BD, baricitinib 4 mg OD, upadacitinib 15 mg OD

**ORAL Surveillance trial (2022):** increased major CV events, malignancy, VTE with tofacitinib vs TNFi in older patients with CV risk

**EMA/FDA:** use only if no TNFi alternative in patients ≥65 yr, smokers, malignancy, CV risk

Pre-biologic screening (essential — viva point)

**TB:** Mantoux/IGRA, CXR; if positive — INH 300 mg/d × 9 months started ≥1 month before biologic

### HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV

### CBC, LFT, RFT

Pregnancy test; contraception counselling

### Surgical

### Synovectomy (rare today)

Arthrodesis, arthroplasty (hip/knee/shoulder) for end-stage joint damage

C1–C2 fixation for atlanto-axial instability

### Carpal tunnel release

Fig 5. Rheumatoid arthritis — treat-to-target DMARD ladder

### Complications

Joint destruction, deformity, functional disability

Premature CV death (leading cause)

### ILD, pulmonary fibrosis

### Cervical myelopathy (atlanto-axial)

### Infections (immunosuppression)

### Lymphoma, skin cancers

### Osteoporosis, fragility fractures

### AA amyloidosis

### Prognosis

Modern treat-to-target therapy achieves remission/low disease activity in 50–80%. Adverse prognostic factors: female, smoking, high titre RF/anti-CCP, early erosions, multiple joint involvement, extra-articular features, high inflammatory markers. Untreated RA shortens life expectancy by 5–10 years, mostly from CV disease.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 RA + ACR 2021 guideline for RA + EULAR 2022 RA management recommendations + Indian Rheumatology Association RA position paper.
