### Definition

Recurrent paroxysmal unilateral severe facial pain in one or more divisions of trigeminal nerve, triggered by innocuous stimuli ('tic douloureux'). 'Suicide disease' due to intensity.

### Epidemiology

**Incidence 4-13/100,000/year; F:** M = 1.5:1; peaks 60-70 y.

Younger onset (< 40 y) → suspect MS or structural cause.

Aetiology / Classification (ICHD-3 / 2016 redefinition)

**Classical TN:** vascular compression of trigeminal root by superior cerebellar artery (90% of cases).

**Secondary TN:** MS (5-10%), tumour (acoustic neuroma, meningioma, epidermoid cyst), AVM, sarcoidosis.

**Idiopathic TN:** no identifiable cause.

### Clinical features

Pain characteristics — diagnostic

Sharp, stabbing, electric-shock-like.

Severe (10/10) — among worst pains known.

Brief — seconds to 2 minutes per attack.

Strictly unilateral (bilateral rare; suggests MS).

**Distribution:** V2 (maxillary) > V3 (mandibular) > V1 (ophthalmic).

**Triggers:** light touch, washing face, shaving, chewing, brushing teeth, cold breeze, talking.

Refractory period after attack.

Remissions and relapses common.

### Examination

NORMAL between attacks in classical TN.

If sensory loss, corneal reflex abnormal, or other CN involved → suspect secondary TN.

### Investigations

MRI brain with high-resolution trigeminal protocol (FIESTA / CISS) + MR angiography — identifies neurovascular conflict and excludes secondary causes.

All patients with TN should have MRI; especially mandatory if age < 40, bilateral, sensory loss, no carbamazepine response.

### Management

### 1. Medical (first-line)

**Carbamazepine:** Carbamazepine: FIRST CHOICE. Start 100-200 mg BD, titrate up to 600-1200 mg/d (max 1800 mg). NNT = 1.7-2.6. Side effects: rash (SJS — HLA-B*1502 in Asians), hyponatraemia, ataxia, drowsiness, leukopenia. Monitor Na, CBC, LFT.

**Oxcarbazepine:** Oxcarbazepine: Better tolerated. 300 mg BD up to 1800 mg. Hyponatraemia still possible.

**Lamotrigine:** Lamotrigine: Adjunct; slow titration (rash, SJS).

**Baclofen:** Baclofen: 30-80 mg/d; especially useful in TN due to MS.

**Gabapentin / Pregabalin:** Gabapentin / Pregabalin: Adjunct; useful when carbamazepine not tolerated.

**Phenytoin:** Phenytoin: IV 250 mg slowly — for acute exacerbation 'crisis'.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: Subcutaneous injection — emerging evidence, 2nd-3rd line.

- Surgical (indicated if medical therapy fails or intolerable AEs)

Microvascular decompression (Jannetta):Microvascular decompression (Jannetta): Posterior fossa craniotomy, Teflon felt between vessel and nerve. BEST long-term results: 80-90% pain-free at 10 y. Best in younger patients with classical TN. Risks: hearing loss, facial palsy, CSF leak, stroke (1%).

Percutaneous procedures (ganglion ablation):Percutaneous procedures (ganglion ablation): Glycerol injection, balloon compression, radiofrequency thermocoagulation. Less invasive but higher recurrence (40-60% at 5 y) and sensory loss (corneal anaesthesia if V1).

Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife):Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife): 70-80% initial relief; effect at 4-6 weeks; useful in elderly / high surgical risk. Recurrence 30-50% at 5 y.

- Treat underlying cause if secondary TN

MS — disease-modifying therapy.

Tumour — resection / radiation.

### Differential diagnosis

Cluster headache (longer, autonomic features, orbital).

SUNCT / SUNA (V1 distribution, autonomic).

Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (V → throat/ear; triggered by swallowing).

Postherpetic neuralgia (history of zoster).

Dental pain, temporomandibular joint disorder, sinusitis.

Atypical facial pain (constant, dull, no trigger).

**Source:** EAN 2019 TN Guidelines; AAN-EFNS 2008; Boloor Ch.15.

### Combined Notes (7 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Background

Intracranial calcifications are common — many physiological, some pathological. Pattern, location and clinical context help diagnosis. CT is far more sensitive than plain X-ray.

### PHYSIOLOGICAL calcifications

Pineal gland (60% after age 20; useful for midline shift assessment).

Choroid plexus (in lateral ventricles, trigone).

Falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli.

Petroclinoid ligaments.

Habenular commissure.

Dura, arachnoid granulations.

### PATHOLOGICAL calcifications

### 1. Infections

Neurocysticercosis — MULTIPLE punctate calcifications, classic in India; often with seizure history.

Tuberculoma — calcified granuloma.

Toxoplasmosis (congenital) — periventricular / scattered cortical; with hydrocephalus.

CMV (congenital) — periventricular calcifications; with microcephaly.

Cryptococcus, hydatid cyst.

Old abscess.

### 2. Tumours

Oligodendroglioma — 70-90% calcify (characteristic).

Astrocytoma (especially low-grade) — 15%.

Craniopharyngioma — suprasellar, mixed solid-cystic with calcification (children).

Meningioma — psammomatous calcification.

Ependymoma.

Pituitary adenoma (rare).

Metastases (osteoblastic — prostate, breast).

### 3. Vascular

Atherosclerosis (carotid siphon).

Aneurysm (curvilinear calcification of wall).

AVM, cavernoma.

Old infarct / haemorrhage.

Subdural haematoma (chronic, calcified).

### 4. Phakomatoses / Congenital

Sturge-Weber syndrome — tram-track / gyriform calcifications along cortex (parieto-occipital).

Tuberous sclerosis — subependymal nodules (basal ganglia, near foramen of Monro).

Neurofibromatosis (rare optic glioma calcification).

### 5. Metabolic / Endocrine

Hypoparathyroidism / pseudohypoparathyroidism — bilateral basal ganglia + cerebellar (Fahr syndrome).

Hyperparathyroidism (rare).

Hypothyroidism (cretinism).

Wilson's disease.

Fahr disease (idiopathic basal ganglia calcification).

### 6. Toxic / Radiation

Lead poisoning.

Post-radiotherapy (mineralising microangiopathy).

Methotrexate-induced leukoencephalopathy.

### 7. Other

Cockayne syndrome (basal ganglia).

Coats plus syndrome.

### Approach by location

### Investigations

CT head (without contrast) — sensitive for calcification.

MRI brain — characterise lesion; calcium is hypointense on T1 and T2 (or use SWI).

Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D (basal ganglia calcifications).

Ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper (Wilson's).

TORCH serology if neonatal.

Cysticercosis ELISA (EITB), stool ova/cyst.

**Source:** Osborn Diagnostic Imaging Brain; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Platelet count <150 × 10⁹/L. Mild: 100–150; moderate: 50–100; severe: <50 (bleeding risk); critical: <20 (spontaneous bleeding risk).

### Mechanistic classification

### 1. Decreased production

**Bone marrow failure:** aplastic anaemia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, metastasis, myelofibrosis).

Megaloblastic anaemia – ineffective megakaryopoiesis.

Viral – HIV, HCV, dengue, EBV, parvovirus.

Drugs – chemotherapy, alcohol, valproate, co-trimoxazole, linezolid, thiazides, methotrexate.

Radiation.

Congenital – Fanconi anaemia, Wiskott-Aldrich, thrombocytopenia with absent radii, May-Hegglin.

### 2. Increased destruction

### Immune (ITP):

– Primary ITP (idiopathic / autoimmune anti-GP IIb/IIIa antibodies)

– Secondary ITP – SLE, HIV, HCV, CLL, lymphoma, drugs (heparin, quinine, sulpha, vancomycin, rifampicin)

### – Post-vaccination, post-viral

**Microangiopathic (MAHA):** TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, preeclampsia.

**Mechanical:** prosthetic valves, ECMO, IABP.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT-II): 4Ts score.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.

### 3. Sequestration

Hypersplenism (cirrhosis, portal hypertension, lymphoma, kala-azar, Gaucher).

### 4. Dilutional

Massive transfusion, large volume fluid resuscitation.

### 5. Pseudo-thrombocytopenia

EDTA-induced platelet clumping; redraw in citrate.

### Clinical features

Mucocutaneous bleeding – petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeds, menorrhagia, haematuria.

GI bleed, intracranial haemorrhage (most feared).

Wet purpura (mucosal bullae) – high bleeding risk.

Splenomegaly – hypersplenism, lymphoma, kala-azar; absent in ITP and BM failure.

Features of underlying cause.

### Investigations

CBC – platelet count, MPV (high in ITP / destruction; low in failure).

Peripheral smear – platelet clumps (pseudo), schistocytes (MAHA), blasts (leukaemia), giant platelets, tear drops, atypical lymphocytes (viral).

**Coagulation:** PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer (DIC).

Reticulocyte count, retic Hb.

LFT, RFT.

HIV, HCV, HBV; ANA; dengue NS1/IgM in endemic.

DAT, blood group, cross-match (in case BT needed).

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP <10%.

Anti-PF4 antibody, 4Ts score, serotonin release – HIT.

Bone marrow biopsy – not routine for ITP but mandatory if elderly, pancytopenia, unusual features, before splenectomy.

USG abdomen – splenomegaly.

### Management (cause-specific)

Primary ITP (commonest haematological clinical scenario)

Treatment indicated when platelets <30 × 10⁹/L OR bleeding.

### First line:

– Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day × 2–4 weeks then taper

– Dexamethasone 40 mg OD × 4 days (high-dose pulse)

– IVIG 1 g/kg/day × 2 days – rapid rise; for severe bleeding, pregnancy, pre-op

– Anti-D 50–75 µg/kg IV (Rh+ve only)

### Second line:

– Rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly × 4

– Thrombopoietin receptor agonists: eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag

– Splenectomy – durable 60–70% response; vaccinations ≥2 weeks pre-op

– Fostamatinib (SYK inhibitor) — newer

Emergency – platelet count <10 + bleeding: IVIG + IV methylprednisolone + platelet transfusion (preferably after IVIG to slow destruction).

### TTP

Urgent plasma exchange daily with FFP replacement.

Steroids high-dose.

Rituximab.

Caplacizumab (anti-vWF).

Avoid platelet transfusion (worsens thrombosis).

### HIT

Stop ALL heparin (including flushes, line locks); remove heparin-coated catheters.

**Non-heparin anticoagulant:** argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOAC.

Do NOT give platelets unless major bleed.

**Confirmation:** ELISA + serotonin release assay.

DIC – treat cause + replace blood products if bleeding (see Q28).

Drug-induced – stop offending drug; usually resolves in days.

Fig 11. Thrombocytopenia — diagnostic algorithm.

Transfusion thresholds (general guide)

**<10 × 10⁹/L:** prophylactic transfusion for all (intracranial haemorrhage risk).

**<20:** prophylactic if sepsis, coagulopathy.

**<50:** prior to most procedures, in bleeding patient.

**<100:** neurosurgery, ophthalmic surgery.

Avoid in TTP, HIT (worsens thrombosis); ITP (only with severe bleed).

### Combined Notes (12 topics)

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

Fig 1. Anaemia workup by MCV.

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

Fig 3. Megaloblastic anaemia — workup and treatment.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.

Fig 5. Sickle cell disease — crisis management.

### Definition

Infusion of haematopoietic stem cells (CD34+) to re-establish marrow function after high-dose chemotherapy / radiotherapy, or to provide a healthy immune system / correct an inherited defect.

### Types

### Based on donor

Autologous – patient's own cells harvested, stored, reinfused (e.g. multiple myeloma, lymphoma).

Allogeneic – HLA-matched donor (sibling, unrelated, haplo-identical, cord blood).

Syngeneic – identical twin.

### Based on source

Bone marrow harvest – iliac crest under anaesthesia.

Peripheral blood stem cells (PBSC) – G-CSF mobilisation + apheresis (commonest, >90% of allogeneic).

Umbilical cord blood – lower stem cell dose, slower engraftment, less GVHD, useful in paediatrics.

### Indications

### Autologous

Multiple myeloma (1st remission).

Relapsed Hodgkin / Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Acute leukaemia in selected cases.

Germ cell tumours (relapsed).

### Allogeneic

AML/ALL high risk or in second CR.

CML – TKI failure or T315I.

MDS, severe aplastic anaemia.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

Thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease.

Inherited metabolic / lysosomal storage disorders.

Fanconi anaemia, congenital marrow failure.

### Process

- Donor evaluation + HLA typing (high-resolution A,B,C,DR,DQ).

- Stem cell mobilisation – G-CSF 10 µg/kg/day × 4–5 days ± plerixafor; apheresis to collect ≥2–5 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg.

### 3. Conditioning regimen:

**– Myeloablative (MAC):** high-dose chemo (busulfan/cyclophosphamide, cyclophosphamide/TBI).

**– Reduced intensity (RIC):** less toxic; for older / co-morbid patients.

- Stem cell infusion (Day 0).

- Engraftment – neutrophils ≥0.5 × 10⁹/L for 3 days (usually 10–28 d); platelets ≥20 × 10⁹/L without transfusion.

- GVHD prophylaxis – calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporin/tacrolimus) + methotrexate, or post-transplant cyclophosphamide for haploidentical.

### Complications

### Early (<100 d)

**Conditioning toxicity:** mucositis, alopecia, infertility, VOD/SOS, cardiotoxicity.

Pancytopenia + infections – bacterial, fungal (aspergillus), viral (CMV, HSV).

Acute GVHD – skin rash, hepatitis, diarrhoea; first 100 days.

Graft failure / rejection.

### Late (>100 d)

Chronic GVHD – scleroderma, sicca syndrome, BOOP, cholestasis.

Opportunistic infections – PJP, CMV, fungal, VZV.

Secondary malignancy.

**Endocrine:** hypothyroidism, infertility, growth failure.

Cataracts, osteoporosis.

Relapse of primary disease.

### Outcomes / Indian context

TRM (Transplant Related Mortality) ~10% autologous, 15–25% allogeneic. Indian centres of excellence – CMC Vellore, Tata Medical Centre Kolkata, AIIMS Delhi, Apollo, Manipal. Cost remains a major barrier; Govt. schemes (RAN, PMJAY) and BMTU at Tata, CMC help.

### Indications

Intolerance to oral iron (GI side effects despite dose modification).

Malabsorption – coeliac disease, gastric surgery, IBD.

Non-compliance.

Continued blood loss exceeding capacity of oral iron.

Pregnancy with severe anaemia in 2nd/3rd trimester or intolerance.

CKD anaemia, especially on EPO therapy.

Heart failure with iron deficiency (functional or absolute).

Need for rapid replenishment (pre-operative).

Anaemia of chronic disease where oral inefficient (hepcidin-mediated block).

### Preparations and doses

Iron sucrose – 100–200 mg slow IV, max 600 mg/week; multiple doses needed; safe in pregnancy.

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM, e.g. Ferinject, Encicarb) – single dose up to 1000 mg over 15 min IV infusion; preferred for rapid correction; weekly if larger doses needed; widely used in India.

Iron isomaltoside / derisomaltose – up to 20 mg/kg in single infusion.

Ferumoxytol – 510 mg IV.

Iron dextran – high dose possible (total dose infusion) but anaphylaxis risk; test dose mandatory; rarely used.

Total iron deficit (Ganzoni formula)

Total iron required (mg) = Weight (kg) × (Target Hb − Actual Hb) × 2.4 + iron stores (500 mg adults / 15 mg/kg <35 kg).

Target Hb typically 15 g/dL (men), 14 g/dL (women); 11 g/dL in pregnancy.

### Adverse effects

**Infusion reaction:** fever, flushing, myalgia, hypotension (usually mild).

Anaphylaxis – rare with newer formulations (~1:200,000 FCM); higher with dextran.

Hypophosphataemia – particularly with FCM and iron isomaltoside (repeated doses).

Extravasation – skin staining (administer in proximal vein, stop if pain at site).

Iron overload – haemochromatosis-like with prolonged unmonitored use.

### Administration precautions

Resuscitation facility available (anaphylaxis).

Monitor BP/pulse/SpO₂.

Avoid in 1st trimester of pregnancy and active infection (except life-threatening anaemia).

Reassess Hb / ferritin / TSAT in 4–8 weeks post-infusion.

### Genetics

X-linked recessive disorder of the hexose monophosphate shunt enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, leading to decreased NADPH and reduced glutathione → RBCs unable to neutralise oxidative stress. Commonest enzymopathy; ~400 million people affected worldwide. Common in Mediterranean, Africa, South-East Asia, parts of India (tribal, ~10%). Confers partial protection against P. falciparum malaria.

### Variants

**Class I:** severe enzyme deficiency + chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia.

**Class II:** severe deficiency, intermittent haemolysis (Mediterranean variant).

**Class III:** moderate deficiency (African A−, most Indian patients).

**Class IV:** normal activity.

### Triggers of haemolysis

**Drugs:** primaquine, dapsone, sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin, ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, rasburicase, methylene blue, sulfasalazine, high-dose aspirin, vitamin K analogues.

Infections – viral hepatitis, pneumonia, typhoid, septicaemia (commonest trigger overall).

Fava beans (favism) – Mediterranean variant.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.

Naphthalene (mothballs), henna.

### Clinical features

Asymptomatic between episodes.

Acute intravascular haemolysis 24–72 h after trigger: fever, malaise, jaundice, dark (cola-coloured) urine, back pain, dyspnoea, AKI in severe cases.

Neonatal jaundice – may need exchange transfusion; kernicterus risk.

Chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia (rare, Class I).

### Investigations

**During crisis:** ↓Hb, ↑retic, ↑indirect bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria.

Peripheral smear – bite cells, blister cells, Heinz bodies (with supravital stain – brilliant cresyl blue), polychromasia.

G6PD enzyme assay – diagnostic. False-negatives during active haemolysis (young RBCs have higher enzyme); repeat after 3 months.

Fluorescent spot test – screening.

DNA analysis – definitive carrier detection.

### Management

Avoid known triggers (drug card, family education).

Treat infection promptly.

**Acute crisis:** hydration, monitor renal function; transfusion if severe (Hb <7).

Folic acid supplementation in chronic haemolysis.

Phototherapy ± exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice.

Screen before starting primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase.

Splenectomy not effective (intravascular haemolysis).

### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

### Combined Notes (12 topics)

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

Fig 1. Anaemia workup by MCV.

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

Fig 3. Megaloblastic anaemia — workup and treatment.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.
