### Definition

X-linked recessive bleeding disorder due to deficiency of coagulation factor VIII (Haemophilia A, 80%) or factor IX (Haemophilia B / Christmas disease, 20%). Haemophilia C is factor XI deficiency, autosomal, milder.

### Severity classification

Severe – factor activity <1%; spontaneous bleeding (joints, muscles).

Moderate – factor activity 1–5%; bleeding with minor trauma.

Mild – factor activity 5–40%; bleeding only with major trauma / surgery.

### Clinical features

Onset in childhood (severe – infancy with circumcision, bruising on crawling).

Haemarthrosis – knee > ankle > elbow > shoulder; recurrent → target joint → chronic synovitis → haemophilic arthropathy.

Muscle haematoma – calf, psoas (causes femoral nerve palsy).

Intracranial haemorrhage – leading cause of death.

Mucosal – epistaxis, haematuria, post-extraction bleed.

GI haemorrhage.

Post-surgical / post-trauma bleed.

Female carriers — usually asymptomatic; some with low factor levels may have menorrhagia.

### Investigations

Prolonged aPTT (intrinsic pathway).

Normal PT, BT, platelet count, fibrinogen.

Mixing study – aPTT corrects with normal plasma (no inhibitor).

Factor VIII or IX assay – diagnostic and severity-grading.

vWF and ristocetin cofactor – exclude vWD.

Inhibitor screen – Bethesda assay (if poor response to factor replacement).

Genetic testing for carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis.

MRI / USG joints for arthropathy and acute bleeds.

### Management (WFH 2020 guidelines + Indian Haemophilia Society)

### Factor replacement (mainstay)

Recombinant factor VIII or IX – first choice (lower viral risk).

Plasma-derived concentrates – alternative.

### Dose calculation:

**– Factor VIII:** dose (IU) = weight (kg) × desired rise (%) × 0.5

**– Factor IX:** dose (IU) = weight (kg) × desired rise (%) × 1.0

### Target levels:

**– Minor bleed:** 30–50%

**– Major bleed/surgery:** 80–100%

**– CNS bleed:** 100% then maintain >50% for 7–14 days

### Adjuvant

Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 µg/kg IV/SC – mild haemophilia A (raises FVIII 2–3 fold); tachyphylaxis with repeated doses.

Tranexamic acid 15–25 mg/kg q8h (mucosal bleeds, dental); avoid in haematuria (clot retention).

Prophylaxis (severe haemophilia, all paediatric)

FVIII 25–40 IU/kg 2–3 times/week (HemA).

FIX 40–60 IU/kg twice/week (HemB).

Emicizumab (bispecific Ab mimicking FVIIIa) – SC weekly/fortnightly/monthly; effective even with inhibitors.

### Inhibitor management

Recombinant FVIIa (NovoSeven) 90 µg/kg q2-3h.

Activated PCC (FEIBA) 50–100 U/kg q6-12h.

Immune tolerance induction (high-dose factor over months).

Emicizumab prophylaxis even with inhibitors.

### Supportive

RICE for acute haemarthrosis – rest, ice, compression, elevation + factor.

Physiotherapy.

Avoid IM injections, aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants.

Hepatitis A/B/HIV vaccination and screening for transfusion-transmitted infections.

Genetic counselling, carrier detection.

### Future therapies

**Gene therapy:** valoctocogene roxaparvovec (HemA, FDA 2023), etranacogene dezaparvovec (HemB, FDA 2022).

Concizumab, marstacimab (anti-TFPI), fitusiran (anti-antithrombin) – non-factor rebalancing therapies.

### Prognosis

With modern factor replacement, life expectancy now approaches normal in high-income settings. Indian context: access to factor concentrates and prophylaxis is improving via Hemophilia Federation of India and Govt. supply, but remains the major prognostic determinant. Joint disease and inhibitor development are main long-term morbidities.

### Definition

Monoclonal proliferation of mature-appearing but functionally incompetent B-lymphocytes (CD5+, CD19+, CD23+) accumulating in blood, marrow, lymph nodes, spleen. The commonest leukaemia in Western adults; less common in India (~10% of all leukaemias). Median age 70 yr; M>F.

### Clinical features

Often asymptomatic – incidental lymphocytosis on routine CBC (25–50%).

Painless generalised lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, inguinal).

Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly.

**B-symptoms:** fever, night sweats, weight loss (late).

Recurrent infections – hypogammaglobulinaemia, T-cell dysfunction (commonest cause of death).

Autoimmune cytopenias – AIHA (positive Coombs), ITP, pure red cell aplasia.

Tonsillar enlargement, Mikulicz syndrome (rare).

Richter's transformation – rapid LN enlargement + B symptoms → DLBCL (5%).

### Investigations

CBC – persistent lymphocytosis >5 × 10⁹/L for >3 months (diagnostic threshold).

Peripheral smear – mature lymphocytes + 'smudge / basket' cells (fragile).

Flow cytometry (diagnostic) – CD5+ CD19+ CD23+ CD20 dim, monoclonal κ or λ, kappa:lambda ratio skewed; CD79b dim.

Bone marrow – ≥30% mature lymphocytes; pattern (nodular, interstitial, diffuse) prognostic.

FISH / cytogenetics – del(17p), del(11q), trisomy 12, del(13q) – prognostic and predictive.

**Molecular:** TP53 mutation, IGHV mutation status (unmutated = worse), NOTCH1, SF3B1 mutations.

Direct Coombs test, reticulocyte count, β₂-microglobulin, serum LDH.

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis – LN, hepatosplenomegaly.

Serum immunoglobulins – often low.

### Staging

### Rai (USA)

**0:** lymphocytosis only (low risk)

**I:** + lymphadenopathy (intermediate)

**II:** + hepatosplenomegaly (intermediate)

**III:** + anaemia Hb<11 (high)

**IV:** + thrombocytopenia <100 (high)

### Binet (Europe)

**A:** <3 nodal areas, no cytopenia (median survival >12 yr)

**B:** ≥3 nodal areas (5–7 yr)

**C:** anaemia/thrombocytopenia (3–4 yr)

Indications for treatment (iwCLL 2018)

Progressive marrow failure (worsening anaemia or thrombocytopenia).

Massive (>6 cm below costal margin) or symptomatic splenomegaly.

Massive nodes (>10 cm) or symptomatic lymphadenopathy.

Lymphocyte doubling time <6 months.

Autoimmune cytopenias refractory to steroids.

Disease-related symptoms – fever, night sweats, weight loss >10%, fatigue.

Asymptomatic – 'watch and wait'.

### Treatment (NCCN / iwCLL)

First line (modern era — chemo-immunotherapy largely replaced)

Targeted oral therapy preferred:

**– BTK inhibitor:** ibrutinib 420 mg OD, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib (continuous).

**– BCL-2 inhibitor:** venetoclax 400 mg OD (ramp-up to avoid TLS) + obinutuzumab (12 cycles, fixed-duration).

Chemo-immunotherapy (older but still used in young, IGHV-mutated, no TP53 abnormality):

– FCR (fludarabine + cyclophosphamide + rituximab)

– BR (bendamustine + rituximab) – older patients

Chlorambucil ± obinutuzumab – frail/elderly.

### Relapsed/refractory

Switch class (BTKi ↔ BCL-2i ± antiCD20).

PI3K inhibitor – idelalisib (toxicity-limited).

Allogeneic HSCT – young, fit, high-risk disease.

CAR-T cells – lisocabtagene (recently approved).

### Supportive

IVIG – recurrent infections + hypogammaglobulinaemia.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal, influenza, COVID; avoid live vaccines.

TMP-SMX prophylaxis (PJP), aciclovir (HSV/VZV) on purine analogues, BTKi etc.

AIHA / ITP – prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; rituximab; splenectomy.

### Prognosis

Highly variable. Median survival 5–20 yr depending on stage and biological markers. Adverse markers: del(17p), TP53 mutation, unmutated IGHV, ZAP-70+, CD38+, β₂-microglobulin elevated.

### Definition

Myeloproliferative neoplasm of haematopoietic stem cells characterised by the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome — reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (p210 protein), a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Accounts for ~15% of adult leukaemias; median age 50 yr in India (younger than West).

### Phases

Chronic phase (CP, 85% at diagnosis): blasts <10%, stable.

**Accelerated phase (AP):** blasts 10–19%, basophils ≥20%, thrombocytopenia <100 not from therapy, or thrombocytosis >1000, additional cytogenetic abnormality, splenomegaly resistant to therapy.

**Blast crisis (BC):** blasts ≥20% in blood/marrow, or extramedullary disease — myeloid (70%) or lymphoid (30%) lineage.

### Clinical features

Insidious onset; many asymptomatic at diagnosis (incidental leukocytosis).

**B-symptoms:** fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats.

Massive splenomegaly (commonest physical finding — often crosses midline) → early satiety, LUQ discomfort/dragging sensation, splenic infarct (sharp pleuritic pain + rub).

Hepatomegaly; lymphadenopathy unusual (red flag for blast crisis).

**Hyperviscosity:** priapism, visual disturbance, tinnitus, stupor (rare).

Gouty arthritis, hyperuricaemia.

Anaemia (pallor), thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis (bleeding/thrombosis).

### Investigations

CBC – marked leukocytosis 50–500 × 10⁹/L with full myeloid spectrum (myelocytes > metamyelocytes > neutrophils); basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis common; mild anaemia.

Peripheral smear – left shift, basophilia (key clue), <10% blasts in CP, no Auer rods.

Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score – LOW or ABSENT (helps differentiate from leukemoid reaction).

**Bone marrow – hypercellular, M:** E 10–30:1, full myeloid maturation; reticulin fibrosis variable.

Cytogenetics – Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in 95%.

FISH for BCR-ABL1 fusion.

RT-PCR for BCR-ABL1 transcript – quantitative on the International Scale (IS); essential for treatment monitoring.

Hyperuricaemia, raised LDH, raised B12 and uric acid.

### Treatment (NCCN / ELN 2020 / Indian NCG)

### First-line — Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKI)

Imatinib 400 mg PO OD (first-generation; affordable; Indian first-line, available via Glivec International Patient Assistance Programme / generic).

Second-generation (high-risk score / intolerance):

– Dasatinib 100 mg OD

– Nilotinib 300 mg BD

– Bosutinib 400 mg OD

### Third-generation (T315I mutation, multiple TKI failure):

– Ponatinib 45 mg OD (significant cardiovascular toxicity)

### – Asciminib (STAMP inhibitor)

### Monitoring (ELN 2020)

Quantitative BCR-ABL1 on IS at 3, 6, 12 months, then every 3 months.

### Optimal milestones:

**– 3 months:** BCR-ABL1 ≤10% (= EMR, early molecular response)

**– 6 months:** ≤1%

**– 12 months:** ≤0.1% (= MMR, major molecular response)

**Deep molecular response:** MR4 (≤0.01%), MR4.5 (≤0.0032%), MR5 (undetectable).

If failing milestones → check adherence + drug levels + BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutations → consider switch TKI.

Treatment-free remission (TFR) trial – consider after ≥2 years of MR4 on TKI; ~50% maintain remission.

### TKI side effects

Imatinib – fluid retention, periorbital oedema, GI, muscle cramps, rash, transaminitis.

### Definition

Toxic syndrome caused by ingestion / inhalation / dermal exposure to organophosphate compounds (parathion, malathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, fenthion, monocrotophos, dimethoate, dichlorvos, etc., and chemical warfare nerve agents — sarin, tabun, VX). Most common cause of poisoning mortality in rural India (deliberate self-poisoning).

### Mechanism

OP compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active serine residue, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. 'Ageing' (loss of an R-group) makes the enzyme inhibition permanent — hence early use of oximes is critical.

Clinical features (cholinergic crisis)

### Muscarinic (DUMBELS / SLUDGEM):

Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

Pulmonary oedema – the major cause of death.

Nicotinic (Days of the Week — MTWThF):

Muscle fasciculation, Tachycardia, Weakness/paralysis (including respiratory), Hypertension, Hyperglycaemia.

### CNS:

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

### Distinct syndromes:

Intermediate syndrome (24–96 h after acute phase): proximal muscle, neck flexor, and respiratory muscle weakness; cranial nerve deficits; lasts 2–3 weeks; needs prolonged ventilation.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN, 1–3 weeks after exposure): distal sensorimotor neuropathy.

### Diagnosis

History of exposure, characteristic odour (garlic/kerosene), DUMBELS toxidrome.

Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (BChE / pseudocholinesterase) – rapid, available – severely depressed.

RBC acetylcholinesterase – more accurate, slower turnaround.

Atropine challenge test – minimal response to therapeutic dose supports diagnosis.

Ancillary – ABG, CK, troponin, ECG (QT prolongation, AV block), CXR (pulmonary oedema), serum amylase (pancreatitis).

### Treatment

### Resuscitation and decontamination

**ABC:** secure airway (suction copious secretions), 100% O₂.

**Decontamination:** remove all clothing, wash skin with soap and water (rescuers wear PPE — secondary contamination risk).

Gastric lavage – only if presentation <1 h, large amount ingested, and airway protected; NOT recommended routinely (aspiration risk).

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

### End-points (must achieve ALL):

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

(iv) Pupil dilation.

**Maintenance:** atropine infusion 10–20% of the cumulative atropinising dose per hour; titrate to keep target signs.

Watch for atropine toxicity – hyperthermia, agitation, ileus, urinary retention; lower infusion accordingly.

### Oxime (pralidoxime / 2-PAM)

Reactivates AChE if given before ageing.

**Dose:** 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 48–72 h. Alternatively: 1 g IV q4-6h.

Most effective in first 24 h, but should be given even later (prolonged release from fat).

Particularly effective against nicotinic (muscle) signs.

### Supportive care

ICU monitoring. Mechanical ventilation often needed for days–weeks. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (prolonged paralysis – use rocuronium or vecuronium).

Seizures – diazepam 5–10 mg IV (does not interact with AChE).

Aggressive electrolyte (K, Mg) replacement; cardiac monitoring.

Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS.

Surveillance for intermediate syndrome (FVC, NIF monitoring).

Avoid β-blockers (worsen bronchospasm), morphine, theophylline, phenothiazines.

### Psychiatric and social

Most cases are deliberate self-poisoning – mandatory psychiatric evaluation; suicide-risk assessment; family counselling; safe-storage advice; pesticide bans (e.g. WHO Class I OP withdrawn in India 2020).

Fig 3. Organophosphate poisoning – emergency management.

### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Combination of wound care, anti-rabies vaccination and (where indicated) rabies immunoglobulin given after exposure to a known or suspected rabid mammal, intended to prevent rabies before CNS invasion. Rabies is uniformly fatal once encephalitic symptoms develop, so PEP must be initiated promptly.

### Categorisation (WHO/NRCP)

**Cat I:** Touching/feeding animal, lick on intact skin. No PEP needed (only wash skin).

**Cat II:** Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleed, licks on broken skin.

**Cat III:** Single/multiple transdermal bites or scratches, contamination of mucous membrane with saliva (lick on mouth/eyes), bat exposures.

Wound management (all categories)

Immediate, thorough cleansing of wound with soap (or detergent) and copious running water for 15 minutes.

Apply povidone iodine, alcohol, or virucidal antiseptic.

Avoid suturing if possible; delayed primary closure after RIG infiltration if essential (face/cosmesis).

Tetanus prophylaxis if not up to date.

Antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) for dirty wounds, deep, puncture, or face/hand bites.

### Vaccine (Cat II and III)

### Cell-culture vaccines (CCEEV)

Purified chick embryo cell vaccine (PCEC) – Rabipur.

Human diploid cell vaccine (HDCV).

Purified Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV) – Verorab.

Purified duck embryo cell vaccine (PDEV).

### Intramuscular (Essen) regimen

1 mL IM (deltoid in adults; anterolateral thigh in children <2 yrs; NEVER gluteus) on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28.

### Intradermal (Thai Red Cross) – preferred in India

0.1 mL ID × 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, 28 (2-2-2-0-2).

Updated WHO 1-week IDRV — days 0, 3, 7 (2 sites each) — adopted India 2018.

Booster (previously immunised within 3 years)

1 mL IM (or 0.1 mL ID × 1 site) on days 0 and 3. No RIG.

Rabies immunoglobulin – RIG (Cat III only)

ERIG 40 IU/kg or HRIG 20 IU/kg.

Infiltrate as much as possible IN and AROUND the wound; remaining IM at site distant from vaccine.

Sensitivity test for ERIG; highly purified ERIG has low reaction rate (1–2%).

Monoclonal antibody cocktails (Rabishield, Twinrab) – alternative.

Give within 7 days of vaccine; do not exceed dose.

### Special situations

Pregnancy / lactation – vaccine and RIG safe.

Immunocompromised – use IM regimen, check titre day 14, consider double dose.

Bat exposure (even without overt bite) – treat as Cat III.

If healthy domestic dog/cat is available for 10-day observation and remains well — PEP may be discontinued.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Toxic syndrome caused by ingestion / inhalation / dermal exposure to organophosphate compounds (parathion, malathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, fenthion, monocrotophos, dimethoate, dichlorvos, etc., and chemical warfare nerve agents — sarin, tabun, VX). Most common cause of poisoning mortality in rural India (deliberate self-poisoning).

### Mechanism

OP compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active serine residue, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. 'Ageing' (loss of an R-group) makes the enzyme inhibition permanent — hence early use of oximes is critical.

Clinical features (cholinergic crisis)

### Muscarinic (DUMBELS / SLUDGEM):

Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

Pulmonary oedema – the major cause of death.

Nicotinic (Days of the Week — MTWThF):

Muscle fasciculation, Tachycardia, Weakness/paralysis (including respiratory), Hypertension, Hyperglycaemia.

### CNS:

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

### Distinct syndromes:

Intermediate syndrome (24–96 h after acute phase): proximal muscle, neck flexor, and respiratory muscle weakness; cranial nerve deficits; lasts 2–3 weeks; needs prolonged ventilation.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN, 1–3 weeks after exposure): distal sensorimotor neuropathy.

### Diagnosis

History of exposure, characteristic odour (garlic/kerosene), DUMBELS toxidrome.

Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (BChE / pseudocholinesterase) – rapid, available – severely depressed.

RBC acetylcholinesterase – more accurate, slower turnaround.

Atropine challenge test – minimal response to therapeutic dose supports diagnosis.

Ancillary – ABG, CK, troponin, ECG (QT prolongation, AV block), CXR (pulmonary oedema), serum amylase (pancreatitis).

### Treatment

### Resuscitation and decontamination

**ABC:** secure airway (suction copious secretions), 100% O₂.

**Decontamination:** remove all clothing, wash skin with soap and water (rescuers wear PPE — secondary contamination risk).

Gastric lavage – only if presentation <1 h, large amount ingested, and airway protected; NOT recommended routinely (aspiration risk).

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

### End-points (must achieve ALL):

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

(iv) Pupil dilation.

**Maintenance:** atropine infusion 10–20% of the cumulative atropinising dose per hour; titrate to keep target signs.

Watch for atropine toxicity – hyperthermia, agitation, ileus, urinary retention; lower infusion accordingly.

### Oxime (pralidoxime / 2-PAM)

Reactivates AChE if given before ageing.

**Dose:** 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 48–72 h. Alternatively: 1 g IV q4-6h.

Most effective in first 24 h, but should be given even later (prolonged release from fat).

Particularly effective against nicotinic (muscle) signs.

### Supportive care

ICU monitoring. Mechanical ventilation often needed for days–weeks. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (prolonged paralysis – use rocuronium or vecuronium).

Seizures – diazepam 5–10 mg IV (does not interact with AChE).

Aggressive electrolyte (K, Mg) replacement; cardiac monitoring.

Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS.

Surveillance for intermediate syndrome (FVC, NIF monitoring).

Avoid β-blockers (worsen bronchospasm), morphine, theophylline, phenothiazines.

### Psychiatric and social

Most cases are deliberate self-poisoning – mandatory psychiatric evaluation; suicide-risk assessment; family counselling; safe-storage advice; pesticide bans (e.g. WHO Class I OP withdrawn in India 2020).

### Definition

PEP is a short course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) administered after a defined exposure to potentially HIV-infected body fluids, with the goal of preventing seroconversion. Effective only if started within 72 hours (ideally <2 hours).

### Categories of exposure

Occupational (needle-stick, mucosal splash)

**Source HIV status:** positive (CD4, viral load checked), negative, or unknown.

**Type of exposure:** percutaneous (large/small hollow needle, solid needle, superficial), mucous membrane, non-intact skin.

Non-occupational (sexual assault, IDU, unprotected sex)

**Highest risk:** receptive anal intercourse, contaminated needle sharing.

Immediate first-aid (any exposure)

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.

### Definition

Envenomation by elapid snakes (Cobra — Naja naja, King cobra — Ophiophagus hannah, Common krait — Bungarus caeruleus) produces a neurotoxic syndrome through α- and β-neurotoxins that block post-synaptic and pre-synaptic neuromuscular transmission respectively, leading to flaccid paralysis. India: cobra and krait are two of the 'Big Four' deadly Indian snakes.

Local features (cobra > krait)

Two fang punctures (krait bite often painless and at night).

Local pain, swelling, blistering, sometimes necrosis (cobra).

Krait – minimal local signs; pain disproportionate to swelling; often patient awakes with abdominal pain at 4–6 a.m.

Systemic features – progressive descending paralysis

Early (30 min – 2 h)

Heaviness of eyelids (ptosis – earliest and commonest sign), external ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, blurred vision.

Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia.

Hypersalivation, profuse sweating, paraesthesiae.

Established neurotoxicity (2–6 h)

Bulbar palsy – pooled secretions, tongue weakness, broken neck sign (cannot lift head off pillow).

Limb weakness – proximal first; progressive descending paralysis.

Respiratory muscle paralysis – the most life-threatening complication; intercostal and diaphragmatic weakness leading to respiratory failure.

Patient is conscious throughout (locked-in pattern unless hypoxic).

### Autonomic features

Cobra – bradycardia, hypotension; krait – sometimes mild hypertension, abdominal pain.

### Krait-specific

Bite often at night while sleeping on the floor; little or no local reaction; severe abdominal pain.

Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia may accompany.

Response to neostigmine usually poor (β-neurotoxin pre-synaptic action — already-released ACh is depleted).

### Investigations and monitoring

20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20-WBCT) – usually normal in pure neurotoxic bite (distinguishes from haemotoxic).

FVC (vital capacity) — if <1 L or falling — intubate.

ABG, electrolytes (krait — hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia).

ECG (arrhythmia).

Edrophonium / neostigmine test (improvement supports diagnosis and helps in management).

### Management (Indian National Snakebite Protocol 2017)

**First aid:** reassure, immobilise limb at heart level, remove rings/tight items, pressure-immobilisation bandage; rapid transport to a centre with ASV and ventilator. AVOID tourniquet/cut/suck/ice/electric shock.

Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV): initial 10 vials (100 mL) in 100–200 mL normal saline IV over 1 hour. Repeat every 6 hours up to maximum 30 vials, based on clinical/lab response.

Adjuvant — Neostigmine 0.5 mg + atropine 0.6 mg IV every 30 min × 5 doses (then 1–2 hourly as needed) — useful especially for cobra envenomation.

Early intubation and mechanical ventilation if FVC <1 L, tidal volume <5 mL/kg, or any respiratory distress.

**Treat ASV reactions:** stop infusion, adrenaline 0.5 mg IM, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV, chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV; resume ASV at slower rate.

Tetanus toxoid, antibiotics if cellulitis or wound necrosis.

Supportive — fluids, vasopressors if hypotensive; psychological support.

Fig 5. Snakebite — Indian National Protocol.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

### Definition

Acute purulent infection of meninges/subarachnoid space, presenting with fever + headache + neck stiffness +/- altered mental status. Medical emergency: untreated >90% mortality, with treatment 15-25%.

Aetiology by age (community-acquired)

**Neonates (0-1 mo):** GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

**1 mo - 50 y:** Streptococcus pneumoniae > Neisseria meningitidis > H. influenzae (now rare with vaccine).

**> 50 y / immunosuppressed:** S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negatives.

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Staph aureus, CoNS, gram-negatives.

**India-specific:** TB meningitis remains common — always consider.

### Clinical features

**Classic triad (only 44%):** fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status.

**≥ 2 of:** fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental → 95% sensitivity.

Kernig (knee extension with hip flexed → pain) and Brudzinski (neck flexion → hip flexion).

**Meningococcal:** petechial / purpuric rash (purpura fulminans = severe).

**Pneumococcal:** associated otitis/sinusitis/pneumonia.

Cranial nerve palsies, seizures, papilloedema, focal deficit.

### Investigations

Blood cultures × 2 BEFORE antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics > 1 h for cultures).

Lumbar puncture — CT first if focal deficit, GCS < 10, papilloedema, new-onset seizure, immunosuppression.

CSF Gram stain (60-90% sens), culture, latex agglutination (S. pneumo, H.influ, Nm, GBS).

**TB:** CSF AFB smear (low sens), GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (rapid + rifampicin resistance), culture.

**PCR:** HSV-1/2 (encephalitis), enterovirus, JC virus.

**Other:** CBC, blood C/S, CRP, procalcitonin, electrolytes (SIADH), HIV test.

### Management

- Resuscitation (within first hour)

**Sepsis bundle:** fluids, vasopressors if shock, oxygen, glucose check.

**Seizure control:** lorazepam, then levetiracetam load.

### 2. Dexamethasone

0.15 mg/kg IV q6h × 4 days, FIRST DOSE before or with first antibiotic.

Reduces mortality in S.pneumo; reduces neuro sequelae (deafness) in H.influenzae.

Stop if non-pneumococcal organism identified.

**TB meningitis:** prednisolone/dex tapered over 6-8 wk (TBM treatment).

- Empirical antibiotics (do NOT delay)

**Adult immunocompetent:** Adult immunocompetent: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h (target trough 15-20).

Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed:Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed: ADD Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria cover).

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Post-neurosurgery / shunt: Vancomycin + Cefepime or Meropenem 2 g q8h.

**Penicillin allergy severe:** Penicillin allergy severe: Vancomycin + Moxifloxacin + TMP-SMX (Listeria).

**Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h:** Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h: If HSV encephalitis suspected (e.g. temporal seizures, behaviour change).

### 4. Pathogen-specific duration

### 5. Adjunctive

Maintain euvolaemia (avoid SIADH).

**ICP management:** head-up 30°, mannitol if raised, ICU monitor.

Audiology test at discharge (especially children — sensorineural deafness).

- Chemoprophylaxis (close contacts)

**Meningococcal:** Rifampicin 600 mg PO BD × 2 d, OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose, OR Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single.

**H. influenzae type b:** Rifampicin 20 mg/kg/d × 4 d for households with child < 4 y unvaccinated.

### 7. Vaccination prevention

Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23 in elderly/asplenic/CKD/HIV).

Meningococcal (MenACWY for hajj pilgrims, students, military, asplenia).

Hib (in National Immunisation Schedule under Pentavalent).

### Complications

Hydrocephalus (communicating > obstructive).

Cerebritis, brain abscess, subdural empyema.

Sensorineural hearing loss (10-30%).

Seizures, epilepsy, cognitive deficits.

Cranial nerve palsies (esp. III, VI, VII, VIII).

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal, adrenal haemorrhage).

SIADH, DIC, septic shock.

### Prognosis

**Treated mortality:** pneumococcal 20-25%, meningococcal 5-10%, H.influ 3-7%.

**Untreated:** > 90% mortality.

10-20% long-term sequelae (deafness, cognitive, epilepsy).

Fig 5. Bacterial meningitis pathway.

**Source:** IDSA Meningitis Guidelines 2017; ICMR Antibiotic Policy 2022; Boloor Ch.15.

### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Pneumonia acquired outside healthcare settings (or within first 48 h of admission). Major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.

### Etiology

### Typical bacterial:

Streptococcus pneumoniae – the leading cause (50–60%); lobar pneumonia, rusty sputum.

Haemophilus influenzae (especially COPD).

Moraxella catarrhalis (COPD).

Staphylococcus aureus – post-influenza, IV drug users, necrotising.

Klebsiella pneumoniae – alcoholics, diabetics; currant-jelly sputum, bulging fissure sign, upper-lobe.

### Atypical:

Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii.

### Viral:

Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, hMPV, adenovirus.

### Special host groups:

Alcoholics – Klebsiella, anaerobes, S. pneumoniae, TB.

Diabetics – Klebsiella, S. aureus, fungi (mucormycosis).

HIV – Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, fungal.

Aspiration – oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus).

Indian context – TB always differential.

### Clinical features

Sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, rusty/blood-stained sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

**Atypical pneumonia:** dry cough, headache, myalgia, GI upset, subacute course.

**Signs of consolidation:** tachypnoea, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, fine crackles.

Sepsis features – tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness.

### Severity (CURB-65)

C – Confusion (AMT ≤8 or new disorientation).

U – Urea > 7 mmol/L (>20 mg/dL).

R – Respiratory rate ≥ 30.

B – BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic.

65 – Age ≥65 years.

**0–1:** home; 2: ward; 3–5: ICU (consider).

Empirical therapy (ICMR 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2019)

**Outpatient:** amoxicillin 1 g TDS 5–7 d (± macrolide if atypical suspected) or doxycycline.

**Ward (CURB-65 = 2):** IV amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ceftriaxone + macrolide.

**ICU (CURB-65 ≥3):** IV ceftriaxone + macrolide OR levofloxacin; add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; add antipseudomonal cover if structural lung disease.

De-escalate based on cultures.

**Supportive:** O₂, fluids, antipyretic, VTE prophylaxis.

GENERAL MEDICINE|47.note:
### Light's criteria

Effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met:

Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5.

Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Causes (mnemonic:** 'Pus, blood, fluid from inflammation')

### Infective:

Parapneumonic effusion / empyema (Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Tuberculous pleural effusion (the commonest cause of exudative effusion in young adults in India – lymphocytic, ADA >40 U/L, biopsy shows granulomas).

Fungal (rare), parasitic (amoebic, hydatid).

Malignancy (commonest cause of exudate in elderly):

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Breast carcinoma.

Lymphoma, leukaemia.

Mesothelioma (asbestos-related).

Ovarian carcinoma (Meigs syndrome with ascites).

Connective tissue / autoimmune:

Rheumatoid arthritis (low glucose, low pH, low complement, RF positive).

SLE.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Pulmonary embolism / infarction.

### Gastrointestinal / abdominal:

Pancreatitis (left-sided, high amylase).

Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave's – high amylase from saliva, low pH).

Subdiaphragmatic abscess.

Post-CABG.

### Drugs:

Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine.

### Other:

Radiation therapy.

Chylothorax (lymphoma, trauma, thoracic-duct obstruction – triglycerides >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons).

Haemothorax (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation).

Yellow nail syndrome.
