### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Pneumonia acquired outside healthcare settings (or within first 48 h of admission). Major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.

### Etiology

### Typical bacterial:

Streptococcus pneumoniae – the leading cause (50–60%); lobar pneumonia, rusty sputum.

Haemophilus influenzae (especially COPD).

Moraxella catarrhalis (COPD).

Staphylococcus aureus – post-influenza, IV drug users, necrotising.

Klebsiella pneumoniae – alcoholics, diabetics; currant-jelly sputum, bulging fissure sign, upper-lobe.

### Atypical:

Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii.

### Viral:

Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, hMPV, adenovirus.

### Special host groups:

Alcoholics – Klebsiella, anaerobes, S. pneumoniae, TB.

Diabetics – Klebsiella, S. aureus, fungi (mucormycosis).

HIV – Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, fungal.

Aspiration – oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus).

Indian context – TB always differential.

### Clinical features

Sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, rusty/blood-stained sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

**Atypical pneumonia:** dry cough, headache, myalgia, GI upset, subacute course.

**Signs of consolidation:** tachypnoea, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, fine crackles.

Sepsis features – tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness.

### Severity (CURB-65)

C – Confusion (AMT ≤8 or new disorientation).

U – Urea > 7 mmol/L (>20 mg/dL).

R – Respiratory rate ≥ 30.

B – BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic.

65 – Age ≥65 years.

**0–1:** home; 2: ward; 3–5: ICU (consider).

Empirical therapy (ICMR 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2019)

**Outpatient:** amoxicillin 1 g TDS 5–7 d (± macrolide if atypical suspected) or doxycycline.

**Ward (CURB-65 = 2):** IV amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ceftriaxone + macrolide.

**ICU (CURB-65 ≥3):** IV ceftriaxone + macrolide OR levofloxacin; add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; add antipseudomonal cover if structural lung disease.

De-escalate based on cultures.

**Supportive:** O₂, fluids, antipyretic, VTE prophylaxis.

GENERAL MEDICINE|50.note:
### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterised by reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness, and clinically by recurrent episodes of wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough – typically worse at night or early morning.

### Etiology and Risk Factors

**Host:** Atopic individuals; family history of asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, ORMDL3, IL-13.

**Environmental:** Allergens (house dust mite, animal dander, pollen, moulds, cockroach), respiratory infections (RSV, rhinovirus), tobacco smoke, indoor/outdoor air pollution, occupational exposures (isocyanates, flour, latex), exercise, cold air.

**Drugs:** β-blockers, aspirin/NSAIDs (AERD/Samter's triad – asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity).

**Triggers:** Emotion, GERD, obesity, OSA, pregnancy.

**Indian context:** Urban air pollution, biomass fuel exposure, and undiagnosed allergic rhinitis are particularly relevant.

### Pathophysiology

Antigen exposure → IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation → release of histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4), prostaglandins → early-phase bronchoconstriction (15–30 min). Cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes → late-phase response (4–8 h) with mucosal oedema, mucus plugging and ongoing inflammation. Chronic inflammation leads to airway remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia) and fixed obstruction. Result: airway hyper-responsiveness, variable airflow limitation, and reversibility with bronchodilators or steroids.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, dry cough, chest tightness – often nocturnal / early morning; symptom-free intervals.

**Pattern:** Diurnal variation; triggers (cold, exercise, allergen, URTI); personal/family atopy.

**Signs:** Tachypnoea, prolonged expiration, bilateral polyphonic wheeze, hyperinflation; eczema, allergic rhinitis. In severe attacks: tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, accessory-muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences.

### Asthma severity in acute attack (BTS/GINA)

**Mild:** PEFR >75%, talking in sentences.

**Moderate:** PEFR 50–75%.

**Acute severe:** PEFR 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, cannot complete sentences.

**Life-threatening:** PEFR <33%, SpO₂ <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, exhaustion, altered consciousness, normal/raised PaCO₂.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) – diurnal variation >20%, drop during attack.

**Spirometry:** Obstructive pattern – FEV1/FVC <0.70, reversibility with bronchodilator (FEV1 ↑≥12% AND ≥200 mL).

**Bronchial provocation:** If spirometry normal but symptoms suggestive – methacholine or histamine challenge (PC20 < 8 mg/mL = positive).

**Labs:** Eosinophil count, total IgE, specific allergen IgE; sputum eosinophil count >2%; fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) >25 ppb in eosinophilic asthma.

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray – usually normal; hyperinflation in exacerbation; rules out pneumothorax, infection.

**ABG:** ABG in acute severe attack (normal/rising PaCO₂ is a warning sign).

**Other:** Skin prick test, RAST for specific allergens; ENT review for nasal polyps.

### Management (GINA 2023 + Indian context)

**Goals:** control symptoms, prevent exacerbations, maintain normal lung function, avoid medication side-effects.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA tracks 1 & 2):

**Step 1:** As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred Track 1) or SABA + low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA used.

**Step 2:** Daily low-dose ICS (budesonide 200–400 µg, fluticasone 100–250 µg) + SABA PRN.

**Step 3:** Low-dose ICS-LABA (budesonide/formoterol) + PRN.

**Step 4:** Medium-dose ICS-LABA + PRN.

**Step 5:** High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on: tiotropium (LAMA), biologics (omalizumab anti-IgE; mepolizumab/reslizumab anti-IL-5; dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast); low-dose oral corticosteroid (last resort).

Acute severe asthma (Indian ICU practice + BTS/GINA):

Sit patient up, high-flow O₂ via mask, target SpO₂ 94–98%.

Salbutamol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebuliser (back-to-back q15min × 3).

Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (or Methylprednisolone 60–125 mg IV) → continue Prednisolone 40–50 mg PO daily × 5 days.

Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min in severe attack.

IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg loading, 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion) only if above measures fail; monitor levels.

Antibiotics only if clear infection (CXR consolidation, purulent sputum, fever).

ICU admission if life-threatening / not improving; intubation for exhaustion, falling PEFR, rising PaCO₂.

### Non-pharmacological:

Trigger avoidance (allergens, smoke, occupational), weight reduction, GERD treatment, treat allergic rhinitis (nasal steroid).

Patient education, written action plan (green-yellow-red zones), inhaler technique (MDI + spacer for children/elderly; turbohaler/DPI for adults).

Annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination for severe.

Allergen immunotherapy in selected cases.

Fig 1. GINA 2023 stepwise management of asthma (Track 1, preferred path with ICS-formoterol reliever).

Fig 2. Acute severe asthma – emergency management algorithm.

### Complications

Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

Aspergillosis (ABPA – worsening asthma + central bronchiectasis + peripheral eosinophilia + raised IgE).

Long-term airway remodelling, fixed obstruction.

**Side-effects of treatment:** oral candidiasis, dysphonia (ICS), osteoporosis, cushingoid features (oral steroids), tremor (β-agonists).

### Prognosis

Most patients have well-controlled disease with modern therapy. Asthma mortality is low but preventable; under-treatment with ICS, over-reliance on SABA, and poor adherence/inhaler technique are the key contributors to fatal asthma.

### Cardiovascular

Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina) – retrosternal, crushing, >20 min, radiation to left arm/jaw.

Stable angina – exertional, <10 min, relieved by rest/GTN.

Aortic dissection – sudden, tearing, between shoulder blades, BP/pulse asymmetry, widened mediastinum.

Pericarditis – sharp, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, rub on auscultation.

Myocarditis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe aortic stenosis.

### Respiratory

Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, risk factors.

Pneumonia, pleurisy – pleuritic, fever, cough.

Pneumothorax – sudden, unilateral, dyspnoea.

Asthma exacerbation, bronchitis.

Lung cancer (chest wall invasion).

### Gastrointestinal

GERD / oesophagitis – retrosternal burning, post-prandial, supine.

Oesophageal spasm – may mimic ACS.

Peptic ulcer disease, gastritis.

Boerhaave's syndrome (oesophageal rupture – Mackler triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema).

Pancreatitis (radiates to back), biliary colic.

### Musculoskeletal

Costochondritis / Tietze's syndrome – localised, reproducible tenderness.

Rib fracture, intercostal muscle strain.

Cervical spondylosis (radicular).

### Other

Herpes zoster (dermatomal).

Anxiety / panic attack – associated with hyperventilation.

Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crisis (acute chest syndrome).

**Approach:** ECG within 10 min in any adult with chest pain; troponin; CXR; consider CT pulmonary angiogram for PE, CT angio for aortic dissection; echocardiography. Wells score, HEART score, GRACE/TIMI guide risk-stratification.

Bronchial breath sounds are produced in the trachea and large airways; they are heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is consolidated or replaced by a sound-conducting medium.

### Characteristics

**Normal site:** Heard over manubrium, trachea normally.

**Components:** Inspiration = expiration in duration; expiration is louder than inspiration; clear gap between them.

**Quality:** High-pitched, harsh.

### Types

Tubular bronchial breathing – classical, heard over consolidation (lobar pneumonia – S. pneumoniae), and over a tense pleural effusion (compressed lung above effusion).

Cavernous breathing – low-pitched, hollow, with reverberating quality (over large lung cavity ≥6 cm communicating with bronchus – TB cavity, lung abscess).

Amphoric breathing – high-pitched, metallic, hollow (like blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle); heard over a smooth-walled cavity (>4 cm) communicating with a bronchus, or over an open pneumothorax. Often associated with metallic tinkling.

Associated signs of consolidation

Increased vocal fremitus, dull percussion note, increased vocal resonance with whispering pectoriloquy and aegophony, fine crackles and bronchial breathing.

Bronchial breathing is heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is more uniform / conducting than normal aerated lung. Causes:

Lobar pneumonia (commonest – S. pneumoniae causing red hepatisation).

Compressed lung above a large pleural effusion (top edge).

Lung abscess opened to bronchus (cavernous, amphoric variants).

Tuberculous cavity (cavernous or amphoric).

Collapse with patent bronchus (paradoxically – consolidation-like transmission).

Mass lesion compressing airway open to large bronchus.

Pulmonary infarction (rare).

Associated signs of consolidation: increased vocal fremitus and resonance, whispering pectoriloquy, aegophony, dull percussion, fine end-inspiratory crackles.

Common inhaled corticosteroids (Indian availability)

Budesonide (Budecort, Pulmicort) – MDI 100/200 µg; DPI 200/400 µg; neb 0.5/1 mg.

Fluticasone propionate (Flohale, Flixotide) – MDI 50/125/250 µg; DPI 100/250/500 µg.

Fluticasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg (once-daily).

Beclomethasone dipropionate (Beclate) – MDI 50/100/250 µg.

Ciclesonide (Alvesco) – MDI 80/160 µg.

Mometasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg.

Combination ICS-LABA inhalers (most prescribed)

Budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort, Foracort) – preferred Track 1 GINA reliever-controller.

Fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide).

Fluticasone furoate + vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta).

Beclomethasone + formoterol.

### Triple-therapy inhalers (ICS-LABA-LAMA)

Fluticasone + umeclidinium + vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta).

Budesonide + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

Beclomethasone + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

### Adverse effects

**Local:** oral candidiasis (Candida albicans – use spacer + rinse mouth), dysphonia, throat irritation.

Systemic (with high dose / long-term): osteoporosis, skin thinning, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, adrenal suppression, increased pneumonia risk in COPD.

### Indications

Asthma – mainstay of controller therapy from GINA Step 1 onwards.

COPD – with LABA in patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥100/300.

Other obstructive airways disease (some forms of bronchiectasis with asthma overlap).

### Class background

Artemisinin (qinghaosu) is a sesquiterpene lactone derived from Artemisia annua (sweet wormwood). It and its semi-synthetic derivatives are the most rapidly acting antimalarials known, cidal against asexual blood stages including ring forms of all Plasmodium species. WHO recommends artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) as first-line in nearly all malaria-endemic countries.

### Available derivatives

**Artemisinin:** Original parent compound; rarely used alone clinically due to poor solubility and short half-life.

**Artesunate:** Water-soluble; available as IV, IM, oral, and rectal suppository (paediatric). Half-life ~45 min.

**Artemether:** Oil-soluble; IM only; long-acting; used in severe malaria when artesunate unavailable.

**Dihydroartemisinin (DHA):** Oral/oil-soluble; used in ACT combinations.

**Artemotil (β-arteether):** Older oral preparation, less common.

Dosage – uncomplicated falciparum (ACT regimens)

Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (AS-SP): Artesunate 4 mg/kg + Sulfadoxine 25 mg/kg + Pyrimethamine 1.25 mg/kg, given over 3 days. NVBDCP first-line in non-NE Indian states.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL, Coartem): 20/120 mg fixed-dose; adult dose 4 tablets BD × 3 days. NVBDCP first-line in North-East India (where SP resistance documented).

Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine (DP, Eurartesim): 40/320 mg; 4 tablets OD × 3 days (adult). Alternative ACT.

**Artesunate-Amodiaquine (AS-AQ):** Artesunate 4 mg/kg + Amodiaquine 10 mg/kg, both OD × 3 days. Used in some African settings.

Severe / complicated malaria

**Artesunate IV:** 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily; minimum 3 doses (24 h); follow with full oral ACT once tolerating oral.

**Artemether IM:** 3.2 mg/kg at hour 0, then 1.6 mg/kg daily × at least 3 days; second-line if artesunate unavailable.

Rectal artesunate (pre-referral, children): 10 mg/kg single dose while arranging transfer.

### Adjunct (gametocidal)

Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (P. falciparum) – kill gametocytes to interrupt transmission; G6PD test or low-dose 0.25 mg/kg single dose may be used safely without test in low-transmission settings (WHO 2018).

### Adverse effects

Generally well tolerated; nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache.

**Rare:** post-artesunate delayed haemolytic anaemia (>5% in some cohorts, 1–3 weeks after IV artesunate; monitor Hb for 4 weeks).

Cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation – piperaquine, lumefantrine).

Avoid in 1st trimester pregnancy where possible (use only if severe / falciparum and benefits outweigh risk – WHO permits in severe malaria across all trimesters).

### Resistance

Greater Mekong subregion (Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand) – partial artemisinin resistance from Pf K13 mutations; delayed parasite clearance.

Africa and India – clinical artemisinin resistance not yet established; surveillance ongoing.

Combination with partner drug (sulfadoxine, lumefantrine, piperaquine) protects against monotherapy resistance.

### Combined Notes (4 topics)

ILDs are a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases characterised by varying degrees of inflammation and fibrosis of the alveolar walls and interstitium, producing restrictive lung disease and impaired gas exchange.

Examples by category (four key examples + classification)

### Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias:

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – usual interstitial pneumonia pattern; older adults; honeycombing.

Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP).

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP).

Acute interstitial pneumonia.

ILD due to known cause:

Connective tissue disease–associated ILD: RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, dermatomyositis (anti-Jo1), Sjögren's, MCTD.

### Definition

Localised collection of pus within the lung parenchyma due to microbial infection, leading to tissue necrosis and cavitation.

### Etiology

**Primary (aspiration):** Aspiration (commonest) – alcoholics, post-anaesthesia, stroke, epilepsy, GERD. Anaerobic flora from oral cavity.

**Secondary:** Bronchial obstruction (carcinoma, foreign body), septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided endocarditis, IV drug use), spread from subphrenic/hepatic abscess.

**Organisms:** Anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides), Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza), Streptococcus milleri, gram-negative bacilli, fungi (immunocompromised).

### Clinical Features

Insidious – fever, malaise, weight loss, night sweats over weeks.

Productive cough with copious foul-smelling sputum (anaerobes); may be blood-stained.

Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

Halitosis.

**Signs:** clubbing (chronic), dull percussion, bronchial/amphoric breathing, post-tussive crackles, signs of consolidation.

### Investigations

CXR – cavity with air-fluid level, surrounding consolidation; usual site posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe (gravity-dependent in supine aspiration).

CT chest – delineates cavity, exclude underlying mass.

Sputum gram stain, AFB, culture (aerobic and anaerobic), cytology.

Bronchoscopy – exclude obstruction, obtain protected specimen, facilitate drainage.

Blood culture (especially in septic embolism, IE).

Echo if right-sided endocarditis suspected.

### Management

Empirical antibiotic with anaerobic cover: IV clindamycin 600 mg q8h, OR β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam), OR metronidazole + ceftriaxone.

Add vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA suspected; add fluconazole/voriconazole if fungal.

**Duration:** 4–6 weeks, IV until clinical improvement then PO (oral amoxicillin-clavulanate + metronidazole).

Postural drainage and physiotherapy to facilitate sputum clearance.

Bronchoscopic drainage if poor response (large cavity >6 cm, obstructing lesion).

Percutaneous catheter drainage in selected (refractory abscess).

Surgical resection (lobectomy/segmentectomy) – rarely needed; indications: persistent abscess despite 6–8 wk antibiotic, massive haemoptysis, suspected malignancy, bronchopleural fistula.

**Treat underlying cause:** dental hygiene, anti-seizure medication, swallow assessment, GERD therapy, treat malignancy if present.

### Complications

Empyema, bronchopleural fistula, massive haemoptysis, septicaemia, metastatic abscess (brain, etc.), amyloidosis (chronic), respiratory failure.

### Local features

Cough (commonest); change in chronic smoker's cough.

Haemoptysis – any new in a smoker > 40 yr → CT chest.

Dyspnoea (bronchial obstruction, effusion, lymphangitis).

Chest pain – pleuritic if pleural involvement; dull ache if chest-wall invasion.

Wheeze (fixed monophonic – endobronchial).

Recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia in the same lobe.

### Regional spread

Hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy).

Pancoast tumour (apical) – ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), shoulder/arm pain, T1 wasting.

Phrenic nerve palsy – elevated hemidiaphragm.

Superior vena cava obstruction – facial/upper-limb oedema, fixed engorged neck veins, Pemberton's sign.

Dysphagia (oesophageal compression), pericardial effusion, malignant pleural effusion, lymphangitis carcinomatosa.

Liver (RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice).

Bone (pain, hypercalcaemia, pathological fractures).

Brain (headache, focal deficit, seizures, personality change).

Adrenals (commonly silent).

Skin and contralateral lung.

Squamous-cell carcinoma → PTHrP → hypercalcaemia.

Small-cell carcinoma → SIADH (hyponatraemia), ectopic ACTH (Cushing's syndrome with hyperpigmentation, hypokalaemia), Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

Clubbing, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (NSCLC, adenocarcinoma).

Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's syndrome – adenocarcinoma).

Acanthosis nigricans, dermatomyositis, anaemia of chronic disease.

### Constitutional

Anorexia, fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats.

CXR, contrast CT chest + upper abdomen + adrenals, PET-CT.

Bronchoscopy + biopsy/brushings; EBUS for nodal sampling; CT-guided biopsy for peripheral lesions; thoracoscopy.

Histology + molecular (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS, PD-L1) for NSCLC.

Brain MRI, bone scan, FBC, LFT, RFT, calcium, sodium.

Silicosis – stone-cutting, quartz, sand-blasting.

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis – coal mining.

Asbestosis – insulation, ship-breaking, construction; pleural plaques, mesothelioma.

Berylliosis – aerospace, ceramics.

Stannosis (tin), siderosis (iron), baritosis (barium).

Farmer's lung – mouldy hay (thermophilic actinomycetes).

Bird-fancier's lung – avian proteins.

Bagassosis – sugarcane waste.

Mushroom-worker's lung.

Humidifier lung.

### Occupational asthma (cause-and-effect)

Isocyanates (paint, polyurethane).

Flour dust (bakers).

Latex (healthcare workers).

Wood dust (cedar – plicatic acid).

Animal proteins (laboratory workers).

### Other

Byssinosis – cotton, flax dust.

Metal-fume fever (zinc oxide fumes, welding).

Occupational malignancies – mesothelioma (asbestos), lung carcinoma (asbestos, silica, radon, chromates).

Toxic gases – chlorine, ammonia, phosgene (acute injury, RADS).

### Definition and classification (DSM-5 / ICD-11)

**Bipolar I:** ≥1 manic episode (≥1 wk or any duration if hospitalised) ± depressive / hypomanic episodes.

**Bipolar II:** ≥1 hypomanic episode (≥4 days, less severe than mania, no psychosis, no severe functional impairment) + ≥1 major depressive episode. NO manic episode ever.

**Cyclothymia:** Numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms for ≥2 years (1 year in children/adolescents) that don't meet full episode criteria.

**Other mood disorders:** MDD (Q2), persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), PMDD, DMDD (children), substance-/medical-induced mood disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** BP-I ~1%, BP-II ~1.1%, sub-threshold ~2.4%; combined ~2.5%.

M=F for BP-I; BP-II commoner in women.

Peak onset 15–25 years; rare new onset >50 (consider organic).

Heritability ~70%; first-degree relative risk 5–10×.

### Etiology

Genetic — polygenic (CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4); high heritability.

Neurochemical — dopaminergic and noradrenergic hyperactivity in mania; serotonergic deficit; second-messenger (inositol monophosphatase, GSK-3β) dysregulation — basis for lithium and valproate action.

Neuroanatomical — ↓ prefrontal cortex, ↑ amygdala activation.

Triggers / precipitants — sleep deprivation, stimulants, antidepressant monotherapy ('switch'), childbirth, seasonal change (spring–summer mania, autumn–winter depression).

### Clinical features

### Manic episode (DSM-5)

Distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood AND ↑ energy/activity, lasting ≥1 wk (any duration if hospitalisation needed), with ≥3 (≥4 if mood only irritable) of:

Inflated self-esteem / grandiosity (may reach delusional).

Decreased need for sleep.

More talkative / pressure of speech.

Flight of ideas / racing thoughts.

Distractibility.

Increase in goal-directed activity / psychomotor agitation.

Excessive involvement in risky activities (spending, sexual indiscretion, business deals).

Marked functional impairment ± psychotic features ± hospitalisation needed.

### Hypomania

Same symptoms but ≥4 days, no psychosis, no marked functional impairment, no hospitalisation needed; observable change from baseline.

### Mixed features

Manic / hypomanic episode with ≥3 depressive symptoms (or vice versa) — high suicide risk.

### Bipolar depression

Same DSM-5 criteria as MDD (see Q2). Often: hypersomnia, hyperphagia, atypical features, psychomotor retardation more than agitation; suicide risk higher than unipolar.

### Course specifiers

Rapid cycling — ≥4 episodes/year (more common in women, hypothyroidism, antidepressant-induced).

With psychotic features (mood-congruent grandiose; or incongruent).

With anxious distress; with melancholic; with atypical; with seasonal pattern; peripartum.

### Differential diagnosis

Substance-induced (cocaine, amphetamines, steroids, antidepressants).

Schizoaffective disorder.

Hyperthyroidism, Cushing's, frontal-lobe lesions, MS, neurosyphilis, HIV.

ADHD (chronic, not episodic).

Borderline personality disorder (mood within minutes-hours, not days-weeks).

### Investigations

**Routine:** CBC, TSH (critical — rule out hyperthyroidism), FBS, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, B12.

**Toxicology:** urine drug screen.

MRI brain if late-onset, focal signs, treatment resistance.

**Pre-lithium:** U&E, TSH, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test in women of child-bearing age, urine specific gravity.

**Pre-valproate:** LFT, CBC, ammonia (if encephalopathy), pregnancy test (teratogen — neural-tube defects, ↓ IQ).

**Pre-carbamazepine:** HLA-B*1502 in Asians (SJS/TEN risk).

### Management

Figure 3. Bipolar disorder management — acute mania vs. depression, lithium monitoring, and lifelong maintenance.

Acute mania / mixed

**First-line:** Lithium (target 0.8–1.2 mEq/L) OR valproate 750–2000 mg/d (level 50–125) OR atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, asenapine, cariprazine).

**Severe / psychotic / agitated:** Combination — lithium or valproate + atypical antipsychotic; add BZD short-term (lorazepam 2 mg IM/PO PRN, max 8 mg/d).

Refractory / unable to use first-line: Carbamazepine 600–1200 mg, oxcarbazepine; ECT for severe / pregnancy / treatment resistance.

STOP antidepressants (they perpetuate mania / mixed states / rapid cycling).

Treat insomnia aggressively — sleep regularisation is therapeutic.

### Acute bipolar depression

**First-line:** Quetiapine 300 mg, olanzapine + fluoxetine combination (OFC), lurasidone 20–120 mg (with food), cariprazine 1.5–3 mg, lamotrigine (slow titration 25 mg/2 wk → 200 mg to ↓ SJS/TEN risk — better for prevention than acute).

**Second-line:** Lithium monotherapy; lithium + SSRI/bupropion (NEVER monotherapy SSRI — switch risk). SSRIs only as add-on to a mood stabiliser, with vigilance for mania switch.

ECT — safe in pregnancy; for severe / suicidal / psychotic.

Maintenance (after acute episode — lifelong if recurrent)

**Lithium — gold standard:** 300–600 mg BD; target 0.6–1.0 mEq/L (12 h post-dose). Only psychotropic with proven anti-suicide effect.

Valproate (sodium valproate / divalproex): 750–2000 mg/d; level 50–125. AVOID in women of child-bearing age (teratogen, ↓ IQ, neural-tube defects); requires reliable contraception per Indian PvPI / MHRA valproate pregnancy-prevention programme.

**Lamotrigine:** Titrate 25 mg → 200 mg/d slowly; best for prevention of depressive recurrences; SJS/TEN risk (worst in first 8 wk; ↑ with rapid titration or with valproate).

**Atypicals:** Quetiapine 300–600 mg, olanzapine 5–20 mg, aripiprazole 15–30 mg, risperidone, asenapine. LAI options (aripiprazole, risperidone) for adherence problems.

**Carbamazepine:** 600–1200 mg/d; SE: hyponatraemia, agranulocytosis, hepatic enzyme induction (↓ OCP, ↓ warfarin), SJS/TEN (HLA-B*1502 Asians).

Lithium monitoring (must know — exam favourite)

**Levels:** 5–7 days after dose change; q3–6 mo when stable. Trough (12 h post-dose).

**Renal:** U&E baseline, q6 mo (long-term: nephrogenic DI, CKD).

**Thyroid:** TSH baseline, q6–12 mo (hypothyroidism in 20%).

**Calcium:** baseline, annually (hyperparathyroidism rare).

**Drug interactions:** NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics (thiazides) raise lithium levels.

Pregnancy — Ebstein's anomaly risk (0.05–0.1%); avoid in 1st trimester if possible; foetal echo at 16–18 wk if exposed.

Lithium toxicity (must recognise — boards favourite)

**Mild (1.5–2.0):** Fine tremor, GI upset, polyuria.

**Moderate (2.0–2.5):** Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, drowsiness, confusion.

**Severe (>2.5):** Seizures, coma, arrhythmias, renal failure, death.

**Management:** Stop lithium, IV NS, treat seizures (BZD), correct hypernatraemia carefully. Haemodialysis if level >4.0 (any), >2.5 with severe symptoms, renal failure, or refractory.

### Non-pharmacological

Psychoeducation (mood charting, relapse signs, medication adherence) — single most effective adjunct.

Interpersonal & Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) — preserve sleep–wake regularity.

Family-Focused Therapy (FFT).

CBT — for residual depressive symptoms.

Avoid substance use (stimulants, cannabis, alcohol).

### Complications

Suicide — completed in ~10–15% of BP-I.

Substance abuse comorbidity ~50%.

Reduced life expectancy 10–15 y (CV, suicide, drugs, smoking).

Functional, occupational, financial impact during manic episodes.

**Medication-related:** lithium nephrotoxicity, valproate teratogenicity, atypical metabolic syndrome.

### Prognosis

Lifelong episodic illness; ~90% have ≥1 recurrence.

Inter-episode functioning often impaired (cognitive, social).

Lithium adherence improves outcome significantly; combination therapy often required.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; CANMAT/ISBD 2018; NICE-CG185; DSM-5; ICD-11.

### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Definition

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterised by reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness, and clinically by recurrent episodes of wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough – typically worse at night or early morning.

### Etiology and Risk Factors

**Host:** Atopic individuals; family history of asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, ORMDL3, IL-13.

**Environmental:** Allergens (house dust mite, animal dander, pollen, moulds, cockroach), respiratory infections (RSV, rhinovirus), tobacco smoke, indoor/outdoor air pollution, occupational exposures (isocyanates, flour, latex), exercise, cold air.

**Drugs:** β-blockers, aspirin/NSAIDs (AERD/Samter's triad – asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity).

**Triggers:** Emotion, GERD, obesity, OSA, pregnancy.

**Indian context:** Urban air pollution, biomass fuel exposure, and undiagnosed allergic rhinitis are particularly relevant.

### Pathophysiology

Antigen exposure → IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation → release of histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4), prostaglandins → early-phase bronchoconstriction (15–30 min). Cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes → late-phase response (4–8 h) with mucosal oedema, mucus plugging and ongoing inflammation. Chronic inflammation leads to airway remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia) and fixed obstruction. Result: airway hyper-responsiveness, variable airflow limitation, and reversibility with bronchodilators or steroids.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, dry cough, chest tightness – often nocturnal / early morning; symptom-free intervals.

**Pattern:** Diurnal variation; triggers (cold, exercise, allergen, URTI); personal/family atopy.

**Signs:** Tachypnoea, prolonged expiration, bilateral polyphonic wheeze, hyperinflation; eczema, allergic rhinitis. In severe attacks: tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, accessory-muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences.

### Asthma severity in acute attack (BTS/GINA)

**Mild:** PEFR >75%, talking in sentences.

**Moderate:** PEFR 50–75%.

**Acute severe:** PEFR 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, cannot complete sentences.

**Life-threatening:** PEFR <33%, SpO₂ <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, exhaustion, altered consciousness, normal/raised PaCO₂.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) – diurnal variation >20%, drop during attack.

**Spirometry:** Obstructive pattern – FEV1/FVC <0.70, reversibility with bronchodilator (FEV1 ↑≥12% AND ≥200 mL).

**Bronchial provocation:** If spirometry normal but symptoms suggestive – methacholine or histamine challenge (PC20 < 8 mg/mL = positive).

**Labs:** Eosinophil count, total IgE, specific allergen IgE; sputum eosinophil count >2%; fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) >25 ppb in eosinophilic asthma.

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray – usually normal; hyperinflation in exacerbation; rules out pneumothorax, infection.

**ABG:** ABG in acute severe attack (normal/rising PaCO₂ is a warning sign).

**Other:** Skin prick test, RAST for specific allergens; ENT review for nasal polyps.

### Management (GINA 2023 + Indian context)

**Goals:** control symptoms, prevent exacerbations, maintain normal lung function, avoid medication side-effects.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA tracks 1 & 2):

**Step 1:** As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred Track 1) or SABA + low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA used.

**Step 2:** Daily low-dose ICS (budesonide 200–400 µg, fluticasone 100–250 µg) + SABA PRN.

**Step 3:** Low-dose ICS-LABA (budesonide/formoterol) + PRN.

**Step 4:** Medium-dose ICS-LABA + PRN.

**Step 5:** High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on: tiotropium (LAMA), biologics (omalizumab anti-IgE; mepolizumab/reslizumab anti-IL-5; dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast); low-dose oral corticosteroid (last resort).

Acute severe asthma (Indian ICU practice + BTS/GINA):

Sit patient up, high-flow O₂ via mask, target SpO₂ 94–98%.

Salbutamol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebuliser (back-to-back q15min × 3).

Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (or Methylprednisolone 60–125 mg IV) → continue Prednisolone 40–50 mg PO daily × 5 days.

Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min in severe attack.

IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg loading, 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion) only if above measures fail; monitor levels.

Antibiotics only if clear infection (CXR consolidation, purulent sputum, fever).

ICU admission if life-threatening / not improving; intubation for exhaustion, falling PEFR, rising PaCO₂.

### Non-pharmacological:

Trigger avoidance (allergens, smoke, occupational), weight reduction, GERD treatment, treat allergic rhinitis (nasal steroid).

Patient education, written action plan (green-yellow-red zones), inhaler technique (MDI + spacer for children/elderly; turbohaler/DPI for adults).

Annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination for severe.

Allergen immunotherapy in selected cases.

Fig 1. GINA 2023 stepwise management of asthma (Track 1, preferred path with ICS-formoterol reliever).

Fig 2. Acute severe asthma – emergency management algorithm.

### Complications

Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

Aspergillosis (ABPA – worsening asthma + central bronchiectasis + peripheral eosinophilia + raised IgE).

Long-term airway remodelling, fixed obstruction.

**Side-effects of treatment:** oral candidiasis, dysphonia (ICS), osteoporosis, cushingoid features (oral steroids), tremor (β-agonists).

### Prognosis

Most patients have well-controlled disease with modern therapy. Asthma mortality is low but preventable; under-treatment with ICS, over-reliance on SABA, and poor adherence/inhaler technique are the key contributors to fatal asthma.

Bronchial breath sounds are produced in the trachea and large airways; they are heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is consolidated or replaced by a sound-conducting medium.

### Characteristics

**Normal site:** Heard over manubrium, trachea normally.

**Components:** Inspiration = expiration in duration; expiration is louder than inspiration; clear gap between them.

**Quality:** High-pitched, harsh.

### Types

Tubular bronchial breathing – classical, heard over consolidation (lobar pneumonia – S. pneumoniae), and over a tense pleural effusion (compressed lung above effusion).

Cavernous breathing – low-pitched, hollow, with reverberating quality (over large lung cavity ≥6 cm communicating with bronchus – TB cavity, lung abscess).

Amphoric breathing – high-pitched, metallic, hollow (like blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle); heard over a smooth-walled cavity (>4 cm) communicating with a bronchus, or over an open pneumothorax. Often associated with metallic tinkling.

Associated signs of consolidation

Increased vocal fremitus, dull percussion note, increased vocal resonance with whispering pectoriloquy and aegophony, fine crackles and bronchial breathing.

### Why it matters

Tobacco smoking is the leading preventable cause of death globally; responsible for COPD, lung cancer, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, PVD, oral and other cancers. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality, slows FEV1 decline in COPD, and is the most effective single intervention in respiratory medicine.

Approach – the '5 A's'

Ask about tobacco use at every visit.

Advise to quit, clearly and personally.

Assess willingness to quit.

Assist – set a quit date, pharmacotherapy, counselling.

Arrange follow-up within 1 week of quit date.

### Behavioural support

Motivational interviewing, brief advice (~5 min) doubles quit rate.

Group or individual cognitive behavioural therapy.

Telephone quit-lines (Indian National Tobacco Quitline 1800-11-2356).

mCessation programme via SMS (India MoHFW).

Identify and avoid triggers; coping strategies.

### Pharmacotherapy (Indian availability)

Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT): patch (24-h, 21/14/7 mg), gum (2/4 mg), lozenge, sublingual tablet, inhaler. Start on quit date; taper over 8–12 weeks. Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) most effective.

Varenicline (Champix) – partial nicotinic α4β2 agonist; 0.5 mg OD × 3 d → 0.5 mg BD × 4 d → 1 mg BD × 11–23 weeks. Highest single-agent efficacy. Monitor for mood change.

Bupropion SR 150 mg OD × 3 d → BD; start 1–2 weeks before quit date; 7–12 weeks. Contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorder.

Cytisine – natural partial nicotinic agonist; emerging option in low-resource settings.

Combination therapy (varenicline + NRT) for heavy smokers.

### Special populations

**Pregnancy:** behavioural support first-line; NRT only if behavioural fails (intermittent forms preferred).

**Adolescents:** behavioural; NRT for ≥10/day smokers.

**Cardiovascular disease:** all therapies safe; bupropion preferred post-MI per some guidelines.

### Indian regulations

Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA) 2003 prohibits advertising, smoking in public places, sale to minors.

85% pictorial warnings on tobacco packages.

Ban on e-cigarettes (PECA 2019).

Lobar pneumonia (commonest – S. pneumoniae causing red hepatisation).

Compressed lung above a large pleural effusion (top edge).

Lung abscess opened to bronchus (cavernous, amphoric variants).

Tuberculous cavity (cavernous or amphoric).

Collapse with patent bronchus (paradoxically – consolidation-like transmission).

Mass lesion compressing airway open to large bronchus.

Pulmonary infarction (rare).

Associated signs of consolidation: increased vocal fremitus and resonance, whispering pectoriloquy, aegophony, dull percussion, fine end-inspiratory crackles.

### Definition

Air in the pleural cavity, causing lung collapse. Classified as spontaneous (primary/secondary), traumatic (penetrating/blunt), or iatrogenic; and by severity as simple, tension, or open.

Risk factors and causes

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP – no underlying lung disease):

Tall, thin young males (apical sub-pleural blebs).

Smoking (×20 risk).

Family history (Marfan syndrome, Birt-Hogg-Dubé).

Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, homocystinuria.

Asthma exacerbation.

Tuberculosis (cavitary disease, India).

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (HIV/AIDS).

Cystic fibrosis, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM – women), Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers), Birt-Hogg-Dubé.

Bronchogenic carcinoma, metastatic disease.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Catamenial pneumothorax – endometriosis (around menstruation).

Thoracentesis, pleural biopsy.

### Definition

Clinical syndrome resulting from excess circulating thyroid hormones (T4 and/or T3). 'Hyperthyroidism' specifically refers to overproduction by the thyroid gland; 'thyrotoxicosis' is the broader term encompassing exogenous and gland-derived excess.

### Causes

Increased synthesis (with high RAIU):

Graves' disease (autoimmune, anti-TSH-receptor antibodies; 60–80% of cases) – diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema.

Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease).

Toxic adenoma (autonomously functioning nodule).

Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow) – iodinated contrast, amiodarone type 1, kelp.

Trophoblastic disease (hyperemesis gravidarum, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) – β-hCG-driven.

### Decreased synthesis (low RAIU):

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain – painful, post-viral, raised ESR).

Silent thyroiditis (painless).

Post-partum thyroiditis (1–6 months post-delivery).

Amiodarone type 2 (destructive thyroiditis).

Drug-induced (lithium withdrawal, IFN-α, IL-2, immune-checkpoint inhibitors).

Exogenous thyroid hormone (factitious thyrotoxicosis – low Tg).

Struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid tissue in ovarian teratoma).

### Clinical features

**Symptoms:** Heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, fatigue, weight loss despite good appetite, anxiety, tremor, restlessness, insomnia, irritability, loose stools, polyuria.

**General signs:** Tachycardia, AF (10–15%), warm moist skin, fine tremor, hyperreflexia, lid retraction and lid lag (any thyrotoxicosis), palmar erythema, onycholysis (Plummer's nails), thinning hair, proximal myopathy, low BMI.

**Goitre:** Diffuse smooth goitre with bruit (Graves'); nodular thyroid (TMNG, adenoma); tender (de Quervain); painless tender-free (silent).

**Ophthalmopathy:** Specific to Graves' disease – exophthalmos, periorbital oedema, chemosis, lid retraction (separate from generalised lid retraction of thyrotoxicosis), proptosis, ophthalmoplegia (especially upgaze), diplopia, optic neuropathy.

**Dermopathy / acropachy:** Specific to Graves' – pretibial myxoedema (non-pitting nodular skin thickening on shins); thyroid acropachy (clubbing-like).

**Emergency presentation:** Thyroid storm (decompensated thyrotoxicosis): fever >39°C, severe tachycardia/AF, vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, agitation, delirium, coma, heart failure; mortality 10–30%. Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 supports diagnosis.

### Investigations

**Biochemistry:** TSH suppressed (<0.01 mIU/L), free T4 elevated (and/or T3 elevated – T3 toxicosis seen in early Graves', toxic nodule).

**Antibodies:** Anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb / TSI) – diagnostic for Graves'. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg often positive but non-specific.

**Imaging:** Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) and scan: diffuse high uptake (Graves'), focal high (adenoma), patchy multifocal (TMNG), low/absent uptake (thyroiditis, exogenous, struma ovarii).

Thyroid USG with Doppler (Graves' shows hyper-vascularity).

Thyroglobulin (low in factitious; raised in others).

ECG (sinus tachycardia, AF), CBC, LFT, glucose, calcium.

### Management

### Symptomatic:

β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg q8h, or atenolol 25–50 mg OD) for tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, AF.

Calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) if β-blocker contraindicated (asthma).

### Anti-thyroid drugs (ATDs):

Carbimazole 20–40 mg/day (or methimazole 15–30 mg/day) – tapered based on TFTs, total course 12–18 months.

Propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg q8h – preferred in first trimester of pregnancy (carbimazole teratogenic – aplasia cutis), thyroid storm, ATD allergy.

Side effects – rash, arthralgia (5%), agranulocytosis (0.3%, warn re: sore throat and fever – stop drug, FBC immediately), hepatitis (PTU more), ANCA vasculitis.

**Monitor:** TFT 4–6 weekly initially; FBC and LFT at baseline.

Radioactive iodine (¹³¹I) — definitive:

Most patients with Graves', TMNG, or toxic adenoma; first-line in USA, second-line in Europe/India after ATD relapse.

**Contraindicated:** pregnancy (avoid 6 months prior), breastfeeding, severe ophthalmopathy (can worsen).

Most become hypothyroid – levothyroxine replacement.

Surgery (total or near-total thyroidectomy):

Large goitre with compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, pregnancy unable to tolerate ATD, severe ophthalmopathy, child-bearing-age women planning pregnancy soon.

**Pre-op:** render euthyroid with ATD; add Lugol's iodine 10 days before surgery to reduce vascularity.

**Complications:** recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hypoparathyroidism, hypothyroidism (need lifelong levothyroxine), bleeding.

### Graves' ophthalmopathy:

Stop smoking (worsens), selenium 100 µg BD × 6 months for mild disease.

**Moderate-severe active:** IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/week × 6 weeks then 250 mg/week × 6 weeks; teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody, expensive); orbital decompression; orbital radiotherapy.

### Thyroid storm:

ICU admission, cooling, IV fluids.

PTU 200–300 mg PO/NG q4h (preferred – blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).

Lugol's iodine 5–10 drops q6h, OR sodium iodide 1 g/day IV — at least 1 h after PTU.

IV propranolol 1 mg/min (max 10 mg).

Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (blocks T4→T3, treats adrenal insufficiency).

Treat precipitant (infection, MI, DKA, surgery).

Cholestyramine, plasmapheresis in refractory cases.

### Pregnancy:

PTU in T1, carbimazole in T2/T3 (lowest effective dose); aim for high-normal fT4. Monitor monthly. β-blocker for symptoms (caution: IUGR).

Fig 5. Thyrotoxicosis – diagnostic and management algorithm.

### Complications

AF, dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, thromboembolism.

Osteoporosis, hypercalcaemia.

Thyroid storm.

Severe ophthalmopathy with optic neuropathy.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis (Asian males).

### Definition

SLE is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by production of antibodies to nuclear antigens, immune-complex deposition and inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, serous membranes and the central nervous system. Female:male ≈ 9:1, peak onset 15–40 yrs; commoner and more severe in South Asians and Afro-Caribbeans.

### Etiology / Risk factors

Genetic — HLA-DR2, DR3; complement deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4); IRF5, STAT4, TREX1

Hormonal — oestrogen excess, oral contraceptives may trigger flares

Environmental — UV light, EBV infection, silica, smoking

**Drug-induced lupus:** hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF, interferon (less renal/CNS, anti-histone +)

Pregnancy can precipitate flare; flares can affect pregnancy

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Defective clearance of apoptotic debris exposes nuclear antigens

Loss of self-tolerance → polyclonal B-cell activation → autoantibody production (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, anti-phospholipid)

Immune complexes deposit in kidneys, skin, vessels → complement activation → tissue injury

Type I interferon signature drives disease activity

Clinical features — multisystem

### Constitutional

Fatigue, fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy

### Mucocutaneous (80%)

Malar (butterfly) rash — spares nasolabial folds

Discoid rash — scarring, dyspigmentation; sun-exposed areas

Subacute cutaneous LE — annular/psoriasiform, photosensitive, anti-Ro/SSA

### Photosensitivity

Painless oral/nasal ulcers (commonly hard palate)

Alopecia (diffuse non-scarring or discoid scarring)

### Raynaud's phenomenon

### Musculoskeletal (90%)

Symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis — non-erosive (Jaccoud's reducible deformity)

Myalgia, true myositis rare

### Avascular necrosis (steroid-related)

Renal — lupus nephritis (LN, 40–60%, more in Indians)

### Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, AKI

ISN/RPS 2003 classes I–VI; III/IV (proliferative) most severe, V membranous

**Renal biopsy:** light microscopy + IF (full-house: IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q) + EM

### Neuropsychiatric (NPSLE)

Seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction

### Stroke (often APLA mediated)

Aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, mononeuritis multiplex

### Cardiopulmonary

Pleuritis, pericarditis (commonest serous involvement)

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (non-bacterial verrucous)

Pneumonitis, shrinking lung syndrome, alveolar haemorrhage, ILD

Premature accelerated atherosclerosis — major late mortality cause

### Haematological

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Coombs+), leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia (ITP-like)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (30–40% of SLE)

Arterial/venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, livedo reticularis

### Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin Ab, anti-β2 GP I

### GI / hepatic

Lupus enteritis (vasculitis), pancreatitis, autoimmune hepatitis overlap

### Diagnostic criteria

**EULAR/ACR 2019 (preferred):** Entry: ANA ≥1:80 (HEp-2 IIF). Then weighted criteria in 7 clinical (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) + 3 immunology domains (APLA, complement, SLE-specific antibodies). Classify SLE if ≥10 points with at least one clinical criterion.

SLICC 2012 / ACR 1997 — alternative criteria

### Investigations

Screening / disease confirmation

ANA by IIF on HEp-2 cells — sensitive (>95%), low specificity

Anti-dsDNA — specific; correlates with disease activity (esp. lupus nephritis)

Anti-Sm — specific (low sensitivity ~20% in Caucasians, ~30% in South Asians)

Anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB — subacute cutaneous, neonatal lupus, Sjögren overlap

### Anti-U1 RNP — MCTD overlap

Anti-histone — drug-induced lupus

### Anti-ribosomal P — NPSLE

Complement / immune complex

C3, C4, CH50 — low in active disease

### Disease activity markers

Urinalysis (proteinuria, RBC casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio

CBC (cytopenias), ESR (CRP may be normal — exception: serositis, infection)

### RFT, LFT, lipid profile

**APLA panel:** LA, ACL IgG/IgM, anti-β2 GP I

Renal biopsy if proteinuria >500 mg/day, active sediment, or rising creatinine

MRI brain for NPSLE; EEG if seizures; CSF if meningitis suspected

Echocardiography for serositis, Libman-Sacks; CXR/HRCT for lung

**SLE disease activity:** SLEDAI-2K, BILAG

### Management

Background therapy — for all SLE patients

Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/d (max 400 mg/d) — reduces flares, mortality, organ damage; baseline + annual ophthalmology after 5 years (retinal toxicity)

Photoprotection — sunscreen SPF ≥50 daily

### Vitamin D 1000–2000 IU/d + calcium

**Vaccines:** annual influenza, pneumococcal, HPV (before immunosuppression); avoid live vaccines if immunosuppressed

Aggressive CV risk-factor management — statin, BP <130/80, glycaemic control

**Pregnancy planning:** pre-conceptional counselling, switch teratogens, low-dose aspirin in APS

Mild disease (skin, joints, mild serositis)

### HCQ + NSAIDs PRN

Topical steroids, tacrolimus for skin

Low-dose prednisolone (≤7.5 mg/d) — minimise long-term use

Methotrexate 10–25 mg/wk for arthritis

Belimumab (anti-BLyS) for refractory mucocutaneous/joint

Moderate disease (haematological, mild renal, serositis)

Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/d, taper

**Steroid-sparing:** azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d, MMF 1–2 g/d, methotrexate

### Belimumab, anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR)

Severe disease — Lupus nephritis class III/IV

**Induction:** IV methylprednisolone pulse 500–1000 mg × 3 days + ONE of:

- Cyclophosphamide — Euro-Lupus 500 mg IV every 2 weeks × 6 doses (less toxic, equivalent efficacy in Caucasians/South Asians)

- Cyclophosphamide — NIH 0.5–1 g/m² monthly × 6 (preferred in severe/African ancestry)

- Mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/d × 6 months (preferred in pregnancy planning, GI tolerance)

**Maintenance:** MMF 1–2 g/d OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d for ≥3 years

**Add:** voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) or belimumab — recent evidence for triple therapy

ACEi/ARB for renoprotection; BP target <130/80

**Class V (membranous):** MMF + steroid; ACEi; consider tacrolimus or rituximab

Severe disease — CNS / haematological crises

Methylprednisolone pulse + cyclophosphamide or rituximab

Plasma exchange for catastrophic APS, TTP-like, alveolar haemorrhage

### Newer/targeted biologics

Belimumab — anti-BLyS; mucocutaneous, joint, mild renal

Anifrolumab — anti-type I interferon receptor; moderate–severe skin/joint disease

Voclosporin — class III/IV/V lupus nephritis (with MMF + steroid)

Rituximab — refractory severe disease (off-label in many countries)

### Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)

**Thrombosis:** warfarin INR 2–3 (arterial: 3–4 or warfarin + LDA); avoid DOACs (TRAPS trial showed inferiority for arterial events)

**Pregnancy + APS:** LMWH + low-dose aspirin throughout

**Catastrophic APS:** anticoag + steroid + plasma exchange + IVIG ± rituximab

### Pregnancy in SLE

Plan in clinical remission ≥6 months

Continue HCQ throughout; LDA from 12 weeks (pre-eclampsia prevention)

**Safe:** HCQ, AZA, calcineurin inhibitors, low-dose steroid

**Stop ≥3 months pre-conception:** MMF, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide

**Anti-Ro+:** neonatal lupus → congenital heart block; foetal echo at 16–28 weeks

Fig 4. SLE — classification + organ-directed management

### Complications

End-stage renal disease (lupus nephritis)

Accelerated atherosclerosis, MI, stroke (leading cause of late death)

### Thrombosis (APS)

Infection (immunosuppression) — bacterial, TB, HZ, opportunistic

Avascular necrosis, osteoporosis (steroid)

Premature ovarian failure (cyclophosphamide)

### Malignancy — NHL, cervical (HPV)

Foetal loss, neonatal lupus, prematurity

### Prognosis

5-yr survival has improved from ~50% (1950s) to >90% with modern treatment. Indian cohorts report 10-yr survival 70–80%. Major causes of early death (≤5 yr): active disease, infection, lupus nephritis. Late death: cardiovascular, ESRD. Adherence to HCQ, control of proteinuria, and CV risk modification are the strongest modifiable predictors.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 SLE + EULAR 2019 SLE management recommendations (update 2023) + ISN/RPS 2003 lupus nephritis classification + Indian Rheumatology Association statement on SLE in Indians (2020).
