Trophoblastic disease (hyperemesis gravidarum, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) – β-hCG-driven.

### Decreased synthesis (low RAIU):

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain – painful, post-viral, raised ESR).

Silent thyroiditis (painless).

Post-partum thyroiditis (1–6 months post-delivery).

Amiodarone type 2 (destructive thyroiditis).

Drug-induced (lithium withdrawal, IFN-α, IL-2, immune-checkpoint inhibitors).

Exogenous thyroid hormone (factitious thyrotoxicosis – low Tg).

Struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid tissue in ovarian teratoma).

### Clinical features

**Symptoms:** Heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, fatigue, weight loss despite good appetite, anxiety, tremor, restlessness, insomnia, irritability, loose stools, polyuria.

**General signs:** Tachycardia, AF (10–15%), warm moist skin, fine tremor, hyperreflexia, lid retraction and lid lag (any thyrotoxicosis), palmar erythema, onycholysis (Plummer's nails), thinning hair, proximal myopathy, low BMI.

**Goitre:** Diffuse smooth goitre with bruit (Graves'); nodular thyroid (TMNG, adenoma); tender (de Quervain); painless tender-free (silent).

**Ophthalmopathy:** Specific to Graves' disease – exophthalmos, periorbital oedema, chemosis, lid retraction (separate from generalised lid retraction of thyrotoxicosis), proptosis, ophthalmoplegia (especially upgaze), diplopia, optic neuropathy.

**Dermopathy / acropachy:** Specific to Graves' – pretibial myxoedema (non-pitting nodular skin thickening on shins); thyroid acropachy (clubbing-like).

**Emergency presentation:** Thyroid storm (decompensated thyrotoxicosis): fever >39°C, severe tachycardia/AF, vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, agitation, delirium, coma, heart failure; mortality 10–30%. Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 supports diagnosis.

### Investigations

**Biochemistry:** TSH suppressed (<0.01 mIU/L), free T4 elevated (and/or T3 elevated – T3 toxicosis seen in early Graves', toxic nodule).

**Antibodies:** Anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb / TSI) – diagnostic for Graves'. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg often positive but non-specific.

**Imaging:** Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) and scan: diffuse high uptake (Graves'), focal high (adenoma), patchy multifocal (TMNG), low/absent uptake (thyroiditis, exogenous, struma ovarii).

Thyroid USG with Doppler (Graves' shows hyper-vascularity).

Thyroglobulin (low in factitious; raised in others).

ECG (sinus tachycardia, AF), CBC, LFT, glucose, calcium.

### Management

### Symptomatic:

β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg q8h, or atenolol 25–50 mg OD) for tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, AF.

Calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) if β-blocker contraindicated (asthma).

### Anti-thyroid drugs (ATDs):

Carbimazole 20–40 mg/day (or methimazole 15–30 mg/day) – tapered based on TFTs, total course 12–18 months.

Propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg q8h – preferred in first trimester of pregnancy (carbimazole teratogenic – aplasia cutis), thyroid storm, ATD allergy.

Side effects – rash, arthralgia (5%), agranulocytosis (0.3%, warn re: sore throat and fever – stop drug, FBC immediately), hepatitis (PTU more), ANCA vasculitis.

**Monitor:** TFT 4–6 weekly initially; FBC and LFT at baseline.

Radioactive iodine (¹³¹I) — definitive:

Most patients with Graves', TMNG, or toxic adenoma; first-line in USA, second-line in Europe/India after ATD relapse.

**Contraindicated:** pregnancy (avoid 6 months prior), breastfeeding, severe ophthalmopathy (can worsen).

Most become hypothyroid – levothyroxine replacement.

Surgery (total or near-total thyroidectomy):

Large goitre with compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, pregnancy unable to tolerate ATD, severe ophthalmopathy, child-bearing-age women planning pregnancy soon.

**Pre-op:** render euthyroid with ATD; add Lugol's iodine 10 days before surgery to reduce vascularity.

**Complications:** recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hypoparathyroidism, hypothyroidism (need lifelong levothyroxine), bleeding.

### Graves' ophthalmopathy:

Stop smoking (worsens), selenium 100 µg BD × 6 months for mild disease.

**Moderate-severe active:** IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/week × 6 weeks then 250 mg/week × 6 weeks; teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody, expensive); orbital decompression; orbital radiotherapy.

### Thyroid storm:

ICU admission, cooling, IV fluids.

PTU 200–300 mg PO/NG q4h (preferred – blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).

Lugol's iodine 5–10 drops q6h, OR sodium iodide 1 g/day IV — at least 1 h after PTU.

IV propranolol 1 mg/min (max 10 mg).

Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (blocks T4→T3, treats adrenal insufficiency).

Treat precipitant (infection, MI, DKA, surgery).

Cholestyramine, plasmapheresis in refractory cases.

### Pregnancy:

PTU in T1, carbimazole in T2/T3 (lowest effective dose); aim for high-normal fT4. Monitor monthly. β-blocker for symptoms (caution: IUGR).

Fig 5. Thyrotoxicosis – diagnostic and management algorithm.

### Complications

AF, dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, thromboembolism.

Osteoporosis, hypercalcaemia.

Thyroid storm.

Severe ophthalmopathy with optic neuropathy.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis (Asian males).

GENERAL MEDICINE|61.note:
### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Overview

**Vaccines available routinely:** Hepatitis A (inactivated/live attenuated) and Hepatitis B (recombinant HBsAg). No vaccine for HCV, HDV (HBV vaccine prevents HDV), HEV (Hecolin licensed in China only; not in WHO/India schedule yet).

### Hepatitis B Vaccine

### Indications (Universal in India — UIP)

**All neonates:** birth dose within 24 h + UIP at 6, 10, 14 wk (pentavalent — DPT-HepB-Hib).

**Catch-up:** 0–1–6-month schedule for unvaccinated children/adolescents/adults.

Healthcare workers (HCWs), medical students, lab personnel, dialysis patients.

Household and sexual contacts of HBsAg+ individuals.

MSM, multiple sexual partners, IDU, recipients of clotting factor concentrate.

Patients with chronic liver disease, on immunosuppression, transplant candidates.

Patients with CKD (especially pre-dialysis) — higher dose schedule (40 µg × 4).

Inmates of correctional facilities, residents of institutional care.

Travellers to endemic regions (Asia, Africa, parts of Latin America).

### Schedules

### Dose

**Adult:** 20 µg IM deltoid (10 µg paediatric).

**Dialysis:** 40 µg × 4 doses (Engerix-B 40 µg).

### Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)

HBIG 0.06 ml/kg IM within 24 h + Hep B vaccine (full course) if source HBsAg+ AND recipient unvaccinated / non-responder.

Vaccinated responder (anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/ml): no PEP needed.

**Neonates of HBsAg+ mothers:** HBIG + Hep B vaccine within 12 h of birth → completes 3-dose schedule; 95% efficacy.

### Precautions / Contraindications

Anaphylaxis to yeast or previous dose.

Defer if acute moderate-severe illness (mild URI not a contraindication).

Pregnancy/lactation — safe (inactivated/recombinant, no live virus).

### Adverse effects

Local injection site pain (commonest), low-grade fever, fatigue.

Anaphylaxis very rare (~ 1 in 600,000).

Demyelinating disease association — refuted by large studies.

Non-responders / serology testing

Check anti-HBs 1–2 mo after final dose in HCWs / immunocompromised.

≥ 10 mIU/ml = responder (lifelong immunity).

< 10 mIU/ml = non-responder → revaccinate 3 more doses; if still negative → test HBsAg (occult infection) and document.

### Hepatitis A Vaccine

Indications (recommended, not yet universal in India)

Children > 1 yr (recommended by IAP in India since 2014).

Travellers to endemic areas, food handlers, MSM, IDU, patients with chronic liver disease (mortality 10× higher), clotting factor recipients, lab personnel handling HAV.

### Schedule

**Inactivated (Havrix, Avaxim):** 2 doses 6 mo apart — > 95% seroconversion, > 25 yr immunity.

**Live attenuated (Indian:** Biovac-A, Bharat Biotech): 1 dose, equivalent immunogenicity.

### Post-exposure

**Healthy 1–40 yr:** HAV vaccine within 2 wk of exposure.

Immunocompromised / > 40 yr / chronic liver disease: HAV-Ig 0.02 ml/kg IM + vaccine (separate site).

### Contraindications/precautions

Anaphylaxis to previous dose, neomycin.

Pregnancy — theoretical risk, generally safe (inactivated).

### Patient Counselling Points

Vaccine is preventive, NOT curative — chronic HBV needs antivirals.

Complete all 3 doses (HBV) at correct intervals; missed dose — resume schedule, do NOT restart.

Hand hygiene, safe water/food (HAV), safe sex, sterile needles (HBV/HCV).

**HBsAg+ individuals:** cannot donate blood/organ; inform sexual partners; household members vaccinate; avoid alcohol; avoid hepatotoxic drugs; monitor LFT, HBV DNA, AFP + USG 6-monthly.

No vaccine for HCV — emphasise primary prevention (safe injection, no shared razors/toothbrushes).

**Pregnant women:** HBsAg screening in 1st trimester (NACO PPTCT); if HBsAg+ HBV DNA > 200,000 → maternal TDF in 3rd trimester to reduce vertical transmission.

Vaccine record card to be maintained (UIP card).

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; NTAGI/India UIP 2024; CDC ACIP 2023; IAP Immunisation 2023.

### Definition

Acute Hep B = clinically and biochemically apparent hepatitis (jaundice, raised ALT) with positive HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM, of < 6 months' duration.

### HBV Antigens and Antibodies

### Phases / Patterns in Acute HBV

- Incubation phase (2–10 wk)

HBsAg + (first to appear, 2–10 wk post-exposure)

HBeAg + (high infectivity)

HBV DNA + (viral replication)

Anti-HBc not yet detectable; patient usually asymptomatic.

- Symptomatic / Acute phase (4–12 wk)

### HBsAg + persists

### HBeAg + (transitioning)

**Hallmark:** Anti-HBc IgM + → DIAGNOSTIC of acute infection

ALT/AST elevated (often > 1000); bilirubin rising.

- Window period (in recovering patients)

HBsAg — (cleared) but anti-HBs not yet detectable

**Sole marker:** Anti-HBc IgM + (sole marker of recent infection)

Important to order anti-HBc IgM, not just HBsAg, in suspected acute hepatitis.

- Recovery phase (months later)

HBsAg −, anti-HBs + (protective immunity)

### Anti-HBc IgG + (lifelong)

HBeAg −, anti-HBe + (early), then anti-HBe levels wane

### Differentiating Acute vs Chronic vs Vaccinated

### Clinical Algorithm

**Step 1:** Order HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM (and total anti-HBc) in any patient with acute hepatitis.

**Step 2:** Both positive → ACUTE Hep B.

**Step 3:** HBsAg + but anti-HBc IgM − → likely CHRONIC HBV with super-infection by another agent (rule out HDV super-infection, HAV/HEV).

**Step 4:** HBsAg − but anti-HBc IgM + → WINDOW PERIOD of resolving acute Hep B.

**Step 5:** Repeat HBsAg at 6 months — persistence = chronic HBV; loss + anti-HBs = recovery.

### Additional Tests in Acute Hepatitis

HBV DNA (PCR quantitative) — helps differentiate replication status.

HDV IgM/IgG — co-infection or super-infection (severe acute / fulminant).

ALT, AST, bilirubin, INR — severity / acute liver failure markers (INR > 1.5 + encephalopathy).

Exclude co-existing HAV, HEV, HCV, HIV.

Management Notes (brief — see Q9 for chronic)

Acute HBV in immunocompetent adults — > 95% recover without antiviral.

Antivirals (TDF/entecavir) considered only in:

Severe acute hepatitis (INR > 1.5, encephalopathy, bilirubin > 10).

Prolonged (> 4 wk) symptomatic illness with persistent HBV DNA.

Immunocompromised host.

Notify (statutorily notifiable disease in India).

Counsel contacts — Hep B vaccine ± HBIG; condom use until anti-HBs +.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.518; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD 2018; EASL 2017.

### Definition

Inflammation of the liver, evidenced by hepatocellular injury (raised ALT > AST, in ratio > 1 except in alcoholic hepatitis where AST > ALT and ratio > 2). Acute (< 6 mo) vs chronic (≥ 6 mo).

### Classification by Aetiology

- Viral (commonest globally)

- Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) — see also tabular list below

**Antibiotics:** amoxicillin-clavulanate (commonest DILI cause), flucloxacillin, macrolides, tetracyclines, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones.

**ATT-DILI:** Antitubercular: INH, rifampicin, pyrazinamide (esp. older, alcoholics, HIV+, hep B/C carriers). Pivotal Indian cause.

**Antifungals:** ketoconazole, voriconazole, terbinafine.

**Antiepileptics:** phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine.

Statins (rare hepatocellular), methotrexate (chronic fibrosis), amiodarone (steatohepatitis-like), azathioprine, allopurinol.

Paracetamol overdose (> 10 g acute or 150 mg/kg) — leading cause of acute liver failure in West (rare in India).

**Anaesthetics:** halothane, enflurane (idiosyncratic).

**Hormones:** oestrogens (cholestatic), androgens, contraceptives.

Chemotherapy / immunomodulators: tamoxifen, MTX, asparaginase, immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICI hepatitis).

**Indian-relevant herbs:** Herbal / supplements — kava, germander, comfrey, green tea extract, Ayurvedic preparations with heavy metals.

**Recreational:** ecstasy, anabolic steroids, cocaine.

### 3. Toxin / Environmental

Alcohol — acute alcoholic hepatitis (high mortality; Maddrey DF > 32 / MELD > 20).

Mushroom (Amanita phalloides — α-amanitin).

Carbon tetrachloride, vinyl chloride, aflatoxin (→ HCC).

Iron overload, copper (Wilson's).

### 4. Autoimmune

Type 1 AIH (ANA, ASMA) — adult women, polyarthralgia.

Type 2 AIH (anti-LKM-1) — children, more severe.

Primary biliary cholangitis (AMA, middle-aged women, pruritus).

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (pANCA, IBD association).

### 5. Metabolic / Genetic

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD / NASH) — most common chronic liver disease in India, related to MetS, obesity, T2DM.

Wilson's disease (autosomal recessive, ATP7B; KF rings, low ceruloplasmin).

Hereditary haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y; iron overload — rare in India).

α1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ).

### 6. Vascular / Hypoxic

Ischaemic hepatitis ('shock liver') — markedly raised AST/ALT, restores rapidly.

Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein outflow obstruction).

Veno-occlusive disease (post-transplant, herbal teas).

Congestive hepatopathy (RHF, TR).

### 7. Infiltrative / Granulomatous

Hepatic TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma, amyloidosis, brucellosis.

### Pattern of LFT Abnormality

### DILI — Common Mechanisms

Direct hepatotoxin (predictable, dose-related): paracetamol, CCl₄.

Idiosyncratic (unpredictable, host-related): INH, halothane, amoxicillin-clavulanate.

**Immune-mediated:** phenytoin (DRESS), allopurinol (HLA-B*5801), anti-TNF.

**Mitochondrial / steatosis:** valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs (didanosine, stavudine).

### Diagnostic Workup

Detailed history — alcohol, drugs/herbal/Ayurvedic, sexual, travel, IDU, occupational.

LFT pattern, INR, albumin.

**Viral serology:** HAV IgM, HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV (+ HCV RNA), HEV IgM, HIV.

**Autoimmune:** ANA, ASMA, AMA, anti-LKM, IgG, IgM, IgA.

**Metabolic:** ferritin, transferrin sat, ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, α1-AT.

USG abdomen ± Doppler; MRI/MRCP if cholestatic.

Liver biopsy if diagnosis unclear or staging needed.

### Management — Principles

Withdraw / treat causative agent (stop drug, antiviral for HBV/HCV, abstinence for alcohol).

Supportive — hydration, antiemetics, vit K if INR raised, glucose monitoring in ALF.

**Specific antidotes:** NAC for paracetamol (within 8–10 h), penicillin G for Amanita, D-penicillamine + zinc for Wilson's.

**Immunosuppression:** prednisolone ± azathioprine for AIH; pred for severe alcoholic hep (Maddrey > 32).

DAA for HCV; antiviral (TDF/entecavir) for chronic HBV with appropriate criteria.

Liver transplant — King's College criteria for paracetamol ALF; MELD-based listing for chronic.

Fig 5. Hepatitis — serological workup.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.515–525; Davidson Ch.22; EASL 2018; NVHCP guidelines.

### Definition

Chronic HCV = anti-HCV positive + HCV RNA detectable for > 6 months. 70–80% of HCV-infected individuals progress to chronicity. Indian estimated prevalence ~ 1%, with regional variation; major IDU and dialysis-associated.

### Goals of Therapy

Achieve sustained virological response (SVR) — undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after end of treatment. Equivalent to cure.

Halt or reverse fibrosis, prevent cirrhosis, HCC.

Improve quality of life, reduce transmission.

### Pre-treatment Assessment

Confirm chronic HCV — HCV RNA (quantitative).

Genotype (with universal pan-genotypic DAA, often skipped in India under NVHCP).

Fibrosis assessment — transient elastography (FibroScan), APRI, FIB-4.

Cirrhosis decompensation — Child-Pugh, MELD.

Co-infection screen — HBV, HIV (modifies treatment).

Renal function (eGFR) — drug choice.

Pregnancy test, drug interactions (especially with HIV ART).

DAA Regimens (current standard — replaces interferon-ribavirin era)

### Pan-genotypic regimens (first-line under Indian NVHCP)

Genotype-Specific (less used now)

**Genotype 1 + 4:** Ledipasvir + Sofosbuvir 12 wk (or 8 wk if non-cirrhotic, low VL).

**Genotype 3:** Sofosbuvir + Daclatasvir × 12 wk ± ribavirin if cirrhotic.

**Genotype 5/6:** Sofosbuvir + Velpatasvir × 12 wk.

### Special Populations

### Decompensated cirrhosis (Child B/C)

AVOID protease inhibitors (glecaprevir, voxilaprevir) — hepatotoxicity.

Use Sofosbuvir + Velpatasvir + Ribavirin × 12 wk (consider liver transplant).

Ribavirin dose by weight (1000 mg if < 75 kg, 1200 mg if ≥ 75 kg).

### HCV + HIV co-infection

Same DAA regimens; check ARV interactions (sofosbuvir + atazanavir/ritonavir — caution).

### HCV + HBV co-infection

Risk of HBV reactivation during DAA → must check HBV status. If HBsAg+ → concurrent HBV antiviral (entecavir/TDF).

Renal failure (eGFR < 30 or dialysis)

Glecaprevir + Pibrentasvir × 12 wk — preferred (no sofosbuvir).

Avoid sofosbuvir-based regimens (renal clearance) if eGFR < 30.

### Pregnancy

DAAs not recommended; defer treatment till after delivery / breastfeeding.

Ribavirin TERATOGENIC — strict contraception for 6 months post-treatment.

Children > 3 yr

**Approved:** Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir, Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir, weight-based dosing.

### Monitoring

Baseline HCV RNA, LFT, CBC, eGFR.

On-treatment LFT at 4 wk (especially if cirrhotic).

End of treatment HCV RNA.

SVR12 — HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment. Negative = cure.

**Cirrhotics:** continue HCC surveillance (AFP + USG 6-monthly) lifelong even after SVR.

### Adverse Effects of DAA

Generally well tolerated; fatigue, headache, nausea.

**Drug interactions:** amiodarone + sofosbuvir → severe bradycardia (avoid); statins (rosuvastatin levels rise); rifampicin and St John's wort reduce DAA levels.

### Indian Programme: NVHCP

National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme launched 2018 — provides FREE DAA (sofosbuvir + daclatasvir or velpatasvir) to all chronic HCV patients in India. Diagnostics also subsidised. India aims to eliminate HCV by 2030 (WHO target).

### Prognosis

SVR > 95% with current DAAs across genotypes. SVR reduces all-cause mortality, liver mortality, HCC incidence, decompensation, and need for transplant. Compensated cirrhotics with SVR can still develop HCC — continue surveillance.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; NVHCP Operational Guidelines 2018; AASLD/IDSA HCV 2023; EASL 2020; APASL 2017.

### Overview

HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae). India is 'intermediate endemic' (HBsAg prevalence 2–7%). Transmission: vertical (commonest in India), horizontal (childhood close contact), parenteral (transfusion, IDU), sexual.

### Viral Markers (Quick Reference)

### Laboratory Diagnosis

### Initial Screening

HBsAg + anti-HBc total (rule out occult HBV).

Anti-HBs — assess vaccine response, prior immunity.

### If HBsAg Positive

Confirm chronicity (> 6 mo) — repeat at 6 mo.

Anti-HBc IgM (acute vs chronic exacerbation).

HBeAg, anti-HBe — define phase.

HBV DNA (quantitative PCR) — viral load.

LFT — ALT, AST, bilirubin, albumin, INR.

Fibrosis assessment — FibroScan, APRI, FIB-4, liver biopsy if uncertain.

HCC surveillance — AFP + USG abdomen 6-monthly.

Co-infection screen — HCV, HDV, HIV.

### Phases of Chronic HBV (EASL/AASLD)

### Indications for Antiviral Therapy

**HBeAg+ chronic hepatitis:** HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/ml + ALT > 2× ULN OR significant fibrosis (Metavir ≥ F2 or FibroScan > 7 kPa).

**HBeAg− chronic hepatitis:** HBV DNA > 2,000 IU/ml + raised ALT or fibrosis.

All cirrhotic patients (compensated/decompensated) with detectable HBV DNA — treat.

Acute liver failure / severe acute hepatitis B.

**Pregnancy:** HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/ml in 3rd trimester → TDF to reduce vertical transmission.

Patients receiving immunosuppression (chemo, rituximab, anti-TNF, transplant): pre-emptive antiviral to prevent reactivation (HBsAg+ definite; isolated anti-HBc+ for high-risk regimens).

### Antiviral Treatment

### First-line Nucleos(t)ide Analogues (NA)

Generally lifelong (especially HBeAg−); stop only if HBsAg seroconversion (rare).

**Monitor:** ALT, HBV DNA 3–6 monthly; HBeAg/anti-HBe annually; creatinine + phosphate for TDF.

### Pegylated Interferon-α (Peg-IFN-α-2a)

180 µg SC weekly × 48 weeks.

**Indications:** young, low viral load, HBeAg+, no cirrhosis, genotype A > D.

**Advantage:** finite duration, sustained response, higher HBsAg loss.

**Limitations:** SE (flu-like, depression, cytopenia), poor tolerability; absolute contraindications in decompensated cirrhosis, pregnancy.

### Prevention

Vaccination (see Q5 for details)

Universal birth-dose Hep B in India (UIP); 3-dose pentavalent at 6, 10, 14 wk.

Catch-up for unvaccinated children and high-risk adults.

Anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/ml = protective.

### Post-Exposure Prophylaxis

HBIG 0.06 ml/kg IM + Hep B vaccine (full schedule) within 24 h for non-vaccinated / non-responder exposed to HBsAg+ source.

### Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT)

Maternal HBsAg screening 1st trimester (NACO).

Maternal TDF 28 wk to delivery if HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/ml.

**Neonate:** HBIG + Hep B vaccine within 12 h of birth → completes UIP schedule. 95% efficacy.

### Other

Screen blood donors universally.

Single-use needles, safe injection practices.

Safe sex / condoms.

Avoid sharing razors, toothbrushes.

Healthcare worker compliance with universal precautions.

### Complications

Cirrhosis (20–30% over 20 yr without treatment).

HCC — risk ~ 0.5%/yr in non-cirrhotic chronic HBV, 2–5%/yr in cirrhotic; even without cirrhosis HBV is direct oncogene (integrates into hepatocyte DNA).

Decompensation, hepatic failure.

**Extra-hepatic:** polyarteritis nodosa, membranous nephropathy, MPGN, essential mixed cryoglobulinaemia.

### Prognosis

**With antiviral therapy:** HBV DNA suppression > 95%, fibrosis regression, ↓ HCC risk by ~50%, prolonged survival. Cure (HBsAg loss) rare ~ 1–3%/yr on NA. India NVHCP free antivirals available.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.519; AASLD 2018; APASL 2015; EASL 2017; NVHCP guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|62.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Definition

Extra-intestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica infection, where trophozoites breach colonic mucosa → portal circulation → hepatic parenchyma → necrotic abscess (classic 'anchovy sauce' aspirate). Most common extra-intestinal amoebic manifestation; right lobe involved in 70–80%. Significant Indian public health burden — endemic across the subcontinent.

### Clinical Features

**Subacute onset (1–4 wk):** fever, RUQ pain (referred to right shoulder), tender hepatomegaly, weight loss, anorexia, sweating.

Recent dysentery only in 10–30% (most have no GI history).

**Examination:** tender enlarged liver (intercostal tenderness — Boas sign), right basal lung dullness/effusion, mild jaundice (15–25%).

**Demographic:** adult male 20–40 yr, alcohol/poor sanitation/lower SES.

### Investigations

### Confirmatory

USG abdomen — single hypoechoic lesion right lobe, no calcification (unlike hydatid), 1st-line in India.

CECT — peripheral enhancement, central necrosis; chronic shows wall.

Serology — IELISA anti-E. histolytica IgG (sensitivity > 90%; persists for years — limits use in re-exposed Indian patients).

Stool antigen (Entamoeba histolytica II ELISA) > microscopy (microscopy can't distinguish from non-pathogenic E. dispar/moshkovskii).

Aspirate (only if needed)

Reddish-brown 'anchovy sauce' pus, sterile bacterial culture, PCR positive for E. histolytica.

### Supportive

CBC — leukocytosis without eosinophilia (eosinophilia suggests hydatid).

LFT — raised ALP > ALT/AST.

CRP raised, blood culture (rule out pyogenic).

### Differentiating Amoebic vs Pyogenic Liver Abscess

### Management

### 1. Medical (primary)

**Tissue amoebicide:** Tissue amoebicide: Metronidazole 800 mg PO TDS × 7–10 d (or tinidazole 2 g OD × 3–5 d — better tolerated).

**Luminal amoebicide:** Luminal amoebicide: Diloxanide furoate 500 mg TDS × 10 d OR paromomycin 25–35 mg/kg/d in 3 divided doses × 7 d (MUST follow tissue amoebicide to eradicate cysts; prevents relapse / spread).

**Supportive:** Supportive: Analgesia, antiemetics, hydration; avoid alcohol with metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction).

### 2. Aspiration / Drainage

Indications for percutaneous (USG-guided) aspiration:

Large abscess (> 5–10 cm) with thin wall and risk of rupture.

Left lobe abscess (risk of rupture into pericardium).

No clinical response to medical Rx within 5–7 d.

Diagnostic doubt (rule out pyogenic).

Pregnancy (avoid metronidazole 1st trimester — drainage preferred).

Imminent rupture / superficial location.

Percutaneous catheter drainage if recurrent or multilocular.

Open surgical drainage — only if percutaneous fails or rupture into peritoneum/pleura.

- Complications & their Management

**Rupture (10%):** pleuropulmonary (commonest — right), peritoneal (acute abdomen), pericardial (left lobe — TAMPONADE → emergency drainage), bronchial fistula (anchovy sputum).

Secondary bacterial infection — broad-spectrum abx + drainage.

Hepatobronchial fistula — usually self-resolves with abscess Rx.

### Prognosis

With appropriate Rx, mortality < 5%. Untreated or complicated (rupture) → 20–40%. Resolution of abscess on imaging takes 3–9 months — not a measure of treatment success (clinical improvement is).

### Public Health / Prevention

Sanitation — boil water, wash hands, wash vegetables (esp. India).

Treat asymptomatic cyst-passers (diloxanide / paromomycin) in households.

Health education in endemic regions; screen food handlers in institutional settings.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.555; Davidson Ch.13 (parasites); WHO 2017; ICMR antibiotic policy 2022.

### Definition

Cirrhosis is end-stage liver disease with fibrosis, regenerative nodules, and architectural distortion. Compensated cirrhosis = no overt clinical decompensation (no ascites, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice). Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally — 'silent' stage.

### Two Stages of Compensated Cirrhosis

Clinical Features of Compensated Cirrhosis (≥ 2 to enumerate)

### General / Constitutional

Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss (usually mild).

Mild non-specific RUQ discomfort.

Often asymptomatic — discovered on routine LFT abnormality, imaging, or evaluation for related condition.

### Cutaneous / Mucocutaneous Stigmata

**Spider naevi:** Spider naevi / spider angiomata (face, neck, upper chest, > 5 = significant).

Palmar erythema (thenar/hypothenar).

Caput medusae (recanalised paraumbilical vein — uncommon in early).

Dupuytren's contracture (alcoholic CLD particularly).

Clubbing (especially in PBC, hepatopulmonary syndrome later).

Leuconychia (white nails, Terry's nails — proximal 2/3 white).

Pruritus (cholestasis component).

Easy bruising — coagulopathy from impaired clotting factor synthesis.

### Hormonal / Endocrine

Gynaecomastia (impaired oestrogen metabolism).

Testicular atrophy, decreased libido, loss of body hair (men).

Amenorrhoea (women).

Parotid enlargement (alcoholic CLD).

Hepatomegaly initially (firm, irregular, nodular) → may shrink in advanced.

Splenomegaly (portal HTN; usually moderate, smooth) — earliest sign of PHT.

Distended abdominal wall veins (caput medusae) — flow away from umbilicus.

No ascites (defining feature of compensated stage).

### Other

Easy fatigability, mild peripheral oedema.

Foetor hepaticus (sweet, musty breath) — usually absent in compensated.

Xanthelasma (cholestatic — PBC).

LFT — may be normal or mildly deranged; albumin low, INR raised, bilirubin may be normal or mildly raised.

**Hyperdynamic circulation labs:** thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism + thrombopoietin reduction), low albumin, raised INR.

FIB-4 score, APRI score — non-invasive fibrosis markers.

Transient elastography (FibroScan) > 12.5 kPa → cirrhosis.

USG abdomen — shrunken nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, varices.

OGD — varices screening.

Liver biopsy — gold standard but increasingly replaced by elastography.

Treat aetiology — antiviral for HBV/HCV, abstinence, weight loss for NAFLD.

Vaccinate against HAV, HBV (if not immune), influenza, pneumococcal.

**Surveillance:** AFP + USG abdomen 6-monthly (HCC, ~ 2–5%/yr).

Screen for varices (OGD baseline; if small varices repeat 2 yr, if large → primary prophylaxis).

Bone density (osteoporosis with cholestatic disease).

Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ATT without monitoring).

Fig 6. Cirrhosis — compensated vs decompensated pathway.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.522; Davidson Ch.22; D'Amico 2006 staging; EASL 2018.

### Definition

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) = hepatic injury attributable to a drug or supplement, after excluding viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes. Accounts for 10% of all acute hepatitis and ~ 50% of acute liver failure in the West.

### Classification by Mechanism

**Intrinsic / Direct:** Intrinsic / Direct: Predictable, dose-dependent, reproducible. e.g. paracetamol (NAPQI metabolite), CCl₄, Amanita phalloides (α-amanitin).

**Idiosyncratic:** Idiosyncratic: Unpredictable, NOT dose-related, latency days–months. e.g. INH, amoxicillin-clavulanate, halothane, phenytoin.

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

### Classification by Pattern (R-value)

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

**R 2–5:** Mixed (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulphonamides).

### Common Hepatotoxic Drugs — by Class

### Indian Context — ATT-DILI

Highest incidence among Asians (~ 8–12%) — important for MBBS.

**Risk factors:** age > 35, female, alcoholism, viral hepatitis B/C carrier, HIV, malnutrition, slow acetylator phenotype (Indian genetic prevalence).

**Pathway:** INH → hydrazine metabolite → CYP2E1 → hepatocyte injury. Rifampicin induces CYP isoenzymes → ↑ INH toxicity; PZA additional risk.

**Monitoring:** baseline + monthly LFT during ATT in high-risk; symptom screening.

Stop ATT if ALT > 5× ULN (asymptomatic) or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms / jaundice.

**Re-introduction:** after LFT normalises, single drug → titrate up (usually rifampicin first → INH → PZA).

**Severe / hepatitic ATT-DILI:** switch to non-hepatotoxic regimen — levofloxacin + ethambutol + injectable (aminoglycoside) ± linezolid.

### Diagnosis

Temporal relationship — onset days to months after starting drug; dechallenge improves LFT.

Exclude viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), autoimmune, biliary (USG/MRCP), metabolic (Wilson's, haemochromatosis).

RUCAM / Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score ≥ 6 = probable.

Liver biopsy — only if diagnosis unclear or atypical.

### Management

WITHDRAW culprit drug immediately.

**Supportive:** hydration, antiemetics, monitor INR + bilirubin.

**Paracetamol:** Specific antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for paracetamol — 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (Rumack-Matthew nomogram).

Penicillin G + silibinin for Amanita.

Carnitine for valproate.

Corticosteroids may help immune-mediated (DRESS, ICI-related hepatitis).

Liver transplant if acute liver failure (King's College criteria for paracetamol, INR > 6.5 / 3 of 5 minor criteria for non-paracetamol).

### Prognosis

Most resolve on dechallenge. 'Hy's law' (ALT > 3× ULN + bilirubin > 2× ULN + no other cause) → 10% mortality. Cholestatic DILI may persist months → vanishing bile duct syndrome.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.22; ACG DILI 2014; Indian Society of Gastroenterology DILI consensus.

### Definition

Clinical manifestations of impaired hepatic synthetic, metabolic, detoxification, and excretory function — may be acute or chronic, compensated or decompensated.

### Signs — Examination Sequence (Head to Toe)

### General / Constitutional

Sallow / icteric complexion (yellow tinge of sclera, mucosa, skin) — bilirubin > 2 mg/dL.

Cachexia, muscle wasting (temporal hollowing, sarcopenia).

Foetor hepaticus — sweet musty breath (dimethyl sulphide from mercaptans).

Altered mentation — drowsiness, confusion, irritability (encephalopathy).

### Hands

Clubbing — chronic liver disease, especially PBC, hepatopulmonary syndrome.

Leuconychia — proximal 2/3 white (Terry's nails) → hypoalbuminaemia.

Palmar erythema — thenar / hypothenar.

Dupuytren's contracture — palmar fascia thickening (alcoholic CLD).

Asterixis (flapping tremor) — hepatic encephalopathy; not specific (also uraemia, CO₂ retention).

Bruising / ecchymoses — coagulopathy (↓ vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X).

Petechiae — thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism, ↓ thrombopoietin).

### Face / Eyes

Icterus — sclera + frenulum.

Xanthelasma — periorbital cholestatic deposits (PBC).

Kayser-Fleischer ring — Wilson's disease.

Parotid enlargement — alcoholic CLD.

Spider naevi on face, neck, upper chest (drainage area of SVC).

### Chest

Spider naevi (> 5 significant).

Gynaecomastia (impaired oestrogen metabolism, also drugs — spironolactone, digoxin).

Loss of axillary / chest hair.

Pleural effusion right > left (hepatic hydrothorax — diaphragmatic defect; transudate, ascitic origin).

### Abdomen

Hepatomegaly initially (firm, irregular, tender) — may shrink in late cirrhosis.

Splenomegaly (portal HTN) — moderate.

Ascites — shifting dullness, fluid thrill (large), umbilicus evertion / hernia.

Caput medusae — recanalised paraumbilical vein → distended abdominal wall veins (flow AWAY from umbilicus, distinguishes from SVC obstruction).

Venous hum (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur) — heard over caput medusae.

Pulsatile liver — TR (cardiac cirrhosis).

Bruit over liver — HCC, hepatic artery aneurysm.

### Hormonal / Genitalia

Testicular atrophy, loss of libido, impotence.

Amenorrhoea (women).

Loss of pubic / body hair.

### Lower limbs

Pitting oedema — hypoalbuminaemia (albumin < 2.5 g/dL).

Bruising — coagulopathy.

Peripheral neuropathy (alcoholic / thiamine deficiency / autoimmune AIH).

### Systemic / Cardiovascular

Hyperdynamic circulation — bounding pulse, low BP, warm peripheries, tachycardia.

Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy — blunted contractile response to stress.

### Major Decompensation Markers (memorise)

### Investigations to Confirm

LFT (AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin/albumin), INR, ammonia.

USG abdomen ± Doppler — shrunken nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, portal flow.

OGD — varices.

Child-Pugh, MELD-Na for severity and prognostication.

### Prognostic Implication

Each decompensation event reduces median survival significantly: compensated cirrhosis ~ 12 yr → after first decompensation ~ 2 yr → second decompensation ~ 6–12 months. Number of decompensations + MELD-Na guide transplant listing.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.523; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD cirrhosis.

### Definition

SLE is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by production of antibodies to nuclear antigens, immune-complex deposition and inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, serous membranes and the central nervous system. Female:male ≈ 9:1, peak onset 15–40 yrs; commoner and more severe in South Asians and Afro-Caribbeans.

### Etiology / Risk factors

Genetic — HLA-DR2, DR3; complement deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4); IRF5, STAT4, TREX1

Hormonal — oestrogen excess, oral contraceptives may trigger flares

Environmental — UV light, EBV infection, silica, smoking

**Drug-induced lupus:** hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF, interferon (less renal/CNS, anti-histone +)

Pregnancy can precipitate flare; flares can affect pregnancy

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Defective clearance of apoptotic debris exposes nuclear antigens

Loss of self-tolerance → polyclonal B-cell activation → autoantibody production (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, anti-phospholipid)

Immune complexes deposit in kidneys, skin, vessels → complement activation → tissue injury

Type I interferon signature drives disease activity

Clinical features — multisystem

### Constitutional

Fatigue, fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy

### Mucocutaneous (80%)

Malar (butterfly) rash — spares nasolabial folds

Discoid rash — scarring, dyspigmentation; sun-exposed areas

Subacute cutaneous LE — annular/psoriasiform, photosensitive, anti-Ro/SSA

### Photosensitivity

Painless oral/nasal ulcers (commonly hard palate)

Alopecia (diffuse non-scarring or discoid scarring)

### Raynaud's phenomenon

### Musculoskeletal (90%)

Symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis — non-erosive (Jaccoud's reducible deformity)

Myalgia, true myositis rare

### Avascular necrosis (steroid-related)

Renal — lupus nephritis (LN, 40–60%, more in Indians)

### Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, AKI

ISN/RPS 2003 classes I–VI; III/IV (proliferative) most severe, V membranous

**Renal biopsy:** light microscopy + IF (full-house: IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q) + EM

### Neuropsychiatric (NPSLE)

Seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction

### Stroke (often APLA mediated)

Aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, mononeuritis multiplex

### Cardiopulmonary

Pleuritis, pericarditis (commonest serous involvement)

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (non-bacterial verrucous)

Pneumonitis, shrinking lung syndrome, alveolar haemorrhage, ILD

Premature accelerated atherosclerosis — major late mortality cause

### Haematological

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Coombs+), leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia (ITP-like)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (30–40% of SLE)

Arterial/venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, livedo reticularis

### Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin Ab, anti-β2 GP I

### GI / hepatic

Lupus enteritis (vasculitis), pancreatitis, autoimmune hepatitis overlap

### Diagnostic criteria

**EULAR/ACR 2019 (preferred):** Entry: ANA ≥1:80 (HEp-2 IIF). Then weighted criteria in 7 clinical (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) + 3 immunology domains (APLA, complement, SLE-specific antibodies). Classify SLE if ≥10 points with at least one clinical criterion.

SLICC 2012 / ACR 1997 — alternative criteria

### Investigations

Screening / disease confirmation

ANA by IIF on HEp-2 cells — sensitive (>95%), low specificity

Anti-dsDNA — specific; correlates with disease activity (esp. lupus nephritis)

Anti-Sm — specific (low sensitivity ~20% in Caucasians, ~30% in South Asians)

Anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB — subacute cutaneous, neonatal lupus, Sjögren overlap

### Anti-U1 RNP — MCTD overlap

Anti-histone — drug-induced lupus

### Anti-ribosomal P — NPSLE

Complement / immune complex

C3, C4, CH50 — low in active disease

### Disease activity markers

Urinalysis (proteinuria, RBC casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio

CBC (cytopenias), ESR (CRP may be normal — exception: serositis, infection)

### RFT, LFT, lipid profile

**APLA panel:** LA, ACL IgG/IgM, anti-β2 GP I

Renal biopsy if proteinuria >500 mg/day, active sediment, or rising creatinine

MRI brain for NPSLE; EEG if seizures; CSF if meningitis suspected

Echocardiography for serositis, Libman-Sacks; CXR/HRCT for lung

**SLE disease activity:** SLEDAI-2K, BILAG

### Management

Background therapy — for all SLE patients

Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/d (max 400 mg/d) — reduces flares, mortality, organ damage; baseline + annual ophthalmology after 5 years (retinal toxicity)

Photoprotection — sunscreen SPF ≥50 daily

### Vitamin D 1000–2000 IU/d + calcium

**Vaccines:** annual influenza, pneumococcal, HPV (before immunosuppression); avoid live vaccines if immunosuppressed

Aggressive CV risk-factor management — statin, BP <130/80, glycaemic control

**Pregnancy planning:** pre-conceptional counselling, switch teratogens, low-dose aspirin in APS

Mild disease (skin, joints, mild serositis)

### HCQ + NSAIDs PRN

Topical steroids, tacrolimus for skin

Low-dose prednisolone (≤7.5 mg/d) — minimise long-term use

Methotrexate 10–25 mg/wk for arthritis

Belimumab (anti-BLyS) for refractory mucocutaneous/joint

Moderate disease (haematological, mild renal, serositis)

Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/d, taper

**Steroid-sparing:** azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d, MMF 1–2 g/d, methotrexate

### Belimumab, anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR)

Severe disease — Lupus nephritis class III/IV

**Induction:** IV methylprednisolone pulse 500–1000 mg × 3 days + ONE of:

- Cyclophosphamide — Euro-Lupus 500 mg IV every 2 weeks × 6 doses (less toxic, equivalent efficacy in Caucasians/South Asians)

- Cyclophosphamide — NIH 0.5–1 g/m² monthly × 6 (preferred in severe/African ancestry)

- Mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/d × 6 months (preferred in pregnancy planning, GI tolerance)

**Maintenance:** MMF 1–2 g/d OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d for ≥3 years

**Add:** voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) or belimumab — recent evidence for triple therapy

ACEi/ARB for renoprotection; BP target <130/80

**Class V (membranous):** MMF + steroid; ACEi; consider tacrolimus or rituximab

Severe disease — CNS / haematological crises

Methylprednisolone pulse + cyclophosphamide or rituximab

Plasma exchange for catastrophic APS, TTP-like, alveolar haemorrhage

### Newer/targeted biologics

Belimumab — anti-BLyS; mucocutaneous, joint, mild renal

Anifrolumab — anti-type I interferon receptor; moderate–severe skin/joint disease

Voclosporin — class III/IV/V lupus nephritis (with MMF + steroid)

Rituximab — refractory severe disease (off-label in many countries)

### Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)

**Thrombosis:** warfarin INR 2–3 (arterial: 3–4 or warfarin + LDA); avoid DOACs (TRAPS trial showed inferiority for arterial events)

**Pregnancy + APS:** LMWH + low-dose aspirin throughout

**Catastrophic APS:** anticoag + steroid + plasma exchange + IVIG ± rituximab

### Pregnancy in SLE

Plan in clinical remission ≥6 months

Continue HCQ throughout; LDA from 12 weeks (pre-eclampsia prevention)

**Safe:** HCQ, AZA, calcineurin inhibitors, low-dose steroid

**Stop ≥3 months pre-conception:** MMF, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide

**Anti-Ro+:** neonatal lupus → congenital heart block; foetal echo at 16–28 weeks

Fig 4. SLE — classification + organ-directed management

### Complications

End-stage renal disease (lupus nephritis)

Accelerated atherosclerosis, MI, stroke (leading cause of late death)

### Thrombosis (APS)

Infection (immunosuppression) — bacterial, TB, HZ, opportunistic

Avascular necrosis, osteoporosis (steroid)

Premature ovarian failure (cyclophosphamide)

### Malignancy — NHL, cervical (HPV)

Foetal loss, neonatal lupus, prematurity

### Prognosis

5-yr survival has improved from ~50% (1950s) to >90% with modern treatment. Indian cohorts report 10-yr survival 70–80%. Major causes of early death (≤5 yr): active disease, infection, lupus nephritis. Late death: cardiovascular, ESRD. Adherence to HCQ, control of proteinuria, and CV risk modification are the strongest modifiable predictors.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 SLE + EULAR 2019 SLE management recommendations (update 2023) + ISN/RPS 2003 lupus nephritis classification + Indian Rheumatology Association statement on SLE in Indians (2020).

First-line drugs and hepatotoxicity

**Isoniazid (H):** Hepatotoxic – stop if ALT >5× ULN (or >3× with symptoms).

**Pyrazinamide (Z):** Most hepatotoxic of the first-line drugs; dose-dependent.

**Rifampicin (R):** Hepatotoxic; also causes orange discoloration of secretions.

Modified regimen for hepatitis / hepatic impairment (NTEP, WHO 2024)

If ALT >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN without – stop all hepatotoxic ATT.

Continue with non-hepatotoxic combination: ethambutol + streptomycin/levofloxacin (+ rifampicin if liver enzymes recovering; reintroduce H or Z sequentially).

**Severe hepatitis:** 2 SH(streptomycin + isoniazid)E + 6 HE OR 9–12 RE + levofloxacin / linezolid based regimen.

**Once LFTs return to normal:** gradually reintroduce R first, then H, last Z (if needed).

Other antimicrobials notable for hepatotoxicity in ATT context

Para-amino salicylic acid (PAS) – hepatotoxic.

Ethionamide / prothionamide – hepatotoxic.

### Definition

**Whipple's triad:** (1) low plasma glucose, (2) symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, (3) relief with raising the glucose. ADA biochemical threshold: <70 mg/dL = level 1; <54 mg/dL = level 2 (clinically significant); requiring third-party assistance = level 3 (severe).

### Symptoms by mechanism

Adrenergic / autonomic (early, glucose ~55–70 mg/dL):

Tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paraesthesiae, tachycardia, pallor.

### Cholinergic:

Sweating, hunger, paraesthesiae.

Neuroglycopenic (later, glucose <55 mg/dL):

Difficulty concentrating, confusion, blurred vision, slurred speech, drowsiness, behavioural change, dizziness, weakness, headache.

**Severe:** seizures, focal neurological deficit (mimics stroke), loss of consciousness, coma, death.

### Hypoglycaemia unawareness:

Loss of adrenergic warning symptoms with recurrent hypoglycaemia (common in long-standing T1DM, autonomic neuropathy, β-blocker use). Patient may go directly to neuroglycopenia and unconsciousness without warning.

Causes (in non-diabetic adults)

Drugs – insulin, sulfonylureas (commonest), alcohol, quinine, pentamidine, ACEi, β-blockers.

Insulinoma – fasting hypoglycaemia, high insulin + C-peptide, low β-hydroxybutyrate (Whipple's triad + supervised 72-h fast).

Critical illness – sepsis, hepatic/renal/cardiac failure.

Hormone deficiency – Addison's, hypopituitarism.

Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia (IGF-2).

Reactive (postprandial) – post-bariatric surgery, idiopathic.

Factitious – surreptitious insulin (low C-peptide) or sulfonylurea (urine screen).

### Management

**Conscious:** 15 g rapid carbohydrate (4 sugar lumps, 3 dextrose tablets, 150 mL fruit juice, 100 mL sweet cola). Recheck in 15 min. Repeat if needed (rule of 15). Follow with complex carbohydrate snack.

Unconscious – IM glucagon 1 mg, OR IV 50 mL of 25% dextrose, then 10% dextrose infusion. Watch for sulfonylurea recurrence (prolonged half-life).

Treat underlying cause; for insulinoma – surgical resection; diazoxide and octreotide as medical bridge.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 RA + ACR 2021 guideline for RA + EULAR 2022 RA management recommendations + Indian Rheumatology Association RA position paper.

### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

### Definition

Single, well-defined, rounded opacity ≤3 cm in diameter, surrounded by normal lung, without associated atelectasis or lymphadenopathy. Important because malignancy must be excluded.

### Differential diagnosis

### Malignant (40%):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (adenocarcinoma commonest in non-smokers).

Carcinoid tumour.

Solitary metastasis (colon, breast, renal, sarcoma, melanoma).

Lymphoma (rare).

### Benign (60%):

Infectious granuloma (tuberculoma – India's commonest), histoplasmoma, cryptococcoma, aspergilloma.

Hamartoma (popcorn calcification).

Lung abscess (early).

Pulmonary AVM.

Round atelectasis.

Rheumatoid nodule.

Wegener's granulomatous nodule.

Bronchogenic cyst, sequestration.

Pulmonary infarct.

### Features suggesting malignancy

Age >50, smoker, size >2 cm, spiculated margin, irregular shape, growth on serial imaging, lack of calcification (or eccentric calcification), upper lobe location, PET-avid (SUV >2.5).

### Features suggesting benignity

Age <40, never-smoker, well-defined smooth margin, central/diffuse/popcorn/laminated calcification, stability >2 years, small (<1 cm), fat density (hamartoma).

### Approach (Fleischner Society 2017)

Compare with previous imaging.

**<6 mm low-risk:** no follow-up; high-risk: optional CT at 12 months.

**6–8 mm:** CT at 6–12 m, then 18–24 m.

**>8 mm:** CT at 3 months and/or PET-CT, biopsy as needed.

Biopsy via CT-guided transthoracic, bronchoscopy (EBUS, navigational), or VATS.

### Spirometry – measurements

FVC – forced vital capacity.

FEV1 – forced expiratory volume in 1st second.

FEV1/FVC ratio (key diagnostic).

PEFR – peak expiratory flow rate.

FEF 25–75% – sensitive to small airway disease.

Flow-volume loop – shape diagnostic (e.g. scalloped in obstruction).

### Patterns

**Obstructive:** FEV1/FVC <0.70; FEV1 reduced; FVC normal or reduced. Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, CF. Reversibility (≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator) supports asthma.

**Restrictive:** FEV1/FVC normal or increased (>0.70); FEV1 and FVC reduced; TLC reduced. ILD, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular, obesity.

**Mixed:** both reduced. Sarcoidosis, advanced bronchiectasis.

### Full PFT (lung volumes, DLCO)

Body plethysmography or helium dilution – TLC, RV, FRC.

DLCO (diffusion capacity) – decreased in emphysema, ILD, anaemia, PE; increased in alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, asthma.

### Indications

Diagnose asthma, COPD, restrictive lung disease.

Monitor disease progression and treatment response.

Pre-operative assessment for thoracic or upper-abdominal surgery.

Occupational lung disease assessment.

Disability evaluation.

### Contraindications (relative)

Recent MI (<1 month), unstable angina, recent eye/abdominal/thoracic surgery, pneumothorax, haemoptysis, severe respiratory distress.

### Definition

Acute occlusion of pulmonary arterial circulation by embolus, most commonly thrombus dislodged from a deep venous thrombus, less commonly air, fat, amniotic fluid, or tumour. Together with DVT, constitutes venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Risk factors (Virchow's triad)

**Stasis:** Recent surgery (especially orthopaedic), prolonged immobilisation, long-haul travel, paralysis, plaster cast.

**Endothelial injury:** Trauma, central venous catheter, pelvic surgery, IBD, vasculitis.

**Hypercoagulability:** Pregnancy and puerperium, OCP/HRT, malignancy (Trousseau), inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin III, prothrombin G20210A), antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, dehydration, nephrotic syndrome.

### Clinical features

Sudden dyspnoea (commonest – >80%), pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis (classic triad in <20%).

**Massive PE:** syncope, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, sudden death.

Tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia, low-grade fever, gallop rhythm, loud P2, raised JVP; pleural rub if infarction.

Signs of DVT in lower limbs – unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness.

### Investigations

Pulse oximetry, ABG (Type 1 RF, A-a gradient widened, respiratory alkalosis).

ECG – sinus tachycardia commonest; S1Q3T3 classical but uncommon; T wave inversion V1–V4; RBBB.

CXR – often normal; Hampton's hump (peripheral wedge), Westermark's sign (oligaemia), Fleischner sign (enlarged PA).

D-dimer – sensitive (>500 ng/mL), not specific; used to exclude PE in low-Wells probability.

CT pulmonary angiogram – investigation of choice.

V/Q scan – if CTPA contraindicated (renal failure, pregnancy).

Echocardiography – RV dilatation/dysfunction (McConnell's sign), pulmonary hypertension; risk-stratifies PE.

Lower-limb compression USS for DVT.

Troponin, BNP – risk stratification.

Thrombophilia screen if unprovoked or recurrent.

### Management

**Risk-stratify:** PESI / sPESI score; haemodynamic stability; RV dysfunction; troponin elevation.

High-risk (massive PE, hypotensive): IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 h, followed by heparin. Surgical or catheter-directed embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated.

Intermediate-risk (sub-massive, RV dysfunction): anticoagulation with LMWH/UFH; consider thrombolysis if deterioration.

**Low-risk:** anticoagulation – LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD), then DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or warfarin INR 2–3. DOACs are first-line (except active cancer – LMWH preferred, or pregnancy – LMWH only).

**Duration:** provoked 3 months; unprovoked ≥6 months or indefinite if low bleeding risk; cancer-associated for as long as cancer active.

IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE on anticoagulation.

**Supportive:** O₂, IV fluids, vasopressors (noradrenaline) if hypotensive.

**Prevention:** VTE risk-assess all medical inpatients; mechanical (compression stockings, IPC) + pharmacological (LMWH 40 mg OD, fondaparinux) prophylaxis.

Fig 7. Acute pulmonary embolism – diagnostic and management algorithm.

(See Q24 above for the comprehensive answer on acute PE. The essence summarised here for this SN.)

### Risk factors

Recent surgery, immobilisation, malignancy, OCP/HRT, pregnancy and puerperium, prior VTE, inherited thrombophilias, antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, smoking, indwelling catheter, long-haul travel, IBD, nephrotic syndrome.

### Investigations

Wells score / Geneva score to estimate probability.

D-dimer for low-probability (rule-out).

CT pulmonary angiogram (first-line).

V/Q scan – pregnancy, renal failure.

Echocardiogram – RV strain, risk-stratify.

Compression USS legs, ECG, troponin, BNP.

### Management

Anticoagulation – LMWH then DOAC or warfarin INR 2-3.

Thrombolysis (alteplase) – haemodynamically unstable.

Surgical / catheter embolectomy – thrombolysis contraindicated.

IVC filter – anticoagulation contraindicated.

**Duration:** 3 months provoked; ≥6 months unprovoked; indefinite if cancer or recurrent.

### Overview

**Renal function tests assess:** (1) GFR, (2) tubular function, (3) glomerular permeability (proteinuria), (4) urinary sediment, (5) renal anatomy. Used for screening, diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of kidney disease.

### 1. Assessment of GFR

Direct (Exogenous Markers — gold standard, research)

Inulin clearance — gold standard; cumbersome.

Iohexol, iothalamate, EDTA clearance — used clinically when accurate GFR needed (transplant donor, chemotherapy dosing).

### Endogenous Markers

**Serum Creatinine (Cr):** Serum Creatinine (Cr): Normal 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (M), 0.6–1.1 (F). Easy, cheap. Limitations:

Affected by muscle mass (low in elderly, women, vegetarians, amputees, sarcopenia).

Insensitive in early CKD ('creatinine-blind range' — GFR can drop to 50% before Cr rises).

Affected by drugs blocking tubular secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine).

Diet — cooked meat ↑ Cr.

**Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas:** Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas: Calculated from serum Cr + age + sex (± race, removed 2021).

CKD-EPI 2021 (PREFERRED — race-free) — most accurate across all ranges.

MDRD — older; less accurate at normal/high GFR.

Cockcroft-Gault — older; uses weight; used for drug dosing.

Schwartz (children) — eGFR = k × height/Cr.

**Creatinine Clearance (24-h):** Creatinine Clearance (24-h): Cr clearance = (Urine Cr × Urine volume) / Plasma Cr. Limitations: incomplete urine collection, overestimates GFR (tubular secretion of Cr 10–15%, more with low GFR). Less used now than eGFR. Adequate collection: Cr × 1.5 (males) / 1.2 (females) g/kg/d.

**Cystatin C:** Cystatin C: Constant cellular production; freely filtered; not reabsorbed; not secreted. Independent of muscle mass. Useful in elderly, sarcopenic, paediatric. CKD-EPI Cr-cystatin C combined — most accurate. Expensive.

**Blood urea / BUN:** Blood urea / BUN: Normal 7–25 mg/dL. Affected by protein intake, GI bleeding (↑), liver disease (↓), hydration. Urea:Cr ratio > 100 → pre-renal / GI bleed.

### 2. Glomerular Permeability — Proteinuria

### Quantification

Dipstick — semi-quantitative; detects albumin > 30 mg/dL. Negative in non-albumin proteinuria (myeloma — light chain).

24-h urine protein — gold standard. Normal < 150 mg/d.

**Spot UACR (urine albumin:** creatinine ratio):

< 30 mg/g — normal

30–300 mg/g — moderately increased (microalbuminuria)

> 300 mg/g — severely increased (macroalbuminuria)

**Spot UPCR (urine protein:** creatinine ratio) — total proteinuria. PCR > 3500 mg/g = nephrotic range.

Urinary protein electrophoresis (UPEP) + immunofixation — myeloma (Bence-Jones).

Sulphosalicylic acid (SSA) test — detects total protein (incl. light chains; dipstick misses).

### Selectivity

**Selective proteinuria:** predominantly albumin (smaller MW) — MCD.

**Non-selective:** albumin + IgG + larger proteins — advanced glomerular disease.

Selectivity index = clearance of IgG / clearance of transferrin; < 0.2 = highly selective.

### 3. Tubular Function Tests

### Concentration / Dilution

Urine osmolality (random) — normal 50–1200 mOsm/kg.

Urine specific gravity — 1.005–1.030.

Water deprivation test — for diabetes insipidus (Uosm < 300 after deprivation).

ADH (DDAVP) challenge — central vs nephrogenic DI.

### Acidification

Urine pH (random) — 5–6.5 normal.

Ammonium chloride loading test — RTA diagnosis (urine pH should fall < 5.5 if normal).

Serum bicarbonate, anion gap, urinary anion gap.

### Tubular Reabsorption / Secretion

Fractional excretion of Na (FENa) — pre-renal vs ATN.

Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) — pre-renal if < 35% (use if on diuretics).

Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO₄) — TmP/GFR (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / GFR) — Fanconi syndrome (< 80%).

Glucosuria with normal serum glucose — proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi).

Aminoaciduria — Fanconi syndrome.

**Tubular markers:** NGAL, KIM-1, IL-18 (research; early AKI biomarkers).

### 4. Urinary Sediment Examination

### 5. Imaging

**Ultrasound (USG) — first-line:** size (10–14 cm normal; < 9 cm = chronic), echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, masses, Doppler (renal artery flow, RVT).

KUB X-ray — radio-opaque stones (calcium, struvite). Cystine = semi-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent.

CT (CECT, KUB) — masses, complex cysts, stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis).

MRI / MRA — RAS, masses (avoid gadolinium if eGFR < 30 — NSF risk).

DTPA scan — split function (each kidney's contribution).

DMSA scan — cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy).

MAG-3 scan — obstruction.

Renal biopsy — definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.

### 6. Other / Specialised

Complement (C3, C4) — see Q3.

Autoantibodies — ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM.

Anti-PLA2R — membranous.

SPEP / UPEP / IFE — myeloma.

Cryoglobulins.

### Approach to Interpretation

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.353; KDIGO CKD 2012; CKD-EPI 2021 race-free.

### Definition

Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) is episodic, reversible digital vasospasm precipitated by cold or emotional stress, classically producing the triphasic colour change of pallor → cyanosis → rubor in the fingers (and less often toes, ears, nose, nipples). Prevalence 3–5%; female:male ≈ 4:1.

### Classification

### Etiology / Causes of secondary RP

**Connective tissue:** systemic sclerosis (>95% have RP), SLE, MCTD, Sjögren's, dermatomyositis, RA

**Drugs:** β-blockers, ergotamine, methylphenidate, cocaine, amphetamines, cisplatin, bleomycin, interferon, sympathomimetic decongestants

**Occupational:** vibration white finger (jackhammer, chainsaw), cold exposure

**Haematological:** cryoglobulinaemia, cold agglutinin disease, polycythaemia, thrombocytosis, paraproteinaemia

**Vascular:** atherosclerosis, thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger), thoracic outlet syndrome, embolism

**Endocrine:** hypothyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid

**Infections:** hepatitis B/C, parvovirus

Neoplasia (paraneoplastic — rare)

### Pathophysiology

Vasoconstriction phase — exaggerated α2-adrenergic response → arteriolar/capillary spasm → pallor

Hypoxia and stasis → deoxygenated blood → cyanosis

Reflex vasodilation on rewarming → reactive hyperaemia → rubor with paraesthesia/burning

**In secondary RP:** structural intimal hyperplasia, endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO, ↑ endothelin-1), platelet activation, oxidative stress

### Clinical features

Triphasic colour change — white → blue → red (not all three required for diagnosis)

Sharply demarcated, symmetric in primary, asymmetric in secondary

Episodes last minutes to hours; provoked by cold (handling cold objects, air-conditioning), emotional stress

Numbness, paraesthesia, burning pain on rewarming

Thumb usually spared in primary; thumb involvement suggests secondary

Digital pitting scars, ulcers, gangrene — red flags for secondary disease (systemic sclerosis especially)

**Look for features of CTD:** sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, calcinosis, dry mouth/eyes, malar rash, arthralgia

Diagnostic criteria — primary Raynaud (Allen-Brown / LeRoy and Medsger)

### Symmetric episodic attacks

Absence of digital ulcer / gangrene / pitting

No clinical features of CTD

### Normal nailfold capillaries

### Negative ANA

### Normal ESR

### Investigations

Bedside — nailfold capillaroscopy

Performed with stereomicroscope, dermatoscope, or videocapillaroscope; cuticle wetted with immersion oil

### Normal in primary RP

**Early scleroderma pattern:** few enlarged loops, no loss; active: many giant capillaries, haemorrhages; late: loss with avascular areas, neoangiogenesis

Strong predictor of CTD development

### Serology

ANA + ENA panel (anti-centromere → limited SSc; anti-Scl-70 → diffuse SSc; anti-RNA polymerase III → renal crisis risk)

### RF, anti-CCP, anti-dsDNA

Complement, cryoglobulin (if symptoms suggest), cold agglutinin

### Other

### CBC, ESR, CRP

### TFT

### Hepatitis B and C serology

### Urinalysis, RFT

Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension if SSc

Doppler / angiography for atypical, asymmetric cases (Buerger, atherosclerosis)

### Management

- Non-pharmacological (most patients with mild primary RP)

Keep warm — gloves, mittens (better than gloves), thermal underwear, hat (significant heat loss from head), warm shoes

### Carry hand-warmers

Avoid sudden temperature change, cold drinks, supermarket freezer aisles

Smoking cessation — strongly advised

Avoid trigger drugs (β-blockers — substitute non-DHP CCB or ACEi)

### Stress management

### Treat underlying disease (CTD)

- Pharmacological — for moderate–severe symptoms

Calcium channel blockers (first line): Nifedipine SR 10–30 mg BD (max 60–90 mg/d) — most evidence. Amlodipine 5–10 mg OD if better tolerated. AE: headache, flushing, ankle oedema, hypotension.

**PDE-5 inhibitors:** Sildenafil 20–50 mg TDS, tadalafil 10–20 mg alternate-day — particularly useful for SSc-associated RP, healing digital ulcers.

**ARBs:** Losartan 50 mg OD

**SSRIs:** Fluoxetine 20 mg/d — modest benefit, avoid β-blocker withdrawal vasospasm

**Topical nitrates:** GTN 2% ointment to digits — useful for severe acute episodes

**Prostacyclin analogues:** Iloprost 0.5–2 ng/kg/min IV × 6 h/day × 5 days — for severe RP, digital ulcers, gangrene threatening (SSc)

**Endothelin antagonists:** Bosentan 62.5–125 mg BD — for recurrent digital ulcers in SSc (prevention; not licensed for healing)

Selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor: Pentoxifylline 400 mg TDS — improves microcirculation

- Surgical / interventional — severe, refractory

Botulinum toxin A injection — palmar/digital sympathetic blockade

Digital sympathectomy — for critical digital ischaemia

Cervical/thoracic sympathectomy (last resort)

Amputation only if irreversible gangrene

### Complications

Digital pits, ulcers, gangrene, autoamputation (secondary RP)

Disability — impaired use of hands for ADLs

Evolution to CTD over months to years (one-third of seemingly primary cases ultimately develop SSc, SLE, etc.)

### Prognosis

Primary Raynaud's has excellent prognosis with conservative measures; symptoms often diminish with age or pregnancy. Secondary Raynaud's prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disease — SSc with frequent ulcers carries significant morbidity. All patients with new RP, especially adult-onset, severe, or asymmetric, need follow-up with serology and capillaroscopy to detect evolving CTD.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 Raynaud's section + EULAR/EUSTAR 2017 SSc treatment recommendations + Wigley 2016 NEJM Raynaud review.
