### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

Approach to a bleeding patient

**Decide:** vascular / platelet / coagulation / mixed.

### Pattern of bleeding:

– Mucocutaneous (petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia) → platelet or vascular.

– Deep (haemarthrosis, muscle haematoma, delayed post-op) → coagulation factor.

– Family history → inherited (haemophilia, vWD).

Tier 1 – screening tests

CBC + peripheral smear – platelet count, morphology, schistocytes.

Bleeding time (BT) – normal 2–7 min; prolonged in thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, vWD.

Prothrombin time (PT) – extrinsic + common pathway (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen). Reported as INR.

Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) – intrinsic + common pathway (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogen).

Thrombin time (TT) – fibrinogen to fibrin step; prolonged in heparin, fibrinogen deficiency, DIC.

Fibrinogen – Clauss method; low in DIC, liver disease.

D-dimer / FDP – elevated in DIC, VTE, sepsis, malignancy.

### Interpretation

Isolated ↑PT – factor VII deficiency, mild warfarin/vitamin K deficiency, mild liver disease.

Isolated ↑aPTT – haemophilia A, B; factor XI deficiency; lupus anticoagulant; heparin; some vWD.

Both ↑PT and ↑aPTT – common pathway deficiency (X, V, II, fibrinogen), severe liver disease, DIC, overdose of warfarin/heparin.

Both normal + bleeding – vWD, factor XIII, mild haemophilia, platelet dysfunction.

Thrombocytopenia – review smear; consider ITP, TTP, DIC, drug, HIT, hypersplenism.

Tier 2 – specific tests

**Mixing studies (50:** 50 with normal plasma) – correction = factor deficiency; no correction = inhibitor.

Factor assays (VIII, IX, XI, XII, II, V, VII, X) – quantitative.

von Willebrand panel – vWF antigen, vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor or GPIb binding), factor VIII; vWF multimer analysis for sub-typing.

Platelet aggregation studies (ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid, ristocetin).

PFA-100 (platelet function under shear).

Bethesda assay – quantify inhibitor titre.

Antiphospholipid panel – lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2 GPI.

Thromboelastography (TEG / ROTEM) – global functional test (theatre, ICU).

ADAMTS-13 – TTP.

Genetic testing for inherited bleeding disorders.

### Thrombophilia screen

Factor V Leiden (APC resistance), prothrombin G20210A.

Protein C, protein S, antithrombin levels.

Antiphospholipid antibodies.

Homocysteine, JAK2 V617F (myeloproliferative).

Defer measurement of natural anticoagulants and thrombophilia testing until 6 weeks after the acute thrombotic event and off anticoagulation.

### Definition

An acquired syndrome of widespread intravascular activation of coagulation, resulting in simultaneous microvascular thrombosis (causing multi-organ dysfunction) and consumption of platelets + clotting factors leading to bleeding. ALWAYS secondary to a triggering condition.

### Etiology

Sepsis – Gram-negative > Gram-positive, fungal (commonest cause in ICU).

Trauma – multiple injuries, head injury, burns, fat embolism.

Obstetric – abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus, septic abortion, HELLP, severe pre-eclampsia.

Malignancy – acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL/M3), mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma (pancreas, prostate, lung).

Vascular – giant haemangioma (Kasabach-Merritt), aortic aneurysm dissection.

Severe hepatic failure.

Severe transfusion reaction.

Snake envenoming – Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper.

Pancreatitis.

Heat stroke.

### Pathophysiology

Trigger (cytokines, tissue factor, endothelial injury) → widespread activation of coagulation cascade → fibrin deposition in microcirculation → consumption of platelets, fibrinogen, factors → impaired fibrinolysis (PAI-1 high in sepsis) → bleeding + microvascular thrombosis → organ failure.

### Clinical features

Bleeding manifestations (most common)

Oozing from venepuncture sites, IV lines, surgical wounds.

Petechiae, ecchymosis, purpura, mucosal bleeding.

GI bleed, haematuria, intracranial haemorrhage.

Post-partum haemorrhage.

### Thrombotic manifestations

Acral cyanosis, purpura fulminans, digital gangrene.

ARDS, AKI (renal cortical necrosis).

Hepatic dysfunction, adrenal infarction (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).

Cerebral microthrombi → altered sensorium.

Features of underlying cause + multi-organ failure.

### Investigations

CBC + smear – thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), schistocytes (~10–50%), anaemia.

**Coagulation:** PT prolonged, aPTT prolonged.

Fibrinogen low (<150 mg/dL; serial fall important).

D-dimer / FDP – markedly elevated.

Thrombin time prolonged.

Antithrombin and protein C levels reduced.

Specific to trigger – blood culture, LFT, renal function, ABG, lactate, β-hCG, peripheral smear for APL/Auer rods.

ISTH overt-DIC scoring (≥5 = overt)

**Platelet count:** >100 = 0, 50–100 = 1, <50 = 2.

**Elevated FDP/D-dimer:** no rise = 0, moderate = 2, strong = 3.

**Prolonged PT:** <3 s = 0, 3–6 s = 1, >6 s = 2.

**Fibrinogen:** ≥1 g/L = 0, <1 g/L = 1.

**Total score ≥5:** overt DIC; repeat daily.

### Management

Cardinal rule – treat the underlying cause

Antibiotics + source control for sepsis.

Delivery / evacuate uterus in obstetric DIC.

ATRA + chemotherapy for APL.

ASV for snake bite.

Tumour resection / chemotherapy.

Supportive – guided by clinical picture, not by labs alone

Active bleeding or pre-procedure:

– Platelet transfusion (target >50 if bleeding, >20 if not)

– FFP 10–15 mL/kg (multiple factor replacement)

– Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (target >1.5–2)

– PRBC to maintain Hb

### Predominantly thrombotic phenotype:

– LMW heparin in selected (e.g. APL, purpura fulminans, large vessel thrombosis) — controversial

Anti-fibrinolytics (tranexamic acid) – avoid as routine; consider only in markedly hyperfibrinolytic state (APL, amniotic embolism), and never alone.

Activated protein C – withdrawn (no benefit).

Recombinant thrombomodulin – under evaluation.

Fig 10. DIC — ISTH score and management algorithm.

### Prognosis

Mortality 40–80%, driven mainly by the underlying cause and organ failure. Early recognition + aggressive treatment of the trigger remains the key to survival.

### Definition

Platelet count <150 × 10⁹/L. Mild: 100–150; moderate: 50–100; severe: <50 (bleeding risk); critical: <20 (spontaneous bleeding risk).

### Mechanistic classification

### 1. Decreased production

**Bone marrow failure:** aplastic anaemia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, metastasis, myelofibrosis).

Megaloblastic anaemia – ineffective megakaryopoiesis.

Viral – HIV, HCV, dengue, EBV, parvovirus.

Drugs – chemotherapy, alcohol, valproate, co-trimoxazole, linezolid, thiazides, methotrexate.

Radiation.

Congenital – Fanconi anaemia, Wiskott-Aldrich, thrombocytopenia with absent radii, May-Hegglin.

### 2. Increased destruction

### Immune (ITP):

– Primary ITP (idiopathic / autoimmune anti-GP IIb/IIIa antibodies)

– Secondary ITP – SLE, HIV, HCV, CLL, lymphoma, drugs (heparin, quinine, sulpha, vancomycin, rifampicin)

### – Post-vaccination, post-viral

**Microangiopathic (MAHA):** TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, preeclampsia.

**Mechanical:** prosthetic valves, ECMO, IABP.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT-II): 4Ts score.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.

### 3. Sequestration

Hypersplenism (cirrhosis, portal hypertension, lymphoma, kala-azar, Gaucher).

### 4. Dilutional

Massive transfusion, large volume fluid resuscitation.

### 5. Pseudo-thrombocytopenia

EDTA-induced platelet clumping; redraw in citrate.

### Clinical features

Mucocutaneous bleeding – petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeds, menorrhagia, haematuria.

GI bleed, intracranial haemorrhage (most feared).

Wet purpura (mucosal bullae) – high bleeding risk.

Splenomegaly – hypersplenism, lymphoma, kala-azar; absent in ITP and BM failure.

Features of underlying cause.

### Investigations

CBC – platelet count, MPV (high in ITP / destruction; low in failure).

Peripheral smear – platelet clumps (pseudo), schistocytes (MAHA), blasts (leukaemia), giant platelets, tear drops, atypical lymphocytes (viral).

**Coagulation:** PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer (DIC).

Reticulocyte count, retic Hb.

LFT, RFT.

HIV, HCV, HBV; ANA; dengue NS1/IgM in endemic.

DAT, blood group, cross-match (in case BT needed).

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP <10%.

Anti-PF4 antibody, 4Ts score, serotonin release – HIT.

Bone marrow biopsy – not routine for ITP but mandatory if elderly, pancytopenia, unusual features, before splenectomy.

USG abdomen – splenomegaly.

### Management (cause-specific)

Primary ITP (commonest haematological clinical scenario)

Treatment indicated when platelets <30 × 10⁹/L OR bleeding.

### First line:

– Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day × 2–4 weeks then taper

– Dexamethasone 40 mg OD × 4 days (high-dose pulse)

– IVIG 1 g/kg/day × 2 days – rapid rise; for severe bleeding, pregnancy, pre-op

– Anti-D 50–75 µg/kg IV (Rh+ve only)

### Second line:

– Rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly × 4

– Thrombopoietin receptor agonists: eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag

– Splenectomy – durable 60–70% response; vaccinations ≥2 weeks pre-op

– Fostamatinib (SYK inhibitor) — newer

Emergency – platelet count <10 + bleeding: IVIG + IV methylprednisolone + platelet transfusion (preferably after IVIG to slow destruction).

### TTP

Urgent plasma exchange daily with FFP replacement.

Steroids high-dose.

Rituximab.

Caplacizumab (anti-vWF).

Avoid platelet transfusion (worsens thrombosis).

### HIT

Stop ALL heparin (including flushes, line locks); remove heparin-coated catheters.

**Non-heparin anticoagulant:** argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOAC.

Do NOT give platelets unless major bleed.

**Confirmation:** ELISA + serotonin release assay.

DIC – treat cause + replace blood products if bleeding (see Q28).

Drug-induced – stop offending drug; usually resolves in days.

Fig 11. Thrombocytopenia — diagnostic algorithm.

Transfusion thresholds (general guide)

**<10 × 10⁹/L:** prophylactic transfusion for all (intracranial haemorrhage risk).

**<20:** prophylactic if sepsis, coagulopathy.

**<50:** prior to most procedures, in bleeding patient.

**<100:** neurosurgery, ophthalmic surgery.

Avoid in TTP, HIT (worsens thrombosis); ITP (only with severe bleed).

GENERAL MEDICINE|78.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Classification

Acute (within 24 h) vs Delayed (after 24 h); Immune vs Non-immune.

ACUTE reactions (within 24 hours)

- Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) – commonest

**Cause:** recipient antibodies vs donor leukocytes; cytokines in stored blood.

**Features:** fever >1°C rise, chills, no haemolysis.

**Mx:** stop transfusion, exclude AHTR & sepsis; paracetamol; leuko-reduced components for future.

- Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) – most feared

**Cause:** ABO incompatibility (clerical error); IgM-mediated, complement-activating, intravascular haemolysis.

**Features:** fever, chills, loin/back pain, dyspnoea, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, DIC, AKI.

**Mx:** STOP TRANSFUSION immediately, IV NS, IV fluids to maintain urine output >100 mL/h, mannitol/frusemide, manage DIC, treat shock; send sample for DAT, compatibility recheck; report to blood bank.

- Allergic / urticarial reaction

**Cause:** recipient IgE vs donor plasma proteins.

**Features:** urticaria, pruritus only; no fever.

**Mx:** stop, antihistamines; can resume slowly if symptoms settle. Washed components for future.

### 4. Anaphylactic reaction

**Cause:** IgA-deficient recipient with anti-IgA; or other severe hypersensitivity.

**Features:** bronchospasm, hypotension, angioedema, shock in first minutes.

**Mx:** STOP, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg, IV fluids, O₂, steroids, antihistamine; IgA-deficient (washed) components in future; check IgA level.

### 5. TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury)

**Cause:** donor anti-leukocyte / HLA / HNA antibodies activate recipient neutrophils → pulmonary capillary leak.

**Features:** acute hypoxaemia + bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion; no LV failure.

**Mx:** stop transfusion, supportive ventilation (lung-protective), supplemental O₂; usually resolves in 48–96 h. Future: male-only plasma (Indian NACO).

### 6. TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload)

**Cause:** volume overload (elderly, cardiac/renal disease, rapid infusion).

**Features:** dyspnoea, raised JVP, basal crackles, hypertension, raised BNP, pulmonary oedema within 6 h.

**Mx:** stop or slow transfusion, sit up, O₂, IV frusemide. Prevent: slow rate (1 mL/kg/h), diuretic between units.

- Bacterial contamination / septic transfusion

**Cause:** contaminated unit (platelets > RBC); Gram +ve and −ve organisms.

**Features:** rigors, high fever, hypotension, shock during/just after transfusion.

**Mx:** STOP, blood cultures (from patient AND unit), broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, supportive.

- Citrate toxicity / hypocalcaemia (massive transfusion)

**Cause:** citrate anticoagulant binds Ca²⁺ when liver metabolism is overwhelmed.

**Features:** paraesthesiae, tetany, arrhythmia, prolonged QT.

**Mx:** IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% slow.

### 9. Hypothermia

**Cause:** rapid infusion of cold blood.

**Mx:** blood warmer.

- Hyperkalaemia (especially stored blood, neonates, AKI)

**Cause:** efflux of K⁺ from stored RBCs.

**Mx:** standard hyperkalaemia management; fresh blood for high-risk groups.

DELAYED reactions (after 24 hours)

- Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)

**Cause:** anamnestic response to minor RBC antigens (Kidd, Duffy, Rh, Kell) in previously sensitised recipient.

**Features:** drop in Hb 3–14 days later, jaundice, positive DAT, occasional haemoglobinuria.

**Mx:** usually supportive; identify antibody for future compatible blood.

- Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD)

**Cause:** viable donor T-lymphocytes engraft in immunosuppressed recipient; rarely in immunocompetent with shared HLA haplotype.

**Features:** 1–4 weeks – fever, skin rash, diarrhoea, hepatitis, pancytopenia; mortality >90%.

**Prevention:** gamma irradiation of cellular components for high-risk groups (HSCT, intrauterine, neonatal exchange, haematological malignancy, granulocyte transfusion).

### 3. Post-transfusion purpura (PTP)

**Cause:** anti-HPA-1a antibody in HPA-1a-negative woman (usually multiparous).

**Features:** severe thrombocytopenia 5–10 days post-transfusion.

**Mx:** IVIG 1 g/kg × 2 days; plasma exchange in severe; HPA-1a-negative units in future.

### 4. Iron overload

**Cause:** chronic transfusion (≥20 units cumulative — thalassaemia, MDS, sickle cell).

**Features:** cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, endocrinopathy (DM, hypogonadism), skin hyperpigmentation.

**Mx:** iron chelation – deferoxamine SC infusion, deferiprone PO, deferasirox PO; target ferritin <1000 µg/L.

### 5. Alloimmunisation

**Cause:** development of antibody against minor RBC antigens.

**Features:** difficulty in finding compatible blood subsequently.

**Prevention:** phenotype-matched blood in chronic transfusion patients.

### 6. Transfusion-transmitted infections (TTI)

**Mandatory NACO screening tests:** HIV (Ag-Ab combo), Hepatitis B (HBsAg), Hepatitis C (anti-HCV), Syphilis (VDRL/RPR), Malaria (rapid Ag); NAT testing for HIV, HBV, HCV in many centres.

Residual risk despite screening: HIV ≈ 1:2 million, HBV ≈ 1:500,000, HCV ≈ 1:1 million (Indian NACO 2023).

**Other transmitted:** CMV (use leuko-reduced for immunocompromised), HTLV, parvovirus, EBV, dengue, chikungunya, malaria, prion (vCJD).

Fig 6. Blood component therapy — components, indications, storage.

### Principle

From a single whole blood unit (450 mL), multiple components can be separated by differential centrifugation, permitting targeted replacement and conservation of a scarce resource. NACO mandates that no whole blood be transfused if components are available.

### Components

### 1. Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC)

**Volume:** ~280 mL with Hct 60–80%.

**Storage:** 4 °C × 35 days (CPDA) / 42 days (SAGM).

**Indication:** symptomatic anaemia, Hb <7 g/dL (stable) or <8 g/dL (cardiac); each unit raises Hb by ~1 g/dL.

**Cross-match:** ABO + Rh compatible, ideally type-specific.

### 2. Platelet concentrate

**Random donor platelet (RDP):** 50–70 mL, 5.5 × 10¹⁰ platelets/unit.

Single donor platelet (SDP / apheresis): 200–300 mL, 3 × 10¹¹ platelets (=6 RDP units).

**Storage:** 20–24 °C with continuous agitation × 5 days.

**Indication:** prophylactic if count <10 × 10⁹/L (or <20 with sepsis/coagulopathy); therapeutic if bleeding; pre-procedure if <50 (or <100 for neurosurgery / ophthalmic); platelet dysfunction (uraemia, drugs).

Each RDP unit raises count by ~5,000–10,000/µL; SDP by 30,000–50,000/µL.

**Contraindications/caution:** TTP, HIT (worsens thrombosis), ITP (transient effect only).

### 3. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)

**Volume:** 200–250 mL; contains all coagulation factors at near-physiological levels.

**Storage:** −30 °C × 1 year; thawed FFP usable 24 h at 1–6 °C.

**Indication:** DIC with bleeding, massive transfusion (>1 blood volume), warfarin reversal with life-threatening bleed (if PCC unavailable), multiple coagulation factor deficiency, TTP/HUS (plasma exchange), liver disease with bleeding.

**Dose:** 10–15 mL/kg (3–4 units in adult).

**Not for:** volume expansion, nutritional support, hypoalbuminaemia.

### 4. Cryoprecipitate

**Volume:** 10–20 mL; rich in fibrinogen (>150 mg), FVIII (>80 IU), vWF, FXIII, fibronectin.

**Storage:** −30 °C × 1 year; thawed usable 6 h.

**Indication:** hypofibrinogenaemia (DIC, massive transfusion, obstetric haemorrhage) – target >1.5 g/L; rare F XIII deficiency; vWD or haemophilia A only if no factor concentrates.

**Dose:** 1 unit per 10 kg; raises fibrinogen by 50 mg/dL.

- Granulocyte concentrate (rarely used)

**Indication:** severe neutropenia (ANC <500) with documented infection failing antibiotics.

Must be irradiated + CMV-safe.

### 6. Specialised preparations

**Leuko-reduced:** prevents FNHTR, alloimmunisation, CMV transmission.

**Irradiated:** prevents TA-GVHD.

**Washed RBC/platelets:** removes plasma — for IgA deficiency, recurrent anaphylactic / severe allergic reactions.

**CMV-negative:** for seronegative pregnant women, premature neonates, BMT recipients.

### Compatibility summary

**PRBC:** ABO + Rh compatible; group O Rh-negative is 'universal donor' in emergency.

**Plasma (FFP / cryo):** ABO compatible (no Rh needed); group AB plasma is 'universal donor'.

**Platelets:** preferably ABO + Rh matched (Rh-negative for Rh-negative females of childbearing age).

### Massive transfusion protocol (MTP)

Defined as ≥10 units PRBC in 24 h, or ≥4 units in 1 h.

**1:** 1:1 ratio – PRBC : FFP : platelets (e.g. 6:6:6).

Tranexamic acid 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 h (within 3 h of trauma).

**Monitor:** Hb, platelets, INR, fibrinogen, calcium, potassium, temperature, ABG, lactate.

Maintain warm patient + warmed blood; calcium replacement if needed.

### Procedure

Spread one drop of fresh anticoagulated (EDTA) or fingerprick blood on a glass slide.

Air-dry, fix in methanol, stain with Leishman's, Wright's or Giemsa stain.

Examine in 'thinly spread' area where RBCs just don't overlap.

### Systematic examination

### RBC

**Size:** normocytic / microcytic / macrocytic.

**Colour:** normochromic / hypochromic.

**Shape:** anisocytosis (variable size), poikilocytosis (variable shape).

**Inclusions:** Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), basophilic stippling (lead, thalassaemia), Pappenheimer bodies, Cabot rings, Heinz bodies (oxidant injury, supravital stain).

### Specific RBC forms:

### – Spherocytes – HS, AIHA, burns

– Schistocytes – MAHA (TTP/HUS/DIC), prosthetic valve

– Target cells – thalassaemia, liver disease, HbC/E, post-splenectomy

– Sickle cells – HbSS

– Tear-drop cells – myelofibrosis, marrow infiltration

– Bite cells / blister cells – G6PD deficiency, oxidant

– Acanthocytes / spur cells – liver disease, abetalipoproteinaemia

– Echinocytes / burr cells – uraemia

– Elliptocytes – hereditary elliptocytosis

– Stomatocytes – hereditary stomatocytosis, alcohol

– Rouleaux – inflammation, MM, macroglobulinaemia

– Nucleated RBCs – severe haemolysis, marrow infiltration, thalassaemia major, severe hypoxia

Polychromasia – young RBCs (= reticulocyte response).

### WBC

Differential count.

**Left shift:** bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes (infection, CML, leukemoid).

Hyper-segmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) – B12/folate deficiency.

Toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, vacuoles – sepsis.

Blasts – acute leukaemia.

Smudge cells – CLL.

Atypical lymphocytes – EBV, CMV, viral infections.

Auer rods – AML.

### Platelets

Count estimate – 1 per oil-immersion field ≈ 15,000/µL (roughly).

Giant platelets – ITP, MPN.

Platelet clumping (EDTA-induced) – pseudo-thrombocytopenia.

### Parasites

Malaria – ring forms (P. falciparum), Schüffner's dots (P. vivax), banana gametocytes.

Microfilariae – W. bancrofti, Brugia (in night sample).

Trypanosomes.

Babesia – Maltese cross.

### Uses

Anaemia classification.

Leukaemia / lymphoma screen.

MAHA / TTP / DIC – schistocytes.

Infection clues – toxic granulation, atypical lymphocytes, parasites.

Platelet quantity & quality.

Confirm auto-analyser flags.

Combined summary of indications (Q10) + hazards (Q9). Cross-reference those answers for full details.

### Indications by component

Whole blood (rarely used)

Massive acute haemorrhage where components are unavailable.

Exchange transfusion in neonates.

### Packed RBC (PRBC)

Acute haemorrhage with Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to specific therapy (e.g. thalassaemia, MDS).

Pre-operative if Hb <8 g/dL and major surgery.

Sickle cell crisis (exchange transfusion in stroke, ACS).

### Platelets

Prophylactic if <10 × 10⁹/L.

Prophylactic <20 × 10⁹/L with sepsis or coagulopathy.

**Pre-procedure:** <50 (most procedures), <100 (CNS, ophthalmic).

Bleeding + thrombocytopenia.

Platelet dysfunction (uraemia, drugs) with bleeding.

**Massive transfusion 1:** 1:1 protocol.

### FFP

DIC with bleeding.

Massive transfusion.

Warfarin reversal with major bleed if PCC unavailable.

Multiple factor deficiency (liver disease + bleeding).

TTP/HUS plasma exchange.

Specific factor deficiency where concentrate unavailable.

### Cryoprecipitate

Hypofibrinogenaemia <1.5 g/L (DIC, obstetric haemorrhage).

vWD, haemophilia A (if factor concentrate unavailable).

Factor XIII deficiency.

Hazards – acute (within 24 h)

FNHTR – cytokines, anti-leukocyte antibody.

AHTR – ABO mismatch, fatal.

Allergic / anaphylactic – IgA deficiency.

TRALI – donor anti-HLA antibody.

TACO – volume overload.

Bacterial contamination, septic shock.

Citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia), hypothermia, hyperkalaemia.

Hazards – delayed (after 24 h)

DHTR – minor antigen alloimmunisation.

TA-GVHD – donor T cells; prevented by irradiation.

PTP – HPA-1a antibody.

Iron overload – chronic transfusion.

Alloimmunisation to RBC, HLA antigens.

Transmitted infections – HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, malaria, CMV, HTLV.

Approach to suspected transfusion reaction

STOP transfusion immediately, maintain IV access with NS.

Recheck blood group and patient identity (clerical error).

Send remaining unit, post-transfusion blood sample, and first urine to blood bank for repeat group, cross-match, DAT.

Cultures from unit and patient if febrile.

**Supportive:** IV fluids, vasopressor, O₂, manage DIC/AKI.

Antihistamine for allergic; adrenaline IM for anaphylaxis; paracetamol + ?leuko-reduced future components for FNHTR.

Report to haemovigilance system (HVS).

### Definition

Toxic syndrome caused by ingestion / inhalation / dermal exposure to organophosphate compounds (parathion, malathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, fenthion, monocrotophos, dimethoate, dichlorvos, etc., and chemical warfare nerve agents — sarin, tabun, VX). Most common cause of poisoning mortality in rural India (deliberate self-poisoning).

### Mechanism

OP compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active serine residue, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. 'Ageing' (loss of an R-group) makes the enzyme inhibition permanent — hence early use of oximes is critical.

Clinical features (cholinergic crisis)

### Muscarinic (DUMBELS / SLUDGEM):

Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

Pulmonary oedema – the major cause of death.

Nicotinic (Days of the Week — MTWThF):

Muscle fasciculation, Tachycardia, Weakness/paralysis (including respiratory), Hypertension, Hyperglycaemia.

### CNS:

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

### Distinct syndromes:

Intermediate syndrome (24–96 h after acute phase): proximal muscle, neck flexor, and respiratory muscle weakness; cranial nerve deficits; lasts 2–3 weeks; needs prolonged ventilation.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN, 1–3 weeks after exposure): distal sensorimotor neuropathy.

### Diagnosis

History of exposure, characteristic odour (garlic/kerosene), DUMBELS toxidrome.

Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (BChE / pseudocholinesterase) – rapid, available – severely depressed.

RBC acetylcholinesterase – more accurate, slower turnaround.

Atropine challenge test – minimal response to therapeutic dose supports diagnosis.

Ancillary – ABG, CK, troponin, ECG (QT prolongation, AV block), CXR (pulmonary oedema), serum amylase (pancreatitis).

### Treatment

### Resuscitation and decontamination

**ABC:** secure airway (suction copious secretions), 100% O₂.

**Decontamination:** remove all clothing, wash skin with soap and water (rescuers wear PPE — secondary contamination risk).

Gastric lavage – only if presentation <1 h, large amount ingested, and airway protected; NOT recommended routinely (aspiration risk).

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

### End-points (must achieve ALL):

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

(iv) Pupil dilation.

**Maintenance:** atropine infusion 10–20% of the cumulative atropinising dose per hour; titrate to keep target signs.

Watch for atropine toxicity – hyperthermia, agitation, ileus, urinary retention; lower infusion accordingly.

### Oxime (pralidoxime / 2-PAM)

Reactivates AChE if given before ageing.

**Dose:** 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 48–72 h. Alternatively: 1 g IV q4-6h.

Most effective in first 24 h, but should be given even later (prolonged release from fat).

Particularly effective against nicotinic (muscle) signs.

### Supportive care

ICU monitoring. Mechanical ventilation often needed for days–weeks. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (prolonged paralysis – use rocuronium or vecuronium).

Seizures – diazepam 5–10 mg IV (does not interact with AChE).

Aggressive electrolyte (K, Mg) replacement; cardiac monitoring.

Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS.

Surveillance for intermediate syndrome (FVC, NIF monitoring).

Avoid β-blockers (worsen bronchospasm), morphine, theophylline, phenothiazines.

### Psychiatric and social

Most cases are deliberate self-poisoning – mandatory psychiatric evaluation; suicide-risk assessment; family counselling; safe-storage advice; pesticide bans (e.g. WHO Class I OP withdrawn in India 2020).

Fig 3. Organophosphate poisoning – emergency management.

### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Combination of wound care, anti-rabies vaccination and (where indicated) rabies immunoglobulin given after exposure to a known or suspected rabid mammal, intended to prevent rabies before CNS invasion. Rabies is uniformly fatal once encephalitic symptoms develop, so PEP must be initiated promptly.

### Categorisation (WHO/NRCP)

**Cat I:** Touching/feeding animal, lick on intact skin. No PEP needed (only wash skin).

**Cat II:** Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleed, licks on broken skin.

**Cat III:** Single/multiple transdermal bites or scratches, contamination of mucous membrane with saliva (lick on mouth/eyes), bat exposures.

Wound management (all categories)

Immediate, thorough cleansing of wound with soap (or detergent) and copious running water for 15 minutes.

Apply povidone iodine, alcohol, or virucidal antiseptic.

Avoid suturing if possible; delayed primary closure after RIG infiltration if essential (face/cosmesis).

Tetanus prophylaxis if not up to date.

Antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) for dirty wounds, deep, puncture, or face/hand bites.

### Vaccine (Cat II and III)

### Cell-culture vaccines (CCEEV)

Purified chick embryo cell vaccine (PCEC) – Rabipur.

Human diploid cell vaccine (HDCV).

Purified Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV) – Verorab.

Purified duck embryo cell vaccine (PDEV).

### Intramuscular (Essen) regimen

1 mL IM (deltoid in adults; anterolateral thigh in children <2 yrs; NEVER gluteus) on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28.

### Intradermal (Thai Red Cross) – preferred in India

0.1 mL ID × 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, 28 (2-2-2-0-2).

Updated WHO 1-week IDRV — days 0, 3, 7 (2 sites each) — adopted India 2018.

Booster (previously immunised within 3 years)

1 mL IM (or 0.1 mL ID × 1 site) on days 0 and 3. No RIG.

Rabies immunoglobulin – RIG (Cat III only)

ERIG 40 IU/kg or HRIG 20 IU/kg.

Infiltrate as much as possible IN and AROUND the wound; remaining IM at site distant from vaccine.

Sensitivity test for ERIG; highly purified ERIG has low reaction rate (1–2%).

Monoclonal antibody cocktails (Rabishield, Twinrab) – alternative.

Give within 7 days of vaccine; do not exceed dose.

### Special situations

Pregnancy / lactation – vaccine and RIG safe.

Immunocompromised – use IM regimen, check titre day 14, consider double dose.

Bat exposure (even without overt bite) – treat as Cat III.

If healthy domestic dog/cat is available for 10-day observation and remains well — PEP may be discontinued.

Fig 1. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis algorithm.

### Definition

PEP is a short course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) administered after a defined exposure to potentially HIV-infected body fluids, with the goal of preventing seroconversion. Effective only if started within 72 hours (ideally <2 hours).

### Categories of exposure

Occupational (needle-stick, mucosal splash)

**Source HIV status:** positive (CD4, viral load checked), negative, or unknown.

**Type of exposure:** percutaneous (large/small hollow needle, solid needle, superficial), mucous membrane, non-intact skin.

Non-occupational (sexual assault, IDU, unprotected sex)

**Highest risk:** receptive anal intercourse, contaminated needle sharing.

Immediate first-aid (any exposure)

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Alternative if dolutegravir contraindicated

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Atazanavir/Ritonavir (300/100 mg) OR Lopinavir/Ritonavir 400/100 mg BD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.
