### Definition

Envenomation by elapid snakes (Cobra — Naja naja, King cobra — Ophiophagus hannah, Common krait — Bungarus caeruleus) produces a neurotoxic syndrome through α- and β-neurotoxins that block post-synaptic and pre-synaptic neuromuscular transmission respectively, leading to flaccid paralysis. India: cobra and krait are two of the 'Big Four' deadly Indian snakes.

Local features (cobra > krait)

Two fang punctures (krait bite often painless and at night).

Local pain, swelling, blistering, sometimes necrosis (cobra).

Krait – minimal local signs; pain disproportionate to swelling; often patient awakes with abdominal pain at 4–6 a.m.

Systemic features – progressive descending paralysis

Early (30 min – 2 h)

Heaviness of eyelids (ptosis – earliest and commonest sign), external ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, blurred vision.

Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia.

Hypersalivation, profuse sweating, paraesthesiae.

Established neurotoxicity (2–6 h)

Bulbar palsy – pooled secretions, tongue weakness, broken neck sign (cannot lift head off pillow).

Limb weakness – proximal first; progressive descending paralysis.

Respiratory muscle paralysis – the most life-threatening complication; intercostal and diaphragmatic weakness leading to respiratory failure.

Patient is conscious throughout (locked-in pattern unless hypoxic).

### Autonomic features

Cobra – bradycardia, hypotension; krait – sometimes mild hypertension, abdominal pain.

### Krait-specific

Bite often at night while sleeping on the floor; little or no local reaction; severe abdominal pain.

Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia may accompany.

Response to neostigmine usually poor (β-neurotoxin pre-synaptic action — already-released ACh is depleted).

### Investigations and monitoring

20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20-WBCT) – usually normal in pure neurotoxic bite (distinguishes from haemotoxic).

FVC (vital capacity) — if <1 L or falling — intubate.

ABG, electrolytes (krait — hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia).

ECG (arrhythmia).

Edrophonium / neostigmine test (improvement supports diagnosis and helps in management).

### Management (Indian National Snakebite Protocol 2017)

**First aid:** reassure, immobilise limb at heart level, remove rings/tight items, pressure-immobilisation bandage; rapid transport to a centre with ASV and ventilator. AVOID tourniquet/cut/suck/ice/electric shock.

Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV): initial 10 vials (100 mL) in 100–200 mL normal saline IV over 1 hour. Repeat every 6 hours up to maximum 30 vials, based on clinical/lab response.

Adjuvant — Neostigmine 0.5 mg + atropine 0.6 mg IV every 30 min × 5 doses (then 1–2 hourly as needed) — useful especially for cobra envenomation.

Early intubation and mechanical ventilation if FVC <1 L, tidal volume <5 mL/kg, or any respiratory distress.

**Treat ASV reactions:** stop infusion, adrenaline 0.5 mg IM, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV, chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV; resume ASV at slower rate.

Tetanus toxoid, antibiotics if cellulitis or wound necrosis.

Supportive — fluids, vasopressors if hypotensive; psychological support.

Fig 5. Snakebite — Indian National Protocol.

GENERAL MEDICINE|83.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Overview

**Renal function tests assess:** (1) GFR, (2) tubular function, (3) glomerular permeability (proteinuria), (4) urinary sediment, (5) renal anatomy. Used for screening, diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of kidney disease.

### 1. Assessment of GFR

Direct (Exogenous Markers — gold standard, research)

Inulin clearance — gold standard; cumbersome.

Iohexol, iothalamate, EDTA clearance — used clinically when accurate GFR needed (transplant donor, chemotherapy dosing).

### Endogenous Markers

**Serum Creatinine (Cr):** Serum Creatinine (Cr): Normal 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (M), 0.6–1.1 (F). Easy, cheap. Limitations:

Affected by muscle mass (low in elderly, women, vegetarians, amputees, sarcopenia).

Insensitive in early CKD ('creatinine-blind range' — GFR can drop to 50% before Cr rises).

Affected by drugs blocking tubular secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine).

Diet — cooked meat ↑ Cr.

**Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas:** Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas: Calculated from serum Cr + age + sex (± race, removed 2021).

CKD-EPI 2021 (PREFERRED — race-free) — most accurate across all ranges.

MDRD — older; less accurate at normal/high GFR.

Cockcroft-Gault — older; uses weight; used for drug dosing.

Schwartz (children) — eGFR = k × height/Cr.

**Creatinine Clearance (24-h):** Creatinine Clearance (24-h): Cr clearance = (Urine Cr × Urine volume) / Plasma Cr. Limitations: incomplete urine collection, overestimates GFR (tubular secretion of Cr 10–15%, more with low GFR). Less used now than eGFR. Adequate collection: Cr × 1.5 (males) / 1.2 (females) g/kg/d.

**Cystatin C:** Cystatin C: Constant cellular production; freely filtered; not reabsorbed; not secreted. Independent of muscle mass. Useful in elderly, sarcopenic, paediatric. CKD-EPI Cr-cystatin C combined — most accurate. Expensive.

**Blood urea / BUN:** Blood urea / BUN: Normal 7–25 mg/dL. Affected by protein intake, GI bleeding (↑), liver disease (↓), hydration. Urea:Cr ratio > 100 → pre-renal / GI bleed.

### 2. Glomerular Permeability — Proteinuria

### Quantification

Dipstick — semi-quantitative; detects albumin > 30 mg/dL. Negative in non-albumin proteinuria (myeloma — light chain).

24-h urine protein — gold standard. Normal < 150 mg/d.

**Spot UACR (urine albumin:** creatinine ratio):

< 30 mg/g — normal

30–300 mg/g — moderately increased (microalbuminuria)

> 300 mg/g — severely increased (macroalbuminuria)

**Spot UPCR (urine protein:** creatinine ratio) — total proteinuria. PCR > 3500 mg/g = nephrotic range.

Urinary protein electrophoresis (UPEP) + immunofixation — myeloma (Bence-Jones).

Sulphosalicylic acid (SSA) test — detects total protein (incl. light chains; dipstick misses).

### Selectivity

**Selective proteinuria:** predominantly albumin (smaller MW) — MCD.

**Non-selective:** albumin + IgG + larger proteins — advanced glomerular disease.

Selectivity index = clearance of IgG / clearance of transferrin; < 0.2 = highly selective.

### 3. Tubular Function Tests

### Concentration / Dilution

Urine osmolality (random) — normal 50–1200 mOsm/kg.

Urine specific gravity — 1.005–1.030.

Water deprivation test — for diabetes insipidus (Uosm < 300 after deprivation).

ADH (DDAVP) challenge — central vs nephrogenic DI.

### Acidification

Urine pH (random) — 5–6.5 normal.

Ammonium chloride loading test — RTA diagnosis (urine pH should fall < 5.5 if normal).

Serum bicarbonate, anion gap, urinary anion gap.

### Tubular Reabsorption / Secretion

Fractional excretion of Na (FENa) — pre-renal vs ATN.

Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) — pre-renal if < 35% (use if on diuretics).

Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO₄) — TmP/GFR (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / GFR) — Fanconi syndrome (< 80%).

Glucosuria with normal serum glucose — proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi).

Aminoaciduria — Fanconi syndrome.

**Tubular markers:** NGAL, KIM-1, IL-18 (research; early AKI biomarkers).

### 4. Urinary Sediment Examination

### 5. Imaging

**Ultrasound (USG) — first-line:** size (10–14 cm normal; < 9 cm = chronic), echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, masses, Doppler (renal artery flow, RVT).

KUB X-ray — radio-opaque stones (calcium, struvite). Cystine = semi-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent.

CT (CECT, KUB) — masses, complex cysts, stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis).

MRI / MRA — RAS, masses (avoid gadolinium if eGFR < 30 — NSF risk).

DTPA scan — split function (each kidney's contribution).

DMSA scan — cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy).

MAG-3 scan — obstruction.

Renal biopsy — definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.

### 6. Other / Specialised

Complement (C3, C4) — see Q3.

Autoantibodies — ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM.

Anti-PLA2R — membranous.

SPEP / UPEP / IFE — myeloma.

Cryoglobulins.

### Approach to Interpretation

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.353; KDIGO CKD 2012; CKD-EPI 2021 race-free.

### Indications

ESRD (eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.73 m²) or imminent ESRD.

Pre-emptive (before dialysis starts) — best survival outcomes.

Failed dialysis (HD / PD) — life expectancy + quality of life improved by transplant.

### Donor Types

### Living Donor

Living related — first-degree relatives (parent, sibling, child).

Living unrelated — spouse, friend (Indian Transplant of Human Organs Act 1994 + Rules 2014 — Authorisation Committee approval mandatory; commercial transplant illegal).

Paired exchange (kidney swap) — incompatible donor-recipient pairs swap.

**Advantages:** best outcomes (5-yr graft survival 90%), shorter waiting, scheduled, less rejection (better HLA match).

**Donor evaluation:** thorough — medical, psychological, social, ethical clearance.

### Deceased Donor (DDKT)

Brain-death donors (donation after brain death — DBD) — standard.

Circulatory death donors (DCD) — newer.

Allocation through state / national registry (NOTTO — National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation, India).

Long waiting list — Indian average wait > 5 years (severe organ shortage).

5-yr graft survival 80%.

### Recipient Pre-transplant Workup

### Comprehensive Assessment

Detailed history + examination, cause of ESRD.

**Cardiac:** ECG, echo, stress test, cardiology consult (CAD risk).

**Infectious:** HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV, CMV, EBV, TB (CXR + IGRA / Mantoux), syphilis, screening for endemic infections (malaria, dengue), dental clearance.

**Malignancy screen:** PSA, mammogram, PAP smear, colonoscopy (age-appropriate).

**Immunology:** ABO blood group, HLA typing (A, B, DR loci), HLA antibody screening (panel reactive antibody — PRA), cross-match.

**Urinary:** USG, MCU (if reflux), urodynamics if indicated.

Psychiatric and social assessment.

**Vaccinations:** pneumococcal, influenza, HBV (40 µg × 4), HZV, COVID-19 — BEFORE transplant.

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Active malignancy (< 2 yr remission usually required).

Active uncontrolled infection.

Severe cardiac disease (uncorrected).

Severe pulmonary disease.

Severe psychiatric disease with poor adherence.

Active substance abuse.

Untreated HIV with non-suppressed viral load.

Short life expectancy < 2 yr from other comorbidity.

### Relative

Age > 70 yr (case-by-case).

Severe peripheral vascular disease.

Obesity BMI > 35.

HBV / HCV (now mostly treatable — DAA).

Recurrent kidney disease risk (FSGS, MPGN, primary oxaluria).

### Surgical Procedure

Kidney placed in extraperitoneal iliac fossa (right preferred — iliac vessels superficial).

Renal artery anastomosed to external iliac (or internal iliac in living donor).

Renal vein to external iliac vein.

Ureter to bladder (Lich-Gregoir extravesical anastomosis with stent).

Native kidneys usually LEFT in place (unless symptomatic — ADPKD, infection, RCC).

Duration 2–4 h; recipient hospital stay 7–14 d.

### Immunosuppression

### Induction (at transplant)

Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R) — standard low-risk.

Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG, rabbit) — high-risk (high PRA, deceased donor, retransplant).

Methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g pulse.

### Maintenance (lifelong)

**Triple therapy:** Calcineurin inhibitor + Antiproliferative + Steroid.

**Calcineurin inhibitor:** Calcineurin inhibitor: Tacrolimus (preferred, trough 5–10 ng/ml) OR cyclosporine 100–200 ng/ml. Side effects: nephrotoxic, neurotoxic (tremor), DM, HTN, gingival hyperplasia (CsA), hirsutism (CsA), alopecia (Tac).

**Antiproliferative:** Antiproliferative: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1–2 g/d OR mycophenolic acid (MPA). Side effects: diarrhoea, leucopenia, infection. Azathioprine alternative (cheaper India).

**Steroid:** Steroid: Prednisolone 10–20 mg/d tapered to 5 mg/d maintenance. Side effects: DM, osteoporosis, infection, weight, cushingoid, cataracts.

Alternative — mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus, everolimus) — replaces CNI in nephrotoxicity.

Belatacept — costimulation blocker; less nephrotoxic.

### Complications

### Surgical (early)

Bleeding, haematoma, lymphocoele.

Renal artery / vein thrombosis (graft loss).

Ureteric leak / obstruction.

Wound infection, dehiscence.

Delayed graft function (need post-transplant dialysis).

### Rejection

**Hyperacute:** Hyperacute: Minutes-hours; pre-formed antibodies (ABO / HLA); thrombosis; graft loss (prevent by cross-match).

Acute cellular (T-cell mediated):Acute cellular (T-cell mediated): Days-weeks. Rising Cr, oliguria, fever. Biopsy: tubulitis, lymphocyte infiltration. Treat: pulse methylpred 500 mg × 3 d → tacrolimus boost; severe: ATG.

**Acute antibody-mediated (AMR):** Acute antibody-mediated (AMR): Donor-specific antibodies. C4d on biopsy, peritubular capillaritis. Treat: plasmapheresis + IVIG + rituximab.

Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA):Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA): Months-years. Gradual Cr rise, proteinuria. Mostly irreversible — optimise immunosuppression, manage as CKD.

Infection (commonest cause of death; from immunosuppression)

**Early (< 1 mo):** nosocomial — wound, UTI, line, surgical site.

**1–6 mo:** opportunistic — CMV (commonest viral), BK polyomavirus (nephropathy), Pneumocystis jirovecii, Aspergillus, mycobacteria.

**Late > 6 mo:** community-acquired + late opportunistic (PML, CMV reactivation).

**Prophylaxis:** cotrimoxazole (PCP) × 6 mo; valganciclovir × 3 mo (CMV mismatch); INH 9 mo (latent TB).

### Malignancy (chronic immunosuppression)

Skin cancers (SCC, BCC) — 100× general population.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD — EBV-driven).

Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

**Solid tumours:** lung, breast, prostate, cervix, GI — moderately ↑ risk.

### Metabolic

New-onset diabetes (NODAT) — tacrolimus, steroid (15–30%).

Hypertension (CNI, steroid).

Hyperlipidaemia (CNI, sirolimus, steroid).

Osteoporosis, avascular necrosis (steroid).

Hyperuricaemia, gout.

### Disease Recurrence in Graft

FSGS (30%), MPGN, IgA, lupus, primary oxaluria — variable.

### Long-term Care

Lifelong immunosuppression + adherence.

Regular monitoring — Cr, eGFR, drug levels, urine ACR.

Vaccinations (avoid live — MMR, varicella, yellow fever; OK inactivated).

Sun protection, skin cancer screening annually.

BP < 130/80, lipid control, glucose control.

Pregnancy possible after 1 yr stable function — switch MMF to AZA pre-conception.

### Outcomes (India)

**Living donor:** 5-yr graft survival 90%; deceased donor: 80%. Patient survival transplant > dialysis at 5 yr (95% vs 35%). Cost (India): initial ₹5–10 lakhs + lifelong immunosuppression ₹15–25k/month. Many state schemes and PMJAY cover transplant. Best modality but limited by organ availability.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.398; THOTA 1994 + Rules 2014; NOTTO India; KDIGO Care of Transplant 2009.

### Principles

Nutrition therapy is foundational in CKD — slows progression, controls complications (electrolyte disturbances, oedema, malnutrition, MBD), and improves quality of life. Individualised by CKD stage, modality (conservative / dialysis / transplant), and comorbidity (DM, HTN, obesity).

### Macronutrients

### Protein

**CKD G3–G5 (non-dialysis):** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (KDOQI 2020). Lower protein slows progression but risks malnutrition; do not go below 0.6 g/kg/d.

**Diabetic CKD:** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (lower in non-diabetic, slightly higher in DKD).

**Maintenance HD:** 1.0–1.2 g/kg/d (replace protein lost in HD).

**Peritoneal dialysis:** 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d (protein lost in dialysate).

**Post-transplant:** 1.0 g/kg/d.

Acute illness / hospitalised CKD: 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d.

50% from high biological value (animal — egg, fish, chicken).

**Indian sources:** dal, paneer, dahi, soya — moderate amounts.

### Calories

25–35 kcal/kg/d (sufficient to prevent protein catabolism).

Lower if BMI > 30; higher if BMI < 22 or muscle wasting.

Adequate carbohydrate to spare protein.

### Fat

30–35% of total calories.

Limit saturated; favour MUFA / PUFA (olive oil, fish oil, nuts in moderation).

Restrict cholesterol < 200 mg/d (atherogenic).

### Electrolytes / Minerals

### Sodium

< 5 g salt/d (= 2 g sodium); ideally < 4 g.

**Avoid:** pickles, papad, namkeen, processed foods, canned, fast food.

Cook with less salt; use spices (cumin, coriander, mint, lime).

Avoid salt substitutes (KCl — hyperK risk in CKD).

### Potassium

Restrict in CKD G4–G5 or hyperK: 2–3 g/d (50–80 mEq).

### AVOID / LIMIT (high K):

**Fruits:** banana, orange, sweet lime, citrus, kiwi, melon, mango, papaya, coconut water, dried fruits (raisin, dates, apricot).

**Vegetables:** tomato, spinach, leafy greens, potato, sweet potato, beans, drumstick, mushroom.

**Other:** salt substitutes, instant coffee, chocolate, nuts.

**ALLOWED (low K):** apple, pear, papaya (small), pineapple, grapes, watermelon (small), guava, cauliflower, cabbage, capsicum, brinjal, lauki, tinda, parwal.

DOUBLE BOIL / LEACH vegetables (peel, cut, soak in warm water 2 h, drain, boil with excess water, discard water) — reduces K by 30–50%.

### Phosphate

**Restrict in CKD G4–G5:** 800–1000 mg/d.

**AVOID:** dairy excess (milk > 250 ml/d, cheese), egg yolk excess, organ meats, nuts, seeds, whole grains (wheat bran, oats), cola drinks, processed food (phosphate additives — well-absorbed).

USE phosphate binders with meals (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum).

Refined cereals (white rice, white bread) lower phosphate than whole grain.

### Calcium

1000–1500 mg/d total (from diet + binders).

Avoid Ca-rich foods + Ca binders + Vit D simultaneously (hypercalcaemia).

### Other Minerals

Magnesium — limit if hyperMg (CKD G4–G5).

Iron — adequate (anaemia); often supplement.

Zinc — supplement if dialysis (loss).

### Fluid

**Pre-dialysis CKD:** 1.5–2 L/d unless oliguric.

**Oliguric:** previous day's urine output + 500 ml insensible.

**On HD:** 500 ml + previous day's urine output; restrict interdialytic weight gain < 5% body weight (~ 1 kg/d).

**PD:** usually liberal (continuous fluid removal).

Include ALL fluids — tea, coffee, soup, milk, fruit juice, ice cream, jelly.

### Vitamins

Water-soluble — supplement on dialysis (lost in dialysate): B1 1.5 mg, B6 5 mg, B12 1 µg, folate 1 mg, C 75 mg, niacin.

Avoid high-dose vitamin C (> 250 mg/d — oxalate nephropathy).

Vitamin D — active form (calcitriol / alfacalcidol) as needed.

AVOID vitamin A (retinol — accumulates).

### Indian Diet Practical Tips

Rice over chapatti for low phosphate (preferred in South India).

Roti / chapati from refined flour preferred over whole wheat.

Egg WHITE (low phosphate, good protein).

**Pulses (dal):** boil in excess water, discard, then cook — reduces K, P.

Limit dahi to 1 small bowl/d (75 g).

Limit fruits to 1 small portion of low-K fruits.

Avoid namkeen, biscuits, instant noodles, papad, pickle, chutney.

**Beverages:** lime water (no salt), weak tea, coconut water AVOID, packaged juice AVOID.

**Eating out:** avoid; if must, choose plain rice + vegetable curry.

### Special Situations

### Diabetic CKD

Restrict refined carbs (white rice, sugar).

Whole grains tolerable in earlier CKD; restrict in advanced (phosphate).

Time meals with insulin/SGLT2i/GLP-1.

### Nephrotic Syndrome

Protein 0.8 g/kg/d (NOT high — accelerates loss).

Strict low salt (oedema).

Low cholesterol, low fat.

Adequate calories.

### Renal Stones (prevention)

High fluid > 2.5 L/d.

Low salt < 5 g/d.

Adequate dietary calcium (NOT supplemental).

Low oxalate (avoid spinach, beetroot, tea, chocolate, nuts, soy, rhubarb) — Ca oxalate stones.

Low purine (uric acid stones).

Low animal protein (Ca oxalate, uric acid).

Citrate (lemon, orange — for non-CKD; risk vs benefit in CKD).

### Monitoring

Weight (dry weight in dialysis).

Serum albumin (> 3.5 — good nutrition), pre-albumin.

Electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, phosphate), Mg.

BP, oedema.

Anthropometry (MUAC, BMI).

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA — gold standard for CKD nutrition).

Dietitian review every 3–6 months.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.408; KDOQI Nutrition CKD 2020; ISN Nutrition; ISN India Renal Diet guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|84.note:
### Definition

Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental disorder characterised by disturbances of thought, perception, affect, volition and social functioning, in a setting of clear consciousness and intact intellect. It is the prototype primary psychotic disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~1% worldwide; M=F.

**Peak onset:** males 15–25 y, females 25–35 y; rare onset <10 y or >50 y.

Heritability ~80%; MZ twin concordance ~50%, sibling risk ~10%, child of one parent ~13%, both parents ~46%.

Higher in lower socio-economic strata (social-drift hypothesis), urban residents, migrants, and winter/spring births.

### Etiology (multifactorial)

**Genetic:** polygenic — DISC1, NRG1, COMT, DRD2, ZNF804A; 22q11.2 deletion.

**Neurodevelopmental:** maternal infection (influenza, toxoplasma) in 2nd trimester, obstetric complications, perinatal hypoxia, advanced paternal age.

**Neurochemical:** mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (positive sx); mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity (negative sx); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin (5-HT2A) dysregulation.

**Neuroanatomic:** ventricular enlargement, ↓ hippocampal & temporal volumes, ↓ prefrontal grey matter.

**Psychosocial:** high expressed emotion in family, urban upbringing, cannabis use in adolescence (dose-related, ↑ risk 2–6 fold).

Pathophysiology — dopamine hypothesis (revised)

Mesolimbic pathway hyperactivity → positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations).

Mesocortical hypoactivity → negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.

Nigrostriatal blockade by typical antipsychotics → extrapyramidal side effects.

Tuberoinfundibular blockade → hyperprolactinaemia.

**Atypicals:** combined D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism — less EPS, better negative-symptom coverage.

Clinical features (Schneider's first-rank symptoms — Kurt Schneider 1959)

Audible thoughts (thought echo) — voice repeats thoughts aloud.

Voices arguing / discussing — third-person auditory hallucinations.

Voices commenting on actions (running commentary).

Thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting.

Made affect, made impulse, made volition (passivity phenomena).

Somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by outside force).

Delusional perception — normal perception with bizarre delusional meaning.

### Positive symptoms

Hallucinations — auditory most common (~70%), then visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory.

Delusions — persecutory (most common), referential, grandiose, religious, somatic, bizarre.

Formal thought disorder — loosening of associations, neologisms, word salad, tangentiality, derailment.

Disorganised behaviour — bizarre dress, posturing, agitation.

Catatonia — stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia/echopraxia.

Negative symptoms (the '5 A's')

Affective flattening — restricted emotional expression.

Alogia — poverty of speech/content.

Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure.

Avolition — loss of motivation/goal-directed behaviour.

Asociality — social withdrawal.

### Cognitive symptoms

Deficits in attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed.

Often pre-morbid and major determinant of long-term functional outcome.

ICD-11 subtypes (subtype-based classification removed in DSM-5 but still asked in Indian exams)

Paranoid — predominant delusions and hallucinations (commonest).

Hebephrenic / disorganised — disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect, thought disorder; early onset, poor prognosis.

Catatonic — motor abnormalities predominate.

Simple — gradual negative-symptom development without positive symptoms.

Residual — past positive symptoms, current chronic negative symptoms.

Undifferentiated — does not fit any category.

### Diagnostic criteria

### DSM-5 schizophrenia

**A. Active-phase symptoms:** ≥2 of: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech, (4) grossly disorganised / catatonic behaviour, (5) negative symptoms. ≥1 must be (1), (2), or (3). Present ≥1 month.

B. Social/occupational dysfunction: Marked impairment in work, interpersonal relations or self-care.

**C. Duration:** Continuous signs ≥6 months (active + prodromal ± residual).

**D. Exclusions:** Schizoaffective + mood disorder with psychotic features excluded; substance / general medical condition excluded.

### ICD-10 schizophrenia (F20)

≥1 'first-rank' (a–d) OR ≥2 'second-rank' (e–h) for ≥1 month:

(a) Thought echo, insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.

(b) Delusions of control, influence or passivity; delusional perception.

(c) 3rd-person auditory hallucinations: voices arguing/discussing or running commentary.

(d) Persistent bizarre delusions (culturally inappropriate).

(e) Persistent hallucinations in any modality with delusions / overvalued ideas.

(f) Breaks / interpolations in train of thought — neologisms, incoherence.

(g) Catatonic behaviour.

(h) Negative symptoms — apathy, paucity of speech, blunted affect.

Differential diagnosis (must exclude)

Investigations (mainly to exclude organic / metabolic causes)

**Bedside:** detailed MSE; cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA); risk assessment (suicide, homicide, vulnerability).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, calcium.

**Infective:** VDRL, HIV serology; CSF if encephalitis suspected.

**Toxicology:** urine drug screen — cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, LSD.

**Imaging:** MRI brain — if first episode, late onset, focal neurological signs, treatment resistance, or atypical course.

**EEG:** if seizures or temporal-lobe epilepsy suspected.

Autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti-NMDA-R) if subacute psychosis with neurological signs.

**Baseline pre-antipsychotic:** ECG (QTc), weight/BMI/waist, fasting lipids, fasting glucose/HbA1c, LFT, prolactin.

### Management

Figure 1. Schizophrenia management — from DSM-5/ICD-10 diagnosis through atypical antipsychotic first-line to clozapine for treatment-resistant disease.

### Acute episode

Ensure safety — assess suicidality, aggression, self-neglect; admit if needed (voluntary / under MHCA 2017).

Address concurrent substance use, malnutrition, infection.

**For agitation:** lorazepam 2–4 mg IM / olanzapine 10 mg IM / haloperidol 5–10 mg IM ± promethazine 25–50 mg IM (rapid tranquillisation per NIMHANS protocol). Avoid IM olanzapine + IM lorazepam together (hypotension, respiratory depression).

### Pharmacotherapy

**First-line:** Atypical (2nd-gen) antipsychotic — start low, titrate weekly to therapeutic range. Risperidone 2–6 mg/d, olanzapine 10–20 mg/d, aripiprazole 10–30 mg/d, quetiapine 300–600 mg/d, ziprasidone 80–160 mg/d, amisulpride 400–800 mg/d. Continue at therapeutic dose ≥4–6 wk before judging response.

**Inadequate response:** Try a 2nd atypical (different agent) or a typical (haloperidol 5–15 mg/d, trifluoperazine 5–20 mg/d, chlorpromazine 300–800 mg/d).

Treatment-resistant (failed ≥2 antipsychotics, ≥6 wk, adequate dose): CLOZAPINE — 12.5 mg → titrate to 300–450 mg/d (max 900 mg). Most effective drug for refractory disease (CATIE, CUtLASS-2). Mandatory monitoring: CBC weekly × 18 wk, then fortnightly to 1 yr, then monthly. Stop if WBC <3,000 or ANC <1,500. Other AEs: myocarditis (esp. 1st month), sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures (dose-related), constipation/ileus, weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia.

Long-acting injectables (LAIs) — for poor adherence: Risperidone LAI 25–50 mg IM q2wk; paliperidone palmitate IM monthly or 3-monthly; aripiprazole LAI monthly; haloperidol decanoate 50–200 mg IM monthly; fluphenazine decanoate 12.5–50 mg IM monthly.

Augmentation in clozapine-resistant: Add ECT, second antipsychotic (amisulpride / aripiprazole), or mood stabiliser (lithium / valproate).

Duration of antipsychotic treatment

**First episode:** continue ≥1–2 years after full remission, then taper slowly.

**Recurrent / multi-episode:** ≥5 years; many patients need lifelong therapy.

Abrupt discontinuation → 80% relapse within 2 years.

Psychosocial interventions (essential — not optional)

Psychoeducation — patient and family; reduces high expressed emotion.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for psychosis (CBT-p) — reduces residual positive symptoms.

Family therapy — reduces relapse.

Supported employment / Individual Placement & Support (IPS).

Social skills training, assertive community treatment (ACT) for severe persistent disease.

Cognitive remediation for cognitive symptoms.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) — indications

Catatonia (response in 80–90%).

Severe suicidality / homicidality.

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (clozapine augmentation).

Severe positive symptoms not responding to ≥6 wk of antipsychotic.

6–12 sessions, 2–3 times per week; modified (anaesthesia + suxamethonium).

Antipsychotic side effects (sub-question — Boloor A372)

Typical (1st-generation) — high-potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine)

**Extrapyramidal:** acute dystonia (hours–days; oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonus → IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg or promethazine 25–50 mg), parkinsonism (days–weeks; bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor → anticholinergic e.g. trihexyphenidyl 2–10 mg/d), akathisia (motor restlessness → propranolol 30–80 mg/d or BZD), tardive dyskinesia (months–years; orobuccolingual choreoathetosis → switch to clozapine, valbenazine or tetrabenazine).

Hyperprolactinaemia → amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, ↓ libido, osteoporosis (esp. risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride).

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, ↑↑ CK, leucocytosis. STOP drug, ICU, IV fluids/cooling, dantrolene 1–2 mg/kg q6h, bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS. Mortality 10–20%.

Lowered seizure threshold (chlorpromazine > others).

QTc prolongation (haloperidol IV, thioridazine — withdrawn).

Typical low-potency (chlorpromazine, thioridazine)

Anticholinergic — dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, ileus.

Antihistaminic — sedation, weight gain.

α-blockade — postural hypotension.

Photosensitivity, blue-grey skin pigmentation; corneal/lens deposits with prolonged use.

Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice with chlorpromazine).

Atypical (2nd-generation) — overall fewer EPS, more metabolic

Metabolic syndrome — weight gain, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance / diabetes (olanzapine + clozapine highest; ziprasidone + aripiprazole + lurasidone lowest).

Risperidone / paliperidone — dose-related EPS and hyperprolactinaemia.

Clozapine — agranulocytosis, myocarditis, sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures, ileus, weight gain, metabolic syndrome.

Quetiapine — sedation, postural hypotension.

Aripiprazole — akathisia (most common SE), impulse-control problems (gambling, hypersexuality).

Ziprasidone, lurasidone — QTc prolongation; lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal food.

Asenapine — sublingual; oral hypoaesthesia, EPS at high dose.

Drugs causing hallucinations (sub-question — Boloor A363)

**Recreational / drugs of abuse:** cannabis, LSD, psilocybin (magic mushroom), mescaline, MDMA (ecstasy), amphetamines, cocaine, PCP, ketamine, alcohol (in withdrawal — DT).

**Anti-Parkinsonian:** levodopa, dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine), amantadine, selegiline.

**Anticholinergics:** atropine, scopolamine, hyoscine, trihexyphenidyl, benztropine; antihistamines (diphenhydramine); TCAs at toxic doses.

**Steroids:** prednisolone (high-dose), ACTH ('steroid psychosis').

**Antimalarials:** chloroquine, mefloquine, primaquine.

**Antibiotics:** ciprofloxacin (CNS), isoniazid, cycloserine, clarithromycin, voriconazole.

**Antivirals:** aciclovir (renal failure), efavirenz, oseltamivir.

**Anaesthetics:** ketamine, nitrous oxide.

Opioids in overdose; tramadol; pentazocine.

**Withdrawal-induced:** alcohol (DT), benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids.

**Others:** digoxin toxicity, β-blockers (lipophilic — propranolol), interferon-α, baclofen withdrawal, lithium toxicity.

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk 5–10% (highest in young males, early course, after discharge).

Violence (small but real; usually against family, often with substance co-use).

Substance abuse comorbidity — ~50% (nicotine, cannabis, alcohol).

Cardiovascular disease — leading cause of premature mortality; antipsychotic metabolic effects + smoking + sedentary lifestyle.

Polydipsia, hyponatraemia.

Homelessness, unemployment, social isolation.

Reduced life expectancy by 15–20 years (suicide + CV disease + suboptimal medical care).

Prognosis (rule of thirds)

≈1/3 substantial recovery, ≈1/3 partial response with relapses, ≈1/3 chronic disabling course.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, late onset, female, prominent positive symptoms, mood symptoms, married, good pre-morbid function, family history of mood disorder, paranoid subtype, identifiable stressor, short duration of untreated psychosis (DUP).

**Poor prognostic factors:** insidious onset, early onset, male, negative symptoms, social withdrawal, family history of schizophrenia, hebephrenic / simple subtype, no precipitant, long DUP, poor pre-morbid function.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; ICMR/NIMHANS — Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia (Indian Psychiatric Society); DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock — Synopsis of Psychiatry 12e.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Light's criteria

Effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met:

Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5.

Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Causes (mnemonic:** 'Pus, blood, fluid from inflammation')

### Infective:

Parapneumonic effusion / empyema (Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Tuberculous pleural effusion (the commonest cause of exudative effusion in young adults in India – lymphocytic, ADA >40 U/L, biopsy shows granulomas).

Fungal (rare), parasitic (amoebic, hydatid).

Malignancy (commonest cause of exudate in elderly):

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Breast carcinoma.

Lymphoma, leukaemia.

Mesothelioma (asbestos-related).

Ovarian carcinoma (Meigs syndrome with ascites).

Connective tissue / autoimmune:

Rheumatoid arthritis (low glucose, low pH, low complement, RF positive).

SLE.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Pulmonary embolism / infarction.

### Gastrointestinal / abdominal:

Pancreatitis (left-sided, high amylase).

Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave's – high amylase from saliva, low pH).

Subdiaphragmatic abscess.

Post-CABG.

### Drugs:

Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine.

### Other:

Radiation therapy.

Chylothorax (lymphoma, trauma, thoracic-duct obstruction – triglycerides >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons).

Haemothorax (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation).

Yellow nail syndrome.

Fig 6. Pleural effusion – diagnostic algorithm using Light's criteria.

### Definition

Exudative ascites = ascitic fluid protein > 2.5 g/dL with low SAAG (< 1.1 g/dL), indicating peritoneal disease with breached capillary integrity. Contrast with transudative ascites (SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL, portal HTN-driven).

### Pathophysiology

Inflammation, infection, or neoplasm of the peritoneum → increased capillary permeability → protein-rich exudate.

SAAG (serum albumin − ascitic albumin) < 1.1 g/dL.

### Causes

- Malignancy (commonest exudative cause)

Peritoneal carcinomatosis (ovarian — Krukenberg, gastric, colon, breast, pancreatic, primary peritoneal mesothelioma).

Hepatocellular carcinoma (when peritoneal seeding; pure HCC ascites is portal-HTN type).

Lymphoma (chylous if thoracic duct obstruction).

### 2. Infections

**Indian context:** Tuberculous peritonitis — Indian endemic; ADA > 40 U/L, lymphocytic, protein > 3 g/dL.

Secondary bacterial peritonitis — bowel perforation, ruptured appendix; polymicrobial, multiple organisms.

Fungal — Candida, Cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis (immunocompromised).

Parasitic — schistosomiasis, hydatid rupture.

### 3. Pancreatic Ascites

Chronic pancreatitis with ductal disruption → leak; amylase > 1000 U/L, lipase very high; SAAG often < 1.1.

### 4. Biliary Ascites

Post-cholecystectomy / trauma / spontaneous gallbladder perforation; ascitic bilirubin > serum bilirubin.

### 5. Chylous Ascites

Lymphatic obstruction — lymphoma, post-surgical, congenital lymphangiectasia, filariasis (India). Milky appearance, TG > 200 mg/dL.

Filarial chyluria + ascites — Indian-relevant; W. bancrofti.

### 6. Connective Tissue / Vasculitis

SLE serositis (rare).

Familial Mediterranean fever — recurrent peritonitis.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis with serosal involvement.

### 7. Endometriosis (rare)

Cyclical ascites in reproductive-age women, low SAAG.

### Approach to Differentiating

### Investigations

Diagnostic paracentesis — cell count, protein, albumin (calculate SAAG), Gram stain + culture (in blood-culture bottles), cytology, ADA, GeneXpert MTB, amylase, TG, bilirubin (selected).

**Bloods:** CBC, LFT, INR, glucose, USG abdomen ± CECT, tumour markers (CA-125 ovarian, CEA colorectal/gastric, AFP HCC).

Laparoscopy + peritoneal biopsy if TB/malignancy suspected and other tests non-diagnostic (gold standard for TB peritonitis).

### Management

Treat underlying cause (chemotherapy, ATT, antibiotics, surgical repair).

Large-volume paracentesis with albumin (8 g/L removed > 5 L) for symptom relief.

**TB peritonitis:** standard ATT (HRZE 2 mo + HR 4 mo per NTEP; extended to 9 mo if extensive/cavitary).

**Malignant:** paracentesis, intraperitoneal chemotherapy (selected), shunts (Denver), palliative care.

Fig 9. Ascites — SAAG-guided workup.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD ascites 2012/21; ICMR TB Peritonitis.

### Combined Notes (50 topics)

### Definition

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterised by reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness, and clinically by recurrent episodes of wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough – typically worse at night or early morning.

### Etiology and Risk Factors

**Host:** Atopic individuals; family history of asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, ORMDL3, IL-13.

**Environmental:** Allergens (house dust mite, animal dander, pollen, moulds, cockroach), respiratory infections (RSV, rhinovirus), tobacco smoke, indoor/outdoor air pollution, occupational exposures (isocyanates, flour, latex), exercise, cold air.

**Drugs:** β-blockers, aspirin/NSAIDs (AERD/Samter's triad – asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity).

**Triggers:** Emotion, GERD, obesity, OSA, pregnancy.

**Indian context:** Urban air pollution, biomass fuel exposure, and undiagnosed allergic rhinitis are particularly relevant.

### Pathophysiology

Antigen exposure → IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation → release of histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4), prostaglandins → early-phase bronchoconstriction (15–30 min). Cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes → late-phase response (4–8 h) with mucosal oedema, mucus plugging and ongoing inflammation. Chronic inflammation leads to airway remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia) and fixed obstruction. Result: airway hyper-responsiveness, variable airflow limitation, and reversibility with bronchodilators or steroids.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, dry cough, chest tightness – often nocturnal / early morning; symptom-free intervals.

**Pattern:** Diurnal variation; triggers (cold, exercise, allergen, URTI); personal/family atopy.

**Signs:** Tachypnoea, prolonged expiration, bilateral polyphonic wheeze, hyperinflation; eczema, allergic rhinitis. In severe attacks: tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, accessory-muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences.

### Asthma severity in acute attack (BTS/GINA)

**Mild:** PEFR >75%, talking in sentences.

**Moderate:** PEFR 50–75%.

**Acute severe:** PEFR 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, cannot complete sentences.

**Life-threatening:** PEFR <33%, SpO₂ <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, exhaustion, altered consciousness, normal/raised PaCO₂.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) – diurnal variation >20%, drop during attack.

**Spirometry:** Obstructive pattern – FEV1/FVC <0.70, reversibility with bronchodilator (FEV1 ↑≥12% AND ≥200 mL).

**Bronchial provocation:** If spirometry normal but symptoms suggestive – methacholine or histamine challenge (PC20 < 8 mg/mL = positive).

**Labs:** Eosinophil count, total IgE, specific allergen IgE; sputum eosinophil count >2%; fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) >25 ppb in eosinophilic asthma.

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray – usually normal; hyperinflation in exacerbation; rules out pneumothorax, infection.

**ABG:** ABG in acute severe attack (normal/rising PaCO₂ is a warning sign).

**Other:** Skin prick test, RAST for specific allergens; ENT review for nasal polyps.

### Management (GINA 2023 + Indian context)

**Goals:** control symptoms, prevent exacerbations, maintain normal lung function, avoid medication side-effects.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA tracks 1 & 2):

**Step 1:** As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred Track 1) or SABA + low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA used.

**Step 2:** Daily low-dose ICS (budesonide 200–400 µg, fluticasone 100–250 µg) + SABA PRN.

**Step 3:** Low-dose ICS-LABA (budesonide/formoterol) + PRN.

**Step 4:** Medium-dose ICS-LABA + PRN.

**Step 5:** High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on: tiotropium (LAMA), biologics (omalizumab anti-IgE; mepolizumab/reslizumab anti-IL-5; dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast); low-dose oral corticosteroid (last resort).

Acute severe asthma (Indian ICU practice + BTS/GINA):

Sit patient up, high-flow O₂ via mask, target SpO₂ 94–98%.

Salbutamol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebuliser (back-to-back q15min × 3).

Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (or Methylprednisolone 60–125 mg IV) → continue Prednisolone 40–50 mg PO daily × 5 days.

Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min in severe attack.

IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg loading, 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion) only if above measures fail; monitor levels.

Antibiotics only if clear infection (CXR consolidation, purulent sputum, fever).

ICU admission if life-threatening / not improving; intubation for exhaustion, falling PEFR, rising PaCO₂.

### Non-pharmacological:

Trigger avoidance (allergens, smoke, occupational), weight reduction, GERD treatment, treat allergic rhinitis (nasal steroid).

Patient education, written action plan (green-yellow-red zones), inhaler technique (MDI + spacer for children/elderly; turbohaler/DPI for adults).

Annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination for severe.

Allergen immunotherapy in selected cases.

Fig 1. GINA 2023 stepwise management of asthma (Track 1, preferred path with ICS-formoterol reliever).

Fig 2. Acute severe asthma – emergency management algorithm.

### Complications

Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

Aspergillosis (ABPA – worsening asthma + central bronchiectasis + peripheral eosinophilia + raised IgE).

Long-term airway remodelling, fixed obstruction.

**Side-effects of treatment:** oral candidiasis, dysphonia (ICS), osteoporosis, cushingoid features (oral steroids), tremor (β-agonists).

### Prognosis

Most patients have well-controlled disease with modern therapy. Asthma mortality is low but preventable; under-treatment with ICS, over-reliance on SABA, and poor adherence/inhaler technique are the key contributors to fatal asthma.

### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

ILDs are a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases characterised by varying degrees of inflammation and fibrosis of the alveolar walls and interstitium, producing restrictive lung disease and impaired gas exchange.

Examples by category (four key examples + classification)

### Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias:

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – usual interstitial pneumonia pattern; older adults; honeycombing.

Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP).

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP).

Acute interstitial pneumonia.

ILD due to known cause:

Connective tissue disease–associated ILD: RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, dermatomyositis (anti-Jo1), Sjögren's, MCTD.

**Drug-induced:** amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin, busulfan, gold, statins.

Radiation pneumonitis.

### Pneumoconioses (occupational):

Silicosis (silica – stone-cutters, quartz miners – egg-shell calcification of hilar nodes).

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis (coal dust – Caplan's syndrome with RA).

Asbestosis (asbestos – pleural plaques, mesothelioma risk).

Berylliosis (aerospace industry).

Byssinosis (cotton dust – Monday-morning chest tightness).

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (organic dusts) – Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay), Bird-fancier's lung (avian proteins).

### Granulomatous ILDs:

Sarcoidosis – multisystem; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + interstitial infiltrates.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

### Other:

Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers).

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women of reproductive age).

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

### Clinical features

Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, fatigue, clubbing (especially IPF and asbestosis).

Velcro-like end-inspiratory crackles at lung bases.

Extra-pulmonary features (rash, arthritis, eye involvement) point to connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis.

### Investigations

HRCT chest is the cornerstone – pattern (UIP, NSIP, OP, HP) often diagnostic.

**Spirometry:** restrictive (FEV1/FVC ≥0.70, ↓TLC, ↓DLCO).

6-minute walk test – desaturation, exercise tolerance.

**Serology:** ANA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Scl70, anti-Jo1, ANCA, IgG precipitins for HP.

BAL (cell differential), transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy if diagnosis unclear.

### Treatment principles

Remove inciting agent (drugs, occupational exposure).

Corticosteroids ± immunosuppressants (azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide) for inflammatory ILDs (NSIP, COP, HP, CTD-ILD).

Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) for IPF and progressive fibrosing ILDs – slow FVC decline.

Long-term O₂ therapy in chronic hypoxia.

Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations.

Lung transplantation in eligible.

### Cardiovascular

Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina) – retrosternal, crushing, >20 min, radiation to left arm/jaw.

Stable angina – exertional, <10 min, relieved by rest/GTN.

Aortic dissection – sudden, tearing, between shoulder blades, BP/pulse asymmetry, widened mediastinum.

Pericarditis – sharp, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, rub on auscultation.

Myocarditis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe aortic stenosis.

### Respiratory

Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, risk factors.

Pneumonia, pleurisy – pleuritic, fever, cough.

Pneumothorax – sudden, unilateral, dyspnoea.

Asthma exacerbation, bronchitis.

Lung cancer (chest wall invasion).

### Gastrointestinal

GERD / oesophagitis – retrosternal burning, post-prandial, supine.

Oesophageal spasm – may mimic ACS.

Peptic ulcer disease, gastritis.

Boerhaave's syndrome (oesophageal rupture – Mackler triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema).

Pancreatitis (radiates to back), biliary colic.

### Musculoskeletal

Costochondritis / Tietze's syndrome – localised, reproducible tenderness.

Rib fracture, intercostal muscle strain.

Cervical spondylosis (radicular).

### Other

Herpes zoster (dermatomal).

Anxiety / panic attack – associated with hyperventilation.

Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crisis (acute chest syndrome).

**Approach:** ECG within 10 min in any adult with chest pain; troponin; CXR; consider CT pulmonary angiogram for PE, CT angio for aortic dissection; echocardiography. Wells score, HEART score, GRACE/TIMI guide risk-stratification.

### Definition

Localised collection of pus within the lung parenchyma due to microbial infection, leading to tissue necrosis and cavitation.

### Etiology

**Primary (aspiration):** Aspiration (commonest) – alcoholics, post-anaesthesia, stroke, epilepsy, GERD. Anaerobic flora from oral cavity.

**Secondary:** Bronchial obstruction (carcinoma, foreign body), septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided endocarditis, IV drug use), spread from subphrenic/hepatic abscess.

**Organisms:** Anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides), Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza), Streptococcus milleri, gram-negative bacilli, fungi (immunocompromised).

### Clinical Features

Insidious – fever, malaise, weight loss, night sweats over weeks.

Productive cough with copious foul-smelling sputum (anaerobes); may be blood-stained.

Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

Halitosis.

**Signs:** clubbing (chronic), dull percussion, bronchial/amphoric breathing, post-tussive crackles, signs of consolidation.

### Investigations

CXR – cavity with air-fluid level, surrounding consolidation; usual site posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe (gravity-dependent in supine aspiration).

CT chest – delineates cavity, exclude underlying mass.

Sputum gram stain, AFB, culture (aerobic and anaerobic), cytology.

Bronchoscopy – exclude obstruction, obtain protected specimen, facilitate drainage.

Blood culture (especially in septic embolism, IE).

Echo if right-sided endocarditis suspected.

### Management

Empirical antibiotic with anaerobic cover: IV clindamycin 600 mg q8h, OR β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam), OR metronidazole + ceftriaxone.

Add vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA suspected; add fluconazole/voriconazole if fungal.

**Duration:** 4–6 weeks, IV until clinical improvement then PO (oral amoxicillin-clavulanate + metronidazole).

Postural drainage and physiotherapy to facilitate sputum clearance.

Bronchoscopic drainage if poor response (large cavity >6 cm, obstructing lesion).

Percutaneous catheter drainage in selected (refractory abscess).

Surgical resection (lobectomy/segmentectomy) – rarely needed; indications: persistent abscess despite 6–8 wk antibiotic, massive haemoptysis, suspected malignancy, bronchopleural fistula.

**Treat underlying cause:** dental hygiene, anti-seizure medication, swallow assessment, GERD therapy, treat malignancy if present.

### Complications

Empyema, bronchopleural fistula, massive haemoptysis, septicaemia, metastatic abscess (brain, etc.), amyloidosis (chronic), respiratory failure.

Haemoptysis = coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract (below the larynx). Massive haemoptysis = >200–600 mL in 24 h.

### Causes by category

### Infective (commonest in India):

Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially cavitary or post-tubercular bronchiectasis with Rasmussen aneurysm).

Bronchiectasis.

Lung abscess.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella, anaerobes).

Pulmonary aspergilloma (mycetoma in old TB cavity).

Paragonimiasis (in endemic areas).

### Neoplastic:

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Bronchial carcinoid.

Metastatic lung tumours.

### Vascular:

Pulmonary embolism with infarction.

Mitral stenosis (pulmonary venous hypertension).

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (HHT/Osler-Weber-Rendu).

Aortobronchial fistula.

### Inflammatory / autoimmune:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-GBM antibody).

SLE-associated pulmonary haemorrhage.

Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis (in children).

Iatrogenic / trauma / coagulopathy:

Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs), thrombolytics.

Bronchoscopic biopsy, transbronchial biopsy.

Tracheostomy, Swan-Ganz catheter (pulmonary artery rupture).

Chest trauma.

Cocaine use.

**Pseudohaemoptysis:** epistaxis, haematemesis swallowed and regurgitated, Serratia marcescens in dentures, oral bleeding.

### Approach

Distinguish from haematemesis (bright red, frothy, alkaline pH, mixed with sputum vs dark red, acidic, with food, melena later).

Stabilise (ABCDE) if massive – airway, position bleeding side down, IV access, group and cross-match.

CXR, CT chest with contrast/CT pulmonary angiogram, bronchoscopy (rigid for massive), echo, CBC, coagulation, sputum AFB.

Massive haemoptysis – ICU, bronchial artery embolisation, endobronchial tamponade, surgical resection if focal source.

### Definition

Air in the pleural cavity, causing lung collapse. Classified as spontaneous (primary/secondary), traumatic (penetrating/blunt), or iatrogenic; and by severity as simple, tension, or open.

Risk factors and causes

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP – no underlying lung disease):

Tall, thin young males (apical sub-pleural blebs).

Smoking (×20 risk).

Family history (Marfan syndrome, Birt-Hogg-Dubé).

Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, homocystinuria.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP – with lung disease):

COPD/emphysema (bullae rupture) – commonest in adults.

Asthma exacerbation.

Tuberculosis (cavitary disease, India).

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (HIV/AIDS).

Cystic fibrosis, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM – women), Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers), Birt-Hogg-Dubé.

Bronchogenic carcinoma, metastatic disease.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Catamenial pneumothorax – endometriosis (around menstruation).

### Traumatic pneumothorax:

**Penetrating:** stab, gunshot.

**Blunt:** rib fracture, deceleration injury.

### Iatrogenic:

Central venous catheterisation (especially subclavian).

Thoracentesis, pleural biopsy.

Transbronchial / transthoracic lung biopsy.

Barotrauma from mechanical ventilation, NIV.

Acupuncture, intercostal nerve block.

**Tension pneumothorax:** any of above with continued air entry through a one-way valve mechanism → mediastinal shift, cardiovascular collapse – emergency.

### Clinical features (brief)

Sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, dry cough.

Decreased breath sounds, hyper-resonance, decreased vocal fremitus on the affected side.

**Tension:** tachycardia, hypotension, tracheal deviation away, raised JVP – needle decompression in 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line immediately, then chest tube.

### Management (brief)

PSP <2 cm rim, no breathlessness: observe + O₂.

**PSP ≥2 cm or breathless:** needle aspiration; if fails, chest tube.

**SSP ≥1 cm or breathless:** chest tube (most cases).

**Recurrent:** VATS pleurodesis or pleurectomy.

Stop smoking, avoid scuba diving and flying (until resolved).

### Light's criteria

Effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met:

Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5.

Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Causes (mnemonic:** 'Pus, blood, fluid from inflammation')

### Infective:

Parapneumonic effusion / empyema (Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Tuberculous pleural effusion (the commonest cause of exudative effusion in young adults in India – lymphocytic, ADA >40 U/L, biopsy shows granulomas).

Fungal (rare), parasitic (amoebic, hydatid).

Malignancy (commonest cause of exudate in elderly):

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Breast carcinoma.

Lymphoma, leukaemia.

Mesothelioma (asbestos-related).

Ovarian carcinoma (Meigs syndrome with ascites).

Connective tissue / autoimmune:

Rheumatoid arthritis (low glucose, low pH, low complement, RF positive).

SLE.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Pulmonary embolism / infarction.

### Gastrointestinal / abdominal:

Pancreatitis (left-sided, high amylase).

Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave's – high amylase from saliva, low pH).

Subdiaphragmatic abscess.

Post-CABG.

### Drugs:

Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine.

### Other:

Radiation therapy.

Chylothorax (lymphoma, trauma, thoracic-duct obstruction – triglycerides >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons).

Haemothorax (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation).

Yellow nail syndrome.

Fig 6. Pleural effusion – diagnostic algorithm using Light's criteria.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

### Definition

Single, well-defined, rounded opacity ≤3 cm in diameter, surrounded by normal lung, without associated atelectasis or lymphadenopathy. Important because malignancy must be excluded.

### Differential diagnosis

### Malignant (40%):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (adenocarcinoma commonest in non-smokers).

Carcinoid tumour.

Solitary metastasis (colon, breast, renal, sarcoma, melanoma).

Lymphoma (rare).

### Benign (60%):

Infectious granuloma (tuberculoma – India's commonest), histoplasmoma, cryptococcoma, aspergilloma.

Hamartoma (popcorn calcification).

Lung abscess (early).

Pulmonary AVM.

Round atelectasis.

Rheumatoid nodule.

Wegener's granulomatous nodule.

Bronchogenic cyst, sequestration.

Pulmonary infarct.

### Features suggesting malignancy

Age >50, smoker, size >2 cm, spiculated margin, irregular shape, growth on serial imaging, lack of calcification (or eccentric calcification), upper lobe location, PET-avid (SUV >2.5).

### Features suggesting benignity

Age <40, never-smoker, well-defined smooth margin, central/diffuse/popcorn/laminated calcification, stability >2 years, small (<1 cm), fat density (hamartoma).
