### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

PUD = mucosal break ≥ 5 mm in the stomach (gastric ulcer) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer) reaching the muscularis mucosae. Common in Indian adults; lifetime prevalence ~ 5–10%.

### Etiology

**H. pylori:** H. pylori: Causes ~ 70% of DU and ~ 50% of GU in India; gram-negative spiral bacillus; urease produces ammonia → ↓ mucosal protection.

**NSAIDs:** NSAIDs: ↓ prostaglandin → ↓ mucosal defence; risk ↑ with age, high dose, prior PUD, concurrent steroids/anticoagulants.

**Other:** Other: Smoking, alcohol, stress (Curling's — burns; Cushing's — head injury), Zollinger-Ellison, hyperparathyroidism, viral (CMV, HSV in immunocompromised).

### Clinical Features

Epigastric burning/gnawing pain.

**DU:** pain 2–3 h after meals, at night, relieved by food/antacids.

**GU:** pain DURING/SOON after meals, food may worsen; weight loss commoner.

Nausea, bloating, early satiety; in chronic — anaemia (occult blood loss).

**Complications:** bleed (haematemesis/melaena), perforation (sudden severe pain, board-like rigidity), gastric outlet obstruction (postprandial vomiting, succussion splash).

### Investigations

### H. pylori testing

**Non-invasive:** urea breath test (UBT, gold standard), stool antigen, serology (only for screening).

**Invasive (during OGD):** rapid urease test (CLO), histology, culture (resistance testing).

**Test prep:** STOP PPI 2 wk and antibiotics 4 wk before UBT/stool/biopsy to avoid false-negative.

### Endoscopy (OGD)

**Indication:** age ≥ 55 with new dyspepsia, alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, anaemia, GI bleed, persistent vomiting, mass), failure of empirical therapy.

All GASTRIC ulcers MUST be biopsied (rule out malignancy) — biopsy edge × 4 + base × 2 + biopsy for H. pylori.

Duodenal ulcers usually do not need biopsy unless atypical.

### Management

### 1. Acid Suppression

**PPI:** pantoprazole 40 mg OD (or omeprazole 20 mg OD, esomeprazole 40 mg OD, rabeprazole 20 mg OD) × 4 weeks (DU) or 6–8 weeks (GU).

Take 30–60 min before breakfast.

H2RA (ranitidine — no longer available due to NDMA; famotidine 20 mg BD) — second-line.

Antacids (Al/Mg hydroxide) for symptom relief.

- H. pylori Eradication (if positive)

Standard triple therapy (clari resistance < 15%):

PPI BD + clarithromycin 500 BD + amoxicillin 1 g BD × 14 days (or metronidazole 500 BD if penicillin-allergic).

Bismuth-based quadruple (if clari resistance > 15% or treatment failure):

PPI BD + bismuth subcitrate 120 mg QID + tetracycline 500 mg QID + metronidazole 400 mg TDS × 10–14 days.

**Concomitant therapy:** PPI + amox + clari + metro × 10–14 d.

**Levofloxacin-based salvage:** PPI + amox + levofloxacin 500 OD × 10–14 d (2nd-line after triple failure).

**Confirm eradication:** UBT or stool antigen ≥ 4 wk after stopping antibiotics, ≥ 2 wk after PPI.

### 3. Lifestyle / Aetiology

Stop NSAIDs (or use COX-2 + PPI / misoprostol cover).

Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation.

Avoid spicy / acidic food during healing phase.

Stress management (less evidence but practiced).

### 4. Complicated PUD

### 5. Follow-up

**DU:** no routine repeat OGD if symptoms resolve.

**GU:** REPEAT OGD at 8–12 weeks to confirm healing and biopsy if not healed (malignancy).

Long-term PPI if continued NSAID, high-risk patients, persistent symptoms.

Fig 7. PUD — H. pylori test-and-treat algorithm.

### Complications

Bleed (15–20%), perforation (5–10%), gastric outlet obstruction (2–5%), gastric cancer (long-standing H. pylori GU), penetration into pancreas (severe back pain).

### Prognosis

Excellent with H. pylori eradication and PPI therapy — recurrence < 5% vs > 70% without eradication. GU has higher malignancy risk (~ 3%) → mandatory follow-up biopsy.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11 p.487; Davidson Ch.21; Maastricht VI/Florence 2022; ICMR antibiotic policy 2022.

### Definition

Loss of oral mucosal continuity exposing underlying connective tissue. May be acute (< 2 wk), subacute (2–6 wk), or chronic (> 6 wk). Persistent ulcers > 3 weeks require malignancy exclusion.

### Etiology

### 1. Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS) — commonest (20%)

### 2. Infections

**Viral:** HSV-1 (primary gingivostomatitis, recurrent herpes labialis), VZV (chickenpox/shingles), HFMD (Coxsackie A16), HIV (multiple persistent), CMV (immunocompromised).

**Bacterial:** syphilis (chancre, mucous patches, gumma), TB (chronic indurated ulcer with undermined edges — usually dorsum of tongue), Vincent's angina (necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis — Borrelia + fusobacterium).

**Fungal:** candidiasis (white plaques, erythematous), histoplasmosis, mucormycosis (uncontrolled DM, COVID-19-associated CAM in India).

### 3. Systemic Diseases

Crohn's disease (cobblestone mucosa, deep linear ulcers).

Coeliac disease (apthous ulcers, glossitis, dental enamel defects).

Behçet's disease — recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy (>3 episodes/yr).

PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) — paeds.

Reiter's syndrome (oral + genital ulcers + arthritis + conjunctivitis).

SLE — palatal ulcers (one of ACR criteria); painless typically.

Pemphigus vulgaris — flaccid bullae → erosions; Nikolsky+.

Mucous membrane pemphigoid — subepithelial, scarring; ocular involvement common.

Lichen planus — Wickham's striae, erosive form painful; pre-malignant.

Erythema multiforme major / SJS-TEN — drug or HSV-triggered, target lesions, conjunctivitis.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome — mucocutaneous with skin involvement.

### 4. Nutritional Deficiencies

B12 (Hunter's glossitis, atrophic), folate, iron (angular cheilitis, glossitis, koilonychia), vitamin C (scurvy — gingival bleeding, swollen gums).

Zinc deficiency.

### 5. Haematological

Neutropenia / agranulocytosis (chemo, drugs — clozapine, methimazole), acute leukaemia, cyclic neutropenia.

### 6. Drugs

Methotrexate, NSAIDs, β-blockers (atenolol), nicorandil (typically painful, large), sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor), bisphosphonates (ONJ — osteonecrosis of jaw).

### 7. Malignancy

**Indian context:** Squamous cell carcinoma (commonest oral malignancy in India — tobacco, areca nut, alcohol). Non-healing > 3 wk ulcer, induration, raised everted edges → biopsy mandatory.

**Pre-malignant lesions:** leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut chewing — Indian endemic), lichen planus.

### 8. Trauma

Mechanical (dental, ill-fitting denture, tongue bite), thermal, chemical (aspirin burn).

### Clinical Approach

**Duration:** acute (HSV, RAS, trauma), chronic (TB, malignancy, autoimmune, drugs).

**Single vs multiple:** single chronic → malignancy/TB; multiple recurrent → RAS, Behçet's, IBD.

Painful (most ulcers) vs painless (syphilis, SLE, TB tongue, malignancy).

Associated features — genital ulcer, eye, GI, skin, fever.

### Investigations

**Blood:** CBC, ESR/CRP, ferritin, B12/folate, HIV serology, fasting glucose, TSH.

**If suspected systemic:** tTG (coeliac), ANA, ANCA, IgA/IgG (Behçet's), VDRL.

Biopsy if non-healing > 3 wk, atypical, suspected malignancy/lichen planus.

Swab for HSV PCR, candida (KOH), syphilis serology (TPHA, VDRL).

### Management

### General

Identify and treat underlying cause.

**Pain relief:** paracetamol, NSAIDs (avoid if drug-induced).

Topical anaesthetic (lignocaine 2% viscous gel) for severe pain.

Antiseptic mouthwash — chlorhexidine 0.2% rinse BD, povidone iodine.

Avoid irritants (spicy, hot, alcohol-containing mouthwash).

### RAS-Specific

**Topical corticosteroids:** triamcinolone 0.1% in adhesive base (Kenalog in Orabase), dexamethasone elixir 0.5 mg/5 ml rinse-and-spit QID.

Tetracycline mouthwash (250 mg in 5 ml water, hold 2 min, spit QID).

**Severe/refractory:** systemic prednisolone 30–60 mg/d short course, colchicine 0.5 mg BD-TDS, thalidomide (severe HIV-related), dapsone, apremilast.

**Address triggers:** stress, food (chocolate, nuts, citrus), smoking cessation.

### Specific Causes

### Prognosis

Variable. RAS — recurrent, lifelong but harmless. Malignancy → 5-yr survival depends on stage. Indian context: oral SCC accounts for ~ 30% of all cancers in men.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; Davidson Ch.21 (mucocutaneous); Indian oral cancer guidelines.

### Definition

A circumscribed break in the duodenal mucosa, extending through the muscularis mucosae, more common than gastric ulcer (4:1 ratio). 95% are located in the duodenal bulb (D1). Aetiology: H. pylori (70–90%), NSAIDs, stress, smoking, alcohol. Peak incidence 25–50 yr; M:F 3:1.

### Clinical Features

Epigastric pain — burning, gnawing, classically 2–3 h after meals (when stomach empty), RELIEVED by food / antacid; night pain awakens patient (1–3 am).

Periodicity — clusters of symptoms over 2–4 wk, then remission weeks-months.

Anorexia, weight loss — UNCOMMON (vs gastric ulcer where often present).

Nausea, vomiting (only if outlet obstruction).

**May present with complication:** bleed (haematemesis, melaena), perforation (sudden severe pain), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting, succussion splash).

**Examination:** epigastric tenderness; usually no other signs in uncomplicated.

### Investigations

### First-line

CBC — anaemia (chronic bleed).

LFT, U&E — exclude alternatives.

ECG — exclude cardiac cause (inferior MI presents with epigastric pain).

### H. pylori Testing (essential)

Endoscopy (OGD) — when needed

**Indications:** > 55 yr new symptoms, ALARM features, failure of empirical Rx, complications (bleed, perforation), recurrent symptoms.

DU appears as round/oval punched-out lesion in bulb with white fibrinous base.

DU biopsy NOT routine (cancer rare); biopsy if atypical site, irregular, refractory.

Antral biopsies × 2 + body biopsies × 2 (Sydney) for H. pylori + premalignant changes.

### Refractory / Atypical

Fasting serum gastrin — rule out Zollinger-Ellison (PPI cessation 1 wk first).

Calcium, PTH (MEN-1).

Crohn's serology, biopsy.

### Management

### Lifestyle

Stop NSAIDs (use paracetamol instead, or COX-2 + PPI if needed).

Stop / reduce smoking, alcohol.

Avoid trigger foods (spicy, caffeine — patient-specific).

Small frequent meals.

Reduce stress.

### Acid Suppression

**PPI:** pantoprazole 40 mg OD or omeprazole 20 mg OD or esomeprazole 40 mg OD × 4 weeks. Best taken 30 min before breakfast.

H2 receptor antagonists (less preferred): ranitidine 150 BD or famotidine 40 OD × 4 wk.

**Antacids (symptomatic adjunct):** Mg/Al hydroxide combination.

Sucralfate 1 g QID — cytoprotective (alternative in pregnancy).

H. pylori Eradication (if positive)

Triple therapy (first-line; if clari resistance < 15% in region):

PPI BD + Amoxicillin 1 g BD + Clarithromycin 500 mg BD × 14 d.

**Penicillin allergy:** replace amox with metronidazole 400 BD.

Bismuth quadruple (preferred in India — high clari resistance):

PPI BD + Bismuth subsalicylate 525 QID + Tetracycline 500 QID + Metronidazole 400 TDS × 10–14 d.

Concomitant (4 drugs, no bismuth): PPI BD + Amox 1g BD + Clari 500 BD + Metro 400 BD × 14 d.

**Sequential:** PPI + Amox × 5 d, then PPI + Clari + Metro × 5 d.

**Salvage (after first failure):** bismuth quadruple if not used, OR PPI + Levofloxacin 500 OD + Amox 1g BD × 10 d.

**Re-test:** UBT or stool antigen 4 weeks after stopping antibiotics; confirm eradication.

### Duration

**Uncomplicated DU:** 4 weeks PPI sufficient.

Complicated (bleed, perforation, large > 2 cm): 8 weeks PPI then UBT.

### Complications

- Bleeding (commonest, 15%)

Haematemesis, melaena. Resuscitate, OGD < 24 h. Forrest classification guides endotherapy (see Q1).

### 2. Perforation (5–10%)

Sudden severe epigastric pain → generalised peritonitis. Erect CXR — free gas under diaphragm. CT abdomen if uncertain.

**Management:** resuscitate, IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam), PPI IV, NG decompression, urgent surgery — Graham's omental patch closure (laparoscopic if available).

### 3. Gastric Outlet Obstruction (2–5%)

Chronic scarring / oedema → vomiting, succussion splash, electrolyte derangement (hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis), weight loss.

**Mx:** NG decompression, IV fluids/electrolytes, PPI; endoscopic balloon dilatation; if refractory — surgery (pyloroplasty, gastrojejunostomy).

### 4. Penetration

Posterior DU into pancreas → unrelenting back-pain, raised amylase.

### 5. Recurrence

10–30%/yr without H. pylori eradication; < 5%/yr after eradication.

Surgical Indications (rare in modern era)

Failure of medical therapy (rare with PPI + eradication).

**Complications:** perforation, refractory bleed, GOO, malignant transformation.

**Procedures:** Highly selective vagotomy + drainage (historical), truncal vagotomy + antrectomy + Billroth I/II, Roux-en-Y reconstruction (modern).

### Prognosis

Excellent with H. pylori eradication and avoidance of NSAIDs. Recurrence reduced from 60%/yr to < 5%/yr. Complications < 5% with appropriate management.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11 p.397; Maastricht VI Consensus 2022; ACG PUD 2017; Davidson Ch.23.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Cardiac Cycle (brief)

Each cycle (~0.8 s at 75 bpm) comprises: (i) atrial systole (0.1 s, the 'a' wave on JVP); (ii) isovolumetric ventricular contraction (S1, AV valves close); (iii) ventricular ejection (~0.3 s, aortic/pulmonary valves open); (iv) isovolumetric relaxation (S2, semilunar valves close); (v) rapid passive ventricular filling (S3 may be heard in HF); (vi) diastasis; with a return to atrial systole. The Wiggers diagram relates ECG, pressure, volume and heart sounds.

### Definition

Heart failure is the clinical syndrome resulting from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, leading to characteristic symptoms (dyspnoea, fatigue, fluid retention) and signs (raised JVP, crepitations, oedema). Classified by ejection fraction (HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%) and timing (acute vs chronic).

### Etiology

**Cardiac:** Ischaemic heart disease/MI (commonest), hypertension, valvular disease (AS, MR, AR), dilated/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease.

**Arrhythmia-induced:** Sustained tachyarrhythmia, AV block.

**High-output:** Anaemia (severe), thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, AV fistula, paget's, septic shock.

**Right HF:** Constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloid).

**Lung-related:** Cor pulmonale (COPD, pulmonary embolism), pulmonary hypertension.

**Drugs/toxins:** Anthracyclines (doxorubicin), trastuzumab, alcohol, cocaine, NSAIDs (precipitate).

### Precipitating Factors (acute decompensation)

**FAIL ME mnemonic:** Forgot medications, Arrhythmia/Anaemia, Infection, Lifestyle (salt/fluid), MI/ischaemia, Endocrine (thyroid, pregnancy).

### Clinical Features

**Left HF symptoms:** Exertional dyspnoea (NYHA I–IV), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, cough with frothy/pink sputum.

**Right HF symptoms:** Ankle oedema, abdominal distension (ascites), RUQ pain (hepatic congestion), anorexia, weight gain.

**Signs:** Tachycardia, tachypnoea, displaced apex, S3 gallop (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF), basal crepitations, pleural effusion, raised JVP, hepatomegaly with hepatojugular reflux, pitting pedal oedema, peripheral cyanosis, cold extremities.

### NYHA functional classification

**Class I:** No limitation of activity.

**Class II:** Slight limitation, comfortable at rest.

**Class III:** Marked limitation, comfortable at rest only.

**Class IV:** Symptoms at rest.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** ECG (rule out ischaemia, arrhythmia, LBBB), CXR (cardiomegaly CTR>50%, Kerley B lines, upper-lobe diversion, pleural effusion), SpO₂.

**Biomarker:** BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL → HF likely. <35/125 essentially rules out HF.

**Echocardiogram:** Most important – LVEF, chamber size, wall motion, valves, diastolic function, PASP.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes, LFT (congestive hepatopathy), glucose, HbA1c, lipid, TSH, urinalysis, iron studies (HF + iron deficiency common).

**Advanced:** Coronary angiography if ischaemic aetiology, cardiac MRI for myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, RHC if pulmonary hypertension or transplant work-up.

### Management

**Goals:** relieve symptoms, prevent hospitalisation, prolong survival.

### Acute / decompensated:

**LMNOP:** Position upright, O₂ to keep SpO₂>92%; NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) if pulmonary oedema and not in shock.

Lasix (furosemide 40–80 mg IV), Morphine 2–4 mg IV (relieves anxiety, venodilator), Nitrate (sublingual or IV if BP adequate), Oxygen, Position upright.

**Inotropes:** Dobutamine, milrinone (if low output, cardiogenic shock) – use in critical care.

**Mechanical:** IABP or LV assist device in refractory shock.

Chronic HFrEF – Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT, '4 pillars'):

**1. ARNI/ACEi/ARB:** Sacubitril/valsartan or ACEi (enalapril/ramipril) or ARB (losartan/valsartan).

**2. β-blocker:** Carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate. Start low, titrate up.

**3. MRA:** Spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone (monitor K+, creatinine).

**4. SGLT2 inhibitor:** Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg OD – benefit irrespective of diabetes.

**Add-on:** Loop diuretic (furosemide/torsemide) for congestion; ivabradine if HR>70 in sinus on max β-blocker; digoxin if AF or refractory symptoms; hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate (esp. in Black patients or ACEi-intolerant).

### Chronic HFpEF:

Treat HTN, AF (rate/rhythm), DM, obesity, sleep apnoea, iron deficiency.

Diuretic for congestion; SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin/dapagliflozin) reduces hospitalisation in HFpEF.

### Device therapy:

ICD if EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months GDMT (primary prevention of sudden death).

CRT (cardiac resynchronisation) if EF ≤35%, LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–IV in sinus rhythm.

### Advanced HF:

LVAD as bridge or destination therapy; cardiac transplantation in eligible patients.

### Lifestyle:

Sodium <2 g/d, fluid <1.5–2 L/d if hyponatraemic or congested, daily weights, exercise rehabilitation, smoking and alcohol cessation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19), patient education for self-monitoring.

Fig 2. Heart failure – diagnosis and management algorithm.

### Complications & Prognosis

Acute decompensation, arrhythmias (AF, VT/VF), sudden cardiac death, thromboembolism, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cachexia, hepatic congestion.

5-year mortality ~50% for symptomatic HFrEF; modern GDMT improves survival significantly.

Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL or rapid drop) produces a hyperdynamic, high-output circulatory state.

**Symptoms:** Tachycardia, palpitations, exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, dizziness/syncope, angina (if underlying CAD).

**Pulse and BP:** Bounding/collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, low diastolic BP.

**Precordium:** Hyperdynamic apex; mid-systolic ejection (haemic) murmur at aortic / pulmonary area; functional mid-diastolic flow rumble at apex/tricuspid area in very severe anaemia; S3 gallop.

**Other:** Venous hum in the neck (Carotid bruit, child-bearing women), capillary pulsations.

**Decompensation:** High-output cardiac failure (anaemic heart failure) – orthopnoea, raised JVP, hepatomegaly, oedema – seen with chronic severe anaemia and pre-existing cardiac disease.

ECG may show non-specific ST/T changes; CXR – cardiomegaly; echo – dilated chambers with preserved EF; biomarkers (troponin, BNP) raised in decompensation.

Cardiovascular causes (mostly Type 1)

Acute pulmonary oedema (LVF, valvular crisis, hypertensive emergency).

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock.

Cardiac tamponade.

### Cardiac Cycle (brief)

Each cycle (~0.8 s at 75 bpm) comprises: (i) atrial systole (0.1 s, the 'a' wave on JVP); (ii) isovolumetric ventricular contraction (S1, AV valves close); (iii) ventricular ejection (~0.3 s, aortic/pulmonary valves open); (iv) isovolumetric relaxation (S2, semilunar valves close); (v) rapid passive ventricular filling (S3 may be heard in HF); (vi) diastasis; with a return to atrial systole. The Wiggers diagram relates ECG, pressure, volume and heart sounds.

### Definition

Heart failure is the clinical syndrome resulting from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, leading to characteristic symptoms (dyspnoea, fatigue, fluid retention) and signs (raised JVP, crepitations, oedema). Classified by ejection fraction (HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%) and timing (acute vs chronic).

### Etiology

**Cardiac:** Ischaemic heart disease/MI (commonest), hypertension, valvular disease (AS, MR, AR), dilated/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease.

**Arrhythmia-induced:** Sustained tachyarrhythmia, AV block.

**High-output:** Anaemia (severe), thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, AV fistula, paget's, septic shock.

**Right HF:** Constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloid).

**Lung-related:** Cor pulmonale (COPD, pulmonary embolism), pulmonary hypertension.

**Drugs/toxins:** Anthracyclines (doxorubicin), trastuzumab, alcohol, cocaine, NSAIDs (precipitate).

### Precipitating Factors (acute decompensation)

**FAIL ME mnemonic:** Forgot medications, Arrhythmia/Anaemia, Infection, Lifestyle (salt/fluid), MI/ischaemia, Endocrine (thyroid, pregnancy).

### Clinical Features

**Left HF symptoms:** Exertional dyspnoea (NYHA I–IV), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, cough with frothy/pink sputum.

**Right HF symptoms:** Ankle oedema, abdominal distension (ascites), RUQ pain (hepatic congestion), anorexia, weight gain.

**Signs:** Tachycardia, tachypnoea, displaced apex, S3 gallop (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF), basal crepitations, pleural effusion, raised JVP, hepatomegaly with hepatojugular reflux, pitting pedal oedema, peripheral cyanosis, cold extremities.

### NYHA functional classification

**Class I:** No limitation of activity.

**Class II:** Slight limitation, comfortable at rest.

**Class III:** Marked limitation, comfortable at rest only.

**Class IV:** Symptoms at rest.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** ECG (rule out ischaemia, arrhythmia, LBBB), CXR (cardiomegaly CTR>50%, Kerley B lines, upper-lobe diversion, pleural effusion), SpO₂.

**Biomarker:** BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL → HF likely. <35/125 essentially rules out HF.

**Echocardiogram:** Most important – LVEF, chamber size, wall motion, valves, diastolic function, PASP.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes, LFT (congestive hepatopathy), glucose, HbA1c, lipid, TSH, urinalysis, iron studies (HF + iron deficiency common).

**Advanced:** Coronary angiography if ischaemic aetiology, cardiac MRI for myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, RHC if pulmonary hypertension or transplant work-up.

**Goals:** relieve symptoms, prevent hospitalisation, prolong survival.

### Acute / decompensated:

**LMNOP:** Position upright, O₂ to keep SpO₂>92%; NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) if pulmonary oedema and not in shock.

Lasix (furosemide 40–80 mg IV), Morphine 2–4 mg IV (relieves anxiety, venodilator), Nitrate (sublingual or IV if BP adequate), Oxygen, Position upright.

**Inotropes:** Dobutamine, milrinone (if low output, cardiogenic shock) – use in critical care.

**1. ARNI/ACEi/ARB:** Sacubitril/valsartan or ACEi (enalapril/ramipril) or ARB (losartan/valsartan).

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

JVP reflects right atrial pressure. Normally <3 cm vertical height above sternal angle (i.e. <8 cm H₂O), seen with patient at 45°, with two visible peaks per beat.

### Positive waves

**a:** atrial contraction.

**c:** transmitted carotid pulse + bulging tricuspid valve into right atrium during isovolumetric RV contraction.

**v:** atrial filling against closed tricuspid valve in ventricular systole.

### Negative waves (descents)

**x:** after a wave – atrial relaxation.

**x′:** after c wave – downward pull of TV during ventricular ejection (true 'x' descent).

**y:** after v wave – TV opens, blood empties into RV.

Abnormal waves – clinical clues

**Large a:** tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, PS, RV hypertrophy.

**Cannon a:** AV dissociation (CHB, ventricular tachycardia, junctional rhythm).

**Absent a:** atrial fibrillation.

**Large v:** tricuspid regurgitation (giant v / cv).

**Steep y descent:** constrictive pericarditis (Friedreich's sign).

**Absent y descent:** tamponade (Beck's), severe RV failure.

Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises with inspiration): constrictive pericarditis.

Pulse character provides important diagnostic clues. Examine for rate, rhythm, volume, character, and symmetry.

**Rate:** Tachycardia (>100), bradycardia (<60).

**Rhythm:** Regular, regularly irregular, irregularly irregular (AF).

### Pulse characters

**Pulsus parvus et tardus:** small-volume, slow-rising → aortic stenosis.

**Water-hammer (Corrigan) pulse:** rapid upstroke and collapse → AR, PDA, AV fistula, high-output states.

**Bisferiens pulse:** two systolic peaks → severe AR, HOCM.

**Dicrotic pulse:** double impulse, one systolic + diastolic, normal volume → constrictive pericarditis, severe tamponade post-pericardiocentesis.

**Pulsus alternans:** alternating strong and weak beats with regular rhythm → severe LV dysfunction.

**Pulsus paradoxus:** fall in SBP >10 mmHg on inspiration → tamponade, severe asthma/COPD, constrictive pericarditis, large PE.

**Pulsus bigeminus:** alternating large and small after sequence → bigeminy.

**Thready:** low-volume.

Radio-radial / radio-femoral delay: delay between brachial and radial → coarctation of aorta, subclavian stenosis.

**Differential / pulseless:** asymmetry → atherosclerosis, dissection, embolism, large-vessel vasculitis (Takayasu).

Classification (rate >100 bpm)

Supraventricular (narrow QRS <120 ms): Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT (e.g. WPW).

**Ventricular (wide QRS ≥120 ms):** Monomorphic VT, polymorphic VT (Torsades de pointes), ventricular fibrillation.

### Clinical Features

Palpitations, dizziness, syncope, dyspnoea, chest discomfort. Symptoms of haemodynamic compromise (hypotension, pulmonary oedema, altered mental status, ongoing chest pain) define an 'unstable' tachycardia.

**AF:** irregularly irregular pulse, absent P waves, varying R-R.

**Flutter:** 'saw-tooth' F waves at 300/min, ventricular rate often 150 (2:1 block).

**VT:** regular wide QRS, AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, often haemodynamic compromise.

### Management Principles

Unstable tachycardia at any rhythm → synchronised DC cardioversion (100–200 J biphasic), except VF/pulseless VT → unsynchronised defibrillation 200 J.

**Stable narrow QRS, regular:** vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage if no bruit) → IV adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg if no effect.

Stable narrow QRS, irregular (AF): rate control with metoprolol/diltiazem; anticoagulate if CHA₂DS₂-VASc indicates; consider rhythm control (cardioversion) if first episode or HF.

**Stable wide QRS:** assume VT until proved otherwise. IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min, repeat once, then 1 mg/min infusion. Avoid verapamil in wide QRS.

**Torsades de pointes:** IV magnesium sulphate 2 g; correct hypokalaemia; stop QT-prolonging drugs; isoproterenol or overdrive pacing.

**Long-term:** AAD therapy, catheter ablation (very effective for AVNRT, WPW, atrial flutter), ICD for sustained VT or VF survivors.

### Definition

STEMI is acute myocardial necrosis due to complete occlusion of a coronary artery, characterised by ST-segment elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous limb leads (or ≥2 mm in V1–V3) or new LBBB, with rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers (troponin I/T).

### Etiology / Risk Factors

**Mechanism:** Atherosclerotic plaque rupture (>90%) → platelet aggregation → coronary thrombosis.

**Non-modifiable:** Age >45 (M), >55 (F); male sex; family history of premature CAD.

**Modifiable:** Smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia (↑LDL, ↓HDL), obesity (BMI >30), sedentary lifestyle, stress.

**Non-atherosclerotic:** Cocaine use, vasculitis (Takayasu, Kawasaki), coronary spasm, embolism, aortic dissection involving ostia.

**Indian context:** South Asians have a 3–4× higher risk of premature CAD at lower BMI; central adiposity, low HDL, high Lp(a) are key Indian risk markers.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic core → platelet adhesion (Glycoprotein Ib–vWF - von Willebrand Factor), activation (TXA2- Thromboxane A2, ADP- Adenosine Diphosphate), aggregation (GP IIb/IIIa - Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa). The resultant fibrin-rich thrombus totally occludes the artery → transmural ischaemia → necrosis from subendocardium outward over 4–6 h. Hence the 'time is muscle' principle.

**Symptoms:** Retrosternal heavy/crushing chest pain, >20 min, radiating to left arm, jaw, epigastrium; not relieved by rest or sublingual GTN.

### Definition

Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) is episodic, reversible digital vasospasm precipitated by cold or emotional stress, classically producing the triphasic colour change of pallor → cyanosis → rubor in the fingers (and less often toes, ears, nose, nipples). Prevalence 3–5%; female:male ≈ 4:1.

### Classification

### Etiology / Causes of secondary RP

**Connective tissue:** systemic sclerosis (>95% have RP), SLE, MCTD, Sjögren's, dermatomyositis, RA

**Drugs:** β-blockers, ergotamine, methylphenidate, cocaine, amphetamines, cisplatin, bleomycin, interferon, sympathomimetic decongestants

**Occupational:** vibration white finger (jackhammer, chainsaw), cold exposure

**Haematological:** cryoglobulinaemia, cold agglutinin disease, polycythaemia, thrombocytosis, paraproteinaemia

**Vascular:** atherosclerosis, thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger), thoracic outlet syndrome, embolism

**Endocrine:** hypothyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid

**Infections:** hepatitis B/C, parvovirus

Neoplasia (paraneoplastic — rare)

### Pathophysiology

Vasoconstriction phase — exaggerated α2-adrenergic response → arteriolar/capillary spasm → pallor

Hypoxia and stasis → deoxygenated blood → cyanosis

Reflex vasodilation on rewarming → reactive hyperaemia → rubor with paraesthesia/burning

**In secondary RP:** structural intimal hyperplasia, endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO, ↑ endothelin-1), platelet activation, oxidative stress

### Clinical features

Triphasic colour change — white → blue → red (not all three required for diagnosis)

Sharply demarcated, symmetric in primary, asymmetric in secondary

Episodes last minutes to hours; provoked by cold (handling cold objects, air-conditioning), emotional stress

Numbness, paraesthesia, burning pain on rewarming

Thumb usually spared in primary; thumb involvement suggests secondary

Digital pitting scars, ulcers, gangrene — red flags for secondary disease (systemic sclerosis especially)

**Look for features of CTD:** sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, calcinosis, dry mouth/eyes, malar rash, arthralgia

Diagnostic criteria — primary Raynaud (Allen-Brown / LeRoy and Medsger)

### Symmetric episodic attacks

Absence of digital ulcer / gangrene / pitting

No clinical features of CTD

### Normal nailfold capillaries

### Negative ANA

### Normal ESR

### Investigations

Bedside — nailfold capillaroscopy

Performed with stereomicroscope, dermatoscope, or videocapillaroscope; cuticle wetted with immersion oil

### Normal in primary RP

**Early scleroderma pattern:** few enlarged loops, no loss; active: many giant capillaries, haemorrhages; late: loss with avascular areas, neoangiogenesis

Strong predictor of CTD development

### Serology

ANA + ENA panel (anti-centromere → limited SSc; anti-Scl-70 → diffuse SSc; anti-RNA polymerase III → renal crisis risk)

### RF, anti-CCP, anti-dsDNA

Complement, cryoglobulin (if symptoms suggest), cold agglutinin

### Other

### CBC, ESR, CRP

### TFT

### Hepatitis B and C serology

### Urinalysis, RFT

Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension if SSc

Doppler / angiography for atypical, asymmetric cases (Buerger, atherosclerosis)

### Management

- Non-pharmacological (most patients with mild primary RP)

Keep warm — gloves, mittens (better than gloves), thermal underwear, hat (significant heat loss from head), warm shoes

### Carry hand-warmers

Avoid sudden temperature change, cold drinks, supermarket freezer aisles

Smoking cessation — strongly advised

Avoid trigger drugs (β-blockers — substitute non-DHP CCB or ACEi)

### Stress management

### Treat underlying disease (CTD)

- Pharmacological — for moderate–severe symptoms

Calcium channel blockers (first line): Nifedipine SR 10–30 mg BD (max 60–90 mg/d) — most evidence. Amlodipine 5–10 mg OD if better tolerated. AE: headache, flushing, ankle oedema, hypotension.

**PDE-5 inhibitors:** Sildenafil 20–50 mg TDS, tadalafil 10–20 mg alternate-day — particularly useful for SSc-associated RP, healing digital ulcers.

**ARBs:** Losartan 50 mg OD

**SSRIs:** Fluoxetine 20 mg/d — modest benefit, avoid β-blocker withdrawal vasospasm

**Topical nitrates:** GTN 2% ointment to digits — useful for severe acute episodes

**Prostacyclin analogues:** Iloprost 0.5–2 ng/kg/min IV × 6 h/day × 5 days — for severe RP, digital ulcers, gangrene threatening (SSc)

**Endothelin antagonists:** Bosentan 62.5–125 mg BD — for recurrent digital ulcers in SSc (prevention; not licensed for healing)

Selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor: Pentoxifylline 400 mg TDS — improves microcirculation

- Surgical / interventional — severe, refractory

Botulinum toxin A injection — palmar/digital sympathetic blockade

Digital sympathectomy — for critical digital ischaemia

Cervical/thoracic sympathectomy (last resort)

Amputation only if irreversible gangrene

### Complications

Digital pits, ulcers, gangrene, autoamputation (secondary RP)

Disability — impaired use of hands for ADLs

Evolution to CTD over months to years (one-third of seemingly primary cases ultimately develop SSc, SLE, etc.)

### Prognosis

Primary Raynaud's has excellent prognosis with conservative measures; symptoms often diminish with age or pregnancy. Secondary Raynaud's prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disease — SSc with frequent ulcers carries significant morbidity. All patients with new RP, especially adult-onset, severe, or asymmetric, need follow-up with serology and capillaroscopy to detect evolving CTD.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 Raynaud's section + EULAR/EUSTAR 2017 SSc treatment recommendations + Wigley 2016 NEJM Raynaud review.

### Combined Notes (10 topics)

Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL or rapid drop) produces a hyperdynamic, high-output circulatory state.

**Symptoms:** Tachycardia, palpitations, exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, dizziness/syncope, angina (if underlying CAD).

**Pulse and BP:** Bounding/collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, low diastolic BP.

**Precordium:** Hyperdynamic apex; mid-systolic ejection (haemic) murmur at aortic / pulmonary area; functional mid-diastolic flow rumble at apex/tricuspid area in very severe anaemia; S3 gallop.

**Other:** Venous hum in the neck (Carotid bruit, child-bearing women), capillary pulsations.

**Decompensation:** High-output cardiac failure (anaemic heart failure) – orthopnoea, raised JVP, hepatomegaly, oedema – seen with chronic severe anaemia and pre-existing cardiac disease.

ECG may show non-specific ST/T changes; CXR – cardiomegaly; echo – dilated chambers with preserved EF; biomarkers (troponin, BNP) raised in decompensation.

Cardiovascular causes (mostly Type 1)

Acute pulmonary oedema (LVF, valvular crisis, hypertensive emergency).

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock.

Cardiac tamponade.

Severe valvular disease – critical AS, acute MR (papillary rupture).

Massive pulmonary embolism (RV failure + hypoxaemia).

High-output failure – severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, sepsis.

Pulmonary hypertension crisis.

### Respiratory causes

### Type 1 (Hypoxaemic):

Pneumonia (bacterial, viral – including COVID-19).

ARDS (sepsis, pancreatitis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion-related TRALI).

Asthma (severe acute).

Pulmonary embolism.

Pneumothorax.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.

### Type 2 (Hypercapnic):

COPD exacerbation (commonest).

Severe asthma (late).

Neuromuscular – GBS, MG crisis, MND, polio, botulism.

CNS depression – opioid overdose, sedatives, brainstem stroke.

Chest-wall – flail chest, kyphoscoliosis, severe obesity (OHS).

Obstructive sleep apnoea.

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.

Fig 5. Sickle cell disease — crisis management.

### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

Tailor therapy to type/etiology.

Monitor response (rise in Hb 1–2 g/dL per month is typical for nutritional anaemias).

### Specific modalities

### 1. Oral iron

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) TDS — first-line for IDA.

Alternate-day dosing 100–200 mg may improve absorption and tolerance.

**AEs:** GI upset, constipation, dark stools.

### 2. Parenteral iron

Iron sucrose, FCM (Ferinject), iron isomaltoside (see Q18).

### 3. Vitamin B12

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week → weekly × 4 weeks → monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Oral 1000–2000 µg/day — feasible alternative.

### 4. Folate

Folic acid 5 mg PO daily × 1–4 months.

Always check/replace B12 first (avoid SACD).

### 5. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)

Epoetin / darbepoetin / roxadustat — CKD, chemo, MDS (see Q33).

### 6. Blood transfusion

Hb <7 g/dL (stable), <8 (cardiac), or symptomatic regardless.

Acute haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to other therapy.

### 7. Disease-modifying agents

Hydroxyurea — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia intermedia.

Lenalidomide — del(5q) MDS.

Luspatercept — β-thalassaemia, MDS-RS.

Eculizumab / ravulizumab — PNH, AIHA (cold).

Caplacizumab — TTP.

- Steroids & immunosuppression

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day — AIHA (first-line).

Rituximab, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide — refractory AIHA, ITP.

ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag — aplastic anaemia.

### 9. Splenectomy

Hereditary spherocytosis, β-thalassaemia, refractory ITP/AIHA.

### 10. Allogeneic HSCT

Curative for severe aplastic anaemia, severe sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia major, Fanconi anaemia, PNH (selected).

- Gene therapy (emerging)

Casgevy / Lyfgenia (CRISPR-edited HSC) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia — FDA-approved 2023.

### Cardiac Cycle (brief)

Each cycle (~0.8 s at 75 bpm) comprises: (i) atrial systole (0.1 s, the 'a' wave on JVP); (ii) isovolumetric ventricular contraction (S1, AV valves close); (iii) ventricular ejection (~0.3 s, aortic/pulmonary valves open); (iv) isovolumetric relaxation (S2, semilunar valves close); (v) rapid passive ventricular filling (S3 may be heard in HF); (vi) diastasis; with a return to atrial systole. The Wiggers diagram relates ECG, pressure, volume and heart sounds.

### Definition

Heart failure is the clinical syndrome resulting from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, leading to characteristic symptoms (dyspnoea, fatigue, fluid retention) and signs (raised JVP, crepitations, oedema). Classified by ejection fraction (HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%) and timing (acute vs chronic).

### Etiology

**Cardiac:** Ischaemic heart disease/MI (commonest), hypertension, valvular disease (AS, MR, AR), dilated/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease.

**Arrhythmia-induced:** Sustained tachyarrhythmia, AV block.

**High-output:** Anaemia (severe), thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, AV fistula, paget's, septic shock.

**Right HF:** Constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloid).

**Lung-related:** Cor pulmonale (COPD, pulmonary embolism), pulmonary hypertension.

**Drugs/toxins:** Anthracyclines (doxorubicin), trastuzumab, alcohol, cocaine, NSAIDs (precipitate).

### Precipitating Factors (acute decompensation)

**FAIL ME mnemonic:** Forgot medications, Arrhythmia/Anaemia, Infection, Lifestyle (salt/fluid), MI/ischaemia, Endocrine (thyroid, pregnancy).

### Clinical Features

**Left HF symptoms:** Exertional dyspnoea (NYHA I–IV), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, cough with frothy/pink sputum.

**Right HF symptoms:** Ankle oedema, abdominal distension (ascites), RUQ pain (hepatic congestion), anorexia, weight gain.

**Signs:** Tachycardia, tachypnoea, displaced apex, S3 gallop (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF), basal crepitations, pleural effusion, raised JVP, hepatomegaly with hepatojugular reflux, pitting pedal oedema, peripheral cyanosis, cold extremities.

### NYHA functional classification

**Class I:** No limitation of activity.

**Class II:** Slight limitation, comfortable at rest.

**Class III:** Marked limitation, comfortable at rest only.

**Class IV:** Symptoms at rest.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** ECG (rule out ischaemia, arrhythmia, LBBB), CXR (cardiomegaly CTR>50%, Kerley B lines, upper-lobe diversion, pleural effusion), SpO₂.

**Biomarker:** BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL → HF likely. <35/125 essentially rules out HF.

**Echocardiogram:** Most important – LVEF, chamber size, wall motion, valves, diastolic function, PASP.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes, LFT (congestive hepatopathy), glucose, HbA1c, lipid, TSH, urinalysis, iron studies (HF + iron deficiency common).

**Advanced:** Coronary angiography if ischaemic aetiology, cardiac MRI for myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, RHC if pulmonary hypertension or transplant work-up.

### Management

**Goals:** relieve symptoms, prevent hospitalisation, prolong survival.

### Acute / decompensated:

**LMNOP:** Position upright, O₂ to keep SpO₂>92%; NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) if pulmonary oedema and not in shock.

Lasix (furosemide 40–80 mg IV), Morphine 2–4 mg IV (relieves anxiety, venodilator), Nitrate (sublingual or IV if BP adequate), Oxygen, Position upright.

**Inotropes:** Dobutamine, milrinone (if low output, cardiogenic shock) – use in critical care.

**Mechanical:** IABP or LV assist device in refractory shock.

Chronic HFrEF – Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT, '4 pillars'):

**1. ARNI/ACEi/ARB:** Sacubitril/valsartan or ACEi (enalapril/ramipril) or ARB (losartan/valsartan).

**2. β-blocker:** Carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate. Start low, titrate up.

**3. MRA:** Spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone (monitor K+, creatinine).

**4. SGLT2 inhibitor:** Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg OD – benefit irrespective of diabetes.

**Add-on:** Loop diuretic (furosemide/torsemide) for congestion; ivabradine if HR>70 in sinus on max β-blocker; digoxin if AF or refractory symptoms; hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate (esp. in Black patients or ACEi-intolerant).

### Chronic HFpEF:

Treat HTN, AF (rate/rhythm), DM, obesity, sleep apnoea, iron deficiency.

Diuretic for congestion; SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin/dapagliflozin) reduces hospitalisation in HFpEF.

### Device therapy:

ICD if EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months GDMT (primary prevention of sudden death).

CRT (cardiac resynchronisation) if EF ≤35%, LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–IV in sinus rhythm.

### Advanced HF:

LVAD as bridge or destination therapy; cardiac transplantation in eligible patients.

### Lifestyle:

Sodium <2 g/d, fluid <1.5–2 L/d if hyponatraemic or congested, daily weights, exercise rehabilitation, smoking and alcohol cessation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19), patient education for self-monitoring.

Fig 2. Heart failure – diagnosis and management algorithm.

### Complications & Prognosis

Acute decompensation, arrhythmias (AF, VT/VF), sudden cardiac death, thromboembolism, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cachexia, hepatic congestion.

5-year mortality ~50% for symptomatic HFrEF; modern GDMT improves survival significantly.

GENERAL MEDICINE|102.note:
Classification (rate >100 bpm)

Supraventricular (narrow QRS <120 ms): Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT (e.g. WPW).

**Ventricular (wide QRS ≥120 ms):** Monomorphic VT, polymorphic VT (Torsades de pointes), ventricular fibrillation.

### Clinical Features

Palpitations, dizziness, syncope, dyspnoea, chest discomfort. Symptoms of haemodynamic compromise (hypotension, pulmonary oedema, altered mental status, ongoing chest pain) define an 'unstable' tachycardia.

**AF:** irregularly irregular pulse, absent P waves, varying R-R.

**Flutter:** 'saw-tooth' F waves at 300/min, ventricular rate often 150 (2:1 block).

**VT:** regular wide QRS, AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, often haemodynamic compromise.

### Management Principles

Unstable tachycardia at any rhythm → synchronised DC cardioversion (100–200 J biphasic), except VF/pulseless VT → unsynchronised defibrillation 200 J.

**Stable narrow QRS, regular:** vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage if no bruit) → IV adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg if no effect.

Stable narrow QRS, irregular (AF): rate control with metoprolol/diltiazem; anticoagulate if CHA₂DS₂-VASc indicates; consider rhythm control (cardioversion) if first episode or HF.

**Stable wide QRS:** assume VT until proved otherwise. IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min, repeat once, then 1 mg/min infusion. Avoid verapamil in wide QRS.

**Torsades de pointes:** IV magnesium sulphate 2 g; correct hypokalaemia; stop QT-prolonging drugs; isoproterenol or overdrive pacing.

**Long-term:** AAD therapy, catheter ablation (very effective for AVNRT, WPW, atrial flutter), ICD for sustained VT or VF survivors.

GENERAL MEDICINE|103.note:
### Combined Notes (45 topics)

### Definition

STEMI is acute myocardial necrosis due to complete occlusion of a coronary artery, characterised by ST-segment elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous limb leads (or ≥2 mm in V1–V3) or new LBBB, with rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers (troponin I/T).

### Etiology / Risk Factors

**Mechanism:** Atherosclerotic plaque rupture (>90%) → platelet aggregation → coronary thrombosis.

**Non-modifiable:** Age >45 (M), >55 (F); male sex; family history of premature CAD.

**Modifiable:** Smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia (↑LDL, ↓HDL), obesity (BMI >30), sedentary lifestyle, stress.

**Non-atherosclerotic:** Cocaine use, vasculitis (Takayasu, Kawasaki), coronary spasm, embolism, aortic dissection involving ostia.

**Indian context:** South Asians have a 3–4× higher risk of premature CAD at lower BMI; central adiposity, low HDL, high Lp(a) are key Indian risk markers.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic core → platelet adhesion (Glycoprotein Ib–vWF - von Willebrand Factor), activation (TXA2- Thromboxane A2, ADP- Adenosine Diphosphate), aggregation (GP IIb/IIIa - Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa). The resultant fibrin-rich thrombus totally occludes the artery → transmural ischaemia → necrosis from subendocardium outward over 4–6 h. Hence the 'time is muscle' principle.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Retrosternal heavy/crushing chest pain, >20 min, radiating to left arm, jaw, epigastrium; not relieved by rest or sublingual GTN.

**Associated:** Sweating, nausea, vomiting, dyspnoea, anxiety (impending doom).

**Atypical:** Diabetic, elderly, and women may have 'silent MI' with dyspnoea, syncope, or epigastric pain only.

**Signs:** Pallor, sweating, tachycardia, hypotension or hypertension; S4 gallop; new MR murmur; basal crepitations if pulmonary oedema; raised JVP (RV infarct).

**Severity:** Killip class I (no failure) → IV (cardiogenic shock).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Random capillary glucose, SpO₂.

**ECG:** ST elevation ≥1 mm in 2 contiguous leads (or ≥2 mm in V1–V3), or new LBBB. Reciprocal ST depression confirms STEMI. Location: anterior (V1–V4 → LAD), inferior (II, III, aVF → RCA), lateral (I, aVL, V5, V6 → LCx), posterior (tall R in V1–V2, ST↓; confirm with V7–V9), RV (V4R).

**Cardiac biomarkers:** Troponin I/T (rise within 3–6 h, peaks 24 h, stays 7–10 d), CK-MB (peaks 24 h, falls 48–72 h – useful for re-infarction).

**Routine labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes, lipid profile, HbA1c, coagulation profile.

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (rule out aortic dissection, pulmonary oedema), echo (regional wall-motion abnormality, EF, complications).

**Definitive:** Coronary angiography (gold standard, guides PCI).

Management (Indian primary; ESC alternative)

**Goal:** reperfusion within the 'golden hour'.

**Initial (MONAH):** Cardiac monitor, IV access, O₂ if SpO₂ <90%, IV morphine 2–4 mg for pain, sublingual nitrate (avoid if hypotensive/RV infarct), Aspirin 325 mg chewed + Clopidogrel 300 mg PO (Ticagrelor 180 mg if going for PCI), atorvastatin 80 mg. Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

**Reperfusion – PCI:** Door-to-balloon <90 min: Primary PCI is the preferred strategy (Indian STEMI program emphasises PCI-capable hubs). LMWH/UFH or bivalirudin peri-procedure.

**Reperfusion – Lysis:** If PCI not available within 90–120 min and onset <12 h: IV thrombolysis with Streptokinase 1.5 MU over 30–60 min or Tenecteplase (weight-based bolus). Door-to-needle <30 min. Pharmaco-invasive strategy: thrombolyse then transfer for PCI within 3–24 h.

Secondary prevention (lifelong/1 yr): Aspirin 75 mg + Clopidogrel/Ticagrelor 1 year (dual antiplatelet), high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg), β-blocker (metoprolol 25–100 mg BD) unless contraindicated, ACEi/ARB (especially anterior MI, EF<40%), MRA (eplerenone) if EF<40% with HF or DM. Sublingual GTN for angina.

**Lifestyle:** Smoking cessation, Mediterranean/DASH diet, weight, exercise 150 min/wk moderate, cardiac rehabilitation, glycaemic and BP control.

Fig 1. STEMI emergency-management pathway.

### Complications

**Arrhythmias:** Ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia, AV blocks (esp. inferior MI), atrial fibrillation, asystole.

**Pump failure:** Acute heart failure / cardiogenic shock (Killip IV, mortality 50–80%).

**Mechanical (3–7 d):** Free-wall rupture (1–7 d, tamponade), VSD (acute MR-like murmur, septal rupture), papillary-muscle rupture (acute MR).

**Thromboembolic:** Mural thrombus → systemic embolism (CVA, mesenteric).

**Pericarditis:** Early (24–48 h, fibrinous) and Dressler's syndrome (2–10 wk, autoimmune).

**Late:** Ventricular aneurysm, chronic heart failure, recurrent angina, anxiety/depression.

### Prognosis

30-day mortality 5–6% with timely PCI; up to 25% without reperfusion. Anterior MI, age >75, low EF, Killip III–IV, and persistent ST elevation predict worse outcome.

### (a) Likely diagnosis

Acute inferior-wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), with possible posterior extension suggested by ST flattening (likely reciprocal depression) in V1–V6.

Inferior MI typically reflects right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion (~80%) or left circumflex (~20%). Right ventricular involvement must be actively excluded as it changes management (avoid nitrates/diuretics, give fluids).

(b) Confirmatory investigations and why

Repeat 12-lead ECG with V4R, V7–V9: Confirm STEMI, identify reciprocal changes; add right-sided leads V4R (RV MI: ST↑ in V4R, sensitivity ~88%) and posterior leads V7–V9 (posterior MI).

**Troponin I/T:** Highly sensitive (rises 3–6 h, peaks 24 h). Confirms myocardial necrosis and quantifies infarct size.

**CK-MB:** Confirms diagnosis, peaks earlier than troponin, useful for re-infarction.

**2-D Echocardiogram:** EF, regional wall-motion abnormality (inferior wall hypokinesia), RV function, mechanical complications.

**Chest X-ray:** Pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly, exclude dissection.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes (K, Mg matter for arrhythmias), HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, coagulation profile, blood glucose.

**Coronary angiography:** Definitive – delineates culprit and other vessels; required if PCI planned.

### (c) Treatment

**Immediate (MONAH):** Cardiac monitoring, IV access, O₂ if SpO₂<90%, semi-recumbent position. IV morphine 2–4 mg for pain. Aspirin 325 mg chewed + Ticagrelor 180 mg (or Clopidogrel 300–600 mg) loading. Atorvastatin 80 mg. UFH 60 U/kg bolus + 12 U/kg/h infusion (or LMWH).

**Caution:** Avoid nitrates and diuretics until RV infarction excluded (preload-dependent). β-blocker withheld initially if HR or BP marginal.

**Reperfusion:** If centre has cath-lab → Primary PCI within 90 min (door-to-balloon). If not → IV Tenecteplase or Streptokinase 1.5 MU over 30 min (door-to-needle <30 min), then pharmaco-invasive transfer.

**RV infarct:** If RV infarct: aggressive IV crystalloid 200–500 mL boluses to keep preload; inotropes (dobutamine) if shock; pace if AV block.

**Discharge:** Aspirin 75 mg lifelong + P2Y12 inhibitor 12 months, atorvastatin 40–80 mg, β-blocker (carvedilol/metoprolol), ACEi (ramipril 5 mg BD titrated), MRA if EF<40%, glycaemic control (HbA1c <7%), BP <130/80, smoking cessation, cardiac rehab.

(d) Complications if untreated

**Arrhythmias:** VF, AV block (RCA territory typically causes complete heart block, often transient).

**Pump failure:** Cardiogenic shock (Killip IV).

**RV:** RV infarction → hypotension despite clear lungs.

**Mechanical:** Free-wall rupture, VSD, papillary-muscle rupture (acute MR), all in days 3–7.

**Thromboembolic:** Mural thrombus → stroke.

**Late:** LV aneurysm, chronic HF, recurrent ischaemia.

**Mortality:** Up to 30% without reperfusion vs ~5% with timely PCI.

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').
