### Definition

Syndrome of chronic GH (and IGF-1) excess in adults after epiphyseal closure. Caused most commonly by a somatotroph pituitary adenoma (95%). 'Gigantism' is the same disease occurring before epiphyseal fusion in children.

### Etiology

Pituitary somatotroph adenoma (95%) – macroadenoma in >70%.

Ectopic GHRH (rare – pancreatic, bronchial neuroendocrine).

Ectopic GH (very rare – pancreatic islet, lymphoma).

Familial – MEN1, McCune-Albright, Carney complex, FIPA.

### Clinical features

### Tumour mass effects:

Headache, bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression), cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus invasion), hyperprolactinaemia (stalk effect).

Hypopituitarism (deficient TSH, ACTH, gonadotropins).

### GH/IGF-1 excess (somatic):

Facial – frontal bossing, prognathism (mandibular protrusion), interdental separation, macroglossia, prominent supraorbital ridges, coarse features, deepening voice (laryngeal soft-tissue enlargement).

Hands and feet – enlargement (need new ring/shoe size); spade-like hands; carpal tunnel syndrome.

Skin – thick, oily, hyperhidrosis, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans.

Cardiovascular – hypertension, biventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, valvular regurgitation, arrhythmias, heart failure (leading cause of death).

Respiratory – obstructive sleep apnoea (very common, ~60%).

Metabolic – insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia.

Endocrine – goitre, multinodular thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia, hypogonadism.

Musculoskeletal – arthropathy (hips, knees, spine), kyphosis, proximal myopathy.

GI – colonic polyps and increased colon cancer risk; visceromegaly (thyroid, heart, liver, kidney, prostate).

Hyperhidrosis, oily skin, body odour.

### Investigations

### Biochemistry:

Serum IGF-1 (age- and sex-matched) – best screening test; elevated.

OGTT with GH measurement – failure of GH suppression to <1 µg/L (or <0.4 with sensitive assay) at 2 h confirms acromegaly.

Prolactin (often co-secreted), TFT, cortisol, FSH/LH, testosterone/oestradiol for pituitary hormone reserve.

### Imaging:

MRI pituitary with contrast – macroadenoma in 70%.

Visual field testing.

### Complications screening:

ECG, echocardiogram.

Polysomnography (OSA).

HbA1c, fasting lipids.

Colonoscopy at diagnosis (then every 3–5 years).

DEXA, hand X-rays.

### Management

### Surgery (first-line):

Transsphenoidal adenomectomy – cures 80–90% of microadenomas and 40–60% of macroadenomas. Performed by expert pituitary surgeon.

Medical (if surgery fails or contraindicated):

Somatostatin receptor analogues (SRL) – octreotide LAR 20–30 mg IM monthly; lanreotide autogel 90–120 mg SC monthly; pasireotide for resistant disease.

Dopamine agonists – cabergoline 0.5–3.5 mg/week (especially if co-secreting prolactin, modest GH excess).

GH receptor antagonist – pegvisomant 10–30 mg SC daily; normalises IGF-1 but does not shrink tumour, so monitor MRI.

### Radiotherapy (third-line):

Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma knife) or fractionated; effect delayed years. Risk of hypopituitarism.

### Treat complications:

Cardiovascular optimisation, OSA – CPAP, diabetes – metformin/GLP-1 RA, surgical correction of jaw/dental.

### Prognosis

Pre-treatment mortality is double that of age-matched controls; normalising IGF-1 restores life expectancy. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; colon cancer surveillance important.

### Definition

Clinical syndrome resulting from deficient circulating thyroid hormone (T4, T3). Classified into primary (thyroid gland failure – high TSH, low fT4), secondary (pituitary – low/normal TSH, low fT4), tertiary (hypothalamic – low TRH/TSH/fT4), and peripheral resistance (rare).

### Etiology

Primary (95% of cases):

Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's) – commonest in iodine-replete areas; anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies; firm goitre.

Iodine deficiency – still prevalent in some Indian regions despite universal salt iodisation.

Post-ablative – thyroidectomy, radioiodine.

Drugs – amiodarone, lithium, IFN-α, IL-2, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, immune-checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. pembrolizumab).

Subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain – initial thyrotoxic, then hypothyroid), silent thyroiditis, post-partum thyroiditis.

Congenital – dyshormonogenesis (Pendred), thyroid agenesis.

Infiltration – haemochromatosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, lymphoma.

### Secondary:

Pituitary adenoma, Sheehan's syndrome, surgery, radiotherapy, lymphocytic hypophysitis.

### Tertiary:

Hypothalamic lesions (craniopharyngioma, sarcoidosis, infiltration).

### Clinical features

**Symptoms:** Cold intolerance, fatigue, weight gain, constipation, menorrhagia, depression, slow mentation.

**Signs (general):** Dry, coarse, cold skin; non-pitting oedema (myxoedema – periorbital, hands/feet, glossal); brittle hair; loss of outer third of eyebrows (Queen Anne sign); puffy face; macroglossia; hoarse voice.

**CVS:** Bradycardia, hypertension (diastolic), low cardiac output, pericardial effusion, hyperlipidaemia, accelerated CAD.

**Neuro:** Hyporeflexia with delayed relaxation phase ('hung up'); carpal tunnel syndrome; proximal myopathy; cerebellar ataxia.

**Respiratory:** Hypoventilation, sleep apnoea, pleural effusion.

**GI:** Slow gut transit – constipation, ileus; ascites.

**Reproductive:** Menstrual irregularity (menorrhagia or amenorrhoea), infertility, hyperprolactinaemia (TRH-driven) → galactorrhoea; in children, growth retardation, cretinism.

**Haem / electrolytes:** Anaemia (normocytic, macrocytic with B12, or microcytic with menorrhagia); hyponatraemia (SIADH-like).

**Severe / emergency:** Myxoedema coma – hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hypotension, hyponatraemia, coma; mortality 30–50%.

### Investigations

**TSH + free T4 (primary:** TSH↑, fT4↓; subclinical: TSH↑, fT4 normal; secondary: TSH ↓/normal, fT4↓).

Anti-TPO ± anti-Tg antibodies (Hashimoto's).

Lipid profile (often dyslipidaemia), CBC, electrolytes (low Na), creatine kinase (often elevated), glucose, prolactin.

ECG (bradycardia, low voltage, T-wave inversion).

USG thyroid if palpable nodule.

MRI pituitary if secondary hypothyroidism suspected.

### Management

### Levothyroxine (T4):

**Starting dose:** 1.6 µg/kg/day in young, otherwise healthy adults (typical 75–125 µg/day).

Elderly / ischaemic heart disease: start 25–50 µg/day, titrate every 4–6 weeks.

**Pregnancy:** increase dose by 25–30% as soon as pregnancy confirmed; target TSH trimester-specific (<2.5 first trimester).

Take on empty stomach, 30 min before food/calcium/iron/PPI/soya, with water.

Recheck TSH after 6–8 weeks; aim TSH 0.5–2.5 mIU/L (1.0–2.5 in patients with cardiovascular risk).

**Subclinical hypothyroidism:** treat if TSH >10 / anti-TPO positive / symptomatic / pregnancy / planning pregnancy / cardiovascular risk.

### Myxoedema coma (emergency):

IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg loading, then 50–100 µg/day (+/- T3 25 µg q8h).

IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q8h (until adrenal insufficiency excluded).

Gentle re-warming, supportive ventilation, treat precipitating infection/MI, careful fluid replacement.

### Counselling:

Lifelong therapy; do not stop without medical advice; explain drug-food interactions; warning symptoms of over- or under-replacement.

### Definition

Clinical syndrome resulting from excess circulating thyroid hormones (T4 and/or T3). 'Hyperthyroidism' specifically refers to overproduction by the thyroid gland; 'thyrotoxicosis' is the broader term encompassing exogenous and gland-derived excess.

### Causes

Increased synthesis (with high RAIU):

Graves' disease (autoimmune, anti-TSH-receptor antibodies; 60–80% of cases) – diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema.

Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease).

Toxic adenoma (autonomously functioning nodule).

Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow) – iodinated contrast, amiodarone type 1, kelp.

Trophoblastic disease (hyperemesis gravidarum, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) – β-hCG-driven.

### Decreased synthesis (low RAIU):

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain – painful, post-viral, raised ESR).

Silent thyroiditis (painless).

Post-partum thyroiditis (1–6 months post-delivery).

Amiodarone type 2 (destructive thyroiditis).

Drug-induced (lithium withdrawal, IFN-α, IL-2, immune-checkpoint inhibitors).

Exogenous thyroid hormone (factitious thyrotoxicosis – low Tg).

Struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid tissue in ovarian teratoma).

### Clinical features

**Symptoms:** Heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, fatigue, weight loss despite good appetite, anxiety, tremor, restlessness, insomnia, irritability, loose stools, polyuria.

**General signs:** Tachycardia, AF (10–15%), warm moist skin, fine tremor, hyperreflexia, lid retraction and lid lag (any thyrotoxicosis), palmar erythema, onycholysis (Plummer's nails), thinning hair, proximal myopathy, low BMI.

**Goitre:** Diffuse smooth goitre with bruit (Graves'); nodular thyroid (TMNG, adenoma); tender (de Quervain); painless tender-free (silent).

**Ophthalmopathy:** Specific to Graves' disease – exophthalmos, periorbital oedema, chemosis, lid retraction (separate from generalised lid retraction of thyrotoxicosis), proptosis, ophthalmoplegia (especially upgaze), diplopia, optic neuropathy.

**Dermopathy / acropachy:** Specific to Graves' – pretibial myxoedema (non-pitting nodular skin thickening on shins); thyroid acropachy (clubbing-like).

**Emergency presentation:** Thyroid storm (decompensated thyrotoxicosis): fever >39°C, severe tachycardia/AF, vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, agitation, delirium, coma, heart failure; mortality 10–30%. Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 supports diagnosis.

### Investigations

**Biochemistry:** TSH suppressed (<0.01 mIU/L), free T4 elevated (and/or T3 elevated – T3 toxicosis seen in early Graves', toxic nodule).

**Antibodies:** Anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb / TSI) – diagnostic for Graves'. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg often positive but non-specific.

**Imaging:** Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) and scan: diffuse high uptake (Graves'), focal high (adenoma), patchy multifocal (TMNG), low/absent uptake (thyroiditis, exogenous, struma ovarii).

Thyroid USG with Doppler (Graves' shows hyper-vascularity).

Thyroglobulin (low in factitious; raised in others).

ECG (sinus tachycardia, AF), CBC, LFT, glucose, calcium.

### Management

### Symptomatic:

β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg q8h, or atenolol 25–50 mg OD) for tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, AF.

Calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) if β-blocker contraindicated (asthma).

### Anti-thyroid drugs (ATDs):

Carbimazole 20–40 mg/day (or methimazole 15–30 mg/day) – tapered based on TFTs, total course 12–18 months.

Propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg q8h – preferred in first trimester of pregnancy (carbimazole teratogenic – aplasia cutis), thyroid storm, ATD allergy.

Side effects – rash, arthralgia (5%), agranulocytosis (0.3%, warn re: sore throat and fever – stop drug, FBC immediately), hepatitis (PTU more), ANCA vasculitis.

**Monitor:** TFT 4–6 weekly initially; FBC and LFT at baseline.

Radioactive iodine (¹³¹I) — definitive:

Most patients with Graves', TMNG, or toxic adenoma; first-line in USA, second-line in Europe/India after ATD relapse.

**Contraindicated:** pregnancy (avoid 6 months prior), breastfeeding, severe ophthalmopathy (can worsen).

Most become hypothyroid – levothyroxine replacement.

Surgery (total or near-total thyroidectomy):

Large goitre with compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, pregnancy unable to tolerate ATD, severe ophthalmopathy, child-bearing-age women planning pregnancy soon.

**Pre-op:** render euthyroid with ATD; add Lugol's iodine 10 days before surgery to reduce vascularity.

**Complications:** recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hypoparathyroidism, hypothyroidism (need lifelong levothyroxine), bleeding.

### Graves' ophthalmopathy:

Stop smoking (worsens), selenium 100 µg BD × 6 months for mild disease.

**Moderate-severe active:** IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/week × 6 weeks then 250 mg/week × 6 weeks; teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody, expensive); orbital decompression; orbital radiotherapy.

### Thyroid storm:

ICU admission, cooling, IV fluids.

PTU 200–300 mg PO/NG q4h (preferred – blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).

Lugol's iodine 5–10 drops q6h, OR sodium iodide 1 g/day IV — at least 1 h after PTU.

IV propranolol 1 mg/min (max 10 mg).

Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (blocks T4→T3, treats adrenal insufficiency).

Treat precipitant (infection, MI, DKA, surgery).

Cholestyramine, plasmapheresis in refractory cases.

### Pregnancy:

PTU in T1, carbimazole in T2/T3 (lowest effective dose); aim for high-normal fT4. Monitor monthly. β-blocker for symptoms (caution: IUGR).

### Complications

AF, dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, thromboembolism.

Osteoporosis, hypercalcaemia.

Thyroid storm.

Severe ophthalmopathy with optic neuropathy.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis (Asian males).

### Definition

**Whipple's triad:** (1) low plasma glucose, (2) symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, (3) relief with raising the glucose. ADA biochemical threshold: <70 mg/dL = level 1; <54 mg/dL = level 2 (clinically significant); requiring third-party assistance = level 3 (severe).

### Symptoms by mechanism

Adrenergic / autonomic (early, glucose ~55–70 mg/dL):

Tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paraesthesiae, tachycardia, pallor.

### Cholinergic:

Sweating, hunger, paraesthesiae.

Neuroglycopenic (later, glucose <55 mg/dL):

Difficulty concentrating, confusion, blurred vision, slurred speech, drowsiness, behavioural change, dizziness, weakness, headache.

**Severe:** seizures, focal neurological deficit (mimics stroke), loss of consciousness, coma, death.

### Hypoglycaemia unawareness:

Loss of adrenergic warning symptoms with recurrent hypoglycaemia (common in long-standing T1DM, autonomic neuropathy, β-blocker use). Patient may go directly to neuroglycopenia and unconsciousness without warning.

Causes (in non-diabetic adults)

Drugs – insulin, sulfonylureas (commonest), alcohol, quinine, pentamidine, ACEi, β-blockers.

Insulinoma – fasting hypoglycaemia, high insulin + C-peptide, low β-hydroxybutyrate (Whipple's triad + supervised 72-h fast).

Critical illness – sepsis, hepatic/renal/cardiac failure.

Hormone deficiency – Addison's, hypopituitarism.

Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia (IGF-2).

Reactive (postprandial) – post-bariatric surgery, idiopathic.

Factitious – surreptitious insulin (low C-peptide) or sulfonylurea (urine screen).

### Management

**Conscious:** 15 g rapid carbohydrate (4 sugar lumps, 3 dextrose tablets, 150 mL fruit juice, 100 mL sweet cola). Recheck in 15 min. Repeat if needed (rule of 15). Follow with complex carbohydrate snack.

Unconscious – IM glucagon 1 mg, OR IV 50 mL of 25% dextrose, then 10% dextrose infusion. Watch for sulfonylurea recurrence (prolonged half-life).

Treat underlying cause; for insulinoma – surgical resection; diazoxide and octreotide as medical bridge.

### DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 → prolong endogenous GLP-1 and GIP → glucose-dependent insulin secretion, glucagon suppression.

**Available agents:** Sitagliptin 100 mg OD (adjust in CKD), vildagliptin 50 mg BD, linagliptin 5 mg OD (no renal adjustment), saxagliptin 5 mg OD, alogliptin 25 mg OD, teneligliptin 20 mg OD (Indian-favoured, cheap).

**Advantages:** Weight-neutral, no hypoglycaemia (when used alone), well tolerated, safe in elderly and CKD (linagliptin).

**Adverse:** Nasopharyngitis, headache, pancreatitis (rare), arthralgia, hypersensitivity. Saxagliptin and alogliptin – HF hospitalisation signal.

**Use:** Add-on to metformin when modest reduction in HbA1c (0.5–0.8%) needed; preferred in elderly with renal impairment.

### SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in renal proximal tubule → ~50–80 g/day urinary glucose loss; mild diuresis, weight loss, BP reduction; pleotropic cardiovascular and renal benefits.

**Available agents:** Empagliflozin 10–25 mg OD, dapagliflozin 10 mg OD, canagliflozin 100–300 mg OD, ertugliflozin 5–15 mg OD.

**Benefits beyond glycaemia:** ↓ Cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation (EMPA-REG, CANVAS, DECLARE, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR); ↓ CKD progression (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD); approved for HFrEF/HFpEF and CKD regardless of diabetes.

**Indications:** Indicated in T2DM with established/high-risk ASCVD, HF, or CKD; modest HbA1c reduction (0.6–1.0%); 2–3 kg weight loss; ↓ systolic BP 3–5 mmHg.

**Adverse:** Genital mycotic infection (candida, women > men), UTI, volume depletion (especially elderly, on diuretics), euglycaemic DKA (omit pre-op, in fasting/illness), Fournier's gangrene, lower-limb amputation (canagliflozin), bone fractures (canagliflozin).

**Contra-/cautions:** Severe renal failure (eGFR <20–25), volume depletion, hypotension, type 1 DM, recurrent UTI, history of euglycaemic DKA.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (covered briefly)

Liraglutide 1.8–3.0 mg SC OD (also for obesity), exenatide BD or weekly XR, dulaglutide 1.5–4.5 mg SC weekly, semaglutide 0.25–2 mg SC weekly (or oral 14 mg OD).

Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) 5–15 mg SC weekly – superior HbA1c and weight reduction.

**Benefits:** HbA1c reduction 1–1.5%, weight loss 3–10 kg, CV and renal benefit.

**Adverse:** nausea/vomiting (titrate dose), pancreatitis (rare), gallstones, thyroid C-cell tumour (rodent, theoretical).

### Definition

Primary adrenocortical insufficiency – deficient cortisol and aldosterone (and adrenal androgens) due to disease of the adrenal cortex. Distinguish from secondary (pituitary ACTH deficiency – cortisol low but aldosterone preserved) and tertiary (hypothalamic).

### Causes

Autoimmune adrenalitis (commonest in West) – isolated or polyglandular (APS-1, APS-2). 21-hydroxylase antibodies.

Tuberculosis (commonest in India) – calcification on CT.

Fungal – histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis (HIV).

HIV-associated – CMV, mycobacterium avium, ketoconazole.

Metastases – lung, breast, lymphoma.

Adrenal haemorrhage – sepsis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen), anticoagulants, antiphospholipid syndrome.

Drugs – ketoconazole, etomidate, mitotane, abiraterone, ipilimumab.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH – classic 21-OH deficiency).

Adrenoleukodystrophy (males; very-long-chain fatty acids).

### Clinical features

**Insidious:** Fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, salt craving, dizziness on standing.

**Hyperpigmentation:** Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, knuckles, scars, oral mucosa, areolae – due to ACTH/MSH excess) – primary only.

**Biochemical:** Postural hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, mild metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia.

**Androgen deficiency:** Loss of pubic/axillary hair (women – adrenal androgen loss); decreased libido.

**Associated:** Vitiligo, autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 DM, premature ovarian failure, pernicious anaemia.

**Emergency:** Addisonian crisis – severe hypotension, shock, fever, vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, eosinophilia; often precipitated by stress (infection, surgery), abrupt steroid withdrawal.

### Investigations

8 a.m. cortisol <100 nmol/L diagnostic; >500 excludes; 100–500 = indeterminate, do Synacthen test.

**Short Synacthen test:** 250 µg IM/IV; cortisol at 0, 30, 60 min. Peak <500 nmol/L = adrenal insufficiency.

Plasma ACTH (high in primary; low/normal in secondary).

21-hydroxylase antibodies (autoimmune).

Plasma renin (high), aldosterone (low) – confirms primary.

Electrolytes (low Na, high K), urea, glucose.

Adrenal imaging – CT (calcification suggests TB/fungal/haemorrhage; enlargement in lymphoma/metastases; atrophy in autoimmune).

Search for TB, HIV.

### Treatment

### Chronic replacement:

Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses (e.g. 10 mg morning, 5 mg noon, 5 mg 4 p.m. – mimic circadian rhythm). Modified-release once-daily preparations available.

Fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg morning – mineralocorticoid replacement.

DHEA 25–50 mg morning – consider in women with low libido/energy.

Sick-day rules (essential education):

Double oral hydrocortisone dose for fever, infection, dental procedure.

Triple for severe illness or surgery.

If vomiting / unable to take orally – IM/SC hydrocortisone (kept at home), seek medical attention.

Steroid card / MedicAlert bracelet; emergency injection kit.

### Addisonian crisis (emergency):

IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, then 100 mg q6h.

IV normal saline 1 L over first hour, then maintain.

Treat precipitant (infection, etc.).

Glucose if hypoglycaemic.

Once stable, taper to oral replacement over 48–72 h.

Fig 6. Adrenal insufficiency – diagnosis and management.

### Definition

Catecholamine-secreting tumour arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (90%) or extra-adrenal sympathetic ganglia (paraganglioma, 10%). 'Rule of 10' – 10% extra-adrenal, 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% familial, 10% in children, 10% normotensive.

### Clinical features

Classic triad – episodic headache, palpitations, profuse sweating; hypertension (sustained, paroxysmal, or normotensive).

Paroxysms – sudden onset, last minutes to hours, triggered by exertion, anxiety, abdominal palpation, anaesthesia, tyramine-rich food, β-blocker monotherapy.

Anxiety, pallor (vasoconstriction), tremor, nausea, weight loss, hyperglycaemia, postural hypotension, polycythaemia.

Associations – MEN-2A/2B, von Hippel-Lindau, NF-1, SDHx mutations, Carney triad.

### Investigations

### Biochemistry (essential):

Plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive) or 24-h urinary fractionated metanephrines (normetanephrine + metanephrine) – elevated >3–4× ULN diagnostic.

False positives with stress, tricyclic antidepressants, decongestants, paracetamol, levodopa, MAO inhibitors – discontinue before testing; clonidine suppression test if equivocal.

### Localisation:

Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis (adrenal mass with avid contrast enhancement, high attenuation on T2 MRI).

¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy – functional imaging.

Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT – sensitive for metastatic / paraganglioma.

### Genetic testing:

All patients with phaeo/paraganglioma – RET (MEN-2), VHL, NF-1, SDHB/D/A/AF2, MAX, TMEM127.

### Treatment

Pre-operative pharmacological preparation (10–14 days, essential):

α-blockade first – phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD, titrate to BP <130/80 and mild postural drop; or doxazosin (alternative).

After α-blockade established, add β-blockade for tachycardia – propranolol 20 mg TDS, atenolol 25–50 mg OD. NEVER start β-blocker before α-blocker (unopposed α can precipitate hypertensive crisis).

Liberal salt intake and fluids (catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction has reduced plasma volume).

Metyrosine (tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor) – additional control in resistant cases.

### Surgery:

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (open if >6 cm or malignant).

Intraoperative anaesthetic care – avoid drugs that release catecholamines (halothane, succinylcholine); BP swings managed with sodium nitroprusside / nicardipine for hypertension, noradrenaline + saline for hypotension after tumour ligation.

Post-op hypotension common (catecholamine withdrawal) – stop α-blocker, give fluids/pressors.

Monitor for residual / recurrent disease with annual plasma/urine metanephrines.

### Malignant / metastatic:

Surgical debulking, ¹³¹I-MIBG therapy, peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy (¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE), chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide + vincristine + dacarbazine), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sunitinib).

Fig 7. Phaeochromocytoma – diagnosis and surgical preparation.

Diagnosis (ADA / RSSDI 2024 – any one)

FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL (after 8-h fast) – confirmed by repeat.

2-h plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during 75 g OGTT.

HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (NGSP/IFCC-aligned method).

Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss).

### Pre-diabetes:

**Impaired fasting glucose:** FPG 100–125 mg/dL.

**Impaired glucose tolerance:** 2-h OGTT 140–199 mg/dL.

HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

### Management

### Lifestyle (always first):

Diet – ICMR-recommended balanced Indian diet, complex carbs 55–60%, protein 12–15%, fat 25–30%, fibre 25–40 g/day, limit saturated fat and refined sugar.

Exercise – 150 min/week moderate aerobic + 2 sessions resistance training.

Weight reduction 5–10% if BMI ≥23 (Asian threshold).

Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation.

Sleep 7–9 h; stress management.

### Pharmacotherapy:

Metformin first-line.

Add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA if ASCVD/HF/CKD/obesity present.

Add DPP-4i, SU, pioglitazone if no specific indications.

Insulin (basal) when HbA1c >9% or symptomatic.

Targets – HbA1c <7% (relax to 7.5–8% in elderly/frail/short life expectancy); BP <130/80; LDL <70 (or <55 with established ASCVD).

### Adjunctive:

Statin – moderate-intensity for all >40 yrs; high-intensity if ASCVD risk >20%.

ACEi/ARB for albuminuria.

Aspirin only for secondary prevention (or primary with high ASCVD risk + low bleeding).

Annual screening – eye (fundus), feet, urine ACR, eGFR, lipids, BP, dental.

Vaccines – influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, hepatitis B.

### Complications of T2DM

### Acute:

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) – elderly, glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, no significant ketosis.
