### Lower GI Bleed — Etiology

### Approach to Differentiation

### Investigations

**UGIB:** OGD first within 24 h.

**LGIB:** colonoscopy within 24 h after bowel prep (PEG); CT angiography first if haemodynamic instability or massive bleed (detects bleed rate ≥ 0.3 ml/min).

**Obscure / occult:** capsule endoscopy → balloon enteroscopy → CT/MR enterography → tagged RBC scan → angiography.

**Meckel's:** Children/young adults with painless massive PR bleed: technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel's scan).

### Management Principles

ABC resuscitation as in Q1.

**UGIB:** PPI ± vasoactive ± antibiotic (if variceal); endoscopic Rx.

**LGIB:** stabilise → colonoscopy with clips/cautery/EBL; angio-embolisation; surgery if uncontrolled.

**Haemorrhoids:** dietary fibre + sitz + topical → banding/sclerotherapy → haemorrhoidectomy.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.534–540; Davidson Ch.22; ACG 2016 LGIB; ESGE 2021.

### Definition

Bleeding from oesophageal or gastric varices in patients with portal hypertension. Defines decompensated cirrhosis; mortality 15–20% per episode (Child C up to 40%).

### Aetiology

**Portal HTN:** cirrhosis (commonest), schistosomiasis (Indian endemic in some regions), portal/splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN.

**Trigger threshold:** HVPG > 12 mm Hg → varices develop; HVPG > 20 mm Hg + active bleed → high failure / rebleed risk.

### Clinical Features

Sudden large-volume haematemesis (often bright red) ± melaena ± haematochezia (massive bleed).

Hypovolaemic shock — tachycardia, hypotension, cool peripheries.

Stigmata of CLD — jaundice, spider naevi, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis (precipitates HE).

Often painless (unlike PUD).

### Investigations

Urgent OGD within 12 h after stabilisation (definitive diagnostic + therapeutic).

**Bloods:** CBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, splenic sequestration), INR, LFT, urea/creatinine, blood gas, cross-match 4–6 units.

Child-Pugh + MELD scoring (prognosis, transplant listing).

USG abdomen + Doppler — portal vein patency, splenomegaly, ascites.

Calculate HVPG (transjugular) when planning TIPS.

### Management

### 1. Initial Resuscitation

ABC, 2 wide-bore cannulae, airway protection if encephalopathic.

Crystalloid + restrictive PRBC transfusion (target Hb 7 g/dL — over-transfusion ↑ portal pressure → rebleed; Villanueva 2013).

Correct coagulopathy carefully — INR target not too aggressive in cirrhotics (rebalanced haemostasis); platelets if < 50,000.

- Pharmacotherapy — START WITHIN 1 H, BEFORE OGD

**Vasoactive (1st-line in India):** Vasoactive (1st-line in India): Terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h × 5 d (2 mg q4h for 24 h → 1 mg q4h thereafter). MOA: V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure.

**Alternative:** Alternative: Octreotide 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d OR somatostatin 250 µg bolus → 250 µg/h.

**Antibiotic prophylaxis:** Antibiotic prophylaxis: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d (reduces SBP + early rebleed + mortality, Garcia-Tsao recommendation).

**PPI:** PPI: IV PPI till endoscopy (in case non-variceal lesion identified).

### 3. Endoscopic Therapy

**Oesophageal varices:** Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) — 1st-line (controls bleeding in ≥ 90%, lower rebleed than sclerotherapy).

Alternative if EVL not feasible: endoscopic sclerotherapy (ethanolamine oleate, polidocanol).

**Gastric varices:** cyanoacrylate (N-butyl) glue injection; BRTO (balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration) if available.

- Failure / Massive bleed

Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (oesophageal + gastric balloon) — bridging only, max 24 h, requires ICU + airway protection (risk of necrosis, aspiration, rupture).

Early TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) < 72 h — indicated in Child B with active bleed or Child C ≤ 13; reduces rebleed + mortality (Garcia-Pagán 2010).

Self-expanding metallic stent (Danis stent) — temporary tamponade alternative.

**Surgical:** emergency portocaval shunt / oesophagogastric devascularisation (rarely needed in TIPS era).

- Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

Non-selective β-blocker — propranolol 40 mg BD titrate to HR 55–60 or carvedilol 6.25 BD (preferred in compensated cirrhosis, also α-blockade).

EVL every 2–4 wk till varices obliterated; surveillance OGD 6-monthly.

Treat underlying liver disease (DAA for HCV, antivirals for HBV, abstinence for alcohol).

Liver transplant evaluation in selected cases.

Fig 4. Variceal bleed — Baveno VII pathway.

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (red wale marks, Child B/C) → NSBB.

Medium/large varices → NSBB OR EVL (patient choice/comorbidity).

**Cirrhosis without varices:** do NOT use NSBB for prevention; OGD surveillance.

### Complications

Rebleed (15–30%), aspiration, HE precipitation, SBP, HRS.

**Sengstaken-related:** oesophageal necrosis, perforation, aspiration.

**TIPS:** encephalopathy (20–30%), stent dysfunction, RV failure.

### Prognosis

6-week mortality after first variceal bleed: Child A 5%, Child B 20%, Child C 30–40%. Improved with vasoactive + endoscopic Rx + abx + early TIPS.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.541; Baveno VII (2022); AASLD 2017; ISG-Indian Society of Gastroenterology.

### Definition

Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) — visualisation of oesophagus, stomach and duodenum (up to D2) using a flexible fibre-optic endoscope. Allows biopsy, cytology, and therapeutic interventions. Should be performed by trained gastroenterologist with anaesthetic support / monitoring.

### Indications

### Diagnostic

Dyspepsia with alarm features ('ALARMS'): Age > 55 with new symptoms, Loss of weight, Anaemia, Recurrent vomiting, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty.

Persistent dyspepsia not responding to PPI / H. pylori eradication.

GORD with alarm features or atypical symptoms.

Dysphagia / odynophagia.

Suspected oesophageal varices in known CLD.

Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia (with colonoscopy).

Coeliac disease — duodenal biopsy.

Suspected upper GI cancer or post-resection surveillance.

Suspected peptic ulcer disease.

Persistent vomiting of unknown cause.

Caustic ingestion (within 12–48 h to assess injury).

**Surveillance:** Barrett's oesophagus, gastric premalignant conditions (atrophic gastritis, IM, dysplasia), post-gastric resection, post-EMR/ESD.

### Therapeutic

Variceal banding (EVL) / sclerotherapy.

Endoscopic haemostasis for ulcer bleed (adrenaline injection, thermal coagulation, mechanical clips, haemospray).

Foreign body removal.

Stricture dilatation (achalasia, peptic, malignant).

Stent placement (oesophageal Ca, GOO).

Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) / submucosal dissection (ESD) — early cancers, polyps.

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) — long-term feeding access.

**Achalasia:** balloon dilatation, botulinum injection, POEM.

ERCP — biliary/pancreatic interventions (separate procedure).

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Suspected perforated viscus.

Severe respiratory compromise (without intubation).

Uncooperative / unstable patient without sedation/anaesthesia support.

### Relative

Recent MI (within 30 days).

Severe coagulopathy (correct INR, platelets first).

Severe COPD, decompensated heart failure.

Suspected aneurysm of aortic arch.

### Pre-Procedure

NBM 6 h for solids, 2 h for clear fluids.

**Informed consent (risks:** perforation 0.05%, bleeding, aspiration, sedation complications).

Stop anticoagulants (per BSG/ESGE guidelines — warfarin INR ≤ 1.5 for high-risk procedures; DOACs hold 24–48 h).

Stop iron / bismuth (interfere with mucosal visualisation).

**Pre-procedure assessment:** vitals, BP, cardiac/respiratory status.

IV access, oxygen, suction.

Topical pharyngeal anaesthesia (lidocaine spray).

**Sedation:** midazolam 2–5 mg IV ± fentanyl 25–50 µg; or propofol (anaesthetist).

Antibiotic prophylaxis NOT routinely required (except cirrhotic + variceal bleed, post-PEG placement, PEH high risk).

### Procedure

Left lateral decubitus position, head tilted forward.

Mouth-guard, bite-block.

Pass endoscope under direct vision → oesophagus → stomach → D1, D2.

**Systematic inspection:** GE junction, fundus retroflexion, pylorus, duodenum.

**Biopsies:** gastric (2 antrum + 2 body + incisura — Sydney protocol), duodenum (4 from D2 if coeliac disease suspected), specific lesions.

Photographic documentation.

Total procedure time 5–15 min (diagnostic), longer for therapeutic.

### Post-Procedure

Monitor vitals 30–60 min in recovery.

Avoid food/fluids till gag reflex returns (60 min if pharyngeal lignocaine).

**Watch for complications:** persistent chest/abdominal pain, haematemesis, breathing difficulty.

Discharge with adult escort if sedated.

No driving 24 h post-sedation.

### Complications (overall 0.1–0.5%)

Perforation (0.03–0.05% diagnostic; higher for therapeutic).

Bleeding (0.03% diagnostic, up to 1% for therapeutic).

Aspiration pneumonia.

**Cardiopulmonary:** arrhythmia, hypoxia (sedation), MI (rare).

Sore throat (transient).

Infection (transient bacteraemia; rare endocarditis).

### Common Findings (Quick Reference)

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Functional GI disorder characterised by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habit, without identifiable structural / biochemical cause. Lifetime prevalence ~ 10% (rising in India with urbanisation, stress, dietary shifts).

### Rome IV Criteria (2016)

Recurrent abdominal pain, on AVERAGE at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, with onset ≥ 6 months ago, associated with ≥ 2 of:

Related to defaecation.

Associated with a change in stool frequency.

Associated with a change in stool form (appearance).

### Subtypes (Bristol Stool Scale 1–7)

### Etiology / Pathophysiology

**Multifactorial:** brain–gut axis dysregulation, visceral hypersensitivity, altered gut motility, post-infectious (10% develop IBS after gastroenteritis), low-grade mucosal inflammation, altered microbiome, bile acid malabsorption, psychological stress, anxiety, depression.

**Genetic predisposition, female:** male ratio 2:1.

### Clinical Features

Recurrent abdominal pain — crampy, lower abdomen, relieved/worsened by defaecation.

Altered bowel habit — diarrhoea, constipation, or alternating.

Bloating, flatulence, urgency, sense of incomplete evacuation, mucus in stool.

**No nocturnal symptoms:** Symptoms WORSE during day, NOT nocturnal.

**Often co-morbid with:** dyspepsia, anxiety/depression, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, migraine.

### RED FLAGS (NOT IBS — investigate further)

Onset > 50 years.

Family history of CRC, IBD, coeliac.

Unintentional weight loss > 5%.

Rectal bleeding, melaena, iron-deficiency anaemia.

Nocturnal symptoms — wake from sleep with pain/diarrhoea.

Fever, abdominal mass, lymphadenopathy.

Persistent diarrhoea, large-volume diarrhoea, steatorrhoea.

Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, calprotectin).

Investigations (minimal in absence of red flags)

CBC, ESR/CRP, TSH, coeliac serology (tTG IgA + total IgA).

Stool routine + microscopy + culture (if diarrhoea-predominant).

Faecal calprotectin (differentiates IBS from IBD — <50 normal, >150 IBD likely).

Lactose H₂ breath test if suspected intolerance.

**Colonoscopy:** if red flags / age > 50, IBS-D refractory, family history CRC/IBD.

OGD + duodenal biopsy if coeliac serology positive.

### Management

### 1. Patient Education and Reassurance

Explain functional nature — chronic, fluctuating, not life-threatening.

Build therapeutic alliance, address fears (cancer / IBD).

### 2. Diet and Lifestyle

Regular small meals; avoid skipping/large meals.

Low-FODMAP diet — 4–6 wk trial (works in 50–75% IBS-D/M).

Increase soluble fibre (psyllium / ispaghula) for IBS-C; AVOID insoluble (wheat bran) — may worsen.

Adequate hydration, regular exercise, stress management, sleep hygiene.

Limit caffeine, alcohol, fatty foods, spicy foods (individualised).

Avoid carbonated beverages, sorbitol-containing chewing gums.

### 3. Pharmacological — Subtype-Specific

### 4. Psychological Interventions

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) — strongest evidence for global improvement.

Gut-directed hypnotherapy.

Mindfulness-based stress reduction, yoga.

### Prognosis

Chronic, fluctuating course. Symptoms persist long-term in 30–50%, but does NOT progress to IBD or CRC. Quality of life impact significant — main treatment goal is symptom relief and improved QoL, not cure.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11 p.475; Davidson Ch.21; Rome IV (2016); ACG IBS 2021; NICE CG61.

### Overview

IBD (UC, Crohn's) treatment uses a step-up or top-down approach based on severity, location, and prognostic factors. Goals: induce + maintain remission, achieve mucosal healing, prevent complications, avoid surgery.

### Classification of IBD Drugs

### 1. Aminosalicylates (5-ASA / Mesalamine)

**Sulfasalazine:** Sulfasalazine: 1–2 g BD-QID. Sulfapyridine + 5-ASA. Cleaved by colonic bacteria. SE: nausea, headache, hypersensitivity, oligospermia (reversible).

**Mesalamine:** Mesalamine: 2.4–4.8 g/d divided. pH-dependent or time-released formulations (Asacol, Pentasa, Salofalk). For colonic and ileal disease.

**Olsalazine, Balsalazide:** Olsalazine, Balsalazide: 5-ASA dimers / azo-bonded; site-specific colonic release.

**Topical 5-ASA:** Topical 5-ASA: Suppositories (proctitis), enemas (left-sided UC) — adjunct or monotherapy.

**Indications:** Indications: Mild-moderate UC (induction + maintenance); less effective in Crohn's (some role in colonic CD).

### 2. Corticosteroids

**Prednisolone:** Prednisolone: 40–60 mg/d PO, taper over 8–12 weeks. Severe UC: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h or methylprednisolone 60 mg/d. Induction only — NOT maintenance.

**Budesonide:** Budesonide: 9 mg/d × 8 wk for mild-moderate ileal/right colonic Crohn's. Topically active; high first-pass metabolism → fewer systemic SE.

**Topical (PR foam/enema):** Topical (PR foam/enema): Hydrocortisone, budesonide foam for distal UC.

Steroid dependence (cannot taper) or refractoriness (failure of high dose for 7–10 d) → step up to immunomodulators or biologics.

Long-term steroid avoidance — bone protection (Ca/Vit D, DEXA), DM/HTN screening, infection.

### 3. Immunomodulators (steroid-sparing)

Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine:Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine: AZA 2–2.5 mg/kg/d (6-MP 1–1.5 mg/kg/d). Check TPMT activity before starting (deficiency → severe myelosuppression). Onset 6–12 wk. Maintenance.

**Methotrexate:** Methotrexate: 25 mg/wk IM/SC × 16 wk → 15 mg/wk maintenance (Crohn's). Folic acid 5 mg/wk. Less effective in UC.

**Cyclosporine:** Cyclosporine: 2 mg/kg/d IV (or 4 mg/kg/d PO) for steroid-refractory severe UC — rescue therapy. Bridge to AZA/biologics. Trough 200–400 ng/mL.

**Tacrolimus:** Tacrolimus: Alternative calcineurin inhibitor.

**Monitoring:** CBC, LFT every 2 wk × first month, then 3-monthly.

**Risks:** bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis (AZA), lymphoma (slightly raised), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (rare in young men on AZA + anti-TNF).

- Biologics (anti-TNF and others)

**Infliximab (anti-TNF):** Infliximab (anti-TNF): 5 mg/kg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk maintenance. Can escalate to 10 mg/kg or every 6 wk if loss of response.

**Adalimumab (anti-TNF):** Adalimumab (anti-TNF): 160 mg SC week 0 → 80 mg week 2 → 40 mg every 2 wk maintenance.

**Golimumab:** Golimumab: 200 mg SC week 0 → 100 mg week 2 → 50–100 mg every 4 wk (UC).

**Certolizumab pegol:** Certolizumab pegol: 400 mg SC at 0, 2, 4 wk → every 4 wk (Crohn's).

**Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7):** Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7): 300 mg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk. Gut-selective; lower infection risk.

**Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40):** Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40): Weight-based loading IV → 90 mg SC every 8–12 wk maintenance. Crohn's + UC.

**Risankizumab (anti-IL23):** Risankizumab (anti-IL23): 600 mg IV at 0, 4, 8 wk → 360 mg SC every 8 wk (Crohn's).

### Pre-biologic screening (essential)

**TB screening:** chest X-ray + Mantoux/IGRA (especially Indian context — high TB burden, anti-TNF reactivates latent TB).

Hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV.

Vaccinate live attenuated BEFORE starting (yellow fever, varicella).

CBC, LFT, albumin baseline.

### 5. Small Molecule Drugs (new class)

**Tofacitinib:** Tofacitinib: Pan-JAK inhibitor; 10 mg BD × 8 wk → 5 mg BD maintenance. Moderate-severe UC. Caution: VTE risk (especially with risk factors), shingles.

**Upadacitinib:** Upadacitinib: JAK1 selective; 45 mg/d × 8 wk → 15 mg/d (or 30 mg/d) maintenance. UC + Crohn's.

**Ozanimod:** Ozanimod: S1P modulator; UC.

**Etrasimod:** Etrasimod: S1P modulator; newer.

### 6. Antibiotics

**Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin:** Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin: For perianal Crohn's, fistulae, abscess, pouchitis. 400 mg TDS + 500 mg BD for 4–8 wk.

**Vancomycin PO:** Vancomycin PO: For C. difficile co-infection.

### 7. Adjunctive / Supportive

Iron supplementation (oral or IV; IV preferred in moderate-severe).

B12 (terminal ileitis / resection).

Vitamin D, calcium (osteoporosis prevention).

Probiotics (some evidence for pouchitis; mild UC).

Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) — emerging in UC, very promising in pouchitis.

### Indication-Based Algorithm

### Ulcerative Colitis

**Mild proctitis/distal:** topical 5-ASA, topical steroid.

**Mild-moderate extensive:** PO + topical 5-ASA, PO steroids if needed.

**Moderate-severe:** PO steroids → AZA → biologic (anti-TNF, vedo, ustek) or tofacitinib.

**Severe:** IV hydrocortisone; day-3 response (Travis criteria — > 8 stools or 3–8 + CRP > 45 = high colectomy risk); rescue infliximab 5 mg/kg or cyclosporine 2 mg/kg/d IV.

**Refractory:** colectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (curative).

### Crohn's Disease

**Mild ileal:** budesonide 9 mg/d.

**Moderate:** PO prednisolone → AZA / methotrexate maintenance.

Severe / fistulating / perianal: anti-TNF ± AZA ('top-down'); anti-TNF + seton for perianal fistulae; metronidazole.

**Stricture:** balloon dilatation; surgery (stricturoplasty, segmental resection).

**Goal:** deep remission (clinical + endoscopic mucosal healing).

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Extra-intestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica infection, where trophozoites breach colonic mucosa → portal circulation → hepatic parenchyma → necrotic abscess (classic 'anchovy sauce' aspirate). Most common extra-intestinal amoebic manifestation; right lobe involved in 70–80%. Significant Indian public health burden — endemic across the subcontinent.

### Clinical Features

**Subacute onset (1–4 wk):** fever, RUQ pain (referred to right shoulder), tender hepatomegaly, weight loss, anorexia, sweating.

Recent dysentery only in 10–30% (most have no GI history).

**Examination:** tender enlarged liver (intercostal tenderness — Boas sign), right basal lung dullness/effusion, mild jaundice (15–25%).

**Demographic:** adult male 20–40 yr, alcohol/poor sanitation/lower SES.

### Investigations

### Confirmatory

USG abdomen — single hypoechoic lesion right lobe, no calcification (unlike hydatid), 1st-line in India.

CECT — peripheral enhancement, central necrosis; chronic shows wall.

Serology — IELISA anti-E. histolytica IgG (sensitivity > 90%; persists for years — limits use in re-exposed Indian patients).

Stool antigen (Entamoeba histolytica II ELISA) > microscopy (microscopy can't distinguish from non-pathogenic E. dispar/moshkovskii).

Aspirate (only if needed)

Reddish-brown 'anchovy sauce' pus, sterile bacterial culture, PCR positive for E. histolytica.

### Supportive

CBC — leukocytosis without eosinophilia (eosinophilia suggests hydatid).

LFT — raised ALP > ALT/AST.

CRP raised, blood culture (rule out pyogenic).

### Differentiating Amoebic vs Pyogenic Liver Abscess

### Management

### 1. Medical (primary)

**Tissue amoebicide:** Tissue amoebicide: Metronidazole 800 mg PO TDS × 7–10 d (or tinidazole 2 g OD × 3–5 d — better tolerated).

**Luminal amoebicide:** Luminal amoebicide: Diloxanide furoate 500 mg TDS × 10 d OR paromomycin 25–35 mg/kg/d in 3 divided doses × 7 d (MUST follow tissue amoebicide to eradicate cysts; prevents relapse / spread).

**Supportive:** Supportive: Analgesia, antiemetics, hydration; avoid alcohol with metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction).

### 2. Aspiration / Drainage

Indications for percutaneous (USG-guided) aspiration:

Large abscess (> 5–10 cm) with thin wall and risk of rupture.

Left lobe abscess (risk of rupture into pericardium).

No clinical response to medical Rx within 5–7 d.

Diagnostic doubt (rule out pyogenic).

Pregnancy (avoid metronidazole 1st trimester — drainage preferred).

Imminent rupture / superficial location.

Percutaneous catheter drainage if recurrent or multilocular.

Open surgical drainage — only if percutaneous fails or rupture into peritoneum/pleura.

- Complications & their Management

**Rupture (10%):** pleuropulmonary (commonest — right), peritoneal (acute abdomen), pericardial (left lobe — TAMPONADE → emergency drainage), bronchial fistula (anchovy sputum).

Secondary bacterial infection — broad-spectrum abx + drainage.

Hepatobronchial fistula — usually self-resolves with abscess Rx.

### Prognosis

With appropriate Rx, mortality < 5%. Untreated or complicated (rupture) → 20–40%. Resolution of abscess on imaging takes 3–9 months — not a measure of treatment success (clinical improvement is).

### Public Health / Prevention

Sanitation — boil water, wash hands, wash vegetables (esp. India).

Treat asymptomatic cyst-passers (diloxanide / paromomycin) in households.

Health education in endemic regions; screen food handlers in institutional settings.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.555; Davidson Ch.13 (parasites); WHO 2017; ICMR antibiotic policy 2022.

### Definition

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) = hepatic injury attributable to a drug or supplement, after excluding viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes. Accounts for 10% of all acute hepatitis and ~ 50% of acute liver failure in the West.

### Classification by Mechanism

**Intrinsic / Direct:** Intrinsic / Direct: Predictable, dose-dependent, reproducible. e.g. paracetamol (NAPQI metabolite), CCl₄, Amanita phalloides (α-amanitin).

**Idiosyncratic:** Idiosyncratic: Unpredictable, NOT dose-related, latency days–months. e.g. INH, amoxicillin-clavulanate, halothane, phenytoin.

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

### Classification by Pattern (R-value)

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

**R 2–5:** Mixed (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulphonamides).

### Common Hepatotoxic Drugs — by Class

### Indian Context — ATT-DILI

Highest incidence among Asians (~ 8–12%) — important for MBBS.

**Risk factors:** age > 35, female, alcoholism, viral hepatitis B/C carrier, HIV, malnutrition, slow acetylator phenotype (Indian genetic prevalence).

**Pathway:** INH → hydrazine metabolite → CYP2E1 → hepatocyte injury. Rifampicin induces CYP isoenzymes → ↑ INH toxicity; PZA additional risk.

**Monitoring:** baseline + monthly LFT during ATT in high-risk; symptom screening.

Stop ATT if ALT > 5× ULN (asymptomatic) or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms / jaundice.

**Re-introduction:** after LFT normalises, single drug → titrate up (usually rifampicin first → INH → PZA).

**Severe / hepatitic ATT-DILI:** switch to non-hepatotoxic regimen — levofloxacin + ethambutol + injectable (aminoglycoside) ± linezolid.

### Diagnosis

Temporal relationship — onset days to months after starting drug; dechallenge improves LFT.

Exclude viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), autoimmune, biliary (USG/MRCP), metabolic (Wilson's, haemochromatosis).

RUCAM / Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score ≥ 6 = probable.

Liver biopsy — only if diagnosis unclear or atypical.

### Management

WITHDRAW culprit drug immediately.

### Definition

Clinical manifestations of impaired hepatic synthetic, metabolic, detoxification, and excretory function — may be acute or chronic, compensated or decompensated.

### Signs — Examination Sequence (Head to Toe)

### General / Constitutional

Sallow / icteric complexion (yellow tinge of sclera, mucosa, skin) — bilirubin > 2 mg/dL.

Cachexia, muscle wasting (temporal hollowing, sarcopenia).

Foetor hepaticus — sweet musty breath (dimethyl sulphide from mercaptans).

Altered mentation — drowsiness, confusion, irritability (encephalopathy).

### Hands

Clubbing — chronic liver disease, especially PBC, hepatopulmonary syndrome.

Leuconychia — proximal 2/3 white (Terry's nails) → hypoalbuminaemia.

Palmar erythema — thenar / hypothenar.

Dupuytren's contracture — palmar fascia thickening (alcoholic CLD).

Asterixis (flapping tremor) — hepatic encephalopathy; not specific (also uraemia, CO₂ retention).

Bruising / ecchymoses — coagulopathy (↓ vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X).

Petechiae — thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism, ↓ thrombopoietin).

### Face / Eyes

Icterus — sclera + frenulum.

Xanthelasma — periorbital cholestatic deposits (PBC).

Kayser-Fleischer ring — Wilson's disease.

Parotid enlargement — alcoholic CLD.

Spider naevi on face, neck, upper chest (drainage area of SVC).

### Chest

Spider naevi (> 5 significant).

Gynaecomastia (impaired oestrogen metabolism, also drugs — spironolactone, digoxin).

Loss of axillary / chest hair.

Pleural effusion right > left (hepatic hydrothorax — diaphragmatic defect; transudate, ascitic origin).

### Abdomen

Hepatomegaly initially (firm, irregular, tender) — may shrink in late cirrhosis.

Splenomegaly (portal HTN) — moderate.

Ascites — shifting dullness, fluid thrill (large), umbilicus evertion / hernia.

Caput medusae — recanalised paraumbilical vein → distended abdominal wall veins (flow AWAY from umbilicus, distinguishes from SVC obstruction).

Venous hum (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur) — heard over caput medusae.

Pulsatile liver — TR (cardiac cirrhosis).

Bruit over liver — HCC, hepatic artery aneurysm.

### Hormonal / Genitalia

Testicular atrophy, loss of libido, impotence.

Amenorrhoea (women).

Loss of pubic / body hair.

### Lower limbs

Pitting oedema — hypoalbuminaemia (albumin < 2.5 g/dL).

Bruising — coagulopathy.

Peripheral neuropathy (alcoholic / thiamine deficiency / autoimmune AIH).

### Systemic / Cardiovascular

Hyperdynamic circulation — bounding pulse, low BP, warm peripheries, tachycardia.

Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy — blunted contractile response to stress.

OGD — varices.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Extra-intestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica infection, where trophozoites breach colonic mucosa → portal circulation → hepatic parenchyma → necrotic abscess (classic 'anchovy sauce' aspirate). Most common extra-intestinal amoebic manifestation; right lobe involved in 70–80%. Significant Indian public health burden — endemic across the subcontinent.

### Clinical Features

**Subacute onset (1–4 wk):** fever, RUQ pain (referred to right shoulder), tender hepatomegaly, weight loss, anorexia, sweating.

Recent dysentery only in 10–30% (most have no GI history).

**Examination:** tender enlarged liver (intercostal tenderness — Boas sign), right basal lung dullness/effusion, mild jaundice (15–25%).

**Demographic:** adult male 20–40 yr, alcohol/poor sanitation/lower SES.

### Investigations

### Confirmatory

USG abdomen — single hypoechoic lesion right lobe, no calcification (unlike hydatid), 1st-line in India.

CECT — peripheral enhancement, central necrosis; chronic shows wall.

Serology — IELISA anti-E. histolytica IgG (sensitivity > 90%; persists for years — limits use in re-exposed Indian patients).

Stool antigen (Entamoeba histolytica II ELISA) > microscopy (microscopy can't distinguish from non-pathogenic E. dispar/moshkovskii).

Aspirate (only if needed)

Reddish-brown 'anchovy sauce' pus, sterile bacterial culture, PCR positive for E. histolytica.

### Supportive

CBC — leukocytosis without eosinophilia (eosinophilia suggests hydatid).

LFT — raised ALP > ALT/AST.

CRP raised, blood culture (rule out pyogenic).

### Differentiating Amoebic vs Pyogenic Liver Abscess

### Management

### 1. Medical (primary)

**Tissue amoebicide:** Tissue amoebicide: Metronidazole 800 mg PO TDS × 7–10 d (or tinidazole 2 g OD × 3–5 d — better tolerated).

**Luminal amoebicide:** Luminal amoebicide: Diloxanide furoate 500 mg TDS × 10 d OR paromomycin 25–35 mg/kg/d in 3 divided doses × 7 d (MUST follow tissue amoebicide to eradicate cysts; prevents relapse / spread).

**Supportive:** Supportive: Analgesia, antiemetics, hydration; avoid alcohol with metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction).

### 2. Aspiration / Drainage

Indications for percutaneous (USG-guided) aspiration:

Large abscess (> 5–10 cm) with thin wall and risk of rupture.

Left lobe abscess (risk of rupture into pericardium).

No clinical response to medical Rx within 5–7 d.

Diagnostic doubt (rule out pyogenic).

Pregnancy (avoid metronidazole 1st trimester — drainage preferred).

Imminent rupture / superficial location.

Percutaneous catheter drainage if recurrent or multilocular.

Open surgical drainage — only if percutaneous fails or rupture into peritoneum/pleura.

- Complications & their Management

**Rupture (10%):** pleuropulmonary (commonest — right), peritoneal (acute abdomen), pericardial (left lobe — TAMPONADE → emergency drainage), bronchial fistula (anchovy sputum).

Secondary bacterial infection — broad-spectrum abx + drainage.

Hepatobronchial fistula — usually self-resolves with abscess Rx.

With appropriate Rx, mortality < 5%. Untreated or complicated (rupture) → 20–40%. Resolution of abscess on imaging takes 3–9 months — not a measure of treatment success (clinical improvement is).

Sanitation — boil water, wash hands, wash vegetables (esp. India).

Treat asymptomatic cyst-passers (diloxanide / paromomycin) in households.

Health education in endemic regions; screen food handlers in institutional settings.

### Definition

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

### Definition

Acute liver failure (ALF) = sudden onset of liver dysfunction (jaundice, coagulopathy INR ≥ 1.5) with hepatic encephalopathy within 26 weeks, in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing liver disease.

### Classification (O'Grady)

### Aetiology (India-relevant)

**Viral:** Hep E (commonest in India, especially in pregnant women — 20% mortality), Hep B, Hep A in children, Hep D super-infection, HSV/CMV/EBV (immunocompromised).

**Drugs:** paracetamol overdose (commonest in West), anti-TB drugs (INH/Rif/PZA — Indian context), phenytoin, valproate, halothane, herbal/Ayurvedic preparations.

**Toxins:** Amanita phalloides mushroom, yellow phosphorus.

Wilson's disease (fulminant presentation in teens/young adults; Coombs-negative haemolysis).

Autoimmune hepatitis (acute severe).

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP syndrome.

Ischaemic hepatitis (shock, Budd-Chiari).

Lymphoma / malignant infiltration.

### Clinical Features

**Prodrome:** malaise, anorexia, nausea, mild jaundice.

Progressive jaundice with deepening encephalopathy.

Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven I–IV; cerebral oedema, raised ICP in advanced).

Coagulopathy → bruising, GI bleed, intracranial haemorrhage.

Hypoglycaemia (impaired gluconeogenesis), metabolic acidosis (lactate).

Renal failure (HRS type 1) in 50%.

Sepsis (Gram-positive > -negative; CONS, Staph aureus, Candida) — high mortality.

**Cardiovascular:** hyperdynamic, then circulatory failure with vasoplegia.

**Respiratory:** ARDS, aspiration pneumonia.

Liver shrinks rapidly on examination.

### Investigations

### Confirm severity

LFT — AST/ALT often > 1000 (often > 10,000 in ischaemic/paracetamol), bilirubin rising, alkaline phosphatase, GGT.

INR ≥ 1.5 (best indicator of synthetic function).

Albumin, ammonia, lactate, ABG, glucose, electrolytes, renal function.

### Aetiology

Paracetamol level (Rumack-Matthew nomogram — > 4 h post-ingestion).

**Viral serology:** HAV IgM, HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM, HCV RNA, HEV IgM, HDV (if HBV+).

**AIH markers:** ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM, IgG.

**Wilson's:** ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper, KF rings, low ALP:bilirubin ratio < 4.

Pregnancy test, USG abdomen (Budd-Chiari Doppler).

Toxic screen — mushroom history, herbal, alcohol.

### Prognostic scores

**KCC:** King's College Criteria (most validated for transplant referral):

**Paracetamol:** arterial pH < 7.30 OR all 3 of (INR > 6.5, Cr > 300 µmol/L, grade III-IV HE).

**Non-paracetamol:** INR > 6.5 OR any 3 of: age < 10 / > 40, non-A non-B / drug-induced / halothane, jaundice > 7 d before HE, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 300 µmol/L.

MELD ≥ 30, Clichy criteria (factor V < 20–30%) — alternatives.

### Management

- ICU care — early referral to liver transplant centre

Intubation if grade III–IV HE; mechanical ventilation.

Head-up 30°, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40), sedation propofol (avoid benzodiazepine).

Maintain CPP > 60 mm Hg; ICP monitoring controversial (high bleeding risk).

Strict glucose monitoring (frequent hypoglycaemia) — IV 10% dextrose.

**Vasopressors:** noradrenaline for hypotension; avoid hyperthermia.

### 2. Specific antidotes

**Paracetamol overdose:** Paracetamol overdose: N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h IV (Prescott regimen); benefit even > 24 h.

**Amanita phalloides:** Amanita phalloides: Penicillin G 1 MU/kg/d + silibinin 5 mg/kg IV.

**Wilson's:** Wilson's: D-penicillamine, plasmapheresis (urgent), liver transplant.

**Autoimmune hepatitis:** Autoimmune hepatitis: Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/d IV — proceed to transplant if no response in 4 days.

**HSV:** HSV: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h IV.

Acute HBV with severe / coag failure:Acute HBV with severe / coag failure: Tenofovir or entecavir.

### 3. Manage complications

**Encephalopathy/cerebral oedema:** lactulose (controversial in ALF — risk of bowel distention), hypertonic saline (target Na 145–155), mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg, hyperventilation as rescue.

**Coagulopathy:** vitamin K 10 mg IV daily; FFP only if active bleeding or pre-procedure (over-correction can mask trends).

**AKI / HRS:** cautious fluid + albumin, RRT (CRRT preferred).

**Sepsis:** low threshold for empirical broad-spectrum abx + antifungal (piperacillin-tazobactam + fluconazole/echinocandin).

**Stress ulcer prophylaxis:** PPI.

Avoid sedatives / hepatotoxic drugs.

Indicated by KCC, MELD ≥ 30, Clichy.

**Without transplant:** mortality 60–90%.

**With transplant:** 1-yr survival 70–80%.

Living-donor liver transplant feasible in India (cost, donor availability).

### 5. Extracorporeal Liver Support

MARS (Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System) — bridge to transplant.

High-volume plasmapheresis — improves survival without transplant (RELIEF trial).

Loss of axillary / chest hair.

Pleural effusion right > left (hepatic hydrothorax — diaphragmatic defect; transudate, ascitic origin).

### Abdomen

Hepatomegaly initially (firm, irregular, tender) — may shrink in late cirrhosis.

Splenomegaly (portal HTN) — moderate.

Ascites — shifting dullness, fluid thrill (large), umbilicus evertion / hernia.

Caput medusae — recanalised paraumbilical vein → distended abdominal wall veins (flow AWAY from umbilicus, distinguishes from SVC obstruction).

Venous hum (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur) — heard over caput medusae.

Pulsatile liver — TR (cardiac cirrhosis).

Bruit over liver — HCC, hepatic artery aneurysm.

### Hormonal / Genitalia

Testicular atrophy, loss of libido, impotence.

Amenorrhoea (women).

Loss of pubic / body hair.

### Lower limbs

Pitting oedema — hypoalbuminaemia (albumin < 2.5 g/dL).

Bruising — coagulopathy.

Peripheral neuropathy (alcoholic / thiamine deficiency / autoimmune AIH).

### Systemic / Cardiovascular

Hyperdynamic circulation — bounding pulse, low BP, warm peripheries, tachycardia.

Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy — blunted contractile response to stress.

### Major Decompensation Markers (memorise)

### Investigations to Confirm

LFT (AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin/albumin), INR, ammonia.

USG abdomen ± Doppler — shrunken nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, portal flow.

OGD — varices.

Child-Pugh, MELD-Na for severity and prognostication.

### Prognostic Implication

Each decompensation event reduces median survival significantly: compensated cirrhosis ~ 12 yr → after first decompensation ~ 2 yr → second decompensation ~ 6–12 months. Number of decompensations + MELD-Na guide transplant listing.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.523; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD cirrhosis.

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Classification by mechanism

Biguanides — Metformin.

Sulfonylureas (insulin secretagogues) — Glibenclamide, glipizide, gliclazide, glimepiride.

Meglitinides — Repaglinide, nateglinide.

Thiazolidinediones (insulin sensitisers) — Pioglitazone.

α-Glucosidase inhibitors — Acarbose, voglibose, miglitol.

DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) — Sitagliptin, vildagliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin, teneligliptin.

SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) — Empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (injectable, except oral semaglutide) — Liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide, semaglutide; tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1).

Amylin analogue — Pramlintide (injectable).

Bile-acid sequestrant — Colesevelam (modest effect).

Dopamine-2 agonist — Bromocriptine QR.

### Key pharmacology

**Metformin:** ↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑ peripheral insulin sensitivity. First-line for T2DM. SE: GI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (rare). CI: eGFR <30. Dose 500–2000 mg/day.

**Sulfonylureas:** Close KATP channels in β-cells → insulin release. Effective and cheap but cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Avoid in renal failure.

**Pioglitazone:** PPARγ agonist → ↑ insulin sensitivity. SE: weight gain, fluid retention, HF, fractures, bladder cancer risk. Useful in NAFLD.

**α-Glucosidase inhibitors:** Inhibit intestinal carbohydrate absorption. SE: flatulence, diarrhoea. Take with first bite of meal.

**DPP-4 inhibitors:** Inhibit DPP-4 → ↑ GLP-1/GIP → glucose-dependent insulin release. Weight neutral, no hypoglycaemia. Safe in CKD (linagliptin needs no dose adjustment).

**SGLT2 inhibitors:** Inhibit SGLT2 in proximal tubule → glycosuria. ↓ Cardiovascular events, ↓ HF hospitalisation, ↓ CKD progression. SE: GU infection, euglycaemic DKA, Fournier gangrene, volume depletion. Indian favoured.

**GLP-1 RA:** Activate GLP-1 receptor → insulin secretion, glucagon suppression, delayed gastric emptying, satiety. Weight loss, CVD and renal benefit. Injectable (except oral semaglutide). SE: nausea, pancreatitis risk, gallstones.

### Choice in Indian T2DM (RSSDI 2024)

**Step 1:** Metformin + lifestyle.

Add SGLT2i if ASCVD / HF / CKD; add GLP-1 RA if ASCVD / weight loss desired; add DPP-4i / SU / pioglitazone otherwise.

Insulin when HbA1c >9% / symptomatic / contraindications to oral.

### Definition

Loss of oral mucosal continuity exposing underlying connective tissue. May be acute (< 2 wk), subacute (2–6 wk), or chronic (> 6 wk). Persistent ulcers > 3 weeks require malignancy exclusion.

### Etiology

### 1. Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS) — commonest (20%)

### 2. Infections

**Viral:** HSV-1 (primary gingivostomatitis, recurrent herpes labialis), VZV (chickenpox/shingles), HFMD (Coxsackie A16), HIV (multiple persistent), CMV (immunocompromised).

**Bacterial:** syphilis (chancre, mucous patches, gumma), TB (chronic indurated ulcer with undermined edges — usually dorsum of tongue), Vincent's angina (necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis — Borrelia + fusobacterium).

**Fungal:** candidiasis (white plaques, erythematous), histoplasmosis, mucormycosis (uncontrolled DM, COVID-19-associated CAM in India).

### 3. Systemic Diseases

Crohn's disease (cobblestone mucosa, deep linear ulcers).

Coeliac disease (apthous ulcers, glossitis, dental enamel defects).

Behçet's disease — recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy (>3 episodes/yr).

PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) — paeds.

Reiter's syndrome (oral + genital ulcers + arthritis + conjunctivitis).

SLE — palatal ulcers (one of ACR criteria); painless typically.

Pemphigus vulgaris — flaccid bullae → erosions; Nikolsky+.

Mucous membrane pemphigoid — subepithelial, scarring; ocular involvement common.

Lichen planus — Wickham's striae, erosive form painful; pre-malignant.

Erythema multiforme major / SJS-TEN — drug or HSV-triggered, target lesions, conjunctivitis.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome — mucocutaneous with skin involvement.

### 4. Nutritional Deficiencies

B12 (Hunter's glossitis, atrophic), folate, iron (angular cheilitis, glossitis, koilonychia), vitamin C (scurvy — gingival bleeding, swollen gums).

Zinc deficiency.

### 5. Haematological

Neutropenia / agranulocytosis (chemo, drugs — clozapine, methimazole), acute leukaemia, cyclic neutropenia.

### 6. Drugs

Methotrexate, NSAIDs, β-blockers (atenolol), nicorandil (typically painful, large), sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor), bisphosphonates (ONJ — osteonecrosis of jaw).

### 7. Malignancy

**Indian context:** Squamous cell carcinoma (commonest oral malignancy in India — tobacco, areca nut, alcohol). Non-healing > 3 wk ulcer, induration, raised everted edges → biopsy mandatory.

**Pre-malignant lesions:** leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut chewing — Indian endemic), lichen planus.

### 8. Trauma

Mechanical (dental, ill-fitting denture, tongue bite), thermal, chemical (aspirin burn).

### Clinical Approach

**Duration:** acute (HSV, RAS, trauma), chronic (TB, malignancy, autoimmune, drugs).

**Single vs multiple:** single chronic → malignancy/TB; multiple recurrent → RAS, Behçet's, IBD.

Painful (most ulcers) vs painless (syphilis, SLE, TB tongue, malignancy).

Associated features — genital ulcer, eye, GI, skin, fever.

### Investigations

**Blood:** CBC, ESR/CRP, ferritin, B12/folate, HIV serology, fasting glucose, TSH.

**If suspected systemic:** tTG (coeliac), ANA, ANCA, IgA/IgG (Behçet's), VDRL.

Biopsy if non-healing > 3 wk, atypical, suspected malignancy/lichen planus.

Swab for HSV PCR, candida (KOH), syphilis serology (TPHA, VDRL).

### Management

### General

Identify and treat underlying cause.

**Pain relief:** paracetamol, NSAIDs (avoid if drug-induced).

Topical anaesthetic (lignocaine 2% viscous gel) for severe pain.

Antiseptic mouthwash — chlorhexidine 0.2% rinse BD, povidone iodine.

Avoid irritants (spicy, hot, alcohol-containing mouthwash).

### RAS-Specific

**Topical corticosteroids:** triamcinolone 0.1% in adhesive base (Kenalog in Orabase), dexamethasone elixir 0.5 mg/5 ml rinse-and-spit QID.

Tetracycline mouthwash (250 mg in 5 ml water, hold 2 min, spit QID).

**Severe/refractory:** systemic prednisolone 30–60 mg/d short course, colchicine 0.5 mg BD-TDS, thalidomide (severe HIV-related), dapsone, apremilast.

**Address triggers:** stress, food (chocolate, nuts, citrus), smoking cessation.

### Specific Causes

### Prognosis

Variable. RAS — recurrent, lifelong but harmless. Malignancy → 5-yr survival depends on stage. Indian context: oral SCC accounts for ~ 30% of all cancers in men.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; Davidson Ch.21 (mucocutaneous); Indian oral cancer guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|136.note:
### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.
