### Definition

Enlargement of lymph nodes >1 cm (>1.5 cm inguinal, >0.5 cm epitrochlear) in 2 or more non-contiguous regions. Localised: one region only.

### Causes (MIAMI mnemonic)

**M – Malignancies:** lymphoma (Hodgkin's, NHL), leukaemia (CLL, ALL), metastatic carcinoma.

**I – Infections:** viral (EBV, CMV, HIV, viral hepatitis), bacterial (TB, syphilis, brucellosis, cat-scratch, rickettsia), protozoal (toxoplasma, kala-azar, trypanosomiasis), fungal (histoplasmosis).

**A – Autoimmune:** SLE, RA, Sjögren's, IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis.

**M – Miscellaneous:** Castleman disease, Kikuchi disease, amyloidosis, lipid storage disorders (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick), Rosai-Dorfman.

**I – Iatrogenic:** drugs (phenytoin – pseudo-lymphoma, carbamazepine, allopurinol, hydralazine).

### Indian-context specifics

Tuberculosis – commonest cause of cervical, mediastinal in India.

Lymphoma – Hodgkin's especially in young; NHL in older.

Kala-azar – Bihar, eastern UP, West Bengal, Jharkhand.

Filariasis – inguinal nodes + epidemiologically endemic.

HIV with TB or lymphoma.

### Approach – history

Duration, growth rate (rapid – infection/aggressive lymphoma; slow – indolent lymphoma/TB).

Pain (infection vs malignant – usually painless).

B symptoms – fever, night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months.

Pruritus (Hodgkin's).

Sexual history, IV drug use, transfusion (HIV).

Animal exposure, occupation, travel, cat scratch.

Drug history.

Contact with TB.

### Approach – examination

**Each node:** size, site, number, consistency, tenderness, mobility, fixation, overlying skin.

### Characteristic patterns:

– TB – matted, firm, occasional sinus (collar-stud abscess)

– Lymphoma – rubbery, painless, discrete; alcohol-induced pain in Hodgkin's

– Metastatic – hard, fixed, irregular

– Acute infective – tender, warm, soft

Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) – GI cancer (Troisier's sign).

Hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, jaundice, skin lesions, tonsils, ENT exam.

### Investigations

CBC + peripheral smear – cytopenias, atypical lymphocytes, blasts.

ESR / CRP.

Mantoux + chest X-ray.

HIV ELISA, hepatitis serology.

Monospot/EBV serology, CMV serology, toxoplasma serology.

ANA, RA factor (autoimmune).

LDH, β₂-microglobulin (lymphoma prognosis).

USG node – size, vascularity, hilum, matting.

FNAC – useful for TB, metastasis; LIMITED for lymphoma subtyping.

Excisional lymph node biopsy – GOLD STANDARD for lymphoma diagnosis; preserves architecture for IHC + flow + cytogenetics.

CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis or FDG-PET/CT – staging.

Bone marrow biopsy – staging.

**Special:** NAAT for TB (GeneXpert MTB/RIF), kala-azar RK39 + bone marrow.

Fig 9. Generalised lymphadenopathy — differential and workup.

### Management

Treat underlying cause. Empirical antibiotics not routinely indicated; never give empirical anti-TB treatment to undiagnosed lymphadenopathy — biopsy first.

GENERAL MEDICINE|139.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Reactive leucocytosis >50 × 10⁹/L with left shift (immature myeloid forms in peripheral blood) that mimics leukaemia but is secondary to a non-haematological cause.

### Causes

Severe infections – pneumonia, septicaemia, TB, Clostridium difficile, miliary TB.

Severe inflammation / haemorrhage / haemolysis.

Severe tissue necrosis – burns, trauma, MI.

Solid tumours – gastric, lung, colon, melanoma (paraneoplastic G-CSF).

Drugs – corticosteroids, lithium, G-CSF, GM-CSF.

DKA, eclampsia.

Severe haemorrhage, haemolysis.

### Differentiation from CML

### Management

Treat the underlying cause; leucocytosis resolves spontaneously.

### Definition

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) = hepatic injury attributable to a drug or supplement, after excluding viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes. Accounts for 10% of all acute hepatitis and ~ 50% of acute liver failure in the West.

### Classification by Mechanism

**Intrinsic / Direct:** Intrinsic / Direct: Predictable, dose-dependent, reproducible. e.g. paracetamol (NAPQI metabolite), CCl₄, Amanita phalloides (α-amanitin).

**Idiosyncratic:** Idiosyncratic: Unpredictable, NOT dose-related, latency days–months. e.g. INH, amoxicillin-clavulanate, halothane, phenytoin.

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

### Classification by Pattern (R-value)

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

**R 2–5:** Mixed (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulphonamides).

### Common Hepatotoxic Drugs — by Class

### Indian Context — ATT-DILI

Highest incidence among Asians (~ 8–12%) — important for MBBS.

**Risk factors:** age > 35, female, alcoholism, viral hepatitis B/C carrier, HIV, malnutrition, slow acetylator phenotype (Indian genetic prevalence).

**Pathway:** INH → hydrazine metabolite → CYP2E1 → hepatocyte injury. Rifampicin induces CYP isoenzymes → ↑ INH toxicity; PZA additional risk.

**Monitoring:** baseline + monthly LFT during ATT in high-risk; symptom screening.

Stop ATT if ALT > 5× ULN (asymptomatic) or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms / jaundice.

**Re-introduction:** after LFT normalises, single drug → titrate up (usually rifampicin first → INH → PZA).

**Severe / hepatitic ATT-DILI:** switch to non-hepatotoxic regimen — levofloxacin + ethambutol + injectable (aminoglycoside) ± linezolid.

### Diagnosis

Temporal relationship — onset days to months after starting drug; dechallenge improves LFT.

Exclude viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), autoimmune, biliary (USG/MRCP), metabolic (Wilson's, haemochromatosis).

RUCAM / Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score ≥ 6 = probable.

Liver biopsy — only if diagnosis unclear or atypical.

### Management

WITHDRAW culprit drug immediately.

**Supportive:** hydration, antiemetics, monitor INR + bilirubin.

**Paracetamol:** Specific antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for paracetamol — 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (Rumack-Matthew nomogram).

Penicillin G + silibinin for Amanita.

Carnitine for valproate.

Corticosteroids may help immune-mediated (DRESS, ICI-related hepatitis).

Liver transplant if acute liver failure (King's College criteria for paracetamol, INR > 6.5 / 3 of 5 minor criteria for non-paracetamol).

### Prognosis

Most resolve on dechallenge. 'Hy's law' (ALT > 3× ULN + bilirubin > 2× ULN + no other cause) → 10% mortality. Cholestatic DILI may persist months → vanishing bile duct syndrome.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.22; ACG DILI 2014; Indian Society of Gastroenterology DILI consensus.

GENERAL MEDICINE|140.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

Dyspnoea may result from metabolic abnormalities driving respiration without primary lung or cardiac disease – usually stimulating central or peripheral chemoreceptors.

### Acidosis

Diabetic ketoacidosis – Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing, compensatory).

Lactic acidosis – sepsis, shock, metformin toxicity, severe exercise.

Uremic acidosis (CKD).

Toxic alcohols – methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates.

### Anaemia

Severe anaemia (any cause) – decreased O₂ delivery → tachypnoea.

### Hypoxaemia (any cause)

Cyanide/carbon-monoxide poisoning – tissue hypoxia.

Methaemoglobinaemia.

### Thyrotoxicosis

Increased metabolic demand.

### Pregnancy

Progesterone stimulates respiratory centre.

### Hypoglycaemia

Sympathetic surge + tachypnoea.

### Drugs/toxins

Salicylates (early respiratory alkalosis), beta-2 agonists, theophylline toxicity.

### Approach

ABG (acid-base status), CBC, glucose, electrolytes, lactate, creatinine, urinalysis, drug screen, TSH, blood gas methaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin.

### Definition

An acid-base disturbance characterised by reduction in blood pH (<7.35) and primary decrease in serum bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L) due to either gain of fixed acid, loss of base, or impaired renal acid excretion. The respiratory compensation (reduced PaCO₂) typically follows Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2.

### Approach – Anion gap

Anion gap (AG) = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO₃-]); normal 8–12 mmol/L. Albumin-corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4 – albumin).

High anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) — 'MUDPILES' or 'KULT-GOLD-MARS'

M – Methanol (formic acid)

### U – Uremia (CKD)

D – Diabetic ketoacidosis / alcoholic / starvation ketoacidosis

P – Paraldehyde, propylene glycol

### I – Isoniazid, iron

L – Lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock, metformin, hypoxia)

### E – Ethylene glycol

### S – Salicylates

Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA / hyperchloraemic):

Diarrhoea (loss of HCO₃).

Renal tubular acidosis (type 1 distal, type 2 proximal, type 4 hyporeninaemic).

Ureteric diversion (uretero-sigmoidostomy).

Pancreatic/biliary fistula.

**Drugs:** acetazolamide, topiramate, cholestyramine.

Saline infusion (dilutional).

Early renal failure.

### Clinical features

Underlying cause-related (DKA – hyperglycaemia, ketones).

Kussmaul respiration (deep, sighing).

Decreased myocardial contractility, hypotension, arrhythmias.

Increased catecholamines + insulin resistance + hyperkalaemia.

Bone demineralisation (chronic).

**CNS:** lethargy, confusion, coma.

### Investigations

### 1. Confirm acidosis

ABG (arterial pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃).

Venous bicarbonate, base excess.

- Calculate anion gap

Serum Na, K, Cl, HCO₃. Calculate AG and corrected AG (for albumin).

- Look for cause (HAGMA)

Glucose + ketones (DKA, alcoholic ketosis).

Serum lactate (lactic acidosis).

Renal function – urea, creatinine, eGFR (uremia).

Osmolar gap >10 mOsm/kg suggests toxic alcohol (methanol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol).

Toxicology screen – salicylate, methanol/ethylene glycol levels, isoniazid.

### 4. NAGMA workup

Urine pH, urine anion gap (UAG = UNa + UK − UCl).

Urine ammonium (low in RTA).

Stool electrolytes / osmolality if diarrhoea.

Renal ultrasound, urine for calcium/citrate.

### Management principles

Treat underlying cause (insulin for DKA, dialysis for uremia, fomepizole/dialysis for toxic alcohols, glucose+B1 for ketoacidosis).

**Sodium bicarbonate:** usually only if pH<7.1 in DKA; <7.2 in lactic acidosis; or in hyperkalaemic acidosis. Routine HCO₃ in DKA is controversial (paradoxical CSF acidosis).

Correct K+; haemodialysis for uremic acidosis, toxic alcohols, severe lactic acidosis with metformin.

GENERAL MEDICINE|143.note:
### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

GENERAL MEDICINE|145.note:
### Definition

SLE is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by production of antibodies to nuclear antigens, immune-complex deposition and inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, serous membranes and the central nervous system. Female:male ≈ 9:1, peak onset 15–40 yrs; commoner and more severe in South Asians and Afro-Caribbeans.

### Etiology / Risk factors

Genetic — HLA-DR2, DR3; complement deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4); IRF5, STAT4, TREX1

Hormonal — oestrogen excess, oral contraceptives may trigger flares

Environmental — UV light, EBV infection, silica, smoking

**Drug-induced lupus:** hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF, interferon (less renal/CNS, anti-histone +)

Pregnancy can precipitate flare; flares can affect pregnancy

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Defective clearance of apoptotic debris exposes nuclear antigens

Loss of self-tolerance → polyclonal B-cell activation → autoantibody production (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, anti-phospholipid)

Immune complexes deposit in kidneys, skin, vessels → complement activation → tissue injury

Type I interferon signature drives disease activity

Clinical features — multisystem

### Constitutional

Fatigue, fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy

### Mucocutaneous (80%)

Malar (butterfly) rash — spares nasolabial folds

Discoid rash — scarring, dyspigmentation; sun-exposed areas

Subacute cutaneous LE — annular/psoriasiform, photosensitive, anti-Ro/SSA

### Photosensitivity

Painless oral/nasal ulcers (commonly hard palate)

Alopecia (diffuse non-scarring or discoid scarring)

### Raynaud's phenomenon

### Musculoskeletal (90%)

Symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis — non-erosive (Jaccoud's reducible deformity)

Myalgia, true myositis rare

### Avascular necrosis (steroid-related)

Renal — lupus nephritis (LN, 40–60%, more in Indians)

### Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, AKI

ISN/RPS 2003 classes I–VI; III/IV (proliferative) most severe, V membranous

**Renal biopsy:** light microscopy + IF (full-house: IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q) + EM

### Neuropsychiatric (NPSLE)

Seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction

### Stroke (often APLA mediated)

Aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, mononeuritis multiplex

### Cardiopulmonary

Pleuritis, pericarditis (commonest serous involvement)

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (non-bacterial verrucous)

Pneumonitis, shrinking lung syndrome, alveolar haemorrhage, ILD

Premature accelerated atherosclerosis — major late mortality cause

### Haematological

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Coombs+), leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia (ITP-like)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (30–40% of SLE)

Arterial/venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, livedo reticularis

### Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin Ab, anti-β2 GP I

### GI / hepatic

Lupus enteritis (vasculitis), pancreatitis, autoimmune hepatitis overlap

### Diagnostic criteria

**EULAR/ACR 2019 (preferred):** Entry: ANA ≥1:80 (HEp-2 IIF). Then weighted criteria in 7 clinical (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) + 3 immunology domains (APLA, complement, SLE-specific antibodies). Classify SLE if ≥10 points with at least one clinical criterion.

SLICC 2012 / ACR 1997 — alternative criteria

### Investigations

Screening / disease confirmation

ANA by IIF on HEp-2 cells — sensitive (>95%), low specificity

Anti-dsDNA — specific; correlates with disease activity (esp. lupus nephritis)

Anti-Sm — specific (low sensitivity ~20% in Caucasians, ~30% in South Asians)

Anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB — subacute cutaneous, neonatal lupus, Sjögren overlap

### Anti-U1 RNP — MCTD overlap

Anti-histone — drug-induced lupus

### Anti-ribosomal P — NPSLE

Complement / immune complex

C3, C4, CH50 — low in active disease

### Disease activity markers

Urinalysis (proteinuria, RBC casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio

CBC (cytopenias), ESR (CRP may be normal — exception: serositis, infection)

### RFT, LFT, lipid profile

**APLA panel:** LA, ACL IgG/IgM, anti-β2 GP I

Renal biopsy if proteinuria >500 mg/day, active sediment, or rising creatinine

MRI brain for NPSLE; EEG if seizures; CSF if meningitis suspected

Echocardiography for serositis, Libman-Sacks; CXR/HRCT for lung

**SLE disease activity:** SLEDAI-2K, BILAG

### Management

Background therapy — for all SLE patients

Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/d (max 400 mg/d) — reduces flares, mortality, organ damage; baseline + annual ophthalmology after 5 years (retinal toxicity)

Photoprotection — sunscreen SPF ≥50 daily

### Vitamin D 1000–2000 IU/d + calcium

**Vaccines:** annual influenza, pneumococcal, HPV (before immunosuppression); avoid live vaccines if immunosuppressed

Aggressive CV risk-factor management — statin, BP <130/80, glycaemic control

**Pregnancy planning:** pre-conceptional counselling, switch teratogens, low-dose aspirin in APS

Mild disease (skin, joints, mild serositis)

### HCQ + NSAIDs PRN

Topical steroids, tacrolimus for skin

Low-dose prednisolone (≤7.5 mg/d) — minimise long-term use

Methotrexate 10–25 mg/wk for arthritis

Belimumab (anti-BLyS) for refractory mucocutaneous/joint

Moderate disease (haematological, mild renal, serositis)

Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/d, taper

**Steroid-sparing:** azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d, MMF 1–2 g/d, methotrexate

### Belimumab, anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR)

Severe disease — Lupus nephritis class III/IV

**Induction:** IV methylprednisolone pulse 500–1000 mg × 3 days + ONE of:

- Cyclophosphamide — Euro-Lupus 500 mg IV every 2 weeks × 6 doses (less toxic, equivalent efficacy in Caucasians/South Asians)

- Cyclophosphamide — NIH 0.5–1 g/m² monthly × 6 (preferred in severe/African ancestry)

- Mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/d × 6 months (preferred in pregnancy planning, GI tolerance)

**Maintenance:** MMF 1–2 g/d OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d for ≥3 years

**Add:** voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) or belimumab — recent evidence for triple therapy

ACEi/ARB for renoprotection; BP target <130/80

Accelerated atherosclerosis, MI, stroke (leading cause of late death)

Premature ovarian failure (cyclophosphamide)

Foetal loss, neonatal lupus, prematurity

### Definition

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetric, erosive, inflammatory polyarthritis predominantly affecting peripheral synovial joints, associated with systemic features and extra-articular manifestations. Prevalence ~0.75% in India; female:male ≈ 3:1; peak onset 30–55 yrs.

### Etiology / Risk factors

**Genetic:** HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (DR4, DR1) — strongest in seropositive RA; PTPN22, STAT4

### Female sex, postpartum

Smoking — major modifiable risk; interacts with shared epitope to drive anti-CCP production

Periodontal disease (Porphyromonas gingivalis citrullination)

Obesity, low birth weight

### Silica dust exposure

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Citrullination of self-proteins → anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) in genetically susceptible host

Synovial hyperplasia (pannus) infiltrated by T cells, B cells, plasma cells, macrophages

**Pro-inflammatory cytokines:** TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, IL-17

Osteoclast activation (RANKL) → bone erosion; matrix metalloproteinases → cartilage destruction

### Clinical features

### Articular

Insidious onset symmetric polyarthritis — MCPs, PIPs, MTPs, wrists, knees, ankles, cervical spine; DIPs and lumbar spine spared

Morning stiffness >30–60 min, improves with activity

Swelling, warmth, tenderness; reduced grip strength

**Late deformities:** ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, hammer toes, hallux valgus

Atlanto-axial subluxation — neck pain, neurological deficit (caution at intubation)

### Systemic

Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anorexia

Extra-articular manifestations (~40%; more in seropositive RA, high anti-CCP, smokers)

**Cutaneous:** rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces — olecranon, Achilles)

**Pulmonary:** ILD (UIP/NSIP), pleural effusion (exudative, low glucose, low pH), Caplan syndrome, bronchiectasis, rheumatoid lung nodules

**Cardiac:** pericarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis, ↑ MI risk (1.5×), cardiomyopathy

**Ocular:** keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren), episcleritis, scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, scleromalacia perforans

**Haematological:** anaemia of chronic disease, Felty's syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), large granular lymphocyte syndrome

**Neurological:** carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitic), atlanto-axial myelopathy

**Vasculitis:** small/medium vessel — digital gangrene, leg ulcers, mononeuritis

**Renal:** AA amyloidosis (long-standing disease), drug nephropathy

**Lymphoma:** 2–4× increased risk, especially DLBCL

**Bone:** peri-articular osteoporosis, systemic osteoporosis

Diagnostic criteria — ACR/EULAR 2010

Score ≥6/10 classifies as definite RA (in a patient with synovitis in ≥1 joint without alternative explanation):

### Investigations

### Inflammatory and serology

RF (IgM-RF) — sensitivity 60–80%, specificity 60–80%

Anti-CCP — sensitivity 60–70%, specificity >95%; prognostic for erosive disease

ESR, CRP — disease activity

### General workup

CBC (ACD, leukopenia in Felty), comprehensive metabolic, LFT, urinalysis

ANA — screen for overlap

HBsAg, anti-HCV, latent TB (Mantoux/IGRA) — pre-biologic

HIV (Indian context, before biologics)

### Imaging

X-ray hands and feet — soft-tissue swelling, juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, deformities, subluxation; cervical spine for atlanto-axial subluxation

Ultrasound joints — synovitis, power Doppler signal, erosions earlier than X-ray

MRI — most sensitive for early synovitis, erosions, bone marrow oedema

### Disease activity

DAS28-ESR or DAS28-CRP (tender + swollen joint count + global + ESR/CRP)

### CDAI, SDAI — alternatives

**Targets:** DAS28 <2.6 = remission; ≤3.2 low; 3.2–5.1 moderate; >5.1 high activity

### Management — treat-to-target

### General

Smoking cessation; weight reduction; physiotherapy and occupational therapy

Patient education; vaccination pre-immunosuppression (influenza, pneumococcal, HBV, HPV); avoid live vaccines on biologics

CV risk assessment and treatment (statin, BP control)

### Symptom relief

NSAIDs at lowest effective dose for short periods

Prednisolone 5–10 mg/d as 'bridge' until DMARD effective; intra-articular steroid for active joints

Avoid long-term steroids — osteoporosis, infection, diabetes

csDMARDs (conventional synthetic) — start within 3 months of diagnosis

**Methotrexate:** Anchor drug. Start 7.5–10 mg/week, titrate to 20–25 mg/week. Co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/wk (not on MTX day). AE: nausea, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, pneumonitis, teratogenicity. Stop 3 months before conception (M and F). Avoid alcohol. Reduce dose in CKD; contraindicated in eGFR <30.

**Sulfasalazine:** 1 g BD–TDS. AE: GI upset, rash, hepatitis, agranulocytosis, G6PD-related haemolysis, oligospermia.

**Hydroxychloroquine:** 200–400 mg/d (≤5 mg/kg). AE: retinal toxicity — eye check baseline + annual after 5 yrs.

**Leflunomide:** 10–20 mg/d (loading 100 mg × 3 days then maintenance — most centres skip loading). AE: hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, hypertension, teratogenicity (very long half-life; cholestyramine washout needed before pregnancy).

**Combination 'triple therapy':** MTX + SSZ + HCQ — Indian-favoured cost-effective combination, comparable efficacy to early biologic in many patients

Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) — after inadequate response to ≥2 csDMARDs

**TNF inhibitors:** etanercept (50 mg SC weekly), adalimumab (40 mg SC q2wk), infliximab (3–10 mg/kg IV q8wk + MTX), golimumab (50 mg SC monthly), certolizumab

**IL-6 inhibitor:** tocilizumab 162 mg SC weekly OR 4–8 mg/kg IV q4wk

**B-cell depletion:** rituximab 1 g IV × 2 (day 0 and 14), every 6 months — RF/anti-CCP-positive; safer in latent TB

**T-cell co-stimulation:** abatacept 125 mg SC weekly OR weight-based IV monthly

**IL-1 inhibitor:** anakinra (rarely used in RA)

Always combine with MTX where tolerated for synergy and reduced anti-drug antibodies

Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) — JAK inhibitors

Tofacitinib 5 mg BD, baricitinib 4 mg OD, upadacitinib 15 mg OD

**ORAL Surveillance trial (2022):** increased major CV events, malignancy, VTE with tofacitinib vs TNFi in older patients with CV risk

**EMA/FDA:** use only if no TNFi alternative in patients ≥65 yr, smokers, malignancy, CV risk

Pre-biologic screening (essential — viva point)

**TB:** Mantoux/IGRA, CXR; if positive — INH 300 mg/d × 9 months started ≥1 month before biologic

### HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV

### CBC, LFT, RFT

Pregnancy test; contraception counselling

### Surgical

### Synovectomy (rare today)

Arthrodesis, arthroplasty (hip/knee/shoulder) for end-stage joint damage

C1–C2 fixation for atlanto-axial instability

### Carpal tunnel release

Fig 5. Rheumatoid arthritis — treat-to-target DMARD ladder

### Complications

Joint destruction, deformity, functional disability

Premature CV death (leading cause)

### ILD, pulmonary fibrosis

### Cervical myelopathy (atlanto-axial)

### Infections (immunosuppression)

### Lymphoma, skin cancers

### Osteoporosis, fragility fractures

### AA amyloidosis

### Prognosis

Modern treat-to-target therapy achieves remission/low disease activity in 50–80%. Adverse prognostic factors: female, smoking, high titre RF/anti-CCP, early erosions, multiple joint involvement, extra-articular features, high inflammatory markers. Untreated RA shortens life expectancy by 5–10 years, mostly from CV disease.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 RA + ACR 2021 guideline for RA + EULAR 2022 RA management recommendations + Indian Rheumatology Association RA position paper.

### Definition

Osteoporosis is a generalised skeletal disorder characterised by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and a consequent increase in fracture risk (WHO 1994). Diagnostic threshold by DXA: T-score ≤ –2.5 SD at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip.

### Etiology / Risk factors

### Primary

Postmenopausal (type I) — accelerated trabecular bone loss from oestrogen deficiency

Senile (type II) — both cortical and trabecular loss, men and women >70 yr

Idiopathic — young adults and juveniles

### Secondary

**Endocrine:** hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing's, hypogonadism, T1DM, GH deficiency

**GI:** malabsorption (celiac, IBD), post-gastrectomy, chronic liver disease

**Renal:** CKD-MBD, RTA, hypercalciuria

**Drugs:** glucocorticoids (>5 mg pred ≥3 months), aromatase inhibitors, GnRH agonists, heparin (long-term), PPI, anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarb), TZDs, SSRIs, SGLT2i (controversial), tenofovir

**Inflammatory:** RA, ankylosing spondylitis, SLE, IBD

**Haematological:** multiple myeloma, mastocytosis, thalassemia, sickle cell, leukemia

**Others:** alcoholism, smoking, prolonged immobilisation, low body weight (<19 kg/m²), low Ca/Vit D intake, sedentary lifestyle

**Genetic:** osteogenesis imperfecta, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, homocystinuria

### Risk-stratification tools

FRAX (WHO) — 10-yr probability of major osteoporotic and hip fracture; treat if hip ≥3% OR major ≥20%

OST (Osteoporosis Self-assessment Tool): [weight – age] × 0.2

### SCORE, ORAI — alternatives

### Pathophysiology

Bone is constantly remodelled in basic multicellular units (BMUs): osteoclasts resorb bone over ~3 weeks, then osteoblasts form new matrix over ~3 months. Coupling is regulated by RANKL/RANK/OPG, Wnt/β-catenin, sclerostin, PTH and 1,25(OH)₂D. In osteoporosis, uncoupling tips the balance toward resorption.

Oestrogen deficiency → ↑ RANKL, ↓ OPG → ↑ osteoclastogenesis + osteoclast lifespan → predominantly trabecular loss

Glucocorticoids → ↓ osteoblast formation + ↑ osteoblast/osteocyte apoptosis + ↓ intestinal Ca absorption + ↑ urinary Ca loss

Senile osteoporosis → ↓ vitamin D synthesis, ↓ intestinal Ca absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism, sarcopenia

**Net result:** thinning of cortices, loss of trabecular connectivity, accumulation of microdamage

### Clinical features

### Asymptomatic (most common)

Detected incidentally on DXA or imaging

Fragility fracture (clinical presentation)

Vertebral compression — sudden mid-back pain, height loss, kyphosis (dowager's hump), restrictive lung disease

Hip fracture (intertrochanteric/femoral neck) — fall from standing height; shortened, externally rotated leg

Distal radius (Colles') — fall on outstretched hand

Pelvic, proximal humerus, ribs

### Examination

Loss of height (>4 cm vs young adult) — measure!

Increased thoracic kyphosis, occiput-to-wall distance >5 cm

Rib-to-pelvis distance <2 finger-breadths suggests vertebral fracture

### Investigations

### Diagnostic — DXA scan

Z-score (premenopausal women, men <50, children) — <–2.0 = 'below expected range for age'

**Sites:** lumbar spine (L1–L4), femoral neck, total hip; use lowest T-score

Workup for secondary cause

### CBC, ESR

Serum Ca (corrected), phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, albumin

### RFT, LFT, TSH

### 25(OH) vitamin D, intact PTH

Testosterone (men), oestradiol/FSH/LH if amenorrhoea

24-h urinary calcium, creatinine; serum and urine electrophoresis if age >50

tTG-IgA for celiac, morning cortisol if Cushing suspected

Bone turnover markers (optional): P1NP (formation), CTX (resorption)

### Imaging

X-ray spine (lateral thoracolumbar): vertebral wedging, biconcavity, crush; Genant semiquantitative grading

VFA (vertebral fracture assessment) on DXA

TBS (trabecular bone score) on DXA — incremental information

QCT spine — volumetric BMD; HR-pQCT (research)

MRI — if malignancy suspected

### Management

- Lifestyle and non-pharmacological

Weight-bearing and resistance exercise ≥30 min, ≥3 days/wk

**Fall prevention:** home safety, vision correction, balance training, gait aids

Smoking cessation; alcohol <2 units/d

Adequate dietary protein 1–1.2 g/kg/d

Hip protectors in nursing-home residents

- Calcium and vitamin D — foundation of all regimens

Elemental calcium 1000–1200 mg/d (diet + supplement)

Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 800–1000 IU/d to keep 25(OH)D ≥30 ng/mL

**Indian protocol:** 60,000 IU cholecalciferol PO weekly × 8 weeks for deficiency, then 60,000 IU monthly maintenance (or 1000–2000 IU daily)

- Pharmacological — first-line

**Bisphosphonates:** Inhibit osteoclasts via farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase inhibition

**Adverse effects:** oesophagitis, hypocalcaemia, acute-phase reaction (IV), osteonecrosis of jaw (rare, ~1:10,000), atypical femoral fracture (long-term >5 yr)

**Contraindications:** GFR <30–35, hypocalcaemia, oesophageal stricture, pregnancy

Drug holiday after 5 yr (oral) or 3 yr (IV) if low risk reassessed

- Second-line / specific situations

**Denosumab:** 60 mg SC every 6 months — fully human monoclonal anti-RANKL; useful in CKD (no dose adjustment), bisphosphonate intolerance. DO NOT skip/stop without follow-on therapy — rebound vertebral fractures.

**Teriparatide (rPTH 1–34):** 20 µg SC daily — anabolic; severe osteoporosis, multiple vertebral fractures, glucocorticoid-induced. Max 24 months lifetime. Follow with antiresorptive to maintain gains.

**Abaloparatide:** PTHrP analogue, 80 µg SC daily — similar use to teriparatide

**Romosozumab:** Anti-sclerostin monoclonal, 210 mg SC monthly × 12 months — very high fracture risk; CV warning, avoid recent MI/stroke

**Raloxifene:** 60 mg PO daily — SERM; reduces vertebral fx, breast Ca; increases VTE and hot flushes

**Hormone therapy:** Reserved for early postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms; not first-line for osteoporosis

**Strontium ranelate:** Withdrawn in many countries — CV risk; not recommended

**Calcitonin (salmon, nasal):** Limited use — analgesic in acute vertebral fracture only

### 5. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIO)

Anyone on prednisolone ≥7.5 mg/d for ≥3 months → start bisphosphonate empirically

DXA baseline + yearly

Lowest effective steroid dose; calcium 1200 + vit D 800 IU

Teriparatide superior to bisphosphonate for high-risk GIO patients

### 6. Monitoring

DXA every 1–2 years on therapy (same machine, same site)

Bone turnover marker (CTX) at 3 months — adherence and response

Calcium, vitamin D, RFT at 3 months and yearly

Fig 1. Osteoporosis — DXA + FRAX driven treatment ladder

### Complications

Vertebral fractures → chronic back pain, kyphosis, restrictive lung disease, reflux, early satiety

**Hip fracture:** 20–30% 1-yr mortality; loss of independence in >50% survivors

Increased risk of subsequent fracture (1 vertebral → 5× risk of another)

**Therapy-related:** ONJ, atypical femoral fracture, hypocalcaemia

### Prognosis

Pharmacotherapy reduces vertebral fracture risk by 40–70% and hip fracture by 20–40% within 1–3 years of treatment. Mortality after hip fracture remains high (~20% at 1 year); ~50% never regain pre-fracture functional status. Early identification and treatment in osteopenia patients at high FRAX risk has the greatest absolute benefit.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 osteoporosis section + ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements 2020 (Ca/Vit D) + Indian Society for Bone and Mineral Research 2022 osteoporosis guidance. ACR/AACE/ISCD international.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 → prolong endogenous GLP-1 and GIP → glucose-dependent insulin secretion, glucagon suppression.

**Available agents:** Sitagliptin 100 mg OD (adjust in CKD), vildagliptin 50 mg BD, linagliptin 5 mg OD (no renal adjustment), saxagliptin 5 mg OD, alogliptin 25 mg OD, teneligliptin 20 mg OD (Indian-favoured, cheap).

**Advantages:** Weight-neutral, no hypoglycaemia (when used alone), well tolerated, safe in elderly and CKD (linagliptin).

**Adverse:** Nasopharyngitis, headache, pancreatitis (rare), arthralgia, hypersensitivity. Saxagliptin and alogliptin – HF hospitalisation signal.

**Use:** Add-on to metformin when modest reduction in HbA1c (0.5–0.8%) needed; preferred in elderly with renal impairment.

### SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in renal proximal tubule → ~50–80 g/day urinary glucose loss; mild diuresis, weight loss, BP reduction; pleotropic cardiovascular and renal benefits.

**Available agents:** Empagliflozin 10–25 mg OD, dapagliflozin 10 mg OD, canagliflozin 100–300 mg OD, ertugliflozin 5–15 mg OD.

**Benefits beyond glycaemia:** ↓ Cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation (EMPA-REG, CANVAS, DECLARE, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR); ↓ CKD progression (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD); approved for HFrEF/HFpEF and CKD regardless of diabetes.

**Indications:** Indicated in T2DM with established/high-risk ASCVD, HF, or CKD; modest HbA1c reduction (0.6–1.0%); 2–3 kg weight loss; ↓ systolic BP 3–5 mmHg.

**Adverse:** Genital mycotic infection (candida, women > men), UTI, volume depletion (especially elderly, on diuretics), euglycaemic DKA (omit pre-op, in fasting/illness), Fournier's gangrene, lower-limb amputation (canagliflozin), bone fractures (canagliflozin).

**Contra-/cautions:** Severe renal failure (eGFR <20–25), volume depletion, hypotension, type 1 DM, recurrent UTI, history of euglycaemic DKA.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (covered briefly)

Liraglutide 1.8–3.0 mg SC OD (also for obesity), exenatide BD or weekly XR, dulaglutide 1.5–4.5 mg SC weekly, semaglutide 0.25–2 mg SC weekly (or oral 14 mg OD).

Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) 5–15 mg SC weekly – superior HbA1c and weight reduction.

**Benefits:** HbA1c reduction 1–1.5%, weight loss 3–10 kg, CV and renal benefit.

**Adverse:** nausea/vomiting (titrate dose), pancreatitis (rare), gallstones, thyroid C-cell tumour (rodent, theoretical).

### Background

Newer insulin analogues have been engineered for tighter, more physiological glycaemic control and reduced hypoglycaemia risk compared with regular human insulin and NPH. They are classified by their pharmacokinetic profile.

### Rapid-acting analogues (prandial)

Lispro – onset 5–15 min, peak 30–60 min, duration 3–4 h.

Aspart – similar profile.

Glulisine.

Faster aspart (Fiasp) – even faster onset (~2 min via niacinamide); post-meal glucose control.

Inhaled human insulin (Afrezza) – very rapid onset.

### Long-acting analogues (basal)

Glargine U-100 (Lantus) – onset 1–2 h, no peak, duration 20–24 h.

Glargine U-300 (Toujeo) – flatter, more reproducible, 24–36 h duration.

Detemir – duration 14–20 h (often twice daily).

Degludec (Tresiba) – ultra-long, duration >42 h, very stable; lower hypoglycaemia risk.

Icodec (once-weekly) – emerging, approved in 2024.

### Pre-mix and biphasic

Pre-mix 70/30 (NPH/regular), 75/25 (lispro protamine/lispro), 70/30 aspart protamine/aspart, 50/50 mixes.

**Co-formulations:** degludec + aspart (Ryzodeg).

### Combined GLP-1/insulin

iGlarLixi (insulin glargine + lixisenatide) – simplifies regimen, better weight profile.

iDegLira (insulin degludec + liraglutide).

### Indications and choice

**T1DM:** basal-bolus regimen (long-acting analogue + rapid-acting with meals) OR insulin pump (continuous SC infusion of rapid-acting).

**T2DM:** basal insulin added when oral therapy insufficient (HbA1c >9% / symptomatic / contraindications). Add prandial later (basal-plus → basal-bolus).

**Pregnancy:** lispro, aspart, detemir; glargine acceptable; degludec limited data.

Newer agents reduce nocturnal hypoglycaemia and weight gain.

### Adverse effects

Hypoglycaemia (commonest), weight gain, injection site reactions (lipohypertrophy/atrophy), allergic reactions (rare), insulin antibodies.

### Indian context

RSSDI emphasises individualised regimens; cost is a major factor; biosimilar insulin analogues (glargine, lispro, aspart) widely available; NPH and regular human insulin remain affordable backup; continuous glucose monitoring increasingly used in T1DM.

### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

### Approach

ICHD-3 classifies > 200 headache types. First task = exclude secondary (dangerous) headache using SNNOOP10 red flags; then classify primary headache.

SNNOOP10 — red flags for secondary headache

S — Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats).

N — Neoplasm (cancer history).

N — Neurological deficit (focal signs, altered consciousness, papilloedema).

O — Onset sudden (thunderclap, peak < 1 min) — SAH until proven otherwise.

O — Older > 50 with new headache (GCA, mass).

P — Pattern change / Progressive.

P — Positional / Precipitated by Valsalva / Cough (raised ICT, Chiari).

P — Papilloedema / Vision change.

P — Pregnancy / Postpartum (CVT, eclampsia, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy).

P — Painful eye + autonomic (cluster, acute angle-closure glaucoma).

P — Posttraumatic.

P — Painkiller overuse / Pathology of immune system (HIV, immunosuppressed).

### PRIMARY headaches (ICHD-3)

### Migraine — see Q6

### Tension-type headache (TTH)

Most common primary headache; 30-78% lifetime.

Bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-moderate, not aggravated by routine activity.

Episodic (< 15 d/mo) or chronic (≥ 15 d/mo).

**Rx:** NSAID; amitriptyline for prevention; lifestyle, stress management.

### Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias

**Cluster headache:** M > F (3:1); strictly unilateral periorbital/temporal; 15-180 min; ipsilateral autonomic (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, ptosis, miosis); agitation/restlessness (vs migraine quiet). Acute: 100% O2 12 L/min × 15 min + sumatriptan 6 mg SC. Prevention: verapamil 240-480 mg, prednisolone bridging, lithium, galcanezumab.

Paroxysmal hemicrania — shorter (2-30 min), more frequent (5-40/d), absolute response to indomethacin.

SUNCT / SUNA — very short (1-600 s), very frequent.

Hemicrania continua — continuous unilateral, indomethacin-responsive.

### Other primary

Primary cough / exertional / sexual headache.

Stabbing headache.

Hypnic headache ('alarm-clock', wakes from sleep, elderly).

New daily persistent headache (NDPH).

### SECONDARY headache causes

### Vascular — thunderclap

SAH (NCCT + LP).

RCVS (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction — pregnancy, vasoactive drugs).

CVT (D-dimer, MR venography — pregnancy, OCP, dehydration, thrombophilia).

Carotid/vertebral dissection.

Pituitary apoplexy.

Hypertensive emergency / PRES.

### Infection

Meningitis (bacterial, TB, viral, fungal).

Encephalitis (HSV — temporal lobe seizures).

Brain abscess (HIV, post-otitis).

Systemic infection (dengue, malaria, enteric fever, COVID-19).

Neurocysticercosis (Indian context — seizure + headache + cyst on imaging).

### Raised ICT

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (young obese F; papilloedema; LP pressure > 25 cm H₂O; Rx weight loss + acetazolamide; CSF diversion if severe).

Brain tumour (worse mornings/Valsalva; progressive).

Hydrocephalus, ventriculitis.

### Inflammatory / autoimmune

Giant cell arteritis (> 50, temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, ESR > 50, biopsy; Rx prednisolone 60 mg/d IMMEDIATELY).

CNS vasculitis.

Tolosa-Hunt (painful ophthalmoplegia).

### Medication / substance

Medication overuse headache (MOH) — analgesics ≥ 15 d/mo, triptans/opioids ≥ 10 d/mo.

Nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors, calcium-channel blockers.

Caffeine withdrawal.

Sinus / facial / dental

Sinusitis (frontal headache + nasal discharge + fever; CT sinuses).

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (red painful eye + halos + nausea — emergency).

Dental, TMJ disorders.

### Cervicogenic

Occipital pain referred from upper cervical joints; aggravated by neck movement.

### Posttraumatic

Post-concussion, subdural haematoma (elderly, alcoholic, anticoagulant).

Investigations (selectively, based on red flags)

NCCT head — first if thunderclap, posttraumatic, focal deficit, altered mental.

LP — if SAH suspected and CT normal, or meningitis.

MRI brain ± MRA/MRV — chronic progressive, atypical features.

ESR, CRP — GCA suspected.

Tonometry — angle-closure glaucoma.

**Other:** HIV, dengue NS1, malaria smear, autoimmune panel.

Fig 8. Headache — red flags and DD.

**Source:** ICHD-3; Do TG et al, BMJ 2019 (SNNOOP10); Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|159.note:
### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.

### Background

Intracranial calcifications are common — many physiological, some pathological. Pattern, location and clinical context help diagnosis. CT is far more sensitive than plain X-ray.

### PHYSIOLOGICAL calcifications

Pineal gland (60% after age 20; useful for midline shift assessment).

Choroid plexus (in lateral ventricles, trigone).

Falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli.

Petroclinoid ligaments.

Habenular commissure.

Dura, arachnoid granulations.

### PATHOLOGICAL calcifications

### 1. Infections

Neurocysticercosis — MULTIPLE punctate calcifications, classic in India; often with seizure history.

Tuberculoma — calcified granuloma.

Toxoplasmosis (congenital) — periventricular / scattered cortical; with hydrocephalus.

CMV (congenital) — periventricular calcifications; with microcephaly.

Cryptococcus, hydatid cyst.

Old abscess.

### 2. Tumours

Oligodendroglioma — 70-90% calcify (characteristic).

Astrocytoma (especially low-grade) — 15%.

Craniopharyngioma — suprasellar, mixed solid-cystic with calcification (children).

Meningioma — psammomatous calcification.

Ependymoma.

Pituitary adenoma (rare).

Metastases (osteoblastic — prostate, breast).

### 3. Vascular

Atherosclerosis (carotid siphon).

Aneurysm (curvilinear calcification of wall).

AVM, cavernoma.

Old infarct / haemorrhage.

Subdural haematoma (chronic, calcified).

### 4. Phakomatoses / Congenital

Sturge-Weber syndrome — tram-track / gyriform calcifications along cortex (parieto-occipital).

Tuberous sclerosis — subependymal nodules (basal ganglia, near foramen of Monro).

Neurofibromatosis (rare optic glioma calcification).

### 5. Metabolic / Endocrine

Hypoparathyroidism / pseudohypoparathyroidism — bilateral basal ganglia + cerebellar (Fahr syndrome).

Hyperparathyroidism (rare).

Hypothyroidism (cretinism).

Wilson's disease.

Fahr disease (idiopathic basal ganglia calcification).

### 6. Toxic / Radiation

Lead poisoning.

Post-radiotherapy (mineralising microangiopathy).

Methotrexate-induced leukoencephalopathy.

### 7. Other

Cockayne syndrome (basal ganglia).

Coats plus syndrome.

### Approach by location

### Investigations

CT head (without contrast) — sensitive for calcification.

MRI brain — characterise lesion; calcium is hypointense on T1 and T2 (or use SWI).

Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D (basal ganglia calcifications).

Ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper (Wilson's).

TORCH serology if neonatal.

Cysticercosis ELISA (EITB), stool ova/cyst.

**Source:** Osborn Diagnostic Imaging Brain; Boloor Ch.15.
