### Definition

Alcohol Use Disorder (DSM-5) is a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment / distress, manifested by ≥2 of 11 criteria in a 12-month period (replacing DSM-IV abuse + dependence). ICD-10 retains alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria) and harmful use. India has the largest population of male alcohol users in Asia; NMHS 2016 estimates prevalence of any alcohol-use disorder at 4.6% in adults (9% in men).

Hazards of alcohol (Boloor A365)

### Neurological

Acute — intoxication, blackouts, traffic accidents, traumatic brain injury, alcohol-induced psychotic disorder.

Withdrawal — tremor, seizures, delirium tremens (see below).

Chronic — Wernicke encephalopathy / Korsakoff psychosis, cerebellar degeneration (truncal ataxia, gait), peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor, painful), optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia), central pontine myelinolysis (with rapid sodium correction), Marchiafava–Bignami disease (corpus callosum demyelination), alcohol-related dementia.

### Gastrointestinal / hepatic

Acute / chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome.

Pancreatitis — acute and chronic (alcohol is the #1 cause of chronic pancreatitis in India after gallstones).

Alcoholic liver disease — fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >32 → steroids/pentoxifylline) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Oesophageal varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal / hepatopulmonary syndromes.

Malabsorption — folate, thiamine, B6, B12, Mg, Zn.

### Cardiovascular

Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcoholic), holiday heart (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke, sudden cardiac death.

### Haematological

Macrocytic anaemia (folate deficiency, direct marrow toxicity), megaloblastic, sideroblastic, haemolysis (Zieve syndrome with hepatitis + hyperlipidaemia), thrombocytopenia, leucopenia.

### Endocrine / metabolic

Hypoglycaemia (gluconeogenesis blocked), ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia / gout, hyperlipidaemia, pseudo-Cushing's.

Hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, infertility, erectile dysfunction.

### Cancer (Group I carcinogen — IARC)

Oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver (HCC), breast, colorectum.

### Obstetric

Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder — microcephaly, growth retardation, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, intellectual disability.

Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm birth.

### Psychiatric

Depression, anxiety, suicide (alcohol present in ~40% of completed suicides in India), insomnia.

Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, pathological jealousy (Othello syndrome).

### Social

Domestic violence, marital breakdown, child neglect, occupational accidents, road traffic accidents, financial ruin, legal issues.

Diagnosis — DSM-5 AUD criteria (≥2 of 11 in 12 months)

**Severity:** 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥6 severe.

Larger amounts / longer than intended.

Persistent desire / unsuccessful attempts to cut down.

Great time spent obtaining / using / recovering.

Craving.

Failure to fulfil role obligations.

Continued use despite social / interpersonal problems.

Important activities given up.

Use in physically hazardous situations.

Continued use despite physical / psychological problems.

Tolerance.

Withdrawal.

ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria — ≥3 of 6 in past year)

Strong desire / compulsion to drink.

Impaired control over use (onset, level, termination).

Withdrawal state on abstinence.

Tolerance.

Neglect of alternative interests.

Persistence despite clearly harmful consequences.

### Screening

**CAGE:** Cut down, Annoyed by criticism, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 = significant.

**AUDIT (WHO, 10 items):** 0–7 low risk, 8–15 hazardous, 16–19 harmful, ≥20 dependence.

AUDIT-C — 3-item screening tool.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (Boloor A373 ★2026)

Figure 6. Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal triage by CIWA-Ar, thiamine-first inpatient protocol, methanol-poisoning pathway and maintenance pharmacotherapy.

Time course (after last drink)

**6–12 h:** Minor withdrawal — tremor, anxiety, nausea, sweating, palpitations, insomnia, headache.

**12–24 h:** Alcoholic hallucinosis — visual / tactile / auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium and orientation (key DDx from DT).

**24–48 h:** Withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic, brief, 1–6 episodes; usually self-limited; 3% progress to status.

**48–96 h (peak 72 h):** Delirium tremens (DT) — clouded sensorium, disorientation, agitation, fluctuating consciousness, fever, autonomic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis), vivid visual / tactile (formication — 'bugs crawling') hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% untreated; 1–2% with modern care.

Risk stratification — CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised)

10 items, scored 0–7 each (orientation 0–4); total 0–67.

<8 — mild, no intervention.

8–15 — moderate, BZD treatment.

16–20 — severe.

>20 — very severe, ICU.

Management of withdrawal — Indian protocol (NIMHANS / AIIMS de-addiction)

**Inpatient if:** CIWA-Ar ≥10, history of DT / withdrawal seizures, severe medical / psychiatric comorbidity, poor support.

Thiamine FIRST, before any glucose (Wernicke prevention) — 100 mg IV/IM TDS × 3 days, then 100 mg PO OD long-term.

Wernicke / Korsakoff treatment dose: thiamine 500 mg IV TDS × 2–3 days → 250 mg IV/IM daily × 3–5 days → 100 mg PO long-term. Also IV Mg replacement (thiamine requires Mg cofactor).

**Benzodiazepines — first-line:** chlordiazepoxide 25–50 mg PO q4–6h symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar guided), tapered over 5–7 days. Diazepam 10–20 mg PO/IV q1–2h for severe.

Lorazepam preferred in hepatic dysfunction, elderly (no active metabolites): 2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h.

Phenobarbital — for refractory / BZD-resistant DT.

IV fluids (NS + 5%D), electrolyte correction — Mg 1–2 g IV q12h, K, PO4.

Multivitamin, folate 5 mg/d.

AVOID antipsychotics as monotherapy (↓ seizure threshold); use only haloperidol low dose if psychosis / agitation persists despite adequate BZD.

AVOID alcohol substitution.

Monitor vital signs q1–2h initially; CIWA-Ar q1–4h.

Treat fever, sepsis, pneumonia (high risk in DT), dehydration, rhabdomyolysis.

### Withdrawal seizures

**Treat acute seizure:** IV lorazepam 2–4 mg or diazepam 10 mg.

**Prevention:** adequate BZD coverage during detox.

Long-term anti-epileptics not needed unless underlying epilepsy.

Maintenance — relapse prevention (anti-craving)

**Naltrexone:** 50 mg PO OD (or 380 mg IM monthly). μ-opioid antagonist; ↓ craving and pleasure of drinking (COMBINE trial). Avoid in liver failure, opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); LFT monitoring.

**Acamprosate:** 666 mg PO TDS (2 g/d in <60 kg). NMDA modulator; ↓ relapse rate (PROJECT MATCH). Safe in liver disease; needs adequate renal function.

**Disulfiram:** 250 mg PO OD (max 500 mg). Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor; causes aversive reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, hypotension) on alcohol ingestion. Supervised dosing (family member). Avoid in CAD, severe psychiatric illness, pregnancy, peripheral neuropathy. Warn re: hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrups, perfumes).

Baclofen (off-label, useful in liver disease): 10–30 mg TDS; GABA-B agonist; reduces craving especially in cirrhotics where naltrexone and disulfiram unsafe (ANRS-BACLOVILLE).

**Topiramate, gabapentin:** Off-label adjuncts.

Psychosocial interventions (cornerstone — often dominate outcome)

Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MI / MET) — stage-of-change-based.

CBT — relapse prevention, coping skills.

12-step facilitation / Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) — Indian chapters widespread.

Family therapy, community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT).

Residential rehabilitation for severe / relapsing.

Treat comorbid depression / anxiety / PTSD.

Indian de-addiction infrastructure: AIIMS NDDTC, NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine, Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP — MoHFW), state-level Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs).

Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning — Boloor A367

Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in adulterated illicit liquor ('hooch'), industrial solvents, anti-freeze, windshield-washer fluid and formalin. Toxic dose ~10 ml; fatal 30 ml.

### Toxicokinetics

Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → FORMALDEHYDE → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → FORMIC ACID — the principal toxin (causes optic neuritis, metabolic acidosis).

### Clinical features

Latent period 12–24 h (longer if co-ingested ethanol).

Phase 1 — CNS depression (mild intoxication / inebriation).

Phase 2 (12–24 h) — N/V, abdominal pain, headache, vertigo.

Phase 3 — visual disturbance ('snowstorm', blurring, blindness), optic disc hyperaemia / oedema → permanent blindness.

Phase 4 — severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) with ↑ osmolar gap, Kussmaul respiration, seizures, coma, parkinsonism (putaminal necrosis), death.

### Investigations

ABG — severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2, HCO3 <10).

Anion gap — high (>20).

Osmolar gap — high (>10 mOsm/kg) early, falls as methanol is metabolised.

Serum methanol level — confirmatory (toxic >20 mg/dL; severe >50).

Fundus — optic disc hyperaemia / oedema.

MRI brain — putaminal haemorrhage / necrosis (classic).

### Management

ABC, IV access, gastric lavage (if <1 h), activated charcoal NOT effective (poorly adsorbed).

Block ADH (prevent toxic metabolite formation):

- FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole) — drug of choice if available; 15 mg/kg IV load → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses → 15 mg/kg q12h thereafter (induces own metabolism). Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL + acidosis resolved + asymptomatic.

- ETHANOL (alternative if no fomepizole) — IV loading 10 ml/kg of 10% ethanol over 30 min → 1.5 ml/kg/h infusion. Target blood ethanol 100 mg/dL. Cheaper and widely available in India.

FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1 mg/kg IV q4–6h (max 50 mg) × 6 doses — accelerates formate metabolism. Folic acid acceptable if folinic unavailable.

Correct acidosis — IV sodium bicarbonate to keep pH >7.2.

HAEMODIALYSIS — definitive removal of methanol and formate. Indications: serum methanol ≥50 mg/dL, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), visual / mental status changes, electrolyte imbalance refractory, renal failure.

Supportive — ICU, mechanical ventilation, treat seizures.

Complications of alcohol use (summary)

Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis (irreversible amnesia, confabulation).

Delirium tremens — mortality 5–15% untreated.

Cirrhosis, HCC, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy.

Suicide, accidental injuries, road traffic accidents.

Family disruption, economic loss, occupational impairment.

### Prognosis

Without treatment — progressive decline, premature mortality.

With comprehensive treatment (pharmacotherapy + psychosocial) — 30–50% achieve sustained remission at 1 year.

Better with stable social support, employment, no comorbid psychiatric illness, motivation for change.

Worse with antisocial personality, depression / suicide history, polysubstance use.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18 + Ch.16 (toxicology); Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Alcohol Use Disorders; NIMHANS / AIIMS NDDTC protocols; COMBINE 2006; PROJECT MATCH; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology — methanol/fomepizole; DSM-5; ICD-10/11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|165.note:
### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|166.note:
### Definition

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetric, erosive, inflammatory polyarthritis predominantly affecting peripheral synovial joints, associated with systemic features and extra-articular manifestations. Prevalence ~0.75% in India; female:male ≈ 3:1; peak onset 30–55 yrs.

### Etiology / Risk factors

**Genetic:** HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (DR4, DR1) — strongest in seropositive RA; PTPN22, STAT4

### Female sex, postpartum

Smoking — major modifiable risk; interacts with shared epitope to drive anti-CCP production

Periodontal disease (Porphyromonas gingivalis citrullination)

Obesity, low birth weight

### Silica dust exposure

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Citrullination of self-proteins → anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) in genetically susceptible host

Synovial hyperplasia (pannus) infiltrated by T cells, B cells, plasma cells, macrophages

**Pro-inflammatory cytokines:** TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, IL-17

Osteoclast activation (RANKL) → bone erosion; matrix metalloproteinases → cartilage destruction

### Clinical features

### Articular

Insidious onset symmetric polyarthritis — MCPs, PIPs, MTPs, wrists, knees, ankles, cervical spine; DIPs and lumbar spine spared

Morning stiffness >30–60 min, improves with activity

Swelling, warmth, tenderness; reduced grip strength

**Late deformities:** ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, hammer toes, hallux valgus

Atlanto-axial subluxation — neck pain, neurological deficit (caution at intubation)

### Systemic

Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anorexia

Extra-articular manifestations (~40%; more in seropositive RA, high anti-CCP, smokers)

**Cutaneous:** rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces — olecranon, Achilles)

**Pulmonary:** ILD (UIP/NSIP), pleural effusion (exudative, low glucose, low pH), Caplan syndrome, bronchiectasis, rheumatoid lung nodules

**Cardiac:** pericarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis, ↑ MI risk (1.5×), cardiomyopathy

**Ocular:** keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren), episcleritis, scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, scleromalacia perforans

**Haematological:** anaemia of chronic disease, Felty's syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), large granular lymphocyte syndrome

**Neurological:** carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitic), atlanto-axial myelopathy

**Vasculitis:** small/medium vessel — digital gangrene, leg ulcers, mononeuritis

**Renal:** AA amyloidosis (long-standing disease), drug nephropathy

**Lymphoma:** 2–4× increased risk, especially DLBCL

**Bone:** peri-articular osteoporosis, systemic osteoporosis

Diagnostic criteria — ACR/EULAR 2010

Score ≥6/10 classifies as definite RA (in a patient with synovitis in ≥1 joint without alternative explanation):

### Investigations

### Inflammatory and serology

RF (IgM-RF) — sensitivity 60–80%, specificity 60–80%

Anti-CCP — sensitivity 60–70%, specificity >95%; prognostic for erosive disease

ESR, CRP — disease activity

### General workup

CBC (ACD, leukopenia in Felty), comprehensive metabolic, LFT, urinalysis

ANA — screen for overlap

HBsAg, anti-HCV, latent TB (Mantoux/IGRA) — pre-biologic

HIV (Indian context, before biologics)

### Imaging

X-ray hands and feet — soft-tissue swelling, juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, deformities, subluxation; cervical spine for atlanto-axial subluxation

Ultrasound joints — synovitis, power Doppler signal, erosions earlier than X-ray

MRI — most sensitive for early synovitis, erosions, bone marrow oedema

### Disease activity

DAS28-ESR or DAS28-CRP (tender + swollen joint count + global + ESR/CRP)

### CDAI, SDAI — alternatives

**Targets:** DAS28 <2.6 = remission; ≤3.2 low; 3.2–5.1 moderate; >5.1 high activity

### Management — treat-to-target

### General

Smoking cessation; weight reduction; physiotherapy and occupational therapy

Patient education; vaccination pre-immunosuppression (influenza, pneumococcal, HBV, HPV); avoid live vaccines on biologics

CV risk assessment and treatment (statin, BP control)

### Symptom relief

NSAIDs at lowest effective dose for short periods

Prednisolone 5–10 mg/d as 'bridge' until DMARD effective; intra-articular steroid for active joints

Avoid long-term steroids — osteoporosis, infection, diabetes

csDMARDs (conventional synthetic) — start within 3 months of diagnosis

**Methotrexate:** Anchor drug. Start 7.5–10 mg/week, titrate to 20–25 mg/week. Co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/wk (not on MTX day). AE: nausea, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, pneumonitis, teratogenicity. Stop 3 months before conception (M and F). Avoid alcohol. Reduce dose in CKD; contraindicated in eGFR <30.

**Sulfasalazine:** 1 g BD–TDS. AE: GI upset, rash, hepatitis, agranulocytosis, G6PD-related haemolysis, oligospermia.

**Hydroxychloroquine:** 200–400 mg/d (≤5 mg/kg). AE: retinal toxicity — eye check baseline + annual after 5 yrs.

**Leflunomide:** 10–20 mg/d (loading 100 mg × 3 days then maintenance — most centres skip loading). AE: hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, hypertension, teratogenicity (very long half-life; cholestyramine washout needed before pregnancy).

**Combination 'triple therapy':** MTX + SSZ + HCQ — Indian-favoured cost-effective combination, comparable efficacy to early biologic in many patients

Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) — after inadequate response to ≥2 csDMARDs

**TNF inhibitors:** etanercept (50 mg SC weekly), adalimumab (40 mg SC q2wk), infliximab (3–10 mg/kg IV q8wk + MTX), golimumab (50 mg SC monthly), certolizumab

**IL-6 inhibitor:** tocilizumab 162 mg SC weekly OR 4–8 mg/kg IV q4wk

**B-cell depletion:** rituximab 1 g IV × 2 (day 0 and 14), every 6 months — RF/anti-CCP-positive; safer in latent TB

**T-cell co-stimulation:** abatacept 125 mg SC weekly OR weight-based IV monthly

**IL-1 inhibitor:** anakinra (rarely used in RA)

Always combine with MTX where tolerated for synergy and reduced anti-drug antibodies

Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) — JAK inhibitors

Tofacitinib 5 mg BD, baricitinib 4 mg OD, upadacitinib 15 mg OD

**ORAL Surveillance trial (2022):** increased major CV events, malignancy, VTE with tofacitinib vs TNFi in older patients with CV risk

**EMA/FDA:** use only if no TNFi alternative in patients ≥65 yr, smokers, malignancy, CV risk

Pre-biologic screening (essential — viva point)

**TB:** Mantoux/IGRA, CXR; if positive — INH 300 mg/d × 9 months started ≥1 month before biologic

### HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV

### CBC, LFT, RFT

Pregnancy test; contraception counselling

### Surgical

### Synovectomy (rare today)

Arthrodesis, arthroplasty (hip/knee/shoulder) for end-stage joint damage

C1–C2 fixation for atlanto-axial instability

### Carpal tunnel release

Fig 5. Rheumatoid arthritis — treat-to-target DMARD ladder

### Complications

Joint destruction, deformity, functional disability

Premature CV death (leading cause)

### ILD, pulmonary fibrosis

### Cervical myelopathy (atlanto-axial)

### Infections (immunosuppression)

### Lymphoma, skin cancers

### Osteoporosis, fragility fractures

### AA amyloidosis

### Prognosis

Modern treat-to-target therapy achieves remission/low disease activity in 50–80%. Adverse prognostic factors: female, smoking, high titre RF/anti-CCP, early erosions, multiple joint involvement, extra-articular features, high inflammatory markers. Untreated RA shortens life expectancy by 5–10 years, mostly from CV disease.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 RA + ACR 2021 guideline for RA + EULAR 2022 RA management recommendations + Indian Rheumatology Association RA position paper.

GENERAL MEDICINE|167.note:
### Definition

Gout is a crystal arthropathy caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and connective tissues, presenting with episodic acute inflammatory arthritis, chronic tophaceous deposits, urate nephropathy and uric acid urolithiasis. Hyperuricaemia is defined as serum urate >7.0 mg/dL in men and >6.0 mg/dL in women.

### Etiology / Risk factors

### Overproduction (10–15%)

### Idiopathic (most common)

**Enzyme defects:** HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan), PRPP synthetase overactivity, G6PD deficiency

**High cell turnover:** leukemia, lymphoma, myeloproliferative, polycythaemia, tumour lysis, haemolysis, psoriasis

**Diet:** high purine — red meat, organ meat, seafood (anchovies, sardines), beer (esp. yeast), fructose-sweetened beverages

### Exercise/strenuous activity

### Underexcretion (85–90%)

### CKD (any cause)

**Drugs:** thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin (<2 g), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, niacin, levodopa

Lead nephropathy (saturnine gout)

Lactic acidosis (alcohol, exercise, starvation)

### Ketoacidosis

### Hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism

### Other risk factors

Male sex, age >40

Obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes

### Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia

Family history (heritability ~60%)

### Pathophysiology

Uric acid is the end-product of purine metabolism (via xanthine oxidase). Humans lack uricase, so urate accumulates. When serum urate exceeds saturation (~6.8 mg/dL at 37°C), MSU crystals precipitate, especially in cooler peripheral joints (1st MTP), in acidic and low-flow tissues, and after sudden urate fluctuations.

**Phase 1:** Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia

**Phase 2:** Acute gouty arthritis — MSU crystals phagocytosed → NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β release → neutrophil recruitment → acute inflammation

**Phase 3:** Intercritical period — asymptomatic between attacks; microcrystals persist

**Phase 4:** Chronic tophaceous gout — large MSU aggregates with foreign-body giant cells, bone erosions ('punched-out')

**Renal:** uric acid stones (radiolucent), urate nephropathy, acute uric acid nephropathy in tumour lysis

### Clinical features

### Acute attack

Sudden onset, often nocturnal, peaks within 24 h

Severely painful, warm, swollen, erythematous joint — patient cannot bear weight on bed sheet

First MTP joint (podagra) in 50%; can affect ankle, midfoot, knee, wrist, elbow

**Triggers:** trauma, surgery, dehydration, alcohol binge, infection, IV contrast, urate fluctuation (start of ULT)

Resolves spontaneously in 5–14 days even without treatment (with desquamation of overlying skin)

Low-grade fever possible — beware mimicking septic arthritis

Chronic tophaceous gout (untreated >5–10 yr)

**Tophi:** nodular MSU deposits — helix of ear, olecranon bursa, Achilles, finger pulps, extensor tendons

May ulcerate and discharge chalky white material

Persistent polyarticular arthritis with deformity, erosions

### Renal manifestations

Uric acid nephrolithiasis — radiolucent, acidic urine

### Chronic urate nephropathy

Acute uric acid nephropathy — tumour lysis, very high urate, AKI

### Investigations

Gold standard — synovial fluid aspiration

**MSU crystals:** needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light (yellow parallel to axis, blue perpendicular)

WBC 10,000–100,000/µL, predominantly neutrophils

Always send Gram stain and culture — exclude septic arthritis (can coexist!)

### Biochemistry

Serum urate (may be normal during acute attack — repeat after 2 weeks)

RFT (urate excretion + drug dosing), eGFR

FBS, lipid profile, BP (associated metabolic syndrome)

**24-h urine uric acid:** >800 mg/24h on regular diet = overproducer

CBC, ESR/CRP (raised in acute attack, normal between)

### Imaging

**X-ray — early normal; chronic:** punched-out erosions with overhanging edges (Martel sign), preserved joint space, soft-tissue tophi

Dual-energy CT (DECT) — colour-codes MSU; sensitive for tophi

Ultrasound — double-contour sign (urate on cartilage), tophi, erosions

### Pre-ULT (urate-lowering) screen

HLA-B*5801 in Asian patients before allopurinol (SJS/TEN risk)

### Baseline LFT for febuxostat

G6PD if rasburicase planned

### Management

- Acute attack — start within 24 h

**First-line — NSAIDs:** Naproxen 500 mg BD, indomethacin 50 mg TDS, or ibuprofen 800 mg TDS × 5–7 days. Avoid if CKD, peptic ulcer, HF, antiplatelet/anticoag.

**Colchicine:** Low-dose ACR regimen: 1.2 mg STAT, then 0.6 mg 1 hour later, then 0.6 mg OD–BD until resolution (max 7–10 days). Avoid in eGFR <30; reduce dose with CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, statins, cyclosporine).

**Glucocorticoids:** Prednisolone 30–40 mg PO daily × 5 days then taper. Methylprednisolone IM 40–80 mg single dose for 1–2 joints. Intra-articular triamcinolone after aspiration if mono/oligoarticular.

**IL-1 inhibitors:** Anakinra, canakinumab — refractory or polyarticular attack in patient with multiple contraindications. Expensive.

DO NOT start, stop or change dose of urate-lowering therapy during an attack (may prolong/precipitate flare). If patient is already on ULT, CONTINUE it.

Rest, ice, elevate the affected joint

- Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) — indications

Recurrent attacks (≥2 per year)

Tophi (clinical or imaging)

### Radiographic erosions

### CKD stage ≥2

### Uric acid nephrolithiasis

First attack with serum urate >9 mg/dL or young age <40

- Xanthine oxidase inhibitors — first choice

**Allopurinol:** Start 100 mg/d (50 mg/d if eGFR <60); titrate by 100 mg every 2–5 weeks to target serum urate <6 mg/dL (<5 if tophi). Max 800 mg/d. Adverse: rash, hepatitis, AHS (allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — fever + DRESS + AKI; 25% mortality). Risk increased with HLA-B*5801 (~5–8% Han Chinese, 4% Indian, 1% European) — screen Asian/at-risk patients before initiation.

**Febuxostat:** 40–80 mg/d, max 120 mg. No dose adjustment in mild–moderate CKD. More potent than allopurinol. CARES trial showed ↑ CV mortality vs allopurinol — caution if established CV disease.

- Uricosurics — when XO inhibitors fail or are contra-indicated

Probenecid 250 mg BD → 500–2000 mg/d; needs eGFR >50, no nephrolithiasis history; alkalinise urine (pH 6.5–7) + good hydration

Lesinurad 200 mg/d — only in combination with XO inhibitor

Benzbromarone — hepatotoxic; restricted

- Recombinant uricase — refractory tophaceous gout

Pegloticase 8 mg IV every 2 weeks; G6PD-deficient patients excluded

Rasburicase — tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis

### 6. ULT-initiation prophylaxis

Co-prescribe colchicine 0.6 mg OD (or low-dose NSAID, or low-dose prednisolone 5 mg) for 3–6 months during ULT initiation to prevent mobilisation flares

### 7. Lifestyle

Weight loss (gradual — rapid weight loss/ketosis triggers attacks)

Limit red/organ meat, seafood

Avoid alcohol (especially beer) and fructose-sweetened drinks

Encourage low-fat dairy, vegetables, cherries, coffee, water 2–3 L/d

Stop thiazide if possible — substitute losartan (uricosuric) or amlodipine

Fig 2. Gout — acute treatment + urate-lowering therapy ladder

### Complications

Chronic destructive tophaceous gout with joint deformity

Uric acid nephrolithiasis, urate nephropathy → CKD progression

Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — SJS/TEN

**Cardiovascular:** associated with hypertension, CAD, metabolic syndrome

Septic arthritis can coexist — always aspirate

### Prognosis

Excellent with adherent ULT. Achievement of target urate <6 mg/dL reduces flare frequency progressively over 12–24 months and shrinks tophi over years. Untreated gout becomes chronic, erosive and polyarticular within 10–20 years. CV and renal comorbidity drive long-term mortality.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 (gout) + ACR 2020 guideline for management of gout + Indian Rheumatology Association recommendation on HLA-B*5801 screening (2021).

GENERAL MEDICINE|169.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Genetics

X-linked recessive disorder of the hexose monophosphate shunt enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, leading to decreased NADPH and reduced glutathione → RBCs unable to neutralise oxidative stress. Commonest enzymopathy; ~400 million people affected worldwide. Common in Mediterranean, Africa, South-East Asia, parts of India (tribal, ~10%). Confers partial protection against P. falciparum malaria.

### Variants

**Class I:** severe enzyme deficiency + chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia.

**Class II:** severe deficiency, intermittent haemolysis (Mediterranean variant).

**Class III:** moderate deficiency (African A−, most Indian patients).

**Class IV:** normal activity.

### Triggers of haemolysis

**Drugs:** primaquine, dapsone, sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin, ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, rasburicase, methylene blue, sulfasalazine, high-dose aspirin, vitamin K analogues.

Infections – viral hepatitis, pneumonia, typhoid, septicaemia (commonest trigger overall).

Fava beans (favism) – Mediterranean variant.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.

Naphthalene (mothballs), henna.

### Clinical features

Asymptomatic between episodes.

Acute intravascular haemolysis 24–72 h after trigger: fever, malaise, jaundice, dark (cola-coloured) urine, back pain, dyspnoea, AKI in severe cases.

Neonatal jaundice – may need exchange transfusion; kernicterus risk.

Chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia (rare, Class I).

### Investigations

**During crisis:** ↓Hb, ↑retic, ↑indirect bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria.

Peripheral smear – bite cells, blister cells, Heinz bodies (with supravital stain – brilliant cresyl blue), polychromasia.

G6PD enzyme assay – diagnostic. False-negatives during active haemolysis (young RBCs have higher enzyme); repeat after 3 months.

Fluorescent spot test – screening.

DNA analysis – definitive carrier detection.

### Management

Avoid known triggers (drug card, family education).

Treat infection promptly.

**Acute crisis:** hydration, monitor renal function; transfusion if severe (Hb <7).

Folic acid supplementation in chronic haemolysis.

Phototherapy ± exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice.

Screen before starting primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase.

Splenectomy not effective (intravascular haemolysis).

GENERAL MEDICINE|170.note:
### Definition

Serum K < 3.5 mmol/L (mild 3.0–3.5, moderate 2.5–3.0, severe < 2.5).

**Pseudohypokalaemia:** leukocytosis (cells take up K in vitro), sample delay.

### Aetiology

- Decreased Intake (rare alone — kidneys conserve K)

Anorexia nervosa, alcoholism, prolonged TPN without K.

- Transcellular Shift (into cells)

Alkalosis (metabolic or respiratory — K shifts in for H⁺).

Insulin (treatment of DKA).

β2-agonists (salbutamol, asthma exacerbation, theophylline).

Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (familial; thyrotoxic PP — Asian males).

Refeeding syndrome.

Vitamin B12 / folate replacement (rapid haematopoiesis).

Barium poisoning, chloroquine, hyperthermia.

### 3. GI Losses

Diarrhoea (large volume — cholera, IBD, VIPoma, laxative abuse).

Vomiting / NG suction (vomit is low in K but causes metabolic alkalosis → renal K loss).

Fistulae, ileostomy, geophagia (clay binds K).

### 4. Renal Losses

Diuretics — thiazide, loop (commonest cause).

**Mineralocorticoid excess:** primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), 2° hyperaldosteronism (RAS, renin-secreting tumour), Cushing's, exogenous steroids, liquorice (glycyrrhizin — inhibits 11β-HSD2 → cortisol acts on MR), 11β-HSD deficiency, Liddle's (gain-of-function ENaC).

Renal tubular acidosis types 1 (distal) and 2 (proximal).

Bartter syndrome (mimics loop diuretic — defect in NKCC2; normal BP, hypoK alkalosis).

Gitelman syndrome (mimics thiazide — defect in NCCT; normal BP, hypoK alkalosis + hypoMg + low urinary Ca).

**Drugs:** amphotericin B, cisplatin, foscarnet, aminoglycosides, ATT (osmotic diuresis).

Polyuric phase of AKI.

Hypomagnesaemia (worsens K wasting; replace Mg FIRST).

DKA (osmotic diuresis).

### 5. Sweat (excessive)

Heat exhaustion, marathon, hot climate.

### Clinical Features

### Cardiovascular

Palpitations, premature beats.

**Arrhythmias:** AF, VT, torsades de pointes (especially with QT prolongation), VF.

Sensitises to digoxin toxicity (additive).

### Neuromuscular

Fatigue, weakness, cramps.

Ascending paralysis (severe — flaccid quadriparesis).

Hyporeflexia, ileus, paralytic.

Respiratory muscle weakness (severe).

Rhabdomyolysis (severe < 2.5).

### Renal

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (long-standing) → polyuria, polydipsia.

Metabolic alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria).

### Endocrine

Impaired insulin release → hyperglycaemia.

### ECG Changes (PROGRESSIVE)

### Investigations

Repeat serum K (non-haemolysed); ABG (acid-base status).

ECG.

Magnesium (replace first), Ca, phosphate, Cr, urea, glucose.

Urine spot K, Cl, Ca, Mg — assess renal vs extra-renal loss.

Urine K < 20 mEq/d → extra-renal (GI, transcellular).

Urine K > 20 mEq/d → renal loss.

TTKG > 4 with hypoK → renal loss.

Renin + aldosterone (suspected mineralocorticoid excess).

Plasma cortisol (Cushing's).

TFT (thyrotoxic periodic paralysis).

Drug history.

### Management

### 1. Replace Potassium

Mild (K 3.0–3.5) + asymptomatic:Mild (K 3.0–3.5) + asymptomatic: Oral KCl 40–80 mEq/d (Slow-K, Span-K, or syrup). 1 g KCl ≈ 13.4 mEq K.

Moderate (K 2.5–3.0) or symptomatic / ECG changes:Moderate (K 2.5–3.0) or symptomatic / ECG changes: Oral KCl 60–80 mEq + IV KCl. IV rate: ≤ 10 mEq/h via peripheral line; max 20 mEq/h via central line under ECG monitoring. Concentration: ≤ 40 mEq/L peripheral, ≤ 60 mEq/L central.

Severe (K < 2.5) or life-threatening:Severe (K < 2.5) or life-threatening: IV KCl 20 mEq/h via central line + ECG monitoring + ICU/HDU. Recheck K every 1–2 h.

**Daily total:** Daily total: Normal deficit estimation: every 0.3 mmol/L below 4 ~ 100 mmol total deficit. Maximum daily IV: 200–400 mEq.

### 2. Replace Magnesium FIRST in Refractory

If hypoMg coexists, K replacement fails. Replace 2 g MgSO₄ IV over 15 min, then 10 g/24h or oral Mg.

### 3. Treat Underlying Cause

Stop diuretic / switch to K-sparing (e.g., spironolactone in Conn's).

ACEi/ARB if 2° aldosteronism.

Adrenalectomy in Conn's adenoma.

Treat thyrotoxicosis (β-blocker + carbimazole + KI).

Treat alkalosis cause; antiemetics; correct acid-base.

### 4. K-Sparing Agents (chronic)

Spironolactone 25–100 mg/d, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene.

Fig 6. Hypokalaemia — workup and management.

### Complications

Cardiac arrest (VT/torsades/VF).

Rhabdomyolysis → AKI.

Paralytic ileus → aspiration.

Hepatic encephalopathy (alkalosis ↑ NH₃ in cirrhosis).

Iatrogenic — IV K extravasation pain; phlebitis; over-correction.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.380; UK Renal Hypokalaemia 2020; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|171.note:
### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

GENERAL MEDICINE|172.note:
### Definition

Progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by motor (TRAP) and non-motor features, caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with α-synuclein-rich Lewy bodies. Prevalence 1% > 60 y, 4% > 80 y. M > F.

### Aetiology

Idiopathic (95%) — environmental + genetic (pesticide exposure, head trauma).

**Genetic:** LRRK2 (commonest dominant), GBA (commonest risk allele), PARK7, PINK1, SNCA, Parkin.

**Secondary parkinsonism:** drugs (typical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), vascular, post-encephalitic, MPTP, manganese, CO poisoning.

**Parkinson-plus:** PSP, MSA, CBD, DLB — usually poor levodopa response, atypical features early.

### Clinical features

### Motor (TRAP)

Tremor — 4-6 Hz pill-rolling resting tremor, asymmetric, decreases with action; appears late in 20%.

Rigidity — cogwheeling (rigidity + tremor); lead-pipe.

Akinesia / Bradykinesia — slow movements, decreased blink, masked facies, micrographia, hypophonia.

Postural instability — late feature; positive pull test; falls.

Gait — stooped posture, short shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, festination, freezing, en-bloc turning.

Non-motor (often precede motor by years)

Hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression (prodromal markers).

**Cognitive:** executive dysfunction → dementia (50% at 10 y).

**Autonomic:** orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, sialorrhoea, sweating.

**Psychiatric:** depression (40%), anxiety, apathy, visual hallucinations (esp. on dopaminergic Rx).

### Diagnosis (UK PDS Brain Bank / MDS 2015)

Bradykinesia + at least one of rest tremor / rigidity.

**Supportive:** asymmetric, levodopa response, dyskinesia on L-dopa, hyposmia, RBD.

Exclude red flags (rapid progression, early falls/dementia/autonomic, symmetry, dysarthria, gaze palsy, early severe autonomic — suggest Parkinson-plus).

### Investigations

Largely clinical. MRI brain — rule out vascular, normal-pressure hydrocephalus.

DAT-SPECT (¹²³I-FP-CIT, 'DaTscan') — confirms presynaptic dopaminergic deficit; differentiates from essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, dystonic tremor. Cannot distinguish PD from Parkinson-plus.

**Levodopa challenge:** > 30% UPDRS improvement supports PD.

MIBG cardiac (denervation in PD/DLB; preserved in MSA).

### Treatment

### 1. Pharmacological (motor)

**Young, functional:** Young, functional: Dopamine agonist first: pramipexole 0.125 mg TDS titrated to 1.5 mg TDS; ropinirole; rotigotine patch. Avoid in elderly (psychosis, ICD).

**Older / disabled:** Older / disabled: Levodopa + carbidopa (Syndopa, Madopar) — 100/25 mg TDS, titrate to effect (max ~1000/250 mg/d).

**MAO-B inhibitor:** MAO-B inhibitor: Rasagiline 1 mg OD, selegiline — modest benefit, neuroprotective in early disease (controversial).

**Anticholinergics:** Anticholinergics: Trihexyphenidyl 2-6 mg/d — for tremor in young; AVOID in elderly (confusion).

**Amantadine:** Amantadine: 100 mg BD-TDS — useful for dyskinesia.

- Motor fluctuations / wearing-off

Increase L-dopa frequency, add COMT inhibitor (entacapone 200 mg with each L-dopa dose; opicapone 50 mg HS).

Add MAO-B inhibitor.

Apomorphine SC (rescue for off periods).

Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) via jejunal tube (Duodopa).

- Advanced / refractory

Deep Brain Stimulation — STN (commonest, motor) or GPi (dyskinesia) — for L-dopa-responsive disabling motor fluctuations/dyskinesia, age < 70, no dementia, no severe depression.

MR-guided focused ultrasound (HiFU) thalamotomy — tremor-dominant, unilateral.

### 4. Non-motor

**Depression:** SSRI, SNRI; avoid TCA (anticholinergic).

**Psychosis:** quetiapine 25-100 mg, clozapine 12.5-50 mg, pimavanserin (5-HT2A inverse agonist).

**Dementia:** rivastigmine (PD dementia and DLB).

**Orthostatic:** fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa, compression stockings.

**Constipation:** macrogol, lubiprostone.

**REM-SBD:** melatonin 3-12 mg HS, clonazepam.

**Drooling:** glycopyrrolate, botox to salivary glands.

### 5. Non-pharmacological

Physiotherapy (LSVT-BIG), speech therapy (LSVT-LOUD), occupational therapy, exercise (boxing, tai chi).

### Drugs to AVOID

Typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine).

Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine (use ondansetron, domperidone).

Tetrabenazine.

### Prognosis

Progressive; treatment slows but does not halt.

Mean survival from diagnosis ~15 y; near-normal lifespan if optimised.

Dementia and falls are main causes of disability.

Fig 6. Parkinson's disease — management ladder.

**Source:** MDS 2015 PD Criteria; NICE PD Guidelines NG71 2017; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|173.note:
### Definition

Renal replacement therapy in which blood is circulated through an extracorporeal circuit and passes through a semi-permeable dialyser membrane against a counter-current dialysate flow. Solutes (urea, K, creatinine, drugs, toxins) move by DIFFUSION down concentration gradient. Water is removed by ULTRAFILTRATION (hydrostatic pressure).

**Modalities:** intermittent haemodialysis (IHD; 4 h × 3/wk standard), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT — CVVH, CVVHD, CVVHDF), sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED), home daily / nocturnal HD, hybrid (CRRT-IHD).

### Principles

- Diffusion (solute removal)

Concentration gradient drives small/middle MW solutes (urea 60, Cr 113, K 39) across membrane. Efficiency depends on: blood/dialysate flow rate, surface area, molecular size + pore size.

- Ultrafiltration (water removal)

Hydrostatic pressure gradient → bulk fluid movement; removes ~ 0.5–1 L/hr.

### 3. Convection

Solvent drag — water carries dissolved solutes. Main mechanism in CRRT (haemofiltration); better removal of middle-MW solutes (β2-microglobulin).

### 4. Adsorption

Some membranes (polysulphone) adsorb protein-bound toxins.

### Components of HD Circuit

Vascular access (see below).

Blood pump (200–400 ml/min flow).

Heparin / citrate anticoagulation.

Dialyser (artificial kidney — hollow-fibre, surface area 1.0–2.0 m²; biocompatible polysulphone / cellulose triacetate).

Dialysate (purified water + electrolytes — Na 138, K 1–3, Ca 1.25, Mg 0.5, HCO₃ 30–35, glucose; counter-current flow 500 ml/min).

Pressure monitors, air detector, blood leak detector.

Reverse osmosis water plant.

### Vascular Access

### Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF) — GOLD STANDARD

Native vessels — radio-cephalic at wrist (preferred), brachio-cephalic at elbow, brachio-basilic transposition.

Patient's own artery and vein anastomosed → vein arterialises (matures) over 6 weeks.

**PLAN AHEAD:** create when eGFR 15–25 (G4 → G5 transition).

Best long-term patency (5-yr 70%); lowest infection.

**Examination:** bruit + thrill on auscultation/palpation.

### Arteriovenous Graft (AVG)

Synthetic (PTFE) graft when veins inadequate.

Used in 2 weeks; lower patency (5-yr 30%); more infections.

### Central Venous Catheter (CVC)

Internal jugular (preferred), femoral, subclavian (avoid — stenosis).

Temporary (non-tunnelled) — acute settings.

Permanent (tunnelled cuffed — Permcath) — bridge to AVF or bridging.

Highest infection (bacteraemia), thrombosis, stenosis.

**Most common reason:** emergent dialysis when AVF not ready.

### Indications for Initiating Dialysis

### Acute (AKI) — AEIOU mnemonic

Acidosis — refractory pH < 7.1.

Electrolytes — K > 6.5 refractory, severe hyperNa/hypoNa, hypercalcaemia.

Intoxication — lithium, salicylate, ethylene glycol, methanol, valproate, metformin.

Overload — refractory pulmonary oedema.

Uraemia — pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding.

### Chronic (ESRD)

**Symptomatic uraemia:** anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, pruritus.

Volume overload despite diuretics.

Hyperkalaemia / acidosis not controlled medically.

Pericarditis, encephalopathy.

Malnutrition.

eGFR 5–10 ml/min/1.73 m² typically (NOT a fixed number; IDEAL trial showed early start ≥ 10 ml/min NO benefit vs late start 5–7).

### Prescription

### Complications

### Intradialytic

Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%):Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%): Causes: excessive UF, hypovolaemia, antihypertensives, cardiac dysfunction, sepsis, Mg/Ca shift. Treat: stop UF, head down, 100–250 ml NS bolus, midodrine pre-HD, reduce dry weight target.

**Cramps:** Cramps: Volume / Na depletion. NS bolus, quinine, vit E.

**Nausea, vomiting:** Nausea, vomiting: Hypotension, dialysate issues. Antiemetics.

**Headache:** Headache: Disequilibrium (rapid urea shifts; cerebral oedema), HTN, caffeine withdrawal.

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome:Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: Rapid initial dialysis → cerebral oedema (urea shifts). Headache, nausea, seizure, coma. Prevention: shorter, gentler first sessions, mannitol.

**First-use syndrome:** First-use syndrome: Type A (anaphylactoid — ethylene oxide sterilant): immediate (stop dialysis, epinephrine, steroids, antihistamine). Type B (chest/back pain): mild, continue.

**Air embolism:** Air embolism: Rare — clamp lines, left lateral Trendelenburg, 100% O₂.

**Haemolysis:** Haemolysis: Mechanical, hypotonic dialysate. Pink plasma. Stop HD.

**Cardiac:** Cardiac: Arrhythmia, ischaemia (electrolyte shifts, hypotension).

**Bleeding:** Bleeding: Heparin-related. Protamine if severe.

### Long-term

**Vascular access:** Vascular access: Thrombosis, stenosis, infection (bacteraemia esp. catheter), aneurysm, steal syndrome, high-output cardiac failure (AVF > 2 L/min).

**Cardiovascular:** Cardiovascular: Major cause of mortality. Accelerated atherosclerosis, LVH, vascular calcification, uraemic cardiomyopathy.

**Anaemia:** Anaemia: Erythropoietin deficiency, iron deficiency, blood loss in circuit, uraemic platelet dysfunction.

**Bone disease (CKD-MBD):** Bone disease (CKD-MBD): 2° hyperparathyroidism, osteitis fibrosa, adynamic bone, β2-microglobulin amyloid (carpal tunnel).

**Infection:** Infection: CRBSI (catheter — Staph aureus, MRSA, MRSE), HBV/HCV transmission (rare in modern era), TB, fungal.

**Malnutrition / protein wasting:** Malnutrition / protein wasting: Anorexia, restrictions, inflammation, protein loss in HD.

**Encephalopathy:** Encephalopathy: Uraemic, aluminium (older — minimal now), thiamine deficiency.

**Psychosocial:** Psychosocial: Depression, sexual dysfunction, financial burden — high suicide risk.

**Other:** Other: Acquired cystic kidney → RCC, gout/pseudogout, restless legs, dementia.

### Comparison with Peritoneal Dialysis (PD)

### Adequacy Assessment

Kt/V (Daugirdas formula) — single-pool > 1.4 per session.

Urea Reduction Ratio (URR) — > 65%.

Weekly Kt/V > 2.0.

**Clinical:** BP control, dry weight, nutrition, symptom resolution.

### Outcomes (India)

1-yr survival on HD ~ 80% (worse than transplant 95%). 5-yr survival ~ 35–40%. Major cause of death: CV disease (45%), infection (20%), withdrawal (5–10%). PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat) and many state schemes (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) cover HD costs. PMNDP (Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme) since 2016 provides free HD across India.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.392; KDIGO Dialysis Initiation 2015; KDOQI; PMNDP 2016; ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas; IDEAL trial.

GENERAL MEDICINE|174.note:
### Definition

Bulbous enlargement of distal phalanges with increased curvature of the nail – a sign of underlying systemic disease (rarely congenital).

Grades / stages (Lovibond)

**Stage 1:** increased fluctuation of nail bed ('boggy', fluctuant), softening of nail-bed.

**Stage 2:** loss of normal Lovibond angle (>180°) – nail-bed angle between nail and proximal nail-fold flattens or becomes obtuse. Schamroth's window (formed by opposing dorsal aspects of distal phalanges of corresponding fingers of the two hands) is obliterated.

**Stage 3:** bulbous swelling and increased curvature of nail with parrot-beak/'drumstick' appearance.

**Stage 4:** hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) – periostitis, painful swelling of wrists, ankles, knees; subperiosteal new bone formation on X-ray.

### Causes

### Pulmonary (commonest):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially adenocarcinoma, squamous; small-cell less commonly).

Mesothelioma.

Bronchiectasis.

Lung abscess.

Empyema.

Cystic fibrosis.

Pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

Pulmonary AV malformation.

Asbestosis.

### Cardiac:

Cyanotic congenital heart disease (Tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger).

Subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Atrial myxoma.

### Gastrointestinal:

Cirrhosis (especially with hepatopulmonary syndrome).

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, UC).

Coeliac disease.

GI lymphoma.

Tropical sprue.

### Other:

Thyroid acropachy (Graves' disease).

Familial / congenital (autosomal dominant) – pachydermoperiostosis.

Unilateral – aortic aneurysm, axillary tumour, Pancoast tumour.

Pseudoclubbing – hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis.

**(Note:** COPD per se does NOT cause clubbing – its presence in COPD should prompt a search for lung cancer or another cause.)

GENERAL MEDICINE|180.note:
### Definition

OCD is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterised by intrusive, unwanted, recurrent thoughts, images or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) performed to neutralise distress, that are time-consuming (>1 hour/day) or cause marked distress / functional impairment. Reclassified in DSM-5 into 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders' (separate from anxiety disorders).

### Epidemiology

Lifetime prevalence ~2–3%; current ~1%.

M=F overall; childhood onset M>F, adult onset F>M.

**Bimodal onset:** 8–12 years and late adolescence / early adulthood (mean ~20 y).

Heritability ~50%; first-degree relative risk 4×.

High comorbidity with depression (40–60%), anxiety, tic disorders / Tourette's, ADHD, autism spectrum, eating disorders.

### Etiology

Genetic — polygenic (SLITRK1, glutamate genes); familial clustering.

Neurochemical — serotonergic dysregulation (basis for high-dose SSRI efficacy); glutamatergic hyperactivity in cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop.

Neuroanatomic — hyperactivity in orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, caudate; CSTC circuit dysfunction.

PANDAS / PANS — sudden-onset OCD with tics in children after streptococcal / autoimmune trigger.

Psychological — behavioural model: obsession → anxiety → compulsion → relief (negative reinforcement). Cognitive model: thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

### Clinical features

Obsessions — common themes

Contamination — germs, dirt, body fluids.

Doubts — gas left on, door unlocked, hit someone while driving.

Symmetry / ordering — things must be 'just right'.

Aggressive / sexual / blasphemous intrusive thoughts (ego-dystonic — patient horrified).

Religious / scrupulosity.

Hoarding (now a separate DSM-5 disorder but historically grouped).

Compulsions — common forms

Washing / cleaning (paired with contamination obsessions).

Checking (paired with doubts).

Counting, repeating, ordering / arranging.

Mental compulsions — silent prayer, counting in head, neutralising thoughts.

Reassurance-seeking.

Key clinical features (boards-style)

Recognised by the patient as own (insight may be variable — 'good/fair/poor/absent insight' specifier in DSM-5).

Ego-dystonic — distressing, unwanted.

Resisted (at least initially).

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) or marked distress / impairment.

**Average delay to treatment:** 7–10 years (shame, lack of awareness).

### DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria

Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both.

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) OR clinically significant distress / impairment.

Not due to substance / medical condition.

Not better explained by another mental disorder.

**Specify:** with good/fair insight, with poor insight, with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related (current/past).

### OCD spectrum (DSM-5 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders')

Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with perceived defect in appearance.

Hoarding disorder.

Trichotillomania (hair-pulling).

Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder.

### Severity assessment

Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) — 10-item, clinician-rated; gold standard. 0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme.

Children's Y-BOCS (CY-BOCS) for paediatric.

Floyd-Padua, Maudsley scales — self-report alternatives.

### Differential diagnosis

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Y-BOCS / CY-BOCS; PHQ-9, GAD-7 for comorbidity.

**Routine:** rule out organic — CBC, TSH, ASO titre (PANDAS in children), B12.

MRI brain if late onset, focal signs, or atypical presentation.

**Pre-treatment baseline:** ECG (QTc) if planning high-dose SSRI / clomipramine; LFT for clomipramine.

### Management

Figure 5. OCD management — Y-BOCS severity triage, high-dose SSRI + ERP, ladder to clomipramine, antipsychotic augmentation and DBS.

### First-line — pharmacotherapy

SSRIs — must use HIGH dose, allow LONG trial: Fluoxetine 40–80 mg/d, sertraline 150–200 mg/d, paroxetine 40–60 mg/d, fluvoxamine 200–300 mg/d, escitalopram 20–40 mg/d, citalopram 40 mg max. Start at standard dose, titrate every 2 wk; allow 10–12 wk trial at maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure.

### First-line — psychotherapy

CBT with ERP (Exposure & Response Prevention): Gold standard; 13–20 sessions. Patient exposed in hierarchy to feared stimulus while being prevented from performing compulsion → habituation + extinction of anxiety. Equally effective as SSRI; combination superior to either alone in moderate–severe.

Cognitive therapy — challenge thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

Inadequate response after 10–12 wk

Step 1 — switch SSRI (different agent at maximum dose × 10–12 wk).

Step 2 — clomipramine (TCA, potent serotonergic) 100–250 mg/d. Highly effective but ECG monitoring (QTc, AV block), sedation, anticholinergic, weight gain, sexual SE, seizure risk; AVOID combining with SSRI without specialist (serotonin syndrome). Often most effective single agent.

Step 3 — augmentation with atypical antipsychotic: risperidone 0.5–3 mg/d, aripiprazole 5–15 mg/d, low-dose haloperidol (esp. with comorbid tics).

Step 4 — intensive ERP / residential programme; combine SSRI + clomipramine (specialist + serial ECG).

Severe refractory OCD (failed ≥3 SSRIs + clomipramine + augmentation + ERP)

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) over orbitofrontal cortex / supplementary motor area.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of ventral capsule / ventral striatum or subthalamic nucleus — FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption.

Ablative neurosurgery (anterior capsulotomy, cingulotomy) — last resort, specialist centres only.

Trial of glutamate modulators (memantine, riluzole, N-acetylcysteine, lamotrigine, ketamine) — experimental.

### Special situations

Paediatric OCD — sertraline / fluoxetine / fluvoxamine licensed; CBT-ERP first line for mild-moderate; combine for severe.

PANDAS / PANS — antibiotics (penicillin, azithromycin); IVIG / plasmapheresis in severe.

Pregnancy — CBT preferred; sertraline / fluoxetine if pharmacotherapy essential.

### Duration

Maintain effective drug ≥1–2 years after response; relapse rate ~50% on stopping. Many patients need lifelong treatment.

Gradual taper over months; monitor for return of symptoms.

### Complications

Functional impairment — work, education, relationships, self-care.

Comorbid depression (40–60%), suicide risk elevated.

Substance abuse — self-medication.

Dermatological — chronic hand-washing → eczema, fissures.

Financial — checking compulsions, hoarding effects.

### Prognosis

Chronic fluctuating course; ~10–20% recover completely, ~50% partial response, ~30% chronic.

**Better prognosis:** shorter duration before treatment, good insight, no comorbidity, family support.

**Worse:** early onset, severe symptoms, hoarding subtype, comorbid tics / autism, poor insight, comorbid depression.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for OCD; NICE-CG31; APA Practice Guideline 2007 (with updates); WFSBP 2008/2012; DSM-5; ICD-11.

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

Haemoptysis = coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract (below the larynx). Massive haemoptysis = >200–600 mL in 24 h.

### Causes by category

### Infective (commonest in India):

Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially cavitary or post-tubercular bronchiectasis with Rasmussen aneurysm).

Bronchiectasis.

Lung abscess.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella, anaerobes).

Pulmonary aspergilloma (mycetoma in old TB cavity).

Paragonimiasis (in endemic areas).

### Neoplastic:

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Bronchial carcinoid.

Metastatic lung tumours.

### Vascular:

Pulmonary embolism with infarction.

Mitral stenosis (pulmonary venous hypertension).

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (HHT/Osler-Weber-Rendu).

Aortobronchial fistula.

### Inflammatory / autoimmune:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-GBM antibody).

SLE-associated pulmonary haemorrhage.

Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis (in children).

Iatrogenic / trauma / coagulopathy:

Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs), thrombolytics.

Bronchoscopic biopsy, transbronchial biopsy.

Tracheostomy, Swan-Ganz catheter (pulmonary artery rupture).

Chest trauma.

Cocaine use.

**Pseudohaemoptysis:** epistaxis, haematemesis swallowed and regurgitated, Serratia marcescens in dentures, oral bleeding.

### Approach

Distinguish from haematemesis (bright red, frothy, alkaline pH, mixed with sputum vs dark red, acidic, with food, melena later).

Stabilise (ABCDE) if massive – airway, position bleeding side down, IV access, group and cross-match.

CXR, CT chest with contrast/CT pulmonary angiogram, bronchoscopy (rigid for massive), echo, CBC, coagulation, sputum AFB.

Massive haemoptysis – ICU, bronchial artery embolisation, endobronchial tamponade, surgical resection if focal source.

GENERAL MEDICINE|184.note:
### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Cardiac Cycle (brief)

Each cycle (~0.8 s at 75 bpm) comprises: (i) atrial systole (0.1 s, the 'a' wave on JVP); (ii) isovolumetric ventricular contraction (S1, AV valves close); (iii) ventricular ejection (~0.3 s, aortic/pulmonary valves open); (iv) isovolumetric relaxation (S2, semilunar valves close); (v) rapid passive ventricular filling (S3 may be heard in HF); (vi) diastasis; with a return to atrial systole. The Wiggers diagram relates ECG, pressure, volume and heart sounds.

### Definition

Heart failure is the clinical syndrome resulting from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, leading to characteristic symptoms (dyspnoea, fatigue, fluid retention) and signs (raised JVP, crepitations, oedema). Classified by ejection fraction (HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%) and timing (acute vs chronic).

### Etiology

**Cardiac:** Ischaemic heart disease/MI (commonest), hypertension, valvular disease (AS, MR, AR), dilated/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease.

**Arrhythmia-induced:** Sustained tachyarrhythmia, AV block.

**High-output:** Anaemia (severe), thyrotoxicosis, beriberi, AV fistula, paget's, septic shock.

**Right HF:** Constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloid).

**Lung-related:** Cor pulmonale (COPD, pulmonary embolism), pulmonary hypertension.

**Drugs/toxins:** Anthracyclines (doxorubicin), trastuzumab, alcohol, cocaine, NSAIDs (precipitate).

### Precipitating Factors (acute decompensation)

**FAIL ME mnemonic:** Forgot medications, Arrhythmia/Anaemia, Infection, Lifestyle (salt/fluid), MI/ischaemia, Endocrine (thyroid, pregnancy).

### Clinical Features
