**Left HF symptoms:** Exertional dyspnoea (NYHA I–IV), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, cough with frothy/pink sputum.

**Right HF symptoms:** Ankle oedema, abdominal distension (ascites), RUQ pain (hepatic congestion), anorexia, weight gain.

**Signs:** Tachycardia, tachypnoea, displaced apex, S3 gallop (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF), basal crepitations, pleural effusion, raised JVP, hepatomegaly with hepatojugular reflux, pitting pedal oedema, peripheral cyanosis, cold extremities.

### NYHA functional classification

**Class I:** No limitation of activity.

**Class II:** Slight limitation, comfortable at rest.

**Class III:** Marked limitation, comfortable at rest only.

**Class IV:** Symptoms at rest.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** ECG (rule out ischaemia, arrhythmia, LBBB), CXR (cardiomegaly CTR>50%, Kerley B lines, upper-lobe diversion, pleural effusion), SpO₂.

**Biomarker:** BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL → HF likely. <35/125 essentially rules out HF.

**Echocardiogram:** Most important – LVEF, chamber size, wall motion, valves, diastolic function, PASP.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes, LFT (congestive hepatopathy), glucose, HbA1c, lipid, TSH, urinalysis, iron studies (HF + iron deficiency common).

**Advanced:** Coronary angiography if ischaemic aetiology, cardiac MRI for myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, RHC if pulmonary hypertension or transplant work-up.

### Management

**Goals:** relieve symptoms, prevent hospitalisation, prolong survival.

### Acute / decompensated:

**LMNOP:** Position upright, O₂ to keep SpO₂>92%; NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) if pulmonary oedema and not in shock.

Lasix (furosemide 40–80 mg IV), Morphine 2–4 mg IV (relieves anxiety, venodilator), Nitrate (sublingual or IV if BP adequate), Oxygen, Position upright.

**Inotropes:** Dobutamine, milrinone (if low output, cardiogenic shock) – use in critical care.

**Mechanical:** IABP or LV assist device in refractory shock.

Chronic HFrEF – Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT, '4 pillars'):

**1. ARNI/ACEi/ARB:** Sacubitril/valsartan or ACEi (enalapril/ramipril) or ARB (losartan/valsartan).

**2. β-blocker:** Carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate. Start low, titrate up.

**3. MRA:** Spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone (monitor K+, creatinine).

**4. SGLT2 inhibitor:** Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg OD – benefit irrespective of diabetes.

**Add-on:** Loop diuretic (furosemide/torsemide) for congestion; ivabradine if HR>70 in sinus on max β-blocker; digoxin if AF or refractory symptoms; hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate (esp. in Black patients or ACEi-intolerant).

### Chronic HFpEF:

Treat HTN, AF (rate/rhythm), DM, obesity, sleep apnoea, iron deficiency.

Diuretic for congestion; SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin/dapagliflozin) reduces hospitalisation in HFpEF.

### Device therapy:

ICD if EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months GDMT (primary prevention of sudden death).

CRT (cardiac resynchronisation) if EF ≤35%, LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–IV in sinus rhythm.

### Advanced HF:

LVAD as bridge or destination therapy; cardiac transplantation in eligible patients.

### Lifestyle:

Sodium <2 g/d, fluid <1.5–2 L/d if hyponatraemic or congested, daily weights, exercise rehabilitation, smoking and alcohol cessation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19), patient education for self-monitoring.

Fig 2. Heart failure – diagnosis and management algorithm.

### Complications & Prognosis

Acute decompensation, arrhythmias (AF, VT/VF), sudden cardiac death, thromboembolism, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cachexia, hepatic congestion.

5-year mortality ~50% for symptomatic HFrEF; modern GDMT improves survival significantly.

### Definition

Inability of respiratory system to meet metabolic needs, defined by ABG: PaO₂ <60 mmHg (8 kPa) breathing room air at sea level, with or without PaCO₂ >50 mmHg (6.5 kPa).

### Classification (gas exchange)

**Type 1 (Hypoxaemic):** PaO₂ <60, PaCO₂ normal or low. Caused by V/Q mismatch or shunt – pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, PE, COPD, asthma early.

Type 2 (Hypercapnic / ventilatory failure): PaO₂ <60, PaCO₂ >50. Caused by alveolar hypoventilation – COPD (commonest), neuromuscular (GBS, MG, MND, polio), chest-wall (kyphoscoliosis, obesity), CNS depression (opiates, stroke), OSA.

Type 3 (Perioperative / atelectasis) – form of type 1, post-operative atelectasis.

Type 4 (Shock) – peri-arrest, low cardiac output.

### Classification (onset)

Acute (hours) – ARDS, asthma, GBS.

Chronic (months/years) – COPD, ILD, neuromuscular.

Acute-on-chronic – COPD exacerbation.

### Clinical Features

**Hypoxia:** dyspnoea, tachypnoea, cyanosis, restlessness, confusion, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias.

**Hypercapnia:** warm peripheries, bounding pulse, headache, flap, drowsy, papilloedema, CO₂ retention narcosis.

### Investigations

ABG (essential), pulse oximetry.

CXR, CT chest as indicated.

Spirometry/PEFR if obstructive disease suspected.

ECG, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, blood sugar.

### Management

Treat underlying cause.

**Type 1:** high-flow O₂ (target SpO₂ 94–98%), HFNC, NIV (CPAP) in pulmonary oedema, invasive ventilation if PaO₂ remains <60 on FiO₂>0.6.

**Type 2 (especially COPD):** controlled O₂ 24–28% Venturi mask, target SpO₂ 88–92%; NIV (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 and PaCO₂ rising; intubate if NIV fails or contraindicated (vomiting, copious secretions, haemodynamic instability, low GCS).

**Supportive:** fluids, nutrition, VTE/stress-ulcer prophylaxis.

Fig 5. Respiratory failure – ABG-based classification and management.

Cardiovascular causes (mostly Type 1)

Acute pulmonary oedema (LVF, valvular crisis, hypertensive emergency).

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock.

Cardiac tamponade.

Severe valvular disease – critical AS, acute MR (papillary rupture).

Massive pulmonary embolism (RV failure + hypoxaemia).

High-output failure – severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, sepsis.

Pulmonary hypertension crisis.

### Respiratory causes

### Type 1 (Hypoxaemic):

Pneumonia (bacterial, viral – including COVID-19).

ARDS (sepsis, pancreatitis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion-related TRALI).

Asthma (severe acute).

Pulmonary embolism.

Pneumothorax.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.

### Type 2 (Hypercapnic):

COPD exacerbation (commonest).

Severe asthma (late).

Neuromuscular – GBS, MG crisis, MND, polio, botulism.

CNS depression – opioid overdose, sedatives, brainstem stroke.

Chest-wall – flail chest, kyphoscoliosis, severe obesity (OHS).

Obstructive sleep apnoea.

### Likely diagnosis

Acute ischaemic stroke (LACS/PACS) involving right middle cerebral artery territory.

**Evidence:** sudden focal deficit (left hemiparesis), preserved cranial nerves and DTRs at presentation, extensor plantar on left (UMN sign), risk factors (IHD 10 y, HTN 5 y irregular), age >60.

**DDx:** intracerebral haemorrhage, TIA, hypoglycaemia, Todd's paralysis, complicated migraine.

Investigations to confirm and assess

- Bedside (within 5 min)

Glucose finger-stick (rule out hypoglycaemia).

ECG (AF? recent MI? new ischaemia? — both cause and risk of tPA).

NIHSS score (severity, decides thrombolysis benefit; here ~6-10).

- Urgent imaging (door-to-CT < 25 min)

**NCCT head:** rule out haemorrhage; may show early ischaemic changes (loss of grey-white differentiation, hyperdense MCA sign). MUST be done before tPA.

CT angiography (CTA) head + neck: large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1, basilar) — eligible for mechanical thrombectomy.

**MRI DWI/FLAIR:** if onset uncertain or 'wake-up' stroke (DWI/FLAIR mismatch = within 4.5 h equivalent).

### 3. Labs

CBC, platelets (need >100,000 for tPA), coagulation (INR < 1.7), creatinine, electrolytes.

Lipid profile, HbA1c, TSH.

- Cardiac source / aetiology work-up

ECG, holter (paroxysmal AF), echocardiogram (LV thrombus, valvular, PFO/ASD with TEE).

**Carotid Doppler / CTA:** significant stenosis > 70% → CEA / stenting.

**Young patient:** thrombophilia panel (APLA, protein C/S, AT-III, factor V Leiden), homocysteine, vasculitis screen.

### Management — time-based

### Hyperacute (0-4.5 h)

**ABC + O2:** ABC + O2: Maintain SpO₂ ≥ 94%. NBM (aspiration risk). Head-up 30°.

**BP control:** BP control: Permissive HTN < 220/120 if NOT thrombolysing; lower to < 185/110 BEFORE tPA (labetalol 10-20 mg IV bolus).

**IV thrombolysis:** IV thrombolysis: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (10% as bolus, 90% over 60 min). Max 90 mg. Onset < 4.5 h.

**Alternative:** Alternative: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus (max 25 mg) — non-inferior, preferred if LVO going to thrombectomy.

**Mechanical thrombectomy:** Mechanical thrombectomy: LVO (ICA, M1, basilar) within 6 h (or 6-24 h if DAWN/DEFUSE-3 mismatch criteria).

Acute (within 24 h)

**Antiplatelet:** aspirin 300 mg PO/PR/NGT loading — start 24 h after tPA, or immediately if no tPA given.

**If TIA / minor stroke:** dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) × 21 days then aspirin alone (CHANCE/POINT trials).

**Statin:** atorvastatin 40-80 mg HS.

**Glucose:** target 140-180 mg/dL; avoid hypoglycaemia.

**Temperature:** paracetamol if T > 37.5 °C.

**DVT prophylaxis:** IPC immediately; LMWH after 24-48 h once haemorrhage excluded.

NPO until formal swallow screen passed.

Cardioembolic source (e.g. AF, post-MI)

**Anticoagulation start:** small stroke day 3, moderate day 6, large day 12 (1-3-6-12 rule).

DOAC (apixaban 5 mg BD / dabigatran 150 mg BD / rivaroxaban 20 mg OD) preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF.

Stroke unit + rehab

Stroke unit admission reduces mortality by 20%.

Early mobilisation, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy.

### Secondary prevention

BP < 130/80; antiplatelet lifelong; high-intensity statin (LDL < 70).

**Lifestyle:** smoking cessation, salt restriction, weight loss, exercise.

Carotid endarterectomy / stenting if symptomatic stenosis > 70%.

Fig 1. Acute ischaemic stroke — emergency department pathway.

**Source:** AHA/ASA 2019 Stroke Guidelines; Indian Stroke Care Pathway 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Acute liver failure (ALF) = sudden onset of liver dysfunction (jaundice, coagulopathy INR ≥ 1.5) with hepatic encephalopathy within 26 weeks, in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing liver disease.

### Classification (O'Grady)

### Aetiology (India-relevant)

**Viral:** Hep E (commonest in India, especially in pregnant women — 20% mortality), Hep B, Hep A in children, Hep D super-infection, HSV/CMV/EBV (immunocompromised).

**Drugs:** paracetamol overdose (commonest in West), anti-TB drugs (INH/Rif/PZA — Indian context), phenytoin, valproate, halothane, herbal/Ayurvedic preparations.

**Toxins:** Amanita phalloides mushroom, yellow phosphorus.

Wilson's disease (fulminant presentation in teens/young adults; Coombs-negative haemolysis).

Autoimmune hepatitis (acute severe).

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP syndrome.

Ischaemic hepatitis (shock, Budd-Chiari).

Lymphoma / malignant infiltration.

### Clinical Features

**Prodrome:** malaise, anorexia, nausea, mild jaundice.

Progressive jaundice with deepening encephalopathy.

Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven I–IV; cerebral oedema, raised ICP in advanced).

Coagulopathy → bruising, GI bleed, intracranial haemorrhage.

Hypoglycaemia (impaired gluconeogenesis), metabolic acidosis (lactate).

Renal failure (HRS type 1) in 50%.

Sepsis (Gram-positive > -negative; CONS, Staph aureus, Candida) — high mortality.

**Cardiovascular:** hyperdynamic, then circulatory failure with vasoplegia.

**Respiratory:** ARDS, aspiration pneumonia.

Liver shrinks rapidly on examination.

### Investigations

### Confirm severity

LFT — AST/ALT often > 1000 (often > 10,000 in ischaemic/paracetamol), bilirubin rising, alkaline phosphatase, GGT.

INR ≥ 1.5 (best indicator of synthetic function).

Albumin, ammonia, lactate, ABG, glucose, electrolytes, renal function.

### Aetiology

Paracetamol level (Rumack-Matthew nomogram — > 4 h post-ingestion).

**Viral serology:** HAV IgM, HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM, HCV RNA, HEV IgM, HDV (if HBV+).

**AIH markers:** ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM, IgG.

**Wilson's:** ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper, KF rings, low ALP:bilirubin ratio < 4.

Pregnancy test, USG abdomen (Budd-Chiari Doppler).

Toxic screen — mushroom history, herbal, alcohol.

### Prognostic scores

**KCC:** King's College Criteria (most validated for transplant referral):

**Paracetamol:** arterial pH < 7.30 OR all 3 of (INR > 6.5, Cr > 300 µmol/L, grade III-IV HE).

**Non-paracetamol:** INR > 6.5 OR any 3 of: age < 10 / > 40, non-A non-B / drug-induced / halothane, jaundice > 7 d before HE, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 300 µmol/L.

MELD ≥ 30, Clichy criteria (factor V < 20–30%) — alternatives.

### Management

- ICU care — early referral to liver transplant centre

Intubation if grade III–IV HE; mechanical ventilation.

Head-up 30°, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40), sedation propofol (avoid benzodiazepine).

Maintain CPP > 60 mm Hg; ICP monitoring controversial (high bleeding risk).

Strict glucose monitoring (frequent hypoglycaemia) — IV 10% dextrose.

**Vasopressors:** noradrenaline for hypotension; avoid hyperthermia.

### 2. Specific antidotes

**Paracetamol overdose:** Paracetamol overdose: N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h IV (Prescott regimen); benefit even > 24 h.

**Amanita phalloides:** Amanita phalloides: Penicillin G 1 MU/kg/d + silibinin 5 mg/kg IV.

**Wilson's:** Wilson's: D-penicillamine, plasmapheresis (urgent), liver transplant.

**Autoimmune hepatitis:** Autoimmune hepatitis: Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/d IV — proceed to transplant if no response in 4 days.

**HSV:** HSV: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h IV.

Acute HBV with severe / coag failure:Acute HBV with severe / coag failure: Tenofovir or entecavir.

### 3. Manage complications

**Encephalopathy/cerebral oedema:** lactulose (controversial in ALF — risk of bowel distention), hypertonic saline (target Na 145–155), mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg, hyperventilation as rescue.

**Coagulopathy:** vitamin K 10 mg IV daily; FFP only if active bleeding or pre-procedure (over-correction can mask trends).

**AKI / HRS:** cautious fluid + albumin, RRT (CRRT preferred).

**Sepsis:** low threshold for empirical broad-spectrum abx + antifungal (piperacillin-tazobactam + fluconazole/echinocandin).

**Stress ulcer prophylaxis:** PPI.

Avoid sedatives / hepatotoxic drugs.

### 4. Liver Transplantation (definitive)

Indicated by KCC, MELD ≥ 30, Clichy.

**Without transplant:** mortality 60–90%.

**With transplant:** 1-yr survival 70–80%.

Living-donor liver transplant feasible in India (cost, donor availability).

### 5. Extracorporeal Liver Support

MARS (Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System) — bridge to transplant.

High-volume plasmapheresis — improves survival without transplant (RELIEF trial).

### Prognosis

Hyperacute (paracetamol) — best spontaneous survival 30–40%. Subacute — worst (10–20%). HEV in pregnancy mortality up to 20–40%. Transplant improves survival to ~ 70% at 1 year.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.520; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD/EASL ALF 2017.

### Definition

Clinical manifestations of impaired hepatic synthetic, metabolic, detoxification, and excretory function — may be acute or chronic, compensated or decompensated.

### Signs — Examination Sequence (Head to Toe)

### General / Constitutional

Sallow / icteric complexion (yellow tinge of sclera, mucosa, skin) — bilirubin > 2 mg/dL.

Cachexia, muscle wasting (temporal hollowing, sarcopenia).

Foetor hepaticus — sweet musty breath (dimethyl sulphide from mercaptans).

Altered mentation — drowsiness, confusion, irritability (encephalopathy).

### Hands

Clubbing — chronic liver disease, especially PBC, hepatopulmonary syndrome.

Leuconychia — proximal 2/3 white (Terry's nails) → hypoalbuminaemia.

Palmar erythema — thenar / hypothenar.

Dupuytren's contracture — palmar fascia thickening (alcoholic CLD).

Asterixis (flapping tremor) — hepatic encephalopathy; not specific (also uraemia, CO₂ retention).

Bruising / ecchymoses — coagulopathy (↓ vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X).

Petechiae — thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism, ↓ thrombopoietin).

### Face / Eyes

Icterus — sclera + frenulum.

Xanthelasma — periorbital cholestatic deposits (PBC).

Kayser-Fleischer ring — Wilson's disease.

Parotid enlargement — alcoholic CLD.

Spider naevi on face, neck, upper chest (drainage area of SVC).

### Chest

Spider naevi (> 5 significant).

Gynaecomastia (impaired oestrogen metabolism, also drugs — spironolactone, digoxin).

Loss of axillary / chest hair.

Pleural effusion right > left (hepatic hydrothorax — diaphragmatic defect; transudate, ascitic origin).

### Abdomen

Hepatomegaly initially (firm, irregular, tender) — may shrink in late cirrhosis.

Splenomegaly (portal HTN) — moderate.

Ascites — shifting dullness, fluid thrill (large), umbilicus evertion / hernia.

Caput medusae — recanalised paraumbilical vein → distended abdominal wall veins (flow AWAY from umbilicus, distinguishes from SVC obstruction).

Venous hum (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur) — heard over caput medusae.

Pulsatile liver — TR (cardiac cirrhosis).

Bruit over liver — HCC, hepatic artery aneurysm.

### Hormonal / Genitalia

Testicular atrophy, loss of libido, impotence.

Amenorrhoea (women).

Loss of pubic / body hair.

### Lower limbs

Pitting oedema — hypoalbuminaemia (albumin < 2.5 g/dL).

Bruising — coagulopathy.

Peripheral neuropathy (alcoholic / thiamine deficiency / autoimmune AIH).

### Systemic / Cardiovascular

Hyperdynamic circulation — bounding pulse, low BP, warm peripheries, tachycardia.

Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy — blunted contractile response to stress.

### Major Decompensation Markers (memorise)

### Investigations to Confirm

LFT (AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin/albumin), INR, ammonia.

USG abdomen ± Doppler — shrunken nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites, portal flow.

OGD — varices.

Child-Pugh, MELD-Na for severity and prognostication.

### Prognostic Implication

Each decompensation event reduces median survival significantly: compensated cirrhosis ~ 12 yr → after first decompensation ~ 2 yr → second decompensation ~ 6–12 months. Number of decompensations + MELD-Na guide transplant listing.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.523; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD cirrhosis.

GENERAL MEDICINE|186.note:
### Definition

Organs anatomically anchored to or in close apposition with the diaphragm, or held within the retroperitoneal/peritoneal compartments that descend with diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration. Useful for distinguishing them from fixed retroperitoneal masses on examination.

### Organs That MOVE with Respiration

### Organs That DO NOT MOVE Significantly with Respiration

Pancreas — retroperitoneal, deep, doesn't move with breathing; pancreatic masses (pseudocyst, tumour) are typically fixed.

Aortic aneurysm — pulsatile, expansile but fixed; differentiates from transmitted aortic pulsation.

Lymph nodes (retroperitoneal / paraaortic) — fixed; para-aortic lymphadenopathy in lymphoma.

Adrenal glands — small, retroperitoneal, normally not palpable.

Inferior vena cava — fixed.

Vertebral column / bony pelvis — fixed.

### Clinical Significance

Moving with respiration → likely intraperitoneal (liver, spleen) or perirenal (kidney) origin.

Fixed on palpation → retroperitoneal mass (pancreatic tumour, aneurysm, lymph nodes).

Bimanual ballotability + moving = kidney typically.

**Spleen:** moves with respiration, dull to percussion, notched on medial border, cannot get above it (vs renal — can get above).

Distinguishing splenomegaly from left renal mass: spleen has notch, dull percussion, cannot get above; kidney is ballotable, has resonant area above, may have flank dullness with lateral position.

### Method of Palpation

**Position:** supine, knees flexed, abdomen relaxed.

Examiner's warm hand placed flat on abdomen, fingers gently flexed.

Patient takes a deep breath in through mouth; examiner feels for organ edge moving down to meet fingertips.

Start in RIF for liver/spleen (avoid missing massive organ), move up to costal margin.

Spleen — palpate from RIF towards left costal margin; turn patient to right lateral decubitus to bring spleen forward.

Kidney — bimanual ballottement; one hand in renal angle posteriorly, other on anterior abdomen.

**Source:** Boloor Clinical Examination Ch.; Hutchison's Clinical Methods 24e.

GENERAL MEDICINE|187.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Acute purulent infection of meninges/subarachnoid space, presenting with fever + headache + neck stiffness +/- altered mental status. Medical emergency: untreated >90% mortality, with treatment 15-25%.

Aetiology by age (community-acquired)

**Neonates (0-1 mo):** GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

**1 mo - 50 y:** Streptococcus pneumoniae > Neisseria meningitidis > H. influenzae (now rare with vaccine).

**> 50 y / immunosuppressed:** S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negatives.

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Staph aureus, CoNS, gram-negatives.

**India-specific:** TB meningitis remains common — always consider.

### Clinical features

**Classic triad (only 44%):** fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status.

**≥ 2 of:** fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental → 95% sensitivity.

Kernig (knee extension with hip flexed → pain) and Brudzinski (neck flexion → hip flexion).

**Meningococcal:** petechial / purpuric rash (purpura fulminans = severe).

**Pneumococcal:** associated otitis/sinusitis/pneumonia.

Cranial nerve palsies, seizures, papilloedema, focal deficit.

### Investigations

Blood cultures × 2 BEFORE antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics > 1 h for cultures).

Lumbar puncture — CT first if focal deficit, GCS < 10, papilloedema, new-onset seizure, immunosuppression.

CSF Gram stain (60-90% sens), culture, latex agglutination (S. pneumo, H.influ, Nm, GBS).

**TB:** CSF AFB smear (low sens), GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (rapid + rifampicin resistance), culture.

**PCR:** HSV-1/2 (encephalitis), enterovirus, JC virus.

**Other:** CBC, blood C/S, CRP, procalcitonin, electrolytes (SIADH), HIV test.

### Management

- Resuscitation (within first hour)

**Sepsis bundle:** fluids, vasopressors if shock, oxygen, glucose check.

**Seizure control:** lorazepam, then levetiracetam load.

### 2. Dexamethasone

0.15 mg/kg IV q6h × 4 days, FIRST DOSE before or with first antibiotic.

Reduces mortality in S.pneumo; reduces neuro sequelae (deafness) in H.influenzae.

Stop if non-pneumococcal organism identified.

**TB meningitis:** prednisolone/dex tapered over 6-8 wk (TBM treatment).

- Empirical antibiotics (do NOT delay)

**Adult immunocompetent:** Adult immunocompetent: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h (target trough 15-20).

Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed:Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed: ADD Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria cover).

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Post-neurosurgery / shunt: Vancomycin + Cefepime or Meropenem 2 g q8h.

**Penicillin allergy severe:** Penicillin allergy severe: Vancomycin + Moxifloxacin + TMP-SMX (Listeria).

**Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h:** Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h: If HSV encephalitis suspected (e.g. temporal seizures, behaviour change).

### 4. Pathogen-specific duration

### 5. Adjunctive

Maintain euvolaemia (avoid SIADH).

**ICP management:** head-up 30°, mannitol if raised, ICU monitor.

Audiology test at discharge (especially children — sensorineural deafness).

- Chemoprophylaxis (close contacts)

**Meningococcal:** Rifampicin 600 mg PO BD × 2 d, OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose, OR Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single.

**H. influenzae type b:** Rifampicin 20 mg/kg/d × 4 d for households with child < 4 y unvaccinated.

### 7. Vaccination prevention

Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23 in elderly/asplenic/CKD/HIV).

Meningococcal (MenACWY for hajj pilgrims, students, military, asplenia).

Hib (in National Immunisation Schedule under Pentavalent).

### Complications

Hydrocephalus (communicating > obstructive).

Cerebritis, brain abscess, subdural empyema.

Sensorineural hearing loss (10-30%).

Seizures, epilepsy, cognitive deficits.

Cranial nerve palsies (esp. III, VI, VII, VIII).

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal, adrenal haemorrhage).

SIADH, DIC, septic shock.

### Prognosis

**Treated mortality:** pneumococcal 20-25%, meningococcal 5-10%, H.influ 3-7%.

**Untreated:** > 90% mortality.

10-20% long-term sequelae (deafness, cognitive, epilepsy).

Fig 5. Bacterial meningitis pathway.

**Source:** IDSA Meningitis Guidelines 2017; ICMR Antibiotic Policy 2022; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) = hepatic injury attributable to a drug or supplement, after excluding viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes. Accounts for 10% of all acute hepatitis and ~ 50% of acute liver failure in the West.

### Classification by Mechanism

**Intrinsic / Direct:** Intrinsic / Direct: Predictable, dose-dependent, reproducible. e.g. paracetamol (NAPQI metabolite), CCl₄, Amanita phalloides (α-amanitin).

**Idiosyncratic:** Idiosyncratic: Unpredictable, NOT dose-related, latency days–months. e.g. INH, amoxicillin-clavulanate, halothane, phenytoin.

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

### Classification by Pattern (R-value)

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

**R 2–5:** Mixed (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulphonamides).

### Common Hepatotoxic Drugs — by Class

### Indian Context — ATT-DILI

Highest incidence among Asians (~ 8–12%) — important for MBBS.

**Risk factors:** age > 35, female, alcoholism, viral hepatitis B/C carrier, HIV, malnutrition, slow acetylator phenotype (Indian genetic prevalence).

**Pathway:** INH → hydrazine metabolite → CYP2E1 → hepatocyte injury. Rifampicin induces CYP isoenzymes → ↑ INH toxicity; PZA additional risk.

**Monitoring:** baseline + monthly LFT during ATT in high-risk; symptom screening.

Stop ATT if ALT > 5× ULN (asymptomatic) or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms / jaundice.

**Re-introduction:** after LFT normalises, single drug → titrate up (usually rifampicin first → INH → PZA).

**Severe / hepatitic ATT-DILI:** switch to non-hepatotoxic regimen — levofloxacin + ethambutol + injectable (aminoglycoside) ± linezolid.

### Diagnosis

Temporal relationship — onset days to months after starting drug; dechallenge improves LFT.

Exclude viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), autoimmune, biliary (USG/MRCP), metabolic (Wilson's, haemochromatosis).

RUCAM / Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score ≥ 6 = probable.

Liver biopsy — only if diagnosis unclear or atypical.

### Management

WITHDRAW culprit drug immediately.

**Supportive:** hydration, antiemetics, monitor INR + bilirubin.

**Paracetamol:** Specific antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for paracetamol — 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (Rumack-Matthew nomogram).

Penicillin G + silibinin for Amanita.

Carnitine for valproate.

Corticosteroids may help immune-mediated (DRESS, ICI-related hepatitis).

Liver transplant if acute liver failure (King's College criteria for paracetamol, INR > 6.5 / 3 of 5 minor criteria for non-paracetamol).

### Prognosis

Most resolve on dechallenge. 'Hy's law' (ALT > 3× ULN + bilirubin > 2× ULN + no other cause) → 10% mortality. Cholestatic DILI may persist months → vanishing bile duct syndrome.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.22; ACG DILI 2014; Indian Society of Gastroenterology DILI consensus.

GENERAL MEDICINE|194.note:
### Definition

Syndrome of chronic GH (and IGF-1) excess in adults after epiphyseal closure. Caused most commonly by a somatotroph pituitary adenoma (95%). 'Gigantism' is the same disease occurring before epiphyseal fusion in children.

### Etiology

Pituitary somatotroph adenoma (95%) – macroadenoma in >70%.

Ectopic GHRH (rare – pancreatic, bronchial neuroendocrine).

Ectopic GH (very rare – pancreatic islet, lymphoma).

Familial – MEN1, McCune-Albright, Carney complex, FIPA.

### Clinical features

### Tumour mass effects:

Headache, bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression), cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus invasion), hyperprolactinaemia (stalk effect).

Hypopituitarism (deficient TSH, ACTH, gonadotropins).

### GH/IGF-1 excess (somatic):

Facial – frontal bossing, prognathism (mandibular protrusion), interdental separation, macroglossia, prominent supraorbital ridges, coarse features, deepening voice (laryngeal soft-tissue enlargement).

Hands and feet – enlargement (need new ring/shoe size); spade-like hands; carpal tunnel syndrome.

Skin – thick, oily, hyperhidrosis, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans.

Cardiovascular – hypertension, biventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, valvular regurgitation, arrhythmias, heart failure (leading cause of death).

Respiratory – obstructive sleep apnoea (very common, ~60%).

Metabolic – insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia.

Endocrine – goitre, multinodular thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia, hypogonadism.

Musculoskeletal – arthropathy (hips, knees, spine), kyphosis, proximal myopathy.

GI – colonic polyps and increased colon cancer risk; visceromegaly (thyroid, heart, liver, kidney, prostate).

Hyperhidrosis, oily skin, body odour.

### Investigations

### Biochemistry:

Serum IGF-1 (age- and sex-matched) – best screening test; elevated.

OGTT with GH measurement – failure of GH suppression to <1 µg/L (or <0.4 with sensitive assay) at 2 h confirms acromegaly.

Prolactin (often co-secreted), TFT, cortisol, FSH/LH, testosterone/oestradiol for pituitary hormone reserve.

### Imaging:

MRI pituitary with contrast – macroadenoma in 70%.

Visual field testing.

### Complications screening:

ECG, echocardiogram.

Polysomnography (OSA).

HbA1c, fasting lipids.

Colonoscopy at diagnosis (then every 3–5 years).

DEXA, hand X-rays.

### Management

### Surgery (first-line):

Transsphenoidal adenomectomy – cures 80–90% of microadenomas and 40–60% of macroadenomas. Performed by expert pituitary surgeon.

Medical (if surgery fails or contraindicated):

Somatostatin receptor analogues (SRL) – octreotide LAR 20–30 mg IM monthly; lanreotide autogel 90–120 mg SC monthly; pasireotide for resistant disease.

Dopamine agonists – cabergoline 0.5–3.5 mg/week (especially if co-secreting prolactin, modest GH excess).

GH receptor antagonist – pegvisomant 10–30 mg SC daily; normalises IGF-1 but does not shrink tumour, so monitor MRI.

### Radiotherapy (third-line):

Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma knife) or fractionated; effect delayed years. Risk of hypopituitarism.

### Treat complications:

Cardiovascular optimisation, OSA – CPAP, diabetes – metformin/GLP-1 RA, surgical correction of jaw/dental.

### Prognosis

Pre-treatment mortality is double that of age-matched controls; normalising IGF-1 restores life expectancy. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; colon cancer surveillance important.

GENERAL MEDICINE|195.note:
### Definition (KDIGO 2012)

CKD = abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for > 3 months with implications for health. Defined by EITHER:

GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m² for > 3 months (with or without kidney damage), OR

Markers of kidney damage for > 3 months: albuminuria (ACR > 30 mg/g), urine sediment abnormalities, electrolyte abnormalities of tubular origin, histology, structural (imaging), history of transplant.

### Aetiology (India + Global)

Top 2 Causes (memorise — 2026 favourite)

- Diabetic nephropathy — commonest cause globally and in India (40–50%).

- Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — second commonest (20–25%).

### Others

Chronic glomerulonephritis (IgA #1 worldwide, lupus, FSGS, membranous).

**Chronic interstitial nephritis:** analgesic nephropathy (NSAIDs, paracetamol), Ayurvedic / herbal nephropathy (Aristolochia — Balkan + Indian), heavy metals.

Polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD — autosomal dominant; PKD1, PKD2 genes).

Obstructive uropathy (chronic stones, BPH, posterior urethral valves in children).

Reflux nephropathy.

HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN — FSGS collapsing variant).

Sickle cell nephropathy.

**Inherited:** Alport syndrome, Fabry disease.

Chronic interstitial nephritis of agricultural communities (CINAC, Mesoamerican; increasing recognition in Indian farmers).

### Staging (KDIGO)

### GFR Categories (G1–G5)

### Albuminuria Categories (A1–A3)

**CKD is reported as:** G[X] A[Y]. E.g., diabetic with eGFR 40 + ACR 250 = G3b A2. Risk increases with both lower GFR and higher albuminuria (KDIGO 'heat map').

Clinical Features (advanced — early stages often asymptomatic)

Anaemia (normocytic normochromic — EPO deficiency, iron deficiency, blood loss).

Bone disease — mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD): osteitis fibrosa cystica (2° hyperparathyroidism), osteomalacia, osteoporosis, vascular calcification.

**Uraemic symptoms:** anorexia, nausea, fatigue, pruritus, sleep disorder.

Volume overload — oedema, pulmonary, HTN.

Acidosis — Kussmaul respiration.

Electrolyte disturbances — hyperK, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia.

Neurological — peripheral neuropathy, restless legs, encephalopathy.

Cardiovascular — accelerated atherosclerosis (LDL, HTN, vascular calcification); leading cause of death in CKD.

Immune dysfunction — recurrent infections.

Endocrine — sexual dysfunction, infertility.

Bleeding tendency — platelet dysfunction (uraemic platelet).

**Skin:** pallor (anaemia), uraemic frost, sallow complexion, half-and-half nails.

### Investigations

### Confirm CKD

Serum creatinine + eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021).

Urinalysis + ACR / PCR (spot).

Confirm chronicity > 3 months (compare past records).

USG renal — small (< 9 cm), echogenic, loss of corticomedullary differentiation = chronic. Normal in DM nephropathy + amyloid + ADPKD (large cysts).

### Identify Cause

Diabetes screen — HbA1c, fasting / random glucose.

BP control history; fundoscopy for diabetic / hypertensive retinopathy.

**Targeted:** ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, SPEP/UPEP, HBV/HCV/HIV, renal biopsy if rapidly progressive or atypical.

Family history (ADPKD, Alport).

Drug history (NSAIDs, Ayurvedic).

### Assess Complications

CBC — anaemia (target Hb 10–11.5 in CKD, KDIGO 2012).

Iron studies (ferritin, TSAT).

Ca, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, ALP.

Lipid profile.

ECG, echo (LVH, pulmonary HTN).

Bone DEXA if indicated.

### Management

### 1. Slow Progression

**BP control:** target < 130/80 (KDIGO 2021). ACEi or ARB FIRST-LINE (if ACR > 30 or HTN) — also reduces proteinuria. Avoid combination ACEi + ARB (ALTITUDE harm).

**Glycaemic control:** HbA1c 6.5–7.5% (individualise; avoid hypoglycaemia).

SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin 10 mg / empagliflozin 10 mg) — REDUCES CKD progression and mortality even in non-diabetic CKD (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY trials).

Non-steroidal MRA — finerenone (KDIGO 2022 for DKD).

Smoking cessation.

Weight loss, exercise.

Statins — all CKD patients with eGFR < 60 (RCP / NICE).

### 2. Manage Complications

**Anaemia:** Anaemia: Iron first (oral ± IV — target ferritin > 100, TSAT > 20%). Then ESA (erythropoietin 50–100 U/kg/wk SC or darbepoetin Q2W) — target Hb 10–11.5; AVOID > 13 (CV risk). HIF-PHI (roxadustat) new option.

**CKD-MBD:** CKD-MBD: Phosphate restriction (800–1000 mg/d). Calcium-containing binders (avoid in vascular calcif), sevelamer, lanthanum, ferric citrate. Calcitriol or paricalcitol if 2° HPT. Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) for severe HPT. Target Ca-P product < 55.

**Acidosis:** Acidosis: Sodium bicarbonate 0.5–1 mEq/kg/d PO if HCO₃ < 22 (slows CKD progression — Boer 2012).

**Volume / HTN:** Volume / HTN: Salt restriction < 5g/d, fluid 1.5L/d. Loop diuretic in advanced CKD (thiazides less effective if eGFR < 30). ACEi/ARB.

**Hyperkalaemia:** Hyperkalaemia: Dietary K restriction (bananas, citrus, potatoes). Stop ACEi/ARB if K > 6 + acidosis. Patiromer / sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for chronic.

**Dyslipidaemia:** Dyslipidaemia: Atorvastatin 20 mg OD or rosuvastatin 10 mg OD.

**Anaemia/uraemia + symptoms:** Anaemia/uraemia + symptoms: Plan RRT (see below).

### 3. Diet & Lifestyle

Low salt < 5 g/d.

Low protein 0.8 g/kg/d (NOT < 0.6 — risk of malnutrition; KDIGO 2020 nutrition).

Low phosphate, low potassium (avoid bananas, citrus, tomatoes, leafy greens).

Adequate calories 25–35 kcal/kg/d.

Fluid as per output (1–1.5 L if oliguric).

### 4. Vaccinations (immunocompromised)

Hepatitis B (40 µg × 4 doses); pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23); annual influenza; COVID-19; HZV (shingles); avoid live vaccines if on immunosuppressants.

- Prepare for RRT (Stage G4: eGFR 15–29)

Early nephrology referral.

**Patient education — modalities:** HD, PD, transplant.

AV fistula creation 6 months before need (forearm preferred — radio-cephalic > brachiocephalic > brachiobasilic). 'Vein preservation' — no IV cannulas in forearm.

PD catheter insertion 2–4 weeks before start.

Pre-emptive transplant — best outcome; if living donor available, before dialysis.

Psychosocial support, advance care planning.

### 6. ESRD (G5)

**Renal replacement:** HD (intermittent or daily home), PD (CAPD, APD), renal transplant (best outcome — see Q14).

**Conservative care (palliative):** for frail / elderly / patient choice — symptom management.

Fig 2. CKD — staging and stepwise management.

### Prognosis

5-year survival of CKD G5 on dialysis ~ 30–40%. Better with transplant (~ 80% at 5 yr). Leading cause of death = CV disease (50%). Lifetime risk of CKD progression to ESRD varies — DM nephropathy without intervention 30% at 10 yr → with SGLT2i / RAS blockade ~ 10%.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.360; KDIGO CKD 2012; KDIGO BP 2021; KDIGO DKD 2022; DAPA-CKD; EMPA-KIDNEY; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|196.note:
### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|198.note:
### Definition

Height < 3rd percentile or > 2 SD below mean for age and sex (or <2 SD below mid-parental target height; or growth velocity < 25th percentile for >6 months).

### Causes

### Normal variants:

Familial (genetic) short stature – normal growth velocity, skeletal age = chronological age, target height matches parents.

Constitutional growth delay – 'late bloomers', delayed bone age, delayed puberty, normal final height.

### Endocrine:

Growth hormone deficiency (idiopathic, pituitary mass, irradiation, septo-optic dysplasia).

Hypothyroidism (acquired or congenital).

Cushing's syndrome / chronic glucocorticoid excess.

Precocious puberty (early growth spurt → early closure → short final height).

Pseudohypoparathyroidism.

### Genetic / syndromic:

Turner syndrome (45,XO – girls).

Noonan syndrome.

Achondroplasia (skeletal dysplasia – disproportionate, large head).

Russell-Silver, Prader-Willi, Down syndrome.

### Chronic illness:

Malnutrition (commonest globally; significant in India).

Coeliac disease, IBD.

Chronic renal disease.

Cyanotic congenital heart disease.

Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, malabsorption.

Chronic infections – TB, HIV.

### Psychosocial:

Psychosocial dwarfism – emotional deprivation, neglect.

### Evaluation

Height, weight, body proportions, head circumference; growth velocity over time on growth chart.

**Mid-parental height:** boys (father + mother + 13)/2; girls (father + mother − 13)/2 (cm).

Bone age (X-ray left wrist + hand) – delayed in endocrine and constitutional; matches chronological in familial.

**Investigations:** CBC, ESR, U&E, calcium, phosphate, LFT, thyroid function, IGF-1, IGFBP-3, GH provocation test (clonidine, insulin tolerance), TTG anti-endomysial (coeliac), karyotype in girls, urinalysis.

### Management

Treat underlying cause (thyroxine for hypothyroid; gluten-free diet for coeliac; nutritional rehabilitation).

Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) – GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, SGA without catch-up, Prader-Willi, idiopathic short stature (some indications).

Optimise nutrition, treat chronic illness.

Counselling, support; refer paediatric endocrinology.

GENERAL MEDICINE|199.note:
### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.

GENERAL MEDICINE|206.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) = hepatic injury attributable to a drug or supplement, after excluding viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes. Accounts for 10% of all acute hepatitis and ~ 50% of acute liver failure in the West.

### Classification by Mechanism

**Intrinsic / Direct:** Intrinsic / Direct: Predictable, dose-dependent, reproducible. e.g. paracetamol (NAPQI metabolite), CCl₄, Amanita phalloides (α-amanitin).

**Idiosyncratic:** Idiosyncratic: Unpredictable, NOT dose-related, latency days–months. e.g. INH, amoxicillin-clavulanate, halothane, phenytoin.

**Immune-mediated:** Immune-mediated: Fever, rash, eosinophilia (DRESS); HLA-linked. e.g. carbamazepine, allopurinol, anti-TNF, sulpha drugs.

**Steatohepatitis-like:** Steatohepatitis-like: Mitochondrial dysfunction. e.g. valproate, amiodarone, NRTIs.

### Classification by Pattern (R-value)

R = (ALT / ULN) ÷ (ALP / ULN)

**R > 5:** Hepatocellular (paracetamol, INH, statins, methyldopa, isoniazid).

**R < 2:** Cholestatic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, oestrogens, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids).

**R 2–5:** Mixed (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulphonamides).

### Common Hepatotoxic Drugs — by Class

### Indian Context — ATT-DILI

Highest incidence among Asians (~ 8–12%) — important for MBBS.

**Risk factors:** age > 35, female, alcoholism, viral hepatitis B/C carrier, HIV, malnutrition, slow acetylator phenotype (Indian genetic prevalence).

**Pathway:** INH → hydrazine metabolite → CYP2E1 → hepatocyte injury. Rifampicin induces CYP isoenzymes → ↑ INH toxicity; PZA additional risk.

**Monitoring:** baseline + monthly LFT during ATT in high-risk; symptom screening.

Stop ATT if ALT > 5× ULN (asymptomatic) or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms / jaundice.

**Re-introduction:** after LFT normalises, single drug → titrate up (usually rifampicin first → INH → PZA).

**Severe / hepatitic ATT-DILI:** switch to non-hepatotoxic regimen — levofloxacin + ethambutol + injectable (aminoglycoside) ± linezolid.

### Diagnosis

Temporal relationship — onset days to months after starting drug; dechallenge improves LFT.

Exclude viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), autoimmune, biliary (USG/MRCP), metabolic (Wilson's, haemochromatosis).

RUCAM / Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score ≥ 6 = probable.

Liver biopsy — only if diagnosis unclear or atypical.

### Management

WITHDRAW culprit drug immediately.

**Supportive:** hydration, antiemetics, monitor INR + bilirubin.

**Paracetamol:** Specific antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for paracetamol — 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (Rumack-Matthew nomogram).

Penicillin G + silibinin for Amanita.

Carnitine for valproate.

Corticosteroids may help immune-mediated (DRESS, ICI-related hepatitis).

Liver transplant if acute liver failure (King's College criteria for paracetamol, INR > 6.5 / 3 of 5 minor criteria for non-paracetamol).

### Prognosis

Most resolve on dechallenge. 'Hy's law' (ALT > 3× ULN + bilirubin > 2× ULN + no other cause) → 10% mortality. Cholestatic DILI may persist months → vanishing bile duct syndrome.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.22; ACG DILI 2014; Indian Society of Gastroenterology DILI consensus.

GENERAL MEDICINE|207.note:
### Definition

OCD is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterised by intrusive, unwanted, recurrent thoughts, images or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) performed to neutralise distress, that are time-consuming (>1 hour/day) or cause marked distress / functional impairment. Reclassified in DSM-5 into 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders' (separate from anxiety disorders).

### Epidemiology

Lifetime prevalence ~2–3%; current ~1%.

M=F overall; childhood onset M>F, adult onset F>M.

**Bimodal onset:** 8–12 years and late adolescence / early adulthood (mean ~20 y).

Heritability ~50%; first-degree relative risk 4×.

High comorbidity with depression (40–60%), anxiety, tic disorders / Tourette's, ADHD, autism spectrum, eating disorders.

### Etiology

Genetic — polygenic (SLITRK1, glutamate genes); familial clustering.

Neurochemical — serotonergic dysregulation (basis for high-dose SSRI efficacy); glutamatergic hyperactivity in cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop.

Neuroanatomic — hyperactivity in orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, caudate; CSTC circuit dysfunction.

PANDAS / PANS — sudden-onset OCD with tics in children after streptococcal / autoimmune trigger.

Psychological — behavioural model: obsession → anxiety → compulsion → relief (negative reinforcement). Cognitive model: thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

### Clinical features

Obsessions — common themes

Contamination — germs, dirt, body fluids.

Doubts — gas left on, door unlocked, hit someone while driving.

Symmetry / ordering — things must be 'just right'.

Aggressive / sexual / blasphemous intrusive thoughts (ego-dystonic — patient horrified).

Religious / scrupulosity.

Hoarding (now a separate DSM-5 disorder but historically grouped).

Compulsions — common forms

Washing / cleaning (paired with contamination obsessions).

Checking (paired with doubts).

Counting, repeating, ordering / arranging.

Mental compulsions — silent prayer, counting in head, neutralising thoughts.

Reassurance-seeking.

Key clinical features (boards-style)

Recognised by the patient as own (insight may be variable — 'good/fair/poor/absent insight' specifier in DSM-5).

Ego-dystonic — distressing, unwanted.

Resisted (at least initially).

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) or marked distress / impairment.

**Average delay to treatment:** 7–10 years (shame, lack of awareness).

### DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria

Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both.

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) OR clinically significant distress / impairment.

Not due to substance / medical condition.

Not better explained by another mental disorder.

**Specify:** with good/fair insight, with poor insight, with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related (current/past).

### OCD spectrum (DSM-5 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders')

Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with perceived defect in appearance.

Hoarding disorder.

Trichotillomania (hair-pulling).

Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder.

### Severity assessment

Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) — 10-item, clinician-rated; gold standard. 0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme.

Children's Y-BOCS (CY-BOCS) for paediatric.

Floyd-Padua, Maudsley scales — self-report alternatives.

### Differential diagnosis

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Y-BOCS / CY-BOCS; PHQ-9, GAD-7 for comorbidity.

**Routine:** rule out organic — CBC, TSH, ASO titre (PANDAS in children), B12.

MRI brain if late onset, focal signs, or atypical presentation.

**Pre-treatment baseline:** ECG (QTc) if planning high-dose SSRI / clomipramine; LFT for clomipramine.

### Management

Figure 5. OCD management — Y-BOCS severity triage, high-dose SSRI + ERP, ladder to clomipramine, antipsychotic augmentation and DBS.

### First-line — pharmacotherapy

SSRIs — must use HIGH dose, allow LONG trial: Fluoxetine 40–80 mg/d, sertraline 150–200 mg/d, paroxetine 40–60 mg/d, fluvoxamine 200–300 mg/d, escitalopram 20–40 mg/d, citalopram 40 mg max. Start at standard dose, titrate every 2 wk; allow 10–12 wk trial at maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure.

### First-line — psychotherapy

CBT with ERP (Exposure & Response Prevention): Gold standard; 13–20 sessions. Patient exposed in hierarchy to feared stimulus while being prevented from performing compulsion → habituation + extinction of anxiety. Equally effective as SSRI; combination superior to either alone in moderate–severe.

Cognitive therapy — challenge thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

Inadequate response after 10–12 wk

Step 1 — switch SSRI (different agent at maximum dose × 10–12 wk).

Step 2 — clomipramine (TCA, potent serotonergic) 100–250 mg/d. Highly effective but ECG monitoring (QTc, AV block), sedation, anticholinergic, weight gain, sexual SE, seizure risk; AVOID combining with SSRI without specialist (serotonin syndrome). Often most effective single agent.

Step 3 — augmentation with atypical antipsychotic: risperidone 0.5–3 mg/d, aripiprazole 5–15 mg/d, low-dose haloperidol (esp. with comorbid tics).

Step 4 — intensive ERP / residential programme; combine SSRI + clomipramine (specialist + serial ECG).

Severe refractory OCD (failed ≥3 SSRIs + clomipramine + augmentation + ERP)

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) over orbitofrontal cortex / supplementary motor area.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of ventral capsule / ventral striatum or subthalamic nucleus — FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption.

Ablative neurosurgery (anterior capsulotomy, cingulotomy) — last resort, specialist centres only.

Trial of glutamate modulators (memantine, riluzole, N-acetylcysteine, lamotrigine, ketamine) — experimental.

### Special situations

Paediatric OCD — sertraline / fluoxetine / fluvoxamine licensed; CBT-ERP first line for mild-moderate; combine for severe.

PANDAS / PANS — antibiotics (penicillin, azithromycin); IVIG / plasmapheresis in severe.

Pregnancy — CBT preferred; sertraline / fluoxetine if pharmacotherapy essential.

### Duration

Maintain effective drug ≥1–2 years after response; relapse rate ~50% on stopping. Many patients need lifelong treatment.

Gradual taper over months; monitor for return of symptoms.

### Complications

Functional impairment — work, education, relationships, self-care.

Comorbid depression (40–60%), suicide risk elevated.

Substance abuse — self-medication.

Dermatological — chronic hand-washing → eczema, fissures.

Financial — checking compulsions, hoarding effects.

### Prognosis

Chronic fluctuating course; ~10–20% recover completely, ~50% partial response, ~30% chronic.

**Better prognosis:** shorter duration before treatment, good insight, no comorbidity, family support.

**Worse:** early onset, severe symptoms, hoarding subtype, comorbid tics / autism, poor insight, comorbid depression.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for OCD; NICE-CG31; APA Practice Guideline 2007 (with updates); WFSBP 2008/2012; DSM-5; ICD-11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|209.note:
### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

GENERAL MEDICINE|210.note:
**Note:** OSA was bundled in the Rheumatology question set in the source question bank. It is delivered in full here rather than the brief respiratory mention.

### Definition

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is recurrent partial (hypopnoea) or complete (apnoea) collapse of the upper airway during sleep, producing intermittent hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, sympathetic surge and arousals. Severity is graded by the Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) on polysomnography.

### Etiology / Risk factors

Obesity (BMI ≥30) — strongest modifiable risk; neck circumference >40 cm

Male sex (2–3×); risk in females rises after menopause

### Age 40–70 yrs

**Craniofacial:** retrognathia, micrognathia, macroglossia, large tonsils, narrow upper airway

**Endocrine:** hypothyroidism, acromegaly, PCOS

Nasal obstruction — DNS, polyps, rhinitis

Alcohol at bedtime, benzodiazepines, opioids, muscle relaxants

### Smoking

### Supine sleeping position

### Genetic syndromes — Down's, Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins

### Family history

### Pathophysiology

Sleep-induced relaxation of upper airway dilator muscles (genioglossus, tensor palatini) → narrowing of pharyngeal lumen

Negative intraluminal pressure during inspiration → collapse

Apnoea → desaturation → hypercapnia → arousal → muscle tone restored → airway reopens with snoring/gasp

Repeated arousals → sleep fragmentation, daytime sleepiness

Intermittent hypoxia → oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, sympathetic activation → hypertension, insulin resistance, atherogenesis

### Clinical features

### Nocturnal

Loud, habitual snoring (reported by partner)

Witnessed apnoeas, choking / gasping arousals

Restless sleep, frequent awakenings

### Nocturia, nocturnal sweating

### Nocturnal angina, palpitations

### Daytime

Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) — Epworth Sleepiness Scale ≥11

Morning headache (CO₂ retention), dry mouth

Poor concentration, memory impairment, irritability

Erectile dysfunction, loss of libido

### Mood disturbance, depression

Motor-vehicle accident risk 2–7× general population

### Examination

BMI, neck circumference, waist-hip ratio

BP — typically resistant hypertension

Crowded oropharynx (Mallampati III–IV), large tonsils, low-lying soft palate

Retrognathia, micrognathia, dental overjet

Nasal exam — septal deviation, polyps

Signs of cor pulmonale / right HF in severe disease

### Investigations

### Screening tools (clinic)

**STOP-BANG:** Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnoeas, BP elevated, BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, Gender male. Score ≥3 high probability; ≥5 = high probability of moderate-severe OSA.

### Berlin questionnaire, NoSAS score, Epworth Sleepiness Scale

Diagnostic — polysomnography (gold standard)

Type 1 — laboratory-based attended PSG with EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, airflow, effort, oximetry, body position, snore

Type 2 — comprehensive home PSG

Type 3 — limited home respiratory polygraphy (airflow, effort, SpO₂, HR) — acceptable for high-pretest-probability uncomplicated OSA

Type 4 — overnight oximetry alone — only as triage

Apnoea = ≥90% airflow drop ≥10 sec; hypopnoea = ≥30% airflow drop with ≥3% desaturation or arousal

### Additional

TSH, fasting glucose / HbA1c, fasting lipids

Echocardiography if pulmonary hypertension suspected

ABG — daytime hypercapnia (>45 mmHg) suggests obesity hypoventilation overlap

ENT evaluation if surgical option considered

### Management

- Lifestyle and behaviour

Weight loss — 10% weight reduction reduces AHI ~26%

Positional therapy — avoid supine sleep (positional alarms, tennis-ball T-shirt) for positional OSA

Avoid alcohol within 3 h of bedtime; avoid sedatives, opioids, benzodiazepines

### Smoking cessation

Sleep hygiene — regular schedule, adequate duration

Treat nasal congestion (saline, intranasal steroid)

- Positive airway pressure (PAP) — first-line for moderate–severe

**CPAP:** Continuous positive airway pressure — first-line. Auto-titrating CPAP (APAP) common in practice. Compliance threshold ≥4 h/night on ≥70% nights. Re-evaluate at 1 month and 3 months for residual AHI, mask leak, side-effects.

**BiPAP / BiLevel:** For coexisting hypoventilation, COPD-OSA overlap, very high pressure requirements, or CPAP intolerance.

**ASV:** Adaptive servo-ventilation — for treatment-emergent central or complex apnoea. Contra-indicated in HFrEF with EF <45% (SERVE-HF).

**Common side-effects:** nasal congestion, mask leak, claustrophobia, dry mouth

### 3. Oral appliances

Mandibular advancement device (MAD) — first-line for mild OSA, snoring, CPAP-intolerant patients

Fitted by trained dentist; titratable

- Surgery — selected patients

Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) — modest efficacy

Tonsillectomy ± adenoidectomy — particularly in children

Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) — most effective surgical option in selected adults

Nasal surgery for septal deviation, polypectomy

Hypoglossal nerve stimulation — implantable; eligibility AHI 15–65, BMI <35

Tracheostomy — last resort, severe life-threatening OSA

Bariatric surgery — morbid obesity; substantial AHI reduction

- Pharmacological — adjunctive only

Modafinil / armodafinil — residual sleepiness despite adequate CPAP (do NOT replace CPAP)

Solriamfetol — newer alerting agent

### Treat hypothyroidism, acromegaly

- Driving and occupational

Counsel about driving safety; restrict commercial driving until effectively treated

Inform DGCA/RTO if professional driver/pilot (jurisdictional)

Fig 3. Obstructive sleep apnoea — STOP-BANG → PSG → CPAP/MAD ladder

### Complications

Systemic hypertension (especially resistant, non-dipping nocturnal)

Coronary artery disease, MI, heart failure

Atrial fibrillation, bradyarrhythmias during sleep

### Stroke (2–3× risk)

Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale

Type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome

### Motor-vehicle accidents

Perioperative complications — difficult intubation, post-op respiratory depression

Depression, cognitive decline; possible accelerated dementia

Sudden cardiac death (peaks at night in OSA, opposite the general circadian pattern)

### Prognosis

With adherent CPAP use, daytime sleepiness, blood pressure, quality of life and accident risk improve within weeks. Long-term treatment reduces cardiovascular events in observational data. Untreated severe OSA carries a relative mortality of 3–4× over 10–15 years. Adherence to CPAP is the major prognostic determinant.

**Source:** AASM Clinical Practice Guidelines on PAP (2019) + Indian Sleep Disorders Association statement on OSA (2014) + Boloor Ch.6 brief OSA section.

GENERAL MEDICINE|213.note:
Productive cough = cough producing sputum. The character, volume, smell, and consistency provide diagnostic clues.

### Causes by chronicity

### Acute (<3 weeks):

Acute bronchitis (viral, bacterial).

Pneumonia (CAP – rusty sputum in pneumococcal, currant-jelly in Klebsiella).

Acute exacerbation of COPD or asthma.

Pulmonary embolism (occasionally with haemoptysis).

### Sub-acute (3–8 weeks):

Post-infectious cough (pertussis, mycoplasma).

Atypical pneumonia.

### Chronic (>8 weeks):

Chronic bronchitis / COPD (Indian biomass-related particularly).

Bronchiectasis (copious purulent sputum, layered on standing).

Pulmonary tuberculosis (purulent ± haemoptysis ± constitutional).

Lung abscess (foul-smelling purulent sputum).

Bronchogenic carcinoma (change in chronic cough, blood-stained).

Asthma (eosinophilic mucoid plugs).

Interstitial lung disease (dry but occasionally mucoid).

Cystic fibrosis (thick, recurrent infections).

GERD-related cough (often nocturnal, with throat clearing).

Character of sputum and clinical clues

**Mucoid (clear/white):** Asthma, allergic bronchitis, viral bronchitis, early bronchiectasis.

Mucopurulent / purulent yellow-green: Bacterial pneumonia, COPD exacerbation.

**Rusty:** Pneumococcal pneumonia.

**Currant-jelly (red-brown):** Klebsiella pneumonia.

**Blood-stained:** TB, lung cancer, bronchiectasis, PE, mitral stenosis, vasculitides.

**Foul-smelling:** Anaerobic lung abscess, bronchiectasis.

**Pink frothy:** Pulmonary oedema.

**Three-layered:** Bronchiectasis (top layer: foam; middle: serous; bottom: pus).

### Approach

History (duration, character, volume, blood, smoking, occupation, TB contact, fever).

Examination (clubbing, lymph nodes, signs of consolidation/cavity/effusion).

CXR ± HRCT, sputum AFB ×2 + CBNAAT (NTEP), sputum culture, CBC, spirometry, bronchoscopy if neoplasm suspected.

GENERAL MEDICINE|214.note:
### Combined Notes (8 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).
