Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Combination of wound care, anti-rabies vaccination and (where indicated) rabies immunoglobulin given after exposure to a known or suspected rabid mammal, intended to prevent rabies before CNS invasion. Rabies is uniformly fatal once encephalitic symptoms develop, so PEP must be initiated promptly.

### Categorisation (WHO/NRCP)

**Cat I:** Touching/feeding animal, lick on intact skin. No PEP needed (only wash skin).

**Cat II:** Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleed, licks on broken skin.

**Cat III:** Single/multiple transdermal bites or scratches, contamination of mucous membrane with saliva (lick on mouth/eyes), bat exposures.

Wound management (all categories)

Immediate, thorough cleansing of wound with soap (or detergent) and copious running water for 15 minutes.

Apply povidone iodine, alcohol, or virucidal antiseptic.

Avoid suturing if possible; delayed primary closure after RIG infiltration if essential (face/cosmesis).

Tetanus prophylaxis if not up to date.

Antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) for dirty wounds, deep, puncture, or face/hand bites.

### Vaccine (Cat II and III)

### Cell-culture vaccines (CCEEV)

Purified chick embryo cell vaccine (PCEC) – Rabipur.

Human diploid cell vaccine (HDCV).

Purified Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV) – Verorab.

Purified duck embryo cell vaccine (PDEV).

### Intramuscular (Essen) regimen

1 mL IM (deltoid in adults; anterolateral thigh in children <2 yrs; NEVER gluteus) on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28.

### Intradermal (Thai Red Cross) – preferred in India

0.1 mL ID × 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, 28 (2-2-2-0-2).

Updated WHO 1-week IDRV — days 0, 3, 7 (2 sites each) — adopted India 2018.

Booster (previously immunised within 3 years)

1 mL IM (or 0.1 mL ID × 1 site) on days 0 and 3. No RIG.

Rabies immunoglobulin – RIG (Cat III only)

ERIG 40 IU/kg or HRIG 20 IU/kg.

Infiltrate as much as possible IN and AROUND the wound; remaining IM at site distant from vaccine.

Sensitivity test for ERIG; highly purified ERIG has low reaction rate (1–2%).

Monoclonal antibody cocktails (Rabishield, Twinrab) – alternative.

Give within 7 days of vaccine; do not exceed dose.

### Special situations

Pregnancy / lactation – vaccine and RIG safe.

Immunocompromised – use IM regimen, check titre day 14, consider double dose.

Bat exposure (even without overt bite) – treat as Cat III.

If healthy domestic dog/cat is available for 10-day observation and remains well — PEP may be discontinued.

Fig 1. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis algorithm.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

PEP is a short course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) administered after a defined exposure to potentially HIV-infected body fluids, with the goal of preventing seroconversion. Effective only if started within 72 hours (ideally <2 hours).

### Categories of exposure

Occupational (needle-stick, mucosal splash)

**Source HIV status:** positive (CD4, viral load checked), negative, or unknown.

**Type of exposure:** percutaneous (large/small hollow needle, solid needle, superficial), mucous membrane, non-intact skin.

Non-occupational (sexual assault, IDU, unprotected sex)

**Highest risk:** receptive anal intercourse, contaminated needle sharing.

Immediate first-aid (any exposure)

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Alternative if dolutegravir contraindicated

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Atazanavir/Ritonavir (300/100 mg) OR Lopinavir/Ritonavir 400/100 mg BD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

GENERAL MEDICINE|215.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Diastolic regurgitation of blood from aorta into LV due to incompetent aortic valve. Causes: bicuspid valve, rheumatic, IE, syphilitic aortitis, Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection.

### Symptoms

**Asymptomatic for years; later:** exertional dyspnoea, palpitations (forceful heartbeat), angina (nocturnal common), syncope, orthopnoea, PND.

Peripheral Signs (eponyms of free aortic regurgitation)

**Pulse pressure:** wide pulse pressure (>50% of systolic), low diastolic.

**Corrigan's pulse:** high-volume, collapsing, water-hammer (with raised arm).

**Corrigan's sign:** visible carotid pulsation.

**De Musset's:** head bobbing with each beat.

**Quincke's:** visible nail-bed capillary pulsation.

**Traube's:** pistol-shot femoral sounds.

**Duroziez's:** to-and-fro femoral murmur on light compression.

**Müller's:** pulsatile uvula.

**Hill's:** popliteal systolic BP >20 mmHg higher than brachial.

**Rosenbach's:** carotid systolic shudder.

**Becker's:** pulsation of liver.

**Landolfi's:** rhythmic pupillary fluctuation.

### Precordial Signs

Apex – hyperdynamic, displaced down and out (volume overload).

Soft S1, soft/absent A2; S3 if LV dysfunction.

**Early diastolic murmur (EDM):** Murmur: high-pitched, early-diastolic, decrescendo, best heard at 3rd–4th left sternal edge with patient leaning forward in expiration. Length correlates with severity.

**Austin Flint murmur:** Mid-diastolic rumble at apex from regurgitant jet hitting anterior MV leaflet – severe AR.

**Associated:** Aortic ejection systolic murmur (functional, due to large stroke volume) common.

### Definition

Narrowing of aortic valve area producing obstruction to LV outflow. Severe when valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4.0 m/s.

### Etiology

**Calcific (degenerative):** >70 yr, most common cause in developed countries.

**Bicuspid aortic valve:** presents 40–60 yr; commonest congenital cause.

**Rheumatic:** commonest cause in India in younger adults; usually with associated MS.

Subvalvular (HOCM, membrane) or supravalvular (Williams syndrome).

### Pathophysiology

Narrow valve → ↑ LV pressure to maintain stroke volume → concentric LV hypertrophy → compliance ↓ → diastolic dysfunction → ↑ LVEDP → pulmonary congestion. Hypertrophied myocardium also has ↑ O₂ demand and impaired subendocardial perfusion → angina. Fixed cardiac output during exertion + reflex vasodilation → syncope. Eventually LV decompensation → systolic failure.

### Clinical Features

Asymptomatic for decades; triad (SAD) of Syncope (exertional), Angina, Dyspnoea heralds critical AS – mean survival without surgery: 5/3/2 years respectively. Sudden cardiac death possible.

### Signs

**Pulse:** slow-rising, low-volume (pulsus parvus et tardus).

Narrow pulse pressure.

**Apex:** heaving, sustained, not displaced (pressure overload).

Systolic thrill at aortic area radiating to carotids.

**Auscultation:** ejection systolic murmur, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo, maximal at aortic area, radiating to carotids; in elderly, harsh murmur may radiate to apex (Gallavardin phenomenon).

S1 normal; S2 softens/absent (calcified valve); paradoxical splitting; S4 (LVH); ejection click in bicuspid valve.

**Severity pointers:** longer murmur peaking later, soft/absent A2, presence of S4, narrow pulse pressure, slow-rising pulse, signs of LVH.

### Investigations

**ECG:** LVH, strain pattern, LBBB late.

**Echocardiography (key):** valve morphology, AVA (planimetry/continuity equation), peak/mean gradient, LV function, LVH.

**CXR:** cardiomegaly, post-stenotic dilatation of aorta, calcified valve.

**Cardiac catheterisation:** gradient, coronary anatomy before surgery.

**Exercise testing:** only if asymptomatic to unmask symptoms.

**Cardiac CT:** TAVR work-up (annulus size, peripheral vascular access).

Natriuretic peptides (BNP) for risk stratification.

### Management

Pharmacotherapy does not alter prognosis; valve replacement is the only definitive treatment.

**Mild–moderate, asymptomatic:** review yearly with echo. Treat HTN cautiously (ACEi/ARB); avoid vasodilators (GTN) and aggressive diuresis in severe AS.

**Severe symptomatic AS:** aortic valve replacement (AVR). Indicated also if asymptomatic with LVEF <50% or undergoing other cardiac surgery.

SAVR (mechanical/bioprosthetic) for younger, lower-risk patients.

TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement) for elderly/high-surgical-risk patients; now extending into intermediate-risk groups.

**Balloon aortic valvuloplasty:** palliative or bridge to surgery, especially in children/young adults with congenital AS.

Endocarditis prophylaxis if history of IE or prosthetic valve.

Fig 4. Aortic stenosis – management decision tree.

GENERAL MEDICINE|216.note:
### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

GENERAL MEDICINE|217.note:
### Definition

SLE is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by production of antibodies to nuclear antigens, immune-complex deposition and inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, serous membranes and the central nervous system. Female:male ≈ 9:1, peak onset 15–40 yrs; commoner and more severe in South Asians and Afro-Caribbeans.

### Etiology / Risk factors

Genetic — HLA-DR2, DR3; complement deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4); IRF5, STAT4, TREX1

Hormonal — oestrogen excess, oral contraceptives may trigger flares

Environmental — UV light, EBV infection, silica, smoking

**Drug-induced lupus:** hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF, interferon (less renal/CNS, anti-histone +)

Pregnancy can precipitate flare; flares can affect pregnancy

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Defective clearance of apoptotic debris exposes nuclear antigens

Loss of self-tolerance → polyclonal B-cell activation → autoantibody production (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, anti-phospholipid)

Immune complexes deposit in kidneys, skin, vessels → complement activation → tissue injury

Type I interferon signature drives disease activity

Clinical features — multisystem

### Constitutional

Fatigue, fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy

### Mucocutaneous (80%)

Malar (butterfly) rash — spares nasolabial folds

Discoid rash — scarring, dyspigmentation; sun-exposed areas

Subacute cutaneous LE — annular/psoriasiform, photosensitive, anti-Ro/SSA

### Photosensitivity

Painless oral/nasal ulcers (commonly hard palate)

Alopecia (diffuse non-scarring or discoid scarring)

### Raynaud's phenomenon

### Musculoskeletal (90%)

Symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis — non-erosive (Jaccoud's reducible deformity)

Myalgia, true myositis rare

### Avascular necrosis (steroid-related)

Renal — lupus nephritis (LN, 40–60%, more in Indians)

### Proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, AKI

ISN/RPS 2003 classes I–VI; III/IV (proliferative) most severe, V membranous

**Renal biopsy:** light microscopy + IF (full-house: IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q) + EM

### Neuropsychiatric (NPSLE)

Seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction

### Stroke (often APLA mediated)

Aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, mononeuritis multiplex

### Cardiopulmonary

Pleuritis, pericarditis (commonest serous involvement)

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (non-bacterial verrucous)

Pneumonitis, shrinking lung syndrome, alveolar haemorrhage, ILD

Premature accelerated atherosclerosis — major late mortality cause

### Haematological

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Coombs+), leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia (ITP-like)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (30–40% of SLE)

Arterial/venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, livedo reticularis

### Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin Ab, anti-β2 GP I

### GI / hepatic

Lupus enteritis (vasculitis), pancreatitis, autoimmune hepatitis overlap

### Diagnostic criteria

**EULAR/ACR 2019 (preferred):** Entry: ANA ≥1:80 (HEp-2 IIF). Then weighted criteria in 7 clinical (constitutional, haematological, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) + 3 immunology domains (APLA, complement, SLE-specific antibodies). Classify SLE if ≥10 points with at least one clinical criterion.

SLICC 2012 / ACR 1997 — alternative criteria

### Investigations

Screening / disease confirmation

ANA by IIF on HEp-2 cells — sensitive (>95%), low specificity

Anti-dsDNA — specific; correlates with disease activity (esp. lupus nephritis)

Anti-Sm — specific (low sensitivity ~20% in Caucasians, ~30% in South Asians)

Anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB — subacute cutaneous, neonatal lupus, Sjögren overlap

### Anti-U1 RNP — MCTD overlap

Anti-histone — drug-induced lupus

### Anti-ribosomal P — NPSLE

Complement / immune complex

C3, C4, CH50 — low in active disease

### Disease activity markers

Urinalysis (proteinuria, RBC casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio

CBC (cytopenias), ESR (CRP may be normal — exception: serositis, infection)

### RFT, LFT, lipid profile

**APLA panel:** LA, ACL IgG/IgM, anti-β2 GP I

Renal biopsy if proteinuria >500 mg/day, active sediment, or rising creatinine

MRI brain for NPSLE; EEG if seizures; CSF if meningitis suspected

Echocardiography for serositis, Libman-Sacks; CXR/HRCT for lung

**SLE disease activity:** SLEDAI-2K, BILAG

### Management

Background therapy — for all SLE patients

Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/d (max 400 mg/d) — reduces flares, mortality, organ damage; baseline + annual ophthalmology after 5 years (retinal toxicity)

Photoprotection — sunscreen SPF ≥50 daily

### Vitamin D 1000–2000 IU/d + calcium

**Vaccines:** annual influenza, pneumococcal, HPV (before immunosuppression); avoid live vaccines if immunosuppressed

Aggressive CV risk-factor management — statin, BP <130/80, glycaemic control

**Pregnancy planning:** pre-conceptional counselling, switch teratogens, low-dose aspirin in APS

Mild disease (skin, joints, mild serositis)

### HCQ + NSAIDs PRN

Topical steroids, tacrolimus for skin

Low-dose prednisolone (≤7.5 mg/d) — minimise long-term use

Methotrexate 10–25 mg/wk for arthritis

Belimumab (anti-BLyS) for refractory mucocutaneous/joint

Moderate disease (haematological, mild renal, serositis)

Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/d, taper

**Steroid-sparing:** azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d, MMF 1–2 g/d, methotrexate

### Belimumab, anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR)

Severe disease — Lupus nephritis class III/IV

**Induction:** IV methylprednisolone pulse 500–1000 mg × 3 days + ONE of:

- Cyclophosphamide — Euro-Lupus 500 mg IV every 2 weeks × 6 doses (less toxic, equivalent efficacy in Caucasians/South Asians)

- Cyclophosphamide — NIH 0.5–1 g/m² monthly × 6 (preferred in severe/African ancestry)

- Mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/d × 6 months (preferred in pregnancy planning, GI tolerance)

**Maintenance:** MMF 1–2 g/d OR azathioprine 2 mg/kg/d for ≥3 years

**Add:** voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) or belimumab — recent evidence for triple therapy

ACEi/ARB for renoprotection; BP target <130/80

**Class V (membranous):** MMF + steroid; ACEi; consider tacrolimus or rituximab

Severe disease — CNS / haematological crises

Methylprednisolone pulse + cyclophosphamide or rituximab

Plasma exchange for catastrophic APS, TTP-like, alveolar haemorrhage

### Newer/targeted biologics

Belimumab — anti-BLyS; mucocutaneous, joint, mild renal

Anifrolumab — anti-type I interferon receptor; moderate–severe skin/joint disease

Voclosporin — class III/IV/V lupus nephritis (with MMF + steroid)

Rituximab — refractory severe disease (off-label in many countries)

### Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)

**Thrombosis:** warfarin INR 2–3 (arterial: 3–4 or warfarin + LDA); avoid DOACs (TRAPS trial showed inferiority for arterial events)

**Pregnancy + APS:** LMWH + low-dose aspirin throughout

**Catastrophic APS:** anticoag + steroid + plasma exchange + IVIG ± rituximab

### Pregnancy in SLE

Plan in clinical remission ≥6 months

Continue HCQ throughout; LDA from 12 weeks (pre-eclampsia prevention)

**Safe:** HCQ, AZA, calcineurin inhibitors, low-dose steroid

**Stop ≥3 months pre-conception:** MMF, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide

**Anti-Ro+:** neonatal lupus → congenital heart block; foetal echo at 16–28 weeks

Fig 4. SLE — classification + organ-directed management

### Complications

End-stage renal disease (lupus nephritis)

Accelerated atherosclerosis, MI, stroke (leading cause of late death)

### Thrombosis (APS)

Infection (immunosuppression) — bacterial, TB, HZ, opportunistic

Avascular necrosis, osteoporosis (steroid)

Premature ovarian failure (cyclophosphamide)

### Malignancy — NHL, cervical (HPV)

Foetal loss, neonatal lupus, prematurity

### Prognosis

5-yr survival has improved from ~50% (1950s) to >90% with modern treatment. Indian cohorts report 10-yr survival 70–80%. Major causes of early death (≤5 yr): active disease, infection, lupus nephritis. Late death: cardiovascular, ESRD. Adherence to HCQ, control of proteinuria, and CV risk modification are the strongest modifiable predictors.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 SLE + EULAR 2019 SLE management recommendations (update 2023) + ISN/RPS 2003 lupus nephritis classification + Indian Rheumatology Association statement on SLE in Indians (2020).

GENERAL MEDICINE|218.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Passage of ≥ 3 unformed stools per day or > 200 g/d stool weight. Classified by duration: acute (< 14 d), persistent (14–30 d), chronic (> 30 d).

### Pathophysiological Classification

Etiology of Acute Diarrhoea (< 14 d) — usually infective

### Viral (commonest worldwide)

Rotavirus (infants — Rotavac in NIS), norovirus, adenovirus 40/41, astrovirus.

### Bacterial

**Watery:** ETEC (traveller's), V. cholerae (rice-water), Bacillus cereus (rice), Staph aureus (toxin, < 6 h onset), Clostridium perfringens.

**Bloody/inflammatory:** Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, EHEC (O157:H7 — HUS), EIEC, Yersinia, C. difficile (post-antibiotic).

### Parasitic

Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery), Giardia lamblia (chronic watery, foul-smelling), Cryptosporidium (immunocompromised), Cyclospora.

### Non-infectious acute

Drugs (antibiotics, metformin, magnesium, PPIs → microscopic colitis, chemo, colchicine, digoxin), food intolerance, ischaemic colitis (sudden severe abdo pain + bloody).

Etiology of Chronic Diarrhoea (> 30 d)

### Clinical Approach

**History:** travel, food (raw seafood/dairy/water source), antibiotic use, sick contacts, occupation, immunocompromise, weight loss (red flag), nocturnal symptoms (organic), blood/mucus (inflammatory), greasy stool (steatorrhoea).

**Examination:** hydration, weight, thyroid, abdominal mass, perianal disease (Crohn's), lymphadenopathy (TB/lymphoma).

**Alarm features:** weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal diarrhoea, age > 50, blood in stool, family history of IBD/CRC, raised inflammatory markers.

### Investigations

### Bedside / Basic

Stool routine, microscopy (RBC/WBC/cysts), occult blood, fat globules.

Stool culture (Shigella, Salmonella, Campy), C. diff toxin/GDH (if recent abx).

Faecal calprotectin (IBD vs IBS) — > 250 µg/g suggests organic.

### Laboratory

CBC, electrolytes (hypokalaemia), TFT, HIV (chronic).

Coeliac serology — tTG IgA + total IgA (Indian seroprevalence ~ 1%).

Faecal elastase < 200 µg/g → exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

### Endoscopy

Colonoscopy + ileoscopy with biopsies (IBD, microscopic colitis, intestinal TB, Ca).

OGD + duodenal biopsy (coeliac, Whipple's, giardia, sprue).

### Special

Lactose H₂ breath test, glucose H₂ for SIBO.

72-h faecal fat (gold standard for steatorrhoea), D-xylose (mucosal vs pancreatic).

Chromogranin A + 24-h urinary 5-HIAA (carcinoid), serum VIP, gastrin (ZES).

CT/MR enterography for Crohn's mapping.

### Management — Principles

Oral rehydration salts (WHO low-osmolarity ORS) — cornerstone for acute.

Zinc 20 mg/d × 14 d for children < 5 yr (Indian IMNCI, reduces duration/recurrence).

IV fluids if severe dehydration (Plan C — 100 ml/kg over 3–6 h).

Empirical antibiotics ONLY if dysentery, severe travelers' diarrhoea, immunocompromised, prolonged > 7 d, or systemic toxicity:

Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3 d (or azithromycin 500 mg OD × 3 d if fluoroquinolone resistance high).

Metronidazole 400 mg TDS × 7–10 d for amoebic / giardiasis.

Vancomycin PO 125 mg QID × 10 d for C. difficile (fidaxomicin if available).

Anti-motility (loperamide) — avoid in dysentery / EHEC / C. diff (prolongs toxin exposure → HUS, toxic megacolon).

**Treat underlying cause:** GFD for coeliac, immunosuppression for IBD, pancreatic enzyme replacement for CP, octreotide for VIPoma/carcinoid.

Fig 3. Diarrhoea — duration-based workup.

### Complications

Dehydration, AKI, hypovolaemic shock.

Electrolyte disturbance — hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis.

HUS (EHEC, Shigella), Reiter's (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), GBS (Campylobacter jejuni).

Toxic megacolon (UC, C. diff), colorectal Ca (long-standing UC, intestinal TB).

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.404; WHO 2017 IMCI; ESPGHAN 2014; IMNCI India.

### Definition

Diarrhoea persisting for > 4 weeks (WHO classification: > 14 days persistent, > 30 days chronic). Decreased stool consistency (Bristol type 6–7) with or without increased frequency or volume. Important to distinguish from frequency without true diarrhoea (e.g., proctitis tenesmus).

### Classification (Pathophysiological)

### 1. Osmotic

Non-absorbed solutes in lumen → water retention.

Stops with fasting.

Stool osmotic gap > 125 mOsm/kg (gap = 290 − 2(Na + K)).

**Causes:** lactose / fructose / sorbitol intolerance, magnesium-containing laxatives, PEG, malabsorption.

### 2. Secretory

Active secretion of fluid/electrolytes; large volume.

Persists with fasting; nocturnal.

Osmotic gap < 50 mOsm/kg.

**Causes:** VIPoma (pancreatic cholera), carcinoid syndrome, gastrinoma, medullary thyroid Ca (calcitonin), bile acid malabsorption, stimulant laxative abuse (senna, bisacodyl), microscopic colitis.

### 3. Inflammatory

Mucosal damage → blood, pus, protein loss.

**Causes:** IBD (UC, CD), microscopic colitis, infections (TB, amoebiasis), ischaemic colitis, radiation enteritis, lymphoma, eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

### 4. Malabsorption / Steatorrhoea

Pale, bulky, offensive, floating stools.

**Causes:** coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue (Indian!), bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Whipple's, lactose intolerance, post-resection short bowel syndrome.

### 5. Motility

**Causes:** IBS-D (Rome IV), diabetic autonomic neuropathy, hyperthyroidism, post-vagotomy, post-cholecystectomy.

### 6. Factitious / Drug-induced

Laxative abuse (eating disorders).

**Drugs:** metformin, colchicine, magnesium-containing antacids, antibiotics, PPI, NSAIDs, chemotherapy.

### Aetiology — Common Indian Causes

Tuberculosis (ileocaecal) — Indian endemic; pain + diarrhoea + weight loss + RIF mass; ileocaecal valve narrowing, conglomerate nodes, ascites with high ADA.

Intestinal parasites — Giardia (cysts on stool, duodenal aspirate), amoebiasis, strongyloidiasis.

Tropical sprue — Indian climate; megaloblastic, glossitis, B12/folate deficiency; responds to folate + tetracycline.

IBD — increasing incidence.

Coeliac disease — under-recognised in India.

Lactose intolerance — prevalent in adults (Asian phenotype).

IBS — commonest functional cause.

Hyperthyroidism, diabetes.

HIV-associated diarrhoea — opportunistic infections (cryptosporidium, isospora, microsporidium, CMV).

Colon cancer — older patients.

### Approach — History

Duration, frequency, volume, consistency (Bristol).

Nocturnal — organic; daytime only — functional.

Blood/mucus → inflammatory.

Steatorrhoea → malabsorption.

Fasting → relieves osmotic, NOT secretory.

Travel history (tropical sprue, infection), HIV risk factors, occupation.

**Drugs:** laxatives, metformin, antibiotics, antacids.

**Diet:** lactose, gluten, FODMAPs.

Weight loss, fever, joint pain (IBD, coeliac).

Surgery history (resection, vagotomy, cholecystectomy).

**Family history:** IBD, coeliac, colon cancer.

**Red flags ALARM:** Age > 50 new symptoms, blood, weight loss, fever, anaemia, family history of colon Ca.

### Examination

BMI, hydration status, pallor (anaemia).

Lymphadenopathy (TB, lymphoma, HIV).

Thyroid (hyperthyroid).

**Skin:** erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum (IBD), dermatitis herpetiformis (coeliac).

**Joints:** arthritis (IBD).

**Abdomen:** mass (RIF — TB), tenderness, scars, hepatosplenomegaly.

**PR exam:** blood, mass, sphincter tone.

### Investigations — Stepwise

First-line (all chronic diarrhoea)

CBC (anaemia, eosinophilia), ESR / CRP (inflammation).

U&E, LFT, blood glucose, TSH.

Coeliac serology — anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA + total IgA (rule out IgA deficiency).

Stool — routine microscopy, culture (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), C. difficile toxin, ova-parasite × 3, Giardia antigen.

Stool fat (Sudan III qualitative or 72-h quantitative > 7 g/d = steatorrhoea).

Faecal calprotectin (> 250 inflammatory, > 50 in symptomatic).

HIV serology.

### Targeted Investigations

**Suspected IBD:** colonoscopy + biopsies, MR enterography.

**Suspected coeliac:** anti-tTG positive → OGD + duodenal biopsies × 4 from D2.

Suspected pancreatic insufficiency: faecal elastase < 100 µg/g.

**Suspected SIBO:** hydrogen breath test (glucose / lactulose).

**Suspected lactose intolerance:** hydrogen breath test (lactose), elimination trial.

**Suspected secretory cause:** serum gastrin, VIP, 5-HIAA (24-h urine), calcitonin, chromogranin A, OctreoScan.

**Suspected TB:** stool/biopsy AFB, mantoux, IGRA, CECT, ileocolonoscopy biopsy + culture, ascitic ADA > 40.

**Suspected microscopic colitis:** colonoscopy with random biopsies (normal-appearing mucosa).

**Suspected laxative abuse:** urine alkalinisation (phenolphthalein turns pink), stool/urine magnesium.

**Suspected bile acid diarrhoea:** 75SeHCAT test (or empirical trial of cholestyramine).

Tumour markers (CEA, CA 125), CECT abdomen (mass, lymphoma).

### Management

Treat underlying cause specifically.

**Rehydration:** ORS, IV fluids if severe.

Empirical antibiotic — NOT for chronic diarrhoea without confirmed infection.

Antidiarrhoeals (loperamide 2 mg up to 16 mg/d) — symptomatic, AVOID in inflammatory, infectious dysentery, C. difficile.

Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam) — bile acid malabsorption.

Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) — pancreatic insufficiency.

Gluten-free diet — coeliac.

Lactose elimination — lactose intolerance.

ATT — TB ileitis.

Octreotide — secretory (carcinoid, VIPoma).

**Address malnutrition:** protein, B12, folate, iron, fat-soluble vitamins, calcium, magnesium.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11 p.405; Davidson Ch.23; WGO Chronic Diarrhoea 2012; Indian guidelines for ileocaecal TB.

GENERAL MEDICINE|219.note:
### Definition

Gout is a crystal arthropathy caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and connective tissues, presenting with episodic acute inflammatory arthritis, chronic tophaceous deposits, urate nephropathy and uric acid urolithiasis. Hyperuricaemia is defined as serum urate >7.0 mg/dL in men and >6.0 mg/dL in women.

### Etiology / Risk factors

### Overproduction (10–15%)

### Idiopathic (most common)

**Enzyme defects:** HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan), PRPP synthetase overactivity, G6PD deficiency

**High cell turnover:** leukemia, lymphoma, myeloproliferative, polycythaemia, tumour lysis, haemolysis, psoriasis

**Diet:** high purine — red meat, organ meat, seafood (anchovies, sardines), beer (esp. yeast), fructose-sweetened beverages

### Exercise/strenuous activity

### Underexcretion (85–90%)

### CKD (any cause)

**Drugs:** thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin (<2 g), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, niacin, levodopa

Lead nephropathy (saturnine gout)

Lactic acidosis (alcohol, exercise, starvation)

### Ketoacidosis

### Hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism

### Other risk factors

Male sex, age >40

Obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes

### Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia

Family history (heritability ~60%)

### Pathophysiology

Uric acid is the end-product of purine metabolism (via xanthine oxidase). Humans lack uricase, so urate accumulates. When serum urate exceeds saturation (~6.8 mg/dL at 37°C), MSU crystals precipitate, especially in cooler peripheral joints (1st MTP), in acidic and low-flow tissues, and after sudden urate fluctuations.

**Phase 1:** Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia

**Phase 2:** Acute gouty arthritis — MSU crystals phagocytosed → NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β release → neutrophil recruitment → acute inflammation

**Phase 3:** Intercritical period — asymptomatic between attacks; microcrystals persist

**Phase 4:** Chronic tophaceous gout — large MSU aggregates with foreign-body giant cells, bone erosions ('punched-out')

**Renal:** uric acid stones (radiolucent), urate nephropathy, acute uric acid nephropathy in tumour lysis

### Clinical features

### Acute attack

Sudden onset, often nocturnal, peaks within 24 h

Severely painful, warm, swollen, erythematous joint — patient cannot bear weight on bed sheet

First MTP joint (podagra) in 50%; can affect ankle, midfoot, knee, wrist, elbow

**Triggers:** trauma, surgery, dehydration, alcohol binge, infection, IV contrast, urate fluctuation (start of ULT)

Resolves spontaneously in 5–14 days even without treatment (with desquamation of overlying skin)

Low-grade fever possible — beware mimicking septic arthritis

Chronic tophaceous gout (untreated >5–10 yr)

**Tophi:** nodular MSU deposits — helix of ear, olecranon bursa, Achilles, finger pulps, extensor tendons

May ulcerate and discharge chalky white material

Persistent polyarticular arthritis with deformity, erosions

### Renal manifestations

Uric acid nephrolithiasis — radiolucent, acidic urine

### Chronic urate nephropathy

Acute uric acid nephropathy — tumour lysis, very high urate, AKI

### Investigations

Gold standard — synovial fluid aspiration

**MSU crystals:** needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light (yellow parallel to axis, blue perpendicular)

WBC 10,000–100,000/µL, predominantly neutrophils

Always send Gram stain and culture — exclude septic arthritis (can coexist!)

### Biochemistry

Serum urate (may be normal during acute attack — repeat after 2 weeks)

RFT (urate excretion + drug dosing), eGFR

FBS, lipid profile, BP (associated metabolic syndrome)

**24-h urine uric acid:** >800 mg/24h on regular diet = overproducer

CBC, ESR/CRP (raised in acute attack, normal between)

### Imaging

**X-ray — early normal; chronic:** punched-out erosions with overhanging edges (Martel sign), preserved joint space, soft-tissue tophi

Dual-energy CT (DECT) — colour-codes MSU; sensitive for tophi

Ultrasound — double-contour sign (urate on cartilage), tophi, erosions

### Pre-ULT (urate-lowering) screen

HLA-B*5801 in Asian patients before allopurinol (SJS/TEN risk)

### Baseline LFT for febuxostat

G6PD if rasburicase planned

### Management

- Acute attack — start within 24 h

**First-line — NSAIDs:** Naproxen 500 mg BD, indomethacin 50 mg TDS, or ibuprofen 800 mg TDS × 5–7 days. Avoid if CKD, peptic ulcer, HF, antiplatelet/anticoag.

**Colchicine:** Low-dose ACR regimen: 1.2 mg STAT, then 0.6 mg 1 hour later, then 0.6 mg OD–BD until resolution (max 7–10 days). Avoid in eGFR <30; reduce dose with CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, statins, cyclosporine).

**Glucocorticoids:** Prednisolone 30–40 mg PO daily × 5 days then taper. Methylprednisolone IM 40–80 mg single dose for 1–2 joints. Intra-articular triamcinolone after aspiration if mono/oligoarticular.

**IL-1 inhibitors:** Anakinra, canakinumab — refractory or polyarticular attack in patient with multiple contraindications. Expensive.

DO NOT start, stop or change dose of urate-lowering therapy during an attack (may prolong/precipitate flare). If patient is already on ULT, CONTINUE it.

Rest, ice, elevate the affected joint

- Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) — indications

Recurrent attacks (≥2 per year)

Tophi (clinical or imaging)

### Radiographic erosions

### CKD stage ≥2

### Uric acid nephrolithiasis

First attack with serum urate >9 mg/dL or young age <40

- Xanthine oxidase inhibitors — first choice

**Allopurinol:** Start 100 mg/d (50 mg/d if eGFR <60); titrate by 100 mg every 2–5 weeks to target serum urate <6 mg/dL (<5 if tophi). Max 800 mg/d. Adverse: rash, hepatitis, AHS (allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — fever + DRESS + AKI; 25% mortality). Risk increased with HLA-B*5801 (~5–8% Han Chinese, 4% Indian, 1% European) — screen Asian/at-risk patients before initiation.

**Febuxostat:** 40–80 mg/d, max 120 mg. No dose adjustment in mild–moderate CKD. More potent than allopurinol. CARES trial showed ↑ CV mortality vs allopurinol — caution if established CV disease.

- Uricosurics — when XO inhibitors fail or are contra-indicated

Probenecid 250 mg BD → 500–2000 mg/d; needs eGFR >50, no nephrolithiasis history; alkalinise urine (pH 6.5–7) + good hydration

Lesinurad 200 mg/d — only in combination with XO inhibitor

Benzbromarone — hepatotoxic; restricted

- Recombinant uricase — refractory tophaceous gout

Pegloticase 8 mg IV every 2 weeks; G6PD-deficient patients excluded

Rasburicase — tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis

### 6. ULT-initiation prophylaxis

Co-prescribe colchicine 0.6 mg OD (or low-dose NSAID, or low-dose prednisolone 5 mg) for 3–6 months during ULT initiation to prevent mobilisation flares

### 7. Lifestyle

Weight loss (gradual — rapid weight loss/ketosis triggers attacks)

Limit red/organ meat, seafood

Avoid alcohol (especially beer) and fructose-sweetened drinks

Encourage low-fat dairy, vegetables, cherries, coffee, water 2–3 L/d

Stop thiazide if possible — substitute losartan (uricosuric) or amlodipine

Fig 2. Gout — acute treatment + urate-lowering therapy ladder

### Complications

Chronic destructive tophaceous gout with joint deformity

Uric acid nephrolithiasis, urate nephropathy → CKD progression

Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — SJS/TEN

**Cardiovascular:** associated with hypertension, CAD, metabolic syndrome

Septic arthritis can coexist — always aspirate

### Prognosis

Excellent with adherent ULT. Achievement of target urate <6 mg/dL reduces flare frequency progressively over 12–24 months and shrinks tophi over years. Untreated gout becomes chronic, erosive and polyarticular within 10–20 years. CV and renal comorbidity drive long-term mortality.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 (gout) + ACR 2020 guideline for management of gout + Indian Rheumatology Association recommendation on HLA-B*5801 screening (2021).

GENERAL MEDICINE|220.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

Dyspnoea may result from metabolic abnormalities driving respiration without primary lung or cardiac disease – usually stimulating central or peripheral chemoreceptors.

### Acidosis

Diabetic ketoacidosis – Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing, compensatory).

Lactic acidosis – sepsis, shock, metformin toxicity, severe exercise.

Uremic acidosis (CKD).

Toxic alcohols – methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates.

### Anaemia

Severe anaemia (any cause) – decreased O₂ delivery → tachypnoea.

### Hypoxaemia (any cause)

Cyanide/carbon-monoxide poisoning – tissue hypoxia.

Methaemoglobinaemia.

### Thyrotoxicosis

Increased metabolic demand.

### Pregnancy

Progesterone stimulates respiratory centre.

### Hypoglycaemia

Sympathetic surge + tachypnoea.

### Drugs/toxins

Salicylates (early respiratory alkalosis), beta-2 agonists, theophylline toxicity.

### Approach

ABG (acid-base status), CBC, glucose, electrolytes, lactate, creatinine, urinalysis, drug screen, TSH, blood gas methaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin.

### Definition

An acid-base disturbance characterised by reduction in blood pH (<7.35) and primary decrease in serum bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L) due to either gain of fixed acid, loss of base, or impaired renal acid excretion. The respiratory compensation (reduced PaCO₂) typically follows Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2.

### Approach – Anion gap

Anion gap (AG) = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO₃-]); normal 8–12 mmol/L. Albumin-corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4 – albumin).

High anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) — 'MUDPILES' or 'KULT-GOLD-MARS'

M – Methanol (formic acid)

### U – Uremia (CKD)

D – Diabetic ketoacidosis / alcoholic / starvation ketoacidosis

P – Paraldehyde, propylene glycol

### I – Isoniazid, iron

L – Lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock, metformin, hypoxia)

### E – Ethylene glycol

### S – Salicylates

Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA / hyperchloraemic):

Diarrhoea (loss of HCO₃).

Renal tubular acidosis (type 1 distal, type 2 proximal, type 4 hyporeninaemic).

Ureteric diversion (uretero-sigmoidostomy).

Pancreatic/biliary fistula.

**Drugs:** acetazolamide, topiramate, cholestyramine.

Saline infusion (dilutional).

Early renal failure.

### Clinical features

Underlying cause-related (DKA – hyperglycaemia, ketones).

Kussmaul respiration (deep, sighing).

Decreased myocardial contractility, hypotension, arrhythmias.

Increased catecholamines + insulin resistance + hyperkalaemia.

Bone demineralisation (chronic).

**CNS:** lethargy, confusion, coma.

### Investigations

### 1. Confirm acidosis

ABG (arterial pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃).

Venous bicarbonate, base excess.

- Calculate anion gap

Serum Na, K, Cl, HCO₃. Calculate AG and corrected AG (for albumin).

- Look for cause (HAGMA)

Glucose + ketones (DKA, alcoholic ketosis).

Serum lactate (lactic acidosis).

Renal function – urea, creatinine, eGFR (uremia).

Osmolar gap >10 mOsm/kg suggests toxic alcohol (methanol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol).

Toxicology screen – salicylate, methanol/ethylene glycol levels, isoniazid.

### 4. NAGMA workup

Urine pH, urine anion gap (UAG = UNa + UK − UCl).

Urine ammonium (low in RTA).

Stool electrolytes / osmolality if diarrhoea.

Renal ultrasound, urine for calcium/citrate.

### Management principles

Treat underlying cause (insulin for DKA, dialysis for uremia, fomepizole/dialysis for toxic alcohols, glucose+B1 for ketoacidosis).

**Sodium bicarbonate:** usually only if pH<7.1 in DKA; <7.2 in lactic acidosis; or in hyperkalaemic acidosis. Routine HCO₃ in DKA is controversial (paradoxical CSF acidosis).

Correct K+; haemodialysis for uremic acidosis, toxic alcohols, severe lactic acidosis with metformin.

### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

GENERAL MEDICINE|221.note:
### Class background

Artemisinin (qinghaosu) is a sesquiterpene lactone derived from Artemisia annua (sweet wormwood). It and its semi-synthetic derivatives are the most rapidly acting antimalarials known, cidal against asexual blood stages including ring forms of all Plasmodium species. WHO recommends artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) as first-line in nearly all malaria-endemic countries.

### Available derivatives

**Artemisinin:** Original parent compound; rarely used alone clinically due to poor solubility and short half-life.

**Artesunate:** Water-soluble; available as IV, IM, oral, and rectal suppository (paediatric). Half-life ~45 min.

**Artemether:** Oil-soluble; IM only; long-acting; used in severe malaria when artesunate unavailable.

**Dihydroartemisinin (DHA):** Oral/oil-soluble; used in ACT combinations.

**Artemotil (β-arteether):** Older oral preparation, less common.

Dosage – uncomplicated falciparum (ACT regimens)

Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (AS-SP): Artesunate 4 mg/kg + Sulfadoxine 25 mg/kg + Pyrimethamine 1.25 mg/kg, given over 3 days. NVBDCP first-line in non-NE Indian states.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL, Coartem): 20/120 mg fixed-dose; adult dose 4 tablets BD × 3 days. NVBDCP first-line in North-East India (where SP resistance documented).

Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine (DP, Eurartesim): 40/320 mg; 4 tablets OD × 3 days (adult). Alternative ACT.

**Artesunate-Amodiaquine (AS-AQ):** Artesunate 4 mg/kg + Amodiaquine 10 mg/kg, both OD × 3 days. Used in some African settings.

Severe / complicated malaria

**Artesunate IV:** 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily; minimum 3 doses (24 h); follow with full oral ACT once tolerating oral.

**Artemether IM:** 3.2 mg/kg at hour 0, then 1.6 mg/kg daily × at least 3 days; second-line if artesunate unavailable.

Rectal artesunate (pre-referral, children): 10 mg/kg single dose while arranging transfer.

### Adjunct (gametocidal)

Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (P. falciparum) – kill gametocytes to interrupt transmission; G6PD test or low-dose 0.25 mg/kg single dose may be used safely without test in low-transmission settings (WHO 2018).

### Adverse effects

Generally well tolerated; nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache.

**Rare:** post-artesunate delayed haemolytic anaemia (>5% in some cohorts, 1–3 weeks after IV artesunate; monitor Hb for 4 weeks).

Cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation – piperaquine, lumefantrine).

Avoid in 1st trimester pregnancy where possible (use only if severe / falciparum and benefits outweigh risk – WHO permits in severe malaria across all trimesters).

### Resistance

Greater Mekong subregion (Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand) – partial artemisinin resistance from Pf K13 mutations; delayed parasite clearance.

Africa and India – clinical artemisinin resistance not yet established; surveillance ongoing.

Combination with partner drug (sulfadoxine, lumefantrine, piperaquine) protects against monotherapy resistance.

GENERAL MEDICINE|223.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### (a) Likely diagnosis

Acute inferior-wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), with possible posterior extension suggested by ST flattening (likely reciprocal depression) in V1–V6.

Inferior MI typically reflects right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion (~80%) or left circumflex (~20%). Right ventricular involvement must be actively excluded as it changes management (avoid nitrates/diuretics, give fluids).

(b) Confirmatory investigations and why

Repeat 12-lead ECG with V4R, V7–V9: Confirm STEMI, identify reciprocal changes; add right-sided leads V4R (RV MI: ST↑ in V4R, sensitivity ~88%) and posterior leads V7–V9 (posterior MI).

**Troponin I/T:** Highly sensitive (rises 3–6 h, peaks 24 h). Confirms myocardial necrosis and quantifies infarct size.

**CK-MB:** Confirms diagnosis, peaks earlier than troponin, useful for re-infarction.

**2-D Echocardiogram:** EF, regional wall-motion abnormality (inferior wall hypokinesia), RV function, mechanical complications.

**Chest X-ray:** Pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly, exclude dissection.

**Labs:** CBC, RFT, electrolytes (K, Mg matter for arrhythmias), HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, coagulation profile, blood glucose.

**Coronary angiography:** Definitive – delineates culprit and other vessels; required if PCI planned.

### (c) Treatment

**Immediate (MONAH):** Cardiac monitoring, IV access, O₂ if SpO₂<90%, semi-recumbent position. IV morphine 2–4 mg for pain. Aspirin 325 mg chewed + Ticagrelor 180 mg (or Clopidogrel 300–600 mg) loading. Atorvastatin 80 mg. UFH 60 U/kg bolus + 12 U/kg/h infusion (or LMWH).

**Caution:** Avoid nitrates and diuretics until RV infarction excluded (preload-dependent). β-blocker withheld initially if HR or BP marginal.

**Reperfusion:** If centre has cath-lab → Primary PCI within 90 min (door-to-balloon). If not → IV Tenecteplase or Streptokinase 1.5 MU over 30 min (door-to-needle <30 min), then pharmaco-invasive transfer.

**RV infarct:** If RV infarct: aggressive IV crystalloid 200–500 mL boluses to keep preload; inotropes (dobutamine) if shock; pace if AV block.

**Discharge:** Aspirin 75 mg lifelong + P2Y12 inhibitor 12 months, atorvastatin 40–80 mg, β-blocker (carvedilol/metoprolol), ACEi (ramipril 5 mg BD titrated), MRA if EF<40%, glycaemic control (HbA1c <7%), BP <130/80, smoking cessation, cardiac rehab.

(d) Complications if untreated

**Arrhythmias:** VF, AV block (RCA territory typically causes complete heart block, often transient).

**Pump failure:** Cardiogenic shock (Killip IV).

**RV:** RV infarction → hypotension despite clear lungs.

**Mechanical:** Free-wall rupture, VSD, papillary-muscle rupture (acute MR), all in days 3–7.

**Thromboembolic:** Mural thrombus → stroke.

**Late:** LV aneurysm, chronic HF, recurrent ischaemia.

**Mortality:** Up to 30% without reperfusion vs ~5% with timely PCI.

### Cardiovascular

Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina) – retrosternal, crushing, >20 min, radiation to left arm/jaw.

Stable angina – exertional, <10 min, relieved by rest/GTN.

Aortic dissection – sudden, tearing, between shoulder blades, BP/pulse asymmetry, widened mediastinum.

Pericarditis – sharp, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, rub on auscultation.

Myocarditis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe aortic stenosis.

### Respiratory

Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, risk factors.

Pneumonia, pleurisy – pleuritic, fever, cough.

Pneumothorax – sudden, unilateral, dyspnoea.

Asthma exacerbation, bronchitis.

Lung cancer (chest wall invasion).

### Gastrointestinal

GERD / oesophagitis – retrosternal burning, post-prandial, supine.

Oesophageal spasm – may mimic ACS.

Peptic ulcer disease, gastritis.

Boerhaave's syndrome (oesophageal rupture – Mackler triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema).

Pancreatitis (radiates to back), biliary colic.

### Musculoskeletal

Costochondritis / Tietze's syndrome – localised, reproducible tenderness.

Rib fracture, intercostal muscle strain.

Cervical spondylosis (radicular).

### Other

Herpes zoster (dermatomal).

Anxiety / panic attack – associated with hyperventilation.

Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crisis (acute chest syndrome).

**Approach:** ECG within 10 min in any adult with chest pain; troponin; CXR; consider CT pulmonary angiogram for PE, CT angio for aortic dissection; echocardiography. Wells score, HEART score, GRACE/TIMI guide risk-stratification.

### Definition

Joint pain (arthralgia) is pain originating from the joint. When accompanied by signs of inflammation (swelling, warmth, erythema, loss of function), it is arthritis. A systematic clinical approach is essential because the differential ranges from benign self-limited to life-threatening (septic arthritis).

Step 1 — Articular vs non-articular

**Articular:** pain on active AND passive ROM, swelling, joint-line tenderness, crepitus

**Periarticular:** tendinitis, bursitis, enthesitis — focal tenderness, pain on resisted movement, normal passive ROM

**Referred:** hip pain from L1 nerve root, shoulder from diaphragm

Step 2 — Inflammatory vs mechanical

Step 3 — Number and pattern of joints involved

### Monoarthritis (1 joint)

**Acute:** septic arthritis (MUST exclude — aspirate!), crystal (gout, pseudogout), trauma, haemarthrosis, OA flare

**Chronic:** TB, fungal, atypical mycobacteria, OA, PVNS, tumour

### Oligoarthritis (2–4 joints)

### Spondyloarthritis (AS, PsA, ReA, IBD-associated)

Crystal — polyarticular gout

### Sarcoidosis (Löfgren's)

### Endocarditis

### Polyarthritis (≥5 joints)

**Symmetric small-joint:** RA, SLE, MCTD, RA-overlap, viral (parvo, HCV, HBV, rubella, chikungunya, dengue)

**Symmetric large-joint:** rheumatic fever, viral

**Asymmetric:** spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis

**DIP-predominant:** OA (Heberden's, Bouchard's), psoriatic

Step 4 — Acute (<6 weeks) vs chronic (≥6 weeks)

### Acute polyarthritis

Viral — parvovirus B19, HBV, HCV, HIV, rubella, chikungunya (common in Indian outbreaks; persistent in 20%), dengue

Post-streptococcal (rheumatic fever, post-strep ReA)

### Reactive — Chlamydia, Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter

### Crystal flare

### Drug-induced lupus

Serum sickness, drug hypersensitivity

### Chronic polyarthritis

### RA, SLE, MCTD, Sjögren

### Spondyloarthritis

Crystal — chronic tophaceous gout, CPPD

### OA

Chronic infection — TB, brucella, Lyme, fungal

### Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis

Paraneoplastic — hypertrophic osteoarthropathy

Step 5 — Extra-articular clues

**Skin:** psoriasis (PsA), malar rash (SLE), erythema migrans (Lyme), gouty tophi, erythema nodosum (sarcoid)

**Nail:** pitting, onycholysis (PsA); splinter haemorrhages (IE, vasculitis)

**Eye:** uveitis (AS, sarcoid, JIA), keratoconjunctivitis sicca (Sjögren), scleritis (RA, vasculitis)

**Mucosa:** oral ulcers (SLE, Behçet, IBD), genital ulcers (Behçet, ReA)

**GI:** diarrhoea (IBD arthritis, ReA), dysphagia (SSc)

**GU:** urethritis (ReA), nephritis (SLE)

**Lung:** ILD (RA, SSc, MCTD), serositis (SLE)

**Neuro:** mononeuritis (vasculitis, RA), seizure (SLE)

### Investigations

All patients with new arthritis

### CBC, ESR, CRP

### Uric acid, RFT, LFT

### Urinalysis

X-ray of affected joints (and contralateral for comparison)

Acute monoarthritis — emergency aspiration

**Synovial fluid:** appearance, cell count, Gram stain + culture, polarised microscopy for crystals

### Targeted serology

RF, anti-CCP — for symmetric polyarthritis

ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, complement — for SLE

### HLA-B27 — spondyloarthritis

ASO, anti-DNase B — post-streptococcal

Hepatitis B, C, HIV, parvovirus, chikungunya IgM, dengue NS1/IgM

ANCA — if vasculitis suspected

Cryoglobulin — purpura, neuropathy

### Imaging

X-ray — bone erosion (RA), syndesmophytes (AS), pencil-in-cup (PsA), tophi, chondrocalcinosis

Ultrasound — synovitis, effusion, erosions, tophi

MRI — early erosions, sacroiliitis, bone oedema

DEXA — pre-treatment baseline if chronic steroid likely

Fig 6. Approach to joint pain — articular vs non-articular → mono vs poly → inflammatory pattern → specific diagnosis

### Initial management principles

Acute monoarthritis = septic arthritis until disproven → aspirate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics empirically, joint washout if pus

**Symptomatic:** NSAIDs (avoid if peptic ulcer, CKD); intra-articular steroid after septic excluded

**Disease-specific:** DMARDs (RA), urate-lowering (gout), antibiotic (Lyme, ReA), antiviral (HCV)

Refer rheumatology for early diagnosis, suspected CTD, refractory disease

Red flags requiring urgent action

Acute monoarthritis with fever — septic

Neurological deficit + back pain — spinal infection / cauda equina

Joint pain + purpura + AKI — vasculitis

Polyarthritis + pleurisy + nephritis — SLE flare

New uveitis + joint pain — sarcoid, AS, Behçet

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 polyarthropathy + Davidson Ch.24 rheumatology approach + Indian Council of Medical Research polyarthritis evaluation algorithm.
