### Combined Notes (2 topics)

Common inhaled corticosteroids (Indian availability)

Budesonide (Budecort, Pulmicort) – MDI 100/200 µg; DPI 200/400 µg; neb 0.5/1 mg.

Fluticasone propionate (Flohale, Flixotide) – MDI 50/125/250 µg; DPI 100/250/500 µg.

Fluticasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg (once-daily).

Beclomethasone dipropionate (Beclate) – MDI 50/100/250 µg.

Ciclesonide (Alvesco) – MDI 80/160 µg.

Mometasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg.

Combination ICS-LABA inhalers (most prescribed)

Budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort, Foracort) – preferred Track 1 GINA reliever-controller.

Fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide).

Fluticasone furoate + vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta).

Beclomethasone + formoterol.

### Triple-therapy inhalers (ICS-LABA-LAMA)

Fluticasone + umeclidinium + vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta).

Budesonide + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

Beclomethasone + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

### Adverse effects

**Local:** oral candidiasis (Candida albicans – use spacer + rinse mouth), dysphonia, throat irritation.

Systemic (with high dose / long-term): osteoporosis, skin thinning, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, adrenal suppression, increased pneumonia risk in COPD.

### Indications

Asthma – mainstay of controller therapy from GINA Step 1 onwards.

COPD – with LABA in patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥100/300.

Other obstructive airways disease (some forms of bronchiectasis with asthma overlap).

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

GENERAL MEDICINE|226.note:
### Definition

Acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis. Commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide after polio eradication. Incidence 1-2/100,000/year.

### Aetiology / Triggers

Antecedent infection 1-3 weeks earlier in 2/3:

- Campylobacter jejuni (commonest, esp. AMAN variant) — molecular mimicry with GM1/GD1a gangliosides.

- CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV, hepatitis E.

- Zika, dengue, chikungunya (Indian relevance).

- SARS-CoV-2 (post-COVID-19).

Post-vaccination (rare — older 1976 swine flu, rabies, influenza).

Post-surgical (rare).

### Variants

AIDP (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy) — commonest in West.

AMAN (Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy) — common in India/Asia, post-Campylobacter, anti-GM1.

AMSAN (sensorimotor axonal) — severe, slower recovery.

**Miller-Fisher:** ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b in 90%.

Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis: + altered sensorium.

Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial.

### Clinical features

Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis (legs → arms → bulbar → respiratory) over hours-days.

Areflexia (or hyporeflexia) — cardinal.

**Sensory:** paraesthesias > objective sensory loss; back/limb pain common.

**Cranial:** bilateral VII (50%), bulbar palsy.

**Autonomic in 70%:** BP swings, arrhythmias, ileus, urinary retention.

Respiratory failure in 25-30% — needs ventilation.

Peak deficit by 2-4 weeks; plateau; then gradual recovery.

### Brighton diagnostic criteria

Bilateral flaccid limb weakness + reduced/absent reflexes + monophasic course (12 h - 28 days) + CSF and/or electrophysiology supportive + no alternative diagnosis.

### Investigations

### Bedside (essential)

Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) — q4h; intubate if < 20 mL/kg.

Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF) — intubate if > -30 cm H₂O.

**Single breath count:** < 19 → impending respiratory failure.

ECG, BP monitoring (autonomic).

### CSF

Albuminocytological dissociation — protein > 0.45 g/L with cells < 10/mm³.

Appears after day 7 (50% positive in first week, 75% by week 2).

Nerve conduction studies (most sensitive in week 1)

**AIDP:** prolonged distal latency, conduction block, slowed velocity, prolonged F-wave latency, abnormal H reflex.

**AMAN:** reduced CMAP amplitude with preserved velocity.

### Antibodies (optional)

Anti-GM1 (AMAN), anti-GQ1b (Miller-Fisher), anti-GD1a.

### Other

MRI spine with Gd — anterior nerve root enhancement.

Stool Campylobacter PCR; serology HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, Zika/dengue if febrile.

**Rule out:** porphyria, lead, botulism, MG, polio, tick paralysis, transverse myelitis.

### Management

- Supportive — most important

ICU admission if rapidly progressive, bulbar dysfunction, autonomic, or FVC < 20 mL/kg.

Mechanical ventilation if FVC < 15 mL/kg, NIF > -30, hypoxia, or aspiration.

**DVT prophylaxis:** LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg SC OD) + IPC.

NG feeds if bulbar; bladder care; physiotherapy from day 1; pressure-area care.

**Pain:** gabapentin 300-1200 mg/d or carbamazepine; opioids if severe.

**Autonomic:** avoid suctioning-induced bradycardia; atropine standby; cautious BP management.

- Disease-modifying (start within 4 weeks of onset)

IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Preferred — easier, equally effective.

OR Plasmapheresis 5 sessions over 1-2 weeks (200-250 mL/kg total).

Both equally effective; DO NOT combine (no added benefit, increased cost).

**Steroids:** NOT INDICATED — multiple RCTs show no benefit; may delay recovery.

### 3. Rehab

Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychological support.

### Prognosis

80% walk unaided at 6 months; 60% full recovery at 1 year.

Mortality 5-10% (resp failure, autonomic, PE, sepsis).

**Poor prognosticators:** rapid progression < 7 d, axonal pattern, age > 60, ventilation needed, severe distal CMAP reduction.

Fig 4. GBS work-up and management.

**Source:** EAN/PNS GBS Guidelines 2023; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|227.note:
### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|228.note:
### Definition

Clinical state resulting from chronic exposure to glucocorticoid excess. 'Cushing's disease' specifically refers to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (the largest single endogenous cause).

### Causes

ACTH-dependent (80% of endogenous):

Cushing's disease (pituitary corticotroph adenoma) – 70%.

Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumours – 10% (small-cell lung carcinoma, bronchial carcinoid, medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, thymic carcinoid, pancreatic neuroendocrine).

Ectopic CRH secretion – rare.

ACTH-independent (20% of endogenous):

Adrenal adenoma.

Adrenal carcinoma.

Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (PPNAD).

Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia.

### Exogenous (commonest overall):

Prolonged use of glucocorticoids (oral, topical, inhaled, intra-articular, intranasal – especially in asthma, COPD, RA, SLE, transplant).

### Clinical features

### Characteristic (high specificity):

Centripetal obesity (truncal), moon facies, buffalo hump, supraclavicular fat pads.

Wide (>1 cm) violaceous striae on abdomen, thighs, breast.

Easy bruising, thin skin.

Proximal muscle weakness ('cushingoid myopathy') – cannot rise from squat.

### Less specific:

Hypertension (sodium retention, mineralocorticoid effect).

Glucose intolerance / overt diabetes mellitus.

Osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, avascular necrosis.

Hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea, erectile dysfunction (adrenal androgen excess).

Depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment, insomnia.

Infections (immune suppression), poor wound healing.

Hypokalaemic alkalosis (especially ectopic ACTH).

Hyperpigmentation (with high ACTH – ectopic and pituitary cause).

Cataract, peptic ulcer, VTE risk.

**Paediatric:** growth failure with weight gain is the cardinal presentation.

### Investigations (overview)

Screening (any 2 positive):

24-h urinary free cortisol (×2 samples) – >3× ULN diagnostic.

Late-night salivary cortisol (×2) – elevated.

Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test – cortisol >50 nmol/L at 8 a.m. = abnormal.

Low-dose dexamethasone (0.5 mg q6h × 48 h) suppression test.

### Localisation:

Plasma ACTH (low <5 = adrenal; normal/high = pituitary/ectopic).

High-dose dexamethasone (8 mg) – suppression supports pituitary.

Pituitary MRI; inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) if MRI ambiguous.

Adrenal CT/MRI if ACTH-independent.

CT chest/abdomen for ectopic source.

### Management (brief)

**Cushing's disease:** transsphenoidal pituitary adenoma resection (first-line); cabergoline / pasireotide / radiotherapy / bilateral adrenalectomy for failures.

**Adrenal cause:** adrenalectomy (laparoscopic).

**Ectopic ACTH:** treat tumour; adrenal-blocking drugs (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mitotane, etomidate) for control while awaiting surgery.

**Exogenous:** taper steroids slowly; never stop abruptly (risk addisonian crisis).

Fig 2. Cushing's syndrome – diagnostic workup algorithm.

GENERAL MEDICINE|229.note:
### Definition

Syndrome of chronic GH (and IGF-1) excess in adults after epiphyseal closure. Caused most commonly by a somatotroph pituitary adenoma (95%). 'Gigantism' is the same disease occurring before epiphyseal fusion in children.

### Etiology

Pituitary somatotroph adenoma (95%) – macroadenoma in >70%.

Ectopic GHRH (rare – pancreatic, bronchial neuroendocrine).

Ectopic GH (very rare – pancreatic islet, lymphoma).

Familial – MEN1, McCune-Albright, Carney complex, FIPA.

### Clinical features

### Tumour mass effects:

Headache, bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression), cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus invasion), hyperprolactinaemia (stalk effect).

Hypopituitarism (deficient TSH, ACTH, gonadotropins).

### GH/IGF-1 excess (somatic):

Facial – frontal bossing, prognathism (mandibular protrusion), interdental separation, macroglossia, prominent supraorbital ridges, coarse features, deepening voice (laryngeal soft-tissue enlargement).

Hands and feet – enlargement (need new ring/shoe size); spade-like hands; carpal tunnel syndrome.

Skin – thick, oily, hyperhidrosis, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans.

Cardiovascular – hypertension, biventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, valvular regurgitation, arrhythmias, heart failure (leading cause of death).

Respiratory – obstructive sleep apnoea (very common, ~60%).

Metabolic – insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia.

Endocrine – goitre, multinodular thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia, hypogonadism.

Musculoskeletal – arthropathy (hips, knees, spine), kyphosis, proximal myopathy.

GI – colonic polyps and increased colon cancer risk; visceromegaly (thyroid, heart, liver, kidney, prostate).

Hyperhidrosis, oily skin, body odour.

### Investigations

### Biochemistry:

Serum IGF-1 (age- and sex-matched) – best screening test; elevated.

OGTT with GH measurement – failure of GH suppression to <1 µg/L (or <0.4 with sensitive assay) at 2 h confirms acromegaly.

Prolactin (often co-secreted), TFT, cortisol, FSH/LH, testosterone/oestradiol for pituitary hormone reserve.

### Imaging:

MRI pituitary with contrast – macroadenoma in 70%.

Visual field testing.

### Complications screening:

ECG, echocardiogram.

Polysomnography (OSA).

HbA1c, fasting lipids.

Colonoscopy at diagnosis (then every 3–5 years).

DEXA, hand X-rays.

### Management

### Surgery (first-line):

Transsphenoidal adenomectomy – cures 80–90% of microadenomas and 40–60% of macroadenomas. Performed by expert pituitary surgeon.

Medical (if surgery fails or contraindicated):

Somatostatin receptor analogues (SRL) – octreotide LAR 20–30 mg IM monthly; lanreotide autogel 90–120 mg SC monthly; pasireotide for resistant disease.

Dopamine agonists – cabergoline 0.5–3.5 mg/week (especially if co-secreting prolactin, modest GH excess).

GH receptor antagonist – pegvisomant 10–30 mg SC daily; normalises IGF-1 but does not shrink tumour, so monitor MRI.

### Radiotherapy (third-line):

Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma knife) or fractionated; effect delayed years. Risk of hypopituitarism.

### Treat complications:

Cardiovascular optimisation, OSA – CPAP, diabetes – metformin/GLP-1 RA, surgical correction of jaw/dental.

### Prognosis

Pre-treatment mortality is double that of age-matched controls; normalising IGF-1 restores life expectancy. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; colon cancer surveillance important.

GENERAL MEDICINE|230.note:
### Definition

A clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation characterised by:

Haematuria (microscopic / macroscopic — 'cola-coloured' urine), with RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs on microscopy (glomerular bleeding).

Hypertension (sodium retention).

Mild–moderate oedema (peri-orbital characteristic; less than nephrotic).

Sub-nephrotic proteinuria (typically < 3.5 g/d).

Variable degree of acute kidney injury (oliguria, ↑ Cr).

**Pathological hallmark:** glomerular inflammation (mesangial / endothelial proliferation, crescents in severe / RPGN).

### Aetiology — Classified by Complement Status

### Low Complement (C3 ± C4 Reduced)

**Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN):** Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN): Group A β-haemolytic Strep pyogenes — pharyngitis (1–2 wk latency) or skin infection (3–6 wk latency). Low C3 normalises by 8 weeks. ASO ↑ (pharyngitis); Anti-DNase B ↑ (skin). Children most commonly. Self-limiting; > 95% recover.

**Lupus nephritis:** Lupus nephritis: SLE — ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm positive. Low C3 AND C4. ISN/RPS classes I–VI. Class IV (diffuse proliferative) — most aggressive; needs steroid + cyclophosphamide / MMF.

**Infective endocarditis:** Infective endocarditis: Subacute IE (Strep viridans). Low C3 + C4. Treat IE — GN resolves.

**MPGN (membranoproliferative):** MPGN (membranoproliferative): Type I — immune-complex (Hep C, lupus, monoclonal Ig). Type II (dense deposit disease) — C3 nephritic factor → persistent C3 activation. Low C3, normal or low C4.

**Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis:** Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis: Type II + III — associated with Hep C; mixed cryoglobulins. Low C4, sometimes low C3.

**Shunt nephritis:** Shunt nephritis: VP shunt infection — staph epidermidis. Low complement.

### Normal Complement

**IgA nephropathy:** IgA nephropathy: Commonest GN worldwide. Mucosal infection-synchronous haematuria (unlike PSGN's 2-week latency). Mesangial IgA deposits on biopsy. Galactose-deficient IgA1. Variable: 25% develop ESRD over 25 yr.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis):Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis): Children. Tetrad: palpable purpura (extensor surfaces, buttocks), arthralgia, abdominal pain, nephritis. Same biopsy as IgA nephropathy.

ANCA-associated vasculitis (Pauci-immune RPGN):ANCA-associated vasculitis (Pauci-immune RPGN): GPA (c-ANCA / PR3) — granulomas, upper airway. MPA (p-ANCA / MPO). EGPA (Churg-Strauss) — eosinophilia, asthma. Crescentic GN. Urgent — steroid + cyclophosphamide / rituximab + plasmapheresis (PEXIVAS — selected).

**Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture):** Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture): Anti-GBM antibody → linear IgG deposition on biopsy. Pulmonary haemorrhage + RPGN (M > F; HLA-DR15). Urgent plasmapheresis + steroids + cyclophosphamide.

**Alport syndrome:** Alport syndrome: Hereditary (X-linked > AR > AD). Type IV collagen defect. Haematuria + sensorineural deafness + ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus, retinal dots).

**Thin basement membrane disease:** Thin basement membrane disease: Benign familial haematuria. Normal renal function.

### Investigations

### Confirm Nephritic Syndrome

**Urinalysis:** dipstick haematuria (3+/4+), proteinuria (1–3+), RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs on phase-contrast microscopy.

24-h urine protein or spot PCR (typically < 3.5 g/d).

Serum creatinine, urea, electrolytes, eGFR.

BP measurement.

### Identify Cause

**Complement:** C3, C4, CH50.

**Autoantibodies:** ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA (c-ANCA = PR3, p-ANCA = MPO), anti-GBM, ASMA.

**Infection:** ASO titre, Anti-DNase B, throat / skin swab, HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV, blood cultures (IE).

Cryoglobulins (Hep C, autoimmune).

SPEP/UPEP, immunoglobulins (myeloma).

CXR + sinus CT (vasculitis), echo (IE).

### Renal Biopsy (gold standard)

**Indicated for:** AKI in nephritic, atypical features, persistent without explanation, RPGN (urgent biopsy), uncertain diagnosis.

**Light microscopy:** proliferative changes (mesangial / endothelial), crescents, necrosis, sclerosis.

**Immunofluorescence:** IgG / IgA / IgM / C3 / C1q deposits.

**Electron microscopy:** dense deposits, foot process effacement, GBM thickness.

### Management — General Principles

### Supportive (all)

Salt + fluid restriction (oedema, HTN).

**BP control:** target < 130/80; ACEi or ARB FIRST-LINE — reduces proteinuria and slows progression.

Loop diuretic (furosemide) for oedema.

Treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis.

RRT if severe AKI / refractory uraemia / fluid overload.

Vaccinations, infection prevention.

### Cause-Specific

**PSGN:** PSGN: Supportive (penicillin if active strep infection; usually self-limiting; diuretic + BP control). Do NOT use steroids.

**IgA nephropathy:** IgA nephropathy: ACEi/ARB. Persistent proteinuria > 1 g/d + GFR preserved → consider 6 months prednisolone (KDIGO 2021 — controversial after STOP-IgA, TESTING).

**Lupus nephritis Class III/IV:** Lupus nephritis Class III/IV: Induction: pulse methylprednisolone 500 mg × 3 d → prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d + IV cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus 500 mg q2wk × 6 doses) OR mycophenolate mofetil (2–3 g/d). Maintenance: low-dose pred + MMF (1–2 g/d) or AZA. Hydroxychloroquine for all.

**ANCA vasculitis (RPGN):** ANCA vasculitis (RPGN): Induction: methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg × 3 d → pred 1 mg/kg/d + IV cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg pulses q2wk) OR rituximab 375 mg/m² × 4 wk (RAVE, RITUXVAS). Plasmapheresis only if severe (Cr > 5.7 or pulmonary haemorrhage) — PEXIVAS 2020. Maintenance: AZA or rituximab. Avacopan (C5a inhibitor) — newer agent.

**Anti-GBM (Goodpasture):** Anti-GBM (Goodpasture): URGENT — plasmapheresis daily × 14 d + steroid + cyclophosphamide (3 mg/kg/d PO). Stop plasmapheresis when anti-GBM negative.

**Cryoglobulinaemia:** Cryoglobulinaemia: Treat underlying (Hep C with DAA — see Q26 GI). Severe → steroid + cyclophosphamide / rituximab.

Infective endocarditis-related GN:Infective endocarditis-related GN: Treat IE with prolonged IV antibiotics.

Fig 3. Nephritic syndrome — complement-guided workup.

### Complications

Hypertensive emergency.

Pulmonary oedema (volume overload).

Progressive renal failure (RPGN — Cr doubles in days/weeks).

Hypertensive encephalopathy, seizures.

Cardiac failure.

### Prognosis

PSGN — excellent (> 95% recover in children); IgA — variable; lupus nephritis with treatment 80% 10-yr renal survival; ANCA / anti-GBM — early treatment crucial; delayed RPGN treatment → ESRD. Renal biopsy result and percentage crescents predict outcome.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.367; KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|231.note:
First-line drugs and hepatotoxicity

**Isoniazid (H):** Hepatotoxic – stop if ALT >5× ULN (or >3× with symptoms).

**Pyrazinamide (Z):** Most hepatotoxic of the first-line drugs; dose-dependent.

**Rifampicin (R):** Hepatotoxic; also causes orange discoloration of secretions.

**Ethambutol (E):** Not hepatotoxic; main risks – optic neuritis (visual acuity), peripheral neuropathy.

Drugs to avoid in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure: H, R, Z.

Modified regimen for hepatitis / hepatic impairment (NTEP, WHO 2024)

If ALT >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN without – stop all hepatotoxic ATT.

Continue with non-hepatotoxic combination: ethambutol + streptomycin/levofloxacin (+ rifampicin if liver enzymes recovering; reintroduce H or Z sequentially).

**Severe hepatitis:** 2 SH(streptomycin + isoniazid)E + 6 HE OR 9–12 RE + levofloxacin / linezolid based regimen.

**Once LFTs return to normal:** gradually reintroduce R first, then H, last Z (if needed).

Other antimicrobials notable for hepatotoxicity in ATT context

Para-amino salicylic acid (PAS) – hepatotoxic.

Ethionamide / prothionamide – hepatotoxic.

Bedaquiline – QT prolongation, mild LFT rise.

Linezolid – BM suppression, neuropathy; mild hepatic.

Monitor LFTs weekly during reintroduction; counsel patient about alcohol cessation, paracetamol limits, no herbal supplements.
