GENERAL MEDICINE|232.note:
### Definition

Needle puncture of the lumbar subarachnoid space (L3-L4 or L4-L5 — below conus at L1-L2 in adults) to obtain CSF for diagnosis OR therapy.

### Indications

### Diagnostic

Suspected meningitis (bacterial, viral, TB, fungal).

Suspected SAH with negative CT (after 6 h ideally).

Demyelinating disease (MS, NMO, ADEM) — oligoclonal bands, IgG index.

GBS / CIDP — albumino-cytological dissociation.

Neoplastic meningitis — cytology.

CNS infections (HSV PCR, NMDA-R Ab, neurocysticercosis).

Paraneoplastic / autoimmune encephalitis.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension — measure opening pressure.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus — large-volume LP for clinical response.

### Therapeutic

Repeated LP in IIH (until acetazolamide effective).

Intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate, cytarabine for ALL/lymphoma).

Intrathecal antibiotics (vancomycin, gentamicin in select cases).

Spinal anaesthesia.

CSF removal in communicating hydrocephalus (occasional).

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Raised ICP with mass effect / focal signs (risk of herniation).

Infection at puncture site.

**Severe bleeding diathesis:** platelets < 50,000, INR > 1.5, on therapeutic anticoagulation.

### Relative

Spinal cord lesion above LP site.

Uncooperative patient.

Lumbar spinal deformity.

### When to do CT BEFORE LP (IDSA criteria)

Immunocompromised state (HIV, transplant, immunosuppressants).

History of CNS disease (mass, stroke, focal infection).

New-onset seizure within 1 week.

Papilloedema.

Abnormal level of consciousness (GCS < 10).

Focal neurological deficit.

Age > 60.

### Procedure (in brief)

**Position:** lateral decubitus, fetal position (knees-to-chest) OR sitting leaning forward.

**Site:** L3-L4 or L4-L5 (line joining posterior superior iliac crests = L4 — Tuffier's line).

Asepsis, local anaesthesia (1-2% lidocaine).

22 G atraumatic spinal needle (Sprotte / Whitacre) — reduces post-LP headache by 50%.

Bevel parallel to longitudinal dural fibres (if cutting needle).

Measure opening pressure (only in lateral decubitus): normal 7-18 cm H₂O.

**Collect 3-4 tubes:** cell count (T1), biochemistry (T2), microbiology (T3), special (cytology/PCR/Ab — T4).

Take 8-12 mL total (more for cytology, PCR).

Remove needle in same plane.

**Post-LP:** supine 1 h with hydration (reduces headache; insufficient evidence but practiced).

### Normal CSF values

### Complications

Post-LP headache (10-30%) — orthostatic, frontal/occipital, due to CSF leak; Rx caffeine, fluids, NSAIDs, bed rest; epidural blood patch if persistent > 72 h.

Cerebral herniation if raised ICP — devastating.

Infection (meningitis, epidural abscess) — rare.

Spinal/epidural haematoma — with bleeding diathesis.

Backache, transient nerve root pain.

Traumatic tap — bloody CSF; differentiate from true SAH by xanthochromia (centrifuge) and clearing in successive tubes.

### Traumatic tap vs SAH

**Source:** IDSA 2017; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|233.note:
### Definition

Excretion of > 150 mg protein per day in adults (> 4 mg/m²/h in children). Specific cut-offs:

**Microalbuminuria:** 30–300 mg/d (ACR 30–300 mg/g) — earliest marker of glomerular damage.

Macroalbuminuria / overt proteinuria: > 300 mg/d (ACR > 300 mg/g).

**Nephrotic-range proteinuria:** > 3.5 g/d (PCR > 3500 mg/g).

**Composition:** 60% albumin, 30% serum globulins, 10% Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein.

### Pathogenetic Classification

- Glomerular Proteinuria (commonest, > 80%)

Damage to glomerular filtration barrier (capillary endothelium, GBM, podocyte foot processes). Predominantly albumin (mid-molecular wt). Heavy proteinuria (nephrotic range) is virtually always glomerular.

**Primary GN:** MCD, FSGS, membranous, IgA nephropathy, MPGN.

**Secondary GN:** diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, lupus nephritis, amyloidosis, HBV/HCV/HIV-related, drug-induced (NSAIDs, gold).

### 2. Tubular Proteinuria

Defective tubular reabsorption of low MW proteins (β2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein, α1-microglobulin). Total < 2 g/d. Albumin minimal.

Acute / chronic interstitial nephritis (NSAIDs, PPIs, antibiotics).

Fanconi syndrome (Wilson, cystinosis, multiple myeloma — light chains damage tubules, tenofovir, aminoglycosides).

Heavy metal toxicity (Cd, Pb, Hg).

Sickle cell disease.

Polycystic kidney disease.

### 3. Overflow Proteinuria

Increased plasma concentration of LMW proteins exceeds tubular reabsorption capacity.

Multiple myeloma — Bence-Jones (free light chains; dipstick NEGATIVE — use SSA).

Intravascular haemolysis — haemoglobinuria.

Rhabdomyolysis — myoglobinuria.

Acute monocytic leukaemia — lysozyme.

### 4. Post-renal / Pseudoproteinuria

UTI (pyuria gives positive dipstick).

Haematuria — RBC lysis releases protein.

Seminal fluid contamination.

Vaginal discharge contamination.

### Causes by Persistence

Transient (benign — no investigation needed)

Fever (febrile proteinuria).

Strenuous exercise.

Cold exposure.

Severe emotional stress / vasoconstriction.

Acute illness, dehydration.

### Orthostatic / Postural Proteinuria

Common in adolescents (3–5%) and tall thin individuals.

Proteinuria when upright; absent on overnight supine sample.

**Diagnose:** split urine collection — first morning void after waking (supine — should be normal); day-time collection (upright — abnormal).

Excellent prognosis; no progression. Usually resolves.

Persistent (always pathological — investigate)

Glomerular disease, tubular disease, overflow — as above.

### Approach / Workup

### Step 1 — Quantify

Dipstick (qualitative — 1+ to 4+, false positive in alkaline urine, false negative in light-chain proteinuria).

Spot UPCR or UACR.

Confirm with 2nd sample (rule out transient).

24-h urine protein for accurate quantification (if needed).

### Step 2 — Characterise

**Urinalysis:** dipstick haematuria + microscopy (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs → glomerular).

Urinary protein electrophoresis + immunofixation (suspect myeloma — Bence-Jones).

SSA (sulphosalicylic acid) test (detects total protein incl. light chains).

Selectivity index (research).

### Step 3 — Identify Cause

Serum creatinine, eGFR, urea, electrolytes, glucose, HbA1c.

BP measurement.

Albumin, lipid profile (if nephrotic range).

ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement, ANCA — if clinical concern.

HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV.

Anti-PLA2R — if membranous suspected.

SPEP, UPEP, IFE, free light chains — > 40 yr or atypical features.

USG renal — size, structure.

Renal biopsy — > 1 g/d persistent, especially with HTN / impaired GFR / haematuria, OR nephrotic range without obvious cause.

### Step 4 — Treat

Cause-specific (see relevant Qs).

ACEi / ARB FIRST-LINE — reduces proteinuria 30–50%, slows progression in CKD.

SGLT2i — proteinuric CKD (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY).

BP target < 130/80; target proteinuria < 1 g/d.

Low salt, weight loss, smoking cessation.

Treat underlying (DM, SLE, infection).

### When to Refer Nephrology

Persistent proteinuria > 1 g/d.

Nephrotic syndrome.

Proteinuria + haematuria or active sediment.

Proteinuria + ↑ Cr / declining GFR.

Proteinuria + HTN difficult to control.

Atypical features — young patient, family history, systemic disease.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.355; KDIGO CKD 2012; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|234.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Classification by mechanism

Biguanides — Metformin.

Sulfonylureas (insulin secretagogues) — Glibenclamide, glipizide, gliclazide, glimepiride.

Meglitinides — Repaglinide, nateglinide.

Thiazolidinediones (insulin sensitisers) — Pioglitazone.

α-Glucosidase inhibitors — Acarbose, voglibose, miglitol.

DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) — Sitagliptin, vildagliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin, teneligliptin.

SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) — Empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (injectable, except oral semaglutide) — Liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide, semaglutide; tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1).

Amylin analogue — Pramlintide (injectable).

Bile-acid sequestrant — Colesevelam (modest effect).

Dopamine-2 agonist — Bromocriptine QR.

### Key pharmacology

**Metformin:** ↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑ peripheral insulin sensitivity. First-line for T2DM. SE: GI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (rare). CI: eGFR <30. Dose 500–2000 mg/day.

**Sulfonylureas:** Close KATP channels in β-cells → insulin release. Effective and cheap but cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Avoid in renal failure.

**Pioglitazone:** PPARγ agonist → ↑ insulin sensitivity. SE: weight gain, fluid retention, HF, fractures, bladder cancer risk. Useful in NAFLD.

**α-Glucosidase inhibitors:** Inhibit intestinal carbohydrate absorption. SE: flatulence, diarrhoea. Take with first bite of meal.

**DPP-4 inhibitors:** Inhibit DPP-4 → ↑ GLP-1/GIP → glucose-dependent insulin release. Weight neutral, no hypoglycaemia. Safe in CKD (linagliptin needs no dose adjustment).

**SGLT2 inhibitors:** Inhibit SGLT2 in proximal tubule → glycosuria. ↓ Cardiovascular events, ↓ HF hospitalisation, ↓ CKD progression. SE: GU infection, euglycaemic DKA, Fournier gangrene, volume depletion. Indian favoured.

**GLP-1 RA:** Activate GLP-1 receptor → insulin secretion, glucagon suppression, delayed gastric emptying, satiety. Weight loss, CVD and renal benefit. Injectable (except oral semaglutide). SE: nausea, pancreatitis risk, gallstones.

### Choice in Indian T2DM (RSSDI 2024)

**Step 1:** Metformin + lifestyle.

Add SGLT2i if ASCVD / HF / CKD; add GLP-1 RA if ASCVD / weight loss desired; add DPP-4i / SU / pioglitazone otherwise.

Insulin when HbA1c >9% / symptomatic / contraindications to oral.

Fig 4. Type 2 DM stepwise management (RSSDI 2024 / ADA Standards of Care 2024).

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

### Definition

Loss of oral mucosal continuity exposing underlying connective tissue. May be acute (< 2 wk), subacute (2–6 wk), or chronic (> 6 wk). Persistent ulcers > 3 weeks require malignancy exclusion.

### Etiology

### 1. Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis (RAS) — commonest (20%)

### 2. Infections

**Viral:** HSV-1 (primary gingivostomatitis, recurrent herpes labialis), VZV (chickenpox/shingles), HFMD (Coxsackie A16), HIV (multiple persistent), CMV (immunocompromised).

**Bacterial:** syphilis (chancre, mucous patches, gumma), TB (chronic indurated ulcer with undermined edges — usually dorsum of tongue), Vincent's angina (necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis — Borrelia + fusobacterium).

**Fungal:** candidiasis (white plaques, erythematous), histoplasmosis, mucormycosis (uncontrolled DM, COVID-19-associated CAM in India).

### 3. Systemic Diseases

Crohn's disease (cobblestone mucosa, deep linear ulcers).

Coeliac disease (apthous ulcers, glossitis, dental enamel defects).

Behçet's disease — recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy (>3 episodes/yr).

PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) — paeds.

Reiter's syndrome (oral + genital ulcers + arthritis + conjunctivitis).

SLE — palatal ulcers (one of ACR criteria); painless typically.

Pemphigus vulgaris — flaccid bullae → erosions; Nikolsky+.

Mucous membrane pemphigoid — subepithelial, scarring; ocular involvement common.

Lichen planus — Wickham's striae, erosive form painful; pre-malignant.

Erythema multiforme major / SJS-TEN — drug or HSV-triggered, target lesions, conjunctivitis.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome — mucocutaneous with skin involvement.

### 4. Nutritional Deficiencies

B12 (Hunter's glossitis, atrophic), folate, iron (angular cheilitis, glossitis, koilonychia), vitamin C (scurvy — gingival bleeding, swollen gums).

Zinc deficiency.

### 5. Haematological

Neutropenia / agranulocytosis (chemo, drugs — clozapine, methimazole), acute leukaemia, cyclic neutropenia.

### 6. Drugs

Methotrexate, NSAIDs, β-blockers (atenolol), nicorandil (typically painful, large), sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor), bisphosphonates (ONJ — osteonecrosis of jaw).

### 7. Malignancy

**Indian context:** Squamous cell carcinoma (commonest oral malignancy in India — tobacco, areca nut, alcohol). Non-healing > 3 wk ulcer, induration, raised everted edges → biopsy mandatory.

**Pre-malignant lesions:** leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut chewing — Indian endemic), lichen planus.

### 8. Trauma

Mechanical (dental, ill-fitting denture, tongue bite), thermal, chemical (aspirin burn).

### Clinical Approach

**Duration:** acute (HSV, RAS, trauma), chronic (TB, malignancy, autoimmune, drugs).

**Single vs multiple:** single chronic → malignancy/TB; multiple recurrent → RAS, Behçet's, IBD.

Painful (most ulcers) vs painless (syphilis, SLE, TB tongue, malignancy).

Associated features — genital ulcer, eye, GI, skin, fever.

### Investigations

**Blood:** CBC, ESR/CRP, ferritin, B12/folate, HIV serology, fasting glucose, TSH.

**If suspected systemic:** tTG (coeliac), ANA, ANCA, IgA/IgG (Behçet's), VDRL.

Biopsy if non-healing > 3 wk, atypical, suspected malignancy/lichen planus.

Swab for HSV PCR, candida (KOH), syphilis serology (TPHA, VDRL).

### Management

### General

Identify and treat underlying cause.

**Pain relief:** paracetamol, NSAIDs (avoid if drug-induced).

Topical anaesthetic (lignocaine 2% viscous gel) for severe pain.

Antiseptic mouthwash — chlorhexidine 0.2% rinse BD, povidone iodine.

Avoid irritants (spicy, hot, alcohol-containing mouthwash).

### RAS-Specific

**Topical corticosteroids:** triamcinolone 0.1% in adhesive base (Kenalog in Orabase), dexamethasone elixir 0.5 mg/5 ml rinse-and-spit QID.

Tetracycline mouthwash (250 mg in 5 ml water, hold 2 min, spit QID).

**Severe/refractory:** systemic prednisolone 30–60 mg/d short course, colchicine 0.5 mg BD-TDS, thalidomide (severe HIV-related), dapsone, apremilast.

**Address triggers:** stress, food (chocolate, nuts, citrus), smoking cessation.

### Specific Causes

### Prognosis

Variable. RAS — recurrent, lifelong but harmless. Malignancy → 5-yr survival depends on stage. Indian context: oral SCC accounts for ~ 30% of all cancers in men.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; Davidson Ch.21 (mucocutaneous); Indian oral cancer guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|235.note:
### Definition

Total serum Ca < 8.5 mg/dL (< 2.12 mmol/L) — adjusted for albumin.

Ionised Ca < 1.1 mmol/L (< 4.4 mg/dL) — physiologically active.

**Albumin-correction formula:** Corrected Ca = total Ca + 0.8 × (4 – serum albumin in g/dL).

**Severe:** total Ca < 7.5 mg/dL or symptomatic.

### Aetiology

### 1. PTH-Related

**Hypoparathyroidism:** Hypoparathyroidism: Surgical (post-thyroidectomy / parathyroidectomy — commonest, transient or permanent), autoimmune (APS-1), congenital (DiGeorge — 22q11.2), Wilson's, haemochromatosis, thalassaemia (iron deposition).

**Pseudohypoparathyroidism:** Pseudohypoparathyroidism: End-organ resistance to PTH (Type 1a — Albright osteodystrophy: short stature, round face, short 4th/5th metacarpal, obesity, hypocalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia, raised PTH).

**Hypomagnesaemia:** Hypomagnesaemia: Functional hypoparathyroidism — Mg required for PTH secretion + action. Common cause.

### 2. Vitamin D Related

Vitamin D deficiency / insufficiency (very common in India — sun avoidance, veiling, dark skin, malabsorption, elderly).

Liver disease (impaired 25-hydroxylation).

CKD (impaired 1α-hydroxylation, ↓ active 1,25-(OH)₂D).

Vitamin D-dependent rickets (Type 1 — 1α-hydroxylase deficiency; Type 2 — receptor mutation).

Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarbitone) — accelerate Vit D catabolism.

### 3. Sequestration / Loss

Acute pancreatitis (saponification — Ca in fat necrosis).

Rhabdomyolysis (Ca deposition in damaged muscle).

Tumour lysis (Ca deposition with phosphate).

Citrate (massive blood transfusion — citrate binds Ca; > 10 units).

Lactic acidosis (Ca chelation).

Phosphate (large IV phosphate load).

Hungry bone syndrome (post-parathyroidectomy — rapid bone mineralisation).

### 4. Other

Sepsis.

**Drugs:** bisphosphonates, denosumab, foscarnet, calcitonin, fluoride.

Severe hyperphosphataemia (CKD, tumour lysis).

Osteoblastic metastases (prostate, breast).

### Clinical Features

Neuromuscular Excitability (cardinal — increased excitability)

Paraesthesia — circumoral, fingertips, toes.

Cramps, muscle spasm, twitches.

TETANY — carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, bronchospasm.

Trousseau's sign — carpal spasm after BP cuff inflation 20 mm above SBP × 3 min.

Chvostek's sign — facial muscle twitching on tapping facial nerve 2 cm anterior to ear lobe.

Seizures — generalised tonic-clonic.

Confusion, anxiety, depression, psychosis.

### Cardiac

Long QT (corrected).

Torsades de pointes.

Hypotension, decreased contractility, refractory heart failure.

### Chronic Hypocalcaemia

Cataracts (subcapsular).

Dry skin, brittle nails, hair loss.

Calcification of basal ganglia (Fahr's), extrapyramidal features.

Dental hypoplasia, enamel defects.

Papilloedema (raised ICP).

### Investigations

Total Ca + albumin → corrected Ca; ionised Ca (preferred if available).

Phosphate (high in hypoparathyroidism / CKD; low in vit D deficiency / Fanconi).

Magnesium (essential — replace first if low).

PTH (low / inappropriately normal in hypoparathyroidism; high in vit D deficiency, CKD).

25-OH vitamin D (< 20 ng/ml = deficiency; < 30 = insufficiency).

Creatinine, eGFR (CKD), urea.

Amylase/lipase (pancreatitis), CK (rhabdomyolysis), uric acid (tumour lysis).

ECG — QT interval.

ALP — high in osteomalacia / rickets.

Urinary Ca — to assess.

**Targeted:** ANA, autoimmune polyendocrine panel; iron studies; 1,25-(OH)₂D.

### Management

### Acute / Symptomatic (Tetany, Seizures, Laryngospasm, Long QT)

Calcium gluconate 10% — 10 ml IV over 10 min (slow!):Calcium gluconate 10% — 10 ml IV over 10 min (slow!): Provides 90 mg elemental Ca. Repeat once if needed. Then start infusion.

**Calcium gluconate infusion:** Calcium gluconate infusion: Mix 100 ml 10% Ca gluconate (= 900 mg elemental Ca) in 1 L 5% dextrose / NS, infuse at 50–100 ml/h. Adjust to maintain Ca > 7.0–8.0. Recheck Ca every 4–6 h.

**CAUTION:** CAUTION: Ca chloride causes tissue necrosis on extravasation — use Ca gluconate via peripheral line. Use central line for Ca chloride. Slow injection (rapid → bradycardia, asystole).

**Magnesium:** Magnesium: REPLACE FIRST if low — 2 g MgSO₄ IV over 15 min, then 10 g/24 h. Hypocalcaemia refractory to Ca until Mg corrected.

### Treat Underlying Cause

Phosphate restriction in tumour lysis / CKD.

Stop bisphosphonates / denosumab.

Treat sepsis, pancreatitis.

### Chronic / Maintenance

**Oral elemental calcium:** Oral elemental calcium: 1–3 g/d in divided doses. Ca carbonate (40% elemental) with meals; Ca citrate if PPI/achlorhydria. Tab Shelcal 500 mg BD-TDS.

**Active vitamin D:** Active vitamin D: Calcitriol 0.25–1 µg/d PO (1,25-(OH)₂D — bypasses renal hydroxylation; essential in CKD and hypoparathyroidism). Alfacalcidol 0.5–1 µg/d alternative.

**Plain vitamin D:** Plain vitamin D: Cholecalciferol 60,000 IU/wk × 8 wk → 60,000 IU/month (Indian schedule for deficiency). Or ergocalciferol.

**Thiazide diuretic:** Thiazide diuretic: Adjunct in hypoparathyroidism — reduces urinary Ca loss, lower oral Ca need.

**Recombinant PTH:** Recombinant PTH: Teriparatide (rPTH 1-34) or Natpara — selected refractory hypoparathyroidism.

**Monitor:** Monitor: Ca, phosphate, Mg, Cr, urinary Ca — every 1–3 mo. Aim Ca at lower end of normal (8.0–9.0) to avoid hypercalciuria.

Fig 7. Hypocalcaemia — workup and stepwise management.

### Complications of Treatment

Hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria → nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis.

Tissue necrosis from extravasated Ca chloride.

Long-term Ca + Vit D → arterial calcification (CKD).

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.385; Endocrine Society Hypoparathyroidism 2016; ICMR Vit D guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|236.note:
### Definition

Alcohol Use Disorder (DSM-5) is a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment / distress, manifested by ≥2 of 11 criteria in a 12-month period (replacing DSM-IV abuse + dependence). ICD-10 retains alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria) and harmful use. India has the largest population of male alcohol users in Asia; NMHS 2016 estimates prevalence of any alcohol-use disorder at 4.6% in adults (9% in men).

Hazards of alcohol (Boloor A365)

### Neurological

Acute — intoxication, blackouts, traffic accidents, traumatic brain injury, alcohol-induced psychotic disorder.

Withdrawal — tremor, seizures, delirium tremens (see below).

Chronic — Wernicke encephalopathy / Korsakoff psychosis, cerebellar degeneration (truncal ataxia, gait), peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor, painful), optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia), central pontine myelinolysis (with rapid sodium correction), Marchiafava–Bignami disease (corpus callosum demyelination), alcohol-related dementia.

### Gastrointestinal / hepatic

Acute / chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome.

Pancreatitis — acute and chronic (alcohol is the #1 cause of chronic pancreatitis in India after gallstones).

Alcoholic liver disease — fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >32 → steroids/pentoxifylline) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Oesophageal varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal / hepatopulmonary syndromes.

Malabsorption — folate, thiamine, B6, B12, Mg, Zn.

### Cardiovascular

Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcoholic), holiday heart (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke, sudden cardiac death.

### Haematological

Macrocytic anaemia (folate deficiency, direct marrow toxicity), megaloblastic, sideroblastic, haemolysis (Zieve syndrome with hepatitis + hyperlipidaemia), thrombocytopenia, leucopenia.

### Endocrine / metabolic

Hypoglycaemia (gluconeogenesis blocked), ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia / gout, hyperlipidaemia, pseudo-Cushing's.

Hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, infertility, erectile dysfunction.

### Cancer (Group I carcinogen — IARC)

Oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver (HCC), breast, colorectum.

### Obstetric

Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder — microcephaly, growth retardation, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, intellectual disability.

Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm birth.

### Psychiatric

Depression, anxiety, suicide (alcohol present in ~40% of completed suicides in India), insomnia.

Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, pathological jealousy (Othello syndrome).

### Social

Domestic violence, marital breakdown, child neglect, occupational accidents, road traffic accidents, financial ruin, legal issues.

Diagnosis — DSM-5 AUD criteria (≥2 of 11 in 12 months)

**Severity:** 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥6 severe.

Larger amounts / longer than intended.

Persistent desire / unsuccessful attempts to cut down.

Great time spent obtaining / using / recovering.

Craving.

Failure to fulfil role obligations.

Continued use despite social / interpersonal problems.

Important activities given up.

Use in physically hazardous situations.

Continued use despite physical / psychological problems.

Tolerance.

Withdrawal.

ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria — ≥3 of 6 in past year)

Strong desire / compulsion to drink.

Impaired control over use (onset, level, termination).

Withdrawal state on abstinence.

Tolerance.

Neglect of alternative interests.

Persistence despite clearly harmful consequences.

### Screening

**CAGE:** Cut down, Annoyed by criticism, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 = significant.

**AUDIT (WHO, 10 items):** 0–7 low risk, 8–15 hazardous, 16–19 harmful, ≥20 dependence.

AUDIT-C — 3-item screening tool.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (Boloor A373 ★2026)

Figure 6. Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal triage by CIWA-Ar, thiamine-first inpatient protocol, methanol-poisoning pathway and maintenance pharmacotherapy.

Time course (after last drink)

**6–12 h:** Minor withdrawal — tremor, anxiety, nausea, sweating, palpitations, insomnia, headache.

**12–24 h:** Alcoholic hallucinosis — visual / tactile / auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium and orientation (key DDx from DT).

**24–48 h:** Withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic, brief, 1–6 episodes; usually self-limited; 3% progress to status.

**48–96 h (peak 72 h):** Delirium tremens (DT) — clouded sensorium, disorientation, agitation, fluctuating consciousness, fever, autonomic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis), vivid visual / tactile (formication — 'bugs crawling') hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% untreated; 1–2% with modern care.

Risk stratification — CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised)

10 items, scored 0–7 each (orientation 0–4); total 0–67.

<8 — mild, no intervention.

8–15 — moderate, BZD treatment.

16–20 — severe.

>20 — very severe, ICU.

Management of withdrawal — Indian protocol (NIMHANS / AIIMS de-addiction)

**Inpatient if:** CIWA-Ar ≥10, history of DT / withdrawal seizures, severe medical / psychiatric comorbidity, poor support.

Thiamine FIRST, before any glucose (Wernicke prevention) — 100 mg IV/IM TDS × 3 days, then 100 mg PO OD long-term.

Wernicke / Korsakoff treatment dose: thiamine 500 mg IV TDS × 2–3 days → 250 mg IV/IM daily × 3–5 days → 100 mg PO long-term. Also IV Mg replacement (thiamine requires Mg cofactor).

**Benzodiazepines — first-line:** chlordiazepoxide 25–50 mg PO q4–6h symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar guided), tapered over 5–7 days. Diazepam 10–20 mg PO/IV q1–2h for severe.

Lorazepam preferred in hepatic dysfunction, elderly (no active metabolites): 2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h.

Phenobarbital — for refractory / BZD-resistant DT.

IV fluids (NS + 5%D), electrolyte correction — Mg 1–2 g IV q12h, K, PO4.

Multivitamin, folate 5 mg/d.

AVOID antipsychotics as monotherapy (↓ seizure threshold); use only haloperidol low dose if psychosis / agitation persists despite adequate BZD.

AVOID alcohol substitution.

Monitor vital signs q1–2h initially; CIWA-Ar q1–4h.

Treat fever, sepsis, pneumonia (high risk in DT), dehydration, rhabdomyolysis.

### Withdrawal seizures

**Treat acute seizure:** IV lorazepam 2–4 mg or diazepam 10 mg.

**Prevention:** adequate BZD coverage during detox.

Long-term anti-epileptics not needed unless underlying epilepsy.

Maintenance — relapse prevention (anti-craving)

**Naltrexone:** 50 mg PO OD (or 380 mg IM monthly). μ-opioid antagonist; ↓ craving and pleasure of drinking (COMBINE trial). Avoid in liver failure, opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); LFT monitoring.

**Acamprosate:** 666 mg PO TDS (2 g/d in <60 kg). NMDA modulator; ↓ relapse rate (PROJECT MATCH). Safe in liver disease; needs adequate renal function.

**Disulfiram:** 250 mg PO OD (max 500 mg). Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor; causes aversive reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, hypotension) on alcohol ingestion. Supervised dosing (family member). Avoid in CAD, severe psychiatric illness, pregnancy, peripheral neuropathy. Warn re: hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrups, perfumes).

Baclofen (off-label, useful in liver disease): 10–30 mg TDS; GABA-B agonist; reduces craving especially in cirrhotics where naltrexone and disulfiram unsafe (ANRS-BACLOVILLE).

**Topiramate, gabapentin:** Off-label adjuncts.

Psychosocial interventions (cornerstone — often dominate outcome)

Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MI / MET) — stage-of-change-based.

CBT — relapse prevention, coping skills.

12-step facilitation / Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) — Indian chapters widespread.

Family therapy, community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT).

Residential rehabilitation for severe / relapsing.

Treat comorbid depression / anxiety / PTSD.

Indian de-addiction infrastructure: AIIMS NDDTC, NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine, Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP — MoHFW), state-level Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs).

Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning — Boloor A367

Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in adulterated illicit liquor ('hooch'), industrial solvents, anti-freeze, windshield-washer fluid and formalin. Toxic dose ~10 ml; fatal 30 ml.

### Toxicokinetics

Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → FORMALDEHYDE → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → FORMIC ACID — the principal toxin (causes optic neuritis, metabolic acidosis).

### Clinical features

Latent period 12–24 h (longer if co-ingested ethanol).

Phase 1 — CNS depression (mild intoxication / inebriation).

Phase 2 (12–24 h) — N/V, abdominal pain, headache, vertigo.

Phase 3 — visual disturbance ('snowstorm', blurring, blindness), optic disc hyperaemia / oedema → permanent blindness.

Phase 4 — severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) with ↑ osmolar gap, Kussmaul respiration, seizures, coma, parkinsonism (putaminal necrosis), death.

### Investigations

ABG — severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2, HCO3 <10).

Anion gap — high (>20).

Osmolar gap — high (>10 mOsm/kg) early, falls as methanol is metabolised.

Serum methanol level — confirmatory (toxic >20 mg/dL; severe >50).

Fundus — optic disc hyperaemia / oedema.

MRI brain — putaminal haemorrhage / necrosis (classic).

### Management

ABC, IV access, gastric lavage (if <1 h), activated charcoal NOT effective (poorly adsorbed).

Block ADH (prevent toxic metabolite formation):

- FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole) — drug of choice if available; 15 mg/kg IV load → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses → 15 mg/kg q12h thereafter (induces own metabolism). Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL + acidosis resolved + asymptomatic.

- ETHANOL (alternative if no fomepizole) — IV loading 10 ml/kg of 10% ethanol over 30 min → 1.5 ml/kg/h infusion. Target blood ethanol 100 mg/dL. Cheaper and widely available in India.

FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1 mg/kg IV q4–6h (max 50 mg) × 6 doses — accelerates formate metabolism. Folic acid acceptable if folinic unavailable.

Correct acidosis — IV sodium bicarbonate to keep pH >7.2.

HAEMODIALYSIS — definitive removal of methanol and formate. Indications: serum methanol ≥50 mg/dL, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), visual / mental status changes, electrolyte imbalance refractory, renal failure.

Supportive — ICU, mechanical ventilation, treat seizures.

Complications of alcohol use (summary)

Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis (irreversible amnesia, confabulation).

Delirium tremens — mortality 5–15% untreated.

Cirrhosis, HCC, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy.

Suicide, accidental injuries, road traffic accidents.

Family disruption, economic loss, occupational impairment.

### Prognosis

Without treatment — progressive decline, premature mortality.

With comprehensive treatment (pharmacotherapy + psychosocial) — 30–50% achieve sustained remission at 1 year.

Better with stable social support, employment, no comorbid psychiatric illness, motivation for change.

Worse with antisocial personality, depression / suicide history, polysubstance use.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18 + Ch.16 (toxicology); Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Alcohol Use Disorders; NIMHANS / AIIMS NDDTC protocols; COMBINE 2006; PROJECT MATCH; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology — methanol/fomepizole; DSM-5; ICD-10/11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|237.note:
### Definition

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a primary mood disorder characterised by pervasive low mood and/or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks with associated biological and cognitive symptoms, causing significant functional impairment, in the absence of a manic / hypomanic episode and not explained by substance or other medical cause.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~12–17% (Indian National Mental Health Survey 2016 reports current prevalence 2.7%, lifetime 5.2%).

**F:** M ≈ 2:1 from menarche to menopause; equal before puberty and after menopause.

Peak onset 20–40 y; can occur at any age including childhood and old age.

Heritability ~40%; 2–4× risk in first-degree relatives.

### Etiology

**Biological:** monoamine deficiency (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine); HPA-axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol, blunted dexamethasone suppression); ↓ BDNF; sleep architecture changes (↓ REM latency, ↑ REM density); cytokine activation (IL-6, TNF-α).

**Genetic:** serotonin transporter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR short allele), BDNF Val66Met.

**Psychosocial:** childhood adversity, recent life events (loss, separation, financial), chronic stress, low social support.

**Medical / drug-induced:** hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, post-stroke, MS, malignancy, vit B12 deficiency, OSA; drugs — steroids, β-blockers (propranolol), interferon, isotretinoin, vigabatrin, levetiracetam, clonidine, methyldopa, OCP, reserpine, varenicline.

### Clinical features (DSM-5 / ICD-10)

Core (≥1 must be present)

Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, ≥2 weeks.

Markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) in almost all activities.

Additional (need ≥4 more to make 5/9 total)

Significant weight loss/gain (>5% in a month) or appetite change.

Insomnia (early-morning awakening classic) or hypersomnia.

Psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable).

Fatigue / loss of energy.

Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

Diminished concentration; indecisiveness.

Recurrent thoughts of death / suicidal ideation / suicide attempt.

Biological ('somatic') features in severe / melancholic depression

Early-morning awakening (≥2 h before usual).

Diurnal variation — mood worst in the morning.

Significant weight loss, loss of libido, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt.

### Severity grading (ICD-10 / DSM-5)

**Mild:** 5 symptoms (≥1 core); mild functional impairment.

**Moderate:** 6–7 symptoms; moderate functional impairment.

**Severe (without psychosis):** ≥8 symptoms; marked impairment ± suicidal intent.

**Severe with psychotic features:** Mood-congruent (poverty, guilt, nihilism — Cotard's syndrome) or incongruent delusions / hallucinations.

### Special subtypes

Atypical depression — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity (responds well to SSRI / MAOI).

Melancholic depression — pervasive anhedonia, non-reactive mood, biological features prominent.

Seasonal affective disorder — winter recurrence with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carb craving (responds to bright-light therapy + SSRI).

Peripartum depression — onset during pregnancy or up to 4 wk postpartum (DSM-5); up to 1 year per clinical practice.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — depressed mood for ≥2 years (1 year in children).

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

### Investigations

**Bedside:** PHQ-9 (severity & screening), Beck Depression Inventory, MADRS, Hamilton-D; risk assessment (suicidal/homicidal intent).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, electrolytes, RFT, LFT, TSH, B12, folate, Ca, vitamin D.

**If clinically indicated:** HIV, VDRL, cortisol/ACTH (Cushing's), MRI brain (atypical/late-onset/neuro signs), polysomnography if OSA suspected.

Drug screen if substance use is plausible.

### Management

Figure 2. Depression management — PHQ-9 triage to SSRI/SNRI ± psychotherapy, with augmentation and ECT for refractory or urgent presentations.

### General

Address suicidality first — assess plan, means, intent; admit (voluntary / MHCA 2017) if high risk; remove means.

Treat underlying medical cause (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, drug-induced).

Sleep hygiene, exercise (aerobic 30 min × 3–5/wk), social activation, avoid alcohol.

### Pharmacotherapy

**Mild:** Watchful waiting + behavioural activation + CBT / IPT alone for 4–8 wk; add SSRI if no improvement or patient preference.

**Moderate–severe:** SSRI + psychotherapy.

**First-line SSRI:** Sertraline 50–200 mg/d, escitalopram 10–20 mg, fluoxetine 20–60 mg, paroxetine 20–50 mg, citalopram 20–40 mg, fluvoxamine 100–300 mg. Start at lowest dose for 1 wk, titrate at 2–4 wk if tolerated. Response judged at 4–6 wk; full effect by 6–8 wk.

**SNRI:** Venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg (BP rise >150 mg), duloxetine 30–60 mg (also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia), desvenlafaxine 50–100 mg.

**Atypical antidepressants:** Mirtazapine 15–45 mg HS (sedation, weight gain — good for insomnia/anorexia); bupropion 150–300 mg (smoker, low libido, no sexual SE — avoid in eating disorders, seizure history); vortioxetine 5–20 mg; vilazodone; agomelatine 25–50 mg (check LFT).

TCA (2nd-line, lethal in overdose): Amitriptyline 75–150 mg, imipramine 75–150 mg, nortriptyline, clomipramine. Useful in severe / melancholic; avoid in cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

**MAOI (rarely used):** Tranylcypromine, phenelzine — tyramine reaction risk; 2-wk wash-out from/to SSRI.

Antipsychotic-augmented for psychotic depression: SSRI/SNRI + atypical (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) or ECT.

### Inadequate response (STAR*D pathway)

Step 1 — optimise SSRI dose to maximum tolerated × 4–6 wk.

Step 2 — switch to another SSRI or to bupropion / venlafaxine / mirtazapine.

**Step 3 — augmentation:** lithium 600–900 mg (target 0.6–0.8 mEq/L), T3 25–50 µg, atypical (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 150–300 mg, olanzapine), or combine antidepressants (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine — 'California rocket fuel').

Step 4 — TCA, MAOI, or ECT.

### Non-pharmacological

CBT — 12–20 sessions; effective in mild–moderate; equally effective to SSRI in mild.

IPT (interpersonal therapy) — useful when relationship/role transition is central.

Behavioural activation, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for recurrent.

Bright-light therapy — for seasonal pattern.

### ECT — indications

Severe / suicidal / psychotic / catatonic depression.

Pregnancy or intolerant of medications.

Treatment-resistant after 2+ trials.

Marked food refusal with starvation.

**Course:** 6–12 sessions, 2–3 per week; modified ECT.

### Newer interventions

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) — FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression.

IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min / intranasal esketamine — rapid (hours) antisuicidal effect; specialised centres only.

Vagus-nerve stimulation, DBS — experimental refractory.

### Duration of treatment

**First episode:** ≥6–9 months after remission, then taper.

**Recurrent (≥2 episodes):** ≥2 years maintenance.

≥3 episodes / severe / chronic / suicidal — consider indefinite.

Taper over weeks–months; avoid abrupt stop (discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, flu-like, paraesthesia; worse with short-half-life SSRIs, e.g. paroxetine).

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk ~6% in clinical depression; ~15% in inpatients.

Substance abuse (esp. alcohol).

Cardiovascular mortality — depression is an independent CV risk factor.

Reduced adherence and worse outcomes in comorbid medical illness (DM, post-MI, stroke, cancer).

Functional impairment, work loss, relationship breakdown.

### Prognosis

Spontaneous remission of untreated single episode 6–13 months; with treatment 3 months.

**Recurrence:** 50% after 1 episode, 70% after 2, 90% after 3.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, identifiable precipitant, female, good pre-morbid functioning, no comorbidity.

**Poor:** severe / psychotic, melancholic features, comorbid substance / personality / medical illness, residual symptoms, longer episode.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression; STAR*D 2006; NICE-CG90; DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock 12e.

GENERAL MEDICINE|239.note:
### Definition

Chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis) affecting skin, peripheral nerves, mucous membranes, eyes, testes, and reticulo-endothelial system. India carries ~60% of global new case burden; leprosy is a notifiable disease (NLEP).

### Classification (WHO operational)

Paucibacillary (PB) – 1–5 skin lesions, smear-negative.

Multibacillary (MB) – >5 lesions or smear-positive.

Single skin lesion – ROM regimen (Rifampicin + Ofloxacin + Minocycline single dose) – discontinued by NLEP 2022 in favour of standard MDT.

### Multi-Drug Therapy (NLEP / WHO 2018)

MB regimen (>5 lesions or smear+): 12 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily (self-administered).

Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered).

PB regimen (1–5 lesions, smear-negative): 6 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine added since 2018 — 300 mg monthly + 50 mg daily.

Dapsone 100 mg daily.

### Paediatric (10–14 yrs)

Rifampicin 450 mg monthly; Clofazimine 150 mg monthly + 50 mg alternate day; Dapsone 50 mg daily.

Children <10 yrs / <40 kg – body-weight-based dosing.

### Treatment of reactions

Type 1 (reversal reaction – upgrade or downgrade)

Continue MDT.

Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, taper over 12–20 weeks; treat neuritis aggressively (preserve nerve function).

Rest, splinting, analgesia.

Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL)

Continue MDT.

**Mild:** NSAIDs.

**Moderate-severe:** Prednisolone 40 mg/day, taper over 8–12 weeks.

Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (refractory ENL; contraindicated in women of childbearing age – teratogenic).

Clofazimine — high dose 300 mg/day × 12 weeks then taper.

Supportive care and rehabilitation

Education on disease, transmission, course.

Wound care, footwear, protective gloves to prevent injuries to insensate areas.

Physiotherapy, splinting for clawed hands, dropped foot.

Reconstructive surgery for established deformities (lagophthalmos, claw hand, foot drop, plantar ulcer).

Eye care – artificial tears, protective glasses, surgery for lagophthalmos.

Social rehabilitation – combating stigma, vocational training, monthly disability allowance for permanent disability ≥40% under NLEP.

Contact tracing and single-dose rifampicin chemoprophylaxis (SDR-PEP – NLEP 2017).

GENERAL MEDICINE|241.note:
### Combined Notes (7 topics)

### Aim

To prevent recurrent attacks of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following an index attack – the only effective way to reduce progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

### Regimens (WHO / Indian National RHD Programme)

**First choice:** Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 21 days (preferred 3-weekly in endemic areas, 4-weekly elsewhere). Use 0.6 MU if <27 kg.

**Oral alternative:** Penicillin V 250 mg PO BD (less reliable, used when injection refused).

**If penicillin-allergic:** Sulfadiazine 1 g PO OD (0.5 g if <30 kg). Avoid in late pregnancy.

**If sulfa-allergic:** Azithromycin 250 mg OD or Erythromycin 250 mg BD.

### Duration (WHO/AHA)

**ARF without carditis:** 5 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 21 yr (whichever is longer).

ARF with carditis and residual valve disease: 10 years after last attack OR until age 40 yr (whichever is longer); often lifelong.

**After valve surgery for RHD:** Lifelong.

### Additional Measures

**Primary prophylaxis:** prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat (penicillin V 10 days or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU single dose).

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/surgical procedures in those with valvular involvement.

Echocardiographic monitoring; annual review.

Address poverty, overcrowding, oral hygiene (RHD is a 'disease of poverty').

Fig 3. Rheumatic heart disease – primary and secondary prophylaxis schema.

### Definition

Presence of fever (≥38°C) together with a cutaneous eruption (macular, maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, petechial, purpuric, or urticarial). The pattern, distribution, and timing of the rash relative to fever are critical clues to aetiology.

Differential by rash morphology

Maculopapular rash + fever

Measles – Koplik's spots, rash spreads cephalo-caudally on day 3–4.

Rubella – posterior/sub-occipital lymphadenopathy, mild fever.

Dengue – flushing, then morbilliform with 'white islands in a sea of red' (convalescent).

Chikungunya – often morbilliform, severe polyarthralgia.

Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.

Roseola infantum (HHV-6) – rash appears as fever falls.

Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) – slapped-cheek.

Secondary syphilis – symmetric palmar/plantar copper-coloured.

Typhoid – discrete 2–4 mm rose spots on trunk (~7th day).

Drug rash – starts 7–14 days after drug; widespread, pruritic.

Acute HIV seroconversion.

Toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV mononucleosis (esp. with ampicillin).

Kawasaki disease (children).

Vesicular / pustular rash + fever

Chickenpox (VZV) – crops in different stages; centripetal.

Herpes zoster – dermatomal, painful.

Hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie A16, EV-71).

Disseminated HSV.

Monkeypox – mostly single stage, peripheral, lymphadenopathy.

Petechial / purpuric rash + fever

Meningococcaemia – non-blanching, may progress to purpura fulminans; sepsis/meningitis.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever – petechiae, melaena, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus (eschar + petechiae).

Leptospirosis severe form (Weil's).

Endocarditis – Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.

Disseminated gonococcaemia.

HSP (children), TTP/DIC.

Erythroderma / desquamation + fever

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (children).

Toxic shock syndrome (staph/strep).

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

DRESS syndrome.

### Approach to investigation

Detailed history – travel, contact, vaccination, drugs, occupation, sexual history, animal exposure, food/water, season/area.

Examine entire skin including palms/soles/scalp/mucosa; check for eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, meningismus, joint involvement.

Basic labs – CBC (eosinophilia → drug/parasite), peripheral smear, platelet count, LFT, RFT, ESR, CRP.

Targeted serology – dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM, leptospira IgM, chikungunya IgM, HIV, hepatitis, VDRL, typhoid (Widal/blood culture).

Blood culture × 2 if endocarditis / sepsis suspected.

Skin biopsy with H&E + direct immunofluorescence if vasculitis or autoimmune cause suspected.

CSF analysis if meningococcal disease suspected (after CT).

Echocardiogram if endocarditis suspected.

### Initial empirical management

Isolate and notify if infectious (measles, rubella, monkeypox, meningococcaemia, viral haemorrhagic fever).

Resuscitate – fluids, oxygen; correct shock.

Empirical antibiotics for serious presumed bacterial infections (meningococcaemia – ceftriaxone 2 g IV; sepsis – broad-spectrum).

Aciclovir for severe varicella / herpes zoster.

Stop suspected offending drug; tailored therapy once aetiology known.

### Definition

Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) or Paratyphi A, B, C. Transmitted by faeco-oral route; endemic in India. Bacteraemic illness with stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and risk of GI perforation.

Clinical features (untreated, classical 4 weeks)

Week 1 – stepladder rising fever, headache, malaise, abdominal discomfort, dry cough, constipation (adults) or diarrhoea (children).

Week 2 – continued high fever, rose spots on trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), coated tongue.

**Week 3 – complications:** intestinal perforation (terminal ileum, 1–3%), GI haemorrhage, typhoid encephalopathy, myocarditis, shock.

Week 4 – gradual defervescence in survivors.

### Investigations

Blood culture – gold standard, positive in week 1 (~80%).

Stool and urine culture – positive from week 2.

Bone marrow culture – most sensitive (>90%).

Widal test (paired sera, ≥4-fold rise) – widely used but false-positive rates high.

Typhidot (IgM/IgG dot ELISA), TUBEX – rapid alternatives.

Salmonella PCR – emerging.

CBC – leucopenia, eosinopenia, raised LFT.

Treatment (Indian context — extensive drug resistance noted)

### First-line (uncomplicated, outpatient)

Azithromycin 1 g PO OD × 7 days (especially XDR Salmonella).

Cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses × 14 days (paediatric, ESBL strains).

First-line (severe / hospitalised)

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 10–14 days (drug of choice for severe cases in India given resistance).

XDR typhoid (Pakistan strain, MDR + FQ + 3rd gen cephalosporin resistant)

Meropenem 1 g IV q8h ± azithromycin.

### Resistance landscape in India

Chloramphenicol, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole – MDR-TB-Salmonella (resistant strains common since 1990s); now obsolete in most centres.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) – widespread decreased susceptibility (DCS) and resistance since 2000s; not recommended empirically.

**Currently:** ceftriaxone and azithromycin are the mainstays.

### Supportive treatment

Adequate hydration, soft diet, antipyretics (paracetamol).

Dexamethasone 3 mg/kg loading then 1 mg/kg q6h × 8 doses – for severe typhoid with shock, encephalopathy, or DIC (reduces mortality).

Surgical referral for ileal perforation, GI bleed, intestinal obstruction.

### Carrier state management

Chronic carrier (Salmonella in stool >1 year) – ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD × 4 weeks (if sensitive), or cholecystectomy if associated gallstones / chronic cholecystitis.

### Prevention

Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Typherix, Typhim Vi) – single 0.5 mL IM, booster every 3 years.

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Typbar TCV) – India, ≥6 months, single dose with long-lasting immunity.

Live oral Ty21a vaccine – 4 capsules every 2 days; booster every 5 years.

Hand hygiene, safe water, food sanitation, milk pasteurisation, sewage disposal.

### Definition

Acute systemic febrile illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus). WHO 2009 case definition – Dengue without warning signs, Dengue with warning signs, Severe dengue. 'Dengue haemorrhagic fever' (DHF, older WHO 1997 nomenclature) approximates dengue with warning signs or severe dengue. Endemic across India; epidemic peaks during/after monsoon.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Secondary infection with a different serotype → antibody-dependent enhancement → cytokine storm → endothelial dysfunction → plasma leak (the hallmark of severe disease) ± bleeding ± organ damage.

### Clinical phases

Febrile phase (days 1–3)

High fever (>39°C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia ('break-bone fever'), arthralgia, anorexia, nausea, flushing of face/neck, transient morbilliform rash, lymphadenopathy.

Tourniquet test positive (>10 petechiae/inch²).

Critical phase (days 4–6; ~24–48 h around defervescence)

Plasma leakage – rising haematocrit, ascites, pleural effusion.

**Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, hepatomegaly (>2 cm), Hct increase + rapid platelet drop.

**Severe dengue:** shock, severe bleeding, organ involvement (hepatitis, myocarditis, encephalitis, AKI).

Recovery phase (days 7–10)

Reabsorption of extravasated fluid; risk of fluid overload, pulmonary oedema; convalescent rash ('isles of white in a sea of red'); fatigue.

### Investigations

CBC – leucopenia (early), thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L), rising haematocrit (>20% baseline indicates plasma leak).

NS1 antigen ELISA – positive day 1–5 of fever.

Dengue IgM – positive from day 5; persists 2–3 months.

Dengue IgG – paired sera, 4-fold rise.

Dengue PCR – days 1–7.

LFT (mild AST/ALT rise), renal function, ABG.

USG abdomen – gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), ascites, pleural effusion (early plasma leak).

CXR – pleural effusion (right > left).

Echo – myocardial involvement.

### Management (WHO 2009 / NVBDCP)

Group A – home / outpatient

Adequate oral fluids (ORS, fruit juice, water).

Paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg q6h (max 4 g/day); AVOID NSAIDs, aspirin, IM injections.

Daily review – clinical assessment, CBC. Return if warning signs.

Group B – admit (warning signs or co-morbidities)

IV crystalloid (0.9% NS or RL) 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h × 2–4 h, then 2–3 mL/kg/h while Hct stable.

Frequent monitoring – HR, BP, RR, urine output (≥0.5 mL/kg/h), haematocrit q4-6 hourly initially.

Stop IV fluids once stable + appetite returning; total fluid duration usually 48 h.

### Group C – severe dengue (ICU)

**Immediate fluid bolus:** NS/RL 20 mL/kg over 15 min, repeat if needed.

If shock persists – colloid (hydroxyethyl starch, dextran) 10–20 mL/kg.

Blood transfusion if significant bleeding or Hct fall + shock (transfuse to maintain Hct 35–40).

Platelets only if active bleeding + count <10 × 10⁹/L, OR <20 with high-risk procedure (no prophylactic platelets).

FFP, cryoprecipitate for DIC.

Inotropes (noradrenaline) if shock persists despite fluids.

Avoid – steroids (no benefit), IV immunoglobulin (no proven role), aspirin / NSAIDs / antiplatelets.

### Convalescent phase

Reduce / stop IV fluids; watch for pulmonary oedema; furosemide if overloaded.

Fig 4. Dengue – classification and stage-based management.

### Prevention

Aedes vector control – source reduction (drain stagnant water), larvicides (temephos), adulticides (insecticide spraying), community awareness.

Personal protection – repellents (DEET), long sleeves, mosquito nets, screens.

Vaccines – Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) approved only for seropositive individuals 9–45 years; Qdenga (TAK-003) approved 2022 EU/Indonesia for all serostatus; not yet in NVBDCP.

Acute febrile arboviral illness caused by chikungunya virus (genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and A. albopictus. Endemic across India with periodic epidemics.

### Clinical features

Incubation 2–12 days.

**Acute phase (1–10 days):** sudden high fever (>39°C), severe symmetrical polyarthralgia/arthritis (wrists, ankles, hands, feet — often crippling, hence the Makonde name 'that which bends up'), myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy.

Subacute/chronic phase (weeks–months): persistent arthralgia / tenosynovitis / chronic arthritis in 30–60% of cases; depression, fatigue.

**Severe forms:** encephalitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, AKI, GBS-like presentation (especially in elderly, neonates, co-morbidities).

### Diagnosis

RT-PCR — first 5–7 days.

IgM ELISA — from day 5 onwards.

IgG — paired sera (4-fold rise).

**CBC:** lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia (less than dengue); LFT (mild rise); raised CRP/ESR.

### Treatment

Supportive only – no specific antiviral.

Paracetamol for fever and pain.

NSAIDs (after dengue excluded) for arthralgia.

Adequate hydration, rest, physiotherapy.

Chronic arthritis – methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine if refractory (>3 months); short steroid courses sometimes used.

### Prevention

Vector control identical to dengue – source reduction, personal protection.

Vaccine (IXCHIQ, Valneva) approved by US FDA Nov 2023 for adults at risk; not yet in NVBDCP.

### Definition

Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by CCHF virus (Nairovirus, Bunyaviridae); transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with infected animal blood/tissue (livestock, slaughterhouse, abattoir workers). Reported in India (Gujarat outbreak 2011, Rajasthan, MP, UP).

Clinical features (4 phases)

Incubation 1–9 days (tick bite); 5–6 days (contact).

Pre-haemorrhagic phase – sudden fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, neck stiffness, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushing.

Haemorrhagic phase (3–5 days) – petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, haematemesis, melaena, haematuria, gingival bleed, hepatomegaly; DIC.

Convalescent phase – weakness, sweating for weeks.

Case-fatality 10–40%.

### Investigations

RT-PCR (BSL-4 lab — NIV Pune in India).

IgM/IgG ELISA.

CBC – leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; raised LFT, CK, LDH; coagulation derangements.

### Treatment

Ribavirin – oral or IV; 30 mg/kg loading, then 16 mg/kg q6h × 4 days, then 8 mg/kg q8h × 6 days (controversial evidence but WHO/Indian guidelines support).

Supportive – fluids, blood components (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, packed cells).

Strict isolation, barrier nursing, BSL-3/4 facilities.

### Prevention

Tick avoidance, protective clothing, repellents.

Acaricides for livestock.

Use of PPE by abattoir/healthcare workers.

Post-exposure ribavirin prophylaxis for healthcare contacts.

Notifiable disease.

### Background

Intracranial calcifications are common — many physiological, some pathological. Pattern, location and clinical context help diagnosis. CT is far more sensitive than plain X-ray.

### PHYSIOLOGICAL calcifications

Pineal gland (60% after age 20; useful for midline shift assessment).

Choroid plexus (in lateral ventricles, trigone).

Falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli.

Petroclinoid ligaments.

Habenular commissure.

Dura, arachnoid granulations.

### PATHOLOGICAL calcifications

### 1. Infections

Neurocysticercosis — MULTIPLE punctate calcifications, classic in India; often with seizure history.

Tuberculoma — calcified granuloma.

Toxoplasmosis (congenital) — periventricular / scattered cortical; with hydrocephalus.

CMV (congenital) — periventricular calcifications; with microcephaly.

Cryptococcus, hydatid cyst.

Old abscess.

### 2. Tumours

Oligodendroglioma — 70-90% calcify (characteristic).

Astrocytoma (especially low-grade) — 15%.

Craniopharyngioma — suprasellar, mixed solid-cystic with calcification (children).

Meningioma — psammomatous calcification.

Ependymoma.

Pituitary adenoma (rare).

Metastases (osteoblastic — prostate, breast).

### 3. Vascular

Atherosclerosis (carotid siphon).

Aneurysm (curvilinear calcification of wall).

AVM, cavernoma.

Old infarct / haemorrhage.

Subdural haematoma (chronic, calcified).

### 4. Phakomatoses / Congenital

Sturge-Weber syndrome — tram-track / gyriform calcifications along cortex (parieto-occipital).

Tuberous sclerosis — subependymal nodules (basal ganglia, near foramen of Monro).

Neurofibromatosis (rare optic glioma calcification).

### 5. Metabolic / Endocrine

Hypoparathyroidism / pseudohypoparathyroidism — bilateral basal ganglia + cerebellar (Fahr syndrome).

Hyperparathyroidism (rare).

Hypothyroidism (cretinism).

Wilson's disease.

Fahr disease (idiopathic basal ganglia calcification).

### 6. Toxic / Radiation

Lead poisoning.

Post-radiotherapy (mineralising microangiopathy).

Methotrexate-induced leukoencephalopathy.

### 7. Other

Cockayne syndrome (basal ganglia).

Coats plus syndrome.

### Approach by location

### Investigations

CT head (without contrast) — sensitive for calcification.

MRI brain — characterise lesion; calcium is hypointense on T1 and T2 (or use SWI).

Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D (basal ganglia calcifications).

Ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper (Wilson's).

TORCH serology if neonatal.

Cysticercosis ELISA (EITB), stool ova/cyst.

### Local features

Cough (commonest); change in chronic smoker's cough.

Haemoptysis – any new in a smoker > 40 yr → CT chest.

Dyspnoea (bronchial obstruction, effusion, lymphangitis).

Wheeze (fixed monophonic – endobronchial).

Recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia in the same lobe.

Skin and contralateral lung.

### Combined Notes (4 topics)

Common inhaled corticosteroids (Indian availability)

Budesonide (Budecort, Pulmicort) – MDI 100/200 µg; DPI 200/400 µg; neb 0.5/1 mg.

Fluticasone propionate (Flohale, Flixotide) – MDI 50/125/250 µg; DPI 100/250/500 µg.

Fluticasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg (once-daily).

Beclomethasone dipropionate (Beclate) – MDI 50/100/250 µg.

Ciclesonide (Alvesco) – MDI 80/160 µg.

Mometasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg.

Combination ICS-LABA inhalers (most prescribed)

Budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort, Foracort) – preferred Track 1 GINA reliever-controller.

Fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide).

Fluticasone furoate + vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta).

Beclomethasone + formoterol.

### Triple-therapy inhalers (ICS-LABA-LAMA)

Fluticasone + umeclidinium + vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta).

Budesonide + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

Beclomethasone + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

### Adverse effects

**Local:** oral candidiasis (Candida albicans – use spacer + rinse mouth), dysphonia, throat irritation.

Systemic (with high dose / long-term): osteoporosis, skin thinning, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, adrenal suppression, increased pneumonia risk in COPD.

### Indications

Asthma – mainstay of controller therapy from GINA Step 1 onwards.

COPD – with LABA in patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥100/300.

Other obstructive airways disease (some forms of bronchiectasis with asthma overlap).

### Definition

Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. Confirmed by gastric scintigraphy showing > 10% retention at 4 h. Commonest cause is diabetic autonomic neuropathy (especially long-standing T1DM/T2DM); idiopathic, post-viral, post-surgical (vagotomy, fundoplication), drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 agonists), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), Parkinson's.

### Symptoms

Early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting (often undigested food hours after meal), upper abdominal pain, weight loss, poor glycaemic control in diabetics (mismatch with insulin).

### Pharmacological Management

### 1. Prokinetics (first-line)

**Metoclopramide:** Metoclopramide: 5–10 mg PO/IV TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. MOA: D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist + acetylcholine release. Black-box warning: tardive dyskinesia (limit to ≤ 12 weeks); extrapyramidal SE, hyperprolactinaemia.

**Domperidone:** Domperidone: 10 mg PO TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. Peripheral D2 antagonist — does NOT cross BBB → fewer EPS. Caution: QT prolongation (avoid in cardiac disease, electrolyte abnormalities); lower dose in elderly; not available in USA but widely used in India.

**Erythromycin:** Erythromycin: 50–250 mg PO TDS (lower dose for prokinesis) or 3 mg/kg IV; motilin receptor agonist. Tachyphylaxis (loss of effect after 2–4 wk) — limit use. Useful as IV in acute settings (e.g. pre-OGD for blood clearance).

**Cisapride:** Cisapride: Withdrawn in most countries (QT prolongation, torsades).

**Prucalopride:** Prucalopride: 1–2 mg OD — 5-HT4 agonist; emerging evidence for refractory gastroparesis.

### 2. Antiemetics (symptomatic)

Ondansetron 4–8 mg PO/IV TDS — 5-HT3 antagonist; first-line for symptom control.

Prochlorperazine, promethazine — alternatives; sedation, EPS.

Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist, for refractory.

### 3. Other / Emerging

Mirtazapine 15 mg HS — TCA-related; appetite + nausea relief.

Botulinum toxin pyloric injection — only short-term (no longer recommended in guidelines).

Ghrelin agonists (relamorelin) — in trials.

### Non-Pharmacological

**Dietary:** small frequent meals (5–6/day), low-fat, low-fibre, soft/liquid consistency.

Strict glycaemic control in diabetics (hyperglycaemia worsens emptying).

Avoid carbonated drinks, alcohol, smoking.

Stop / reduce offending drugs (opioids, GLP-1 agonists if possible, anticholinergics).

Vitamin / micronutrient supplementation (chronic malnutrition risk).

### Refractory Cases

Gastric electrical stimulation (Enterra device) — FDA HUD; selected refractory cases.

Pyloroplasty / G-POEM (gastric per-oral endoscopic myotomy).

**Surgical:** subtotal gastrectomy, jejunostomy feeding tube.

TPN in severe cachexia.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ACG Gastroparesis 2022; AGA 2022.

### Overview

IBD (UC, Crohn's) treatment uses a step-up or top-down approach based on severity, location, and prognostic factors. Goals: induce + maintain remission, achieve mucosal healing, prevent complications, avoid surgery.

### Classification of IBD Drugs

### 1. Aminosalicylates (5-ASA / Mesalamine)

**Sulfasalazine:** Sulfasalazine: 1–2 g BD-QID. Sulfapyridine + 5-ASA. Cleaved by colonic bacteria. SE: nausea, headache, hypersensitivity, oligospermia (reversible).

**Mesalamine:** Mesalamine: 2.4–4.8 g/d divided. pH-dependent or time-released formulations (Asacol, Pentasa, Salofalk). For colonic and ileal disease.

**Olsalazine, Balsalazide:** Olsalazine, Balsalazide: 5-ASA dimers / azo-bonded; site-specific colonic release.

**Topical 5-ASA:** Topical 5-ASA: Suppositories (proctitis), enemas (left-sided UC) — adjunct or monotherapy.

**Indications:** Indications: Mild-moderate UC (induction + maintenance); less effective in Crohn's (some role in colonic CD).

### 2. Corticosteroids

**Prednisolone:** Prednisolone: 40–60 mg/d PO, taper over 8–12 weeks. Severe UC: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h or methylprednisolone 60 mg/d. Induction only — NOT maintenance.

**Budesonide:** Budesonide: 9 mg/d × 8 wk for mild-moderate ileal/right colonic Crohn's. Topically active; high first-pass metabolism → fewer systemic SE.

**Topical (PR foam/enema):** Topical (PR foam/enema): Hydrocortisone, budesonide foam for distal UC.

Steroid dependence (cannot taper) or refractoriness (failure of high dose for 7–10 d) → step up to immunomodulators or biologics.

Long-term steroid avoidance — bone protection (Ca/Vit D, DEXA), DM/HTN screening, infection.

### 3. Immunomodulators (steroid-sparing)

Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine:Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine: AZA 2–2.5 mg/kg/d (6-MP 1–1.5 mg/kg/d). Check TPMT activity before starting (deficiency → severe myelosuppression). Onset 6–12 wk. Maintenance.

**Methotrexate:** Methotrexate: 25 mg/wk IM/SC × 16 wk → 15 mg/wk maintenance (Crohn's). Folic acid 5 mg/wk. Less effective in UC.

**Cyclosporine:** Cyclosporine: 2 mg/kg/d IV (or 4 mg/kg/d PO) for steroid-refractory severe UC — rescue therapy. Bridge to AZA/biologics. Trough 200–400 ng/mL.

**Tacrolimus:** Tacrolimus: Alternative calcineurin inhibitor.

**Monitoring:** CBC, LFT every 2 wk × first month, then 3-monthly.

**Risks:** bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis (AZA), lymphoma (slightly raised), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (rare in young men on AZA + anti-TNF).

- Biologics (anti-TNF and others)

**Infliximab (anti-TNF):** Infliximab (anti-TNF): 5 mg/kg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk maintenance. Can escalate to 10 mg/kg or every 6 wk if loss of response.

**Adalimumab (anti-TNF):** Adalimumab (anti-TNF): 160 mg SC week 0 → 80 mg week 2 → 40 mg every 2 wk maintenance.

**Golimumab:** Golimumab: 200 mg SC week 0 → 100 mg week 2 → 50–100 mg every 4 wk (UC).

**Certolizumab pegol:** Certolizumab pegol: 400 mg SC at 0, 2, 4 wk → every 4 wk (Crohn's).

**Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7):** Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7): 300 mg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk. Gut-selective; lower infection risk.

**Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40):** Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40): Weight-based loading IV → 90 mg SC every 8–12 wk maintenance. Crohn's + UC.

**Risankizumab (anti-IL23):** Risankizumab (anti-IL23): 600 mg IV at 0, 4, 8 wk → 360 mg SC every 8 wk (Crohn's).

### Pre-biologic screening (essential)

**TB screening:** chest X-ray + Mantoux/IGRA (especially Indian context — high TB burden, anti-TNF reactivates latent TB).

Hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV.

Vaccinate live attenuated BEFORE starting (yellow fever, varicella).

CBC, LFT, albumin baseline.

### 5. Small Molecule Drugs (new class)

**Tofacitinib:** Tofacitinib: Pan-JAK inhibitor; 10 mg BD × 8 wk → 5 mg BD maintenance. Moderate-severe UC. Caution: VTE risk (especially with risk factors), shingles.

**Upadacitinib:** Upadacitinib: JAK1 selective; 45 mg/d × 8 wk → 15 mg/d (or 30 mg/d) maintenance. UC + Crohn's.

**Ozanimod:** Ozanimod: S1P modulator; UC.

**Etrasimod:** Etrasimod: S1P modulator; newer.

### 6. Antibiotics

**Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin:** Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin: For perianal Crohn's, fistulae, abscess, pouchitis. 400 mg TDS + 500 mg BD for 4–8 wk.

**Vancomycin PO:** Vancomycin PO: For C. difficile co-infection.

### 7. Adjunctive / Supportive

Iron supplementation (oral or IV; IV preferred in moderate-severe).

B12 (terminal ileitis / resection).

Vitamin D, calcium (osteoporosis prevention).

Probiotics (some evidence for pouchitis; mild UC).

Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) — emerging in UC, very promising in pouchitis.

### Indication-Based Algorithm

### Ulcerative Colitis

**Mild proctitis/distal:** topical 5-ASA, topical steroid.

**Mild-moderate extensive:** PO + topical 5-ASA, PO steroids if needed.

**Moderate-severe:** PO steroids → AZA → biologic (anti-TNF, vedo, ustek) or tofacitinib.

**Severe:** IV hydrocortisone; day-3 response (Travis criteria — > 8 stools or 3–8 + CRP > 45 = high colectomy risk); rescue infliximab 5 mg/kg or cyclosporine 2 mg/kg/d IV.

**Refractory:** colectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (curative).

### Crohn's Disease

**Mild ileal:** budesonide 9 mg/d.

**Moderate:** PO prednisolone → AZA / methotrexate maintenance.

Severe / fistulating / perianal: anti-TNF ± AZA ('top-down'); anti-TNF + seton for perianal fistulae; metronidazole.

**Stricture:** balloon dilatation; surgery (stricturoplasty, segmental resection).

**Goal:** deep remission (clinical + endoscopic mucosal healing).

Fig 10. IBD — UC vs Crohn's stepwise algorithm.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ECCO 2022 UC + Crohn's guidelines; ACG 2019; ISG IBD India consensus.

### Definition

Portal hypertension = pathological elevation of pressure in the portal venous system, diagnosed clinically (varices, splenomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy) or by hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) > 5 mm Hg (clinically significant > 10 mm Hg; variceal threshold > 12).

### Classification by Site of Obstruction

**Pre-hepatic:** portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis (post-pancreatitis), schistosomiasis (Indian).

**Intra-hepatic:** cirrhosis (commonest), idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN (NCIPH/INCPH — important in India), nodular regenerative hyperplasia, primary biliary cholangitis.

**Post-hepatic:** Budd-Chiari, IVC obstruction, constrictive pericarditis, right heart failure.

### Drug Classes

### 1. Non-Selective Beta-Blockers (NSBB) — first-line

**Propranolol:** Propranolol: Start 20–40 mg BD → titrate to HR 55–60 bpm (or 25% reduction from baseline). Max 320 mg/d. β1 + β2 blockade → reduced cardiac output + splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal flow + pressure.

**Nadolol:** Nadolol: 20–80 mg/d. Longer half-life, once-daily dosing; preferred over propranolol in some patients (less compliance issues).

**Carvedilol:** Carvedilol: 6.25 mg BD → titrate to 12.5 BD (or 25 mg/d in some). Non-selective β + α1 antagonism → further reduces portal pressure via intrahepatic vasodilation. Preferred in compensated cirrhosis (Baveno VII).

**Goals:** Goals: ↓ HVPG > 20% from baseline OR ≤ 12 mm Hg → reduces variceal bleed and mortality.

**Contraindications:** Contraindications: Severe asthma/COPD, bradycardia (HR < 55), AV block, decompensated heart failure, refractory ascites (caution — may worsen).

**Indications:** Indications: Primary prophylaxis (medium/large varices, or small varices with high-risk features), secondary prophylaxis after first variceal bleed.

### 2. Vasoactive Drugs for Acute Variceal Bleed

Terlipressin (1st-line in India):Terlipressin (1st-line in India): 2 mg IV bolus q4h × 24–48 h → 1 mg q4h × 5 d total. Vasopressin analogue → V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure. Indian context: cheap, widely available, DOC for acute variceal bleed + HRS.

**Octreotide:** Octreotide: 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Somatostatin analogue → inhibits splanchnic vasodilator release (glucagon, VIP) → ↓ portal flow. Useful when terlipressin unavailable.

**Somatostatin:** Somatostatin: 250 µg IV bolus → 250 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Less commonly used in India.

**Vasopressin:** Vasopressin: Largely replaced — significant systemic vasoconstriction (coronary, mesenteric, peripheral) → ischaemic complications.

### 3. Antibiotics in Variceal Bleed

**Ceftriaxone:** Ceftriaxone: 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d. Reduces SBP, rebleed risk, and mortality (Garcia-Tsao). Norfloxacin 400 mg BD PO as alternative in countries with low quinolone resistance.

### 4. Diuretics for Ascites

**Spironolactone:** Spironolactone: 100 mg/d → titrate to 400 mg/d (in 100 mg increments). First-line; competitive aldosterone antagonist. SE: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia.

**Furosemide:** Furosemide: Add 40 mg/d → titrate to 160 mg/d. Combined with spironolactone in 100:40 ratio. Loop diuretic; SE: hypokalaemia, AKI, hyponatraemia.

**Amiloride:** Amiloride: Alternative to spironolactone; no gynaecomastia. Less potent.

**Goals:** Goals: Daily weight loss ≤ 0.5 kg (no oedema) / ≤ 1 kg (with oedema). Daily Na restriction 88 mmol (2 g sodium).

**Caution:** Caution: Watch for HRS, encephalopathy (over-diuresis), hyponatraemia (Na < 125 → stop diuretics).

### 5. Albumin

**Indicated for:** large-volume paracentesis (8 g per L removed > 5 L); SBP (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 — reduces HRS, mortality); HRS (1 g/kg day 1 then 20–40 g/d); spontaneous decompensation with hypoalbuminaemia.

### 6. HRS-Specific

**Terlipressin + Albumin:** Terlipressin + Albumin: Terlipressin 1 mg q4–6 h IV (titrate to 2 mg q4h) + albumin 1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/d × 5–14 d. Reverses HRS in 30–50%.

**Noradrenaline + Albumin:** Noradrenaline + Albumin: 0.5–3 mg/h infusion (target MAP rise 10 mm Hg) — alternative in ICU.

Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin:Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin: Less effective; outpatient alternative.

### 7. Hepatic Encephalopathy

Lactulose 30–45 ml TDS → titrate to 2–3 soft stools/d.

Rifaximin 550 mg BD — maintenance / recurrent.

See Q14 for full details.

- Statins (emerging in compensated cirrhosis)

Simvastatin 20–40 mg/d — improves liver microcirculation, reduces portal pressure, may improve survival (Abraldes 2016, EASL 2018). Caution in decompensated.

### Comprehensive Algorithm

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (Child B/C, red wale marks) → NSBB or carvedilol.

Medium/large varices → NSBB / carvedilol OR EVL.

**Combined NSBB + EVL:** NOT recommended primarily.

Acute Bleed (within 12 h)

Resuscitate (restrictive Hb 7), terlipressin + ceftriaxone + IV PPI; urgent OGD with EVL.

Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

NSBB / carvedilol + EVL every 2–4 wk till varices eradicated.

**Refractory:** TIPS / liver transplant evaluation.
