### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

### Definition

Recurrent paroxysmal unilateral severe facial pain in one or more divisions of trigeminal nerve, triggered by innocuous stimuli ('tic douloureux'). 'Suicide disease' due to intensity.

### Epidemiology

**Incidence 4-13/100,000/year; F:** M = 1.5:1; peaks 60-70 y.

Younger onset (< 40 y) → suspect MS or structural cause.

Aetiology / Classification (ICHD-3 / 2016 redefinition)

**Classical TN:** vascular compression of trigeminal root by superior cerebellar artery (90% of cases).

**Secondary TN:** MS (5-10%), tumour (acoustic neuroma, meningioma, epidermoid cyst), AVM, sarcoidosis.

**Idiopathic TN:** no identifiable cause.

### Clinical features

Pain characteristics — diagnostic

Sharp, stabbing, electric-shock-like.

Severe (10/10) — among worst pains known.

Brief — seconds to 2 minutes per attack.

Strictly unilateral (bilateral rare; suggests MS).

**Distribution:** V2 (maxillary) > V3 (mandibular) > V1 (ophthalmic).

**Triggers:** light touch, washing face, shaving, chewing, brushing teeth, cold breeze, talking.

Refractory period after attack.

Remissions and relapses common.

### Examination

NORMAL between attacks in classical TN.

If sensory loss, corneal reflex abnormal, or other CN involved → suspect secondary TN.

### Investigations

MRI brain with high-resolution trigeminal protocol (FIESTA / CISS) + MR angiography — identifies neurovascular conflict and excludes secondary causes.

All patients with TN should have MRI; especially mandatory if age < 40, bilateral, sensory loss, no carbamazepine response.

### Management

### 1. Medical (first-line)

**Carbamazepine:** Carbamazepine: FIRST CHOICE. Start 100-200 mg BD, titrate up to 600-1200 mg/d (max 1800 mg). NNT = 1.7-2.6. Side effects: rash (SJS — HLA-B*1502 in Asians), hyponatraemia, ataxia, drowsiness, leukopenia. Monitor Na, CBC, LFT.

**Oxcarbazepine:** Oxcarbazepine: Better tolerated. 300 mg BD up to 1800 mg. Hyponatraemia still possible.

**Lamotrigine:** Lamotrigine: Adjunct; slow titration (rash, SJS).

**Baclofen:** Baclofen: 30-80 mg/d; especially useful in TN due to MS.

**Gabapentin / Pregabalin:** Gabapentin / Pregabalin: Adjunct; useful when carbamazepine not tolerated.

**Phenytoin:** Phenytoin: IV 250 mg slowly — for acute exacerbation 'crisis'.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: Subcutaneous injection — emerging evidence, 2nd-3rd line.

- Surgical (indicated if medical therapy fails or intolerable AEs)

Microvascular decompression (Jannetta):Microvascular decompression (Jannetta): Posterior fossa craniotomy, Teflon felt between vessel and nerve. BEST long-term results: 80-90% pain-free at 10 y. Best in younger patients with classical TN. Risks: hearing loss, facial palsy, CSF leak, stroke (1%).

Percutaneous procedures (ganglion ablation):Percutaneous procedures (ganglion ablation): Glycerol injection, balloon compression, radiofrequency thermocoagulation. Less invasive but higher recurrence (40-60% at 5 y) and sensory loss (corneal anaesthesia if V1).

Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife):Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife): 70-80% initial relief; effect at 4-6 weeks; useful in elderly / high surgical risk. Recurrence 30-50% at 5 y.

- Treat underlying cause if secondary TN

MS — disease-modifying therapy.

Tumour — resection / radiation.

### Differential diagnosis

Cluster headache (longer, autonomic features, orbital).

SUNCT / SUNA (V1 distribution, autonomic).

Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (V → throat/ear; triggered by swallowing).

Postherpetic neuralgia (history of zoster).

Dental pain, temporomandibular joint disorder, sinusitis.

Atypical facial pain (constant, dull, no trigger).

**Source:** EAN 2019 TN Guidelines; AAN-EFNS 2008; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|271.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Definition

Bleeding proximal to ligament of Treitz, presenting as haematemesis (fresh red / coffee-ground), melaena (≥ 50 ml from upper GI), or occasionally haematochezia in massive bleeds (≥ 1 L) with rapid transit. Accounts for ~80% of acute GI bleeds; mortality 6–10%.

### Etiology

Peptic ulcer disease (35–50%) — duodenal > gastric; NSAIDs, H. pylori, stress.

Oesophagogastric varices (10–20%) — cirrhosis with portal HTN; high mortality.

Mallory-Weiss tear (5–10%) — vomiting/retching, longitudinal mucosal tear at GE junction.

Erosive oesophagitis / gastritis / duodenitis.

Dieulafoy lesion (submucosal artery, lesser curve).

Upper GI malignancy (gastric, oesophageal).

**Vascular:** angiodysplasia, GAVE (watermelon stomach), aortoenteric fistula.

Iatrogenic — post-endoscopy, post-sphincterotomy.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Symptoms: Haematemesis, melaena, syncope, weakness, epigastric pain (PUD), retching → haematemesis (Mallory-Weiss).

**Signs of shock:** Signs of shock: Tachycardia, hypotension, cool peripheries, delayed CRT, oliguria, altered sensorium.

**Stigmata of CLD:** Stigmata of CLD: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis → suggests variceal source.

**PR exam:** PR exam: Mandatory — melaena confirms upper GI source if not from iron/bismuth/spinach.

### Investigations

### Bedside

Vitals + GCS + capillary refill + tilt test (drop SBP > 20 mm = > 1 L loss).

ECG (rule out MI from anaemia/shock, especially elderly).

NG tube only if diagnostic doubt (not routine).

### Laboratory

CBC — Hb may be normal initially (haemoconcentration); reticulocyte for chronicity.

Urea/creatinine — disproportionate ↑ urea suggests UGI source (protein load).

LFT (cirrhosis screen), INR, APTT — coagulopathy correction.

Group & save, cross-match 4–6 units, blood gas (lactate, base deficit).

### Risk stratification

**GBS:** Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) — pre-endoscopy; GBS = 0–1 → outpatient endoscopy safe; ≥ 2 admit.

**Rockall:** Rockall score — post-endoscopy, mortality prediction (age, shock, comorbidity, endoscopic Dx, stigmata).

**AIMS65:** AIMS65 — albumin < 3, INR > 1.5, mental status, SBP ≤ 90, age > 65.

### Endoscopy (definitive)

Within 24 h of stabilisation; within 12 h if haemodynamic instability or known cirrhosis.

Diagnostic + therapeutic (injection, thermal, clips, banding).

**Forrest classification for PUD:** Ia spurting > Ib oozing > IIa visible vessel > IIb adherent clot > IIc flat pigment > III clean base.

### Management

### 1. Resuscitation (ABC)

2 large-bore (16-18G) IV cannulae; airway protection if encephalopathic / massive bleed.

Crystalloid bolus (Ringer's lactate / NS) 20 ml/kg; titrate to MAP ≥ 65, UO ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/h.

**Restrictive transfusion:** PRBC transfusion threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL (Hb < 8 if active cardiac disease).

**Correct coagulopathy:** FFP if INR > 1.5 + active bleed; platelets if < 50,000; reverse warfarin (4F-PCC + vit K); reverse DOAC (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet for FXa).

### 2. Pharmacotherapy

**PPI:** PPI: IV pantoprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/h infusion × 72 h (continue PO 40 mg BD after).

Vasoactive (if suspected variceal):Vasoactive (if suspected variceal): Terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h × 5 d (1st-line in India) OR octreotide 50 µg bolus → 50 µg/h × 5 d.

Prophylactic antibiotics (variceal/cirrhotic):Prophylactic antibiotics (variceal/cirrhotic): Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d (reduces SBP + rebleed; mortality benefit).

**Prokinetic before endoscopy:** Prokinetic before endoscopy: Erythromycin 250 mg IV 30–60 min before OGD (improves visualisation).

### 3. Endoscopic therapy

**PUD Forrest Ia–IIb:** dual therapy (adrenaline injection + thermal/clip).

**Oesophageal varices:** endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) — first-line.

**Gastric varices:** cyanoacrylate (N-butyl) glue injection.

**Mallory-Weiss:** usually self-limiting; if bleeding — clips, adrenaline.

### 4. Failed endoscopic Rx

Repeat endoscopy first (especially if rebleed within 24 h).

**Variceal:** Sengstaken-Blakemore (max 24 h) → early TIPS < 72 h (Child B/C).

**PUD:** angiographic embolisation (gastroduodenal artery for DU posterior bleed); surgery (over-sewing, antrectomy, oesophagogastrectomy) — last resort.

### 5. Post-bleed care

**PUD:** H. pylori test/treat; stop NSAIDs; long-term PPI if can't avoid NSAID.

**Variceal:** non-selective β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg BD titrate to HR 55) + repeat EVL every 2–4 wk till eradication.

**Cirrhotics:** surveillance OGD, MELD/Child-Pugh re-score, transplant evaluation.

Fig 1. UGI bleed — risk-stratified algorithm.

### Complications

Shock, AKI, hypoxic encephalopathy.

Aspiration pneumonia (esp. variceal bleed + encephalopathy).

Transfusion reactions, TRALI, TACO.

Rebleed (15–20%), need for surgery (~5%).

**Cirrhotics:** decompensation, HE, HRS, SBP.

### Prognosis

Overall mortality 6–10%. Variceal bleed in Child C — 6-week mortality 30–40%. PUD bleed mortality < 5% with timely endoscopy. Restrictive transfusion (Villanueva) improves survival vs liberal.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12; Davidson Ch.21; NICE NG12 (2016); Baveno VII (2022).

### Definition

Upper GI bleed (UGIB) = bleeding proximal to ligament of Treitz (haematemesis/melaena/coffee-ground). Lower GI bleed (LGIB) = bleeding distal to it (haematochezia, fresh PR bleed). Mid-GI bleed = small bowel between papilla and ileocaecal valve (obscure source — capsule/enteroscopy).

### Upper GI Bleed — Etiology

### Lower GI Bleed — Etiology

### Approach to Differentiation

### Investigations

**UGIB:** OGD first within 24 h.

**LGIB:** colonoscopy within 24 h after bowel prep (PEG); CT angiography first if haemodynamic instability or massive bleed (detects bleed rate ≥ 0.3 ml/min).

**Obscure / occult:** capsule endoscopy → balloon enteroscopy → CT/MR enterography → tagged RBC scan → angiography.

**Meckel's:** Children/young adults with painless massive PR bleed: technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel's scan).

### Management Principles

ABC resuscitation as in Q1.

**UGIB:** PPI ± vasoactive ± antibiotic (if variceal); endoscopic Rx.

**LGIB:** stabilise → colonoscopy with clips/cautery/EBL; angio-embolisation; surgery if uncontrolled.

**Haemorrhoids:** dietary fibre + sitz + topical → banding/sclerotherapy → haemorrhoidectomy.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.534–540; Davidson Ch.22; ACG 2016 LGIB; ESGE 2021.

### Definition

Bleeding from oesophageal or gastric varices in patients with portal hypertension. Defines decompensated cirrhosis; mortality 15–20% per episode (Child C up to 40%).

### Aetiology

**Portal HTN:** cirrhosis (commonest), schistosomiasis (Indian endemic in some regions), portal/splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN.

**Trigger threshold:** HVPG > 12 mm Hg → varices develop; HVPG > 20 mm Hg + active bleed → high failure / rebleed risk.

### Clinical Features

Sudden large-volume haematemesis (often bright red) ± melaena ± haematochezia (massive bleed).

Hypovolaemic shock — tachycardia, hypotension, cool peripheries.

Stigmata of CLD — jaundice, spider naevi, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis (precipitates HE).

Often painless (unlike PUD).

### Investigations

Urgent OGD within 12 h after stabilisation (definitive diagnostic + therapeutic).

**Bloods:** CBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, splenic sequestration), INR, LFT, urea/creatinine, blood gas, cross-match 4–6 units.

Child-Pugh + MELD scoring (prognosis, transplant listing).

USG abdomen + Doppler — portal vein patency, splenomegaly, ascites.

Calculate HVPG (transjugular) when planning TIPS.

### Management

### 1. Initial Resuscitation

ABC, 2 wide-bore cannulae, airway protection if encephalopathic.

Crystalloid + restrictive PRBC transfusion (target Hb 7 g/dL — over-transfusion ↑ portal pressure → rebleed; Villanueva 2013).

Correct coagulopathy carefully — INR target not too aggressive in cirrhotics (rebalanced haemostasis); platelets if < 50,000.

- Pharmacotherapy — START WITHIN 1 H, BEFORE OGD

**Vasoactive (1st-line in India):** Vasoactive (1st-line in India): Terlipressin 2 mg IV q4h × 5 d (2 mg q4h for 24 h → 1 mg q4h thereafter). MOA: V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure.

**Alternative:** Alternative: Octreotide 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d OR somatostatin 250 µg bolus → 250 µg/h.

**Antibiotic prophylaxis:** Antibiotic prophylaxis: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d (reduces SBP + early rebleed + mortality, Garcia-Tsao recommendation).

**PPI:** PPI: IV PPI till endoscopy (in case non-variceal lesion identified).

### 3. Endoscopic Therapy

**Oesophageal varices:** Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) — 1st-line (controls bleeding in ≥ 90%, lower rebleed than sclerotherapy).

Alternative if EVL not feasible: endoscopic sclerotherapy (ethanolamine oleate, polidocanol).

**Gastric varices:** cyanoacrylate (N-butyl) glue injection; BRTO (balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration) if available.

- Failure / Massive bleed

Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (oesophageal + gastric balloon) — bridging only, max 24 h, requires ICU + airway protection (risk of necrosis, aspiration, rupture).

Early TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) < 72 h — indicated in Child B with active bleed or Child C ≤ 13; reduces rebleed + mortality (Garcia-Pagán 2010).

Self-expanding metallic stent (Danis stent) — temporary tamponade alternative.

**Surgical:** emergency portocaval shunt / oesophagogastric devascularisation (rarely needed in TIPS era).

- Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

Non-selective β-blocker — propranolol 40 mg BD titrate to HR 55–60 or carvedilol 6.25 BD (preferred in compensated cirrhosis, also α-blockade).

EVL every 2–4 wk till varices obliterated; surveillance OGD 6-monthly.

Treat underlying liver disease (DAA for HCV, antivirals for HBV, abstinence for alcohol).

Liver transplant evaluation in selected cases.

Fig 4. Variceal bleed — Baveno VII pathway.

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (red wale marks, Child B/C) → NSBB.

Medium/large varices → NSBB OR EVL (patient choice/comorbidity).

**Cirrhosis without varices:** do NOT use NSBB for prevention; OGD surveillance.

### Complications

Rebleed (15–30%), aspiration, HE precipitation, SBP, HRS.

**Sengstaken-related:** oesophageal necrosis, perforation, aspiration.

**TIPS:** encephalopathy (20–30%), stent dysfunction, RV failure.

### Prognosis

6-week mortality after first variceal bleed: Child A 5%, Child B 20%, Child C 30–40%. Improved with vasoactive + endoscopic Rx + abx + early TIPS.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.541; Baveno VII (2022); AASLD 2017; ISG-Indian Society of Gastroenterology.

### Definition

Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) — visualisation of oesophagus, stomach and duodenum (up to D2) using a flexible fibre-optic endoscope. Allows biopsy, cytology, and therapeutic interventions. Should be performed by trained gastroenterologist with anaesthetic support / monitoring.

### Indications

### Diagnostic

Dyspepsia with alarm features ('ALARMS'): Age > 55 with new symptoms, Loss of weight, Anaemia, Recurrent vomiting, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty.

Persistent dyspepsia not responding to PPI / H. pylori eradication.

GORD with alarm features or atypical symptoms.

Dysphagia / odynophagia.

Suspected oesophageal varices in known CLD.

Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia (with colonoscopy).

Coeliac disease — duodenal biopsy.

Suspected upper GI cancer or post-resection surveillance.

Suspected peptic ulcer disease.

Persistent vomiting of unknown cause.

Caustic ingestion (within 12–48 h to assess injury).

**Surveillance:** Barrett's oesophagus, gastric premalignant conditions (atrophic gastritis, IM, dysplasia), post-gastric resection, post-EMR/ESD.

### Therapeutic

Variceal banding (EVL) / sclerotherapy.

Endoscopic haemostasis for ulcer bleed (adrenaline injection, thermal coagulation, mechanical clips, haemospray).

Foreign body removal.

Stricture dilatation (achalasia, peptic, malignant).

Stent placement (oesophageal Ca, GOO).

Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) / submucosal dissection (ESD) — early cancers, polyps.

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) — long-term feeding access.

**Achalasia:** balloon dilatation, botulinum injection, POEM.

ERCP — biliary/pancreatic interventions (separate procedure).

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Suspected perforated viscus.

Severe respiratory compromise (without intubation).

Uncooperative / unstable patient without sedation/anaesthesia support.

### Relative

Recent MI (within 30 days).

Severe coagulopathy (correct INR, platelets first).

Severe COPD, decompensated heart failure.

Suspected aneurysm of aortic arch.

### Pre-Procedure

NBM 6 h for solids, 2 h for clear fluids.

**Informed consent (risks:** perforation 0.05%, bleeding, aspiration, sedation complications).

Stop anticoagulants (per BSG/ESGE guidelines — warfarin INR ≤ 1.5 for high-risk procedures; DOACs hold 24–48 h).

Stop iron / bismuth (interfere with mucosal visualisation).

**Pre-procedure assessment:** vitals, BP, cardiac/respiratory status.

IV access, oxygen, suction.

Topical pharyngeal anaesthesia (lidocaine spray).

**Sedation:** midazolam 2–5 mg IV ± fentanyl 25–50 µg; or propofol (anaesthetist).

Antibiotic prophylaxis NOT routinely required (except cirrhotic + variceal bleed, post-PEG placement, PEH high risk).

### Procedure

Left lateral decubitus position, head tilted forward.

Mouth-guard, bite-block.

Pass endoscope under direct vision → oesophagus → stomach → D1, D2.

**Systematic inspection:** GE junction, fundus retroflexion, pylorus, duodenum.

**Biopsies:** gastric (2 antrum + 2 body + incisura — Sydney protocol), duodenum (4 from D2 if coeliac disease suspected), specific lesions.

Photographic documentation.

Total procedure time 5–15 min (diagnostic), longer for therapeutic.

### Post-Procedure

Monitor vitals 30–60 min in recovery.

Avoid food/fluids till gag reflex returns (60 min if pharyngeal lignocaine).

**Watch for complications:** persistent chest/abdominal pain, haematemesis, breathing difficulty.

Discharge with adult escort if sedated.

No driving 24 h post-sedation.

### Complications (overall 0.1–0.5%)

Perforation (0.03–0.05% diagnostic; higher for therapeutic).

Bleeding (0.03% diagnostic, up to 1% for therapeutic).

Aspiration pneumonia.

**Cardiopulmonary:** arrhythmia, hypoxia (sedation), MI (rare).

Sore throat (transient).

Infection (transient bacteraemia; rare endocarditis).

### Combined Notes (6 topics)

### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

### Definition

Single, well-defined, rounded opacity ≤3 cm in diameter, surrounded by normal lung, without associated atelectasis or lymphadenopathy. Important because malignancy must be excluded.

### Differential diagnosis

### Malignant (40%):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (adenocarcinoma commonest in non-smokers).

Carcinoid tumour.

Solitary metastasis (colon, breast, renal, sarcoma, melanoma).

Lymphoma (rare).

### Benign (60%):

Infectious granuloma (tuberculoma – India's commonest), histoplasmoma, cryptococcoma, aspergilloma.

Hamartoma (popcorn calcification).

Lung abscess (early).

Pulmonary AVM.

Round atelectasis.

Rheumatoid nodule.

Wegener's granulomatous nodule.

Bronchogenic cyst, sequestration.

Pulmonary infarct.

### Features suggesting malignancy

Age >50, smoker, size >2 cm, spiculated margin, irregular shape, growth on serial imaging, lack of calcification (or eccentric calcification), upper lobe location, PET-avid (SUV >2.5).

### Features suggesting benignity

Age <40, never-smoker, well-defined smooth margin, central/diffuse/popcorn/laminated calcification, stability >2 years, small (<1 cm), fat density (hamartoma).

### Approach (Fleischner Society 2017)

Compare with previous imaging.

**<6 mm low-risk:** no follow-up; high-risk: optional CT at 12 months.

**6–8 mm:** CT at 6–12 m, then 18–24 m.

**>8 mm:** CT at 3 months and/or PET-CT, biopsy as needed.

Biopsy via CT-guided transthoracic, bronchoscopy (EBUS, navigational), or VATS.

### Spirometry – measurements

FVC – forced vital capacity.

FEV1 – forced expiratory volume in 1st second.

FEV1/FVC ratio (key diagnostic).

PEFR – peak expiratory flow rate.

FEF 25–75% – sensitive to small airway disease.

Flow-volume loop – shape diagnostic (e.g. scalloped in obstruction).

### Patterns

**Obstructive:** FEV1/FVC <0.70; FEV1 reduced; FVC normal or reduced. Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, CF. Reversibility (≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator) supports asthma.

**Restrictive:** FEV1/FVC normal or increased (>0.70); FEV1 and FVC reduced; TLC reduced. ILD, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular, obesity.

**Mixed:** both reduced. Sarcoidosis, advanced bronchiectasis.

### Full PFT (lung volumes, DLCO)

Body plethysmography or helium dilution – TLC, RV, FRC.

DLCO (diffusion capacity) – decreased in emphysema, ILD, anaemia, PE; increased in alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, asthma.

### Indications

Diagnose asthma, COPD, restrictive lung disease.

Monitor disease progression and treatment response.

Pre-operative assessment for thoracic or upper-abdominal surgery.

Occupational lung disease assessment.

Disability evaluation.

### Contraindications (relative)

Recent MI (<1 month), unstable angina, recent eye/abdominal/thoracic surgery, pneumothorax, haemoptysis, severe respiratory distress.

### Definition

Acute occlusion of pulmonary arterial circulation by embolus, most commonly thrombus dislodged from a deep venous thrombus, less commonly air, fat, amniotic fluid, or tumour. Together with DVT, constitutes venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Risk factors (Virchow's triad)

**Stasis:** Recent surgery (especially orthopaedic), prolonged immobilisation, long-haul travel, paralysis, plaster cast.

**Endothelial injury:** Trauma, central venous catheter, pelvic surgery, IBD, vasculitis.

**Hypercoagulability:** Pregnancy and puerperium, OCP/HRT, malignancy (Trousseau), inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin III, prothrombin G20210A), antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, dehydration, nephrotic syndrome.

### Clinical features

Sudden dyspnoea (commonest – >80%), pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis (classic triad in <20%).

**Massive PE:** syncope, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, sudden death.

Tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia, low-grade fever, gallop rhythm, loud P2, raised JVP; pleural rub if infarction.

Signs of DVT in lower limbs – unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness.

### Investigations

Pulse oximetry, ABG (Type 1 RF, A-a gradient widened, respiratory alkalosis).

ECG – sinus tachycardia commonest; S1Q3T3 classical but uncommon; T wave inversion V1–V4; RBBB.

CXR – often normal; Hampton's hump (peripheral wedge), Westermark's sign (oligaemia), Fleischner sign (enlarged PA).

D-dimer – sensitive (>500 ng/mL), not specific; used to exclude PE in low-Wells probability.

CT pulmonary angiogram – investigation of choice.

V/Q scan – if CTPA contraindicated (renal failure, pregnancy).

Echocardiography – RV dilatation/dysfunction (McConnell's sign), pulmonary hypertension; risk-stratifies PE.

Lower-limb compression USS for DVT.

Troponin, BNP – risk stratification.

Thrombophilia screen if unprovoked or recurrent.

### Management

**Risk-stratify:** PESI / sPESI score; haemodynamic stability; RV dysfunction; troponin elevation.

High-risk (massive PE, hypotensive): IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 h, followed by heparin. Surgical or catheter-directed embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated.

Intermediate-risk (sub-massive, RV dysfunction): anticoagulation with LMWH/UFH; consider thrombolysis if deterioration.

**Low-risk:** anticoagulation – LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD), then DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or warfarin INR 2–3. DOACs are first-line (except active cancer – LMWH preferred, or pregnancy – LMWH only).

**Duration:** provoked 3 months; unprovoked ≥6 months or indefinite if low bleeding risk; cancer-associated for as long as cancer active.

IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE on anticoagulation.

**Supportive:** O₂, IV fluids, vasopressors (noradrenaline) if hypotensive.

**Prevention:** VTE risk-assess all medical inpatients; mechanical (compression stockings, IPC) + pharmacological (LMWH 40 mg OD, fondaparinux) prophylaxis.

Fig 7. Acute pulmonary embolism – diagnostic and management algorithm.

(See Q24 above for the comprehensive answer on acute PE. The essence summarised here for this SN.)

### Risk factors

Recent surgery, immobilisation, malignancy, OCP/HRT, pregnancy and puerperium, prior VTE, inherited thrombophilias, antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, smoking, indwelling catheter, long-haul travel, IBD, nephrotic syndrome.

### Investigations

Wells score / Geneva score to estimate probability.

D-dimer for low-probability (rule-out).

CT pulmonary angiogram (first-line).

V/Q scan – pregnancy, renal failure.

Echocardiogram – RV strain, risk-stratify.

Compression USS legs, ECG, troponin, BNP.

### Management

Anticoagulation – LMWH then DOAC or warfarin INR 2-3.

Thrombolysis (alteplase) – haemodynamically unstable.

Surgical / catheter embolectomy – thrombolysis contraindicated.

IVC filter – anticoagulation contraindicated.

**Duration:** 3 months provoked; ≥6 months unprovoked; indefinite if cancer or recurrent.

### Overview

**Renal function tests assess:** (1) GFR, (2) tubular function, (3) glomerular permeability (proteinuria), (4) urinary sediment, (5) renal anatomy. Used for screening, diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of kidney disease.

### 1. Assessment of GFR

Direct (Exogenous Markers — gold standard, research)

Inulin clearance — gold standard; cumbersome.

Iohexol, iothalamate, EDTA clearance — used clinically when accurate GFR needed (transplant donor, chemotherapy dosing).

### Endogenous Markers

**Serum Creatinine (Cr):** Serum Creatinine (Cr): Normal 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (M), 0.6–1.1 (F). Easy, cheap. Limitations:

Affected by muscle mass (low in elderly, women, vegetarians, amputees, sarcopenia).

Insensitive in early CKD ('creatinine-blind range' — GFR can drop to 50% before Cr rises).

Affected by drugs blocking tubular secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine).

Diet — cooked meat ↑ Cr.

**Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas:** Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas: Calculated from serum Cr + age + sex (± race, removed 2021).

CKD-EPI 2021 (PREFERRED — race-free) — most accurate across all ranges.

MDRD — older; less accurate at normal/high GFR.

Cockcroft-Gault — older; uses weight; used for drug dosing.

Schwartz (children) — eGFR = k × height/Cr.

**Creatinine Clearance (24-h):** Creatinine Clearance (24-h): Cr clearance = (Urine Cr × Urine volume) / Plasma Cr. Limitations: incomplete urine collection, overestimates GFR (tubular secretion of Cr 10–15%, more with low GFR). Less used now than eGFR. Adequate collection: Cr × 1.5 (males) / 1.2 (females) g/kg/d.

**Cystatin C:** Cystatin C: Constant cellular production; freely filtered; not reabsorbed; not secreted. Independent of muscle mass. Useful in elderly, sarcopenic, paediatric. CKD-EPI Cr-cystatin C combined — most accurate. Expensive.

**Blood urea / BUN:** Blood urea / BUN: Normal 7–25 mg/dL. Affected by protein intake, GI bleeding (↑), liver disease (↓), hydration. Urea:Cr ratio > 100 → pre-renal / GI bleed.

### 2. Glomerular Permeability — Proteinuria

### Quantification

Dipstick — semi-quantitative; detects albumin > 30 mg/dL. Negative in non-albumin proteinuria (myeloma — light chain).

24-h urine protein — gold standard. Normal < 150 mg/d.

**Spot UACR (urine albumin:** creatinine ratio):

< 30 mg/g — normal

30–300 mg/g — moderately increased (microalbuminuria)

> 300 mg/g — severely increased (macroalbuminuria)

**Spot UPCR (urine protein:** creatinine ratio) — total proteinuria. PCR > 3500 mg/g = nephrotic range.

Urinary protein electrophoresis (UPEP) + immunofixation — myeloma (Bence-Jones).

Sulphosalicylic acid (SSA) test — detects total protein (incl. light chains; dipstick misses).

### Selectivity

**Selective proteinuria:** predominantly albumin (smaller MW) — MCD.

**Non-selective:** albumin + IgG + larger proteins — advanced glomerular disease.

Selectivity index = clearance of IgG / clearance of transferrin; < 0.2 = highly selective.

### 3. Tubular Function Tests

### Concentration / Dilution

Urine osmolality (random) — normal 50–1200 mOsm/kg.

Urine specific gravity — 1.005–1.030.

Water deprivation test — for diabetes insipidus (Uosm < 300 after deprivation).

ADH (DDAVP) challenge — central vs nephrogenic DI.

### Acidification

Urine pH (random) — 5–6.5 normal.

Ammonium chloride loading test — RTA diagnosis (urine pH should fall < 5.5 if normal).

Serum bicarbonate, anion gap, urinary anion gap.

### Tubular Reabsorption / Secretion

Fractional excretion of Na (FENa) — pre-renal vs ATN.

Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) — pre-renal if < 35% (use if on diuretics).

Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO₄) — TmP/GFR (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / GFR) — Fanconi syndrome (< 80%).

Glucosuria with normal serum glucose — proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi).

Aminoaciduria — Fanconi syndrome.

**Tubular markers:** NGAL, KIM-1, IL-18 (research; early AKI biomarkers).

### 4. Urinary Sediment Examination

### 5. Imaging

**Ultrasound (USG) — first-line:** size (10–14 cm normal; < 9 cm = chronic), echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, masses, Doppler (renal artery flow, RVT).

KUB X-ray — radio-opaque stones (calcium, struvite). Cystine = semi-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent.

CT (CECT, KUB) — masses, complex cysts, stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis).

MRI / MRA — RAS, masses (avoid gadolinium if eGFR < 30 — NSF risk).

DTPA scan — split function (each kidney's contribution).

DMSA scan — cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy).

MAG-3 scan — obstruction.

Renal biopsy — definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.

### 6. Other / Specialised

Complement (C3, C4) — see Q3.

Autoantibodies — ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM.

Anti-PLA2R — membranous.

SPEP / UPEP / IFE — myeloma.

Cryoglobulins.

### Approach to Interpretation

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.353; KDIGO CKD 2012; CKD-EPI 2021 race-free.

### Definition

Alcohol Use Disorder (DSM-5) is a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment / distress, manifested by ≥2 of 11 criteria in a 12-month period (replacing DSM-IV abuse + dependence). ICD-10 retains alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria) and harmful use. India has the largest population of male alcohol users in Asia; NMHS 2016 estimates prevalence of any alcohol-use disorder at 4.6% in adults (9% in men).

Hazards of alcohol (Boloor A365)

### Neurological

Acute — intoxication, blackouts, traffic accidents, traumatic brain injury, alcohol-induced psychotic disorder.

Withdrawal — tremor, seizures, delirium tremens (see below).

Chronic — Wernicke encephalopathy / Korsakoff psychosis, cerebellar degeneration (truncal ataxia, gait), peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor, painful), optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia), central pontine myelinolysis (with rapid sodium correction), Marchiafava–Bignami disease (corpus callosum demyelination), alcohol-related dementia.

### Gastrointestinal / hepatic

Acute / chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome.

Pancreatitis — acute and chronic (alcohol is the #1 cause of chronic pancreatitis in India after gallstones).

Alcoholic liver disease — fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >32 → steroids/pentoxifylline) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Oesophageal varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal / hepatopulmonary syndromes.

Malabsorption — folate, thiamine, B6, B12, Mg, Zn.

### Cardiovascular

Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcoholic), holiday heart (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke, sudden cardiac death.

### Haematological

Macrocytic anaemia (folate deficiency, direct marrow toxicity), megaloblastic, sideroblastic, haemolysis (Zieve syndrome with hepatitis + hyperlipidaemia), thrombocytopenia, leucopenia.

### Endocrine / metabolic

Hypoglycaemia (gluconeogenesis blocked), ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia / gout, hyperlipidaemia, pseudo-Cushing's.

Hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, infertility, erectile dysfunction.

### Cancer (Group I carcinogen — IARC)

Oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver (HCC), breast, colorectum.

### Obstetric

Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder — microcephaly, growth retardation, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, intellectual disability.

Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm birth.

### Psychiatric

Depression, anxiety, suicide (alcohol present in ~40% of completed suicides in India), insomnia.

Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, pathological jealousy (Othello syndrome).

### Social

Domestic violence, marital breakdown, child neglect, occupational accidents, road traffic accidents, financial ruin, legal issues.

Diagnosis — DSM-5 AUD criteria (≥2 of 11 in 12 months)

**Severity:** 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥6 severe.

Larger amounts / longer than intended.

Persistent desire / unsuccessful attempts to cut down.

Great time spent obtaining / using / recovering.

Craving.

Failure to fulfil role obligations.

Continued use despite social / interpersonal problems.

Important activities given up.

Use in physically hazardous situations.

Continued use despite physical / psychological problems.

Tolerance.

Withdrawal.

ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria — ≥3 of 6 in past year)

Strong desire / compulsion to drink.

Impaired control over use (onset, level, termination).

Withdrawal state on abstinence.

Tolerance.

Neglect of alternative interests.

Persistence despite clearly harmful consequences.

### Screening

**CAGE:** Cut down, Annoyed by criticism, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 = significant.

**AUDIT (WHO, 10 items):** 0–7 low risk, 8–15 hazardous, 16–19 harmful, ≥20 dependence.

AUDIT-C — 3-item screening tool.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (Boloor A373 ★2026)

Figure 6. Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal triage by CIWA-Ar, thiamine-first inpatient protocol, methanol-poisoning pathway and maintenance pharmacotherapy.

Time course (after last drink)

**6–12 h:** Minor withdrawal — tremor, anxiety, nausea, sweating, palpitations, insomnia, headache.

**12–24 h:** Alcoholic hallucinosis — visual / tactile / auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium and orientation (key DDx from DT).

**24–48 h:** Withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic, brief, 1–6 episodes; usually self-limited; 3% progress to status.

**48–96 h (peak 72 h):** Delirium tremens (DT) — clouded sensorium, disorientation, agitation, fluctuating consciousness, fever, autonomic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis), vivid visual / tactile (formication — 'bugs crawling') hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% untreated; 1–2% with modern care.

Risk stratification — CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised)

10 items, scored 0–7 each (orientation 0–4); total 0–67.

<8 — mild, no intervention.

8–15 — moderate, BZD treatment.

16–20 — severe.

>20 — very severe, ICU.

Management of withdrawal — Indian protocol (NIMHANS / AIIMS de-addiction)

**Inpatient if:** CIWA-Ar ≥10, history of DT / withdrawal seizures, severe medical / psychiatric comorbidity, poor support.

Thiamine FIRST, before any glucose (Wernicke prevention) — 100 mg IV/IM TDS × 3 days, then 100 mg PO OD long-term.

Wernicke / Korsakoff treatment dose: thiamine 500 mg IV TDS × 2–3 days → 250 mg IV/IM daily × 3–5 days → 100 mg PO long-term. Also IV Mg replacement (thiamine requires Mg cofactor).

**Benzodiazepines — first-line:** chlordiazepoxide 25–50 mg PO q4–6h symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar guided), tapered over 5–7 days. Diazepam 10–20 mg PO/IV q1–2h for severe.

Lorazepam preferred in hepatic dysfunction, elderly (no active metabolites): 2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h.

Phenobarbital — for refractory / BZD-resistant DT.

IV fluids (NS + 5%D), electrolyte correction — Mg 1–2 g IV q12h, K, PO4.

Multivitamin, folate 5 mg/d.

AVOID antipsychotics as monotherapy (↓ seizure threshold); use only haloperidol low dose if psychosis / agitation persists despite adequate BZD.

AVOID alcohol substitution.

Monitor vital signs q1–2h initially; CIWA-Ar q1–4h.

Treat fever, sepsis, pneumonia (high risk in DT), dehydration, rhabdomyolysis.

### Withdrawal seizures

**Treat acute seizure:** IV lorazepam 2–4 mg or diazepam 10 mg.

**Prevention:** adequate BZD coverage during detox.

Long-term anti-epileptics not needed unless underlying epilepsy.

Maintenance — relapse prevention (anti-craving)

**Naltrexone:** 50 mg PO OD (or 380 mg IM monthly). μ-opioid antagonist; ↓ craving and pleasure of drinking (COMBINE trial). Avoid in liver failure, opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); LFT monitoring.

**Acamprosate:** 666 mg PO TDS (2 g/d in <60 kg). NMDA modulator; ↓ relapse rate (PROJECT MATCH). Safe in liver disease; needs adequate renal function.

**Disulfiram:** 250 mg PO OD (max 500 mg). Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor; causes aversive reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, hypotension) on alcohol ingestion. Supervised dosing (family member). Avoid in CAD, severe psychiatric illness, pregnancy, peripheral neuropathy. Warn re: hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrups, perfumes).

Baclofen (off-label, useful in liver disease): 10–30 mg TDS; GABA-B agonist; reduces craving especially in cirrhotics where naltrexone and disulfiram unsafe (ANRS-BACLOVILLE).

**Topiramate, gabapentin:** Off-label adjuncts.

Psychosocial interventions (cornerstone — often dominate outcome)

Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MI / MET) — stage-of-change-based.

CBT — relapse prevention, coping skills.

12-step facilitation / Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) — Indian chapters widespread.

Family therapy, community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT).

Residential rehabilitation for severe / relapsing.

Treat comorbid depression / anxiety / PTSD.

Indian de-addiction infrastructure: AIIMS NDDTC, NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine, Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP — MoHFW), state-level Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs).

Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning — Boloor A367

Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in adulterated illicit liquor ('hooch'), industrial solvents, anti-freeze, windshield-washer fluid and formalin. Toxic dose ~10 ml; fatal 30 ml.

### Toxicokinetics

Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → FORMALDEHYDE → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → FORMIC ACID — the principal toxin (causes optic neuritis, metabolic acidosis).

### Clinical features

Latent period 12–24 h (longer if co-ingested ethanol).

Phase 1 — CNS depression (mild intoxication / inebriation).

Phase 2 (12–24 h) — N/V, abdominal pain, headache, vertigo.

Phase 3 — visual disturbance ('snowstorm', blurring, blindness), optic disc hyperaemia / oedema → permanent blindness.

Phase 4 — severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) with ↑ osmolar gap, Kussmaul respiration, seizures, coma, parkinsonism (putaminal necrosis), death.

### Investigations

ABG — severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2, HCO3 <10).

Anion gap — high (>20).

Osmolar gap — high (>10 mOsm/kg) early, falls as methanol is metabolised.

Serum methanol level — confirmatory (toxic >20 mg/dL; severe >50).

Fundus — optic disc hyperaemia / oedema.

MRI brain — putaminal haemorrhage / necrosis (classic).

### Management

ABC, IV access, gastric lavage (if <1 h), activated charcoal NOT effective (poorly adsorbed).

Block ADH (prevent toxic metabolite formation):

- FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole) — drug of choice if available; 15 mg/kg IV load → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses → 15 mg/kg q12h thereafter (induces own metabolism). Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL + acidosis resolved + asymptomatic.

- ETHANOL (alternative if no fomepizole) — IV loading 10 ml/kg of 10% ethanol over 30 min → 1.5 ml/kg/h infusion. Target blood ethanol 100 mg/dL. Cheaper and widely available in India.

FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1 mg/kg IV q4–6h (max 50 mg) × 6 doses — accelerates formate metabolism. Folic acid acceptable if folinic unavailable.

Correct acidosis — IV sodium bicarbonate to keep pH >7.2.

HAEMODIALYSIS — definitive removal of methanol and formate. Indications: serum methanol ≥50 mg/dL, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), visual / mental status changes, electrolyte imbalance refractory, renal failure.

Supportive — ICU, mechanical ventilation, treat seizures.

Complications of alcohol use (summary)

Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis (irreversible amnesia, confabulation).

Delirium tremens — mortality 5–15% untreated.

Cirrhosis, HCC, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy.

Suicide, accidental injuries, road traffic accidents.

Family disruption, economic loss, occupational impairment.

### Prognosis

Without treatment — progressive decline, premature mortality.

With comprehensive treatment (pharmacotherapy + psychosocial) — 30–50% achieve sustained remission at 1 year.

Better with stable social support, employment, no comorbid psychiatric illness, motivation for change.

Worse with antisocial personality, depression / suicide history, polysubstance use.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18 + Ch.16 (toxicology); Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Alcohol Use Disorders; NIMHANS / AIIMS NDDTC protocols; COMBINE 2006; PROJECT MATCH; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology — methanol/fomepizole; DSM-5; ICD-10/11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|278.note:
### Combined Notes (5 topics)

Common inhaled corticosteroids (Indian availability)

Budesonide (Budecort, Pulmicort) – MDI 100/200 µg; DPI 200/400 µg; neb 0.5/1 mg.

Fluticasone propionate (Flohale, Flixotide) – MDI 50/125/250 µg; DPI 100/250/500 µg.

Fluticasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg (once-daily).

Beclomethasone dipropionate (Beclate) – MDI 50/100/250 µg.

Ciclesonide (Alvesco) – MDI 80/160 µg.

Mometasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg.

Combination ICS-LABA inhalers (most prescribed)

Budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort, Foracort) – preferred Track 1 GINA reliever-controller.

Fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide).

Fluticasone furoate + vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta).

Beclomethasone + formoterol.

### Triple-therapy inhalers (ICS-LABA-LAMA)

Fluticasone + umeclidinium + vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta).

Budesonide + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

Beclomethasone + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

### Adverse effects

**Local:** oral candidiasis (Candida albicans – use spacer + rinse mouth), dysphonia, throat irritation.

Systemic (with high dose / long-term): osteoporosis, skin thinning, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, adrenal suppression, increased pneumonia risk in COPD.

### Indications

Asthma – mainstay of controller therapy from GINA Step 1 onwards.

COPD – with LABA in patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥100/300.

Other obstructive airways disease (some forms of bronchiectasis with asthma overlap).

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

### Definition

Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. Confirmed by gastric scintigraphy showing > 10% retention at 4 h. Commonest cause is diabetic autonomic neuropathy (especially long-standing T1DM/T2DM); idiopathic, post-viral, post-surgical (vagotomy, fundoplication), drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 agonists), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), Parkinson's.

### Symptoms

Early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting (often undigested food hours after meal), upper abdominal pain, weight loss, poor glycaemic control in diabetics (mismatch with insulin).

### Pharmacological Management

### 1. Prokinetics (first-line)

**Metoclopramide:** Metoclopramide: 5–10 mg PO/IV TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. MOA: D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist + acetylcholine release. Black-box warning: tardive dyskinesia (limit to ≤ 12 weeks); extrapyramidal SE, hyperprolactinaemia.

**Domperidone:** Domperidone: 10 mg PO TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. Peripheral D2 antagonist — does NOT cross BBB → fewer EPS. Caution: QT prolongation (avoid in cardiac disease, electrolyte abnormalities); lower dose in elderly; not available in USA but widely used in India.

**Erythromycin:** Erythromycin: 50–250 mg PO TDS (lower dose for prokinesis) or 3 mg/kg IV; motilin receptor agonist. Tachyphylaxis (loss of effect after 2–4 wk) — limit use. Useful as IV in acute settings (e.g. pre-OGD for blood clearance).

**Cisapride:** Cisapride: Withdrawn in most countries (QT prolongation, torsades).

**Prucalopride:** Prucalopride: 1–2 mg OD — 5-HT4 agonist; emerging evidence for refractory gastroparesis.

### 2. Antiemetics (symptomatic)

Ondansetron 4–8 mg PO/IV TDS — 5-HT3 antagonist; first-line for symptom control.

Prochlorperazine, promethazine — alternatives; sedation, EPS.

Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist, for refractory.

### 3. Other / Emerging

Mirtazapine 15 mg HS — TCA-related; appetite + nausea relief.

Botulinum toxin pyloric injection — only short-term (no longer recommended in guidelines).

Ghrelin agonists (relamorelin) — in trials.

### Non-Pharmacological

**Dietary:** small frequent meals (5–6/day), low-fat, low-fibre, soft/liquid consistency.

Strict glycaemic control in diabetics (hyperglycaemia worsens emptying).

Avoid carbonated drinks, alcohol, smoking.

Stop / reduce offending drugs (opioids, GLP-1 agonists if possible, anticholinergics).

Vitamin / micronutrient supplementation (chronic malnutrition risk).

### Refractory Cases

Gastric electrical stimulation (Enterra device) — FDA HUD; selected refractory cases.

Pyloroplasty / G-POEM (gastric per-oral endoscopic myotomy).

**Surgical:** subtotal gastrectomy, jejunostomy feeding tube.

TPN in severe cachexia.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ACG Gastroparesis 2022; AGA 2022.

### Overview

IBD (UC, Crohn's) treatment uses a step-up or top-down approach based on severity, location, and prognostic factors. Goals: induce + maintain remission, achieve mucosal healing, prevent complications, avoid surgery.

### Classification of IBD Drugs

### 1. Aminosalicylates (5-ASA / Mesalamine)

**Sulfasalazine:** Sulfasalazine: 1–2 g BD-QID. Sulfapyridine + 5-ASA. Cleaved by colonic bacteria. SE: nausea, headache, hypersensitivity, oligospermia (reversible).

**Mesalamine:** Mesalamine: 2.4–4.8 g/d divided. pH-dependent or time-released formulations (Asacol, Pentasa, Salofalk). For colonic and ileal disease.

**Olsalazine, Balsalazide:** Olsalazine, Balsalazide: 5-ASA dimers / azo-bonded; site-specific colonic release.

**Topical 5-ASA:** Topical 5-ASA: Suppositories (proctitis), enemas (left-sided UC) — adjunct or monotherapy.

**Indications:** Indications: Mild-moderate UC (induction + maintenance); less effective in Crohn's (some role in colonic CD).

### 2. Corticosteroids

**Prednisolone:** Prednisolone: 40–60 mg/d PO, taper over 8–12 weeks. Severe UC: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h or methylprednisolone 60 mg/d. Induction only — NOT maintenance.

**Budesonide:** Budesonide: 9 mg/d × 8 wk for mild-moderate ileal/right colonic Crohn's. Topically active; high first-pass metabolism → fewer systemic SE.

**Topical (PR foam/enema):** Topical (PR foam/enema): Hydrocortisone, budesonide foam for distal UC.

Steroid dependence (cannot taper) or refractoriness (failure of high dose for 7–10 d) → step up to immunomodulators or biologics.

Long-term steroid avoidance — bone protection (Ca/Vit D, DEXA), DM/HTN screening, infection.

### 3. Immunomodulators (steroid-sparing)

Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine:Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine: AZA 2–2.5 mg/kg/d (6-MP 1–1.5 mg/kg/d). Check TPMT activity before starting (deficiency → severe myelosuppression). Onset 6–12 wk. Maintenance.

**Methotrexate:** Methotrexate: 25 mg/wk IM/SC × 16 wk → 15 mg/wk maintenance (Crohn's). Folic acid 5 mg/wk. Less effective in UC.

**Cyclosporine:** Cyclosporine: 2 mg/kg/d IV (or 4 mg/kg/d PO) for steroid-refractory severe UC — rescue therapy. Bridge to AZA/biologics. Trough 200–400 ng/mL.

**Tacrolimus:** Tacrolimus: Alternative calcineurin inhibitor.

**Monitoring:** CBC, LFT every 2 wk × first month, then 3-monthly.

**Risks:** bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis (AZA), lymphoma (slightly raised), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (rare in young men on AZA + anti-TNF).

- Biologics (anti-TNF and others)

**Infliximab (anti-TNF):** Infliximab (anti-TNF): 5 mg/kg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk maintenance. Can escalate to 10 mg/kg or every 6 wk if loss of response.

**Adalimumab (anti-TNF):** Adalimumab (anti-TNF): 160 mg SC week 0 → 80 mg week 2 → 40 mg every 2 wk maintenance.

**Golimumab:** Golimumab: 200 mg SC week 0 → 100 mg week 2 → 50–100 mg every 4 wk (UC).

**Certolizumab pegol:** Certolizumab pegol: 400 mg SC at 0, 2, 4 wk → every 4 wk (Crohn's).

**Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7):** Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7): 300 mg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk. Gut-selective; lower infection risk.

**Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40):** Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40): Weight-based loading IV → 90 mg SC every 8–12 wk maintenance. Crohn's + UC.

**Risankizumab (anti-IL23):** Risankizumab (anti-IL23): 600 mg IV at 0, 4, 8 wk → 360 mg SC every 8 wk (Crohn's).

### Pre-biologic screening (essential)

**TB screening:** chest X-ray + Mantoux/IGRA (especially Indian context — high TB burden, anti-TNF reactivates latent TB).

Hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV.

Vaccinate live attenuated BEFORE starting (yellow fever, varicella).

CBC, LFT, albumin baseline.

### 5. Small Molecule Drugs (new class)

**Tofacitinib:** Tofacitinib: Pan-JAK inhibitor; 10 mg BD × 8 wk → 5 mg BD maintenance. Moderate-severe UC. Caution: VTE risk (especially with risk factors), shingles.

**Upadacitinib:** Upadacitinib: JAK1 selective; 45 mg/d × 8 wk → 15 mg/d (or 30 mg/d) maintenance. UC + Crohn's.

**Ozanimod:** Ozanimod: S1P modulator; UC.

**Etrasimod:** Etrasimod: S1P modulator; newer.

### 6. Antibiotics

**Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin:** Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin: For perianal Crohn's, fistulae, abscess, pouchitis. 400 mg TDS + 500 mg BD for 4–8 wk.

**Vancomycin PO:** Vancomycin PO: For C. difficile co-infection.

### 7. Adjunctive / Supportive

Iron supplementation (oral or IV; IV preferred in moderate-severe).

B12 (terminal ileitis / resection).

Vitamin D, calcium (osteoporosis prevention).

Probiotics (some evidence for pouchitis; mild UC).

Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) — emerging in UC, very promising in pouchitis.

### Indication-Based Algorithm

### Ulcerative Colitis

**Mild proctitis/distal:** topical 5-ASA, topical steroid.

**Mild-moderate extensive:** PO + topical 5-ASA, PO steroids if needed.

**Moderate-severe:** PO steroids → AZA → biologic (anti-TNF, vedo, ustek) or tofacitinib.

**Severe:** IV hydrocortisone; day-3 response (Travis criteria — > 8 stools or 3–8 + CRP > 45 = high colectomy risk); rescue infliximab 5 mg/kg or cyclosporine 2 mg/kg/d IV.

**Refractory:** colectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (curative).

### Crohn's Disease

**Mild ileal:** budesonide 9 mg/d.

**Moderate:** PO prednisolone → AZA / methotrexate maintenance.

Severe / fistulating / perianal: anti-TNF ± AZA ('top-down'); anti-TNF + seton for perianal fistulae; metronidazole.

**Stricture:** balloon dilatation; surgery (stricturoplasty, segmental resection).

**Goal:** deep remission (clinical + endoscopic mucosal healing).

Fig 10. IBD — UC vs Crohn's stepwise algorithm.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ECCO 2022 UC + Crohn's guidelines; ACG 2019; ISG IBD India consensus.

### Definition

Portal hypertension = pathological elevation of pressure in the portal venous system, diagnosed clinically (varices, splenomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy) or by hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) > 5 mm Hg (clinically significant > 10 mm Hg; variceal threshold > 12).

### Classification by Site of Obstruction

**Pre-hepatic:** portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis (post-pancreatitis), schistosomiasis (Indian).

**Intra-hepatic:** cirrhosis (commonest), idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN (NCIPH/INCPH — important in India), nodular regenerative hyperplasia, primary biliary cholangitis.

**Post-hepatic:** Budd-Chiari, IVC obstruction, constrictive pericarditis, right heart failure.

### Drug Classes

### 1. Non-Selective Beta-Blockers (NSBB) — first-line

**Propranolol:** Propranolol: Start 20–40 mg BD → titrate to HR 55–60 bpm (or 25% reduction from baseline). Max 320 mg/d. β1 + β2 blockade → reduced cardiac output + splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal flow + pressure.

**Nadolol:** Nadolol: 20–80 mg/d. Longer half-life, once-daily dosing; preferred over propranolol in some patients (less compliance issues).

**Carvedilol:** Carvedilol: 6.25 mg BD → titrate to 12.5 BD (or 25 mg/d in some). Non-selective β + α1 antagonism → further reduces portal pressure via intrahepatic vasodilation. Preferred in compensated cirrhosis (Baveno VII).

**Goals:** Goals: ↓ HVPG > 20% from baseline OR ≤ 12 mm Hg → reduces variceal bleed and mortality.

**Contraindications:** Contraindications: Severe asthma/COPD, bradycardia (HR < 55), AV block, decompensated heart failure, refractory ascites (caution — may worsen).

**Indications:** Indications: Primary prophylaxis (medium/large varices, or small varices with high-risk features), secondary prophylaxis after first variceal bleed.

### 2. Vasoactive Drugs for Acute Variceal Bleed

Terlipressin (1st-line in India):Terlipressin (1st-line in India): 2 mg IV bolus q4h × 24–48 h → 1 mg q4h × 5 d total. Vasopressin analogue → V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure. Indian context: cheap, widely available, DOC for acute variceal bleed + HRS.

**Octreotide:** Octreotide: 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Somatostatin analogue → inhibits splanchnic vasodilator release (glucagon, VIP) → ↓ portal flow. Useful when terlipressin unavailable.

**Somatostatin:** Somatostatin: 250 µg IV bolus → 250 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Less commonly used in India.

**Vasopressin:** Vasopressin: Largely replaced — significant systemic vasoconstriction (coronary, mesenteric, peripheral) → ischaemic complications.

### 3. Antibiotics in Variceal Bleed

**Ceftriaxone:** Ceftriaxone: 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d. Reduces SBP, rebleed risk, and mortality (Garcia-Tsao). Norfloxacin 400 mg BD PO as alternative in countries with low quinolone resistance.

### 4. Diuretics for Ascites

**Spironolactone:** Spironolactone: 100 mg/d → titrate to 400 mg/d (in 100 mg increments). First-line; competitive aldosterone antagonist. SE: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia.

**Furosemide:** Furosemide: Add 40 mg/d → titrate to 160 mg/d. Combined with spironolactone in 100:40 ratio. Loop diuretic; SE: hypokalaemia, AKI, hyponatraemia.

**Amiloride:** Amiloride: Alternative to spironolactone; no gynaecomastia. Less potent.

**Goals:** Goals: Daily weight loss ≤ 0.5 kg (no oedema) / ≤ 1 kg (with oedema). Daily Na restriction 88 mmol (2 g sodium).

**Caution:** Caution: Watch for HRS, encephalopathy (over-diuresis), hyponatraemia (Na < 125 → stop diuretics).

### 5. Albumin

**Indicated for:** large-volume paracentesis (8 g per L removed > 5 L); SBP (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 — reduces HRS, mortality); HRS (1 g/kg day 1 then 20–40 g/d); spontaneous decompensation with hypoalbuminaemia.

### 6. HRS-Specific

**Terlipressin + Albumin:** Terlipressin + Albumin: Terlipressin 1 mg q4–6 h IV (titrate to 2 mg q4h) + albumin 1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/d × 5–14 d. Reverses HRS in 30–50%.

**Noradrenaline + Albumin:** Noradrenaline + Albumin: 0.5–3 mg/h infusion (target MAP rise 10 mm Hg) — alternative in ICU.

Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin:Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin: Less effective; outpatient alternative.

### 7. Hepatic Encephalopathy

Lactulose 30–45 ml TDS → titrate to 2–3 soft stools/d.

Rifaximin 550 mg BD — maintenance / recurrent.

See Q14 for full details.

- Statins (emerging in compensated cirrhosis)

Simvastatin 20–40 mg/d — improves liver microcirculation, reduces portal pressure, may improve survival (Abraldes 2016, EASL 2018). Caution in decompensated.

### Comprehensive Algorithm

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (Child B/C, red wale marks) → NSBB or carvedilol.

Medium/large varices → NSBB / carvedilol OR EVL.

**Combined NSBB + EVL:** NOT recommended primarily.

Acute Bleed (within 12 h)

Resuscitate (restrictive Hb 7), terlipressin + ceftriaxone + IV PPI; urgent OGD with EVL.

Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

NSBB / carvedilol + EVL every 2–4 wk till varices eradicated.

**Refractory:** TIPS / liver transplant evaluation.

Fig 11. Portal HTN — drug algorithm.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.541; Baveno VII (2022); AASLD 2017; EASL 2018; Indian Society of Gastroenterology (ISG) Consensus.

GENERAL MEDICINE|279.note:
Haemoptysis = coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract (below the larynx). Massive haemoptysis = >200–600 mL in 24 h.

### Causes by category

### Infective (commonest in India):

Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially cavitary or post-tubercular bronchiectasis with Rasmussen aneurysm).

Bronchiectasis.

Lung abscess.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella, anaerobes).

Pulmonary aspergilloma (mycetoma in old TB cavity).

Paragonimiasis (in endemic areas).

### Neoplastic:

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Bronchial carcinoid.

Metastatic lung tumours.

### Vascular:

Pulmonary embolism with infarction.

Mitral stenosis (pulmonary venous hypertension).

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (HHT/Osler-Weber-Rendu).

Aortobronchial fistula.

### Inflammatory / autoimmune:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

Goodpasture's syndrome (anti-GBM antibody).

SLE-associated pulmonary haemorrhage.

Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis (in children).

Iatrogenic / trauma / coagulopathy:

Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs), thrombolytics.

Bronchoscopic biopsy, transbronchial biopsy.

Tracheostomy, Swan-Ganz catheter (pulmonary artery rupture).

Chest trauma.

Cocaine use.

**Pseudohaemoptysis:** epistaxis, haematemesis swallowed and regurgitated, Serratia marcescens in dentures, oral bleeding.

### Approach

Distinguish from haematemesis (bright red, frothy, alkaline pH, mixed with sputum vs dark red, acidic, with food, melena later).

Stabilise (ABCDE) if massive – airway, position bleeding side down, IV access, group and cross-match.

CXR, CT chest with contrast/CT pulmonary angiogram, bronchoscopy (rigid for massive), echo, CBC, coagulation, sputum AFB.

Massive haemoptysis – ICU, bronchial artery embolisation, endobronchial tamponade, surgical resection if focal source.
