### Combined Notes (8 topics)

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

Fig 1. Anaemia workup by MCV.

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

Fig 3. Megaloblastic anaemia — workup and treatment.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.

Fig 5. Sickle cell disease — crisis management.

### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

Tailor therapy to type/etiology.

Monitor response (rise in Hb 1–2 g/dL per month is typical for nutritional anaemias).

### Specific modalities

### 1. Oral iron

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) TDS — first-line for IDA.

Alternate-day dosing 100–200 mg may improve absorption and tolerance.

**AEs:** GI upset, constipation, dark stools.

### 2. Parenteral iron

Iron sucrose, FCM (Ferinject), iron isomaltoside (see Q18).

### 3. Vitamin B12

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week → weekly × 4 weeks → monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Oral 1000–2000 µg/day — feasible alternative.

### 4. Folate

Folic acid 5 mg PO daily × 1–4 months.

Always check/replace B12 first (avoid SACD).

### 5. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)

Epoetin / darbepoetin / roxadustat — CKD, chemo, MDS (see Q33).

### 6. Blood transfusion

Hb <7 g/dL (stable), <8 (cardiac), or symptomatic regardless.

Acute haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to other therapy.

### 7. Disease-modifying agents

Hydroxyurea — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia intermedia.

Lenalidomide — del(5q) MDS.

Luspatercept — β-thalassaemia, MDS-RS.

Eculizumab / ravulizumab — PNH, AIHA (cold).

Caplacizumab — TTP.

- Steroids & immunosuppression

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day — AIHA (first-line).

Rituximab, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide — refractory AIHA, ITP.

ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag — aplastic anaemia.

### 9. Splenectomy

Hereditary spherocytosis, β-thalassaemia, refractory ITP/AIHA.

### 10. Allogeneic HSCT

Curative for severe aplastic anaemia, severe sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia major, Fanconi anaemia, PNH (selected).

- Gene therapy (emerging)

Casgevy / Lyfgenia (CRISPR-edited HSC) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia — FDA-approved 2023.

### Combined Notes (10 topics)

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

Fig 1. Anaemia workup by MCV.

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.

Fig 5. Sickle cell disease — crisis management.

### Indications

Intolerance to oral iron (GI side effects despite dose modification).

Malabsorption – coeliac disease, gastric surgery, IBD.

Non-compliance.

Continued blood loss exceeding capacity of oral iron.

Pregnancy with severe anaemia in 2nd/3rd trimester or intolerance.

CKD anaemia, especially on EPO therapy.

Heart failure with iron deficiency (functional or absolute).

Need for rapid replenishment (pre-operative).

Anaemia of chronic disease where oral inefficient (hepcidin-mediated block).

### Preparations and doses

Iron sucrose – 100–200 mg slow IV, max 600 mg/week; multiple doses needed; safe in pregnancy.

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM, e.g. Ferinject, Encicarb) – single dose up to 1000 mg over 15 min IV infusion; preferred for rapid correction; weekly if larger doses needed; widely used in India.

Iron isomaltoside / derisomaltose – up to 20 mg/kg in single infusion.

Ferumoxytol – 510 mg IV.

Iron dextran – high dose possible (total dose infusion) but anaphylaxis risk; test dose mandatory; rarely used.

Total iron deficit (Ganzoni formula)

Total iron required (mg) = Weight (kg) × (Target Hb − Actual Hb) × 2.4 + iron stores (500 mg adults / 15 mg/kg <35 kg).

Target Hb typically 15 g/dL (men), 14 g/dL (women); 11 g/dL in pregnancy.

### Adverse effects

**Infusion reaction:** fever, flushing, myalgia, hypotension (usually mild).

Anaphylaxis – rare with newer formulations (~1:200,000 FCM); higher with dextran.

Hypophosphataemia – particularly with FCM and iron isomaltoside (repeated doses).

Extravasation – skin staining (administer in proximal vein, stop if pain at site).

Iron overload – haemochromatosis-like with prolonged unmonitored use.

### Administration precautions

Resuscitation facility available (anaphylaxis).

Monitor BP/pulse/SpO₂.

Avoid in 1st trimester of pregnancy and active infection (except life-threatening anaemia).

Reassess Hb / ferritin / TSAT in 4–8 weeks post-infusion.

### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

Tailor therapy to type/etiology.

Monitor response (rise in Hb 1–2 g/dL per month is typical for nutritional anaemias).

### Specific modalities

### 1. Oral iron

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) TDS — first-line for IDA.

Alternate-day dosing 100–200 mg may improve absorption and tolerance.

**AEs:** GI upset, constipation, dark stools.

### 2. Parenteral iron

Iron sucrose, FCM (Ferinject), iron isomaltoside (see Q18).

### 3. Vitamin B12

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week → weekly × 4 weeks → monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Oral 1000–2000 µg/day — feasible alternative.

### 4. Folate

Folic acid 5 mg PO daily × 1–4 months.

Always check/replace B12 first (avoid SACD).

### 5. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)

Epoetin / darbepoetin / roxadustat — CKD, chemo, MDS (see Q33).

### 6. Blood transfusion

Hb <7 g/dL (stable), <8 (cardiac), or symptomatic regardless.

Acute haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to other therapy.

### 7. Disease-modifying agents

Hydroxyurea — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia intermedia.

Lenalidomide — del(5q) MDS.

Luspatercept — β-thalassaemia, MDS-RS.

Eculizumab / ravulizumab — PNH, AIHA (cold).

Caplacizumab — TTP.

- Steroids & immunosuppression

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day — AIHA (first-line).

Rituximab, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide — refractory AIHA, ITP.

ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag — aplastic anaemia.

### 9. Splenectomy

Hereditary spherocytosis, β-thalassaemia, refractory ITP/AIHA.

### 10. Allogeneic HSCT

Curative for severe aplastic anaemia, severe sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia major, Fanconi anaemia, PNH (selected).

- Gene therapy (emerging)

Casgevy / Lyfgenia (CRISPR-edited HSC) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia — FDA-approved 2023.

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Classification

Acute (within 24 h) vs Delayed (after 24 h); Immune vs Non-immune.

ACUTE reactions (within 24 hours)

- Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) – commonest

**Cause:** recipient antibodies vs donor leukocytes; cytokines in stored blood.

**Features:** fever >1°C rise, chills, no haemolysis.

**Mx:** stop transfusion, exclude AHTR & sepsis; paracetamol; leuko-reduced components for future.

- Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) – most feared

**Cause:** ABO incompatibility (clerical error); IgM-mediated, complement-activating, intravascular haemolysis.

**Features:** fever, chills, loin/back pain, dyspnoea, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, DIC, AKI.

**Mx:** STOP TRANSFUSION immediately, IV NS, IV fluids to maintain urine output >100 mL/h, mannitol/frusemide, manage DIC, treat shock; send sample for DAT, compatibility recheck; report to blood bank.

- Allergic / urticarial reaction

**Cause:** recipient IgE vs donor plasma proteins.

**Features:** urticaria, pruritus only; no fever.

**Mx:** stop, antihistamines; can resume slowly if symptoms settle. Washed components for future.

### 4. Anaphylactic reaction

**Cause:** IgA-deficient recipient with anti-IgA; or other severe hypersensitivity.

**Features:** bronchospasm, hypotension, angioedema, shock in first minutes.

**Mx:** STOP, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg, IV fluids, O₂, steroids, antihistamine; IgA-deficient (washed) components in future; check IgA level.

### 5. TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury)

**Cause:** donor anti-leukocyte / HLA / HNA antibodies activate recipient neutrophils → pulmonary capillary leak.

**Features:** acute hypoxaemia + bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion; no LV failure.

**Mx:** stop transfusion, supportive ventilation (lung-protective), supplemental O₂; usually resolves in 48–96 h. Future: male-only plasma (Indian NACO).

### 6. TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload)

**Cause:** volume overload (elderly, cardiac/renal disease, rapid infusion).

**Features:** dyspnoea, raised JVP, basal crackles, hypertension, raised BNP, pulmonary oedema within 6 h.

**Mx:** stop or slow transfusion, sit up, O₂, IV frusemide. Prevent: slow rate (1 mL/kg/h), diuretic between units.

- Bacterial contamination / septic transfusion

**Cause:** contaminated unit (platelets > RBC); Gram +ve and −ve organisms.

**Features:** rigors, high fever, hypotension, shock during/just after transfusion.

**Mx:** STOP, blood cultures (from patient AND unit), broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, supportive.

- Citrate toxicity / hypocalcaemia (massive transfusion)

**Cause:** citrate anticoagulant binds Ca²⁺ when liver metabolism is overwhelmed.

**Features:** paraesthesiae, tetany, arrhythmia, prolonged QT.

**Mx:** IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% slow.

### 9. Hypothermia

**Cause:** rapid infusion of cold blood.

**Mx:** blood warmer.

- Hyperkalaemia (especially stored blood, neonates, AKI)

**Cause:** efflux of K⁺ from stored RBCs.

**Mx:** standard hyperkalaemia management; fresh blood for high-risk groups.

DELAYED reactions (after 24 hours)

- Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)

**Cause:** anamnestic response to minor RBC antigens (Kidd, Duffy, Rh, Kell) in previously sensitised recipient.

**Features:** drop in Hb 3–14 days later, jaundice, positive DAT, occasional haemoglobinuria.

**Mx:** usually supportive; identify antibody for future compatible blood.

- Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD)

**Cause:** viable donor T-lymphocytes engraft in immunosuppressed recipient; rarely in immunocompetent with shared HLA haplotype.

**Features:** 1–4 weeks – fever, skin rash, diarrhoea, hepatitis, pancytopenia; mortality >90%.

**Prevention:** gamma irradiation of cellular components for high-risk groups (HSCT, intrauterine, neonatal exchange, haematological malignancy, granulocyte transfusion).

### 3. Post-transfusion purpura (PTP)

**Cause:** anti-HPA-1a antibody in HPA-1a-negative woman (usually multiparous).

**Features:** severe thrombocytopenia 5–10 days post-transfusion.

**Mx:** IVIG 1 g/kg × 2 days; plasma exchange in severe; HPA-1a-negative units in future.

### 4. Iron overload

**Cause:** chronic transfusion (≥20 units cumulative — thalassaemia, MDS, sickle cell).

**Features:** cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, endocrinopathy (DM, hypogonadism), skin hyperpigmentation.

**Mx:** iron chelation – deferoxamine SC infusion, deferiprone PO, deferasirox PO; target ferritin <1000 µg/L.

### 5. Alloimmunisation

**Cause:** development of antibody against minor RBC antigens.

**Features:** difficulty in finding compatible blood subsequently.

**Prevention:** phenotype-matched blood in chronic transfusion patients.

### 6. Transfusion-transmitted infections (TTI)

**Mandatory NACO screening tests:** HIV (Ag-Ab combo), Hepatitis B (HBsAg), Hepatitis C (anti-HCV), Syphilis (VDRL/RPR), Malaria (rapid Ag); NAT testing for HIV, HBV, HCV in many centres.

Residual risk despite screening: HIV ≈ 1:2 million, HBV ≈ 1:500,000, HCV ≈ 1:1 million (Indian NACO 2023).

**Other transmitted:** CMV (use leuko-reduced for immunocompromised), HTLV, parvovirus, EBV, dengue, chikungunya, malaria, prion (vCJD).

Fig 6. Blood component therapy — components, indications, storage.

### Principle

From a single whole blood unit (450 mL), multiple components can be separated by differential centrifugation, permitting targeted replacement and conservation of a scarce resource. NACO mandates that no whole blood be transfused if components are available.

### Components

### 1. Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC)

**Volume:** ~280 mL with Hct 60–80%.

**Storage:** 4 °C × 35 days (CPDA) / 42 days (SAGM).

**Indication:** symptomatic anaemia, Hb <7 g/dL (stable) or <8 g/dL (cardiac); each unit raises Hb by ~1 g/dL.

**Cross-match:** ABO + Rh compatible, ideally type-specific.

### 2. Platelet concentrate

**Random donor platelet (RDP):** 50–70 mL, 5.5 × 10¹⁰ platelets/unit.

Single donor platelet (SDP / apheresis): 200–300 mL, 3 × 10¹¹ platelets (=6 RDP units).

**Storage:** 20–24 °C with continuous agitation × 5 days.

**Indication:** prophylactic if count <10 × 10⁹/L (or <20 with sepsis/coagulopathy); therapeutic if bleeding; pre-procedure if <50 (or <100 for neurosurgery / ophthalmic); platelet dysfunction (uraemia, drugs).

Each RDP unit raises count by ~5,000–10,000/µL; SDP by 30,000–50,000/µL.

**Contraindications/caution:** TTP, HIT (worsens thrombosis), ITP (transient effect only).

### 3. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)

**Volume:** 200–250 mL; contains all coagulation factors at near-physiological levels.

**Storage:** −30 °C × 1 year; thawed FFP usable 24 h at 1–6 °C.

**Indication:** DIC with bleeding, massive transfusion (>1 blood volume), warfarin reversal with life-threatening bleed (if PCC unavailable), multiple coagulation factor deficiency, TTP/HUS (plasma exchange), liver disease with bleeding.

**Dose:** 10–15 mL/kg (3–4 units in adult).

**Not for:** volume expansion, nutritional support, hypoalbuminaemia.

### 4. Cryoprecipitate

**Volume:** 10–20 mL; rich in fibrinogen (>150 mg), FVIII (>80 IU), vWF, FXIII, fibronectin.

**Storage:** −30 °C × 1 year; thawed usable 6 h.

**Indication:** hypofibrinogenaemia (DIC, massive transfusion, obstetric haemorrhage) – target >1.5 g/L; rare F XIII deficiency; vWD or haemophilia A only if no factor concentrates.

**Dose:** 1 unit per 10 kg; raises fibrinogen by 50 mg/dL.

- Granulocyte concentrate (rarely used)

**Indication:** severe neutropenia (ANC <500) with documented infection failing antibiotics.

Must be irradiated + CMV-safe.

### 6. Specialised preparations

**Leuko-reduced:** prevents FNHTR, alloimmunisation, CMV transmission.

**Irradiated:** prevents TA-GVHD.

**Washed RBC/platelets:** removes plasma — for IgA deficiency, recurrent anaphylactic / severe allergic reactions.

**CMV-negative:** for seronegative pregnant women, premature neonates, BMT recipients.

### Compatibility summary

**PRBC:** ABO + Rh compatible; group O Rh-negative is 'universal donor' in emergency.

**Plasma (FFP / cryo):** ABO compatible (no Rh needed); group AB plasma is 'universal donor'.

**Platelets:** preferably ABO + Rh matched (Rh-negative for Rh-negative females of childbearing age).

### Massive transfusion protocol (MTP)

Defined as ≥10 units PRBC in 24 h, or ≥4 units in 1 h.

**1:** 1:1 ratio – PRBC : FFP : platelets (e.g. 6:6:6).

Tranexamic acid 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 h (within 3 h of trauma).

**Monitor:** Hb, platelets, INR, fibrinogen, calcium, potassium, temperature, ABG, lactate.

Maintain warm patient + warmed blood; calcium replacement if needed.

### Procedure

Spread one drop of fresh anticoagulated (EDTA) or fingerprick blood on a glass slide.

Air-dry, fix in methanol, stain with Leishman's, Wright's or Giemsa stain.

Examine in 'thinly spread' area where RBCs just don't overlap.

### Systematic examination

### RBC

**Size:** normocytic / microcytic / macrocytic.

**Colour:** normochromic / hypochromic.

**Shape:** anisocytosis (variable size), poikilocytosis (variable shape).

**Inclusions:** Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), basophilic stippling (lead, thalassaemia), Pappenheimer bodies, Cabot rings, Heinz bodies (oxidant injury, supravital stain).

### Specific RBC forms:

### – Spherocytes – HS, AIHA, burns

– Schistocytes – MAHA (TTP/HUS/DIC), prosthetic valve

– Target cells – thalassaemia, liver disease, HbC/E, post-splenectomy

– Sickle cells – HbSS

– Tear-drop cells – myelofibrosis, marrow infiltration

– Bite cells / blister cells – G6PD deficiency, oxidant

– Acanthocytes / spur cells – liver disease, abetalipoproteinaemia

– Echinocytes / burr cells – uraemia

– Elliptocytes – hereditary elliptocytosis

– Stomatocytes – hereditary stomatocytosis, alcohol

– Rouleaux – inflammation, MM, macroglobulinaemia

– Nucleated RBCs – severe haemolysis, marrow infiltration, thalassaemia major, severe hypoxia

Polychromasia – young RBCs (= reticulocyte response).

### WBC

Differential count.

**Left shift:** bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes (infection, CML, leukemoid).

Hyper-segmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) – B12/folate deficiency.

Toxic granulation, Döhle bodies, vacuoles – sepsis.

Blasts – acute leukaemia.

Smudge cells – CLL.

Atypical lymphocytes – EBV, CMV, viral infections.

Auer rods – AML.

### Platelets

Count estimate – 1 per oil-immersion field ≈ 15,000/µL (roughly).

Giant platelets – ITP, MPN.

Platelet clumping (EDTA-induced) – pseudo-thrombocytopenia.

### Parasites

Malaria – ring forms (P. falciparum), Schüffner's dots (P. vivax), banana gametocytes.

Microfilariae – W. bancrofti, Brugia (in night sample).

Trypanosomes.

Babesia – Maltese cross.

### Uses

Anaemia classification.

Leukaemia / lymphoma screen.

MAHA / TTP / DIC – schistocytes.

Infection clues – toxic granulation, atypical lymphocytes, parasites.

Platelet quantity & quality.

Confirm auto-analyser flags.

### Definition

Reactive leucocytosis >50 × 10⁹/L with left shift (immature myeloid forms in peripheral blood) that mimics leukaemia but is secondary to a non-haematological cause.

### Causes

Severe infections – pneumonia, septicaemia, TB, Clostridium difficile, miliary TB.

Severe inflammation / haemorrhage / haemolysis.

Severe tissue necrosis – burns, trauma, MI.

Solid tumours – gastric, lung, colon, melanoma (paraneoplastic G-CSF).

Drugs – corticosteroids, lithium, G-CSF, GM-CSF.

DKA, eclampsia.

Severe haemorrhage, haemolysis.

### Differentiation from CML

### Management

Treat the underlying cause; leucocytosis resolves spontaneously.

Combined summary of indications (Q10) + hazards (Q9). Cross-reference those answers for full details.

### Indications by component

Whole blood (rarely used)

Massive acute haemorrhage where components are unavailable.

Exchange transfusion in neonates.

### Packed RBC (PRBC)

Acute haemorrhage with Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to specific therapy (e.g. thalassaemia, MDS).

Pre-operative if Hb <8 g/dL and major surgery.

Sickle cell crisis (exchange transfusion in stroke, ACS).

### Platelets

Prophylactic if <10 × 10⁹/L.

Prophylactic <20 × 10⁹/L with sepsis or coagulopathy.

**Pre-procedure:** <50 (most procedures), <100 (CNS, ophthalmic).

Bleeding + thrombocytopenia.

Platelet dysfunction (uraemia, drugs) with bleeding.

**Massive transfusion 1:** 1:1 protocol.

### FFP

DIC with bleeding.

Massive transfusion.

Warfarin reversal with major bleed if PCC unavailable.

Multiple factor deficiency (liver disease + bleeding).

TTP/HUS plasma exchange.

Specific factor deficiency where concentrate unavailable.

### Cryoprecipitate

Hypofibrinogenaemia <1.5 g/L (DIC, obstetric haemorrhage).

vWD, haemophilia A (if factor concentrate unavailable).

Factor XIII deficiency.

Hazards – acute (within 24 h)

FNHTR – cytokines, anti-leukocyte antibody.

AHTR – ABO mismatch, fatal.

Allergic / anaphylactic – IgA deficiency.

TRALI – donor anti-HLA antibody.

TACO – volume overload.

Bacterial contamination, septic shock.

Citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia), hypothermia, hyperkalaemia.

Hazards – delayed (after 24 h)

DHTR – minor antigen alloimmunisation.

TA-GVHD – donor T cells; prevented by irradiation.

PTP – HPA-1a antibody.

Iron overload – chronic transfusion.

Alloimmunisation to RBC, HLA antigens.

Transmitted infections – HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, malaria, CMV, HTLV.

Approach to suspected transfusion reaction

STOP transfusion immediately, maintain IV access with NS.

Recheck blood group and patient identity (clerical error).

Send remaining unit, post-transfusion blood sample, and first urine to blood bank for repeat group, cross-match, DAT.

Cultures from unit and patient if febrile.

**Supportive:** IV fluids, vasopressor, O₂, manage DIC/AKI.

Antihistamine for allergic; adrenaline IM for anaphylaxis; paracetamol + ?leuko-reduced future components for FNHTR.

Report to haemovigilance system (HVS).

**Indication:** severe neutropenia (ANC <500) with documented infection failing antibiotics.

**CMV-negative:** for seronegative pregnant women, premature neonates, BMT recipients.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Monoclonal proliferation of mature-appearing but functionally incompetent B-lymphocytes (CD5+, CD19+, CD23+) accumulating in blood, marrow, lymph nodes, spleen. The commonest leukaemia in Western adults; less common in India (~10% of all leukaemias). Median age 70 yr; M>F.

### Clinical features

Often asymptomatic – incidental lymphocytosis on routine CBC (25–50%).

Painless generalised lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, inguinal).

Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly.

**B-symptoms:** fever, night sweats, weight loss (late).

Recurrent infections – hypogammaglobulinaemia, T-cell dysfunction (commonest cause of death).

Autoimmune cytopenias – AIHA (positive Coombs), ITP, pure red cell aplasia.

Tonsillar enlargement, Mikulicz syndrome (rare).

Richter's transformation – rapid LN enlargement + B symptoms → DLBCL (5%).

### Investigations

CBC – persistent lymphocytosis >5 × 10⁹/L for >3 months (diagnostic threshold).

Peripheral smear – mature lymphocytes + 'smudge / basket' cells (fragile).

Flow cytometry (diagnostic) – CD5+ CD19+ CD23+ CD20 dim, monoclonal κ or λ, kappa:lambda ratio skewed; CD79b dim.

Bone marrow – ≥30% mature lymphocytes; pattern (nodular, interstitial, diffuse) prognostic.

FISH / cytogenetics – del(17p), del(11q), trisomy 12, del(13q) – prognostic and predictive.

**Molecular:** TP53 mutation, IGHV mutation status (unmutated = worse), NOTCH1, SF3B1 mutations.

Direct Coombs test, reticulocyte count, β₂-microglobulin, serum LDH.

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis – LN, hepatosplenomegaly.

Serum immunoglobulins – often low.

### Staging

### Rai (USA)

**0:** lymphocytosis only (low risk)

**I:** + lymphadenopathy (intermediate)

**II:** + hepatosplenomegaly (intermediate)

**III:** + anaemia Hb<11 (high)

**IV:** + thrombocytopenia <100 (high)

### Binet (Europe)

**A:** <3 nodal areas, no cytopenia (median survival >12 yr)

**B:** ≥3 nodal areas (5–7 yr)

**C:** anaemia/thrombocytopenia (3–4 yr)

Indications for treatment (iwCLL 2018)

Progressive marrow failure (worsening anaemia or thrombocytopenia).

Massive (>6 cm below costal margin) or symptomatic splenomegaly.

Massive nodes (>10 cm) or symptomatic lymphadenopathy.

Lymphocyte doubling time <6 months.

Autoimmune cytopenias refractory to steroids.

Disease-related symptoms – fever, night sweats, weight loss >10%, fatigue.

Asymptomatic – 'watch and wait'.

### Treatment (NCCN / iwCLL)

First line (modern era — chemo-immunotherapy largely replaced)

Targeted oral therapy preferred:

**– BTK inhibitor:** ibrutinib 420 mg OD, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib (continuous).

**– BCL-2 inhibitor:** venetoclax 400 mg OD (ramp-up to avoid TLS) + obinutuzumab (12 cycles, fixed-duration).

Chemo-immunotherapy (older but still used in young, IGHV-mutated, no TP53 abnormality):

– FCR (fludarabine + cyclophosphamide + rituximab)

– BR (bendamustine + rituximab) – older patients

Chlorambucil ± obinutuzumab – frail/elderly.

### Relapsed/refractory

Switch class (BTKi ↔ BCL-2i ± antiCD20).

PI3K inhibitor – idelalisib (toxicity-limited).

Allogeneic HSCT – young, fit, high-risk disease.

CAR-T cells – lisocabtagene (recently approved).

### Supportive

IVIG – recurrent infections + hypogammaglobulinaemia.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal, influenza, COVID; avoid live vaccines.

TMP-SMX prophylaxis (PJP), aciclovir (HSV/VZV) on purine analogues, BTKi etc.

AIHA / ITP – prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; rituximab; splenectomy.

### Prognosis

Highly variable. Median survival 5–20 yr depending on stage and biological markers. Adverse markers: del(17p), TP53 mutation, unmutated IGHV, ZAP-70+, CD38+, β₂-microglobulin elevated.

### Definition

Myeloproliferative neoplasm of haematopoietic stem cells characterised by the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome — reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (p210 protein), a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Accounts for ~15% of adult leukaemias; median age 50 yr in India (younger than West).

### Phases

Chronic phase (CP, 85% at diagnosis): blasts <10%, stable.

**Accelerated phase (AP):** blasts 10–19%, basophils ≥20%, thrombocytopenia <100 not from therapy, or thrombocytosis >1000, additional cytogenetic abnormality, splenomegaly resistant to therapy.

**Blast crisis (BC):** blasts ≥20% in blood/marrow, or extramedullary disease — myeloid (70%) or lymphoid (30%) lineage.

### Clinical features

Insidious onset; many asymptomatic at diagnosis (incidental leukocytosis).

**B-symptoms:** fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats.

Massive splenomegaly (commonest physical finding — often crosses midline) → early satiety, LUQ discomfort/dragging sensation, splenic infarct (sharp pleuritic pain + rub).

Hepatomegaly; lymphadenopathy unusual (red flag for blast crisis).

**Hyperviscosity:** priapism, visual disturbance, tinnitus, stupor (rare).

Gouty arthritis, hyperuricaemia.

Anaemia (pallor), thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis (bleeding/thrombosis).

### Investigations

CBC – marked leukocytosis 50–500 × 10⁹/L with full myeloid spectrum (myelocytes > metamyelocytes > neutrophils); basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis common; mild anaemia.

Peripheral smear – left shift, basophilia (key clue), <10% blasts in CP, no Auer rods.

Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score – LOW or ABSENT (helps differentiate from leukemoid reaction).

**Bone marrow – hypercellular, M:** E 10–30:1, full myeloid maturation; reticulin fibrosis variable.

Cytogenetics – Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in 95%.

FISH for BCR-ABL1 fusion.

RT-PCR for BCR-ABL1 transcript – quantitative on the International Scale (IS); essential for treatment monitoring.

Hyperuricaemia, raised LDH, raised B12 and uric acid.

### Treatment (NCCN / ELN 2020 / Indian NCG)

### First-line — Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKI)

Imatinib 400 mg PO OD (first-generation; affordable; Indian first-line, available via Glivec International Patient Assistance Programme / generic).

Second-generation (high-risk score / intolerance):

– Dasatinib 100 mg OD

– Nilotinib 300 mg BD

– Bosutinib 400 mg OD

### Third-generation (T315I mutation, multiple TKI failure):

– Ponatinib 45 mg OD (significant cardiovascular toxicity)

### – Asciminib (STAMP inhibitor)

### Monitoring (ELN 2020)

Quantitative BCR-ABL1 on IS at 3, 6, 12 months, then every 3 months.

### Optimal milestones:

**– 3 months:** BCR-ABL1 ≤10% (= EMR, early molecular response)

**– 6 months:** ≤1%

**– 12 months:** ≤0.1% (= MMR, major molecular response)

**Deep molecular response:** MR4 (≤0.01%), MR4.5 (≤0.0032%), MR5 (undetectable).

If failing milestones → check adherence + drug levels + BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutations → consider switch TKI.

Treatment-free remission (TFR) trial – consider after ≥2 years of MR4 on TKI; ~50% maintain remission.

### TKI side effects

Imatinib – fluid retention, periorbital oedema, GI, muscle cramps, rash, transaminitis.

Dasatinib – pleural effusion, pulmonary hypertension.

Nilotinib – hyperglycaemia, pancreatitis, QT prolongation, peripheral vascular disease.

Ponatinib – arterial thrombosis, hypertension, pancreatitis.

### Advanced phase

**Accelerated/blast:** second/third-generation TKI + chemotherapy (AML induction for myeloid BC, ALL regimen for lymphoid BC) → allogeneic HSCT in responders.

### Allogeneic HSCT

**Indications:** TKI failure, T315I unfit for ponatinib, advanced phase, paediatric.

Curative but with significant mortality (TRM 15–30%).

### Supportive

Hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase for TLS prophylaxis (initial cytoreduction).

Hydroxyurea 30 mg/kg for rapid cytoreduction while awaiting cytogenetics.

Leukapheresis if symptomatic hyperleukocytosis.

### Prognosis

Pre-TKI era median survival 3–5 yr. With imatinib, 10-yr OS ~85% in chronic phase. CML is now a chronic disease with near-normal life expectancy in TKI-responsive patients. Risk scores: Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS, ELTS.

### Definition

Reactive leucocytosis >50 × 10⁹/L with left shift (immature myeloid forms in peripheral blood) that mimics leukaemia but is secondary to a non-haematological cause.

### Causes

Severe infections – pneumonia, septicaemia, TB, Clostridium difficile, miliary TB.

Severe inflammation / haemorrhage / haemolysis.

Severe tissue necrosis – burns, trauma, MI.

Solid tumours – gastric, lung, colon, melanoma (paraneoplastic G-CSF).

Drugs – corticosteroids, lithium, G-CSF, GM-CSF.

DKA, eclampsia.

Severe haemorrhage, haemolysis.

### Management

Treat the underlying cause; leucocytosis resolves spontaneously.
