### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

Tailor therapy to type/etiology.

Monitor response (rise in Hb 1–2 g/dL per month is typical for nutritional anaemias).

### Specific modalities

### 1. Oral iron

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) TDS — first-line for IDA.

Alternate-day dosing 100–200 mg may improve absorption and tolerance.

**AEs:** GI upset, constipation, dark stools.

### 2. Parenteral iron

Iron sucrose, FCM (Ferinject), iron isomaltoside (see Q18).

### 3. Vitamin B12

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week → weekly × 4 weeks → monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Oral 1000–2000 µg/day — feasible alternative.

### 4. Folate

Folic acid 5 mg PO daily × 1–4 months.

Always check/replace B12 first (avoid SACD).

### 5. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)

Epoetin / darbepoetin / roxadustat — CKD, chemo, MDS (see Q33).

### 6. Blood transfusion

Hb <7 g/dL (stable), <8 (cardiac), or symptomatic regardless.

Acute haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to other therapy.

### 7. Disease-modifying agents

Hydroxyurea — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia intermedia.

Lenalidomide — del(5q) MDS.

Luspatercept — β-thalassaemia, MDS-RS.

Eculizumab / ravulizumab — PNH, AIHA (cold).

Caplacizumab — TTP.

- Steroids & immunosuppression

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day — AIHA (first-line).

Rituximab, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide — refractory AIHA, ITP.

ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag — aplastic anaemia.

### 9. Splenectomy

Hereditary spherocytosis, β-thalassaemia, refractory ITP/AIHA.

### 10. Allogeneic HSCT

Curative for severe aplastic anaemia, severe sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia major, Fanconi anaemia, PNH (selected).

- Gene therapy (emerging)

Casgevy / Lyfgenia (CRISPR-edited HSC) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia — FDA-approved 2023.

### Combined Notes (8 topics)

### Definition

Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass / haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and altitude, sufficient to impair oxygen delivery to tissues. WHO cut-offs: men <13 g/dL, non-pregnant women <12 g/dL, pregnant women <11 g/dL, children 6 mo–5 yr <11 g/dL.

Aetiology — by mechanism

### 1. Decreased production

**Nutritional:** Iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency.

**Marrow failure:** Aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, MDS, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, mets, myelofibrosis).

**Reduced EPO:** ↓Erythropoietin – chronic kidney disease.

**Chronic disease / endocrine:** Anaemia of chronic disease, hypothyroid, hypogonadism, hypopituitarism.

- Increased destruction (haemolysis)

**Intrinsic / inherited:** Membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, PNH. Enzyme: G6PD, pyruvate kinase. Haemoglobin: sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

**Extrinsic / acquired:** Autoimmune (warm/cold), drug-induced, mechanical (valves, MAHA, TTP, HUS, DIC), infection (malaria, clostridia), hypersplenism, burns.

### 3. Blood loss

**Acute:** Trauma, surgery, peptic ulcer haemorrhage, ruptured ectopic.

**Chronic:** GI (haemorrhoids, peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm), menstrual, urinary, repeated phlebotomy.

Classification — morphological (by MCV)

Microcytic hypochromic (MCV <80 fL, MCH <27 pg)

Iron deficiency anaemia (commonest worldwide and in India).

Thalassaemia (α and β).

Anaemia of chronic disease (some).

Sideroblastic anaemia.

Lead poisoning.

Normocytic normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL)

Acute blood loss (early).

Anaemia of chronic disease.

Renal failure (↓EPO).

Aplastic anaemia.

Bone marrow infiltration.

Endocrine (hypothyroid, hypopituitary).

Mixed deficiency.

### Macrocytic (MCV >100 fL)

Megaloblastic – vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, AZT, phenytoin).

Non-megaloblastic – alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroid, MDS, reticulocytosis, drugs.

### Aetiological work-up

CBC with peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, MCV/MCH/MCHC.

Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

Vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid.

LFT, RFT, TFT.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC if thalassaemia / sickle suspected.

Direct Coombs test, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin if haemolysis suspected.

G6PD assay; PNH flow cytometry (CD55, CD59).

Bone marrow biopsy + cytogenetics for pancytopenia, macrocytosis with cytopenias, suspected leukaemia/MDS.

Endoscopy, colonoscopy if GI blood loss suspected.

Stool ova / parasites (hookworm).

Fig 1. Anaemia workup by MCV.

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Definition

Macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors, leading to nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with large, immature nuclei in red cell precursors. Most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

### Etiology

### Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Dietary:** Strict vegan, prolonged starvation.

**Gastric:** Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor); commonest cause in elderly. Post-gastrectomy.

**Intestinal:** Ileal resection or Crohn's, blind loop, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium), tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Metformin (chronic, ~30%), PPI, H2 blockers, nitrous oxide.

### Folate deficiency

**Dietary:** Inadequate diet (elderly, alcoholic).

**Increased demand:** Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic haemolytic anaemia, exfoliative skin disease, malignancy, haemodialysis.

**Malabsorption:** Coeliac disease, tropical sprue.

**Drugs:** Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfasalazine, alcohol.

Drug-induced (non-megaloblastic mechanism mimicking)

Hydroxyurea, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, AZT (HIV), anti-retrovirals.

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations).

Mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis → indirect hyperbilirubinaemia).

Glossitis (beefy red, smooth tongue – Hunter's glossitis).

Angular cheilitis.

Mild splenomegaly.

Loss of appetite, weight loss.

Neurological – B12 deficiency only

**Subacute combined degeneration:** symmetrical paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint position sense, ataxia, Romberg's positive, spasticity, extensor plantars; preserves pain and temperature; may have urinary incontinence.

Peripheral neuropathy.

Optic atrophy.

Cognitive – memory loss, dementia, irritability, psychosis ('megaloblastic madness').

**Note:** folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological deficits.

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia common; MCV markedly elevated (>110 fL); high RDW.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of cells, or any 6-lobed), Howell-Jolly bodies, Cabot rings.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (200–300 borderline).

Serum folate <4 ng/mL.

Red cell folate – better marker of body folate stores.

Homocysteine ↑ (both); methylmalonic acid (MMA) ↑ only in B12 deficiency (useful when serum B12 borderline).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific, ~70% sensitive) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive, less specific) for pernicious anaemia.

Schilling test (historical).

Bone marrow – hypercellular, megaloblastic erythroid precursors, giant metamyelocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis (rarely needed).

Endoscopy if pernicious anaemia suspected (atrophic gastritis, ↑gastric cancer risk).

Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

### Management

### B12 replacement

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Cyanocobalamin – equally effective; 1000 µg IM same schedule.

High-dose oral B12 1000–2000 µg/day – effective alternative even in pernicious anaemia (~1% absorbed passively without IF).

Treat underlying cause (stop offending drug, diet advice for vegan, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth).

### Folate replacement

Folic acid 5 mg PO OD × 4 months.

ALWAYS check and replace B12 first (folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate / worsen sub-acute combined degeneration).

**Pregnancy:** 400 µg/day prophylactic; 5 mg/day if previous neural tube defect or on AED.

### Supportive

Avoid transfusion unless decompensation; risk of fluid overload (slow infusion + diuretic).

Treat hypokalaemia during reticulocyte response (rapid K+ uptake by new cells).

Cancel hypothyroid screen in pernicious anaemia (associated autoimmune disorders).

### Response

Reticulocytosis peaks at day 7.

Hb rises 1 g/dL per week; normalises in 6–8 weeks.

MCV normalises by 6–8 weeks.

Neurological improvement may take months; pre-existing axonal damage may not fully recover.

### Definition

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with antibody-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and hence malabsorption of vitamin B12 from the terminal ileum. The commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 deficiency in adults, especially in the elderly.

### Etiology / pathogenesis

Autoimmune – anti-parietal cell antibody (90%) destroys parietal cells; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (50–70%) neutralises secreted IF.

Genetic predisposition – HLA-DR2, DR4, DR5.

Associated with other autoimmune disorders – Hashimoto's, Graves', Addison's, vitiligo, type 1 DM (~30%).

**Female:** Male ≈ 2:1; peak age 60+ yr.

### Clinical features

### General

Insidious onset – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, palpitations.

Slight lemon-yellow tinge (anaemia + jaundice from ineffective erythropoiesis).

### GI

Glossitis (beefy red tongue – Hunter's glossitis), angular cheilitis.

Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhoea.

Neurological (SACD — Sub-Acute Combined Degeneration of spinal cord)

Symmetric paraesthesiae in feet > hands, gait unsteadiness, Romberg's positive, loss of vibration & joint position sense (dorsal columns).

Spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars (lateral columns).

Mixed UMN + LMN signs.

Optic atrophy, dementia, megaloblastic madness.

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, MCV >100 fL, low retic.

Peripheral smear – oval macrocytes, hyper-segmented neutrophils.

Serum B12 <200 pg/mL (often <100).

Anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~95%).

Anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90%, less specific).

Schilling test (largely abandoned).

Serum gastrin – elevated (loss of acid feedback).

Serum pepsinogen-I – low.

Endoscopy with biopsy – atrophic body gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (screen for gastric cancer – ↑3× risk).

### Treatment

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly LIFELONG.

Oral high-dose B12 1000–2000 µg daily — feasible alternative even without IF (passive absorption).

Folate 5 mg PO if combined deficiency (only after B12 started).

Treat associated autoimmune disorders.

Periodic upper GI endoscopy surveillance for gastric carcinoma.

### Prognosis

Excellent if treated; haematological recovery in 6–8 weeks; neurological deficits may take months to improve and may be incomplete if of long duration (>6 months).

### Definition

Anaemia due to premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with bone marrow unable to compensate. Haemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular, inherited or acquired.

### Classification with examples

### Inherited (intra-corpuscular)

**Membrane:** Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.

**Enzyme:** G6PD deficiency (X-linked), pyruvate kinase deficiency.

**Haemoglobin:** Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia α/β, HbC, HbE, HbD.

### Acquired (extra-corpuscular)

**Immune:** Warm AIHA (IgG, idiopathic, SLE, CLL, lymphoma, drugs), cold AIHA (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, idiopathic), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), drug-induced (methyl-dopa, penicillin, cephalosporins), transfusion reaction.

**Non-immune:** Mechanical (prosthetic valve, march haemoglobinuria), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, vasculitis, malignant hypertension), infection (malaria, clostridia, babesiosis), drugs/chemicals (dapsone, sulphonamides, snake venom, lead), burns, hypersplenism.

**Clonal:** PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria) — acquired PIG-A mutation; CD55/CD59 deficient cells.

### Clinical features

Symptoms of anaemia + jaundice + dark urine.

Splenomegaly (extravascular haemolysis).

Gallstones (pigment stones – chronic haemolysis).

Leg ulcers, family history (inherited).

**Acute intravascular:** fever, rigor, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, AKI, shock (e.g. mismatched transfusion).

### Investigations

### Evidence of haemolysis

CBC – normocytic anaemia (high MCV if marked reticulocytosis); raised RDW.

Reticulocyte count – elevated (compensatory).

Indirect bilirubin – elevated (jaundice).

LDH – elevated.

Haptoglobin – low (binds free Hb).

Urine urobilinogen – elevated.

**Intravascular markers:** plasma free Hb, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia (Schumm's test).

### Evidence of compensation

Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia (M:E reversed).

### Aetiological work-up

Peripheral smear – key findings (spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite cells, Heinz bodies, target cells).

Direct Coombs test (DAT) – positive in AIHA.

Hb electrophoresis / HPLC – sickle, thalassaemia, HbC, HbE.

G6PD assay (after acute crisis subsides).

Osmotic fragility test – HS (now flow cytometry – EMA binding).

Sucrose lysis, Ham's acid lysis, flow cytometry CD55/CD59 – PNH.

Cold agglutinin titre, Donath-Landsteiner test.

ANA, anti-dsDNA (SLE workup).

Mantoux, blood culture, mycoplasma serology, hepatitis panel.

ADAMTS-13 activity – TTP.

Echo for prosthetic valves.

Fig 4. Haemolytic anaemia — diagnostic algorithm.

### Brief management notes

AIHA – steroids 1 mg/kg/day prednisolone; rituximab / splenectomy if refractory.

G6PD – avoid triggers (sulpha, dapsone, primaquine, fava beans); supportive in crisis.

TTP – urgent plasma exchange + steroids; rituximab/caplacizumab.

PNH – eculizumab/ravulizumab; allogeneic HSCT for selected.

Inherited HA – folate supplementation, avoid triggers, transfusion + iron chelation (β-thal), splenectomy (HS, β-thal).

### Definition

Autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6, producing HbS). Homozygous (HbSS) is sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) is sickle cell trait. In India, prevalent in tribal populations of central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka) with carrier rate up to 30% in some communities — National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission launched 2023.

### Pathophysiology

Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into rigid fibres, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. Sickled cells: (1) obstruct microcirculation → vaso-occlusion → ischaemic injury; (2) have reduced lifespan (~20 days) → chronic haemolytic anaemia; (3) cause repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia → increased risk of encapsulated organism infections.

### Clinical features

### Anaemia and haemolysis

Chronic haemolytic anaemia from infancy (after foetal Hb wanes).

Jaundice, gallstones.

Aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19).

### Vaso-occlusive crises (commonest)

Painful crisis – bones, joints, chest, abdomen; triggered by cold, dehydration, infection, hypoxia.

Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children.

Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, new infiltrate, hypoxia (leading cause of mortality).

Stroke (mainly ischaemic in children, haemorrhagic in adults).

Priapism.

Avascular necrosis of femoral head, leg ulcers.

**Renal:** papillary necrosis, isosthenuria, FSGS, hyposthenuria.

### Sequestration crisis

Splenic sequestration – sudden splenomegaly, hypovolaemic shock (children); recurrent leads to autosplenectomy.

Hepatic sequestration in older patients.

Functional asplenia – risk of overwhelming sepsis with S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Salmonella osteomyelitis.

### Investigations

CBC – Hb 6–9 g/dL, retic 5–20%, MCV usually normal or raised.

Peripheral smear – sickled cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), polychromasia, nucleated RBCs.

Sickling test (sodium metabisulfite) – screening.

Hb electrophoresis or HPLC – HbS predominant (>80%), HbF variable; no HbA in SS disease.

Solubility test – screening only (positive in both trait and disease).

DNA analysis – prenatal diagnosis, definitive.

Imaging – X-ray (H-shaped vertebrae, avascular necrosis), MRI brain (stroke), CXR (ACS).

Transcranial Doppler USG – annual screening 2–16 yr for stroke risk.

### Management

### Acute crisis (vaso-occlusive)

Hydration – 1.5× maintenance (IV fluids or oral).

Oxygen if SpO₂ <95%.

Analgesia – opioids (IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg, then PCA), paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

Warmth, treat trigger, antibiotics if infection.

Acute chest syndrome – broad-spectrum antibiotics, transfusion (simple or exchange to keep HbS <30%), BiPAP / ventilation if hypoxic.

Stroke – exchange transfusion urgently; long-term transfusion programme.

### Chronic Mx

Hydroxyurea 15–35 mg/kg/day – induces HbF, decreases VOC, ACS, hospitalisation, mortality. Monitor CBC, LFT.

Folate 5 mg/day.

Vaccinations – pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, Hepatitis B, annual influenza.

Penicillin V prophylaxis 125–250 mg BD from age 2 months to 5 years.

L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab (newer agents).

Iron chelation if transfusion-related overload (deferasirox).

Allogeneic HSCT – curative; consider in severe disease with HLA-matched donor.

Gene therapy – exa-cel, lovo-cel approved FDA 2023.

Genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis.

Fig 5. Sickle cell disease — crisis management.

### Definition

Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity <25%, or 25–50% with <30% residual haematopoietic cells), in the absence of infiltration, fibrosis or dyserythropoiesis.

### Severity (Camitta criteria)

**Severe (SAA):** bone marrow <25% + 2 of: neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, retic <60 × 10⁹/L (or corrected <1%).

**Very severe (VSAA):** SAA + neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L.

**Non-severe:** peripheral pancytopenia not meeting SAA criteria.

### Etiology

### Idiopathic (70–80%)

### Acquired

Drugs – chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs (phenyl-butazone), antithyroid (carbimazole, PTU), gold, chemotherapy.

Toxins – benzene, pesticides, hair dyes.

Radiation.

Viral – hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C in 2–10%), EBV, parvovirus B19 (pure red cell aplasia), HIV.

Autoimmune – SLE, eosinophilic fasciitis.

Pregnancy.

PNH (overlap).

### Inherited

Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive; café-au-lait spots, short stature, radial ray defects, chromosomal breaks).

Dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, leucoplakia, skin pigmentation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (pancreatic insufficiency).

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (pure red cell aplasia in infancy).

### Clinical features

Anaemia symptoms – pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea.

Neutropenia – recurrent infections, mouth ulcers, sepsis.

Thrombocytopenia – mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, menorrhagia.

No organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy (key — distinguishes from acute leukaemia / infiltrative).

### Investigations

CBC – pancytopenia; normocytic or macrocytic anaemia; low absolute retic.

Peripheral smear – no blasts, no dysplasia.

Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy – hypocellular, fatty replacement; no blasts, no fibrosis.

Cytogenetics – exclude MDS / hypoplastic MDS.

Flow cytometry – exclude PNH (CD55/CD59 deficient cells).

Chromosome breakage with mitomycin C / DEB – Fanconi.

Telomere length – dyskeratosis congenita.

Viral serology – hepatitis, HIV, EBV, parvovirus B19.

Autoimmune work-up (ANA).

Vit B12 / folate to exclude.

### Management

### Supportive (all patients)

Transfusion support – PRBC for symptomatic anaemia; platelets if <10 prophylactic, <20 with fever, bleeding. Use leuko-reduced + irradiated components (preserve HSCT eligibility).

Neutropenic precautions; broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem) for febrile neutropenia.

Antifungal (voriconazole) prophylaxis if prolonged.

G-CSF only for active infection, not routine.

### Definitive

Allogeneic HSCT from HLA-matched sibling – first choice for SAA <40 yr (overall survival >80%).

Immunosuppressive therapy (IST) – if HSCT not feasible:

– ATG (antithymocyte globulin, horse > rabbit) 40 mg/kg/day × 4 days

– Cyclosporine 5 mg/kg/day for ≥6 months (level 150–250 ng/mL)

– Eltrombopag 150 mg/day (TPO-RA) – added upfront (improves response from 60% to 85%)

Matched unrelated donor / haploidentical HSCT if IST fails.

Androgens (oxymetholone, danazol) – limited efficacy.

### Specific situations

Fanconi – reduced-intensity conditioning for HSCT (severe DNA repair defect).

Pregnancy-associated – may remit post-partum.

PNH with marrow failure – eculizumab + HSCT.

### Prognosis

Untreated SAA mortality >70% within 1 year. Modern HSCT OS 70–90% (sibling donor); IST response 60–80% with eltrombopag. Late risks – relapse, clonal evolution to MDS/AML/PNH.

### General principles

Treat the underlying cause — anaemia is a symptom.

Tailor therapy to type/etiology.

Monitor response (rise in Hb 1–2 g/dL per month is typical for nutritional anaemias).

### Specific modalities

### 1. Oral iron

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental iron) TDS — first-line for IDA.

Alternate-day dosing 100–200 mg may improve absorption and tolerance.

**AEs:** GI upset, constipation, dark stools.

### 2. Parenteral iron

Iron sucrose, FCM (Ferinject), iron isomaltoside (see Q18).

### 3. Vitamin B12

Hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week → weekly × 4 weeks → monthly lifelong (pernicious anaemia).

Oral 1000–2000 µg/day — feasible alternative.

### 4. Folate

Folic acid 5 mg PO daily × 1–4 months.

Always check/replace B12 first (avoid SACD).

### 5. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)

Epoetin / darbepoetin / roxadustat — CKD, chemo, MDS (see Q33).

### 6. Blood transfusion

Hb <7 g/dL (stable), <8 (cardiac), or symptomatic regardless.

Acute haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability.

Chronic anaemia not responsive to other therapy.

### 7. Disease-modifying agents

Hydroxyurea — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia intermedia.

Lenalidomide — del(5q) MDS.

Luspatercept — β-thalassaemia, MDS-RS.

Eculizumab / ravulizumab — PNH, AIHA (cold).

Caplacizumab — TTP.

- Steroids & immunosuppression

Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day — AIHA (first-line).

Rituximab, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide — refractory AIHA, ITP.

ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag — aplastic anaemia.

### 9. Splenectomy

Hereditary spherocytosis, β-thalassaemia, refractory ITP/AIHA.

### 10. Allogeneic HSCT

Curative for severe aplastic anaemia, severe sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia major, Fanconi anaemia, PNH (selected).

- Gene therapy (emerging)

Casgevy / Lyfgenia (CRISPR-edited HSC) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia — FDA-approved 2023.

### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### Classification

Asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Uncomplicated cystitis – healthy non-pregnant women.

Complicated UTI – men, pregnant women, catheter-associated, structural abnormality, immunocompromised.

Pyelonephritis – fever, flank pain, costovertebral tenderness.

Urosepsis – SIRS + UTI source.

Recurrent UTI – ≥2 episodes/6 mo or ≥3/year.

### Common organisms

E. coli (70–95% community; less in hospital).

Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus (young women).

Hospital / catheter — ESBL E. coli, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Candida.

### Investigations

Urinalysis – leukocyte esterase, nitrite, pyuria (>10 WBC/HPF), bacteriuria.

Urine culture and sensitivity — gold standard; ≥10⁵ CFU/mL in midstream sample (or ≥10² in symptomatic women, ≥10³ in men, any growth in suprapubic aspirate).

CBC, CRP, blood culture (pyelonephritis/urosepsis).

USG / CT in complicated UTI, pyelonephritis with poor response, recurrent UTI.

Treatment (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022)

### Asymptomatic bacteriuria

**Treat ONLY in:** pregnancy, before urological procedure with mucosal trauma, renal transplant within 1 month.

Uncomplicated cystitis (non-pregnant women)

Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD × 5 days (first-line, ICMR; avoid in eGFR <30, pyelonephritis).

Fosfomycin 3 g sachet single dose (alternative).

Co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg BD × 3 days (if local resistance <20%).

Fluoroquinolones (norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin) – reserved due to resistance and ICMR de-emphasis.

### UTI in pregnancy

Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 7 days (if sensitive).

Cefalexin 500 mg TDS × 7 days.

Nitrofurantoin (avoid term/G6PD).

Avoid fluoroquinolones, co-trimoxazole (1st trimester).

### UTI in men

Always treated as complicated. Co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin × 7 days; consider prostate involvement — fluoroquinolone × 14 days.

Pyelonephritis (admit if vomiting/septic/pregnant)

**Outpatient:** ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 7 days OR co-trimoxazole × 14 days OR oral cefpodoxime 200 mg BD × 14 days.

**Inpatient:** ceftriaxone 1 g OD IV OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q8h IV; tailor per culture; switch oral when afebrile × 24 h; total 10–14 days.

Urosepsis / septic shock

Carbapenem (meropenem 1 g q8h) + supportive ICU care; cover ESBL/MDR organisms; review based on culture; rule out obstruction (urgent decompression with stent / nephrostomy).

### Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)

Remove or change catheter; culture from new sample; targeted antibiotic × 7 days (or 14 if delayed response).

### Recurrent UTI

Self-start therapy with patient's preferred antibiotic; post-coital prophylaxis (single-dose nitrofurantoin 50 mg or TMP-SMX) if related; continuous low-dose prophylaxis 6 months in selected cases; cranberry, methenamine, vaginal oestrogen in post-menopausal women.

### Non-antibiotic measures

Hydration, regular voiding, wiping technique, urinate after intercourse, avoid spermicides; treat underlying obstruction/stone/reflux.

### Functions

Major DESCENDING motor pathway. Carries voluntary skilled movement signals from motor cortex to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord (lateral CST) and brainstem (corticobulbar tract). Phylogenetically newest; most developed in primates and humans.

### Anatomy — pathway

Origin (30% from primary motor cortex / Brodmann area 4; 30% from premotor / SMA / area 6; 40% from parietal cortex / sensory areas).

Largest cells = Betz cells in layer V of primary motor cortex.

### Axons descend through:

- Corona radiata.

- Posterior limb of internal capsule (somatotopy: face anterior, leg posterior).

- Cerebral peduncle (middle 3/5).

- Ventral pons.

- Pyramids of medulla.

Decussation (pyramidal decussation) at caudal medulla:

- 80% cross → LATERAL corticospinal tract (contralateral; controls distal limb muscles).

- 20% do NOT cross → ANTERIOR (ventral) corticospinal tract (ipsilateral, crosses at segmental level; axial / proximal muscles).

Synapses with α-motor neurons in anterior horn (most via interneurons; only ~5-10% monosynaptic, for fine distal movements).

Lateral CST descends in lateral funiculus; anterior CST in anterior funiculus.

Corticobulbar tract (analogous for brainstem)

Innervates motor nuclei of cranial nerves V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII bilaterally — EXCEPT:

- Lower face (CN VII) — only CONTRALATERAL input → UMN lesion spares forehead.

- Genioglossus (CN XII) — only CONTRALATERAL → tongue deviates away from lesion (UMN) / toward (LMN).

### Lesions — UMN syndrome

### Clinical features (UMN signs)

Hypertonia — spastic / clasp-knife (post-acute; initially flaccid in spinal shock).

Hyperreflexia — DTRs brisk; clonus.

Extensor plantar response (Babinski).

Loss of superficial reflexes (abdominal, cremasteric).

**Pyramidal weakness pattern:** weakness of upper-limb extensors > flexors; lower-limb flexors > extensors.

No or late mild wasting (disuse atrophy).

No fasciculation.

Loss of fine skilled movements (especially distal).

Lesion location → clinical pattern

### Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemicord)

IPSILATERAL UMN weakness below lesion (lateral CST).

IPSILATERAL loss of vibration / proprioception below (posterior column).

CONTRALATERAL loss of pain / temperature 1-2 segments below (spinothalamic — crosses at cord level).

### Causes of CST damage

Stroke (commonest — internal capsule lacunar, MCA territory).

Trauma (brain or spinal cord).

Tumour (glioma, meningioma, metastases, spinal tumour).

MS, NMO-SD, ATM.

ALS / MND (combined UMN + LMN — fasciculation + brisk reflexes = pathognomonic).

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.

SACD (B12).

HTLV-1 tropical spastic paraparesis.

Spinal cord compression (Pott's spine, disc).

Cerebral palsy, perinatal hypoxia.

### Investigations

MRI brain / whole spine — localise lesion.

EMG/NCS — differentiate UMN from LMN, identify MND.

Cause-specific (B12, HIV, HTLV-1, MS work-up).

**Source:** Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy; Davidson Ch.27; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Acute Hep B = clinically and biochemically apparent hepatitis (jaundice, raised ALT) with positive HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM, of < 6 months' duration.

### HBV Antigens and Antibodies

### Phases / Patterns in Acute HBV

- Incubation phase (2–10 wk)

HBsAg + (first to appear, 2–10 wk post-exposure)

HBeAg + (high infectivity)

HBV DNA + (viral replication)

Anti-HBc not yet detectable; patient usually asymptomatic.

- Symptomatic / Acute phase (4–12 wk)

### HBsAg + persists

### HBeAg + (transitioning)

**Hallmark:** Anti-HBc IgM + → DIAGNOSTIC of acute infection

ALT/AST elevated (often > 1000); bilirubin rising.

- Window period (in recovering patients)

HBsAg — (cleared) but anti-HBs not yet detectable

**Sole marker:** Anti-HBc IgM + (sole marker of recent infection)

Important to order anti-HBc IgM, not just HBsAg, in suspected acute hepatitis.

- Recovery phase (months later)

HBsAg −, anti-HBs + (protective immunity)

### Anti-HBc IgG + (lifelong)

HBeAg −, anti-HBe + (early), then anti-HBe levels wane

### Differentiating Acute vs Chronic vs Vaccinated

### Clinical Algorithm

**Step 1:** Order HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM (and total anti-HBc) in any patient with acute hepatitis.

**Step 2:** Both positive → ACUTE Hep B.

**Step 3:** HBsAg + but anti-HBc IgM − → likely CHRONIC HBV with super-infection by another agent (rule out HDV super-infection, HAV/HEV).

**Step 4:** HBsAg − but anti-HBc IgM + → WINDOW PERIOD of resolving acute Hep B.

**Step 5:** Repeat HBsAg at 6 months — persistence = chronic HBV; loss + anti-HBs = recovery.

### Additional Tests in Acute Hepatitis

HBV DNA (PCR quantitative) — helps differentiate replication status.

HDV IgM/IgG — co-infection or super-infection (severe acute / fulminant).

ALT, AST, bilirubin, INR — severity / acute liver failure markers (INR > 1.5 + encephalopathy).

Exclude co-existing HAV, HEV, HCV, HIV.

Management Notes (brief — see Q9 for chronic)

Acute HBV in immunocompetent adults — > 95% recover without antiviral.

Antivirals (TDF/entecavir) considered only in:

Severe acute hepatitis (INR > 1.5, encephalopathy, bilirubin > 10).

Prolonged (> 4 wk) symptomatic illness with persistent HBV DNA.

Immunocompromised host.

Notify (statutorily notifiable disease in India).

Counsel contacts — Hep B vaccine ± HBIG; condom use until anti-HBs +.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.12 p.518; Davidson Ch.22; AASLD 2018; EASL 2017.

### Definition + Classification

UTI = microbial infection of any part of urinary tract — lower (urethra, bladder = cystitis) or upper (ureter, kidney = pyelonephritis).

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ABU) — significant culture without symptoms.

Uncomplicated UTI — non-pregnant, premenopausal female, no structural / functional abnormality, immunocompetent.

**Complicated UTI — all others:** male, pregnant, child, diabetic, structural abnormality (stones, catheter, BPH, neurogenic bladder), renal transplant, immunosuppression, post-operative, hospital-acquired.

Recurrent UTI — ≥ 2 in 6 months OR ≥ 3 in 12 months.

**Significant bacteriuria:** ≥ 10⁵ CFU/ml midstream; ≥ 10² in symptomatic women; ANY growth in suprapubic aspirate.

### Aetiology

### Uropathogens

Escherichia coli — 75–95% of uncomplicated UTI (UPEC strain).

Staphylococcus saprophyticus — 5–10% in young sexually active women.

Klebsiella, Proteus (struvite stones — urease), Enterococcus.

Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Citrobacter — complicated / catheter-associated / hospital-acquired.

Candida (catheter, immunocompromised, broad-spectrum antibiotics).

Mycobacterium tuberculosis — sterile pyuria + haematuria, papillary necrosis.

Schistosomiasis (haematobium — endemic regions; bladder fibrosis).

### Predisposing Factors

Female sex (short urethra, proximity to anus).

Sexual activity ('honeymoon cystitis').

Spermicide, diaphragm use.

Pregnancy (urinary stasis, glucosuria, ureteric dilation).

Menopause (oestrogen deficiency → altered vaginal flora).

Diabetes mellitus (glucosuria, immune dysfunction, neurogenic bladder).

**Urinary stasis:** BPH, neurogenic bladder, pregnancy, stones, strictures.

Catheter (CAUTI risk 5–8% per day).

Vesicoureteric reflux (children).

Immunocompromise (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy).

### Clinical Features

### Cystitis (lower UTI)

Dysuria (burning), frequency, urgency.

Suprapubic pain.

Haematuria (terminal — end of stream).

Cloudy / foul-smelling urine.

No fever (low-grade if any).

### Pyelonephritis (upper UTI)

High fever > 38.5°C, chills, rigors.

Flank / loin pain (unilateral often), costovertebral angle tenderness (Murphy's sign positive).

Nausea, vomiting.

Lower UTI symptoms (often coexist).

Systemic features — confusion (especially elderly), hypotension (sepsis).

### Prostatitis (male)

Fever, perineal / suprapubic pain, dysuria, urinary retention.

Tender boggy prostate on DRE.

### Catheter-associated (CAUTI)

Fever, sepsis ± local symptoms; pyuria may be present without true infection (colonisation).

### Atypical Presentations

Elderly — confusion, falls, delirium, sepsis without classical urinary symptoms.

Diabetic — emphysematous pyelonephritis / cystitis (gas in tissue), perinephric abscess.

Children — failure to thrive, fever without focus.

### Investigations

### Bedside / Initial

**Urinalysis:** leucocyte esterase + nitrite (90% sensitivity for enterobacteriaceae); haematuria; proteinuria.

**Urine microscopy:** WBCs (≥ 10/HPF = pyuria), bacteria, RBCs, casts (WBC casts → pyelonephritis).

Urine culture + sensitivity (gold standard; pre-antibiotic if possible).

### If Pyelonephritis / Complicated / Sepsis

CBC (leucocytosis), CRP, procalcitonin.

Serum Cr, urea, electrolytes.

Blood culture × 2 (especially if pyelonephritis with bacteraemia).

Lactate, ABG (sepsis).

USG renal — abscess, stone, obstruction.

CECT KUB if not improving after 72 h, suspected emphysematous PN, abscess.

### Recurrent / Atypical

USG bladder + post-void residual (BPH, retention).

Cystoscopy.

Urodynamics if neurogenic bladder suspected.

DMSA scan for scarring (children with recurrent UTI).

Voiding cystourethrogram (VUR — children).

TB workup (3 first morning AFB + culture) if sterile pyuria.

### Management

### Uncomplicated Cystitis (premenopausal, non-pregnant)

Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BD × 5 days (FIRST-LINE; avoid if eGFR < 30, 3rd trimester pregnancy).

Fosfomycin 3 g PO single dose (preferred in pregnancy, eGFR < 30).

Trimethoprim 200 mg PO BD × 3 days OR cotrimoxazole DS BD × 3 days (if local resistance < 20%; AVOID 1st trimester pregnancy).

Pivmecillinam 400 mg PO TDS × 3–5 d (Europe).

Cefalexin 500 mg PO QID × 7 d (alternative).

Cipro 250 mg BD × 3 d / levofloxacin 250 mg OD × 3 d — reserve for resistance (side effects: tendon rupture, QT, dysglycaemia, neuropathy).

Phenazopyridine 200 mg TDS × 2 d for symptom relief (orange urine).

Hydration, frequent voiding.

### Acute Pyelonephritis

**Mild — outpatient:** ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BD × 7 d (or co-amoxiclav 625 mg TDS / cefuroxime 500 BD × 10–14 d).

Moderate-severe — admit, IV antibiotics:

### Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV OD (FIRST-LINE), OR

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g TDS (severe, immunocompromised), OR

### Meropenem 1 g TDS (severe sepsis, ESBL), OR

Aminoglycoside (gentamicin 5 mg/kg OD) — short course; renal monitor.

Step down to oral after fever down + culture-guided (cipro 500 BD).

Duration 10–14 days.

IV fluids, analgesics (paracetamol), antiemetics.

Treat sepsis as per Surviving Sepsis Campaign (fluid resus, lactate, source control).

Relieve obstruction urgently (stone, hydronephrosis) — nephrostomy / stent.

### Pregnancy

ALWAYS treat ABU (10% risk of pyelonephritis without treatment).

**Cystitis:** cefalexin 500 BD × 7 d, fosfomycin 3 g single dose, nitrofurantoin 100 BD × 5 d (avoid 3rd trimester — neonatal haemolytic anaemia).

**AVOID:** fluoroquinolones (cartilage), trimethoprim (1st trimester — folate antagonist), tetracyclines (teeth), aminoglycosides (ototoxic foetus — if absolutely needed in PN).

**Pyelonephritis:** IV ceftriaxone in hospital, then oral cefalexin / cefuroxime — total 10–14 d.

### Catheter-Associated UTI

Replace catheter (≥ 7 days in situ) — old biofilm.

Treat symptomatic only — ABU in catheterised patients does NOT need treatment (except pre-urological procedure, pregnancy, neutropenia).

Culture-guided antibiotics; avoid prolonged courses (resistance).

### Asymptomatic Bacteriuria

**TREAT only:** pregnancy, before urological procedure with mucosal breach, renal transplant (first 1 mo).

**DO NOT TREAT:** elderly, diabetic, catheter, dialysis, SCI (resistance, C. difficile, no benefit).

### Recurrent UTI

**Behavioural:** post-coital voiding, hygiene, hydration, cranberry juice (weak evidence), avoid spermicide/diaphragm.

Topical vaginal oestrogen — post-menopausal.

Self-start short course at symptom onset.

Post-coital prophylaxis — nitrofurantoin 50 mg or cotrimoxazole single dose.

Continuous low-dose prophylaxis — nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg OD × 6–12 mo (monitor pulmonary fibrosis).

Methenamine hippurate (alternative non-antibiotic).

D-mannose (anti-adhesion; weak evidence).

Vaccines (uropathogenic E. coli — emerging).

Fig 8. UTI — diagnosis and management pathway.

### Complications

Sepsis, septic shock (5% of pyelonephritis).

Perinephric / renal abscess.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis (diabetic — high mortality; surgical drainage / nephrectomy).

Papillary necrosis (DM, NSAID, sickle cell).

Chronic pyelonephritis → CKD scarring (VUR-related).

Renal stone formation (urease-producing — Proteus).

Pre-term labour, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia (pregnancy).

Bacteraemia, endocarditis (rare).

C. difficile colitis (antibiotic-related).

### Prevention

Adequate hydration > 2 L/d.

Frequent voiding, no holding.

Front-to-back wiping (women).

Post-coital voiding.

Cotton underwear.

Catheter avoidance / earliest removal.

Strict asepsis for catheterisation; closed drainage system.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.388; IDSA Uncomplicated UTI 2010; EAU 2023; ICMR Antibiotic Policy 2022; RCOG (pregnancy).

GENERAL MEDICINE|303.note:
### Definition

PEP is a short course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) administered after a defined exposure to potentially HIV-infected body fluids, with the goal of preventing seroconversion. Effective only if started within 72 hours (ideally <2 hours).

### Categories of exposure

Occupational (needle-stick, mucosal splash)

**Source HIV status:** positive (CD4, viral load checked), negative, or unknown.

**Type of exposure:** percutaneous (large/small hollow needle, solid needle, superficial), mucous membrane, non-intact skin.

Non-occupational (sexual assault, IDU, unprotected sex)

**Highest risk:** receptive anal intercourse, contaminated needle sharing.

Immediate first-aid (any exposure)

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Alternative if dolutegravir contraindicated

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Atazanavir/Ritonavir (300/100 mg) OR Lopinavir/Ritonavir 400/100 mg BD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|304.note:
### Definition

Acute toxin-mediated disease caused by tetanospasmin from Clostridium tetani (gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus); typically follows contamination of a wound with soil/dust. Incubation 3–21 days. Notifiable disease in India.

### Forms

Generalised tetanus (commonest, 80%).

Localised tetanus – muscle rigidity near wound.

Cephalic tetanus – cranial nerve involvement (head/neck wound).

Neonatal tetanus – through umbilical stump contamination (largely eliminated in India after MNTE certification 2015).

### Clinical features

### Early

Trismus (lockjaw) – earliest and commonest.

Risus sardonicus – facial grin from sustained spasm.

Stiff neck, dysphagia.

### Established

Generalised muscle rigidity – axial > limb.

Opisthotonos – arching of back from sustained extensor spasm.

Reflex spasms – provoked by stimuli (touch, sound, light); may obstruct airway, fracture vertebrae, ventilate poorly.

Autonomic dysfunction (severe tetanus) – labile BP, tachycardia/bradycardia, arrhythmia, profuse sweating, fever; leading cause of death.

Consciousness intact throughout (cortex spared).

### Severity – Ablett's grading

Grade I (mild) – trismus only.

Grade II (moderate) – trismus + spasms.

Grade III (severe) – trismus + spasms + respiratory difficulty + dysphagia.

Grade IV (very severe) – grade III + autonomic instability.

### Diagnosis

Clinical – history of wound + characteristic spasms.

Spatula test – touch posterior pharynx → reflex jaw closure (highly suggestive).

Wound culture for C. tetani – low yield; serology unhelpful.

### Treatment

### Neutralise unbound toxin

Human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG) 3000–6000 IU IM (or 500 IU intrathecal in research settings).

Equine ATS 1 lac (100 000) units IM after sensitivity test (if HTIG unavailable).

### Eliminate source

Wound debridement and cleansing.

Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h × 7–10 days (drug of choice; penicillin is GABA-antagonist – may worsen spasms).

Control rigidity and spasms

Quiet, dark, calm ICU environment.

Diazepam 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV q1–4h (titrate to control spasms); OR Midazolam infusion.

Magnesium sulphate infusion (40 mg/kg loading, then 1–3 g/h in adults) for autonomic instability and spasms.

Neuromuscular blockade (vecuronium / rocuronium) if diaphragmatic spasms — requires mechanical ventilation.

### Manage autonomic dysfunction

Labetalol or esmolol for sympathetic surges; avoid β-blockers alone (unopposed α effect).

Magnesium sulphate as above.

Clonidine, morphine for sympathetic over-activity.

### Supportive

Airway protection — early tracheostomy if prolonged ventilation anticipated; nasogastric feeding; DVT prophylaxis; pressure-area care.

Fluid and electrolyte balance.

Treat secondary infections (pneumonia, UTI).

Active immunisation (essential — tetanus does not confer immunity)

Tetanus toxoid (TT) – 3-dose primary series (0, 4 weeks, 6–12 months).

Routine immunisation under UIP – DPT 6/10/14 weeks, booster 16–24 months and 5–6 years; Td booster 10/16 years and during pregnancy.

### Prevention (wound-related TT prophylaxis)

Clean minor wound, fully immunised – no TT needed.

Clean minor wound, incomplete/unknown – TT booster (Td).

Tetanus-prone wound, fully immunised – TT booster if last dose >5 years ago.

Tetanus-prone wound, incomplete/unknown – TT + HTIG 250 IU IM.

### Prognosis

Mortality – mild 0–10%, severe 25–60% (autonomic instability is leading cause of death). Full recovery in survivors usually complete after 4–6 weeks. Always immunise after recovery — natural disease is not immunising.

GENERAL MEDICINE|306.note:
### Definitions (Sepsis-3, 2016)

**Sepsis:** life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA score increase ≥2 from baseline).

**Septic shock:** subset of sepsis with circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities profound enough to substantially increase mortality. Persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mm Hg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

qSOFA (bedside screening, ≥2 of 3 = high risk): RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100 mm Hg.

### Diagnosis

Clinical – fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered mental status, oliguria, mottled skin, hypotension.

Source identification – chest/abdomen/urine/skin/CNS/lines/wounds.

Labs – CBC, lactate (>2 mmol/L), CRP, procalcitonin, ABG, creatinine, bilirubin, coagulation, blood cultures × 2 BEFORE antibiotics.

Imaging – CXR, USG abdomen/CT to find source.

Cultures from sputum, urine, wound, CSF as indicated.

### Management (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

### Hour-1 bundle

Measure lactate; remeasure if initial >2 mmol/L.

Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics.

Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.

Begin crystalloid 30 mL/kg IV if hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L.

Apply vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluid resuscitation – noradrenaline first.

### Antibiotic choice (empirical)

Community-acquired – piperacillin-tazobactam OR ceftriaxone + azithromycin; add vancomycin if MRSA risk.

Hospital-acquired – piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem ± vancomycin.

Suspected source – urinary (ceftriaxone, carbapenem), abdominal (piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole), CNS (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + ampicillin), skin/soft tissue (piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin if necrotising), febrile neutropaenia (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime ± vancomycin).

Add antifungal (echinocandin) if Candida risk.

De-escalate based on culture in 48–72 h; total duration usually 7–10 days.

### Haemodynamic support

First-line vasopressor – noradrenaline (norepinephrine), titrate to MAP ≥65 mm Hg.

Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min if noradrenaline >0.5 µg/kg/min.

Add adrenaline if refractory.

Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg q6h IV or continuous infusion) if vasopressor-refractory shock.

Target lactate clearance >10%/h.

### Source control

Drain abscess (percutaneous/surgical).

Remove infected lines / urinary catheter.

Debride necrotic tissue.

Decompress obstructed urinary tract / biliary tree.

Source control should be achieved within 6–12 hours of diagnosis.

### Supportive ICU care

Mechanical ventilation if ARDS (low TV 6 mL/kg, PEEP, plateau <30 cm H₂O, prone if PaO₂/FiO₂ <150).

Glycaemic control – target 140–180 mg/dL.

VTE prophylaxis (heparin LMWH).

Stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI).

Renal replacement therapy for AKI.

Enteral nutrition started early (within 24–48 h).

Blood transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL (target 7–9).

Fig 7. Sepsis & septic shock – SSC 2021 Hour-1 bundle.

GENERAL MEDICINE|307.note:
### Definition

Toxic syndrome caused by ingestion / inhalation / dermal exposure to organophosphate compounds (parathion, malathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, fenthion, monocrotophos, dimethoate, dichlorvos, etc., and chemical warfare nerve agents — sarin, tabun, VX). Most common cause of poisoning mortality in rural India (deliberate self-poisoning).

### Mechanism

OP compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active serine residue, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. 'Ageing' (loss of an R-group) makes the enzyme inhibition permanent — hence early use of oximes is critical.

Clinical features (cholinergic crisis)

### Muscarinic (DUMBELS / SLUDGEM):

Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

Pulmonary oedema – the major cause of death.

Nicotinic (Days of the Week — MTWThF):

Muscle fasciculation, Tachycardia, Weakness/paralysis (including respiratory), Hypertension, Hyperglycaemia.

### CNS:

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

### Distinct syndromes:

Intermediate syndrome (24–96 h after acute phase): proximal muscle, neck flexor, and respiratory muscle weakness; cranial nerve deficits; lasts 2–3 weeks; needs prolonged ventilation.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN, 1–3 weeks after exposure): distal sensorimotor neuropathy.

### Diagnosis

History of exposure, characteristic odour (garlic/kerosene), DUMBELS toxidrome.

Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (BChE / pseudocholinesterase) – rapid, available – severely depressed.

RBC acetylcholinesterase – more accurate, slower turnaround.

Atropine challenge test – minimal response to therapeutic dose supports diagnosis.

Ancillary – ABG, CK, troponin, ECG (QT prolongation, AV block), CXR (pulmonary oedema), serum amylase (pancreatitis).

### Treatment

### Resuscitation and decontamination

**ABC:** secure airway (suction copious secretions), 100% O₂.

**Decontamination:** remove all clothing, wash skin with soap and water (rescuers wear PPE — secondary contamination risk).

Gastric lavage – only if presentation <1 h, large amount ingested, and airway protected; NOT recommended routinely (aspiration risk).

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

### End-points (must achieve ALL):

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

(iv) Pupil dilation.

**Maintenance:** atropine infusion 10–20% of the cumulative atropinising dose per hour; titrate to keep target signs.

Watch for atropine toxicity – hyperthermia, agitation, ileus, urinary retention; lower infusion accordingly.

### Oxime (pralidoxime / 2-PAM)

Reactivates AChE if given before ageing.

**Dose:** 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 48–72 h. Alternatively: 1 g IV q4-6h.

Most effective in first 24 h, but should be given even later (prolonged release from fat).

Particularly effective against nicotinic (muscle) signs.

### Supportive care

ICU monitoring. Mechanical ventilation often needed for days–weeks. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (prolonged paralysis – use rocuronium or vecuronium).

Seizures – diazepam 5–10 mg IV (does not interact with AChE).

Aggressive electrolyte (K, Mg) replacement; cardiac monitoring.

Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS.

Surveillance for intermediate syndrome (FVC, NIF monitoring).

Avoid β-blockers (worsen bronchospasm), morphine, theophylline, phenothiazines.

### Psychiatric and social

Most cases are deliberate self-poisoning – mandatory psychiatric evaluation; suicide-risk assessment; family counselling; safe-storage advice; pesticide bans (e.g. WHO Class I OP withdrawn in India 2020).

Fig 3. Organophosphate poisoning – emergency management.

GENERAL MEDICINE|308.note:
### Definition

Envenomation by elapid snakes (Cobra — Naja naja, King cobra — Ophiophagus hannah, Common krait — Bungarus caeruleus) produces a neurotoxic syndrome through α- and β-neurotoxins that block post-synaptic and pre-synaptic neuromuscular transmission respectively, leading to flaccid paralysis. India: cobra and krait are two of the 'Big Four' deadly Indian snakes.

Local features (cobra > krait)

Two fang punctures (krait bite often painless and at night).

Local pain, swelling, blistering, sometimes necrosis (cobra).

Krait – minimal local signs; pain disproportionate to swelling; often patient awakes with abdominal pain at 4–6 a.m.

Systemic features – progressive descending paralysis

Early (30 min – 2 h)

Heaviness of eyelids (ptosis – earliest and commonest sign), external ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, blurred vision.

Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia.

Hypersalivation, profuse sweating, paraesthesiae.

Established neurotoxicity (2–6 h)

Bulbar palsy – pooled secretions, tongue weakness, broken neck sign (cannot lift head off pillow).

Limb weakness – proximal first; progressive descending paralysis.

Respiratory muscle paralysis – the most life-threatening complication; intercostal and diaphragmatic weakness leading to respiratory failure.

Patient is conscious throughout (locked-in pattern unless hypoxic).

### Autonomic features

Cobra – bradycardia, hypotension; krait – sometimes mild hypertension, abdominal pain.

### Krait-specific

Bite often at night while sleeping on the floor; little or no local reaction; severe abdominal pain.

Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia may accompany.

Response to neostigmine usually poor (β-neurotoxin pre-synaptic action — already-released ACh is depleted).

### Investigations and monitoring

20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20-WBCT) – usually normal in pure neurotoxic bite (distinguishes from haemotoxic).

FVC (vital capacity) — if <1 L or falling — intubate.

ABG, electrolytes (krait — hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia).

ECG (arrhythmia).

Edrophonium / neostigmine test (improvement supports diagnosis and helps in management).

### Management (Indian National Snakebite Protocol 2017)

**First aid:** reassure, immobilise limb at heart level, remove rings/tight items, pressure-immobilisation bandage; rapid transport to a centre with ASV and ventilator. AVOID tourniquet/cut/suck/ice/electric shock.

Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV): initial 10 vials (100 mL) in 100–200 mL normal saline IV over 1 hour. Repeat every 6 hours up to maximum 30 vials, based on clinical/lab response.

Adjuvant — Neostigmine 0.5 mg + atropine 0.6 mg IV every 30 min × 5 doses (then 1–2 hourly as needed) — useful especially for cobra envenomation.

Early intubation and mechanical ventilation if FVC <1 L, tidal volume <5 mL/kg, or any respiratory distress.

**Treat ASV reactions:** stop infusion, adrenaline 0.5 mg IM, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV, chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV; resume ASV at slower rate.

Tetanus toxoid, antibiotics if cellulitis or wound necrosis.

Supportive — fluids, vasopressors if hypotensive; psychological support.

Fig 5. Snakebite — Indian National Protocol.

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

### Definition

Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) – E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Candida.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) – Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Staph aureus, MRSA.

Surgical site infection (SSI) – Staph aureus, Staph epidermidis, E. coli.

Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) – coagulase-negative Staph, Staph aureus, Candida, Enterococcus.

Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea – following broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Skin and soft tissue – pressure ulcers, IV-line cellulitis.

Multi-drug-resistant organisms – MRSA, VRE, ESBL/CRE Enterobacteriaceae, MDR Acinetobacter, Candida auris.

Patient – age extremes, immunosuppression, malnutrition, diabetes, malignancy, prolonged stay, ICU admission.

Procedural – surgery, dialysis, parenteral nutrition.

Environmental – overcrowding, poor hygiene, contaminated equipment.

Standard precautions – PPE, safe injection practices, sharps disposal, respiratory hygiene.

Cleaning and disinfection of environment and equipment.

Linen and waste management; biomedical waste segregation (BMW rules 2016).

Contact (MRSA, C. difficile, MDR Gram-negatives) – gown + gloves; single room.

Droplet (influenza, meningococcus) – surgical mask + eye protection.

CAUTI – avoid unnecessary catheterisation, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, daily review of need, prompt removal.

CLABSI – maximum barrier precautions during insertion, chlorhexidine skin prep, subclavian preferred, daily review, chlorhexidine bathing.

VAP – head elevation 30°, daily sedation hold + spontaneous breathing trial, oral chlorhexidine, PUD prophylaxis only if indicated.

SSI – preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 min of incision, normothermia, glucose control, hair clipping (not shaving), aseptic technique.

Hospital antibiotic policy (ICMR 2022).

Restrict last-resort antibiotics; de-escalation; appropriate duration.

Surveillance for HAIs (NABH, NABL, CDC NHSN models).

GENERAL MEDICINE|312.note:
### Definition

PEP is a short course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) administered after a defined exposure to potentially HIV-infected body fluids, with the goal of preventing seroconversion. Effective only if started within 72 hours (ideally <2 hours).

### Categories of exposure

Occupational (needle-stick, mucosal splash)

**Source HIV status:** positive (CD4, viral load checked), negative, or unknown.

**Type of exposure:** percutaneous (large/small hollow needle, solid needle, superficial), mucous membrane, non-intact skin.

Non-occupational (sexual assault, IDU, unprotected sex)

**Highest risk:** receptive anal intercourse, contaminated needle sharing.

Immediate first-aid (any exposure)

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Alternative if dolutegravir contraindicated

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Atazanavir/Ritonavir (300/100 mg) OR Lopinavir/Ritonavir 400/100 mg BD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|314.note:
### Definition

Severe / complicated malaria is P. falciparum (or rarely P. vivax) infection with parasitaemia and one or more clinical or laboratory features of vital-organ dysfunction. WHO 2015 criteria are used. Mortality 10–30% with treatment, near 100% untreated.

WHO criteria for severe malaria (any one + parasitaemia)

Cerebral malaria — GCS <11, repeated seizures (≥2 in 24 h), coma.

Severe anaemia — Hb <7 g/dL (adults) / <5 g/dL (children).

AKI — creatinine >265 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) or urea >20 mmol/L.

Jaundice — bilirubin >50 µmol/L (3 mg/dL) + parasitaemia >100 000/µL or other organ dysfunction.

Hypoglycaemia — glucose <2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL).

Acidosis — base deficit >8, HCO₃ <15, lactate >5 mmol/L.

Pulmonary oedema / ARDS.

Significant bleeding / DIC.

Shock (SBP <80 adults; cold extremities, capillary refill >3 s).

Hyperparasitaemia — >10% in falciparum.

Hyperpyrexia >40°C.

### Investigations

### Diagnostic

Peripheral smear (thick + thin) – gold standard; species, parasitaemia %.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP-2 (Pf) or pLDH (all species); useful when smear unavailable.

PCR – speciation in mixed/low parasitaemia/research.

Severity / complications work-up

CBC – severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Glucose (frequently low; especially with quinine).

Urea, creatinine, electrolytes.

LFT – bilirubin, AST/ALT.

ABG – metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia.

Coagulation – PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (DIC).

Urinalysis – haemoglobinuria, haematuria.

CXR – pulmonary oedema; CT/MRI brain (if cerebral malaria, to rule out other causes).

Blood culture (concomitant bacteraemia common in children).

### Management (NVBDCP / WHO)

Antimalarial therapy – severe falciparum

Artesunate IV 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then daily until patient can take oral.

Minimum 24 h of IV artesunate (3 doses) – then switch to full oral ACT × 3 days + primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose (Pf gametocyte clearance, exclude G6PD-deficiency in severe).

Quinine 20 mg/kg IV loading (over 4 h) then 10 mg/kg q8h – second-line if artesunate unavailable; cardiac and glucose monitoring essential.

Supportive care – tailored to complication

Cerebral malaria – ICU airway protection, control seizures (diazepam, phenytoin), bedside glucose hourly, mannitol or ventilation for raised ICP (avoid steroids – harmful).

Severe anaemia – packed cells.

AKI – cautious fluids, monitor urine output, dialysis if indicated (fluid overload, K+ >6.5, uremia, acidosis pH <7.2).

ARDS – non-invasive or invasive ventilation; restrictive fluid strategy.

Shock – fluid challenge (cautious), vasopressors, source-control for sepsis; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics if Gram-negative co-infection suspected.

Hypoglycaemia – 25% dextrose 100 mL IV, then 10% infusion; frequent monitoring.

Acidosis – correct hypovolaemia + hypoglycaemia first; bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

Exchange transfusion – consider if parasitaemia >30% with organ failure (evidence weak).

DIC – platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate.

Avoid – steroids, prophylactic anticonvulsants, heparin, adrenaline, urea-based diuretics.

Fig 2. Malaria – diagnosis and management (NVBDCP).

### Prognosis

Even with optimal care, mortality 10–30% in severe falciparum. Cerebral malaria survivors may have neurological sequelae (seizures, cognitive deficits). Pregnancy carries higher mortality. Early IV artesunate is the single most important predictor of survival.

Wash wound with soap and water (do not squeeze, do not use bleach).

Irrigate mucous membranes with copious water/saline.

Report to ICTC / occupational health within 1–2 hours.

### NACO 2023 PEP regimen

### Recommended (preferred 3-drug)

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + Lamivudine 300 mg + Dolutegravir 50 mg — TLD — 1 tablet OD × 28 days.

Alternative if dolutegravir contraindicated

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Atazanavir/Ritonavir (300/100 mg) OR Lopinavir/Ritonavir 400/100 mg BD × 28 days.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Raltegravir 400 mg BD × 28 days (pregnancy alternative).

### Paediatric

Age- and weight-appropriate dosing of AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or DTG (per NACO).

### Timing

Start as soon as possible after exposure (ideally within 2 hours; up to 72 hours). Beyond 72 hours, not effective.

**Duration:** 28 days.

### Pre-PEP testing

Source patient – rapid HIV test, hepatitis B and C status.

Exposed person – baseline HIV antibody test, hepatitis B antibody status, pregnancy test (women), LFT, creatinine.

### Follow-up testing

HIV antibody / 4th-gen antigen-antibody – at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months (extended to 12 months if hepatitis C co-exposure).

Hepatitis B surface antigen / antibody.

Hepatitis C antibody at 6 months ± PCR.

LFT, creatinine at 2 weeks; symptomatic review.

### Counselling

Risk explanation; condom use during follow-up; defer blood donation, organ donation, pregnancy; importance of completing 28-day course; psychological support.

### Side effects of TLD

GI upset, headache, fatigue, insomnia, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction (tenofovir), neuropsychiatric (DTG – rare).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – brief mention

Tenofovir/Emtricitabine 300/200 mg OD daily for ongoing risk (MSM, sero-discordant couples, IDU); also CAB-LA injectable every 8 weeks; recommended in updated NACO 2023 guidelines.
