Water deprivation test — for diabetes insipidus (Uosm < 300 after deprivation).

ADH (DDAVP) challenge — central vs nephrogenic DI.

### Acidification

Urine pH (random) — 5–6.5 normal.

Ammonium chloride loading test — RTA diagnosis (urine pH should fall < 5.5 if normal).

Serum bicarbonate, anion gap, urinary anion gap.

### Tubular Reabsorption / Secretion

Fractional excretion of Na (FENa) — pre-renal vs ATN.

Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) — pre-renal if < 35% (use if on diuretics).

Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO₄) — TmP/GFR (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / GFR) — Fanconi syndrome (< 80%).

Glucosuria with normal serum glucose — proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi).

Aminoaciduria — Fanconi syndrome.

**Tubular markers:** NGAL, KIM-1, IL-18 (research; early AKI biomarkers).

### 4. Urinary Sediment Examination

### 5. Imaging

**Ultrasound (USG) — first-line:** size (10–14 cm normal; < 9 cm = chronic), echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, masses, Doppler (renal artery flow, RVT).

KUB X-ray — radio-opaque stones (calcium, struvite). Cystine = semi-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent.

CT (CECT, KUB) — masses, complex cysts, stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis).

MRI / MRA — RAS, masses (avoid gadolinium if eGFR < 30 — NSF risk).

DTPA scan — split function (each kidney's contribution).

DMSA scan — cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy).

MAG-3 scan — obstruction.

Renal biopsy — definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.

### 6. Other / Specialised

Complement (C3, C4) — see Q3.

Autoantibodies — ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM.

Anti-PLA2R — membranous.

SPEP / UPEP / IFE — myeloma.

Cryoglobulins.

### Approach to Interpretation

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.353; KDIGO CKD 2012; CKD-EPI 2021 race-free.

### Indications

ESRD (eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.73 m²) or imminent ESRD.

Pre-emptive (before dialysis starts) — best survival outcomes.

Failed dialysis (HD / PD) — life expectancy + quality of life improved by transplant.

### Donor Types

### Living Donor

Living related — first-degree relatives (parent, sibling, child).

Living unrelated — spouse, friend (Indian Transplant of Human Organs Act 1994 + Rules 2014 — Authorisation Committee approval mandatory; commercial transplant illegal).

Paired exchange (kidney swap) — incompatible donor-recipient pairs swap.

**Advantages:** best outcomes (5-yr graft survival 90%), shorter waiting, scheduled, less rejection (better HLA match).

**Donor evaluation:** thorough — medical, psychological, social, ethical clearance.

### Deceased Donor (DDKT)

Brain-death donors (donation after brain death — DBD) — standard.

Circulatory death donors (DCD) — newer.

Allocation through state / national registry (NOTTO — National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation, India).

Long waiting list — Indian average wait > 5 years (severe organ shortage).

5-yr graft survival 80%.

### Recipient Pre-transplant Workup

### Comprehensive Assessment

Detailed history + examination, cause of ESRD.

**Cardiac:** ECG, echo, stress test, cardiology consult (CAD risk).

**Infectious:** HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV, CMV, EBV, TB (CXR + IGRA / Mantoux), syphilis, screening for endemic infections (malaria, dengue), dental clearance.

**Malignancy screen:** PSA, mammogram, PAP smear, colonoscopy (age-appropriate).

**Immunology:** ABO blood group, HLA typing (A, B, DR loci), HLA antibody screening (panel reactive antibody — PRA), cross-match.

**Urinary:** USG, MCU (if reflux), urodynamics if indicated.

Psychiatric and social assessment.

**Vaccinations:** pneumococcal, influenza, HBV (40 µg × 4), HZV, COVID-19 — BEFORE transplant.

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Active malignancy (< 2 yr remission usually required).

Active uncontrolled infection.

Severe cardiac disease (uncorrected).

Severe pulmonary disease.

Severe psychiatric disease with poor adherence.

Active substance abuse.

Untreated HIV with non-suppressed viral load.

Short life expectancy < 2 yr from other comorbidity.

### Relative

Age > 70 yr (case-by-case).

Severe peripheral vascular disease.

Obesity BMI > 35.

HBV / HCV (now mostly treatable — DAA).

Recurrent kidney disease risk (FSGS, MPGN, primary oxaluria).

### Surgical Procedure

Kidney placed in extraperitoneal iliac fossa (right preferred — iliac vessels superficial).

Renal artery anastomosed to external iliac (or internal iliac in living donor).

Renal vein to external iliac vein.

Ureter to bladder (Lich-Gregoir extravesical anastomosis with stent).

Native kidneys usually LEFT in place (unless symptomatic — ADPKD, infection, RCC).

Duration 2–4 h; recipient hospital stay 7–14 d.

### Immunosuppression

### Induction (at transplant)

Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R) — standard low-risk.

Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG, rabbit) — high-risk (high PRA, deceased donor, retransplant).

Methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g pulse.

### Maintenance (lifelong)

**Triple therapy:** Calcineurin inhibitor + Antiproliferative + Steroid.

**Calcineurin inhibitor:** Calcineurin inhibitor: Tacrolimus (preferred, trough 5–10 ng/ml) OR cyclosporine 100–200 ng/ml. Side effects: nephrotoxic, neurotoxic (tremor), DM, HTN, gingival hyperplasia (CsA), hirsutism (CsA), alopecia (Tac).

**Antiproliferative:** Antiproliferative: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1–2 g/d OR mycophenolic acid (MPA). Side effects: diarrhoea, leucopenia, infection. Azathioprine alternative (cheaper India).

**Steroid:** Steroid: Prednisolone 10–20 mg/d tapered to 5 mg/d maintenance. Side effects: DM, osteoporosis, infection, weight, cushingoid, cataracts.

Alternative — mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus, everolimus) — replaces CNI in nephrotoxicity.

Belatacept — costimulation blocker; less nephrotoxic.

### Complications

### Surgical (early)

Bleeding, haematoma, lymphocoele.

Renal artery / vein thrombosis (graft loss).

Ureteric leak / obstruction.

Wound infection, dehiscence.

Delayed graft function (need post-transplant dialysis).

### Rejection

**Hyperacute:** Hyperacute: Minutes-hours; pre-formed antibodies (ABO / HLA); thrombosis; graft loss (prevent by cross-match).

Acute cellular (T-cell mediated):Acute cellular (T-cell mediated): Days-weeks. Rising Cr, oliguria, fever. Biopsy: tubulitis, lymphocyte infiltration. Treat: pulse methylpred 500 mg × 3 d → tacrolimus boost; severe: ATG.

**Acute antibody-mediated (AMR):** Acute antibody-mediated (AMR): Donor-specific antibodies. C4d on biopsy, peritubular capillaritis. Treat: plasmapheresis + IVIG + rituximab.

Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA):Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA): Months-years. Gradual Cr rise, proteinuria. Mostly irreversible — optimise immunosuppression, manage as CKD.

Infection (commonest cause of death; from immunosuppression)

**Early (< 1 mo):** nosocomial — wound, UTI, line, surgical site.

**1–6 mo:** opportunistic — CMV (commonest viral), BK polyomavirus (nephropathy), Pneumocystis jirovecii, Aspergillus, mycobacteria.

**Late > 6 mo:** community-acquired + late opportunistic (PML, CMV reactivation).

**Prophylaxis:** cotrimoxazole (PCP) × 6 mo; valganciclovir × 3 mo (CMV mismatch); INH 9 mo (latent TB).

### Malignancy (chronic immunosuppression)

Skin cancers (SCC, BCC) — 100× general population.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD — EBV-driven).

Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

**Solid tumours:** lung, breast, prostate, cervix, GI — moderately ↑ risk.

### Metabolic

New-onset diabetes (NODAT) — tacrolimus, steroid (15–30%).

Hypertension (CNI, steroid).

Hyperlipidaemia (CNI, sirolimus, steroid).

Osteoporosis, avascular necrosis (steroid).

Hyperuricaemia, gout.

### Disease Recurrence in Graft

FSGS (30%), MPGN, IgA, lupus, primary oxaluria — variable.

### Long-term Care

Lifelong immunosuppression + adherence.

Regular monitoring — Cr, eGFR, drug levels, urine ACR.

Vaccinations (avoid live — MMR, varicella, yellow fever; OK inactivated).

Sun protection, skin cancer screening annually.

BP < 130/80, lipid control, glucose control.

Pregnancy possible after 1 yr stable function — switch MMF to AZA pre-conception.

### Outcomes (India)

**Living donor:** 5-yr graft survival 90%; deceased donor: 80%. Patient survival transplant > dialysis at 5 yr (95% vs 35%). Cost (India): initial ₹5–10 lakhs + lifelong immunosuppression ₹15–25k/month. Many state schemes and PMJAY cover transplant. Best modality but limited by organ availability.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.398; THOTA 1994 + Rules 2014; NOTTO India; KDIGO Care of Transplant 2009.

### Principles

Nutrition therapy is foundational in CKD — slows progression, controls complications (electrolyte disturbances, oedema, malnutrition, MBD), and improves quality of life. Individualised by CKD stage, modality (conservative / dialysis / transplant), and comorbidity (DM, HTN, obesity).

### Macronutrients

### Protein

**CKD G3–G5 (non-dialysis):** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (KDOQI 2020). Lower protein slows progression but risks malnutrition; do not go below 0.6 g/kg/d.

**Diabetic CKD:** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (lower in non-diabetic, slightly higher in DKD).

**Maintenance HD:** 1.0–1.2 g/kg/d (replace protein lost in HD).

**Peritoneal dialysis:** 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d (protein lost in dialysate).

**Post-transplant:** 1.0 g/kg/d.

Acute illness / hospitalised CKD: 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d.

50% from high biological value (animal — egg, fish, chicken).

**Indian sources:** dal, paneer, dahi, soya — moderate amounts.

### Calories

25–35 kcal/kg/d (sufficient to prevent protein catabolism).

Lower if BMI > 30; higher if BMI < 22 or muscle wasting.

Adequate carbohydrate to spare protein.

### Fat

30–35% of total calories.

Limit saturated; favour MUFA / PUFA (olive oil, fish oil, nuts in moderation).

Restrict cholesterol < 200 mg/d (atherogenic).

### Electrolytes / Minerals

### Sodium

< 5 g salt/d (= 2 g sodium); ideally < 4 g.

**Avoid:** pickles, papad, namkeen, processed foods, canned, fast food.

Cook with less salt; use spices (cumin, coriander, mint, lime).

Avoid salt substitutes (KCl — hyperK risk in CKD).

### Potassium

Restrict in CKD G4–G5 or hyperK: 2–3 g/d (50–80 mEq).

### AVOID / LIMIT (high K):

**Fruits:** banana, orange, sweet lime, citrus, kiwi, melon, mango, papaya, coconut water, dried fruits (raisin, dates, apricot).

**Vegetables:** tomato, spinach, leafy greens, potato, sweet potato, beans, drumstick, mushroom.

**Other:** salt substitutes, instant coffee, chocolate, nuts.

**ALLOWED (low K):** apple, pear, papaya (small), pineapple, grapes, watermelon (small), guava, cauliflower, cabbage, capsicum, brinjal, lauki, tinda, parwal.

DOUBLE BOIL / LEACH vegetables (peel, cut, soak in warm water 2 h, drain, boil with excess water, discard water) — reduces K by 30–50%.

### Phosphate

**Restrict in CKD G4–G5:** 800–1000 mg/d.

**AVOID:** dairy excess (milk > 250 ml/d, cheese), egg yolk excess, organ meats, nuts, seeds, whole grains (wheat bran, oats), cola drinks, processed food (phosphate additives — well-absorbed).

USE phosphate binders with meals (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum).

Refined cereals (white rice, white bread) lower phosphate than whole grain.

### Calcium

1000–1500 mg/d total (from diet + binders).

Avoid Ca-rich foods + Ca binders + Vit D simultaneously (hypercalcaemia).

### Other Minerals

Magnesium — limit if hyperMg (CKD G4–G5).

Iron — adequate (anaemia); often supplement.

Zinc — supplement if dialysis (loss).

### Fluid

**Pre-dialysis CKD:** 1.5–2 L/d unless oliguric.

**Oliguric:** previous day's urine output + 500 ml insensible.

**On HD:** 500 ml + previous day's urine output; restrict interdialytic weight gain < 5% body weight (~ 1 kg/d).

**PD:** usually liberal (continuous fluid removal).

Include ALL fluids — tea, coffee, soup, milk, fruit juice, ice cream, jelly.

### Vitamins

Water-soluble — supplement on dialysis (lost in dialysate): B1 1.5 mg, B6 5 mg, B12 1 µg, folate 1 mg, C 75 mg, niacin.

Avoid high-dose vitamin C (> 250 mg/d — oxalate nephropathy).

Vitamin D — active form (calcitriol / alfacalcidol) as needed.

AVOID vitamin A (retinol — accumulates).

### Indian Diet Practical Tips

Rice over chapatti for low phosphate (preferred in South India).

Roti / chapati from refined flour preferred over whole wheat.

Egg WHITE (low phosphate, good protein).

**Pulses (dal):** boil in excess water, discard, then cook — reduces K, P.

Limit dahi to 1 small bowl/d (75 g).

Limit fruits to 1 small portion of low-K fruits.

Avoid namkeen, biscuits, instant noodles, papad, pickle, chutney.

**Beverages:** lime water (no salt), weak tea, coconut water AVOID, packaged juice AVOID.

**Eating out:** avoid; if must, choose plain rice + vegetable curry.

### Special Situations

### Diabetic CKD

Restrict refined carbs (white rice, sugar).

Whole grains tolerable in earlier CKD; restrict in advanced (phosphate).

Time meals with insulin/SGLT2i/GLP-1.

### Nephrotic Syndrome

Protein 0.8 g/kg/d (NOT high — accelerates loss).

Strict low salt (oedema).

Low cholesterol, low fat.

Adequate calories.

### Renal Stones (prevention)

High fluid > 2.5 L/d.

Low salt < 5 g/d.

Adequate dietary calcium (NOT supplemental).

Low oxalate (avoid spinach, beetroot, tea, chocolate, nuts, soy, rhubarb) — Ca oxalate stones.

Low purine (uric acid stones).

Low animal protein (Ca oxalate, uric acid).

Citrate (lemon, orange — for non-CKD; risk vs benefit in CKD).

### Monitoring

Weight (dry weight in dialysis).

Serum albumin (> 3.5 — good nutrition), pre-albumin.

Electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, phosphate), Mg.

BP, oedema.

Anthropometry (MUAC, BMI).

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA — gold standard for CKD nutrition).

Dietitian review every 3–6 months.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.408; KDOQI Nutrition CKD 2020; ISN Nutrition; ISN India Renal Diet guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|333.note:
### Definition

Renal replacement therapy in which blood is circulated through an extracorporeal circuit and passes through a semi-permeable dialyser membrane against a counter-current dialysate flow. Solutes (urea, K, creatinine, drugs, toxins) move by DIFFUSION down concentration gradient. Water is removed by ULTRAFILTRATION (hydrostatic pressure).

**Modalities:** intermittent haemodialysis (IHD; 4 h × 3/wk standard), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT — CVVH, CVVHD, CVVHDF), sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED), home daily / nocturnal HD, hybrid (CRRT-IHD).

### Principles

- Diffusion (solute removal)

Concentration gradient drives small/middle MW solutes (urea 60, Cr 113, K 39) across membrane. Efficiency depends on: blood/dialysate flow rate, surface area, molecular size + pore size.

- Ultrafiltration (water removal)

Hydrostatic pressure gradient → bulk fluid movement; removes ~ 0.5–1 L/hr.

### 3. Convection

Solvent drag — water carries dissolved solutes. Main mechanism in CRRT (haemofiltration); better removal of middle-MW solutes (β2-microglobulin).

### 4. Adsorption

Some membranes (polysulphone) adsorb protein-bound toxins.

### Components of HD Circuit

Vascular access (see below).

Blood pump (200–400 ml/min flow).

Heparin / citrate anticoagulation.

Dialyser (artificial kidney — hollow-fibre, surface area 1.0–2.0 m²; biocompatible polysulphone / cellulose triacetate).

Dialysate (purified water + electrolytes — Na 138, K 1–3, Ca 1.25, Mg 0.5, HCO₃ 30–35, glucose; counter-current flow 500 ml/min).

Pressure monitors, air detector, blood leak detector.

Reverse osmosis water plant.

### Vascular Access

### Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF) — GOLD STANDARD

Native vessels — radio-cephalic at wrist (preferred), brachio-cephalic at elbow, brachio-basilic transposition.

Patient's own artery and vein anastomosed → vein arterialises (matures) over 6 weeks.

**PLAN AHEAD:** create when eGFR 15–25 (G4 → G5 transition).

Best long-term patency (5-yr 70%); lowest infection.

**Examination:** bruit + thrill on auscultation/palpation.

### Arteriovenous Graft (AVG)

Synthetic (PTFE) graft when veins inadequate.

Used in 2 weeks; lower patency (5-yr 30%); more infections.

### Central Venous Catheter (CVC)

Internal jugular (preferred), femoral, subclavian (avoid — stenosis).

Temporary (non-tunnelled) — acute settings.

Permanent (tunnelled cuffed — Permcath) — bridge to AVF or bridging.

Highest infection (bacteraemia), thrombosis, stenosis.

**Most common reason:** emergent dialysis when AVF not ready.

### Indications for Initiating Dialysis

### Acute (AKI) — AEIOU mnemonic

Acidosis — refractory pH < 7.1.

Electrolytes — K > 6.5 refractory, severe hyperNa/hypoNa, hypercalcaemia.

Intoxication — lithium, salicylate, ethylene glycol, methanol, valproate, metformin.

Overload — refractory pulmonary oedema.

Uraemia — pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding.

### Chronic (ESRD)

**Symptomatic uraemia:** anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, pruritus.

Volume overload despite diuretics.

Hyperkalaemia / acidosis not controlled medically.

Pericarditis, encephalopathy.

Malnutrition.

eGFR 5–10 ml/min/1.73 m² typically (NOT a fixed number; IDEAL trial showed early start ≥ 10 ml/min NO benefit vs late start 5–7).

### Prescription

### Complications

### Intradialytic

Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%):Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%): Causes: excessive UF, hypovolaemia, antihypertensives, cardiac dysfunction, sepsis, Mg/Ca shift. Treat: stop UF, head down, 100–250 ml NS bolus, midodrine pre-HD, reduce dry weight target.

**Cramps:** Cramps: Volume / Na depletion. NS bolus, quinine, vit E.

**Nausea, vomiting:** Nausea, vomiting: Hypotension, dialysate issues. Antiemetics.

**Headache:** Headache: Disequilibrium (rapid urea shifts; cerebral oedema), HTN, caffeine withdrawal.

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome:Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: Rapid initial dialysis → cerebral oedema (urea shifts). Headache, nausea, seizure, coma. Prevention: shorter, gentler first sessions, mannitol.

**First-use syndrome:** First-use syndrome: Type A (anaphylactoid — ethylene oxide sterilant): immediate (stop dialysis, epinephrine, steroids, antihistamine). Type B (chest/back pain): mild, continue.

**Air embolism:** Air embolism: Rare — clamp lines, left lateral Trendelenburg, 100% O₂.

**Haemolysis:** Haemolysis: Mechanical, hypotonic dialysate. Pink plasma. Stop HD.

**Cardiac:** Cardiac: Arrhythmia, ischaemia (electrolyte shifts, hypotension).

**Bleeding:** Bleeding: Heparin-related. Protamine if severe.

### Long-term

**Vascular access:** Vascular access: Thrombosis, stenosis, infection (bacteraemia esp. catheter), aneurysm, steal syndrome, high-output cardiac failure (AVF > 2 L/min).

**Cardiovascular:** Cardiovascular: Major cause of mortality. Accelerated atherosclerosis, LVH, vascular calcification, uraemic cardiomyopathy.

**Anaemia:** Anaemia: Erythropoietin deficiency, iron deficiency, blood loss in circuit, uraemic platelet dysfunction.

**Bone disease (CKD-MBD):** Bone disease (CKD-MBD): 2° hyperparathyroidism, osteitis fibrosa, adynamic bone, β2-microglobulin amyloid (carpal tunnel).

**Infection:** Infection: CRBSI (catheter — Staph aureus, MRSA, MRSE), HBV/HCV transmission (rare in modern era), TB, fungal.

**Malnutrition / protein wasting:** Malnutrition / protein wasting: Anorexia, restrictions, inflammation, protein loss in HD.

**Encephalopathy:** Encephalopathy: Uraemic, aluminium (older — minimal now), thiamine deficiency.

**Psychosocial:** Psychosocial: Depression, sexual dysfunction, financial burden — high suicide risk.

**Other:** Other: Acquired cystic kidney → RCC, gout/pseudogout, restless legs, dementia.

### Comparison with Peritoneal Dialysis (PD)

### Adequacy Assessment

Kt/V (Daugirdas formula) — single-pool > 1.4 per session.

Urea Reduction Ratio (URR) — > 65%.

Weekly Kt/V > 2.0.

**Clinical:** BP control, dry weight, nutrition, symptom resolution.

### Outcomes (India)

1-yr survival on HD ~ 80% (worse than transplant 95%). 5-yr survival ~ 35–40%. Major cause of death: CV disease (45%), infection (20%), withdrawal (5–10%). PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat) and many state schemes (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) cover HD costs. PMNDP (Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme) since 2016 provides free HD across India.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.392; KDIGO Dialysis Initiation 2015; KDOQI; PMNDP 2016; ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas; IDEAL trial.

GENERAL MEDICINE|334.note:
### Definition (Tetrad)

Heavy proteinuria > 3.5 g/d (or PCR > 3.5 g/g; in children > 40 mg/m²/h).

Hypoalbuminaemia < 3 g/dL (often < 2.5).

Generalised oedema (peri-orbital morning, peripheral evening, anasarca, ascites, pleural effusion).

Hyperlipidaemia (↑ cholesterol > 250, triglycerides).

**Pathology:** damage to glomerular filtration barrier → loss of selectivity for protein. Lipiduria (oval fat bodies / Maltese cross under polarised light) is associated.

### Aetiology — Primary vs Secondary

### Primary (Idiopathic) Glomerular Diseases

**Minimal Change Disease (MCD):** Minimal Change Disease (MCD): Commonest in CHILDREN (~90% paediatric NS). Normal LM; foot process effacement on EM. Selective proteinuria (albumin > IgG). Highly steroid-responsive. T-cell / cytokine-mediated. Adult MCD ~10% of adult NS.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS):Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Commonest in ADULTS (especially African descent — APOL1 risk allele). Primary or secondary (HIV — collapsing variant, heroin, obesity, reflux nephropathy, sickle cell). Variable steroid response. Anti-suPAR Ab in some.

**Membranous Nephropathy:** Membranous Nephropathy: Common cause in adults. Anti-PLA2R autoantibody (70–80% — diagnostic). THSD7A (5%). Secondary causes: SLE (Class V), Hep B, malignancy (solid tumours — lung, breast, colon — esp > 65 yr), drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs). Spike + dome on EM.

Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN):Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN): Immune-complex (Type I) or C3 glomerulopathy. Mixed nephritic-nephrotic features. Hep C, monoclonal gammopathy.

**IgA nephropathy:** IgA nephropathy: Usually nephritic but can present as NS.

### Secondary

**Diabetic nephropathy:** Diabetic nephropathy: Commonest cause overall in adults (commoner than primary GN in older diabetic). See Q5 for details.

**Amyloidosis:** Amyloidosis: AL (light chain — myeloma association) or AA (chronic inflammation — RA, TB, IBD, Indian context). Congo red apple-green birefringence. SAP scan, biopsy.

**Lupus nephritis Class V:** Lupus nephritis Class V: Membranous pattern; SLE features.

**Viral:** Viral: Hep B → membranous (children); Hep C → MPGN / cryoglobulinaemia; HIV → collapsing FSGS (HIVAN).

**Drugs:** Drugs: NSAIDs (MCD + AIN), gold, penicillamine, captopril, lithium (FSGS), bisphosphonates (collapsing).

**Malignancy:** Malignancy: Solid tumour membranous (esp > 65 yr), lymphoma → MCD.

**Congenital:** Congenital: Finnish-type CNS (NPHS1 mutation), denys-Drash (WT1).

### Clinical Features

Oedema — onset peri-orbital (morning), progresses to pitting peripheral, ascites, pleural effusion, anasarca; weight gain.

Froamy urine (proteinuria).

Lethargy, malabsorption (oedematous bowel), poor appetite.

Hypotension if severe hypoalbuminaemia (rare).

**Complications-related:** VTE (DVT, renal vein thrombosis — flank pain, AKI), infection (peritonitis pneumococcal in children, encapsulated organisms), AKI.

Secondary cause features (DM control, weight, joints, skin).

**Underlying examination:** BP, fundoscopy, lymph nodes, breast, prostate.

### Investigations

### Confirm Nephrotic Syndrome

**Urinalysis:** dipstick proteinuria 3+/4+; microscopy: oval fat bodies, Maltese cross.

24-h urine protein OR spot PCR / ACR — PCR > 3500 mg/g diagnostic.

Serum albumin, total protein.

Lipid profile.

Creatinine, urea, electrolytes, eGFR.

### Identify Cause

HbA1c, fasting glucose (DM).

ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement (lupus).

Anti-PLA2R antibody (membranous — diagnostic if high).

HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV.

SPEP/UPEP, free light chains, serum IFE, immunoglobulins (amyloid, myeloma).

Cryoglobulins (HCV, MPGN).

Age-appropriate malignancy screen (CXR, mammogram, PSA, colonoscopy, CECT abd) in adults > 65 with membranous.

Renal biopsy (essential in adults with NS; in children empirical steroid if typical MCD; biopsy if atypical features — see below).

### Indications for Biopsy

All adults with new NS.

Children with atypical features: age < 1 or > 12 yr, haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment, low complement, steroid resistance.

Steroid-dependent / frequently relapsing NS.

### Management

### 1. General Supportive Measures

**Oedema:** Oedema: Salt restrict (< 5g/d), fluid 1–1.5 L/d. Loop diuretic — furosemide 40–250 mg/d (often IV in severe; high doses needed due to albumin binding). Combination with thiazide / metolazone if refractory.

**Anasarca / albumin < 2:** Anasarca / albumin < 2: Cautious IV albumin (20% 100 ml) + furosemide if severe respiratory compromise. Routine albumin NOT recommended — short-lived effect.

**BP + proteinuria reduction:** BP + proteinuria reduction: ACEi (ramipril 10 mg) or ARB (losartan 100 mg, telmisartan 80 mg). Target BP < 130/80, proteinuria < 1 g/d.

**Dyslipidaemia:** Dyslipidaemia: Atorvastatin 20–40 mg or rosuvastatin 10–20 mg.

**Diet:** Diet: Protein 0.8–1.0 g/kg/d (NOT high protein — accelerates progression). Low salt, low fat, low cholesterol.

**VTE prophylaxis:** VTE prophylaxis: LMWH if albumin < 2.5 + other risk (immobility, history of thrombosis, PE/DVT/RVT). Long-term anticoagulation if RVT (warfarin 6 mo INR 2–3).

**Infection prophylaxis:** Infection prophylaxis: Pneumococcal vaccination (PCV13 + PPSV23); annual influenza; treat infections promptly.

**Vit D + Ca supplementation:** Vit D + Ca supplementation: Vitamin D-binding protein loss.

**Iron:** Iron: Transferrin loss → IDA.

**Treat secondary cause:** Treat secondary cause: DM control, BP, treat underlying.

### 2. Disease-Specific Treatment

**MCD (children):** MCD (children): Empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60 mg) × 4 wk → 40 mg/m² alternate days × 4 wk → taper over 12 wk (ISKDC). 90% respond within 2 wk. Frequent relapse → cyclophosphamide / mycophenolate / cyclosporine / rituximab.

**MCD (adults):** MCD (adults): Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d (max 80) × 4–16 wk till remission → taper. Slower response. Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) for steroid-resistant.

**FSGS:** FSGS: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d × 12 wk → taper if response. Steroid-resistant: cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/d × 6 mo (KDIGO 2021). Rituximab for selected. APOL1 gene-related considerations.

**Membranous nephropathy:** Membranous nephropathy: First 6 months: conservative (ACEi/ARB, monitor anti-PLA2R, GFR). If persistent NS / progressive: rituximab 1 g × 2 doses (preferred — MENTOR 2019) OR Ponticelli regimen (alternating monthly methylpred + oral chlorambucil/cyclophosphamide × 6 mo) OR cyclosporine + low-dose steroid.

**Lupus Class V:** Lupus Class V: Steroid + MMF / CNI (similar to Class III/IV but milder). Hydroxychloroquine.

**Diabetic nephropathy:** Diabetic nephropathy: See Q5 — strict glycaemic control, ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA.

**Amyloidosis:** Amyloidosis: AL: chemotherapy directed at clonal plasma cells (bortezomib + dex; autologous SCT in fit). AA: treat underlying inflammation (RA → biologics, TB → ATT). Specific anti-amyloid: tafamidis (TTR), patisiran.

**HBV / HCV / HIV-related:** HBV / HCV / HIV-related: Antivirals — HBV (TDF/entecavir), HCV (DAA), HIV (ART) — often resolves GN.

**NSAID / drug-induced:** NSAID / drug-induced: Stop offending agent → usually resolves.

Fig 4. Nephrotic syndrome — diagnostic and management pathway.

### Complications

Venous thromboembolism (DVT 25%, renal vein thrombosis 30% in membranous, PE) — loss of antithrombin III; high ATIII deficiency risk.

Infection — encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae peritonitis in children); loss of immunoglobulins.

AKI — pre-renal from over-diuresis, or renal vein thrombosis.

Hyperlipidaemia → CV disease.

Malnutrition — protein loss, oedematous bowel malabsorption.

Vitamin D deficiency, calcium deficiency.

Anaemia (transferrin loss + EPO loss).

Hypothyroidism (TBG loss).

Steroid SE — osteoporosis, DM, infection, cushingoid, growth retardation in children.

### Prognosis

Highly variable by aetiology. MCD: > 90% remission with steroids; 70% relapse but generally good long-term renal function. FSGS: ESRD in 30–50% over 10 yr (worse if steroid-resistant). Membranous: ~30% spontaneous remission, 30% partial remission, 30% progressive; anti-PLA2R titre predicts treatment response. Lupus V: depends on activity + chronicity.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.371; KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; ISKDC; MENTOR 2019; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|335.note:
### Definition

Macroscopic (gross) haematuria — visible red / brown / 'cola' urine to the naked eye (as little as 1 ml blood per litre).

Microscopic haematuria — ≥ 3 RBCs/HPF on microscopy of a centrifuged urine sample, in 2 of 3 properly-collected specimens.

**Dipstick:** detects haem from RBC, free Hb, myoglobin — false positives in haemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria (NO RBCs on microscopy). Always confirm with microscopy.

### Causes — Anatomical Classification

### Glomerular (medical haematuria)

**Microscopy:** dysmorphic RBCs (> 30% by Köhler criteria), RBC casts, proteinuria, acanthocytes (G1 cells — pathognomonic).

**Primary GN:** IgA nephropathy (#1 — synpharyngitic gross haematuria), MPGN, MCD.

**Secondary GN:** PSGN, lupus, ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM, HSP, IE.

**Hereditary:** Alport (X-linked; haematuria + deafness + ocular), thin BM disease (benign familial).

### Renal Parenchymal / Tubulointerstitial

ATN (rare).

Acute interstitial nephritis (drug — NSAID, PPI, β-lactam).

Polycystic kidney disease (cyst rupture).

Renal cell carcinoma.

Renal trauma, infarction.

Pyelonephritis.

Renal TB ('sterile pyuria' + haematuria classic).

Papillary necrosis (DM, sickle, analgesic, TB, obstruction).

Loin-pain haematuria syndrome.

Urological (surgical haematuria) — typically isomorphic RBCs, no casts

Stones — kidney, ureteric, bladder (40% of stones present with haematuria).

UTI — cystitis, urethritis, prostatitis, pyelonephritis.

### Malignancy:

RCC (often painless gross haematuria > 50 yr — 'triad' of haematuria + flank pain + mass).

Bladder cancer (transitional cell — > 40 yr, smoker, dye/aniline exposure).

Prostate cancer (with metastasis or local invasion).

Upper tract urothelial cancer (smoker, phenacetin, Balkan nephropathy).

BPH (passive haematuria from vascular prostate).

Trauma — renal, ureteric, bladder, urethral.

Schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium — granular bladder; squamous cell Ca risk).

Foreign body, instrumentation, post-catheterisation.

Bladder endometriosis (cyclical, perimenstrual).

### Bleeding Diathesis / Systemic

Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) — usually unmasks underlying lesion; always investigate.

Thrombocytopenia, haemophilia, vWF disease.

Sickle cell trait / disease — papillary necrosis, renal medullary Ca.

### Mimics — Investigate Negative

Haemoglobinuria — intravascular haemolysis.

Myoglobinuria — rhabdomyolysis.

Beeturia — beetroot (10% of population).

Drugs — rifampicin, phenazopyridine, senna, methyldopa, doxorubicin.

Porphyria.

Menstrual contamination.

Factitious (Munchausen).

### Approach to Investigation

### Step 1 — Confirm True Haematuria

Repeat urinalysis 2–3 times (exclude transient — exercise, fever, menses, sexual intercourse).

Dipstick positive + microscopy NO RBCs → think haemoglobinuria / myoglobinuria.

Dipstick positive + microscopy with RBCs → true haematuria.

Step 2 — Localise (glomerular vs urological)

### Step 3 — Targeted Investigations

**All:** serum Cr, eGFR, U+E, CBC, coagulation, urine culture, ACR/PCR.

Glomerular workup (see Q3 nephritic): complement, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, HBV/HCV, ASO, renal biopsy.

### Urological workup:

USG renal + bladder (first-line) — stones, mass, hydronephrosis, residual.

CT urography — stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis), upper tract masses.

Cystoscopy — definitive for bladder lesions; indicated in > 35 yr with unexplained gross haematuria or persistent microscopic + risk factors.

Urine cytology — bladder malignancy screening; low sensitivity for low-grade.

PSA in men > 50 yr or with prostatic symptoms.

Urine AFB + culture × 3 — if sterile pyuria + haematuria (renal TB).

### Indications for Urgent Urology Referral

Visible (gross) haematuria — any age (think malignancy until proven otherwise).

Microscopic haematuria + ANY of: age > 35–40 yr, smoking history, occupational dye / chemical exposure, prior pelvic irradiation, phenacetin / cyclophosphamide exposure, recurrent UTI / pyelonephritis, irritative voiding symptoms.

### Indications for Urgent Nephrology Referral

Active urinary sediment (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs).

Haematuria + proteinuria > 500 mg/d.

Haematuria + AKI / ↓ eGFR.

Haematuria + HTN.

Systemic features (rash, joints, fever, haemoptysis).

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.357; AUA Microhaematuria 2020; Davidson Ch.17.

GENERAL MEDICINE|336.note:
### Definition

Acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis. Commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide after polio eradication. Incidence 1-2/100,000/year.

### Aetiology / Triggers

Antecedent infection 1-3 weeks earlier in 2/3:

- Campylobacter jejuni (commonest, esp. AMAN variant) — molecular mimicry with GM1/GD1a gangliosides.

- CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV, hepatitis E.

- Zika, dengue, chikungunya (Indian relevance).

- SARS-CoV-2 (post-COVID-19).

Post-vaccination (rare — older 1976 swine flu, rabies, influenza).

Post-surgical (rare).

### Variants

AIDP (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy) — commonest in West.

AMAN (Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy) — common in India/Asia, post-Campylobacter, anti-GM1.

AMSAN (sensorimotor axonal) — severe, slower recovery.

**Miller-Fisher:** ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b in 90%.

Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis: + altered sensorium.

Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial.

### Clinical features

Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis (legs → arms → bulbar → respiratory) over hours-days.

Areflexia (or hyporeflexia) — cardinal.

**Sensory:** paraesthesias > objective sensory loss; back/limb pain common.

**Cranial:** bilateral VII (50%), bulbar palsy.

**Autonomic in 70%:** BP swings, arrhythmias, ileus, urinary retention.

Respiratory failure in 25-30% — needs ventilation.

Peak deficit by 2-4 weeks; plateau; then gradual recovery.

### Brighton diagnostic criteria

Bilateral flaccid limb weakness + reduced/absent reflexes + monophasic course (12 h - 28 days) + CSF and/or electrophysiology supportive + no alternative diagnosis.

### Investigations

### Bedside (essential)

Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) — q4h; intubate if < 20 mL/kg.

Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF) — intubate if > -30 cm H₂O.

**Single breath count:** < 19 → impending respiratory failure.

ECG, BP monitoring (autonomic).

### CSF

Albuminocytological dissociation — protein > 0.45 g/L with cells < 10/mm³.

Appears after day 7 (50% positive in first week, 75% by week 2).

Nerve conduction studies (most sensitive in week 1)

**AIDP:** prolonged distal latency, conduction block, slowed velocity, prolonged F-wave latency, abnormal H reflex.

**AMAN:** reduced CMAP amplitude with preserved velocity.

### Antibodies (optional)

Anti-GM1 (AMAN), anti-GQ1b (Miller-Fisher), anti-GD1a.

### Other

MRI spine with Gd — anterior nerve root enhancement.

Stool Campylobacter PCR; serology HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, Zika/dengue if febrile.

**Rule out:** porphyria, lead, botulism, MG, polio, tick paralysis, transverse myelitis.

### Management

- Supportive — most important

ICU admission if rapidly progressive, bulbar dysfunction, autonomic, or FVC < 20 mL/kg.

Mechanical ventilation if FVC < 15 mL/kg, NIF > -30, hypoxia, or aspiration.

**DVT prophylaxis:** LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg SC OD) + IPC.

NG feeds if bulbar; bladder care; physiotherapy from day 1; pressure-area care.

**Pain:** gabapentin 300-1200 mg/d or carbamazepine; opioids if severe.

**Autonomic:** avoid suctioning-induced bradycardia; atropine standby; cautious BP management.

- Disease-modifying (start within 4 weeks of onset)

IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Preferred — easier, equally effective.

OR Plasmapheresis 5 sessions over 1-2 weeks (200-250 mL/kg total).

Both equally effective; DO NOT combine (no added benefit, increased cost).

**Steroids:** NOT INDICATED — multiple RCTs show no benefit; may delay recovery.

### 3. Rehab

Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychological support.

### Prognosis

80% walk unaided at 6 months; 60% full recovery at 1 year.

Mortality 5-10% (resp failure, autonomic, PE, sepsis).

**Poor prognosticators:** rapid progression < 7 d, axonal pattern, age > 60, ventilation needed, severe distal CMAP reduction.

Fig 4. GBS work-up and management.

**Source:** EAN/PNS GBS Guidelines 2023; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|337.note:
### Definition

Disorder of peripheral nervous system, presenting with sensory, motor, autonomic, or mixed symptoms. Most common — distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP).

### Classification

By number of nerves

Mononeuropathy — single nerve (carpal tunnel, foot drop).

Mononeuritis multiplex — multiple non-contiguous nerves (vasculitis classic).

Polyneuropathy — symmetric, distal (length-dependent).

### By fibres

Motor / Sensory / Autonomic / Mixed.

### By pathology

Demyelinating (slow NCV).

Axonal (low amplitude).

Mixed.

### By course

**Acute (< 4 weeks):** GBS, toxic, porphyria.

Subacute (4-8 weeks).

**Chronic (> 8 weeks):** diabetic, CIDP, hereditary.

### AETIOLOGY (DANG THE RAPIST mnemonic / systematic)

### 1. Metabolic / Endocrine

Diabetes mellitus — COMMONEST cause worldwide. Distal symmetric, autonomic, mononeuropathy, femoral amyotrophy. Dependent on glycaemic control.

Hypothyroidism (carpal tunnel, mild DSP).

Chronic kidney disease (uraemic neuropathy).

Liver failure (chronic).

### 2. Nutritional

Vitamin B12 deficiency (SACD + PN).

Folate, vitamin B1 (Wernicke, beriberi — wet/dry).

Vitamin B6 deficiency (INH neuropathy) or EXCESS (pyridoxine megadose neuropathy).

Vitamin E (cerebellar + PN).

Copper deficiency (myeloneuropathy — gastric bypass, zinc overuse).

Strachan syndrome (multinutrient — Cuban / Tanzanian epidemic).

### 3. Toxic

Alcohol (chronic — thiamine + direct toxic).

**Heavy metals:** lead (motor; wrist drop), arsenic (sensorimotor), mercury, thallium.

**Drugs:** vincristine, cisplatin, oxaliplatin, paclitaxel, bortezomib (chemo); isoniazid (without pyridoxine), metronidazole (high dose), nitrofurantoin, dapsone, amiodarone, hydralazine, statins, colchicine.

Organophosphates (delayed neuropathy after acute toxicity).

n-Hexane (glue-sniffing).

Acrylamide.

### 4. Infections

Leprosy (Hansen's) — COMMONEST treatable cause in India. Mononeuritis multiplex; ulnar > median, common peroneal, posterior tibial, sural, supraorbital. Skin patches with sensory loss.

HIV (DSP — late; ART-related neuropathy — d4T, ddI).

Herpes zoster (post-herpetic neuralgia).

Lyme disease.

Diphtheria, botulism (rare in India now).

Hepatitis B/C, syphilis.

### 5. Immune / Inflammatory

GBS / CIDP.

Multifocal motor neuropathy (anti-GM1).

**Vasculitis:** polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA vasculitis (EGPA, GPA, MPA), cryoglobulinaemia, SLE, Sjögren's, RA. Often mononeuritis multiplex.

**Paraproteinaemic:** MGUS, multiple myeloma, Waldenström, POEMS, amyloidosis (AL > AA > hATTR).

Paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, SCLC; subacute sensory neuronopathy).

### 6. Hereditary

Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) types 1 (demyelinating, PMP22) > 2 (axonal). 'Inverted champagne bottle' legs, pes cavus, hammer toes.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSAN).

Familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR — transthyretin).

Refsum disease (phytanic acid).

Porphyria (intermittent acute; motor predominant; abdominal pain).

Fabry disease.

- Trauma / compressive

Carpal tunnel syndrome (median, commonest entrapment).

Ulnar at elbow.

Common peroneal at fibular head.

Meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous).

Saturday night palsy (radial).

### 8. Critical illness

Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) — acquired in ICU; flaccid weakness.

### 9. Idiopathic

30% remain idiopathic ('cryptogenic axonal polyneuropathy').

### Approach / Investigations

Step 1 — characterise

Distribution (length-dependent vs MM vs cranial), onset, fibres involved (sensory > motor / motor > sensory / autonomic).

Family history; drug history; alcohol; occupational exposure; nutrition; recent infection.

Step 2 — first-line bloods

CBC, ESR, glucose, HbA1c, B12, folate, TSH, U+E, LFT, vitamin D.

HIV, VDRL, hepatitis B/C.

Serum protein electrophoresis + immunofixation (paraproteinaemia).

### Step 3 — NCS / EMG

Distinguish axonal vs demyelinating, length-dependent vs MM, focal vs diffuse, severity.

Step 4 — targeted second-line

ANA, ENA, ANCA, RF, cryoglobulins.

Heavy metals (lead, arsenic) if exposure.

GBS panel (anti-GM1, GQ1b).

Anti-MAG, anti-GD1a (paraproteinaemic / motor neuropathy).

Lyme serology.

Slit-skin smear for AFB (leprosy).

Genetic testing (CMT, hATTR).

Fat pad / nerve biopsy (amyloidosis, vasculitis).

CSF (CIDP — albumino-cytological dissociation).

### Management — overview

Treat the underlying cause (glycaemic control, vitamin replacement, MDT for leprosy, IVIG/steroids for CIDP, stop offending drug, treat vasculitis).

**Neuropathic pain:** gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, duloxetine, carbamazepine; topical capsaicin, lidocaine.

Physiotherapy, OT, gait aids, foot care (especially diabetic).

Surgical decompression for entrapment.

**Source:** Davidson Ch.27; Boloor Ch.15; NLEP Operational Manual.

GENERAL MEDICINE|338.note:
### Definition (ILAE 2014)

Disease of the brain defined by ANY of: (a) at least 2 unprovoked seizures > 24 h apart, or (b) one unprovoked seizure + recurrence risk ≥ 60% over 10 y, or (c) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

### Classification (ILAE 2017)

### By seizure type

FOCAL onset — aware (formerly simple partial) vs impaired awareness (complex partial).

- Motor onset (automatisms, atonic, clonic, epileptic spasms, hyperkinetic, myoclonic, tonic).

- Non-motor onset (autonomic, behaviour arrest, cognitive, emotional, sensory).

- Focal → bilateral tonic-clonic (formerly secondarily generalised).

GENERALIZED onset — motor (tonic-clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, atonic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor (typical absence, atypical absence, myoclonic, eyelid myoclonia).

UNKNOWN onset.

### By epilepsy type

Focal, generalized, combined generalized + focal, unknown.

### By aetiology

Structural (stroke, tumour, trauma, malformation, hippocampal sclerosis).

Genetic (CDKL5, SCN1A — Dravet, GLUT1).

Infectious (neurocysticercosis — commonest in India; TB, HIV, JE, meningitis sequelae).

Metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, mitochondrial).

Immune (NMDA-R encephalitis, LGI-1, GAD).

Unknown.

### Common syndromes

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) — adolescent, morning myoclonic jerks + GTCS + absence; best Rx valproate (males), levetiracetam (women of child-bearing age).

Childhood absence epilepsy — ethosuximide first-line.

Lennox-Gastaut — multiple seizure types, intellectual disability, slow spike-wave.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis — drug-resistant, surgical candidates.

Dravet syndrome — SCN1A, intractable seizures starting in infancy.

### Investigations

EEG — interictal epileptiform discharges (sensitivity ~30% one record; sleep-deprived/prolonged EEG improves to 80%).

MRI brain — protocol with hippocampal cuts (3T preferred); identifies structural cause.

**Biochemistry:** glucose, calcium, sodium, magnesium, urea, LFTs.

Toxicology, ASD levels (if relevant).

ECG to exclude convulsive syncope.

**Specific:** NCC serology + imaging (India), HIV, autoimmune Ab panel, genetic testing.

### Management

### 1. General

**Counselling:** driving (no driving for 1 y after seizure-free in India per AERB; varies by region), swimming alone avoided, height work, alcohol.

Identify and avoid triggers (sleep deprivation, flashing lights, fever, alcohol withdrawal).

Treat aetiology — Rx NCC, control glucose, etc.

- Antiseizure drugs (ASDs)

### 3. Newer drugs

Brivaracetam (SV2A — newer levetiracetam analog, fewer behavioural AEs).

Lacosamide (slow Na-channel inactivation; focal).

Perampanel (AMPA antagonist; focal + GTCS).

Eslicarbazepine (carbamazepine class, OD).

Cannabidiol (Epidiolex — Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut, tuberous sclerosis).

Cenobamate (focal refractory; PRECISE-1).

Fenfluramine (Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut).

Stiripentol (Dravet adjunct).

### 4. Withdrawal of ASD

Consider after 2-5 y seizure-free; taper over 6-12 months. Relapse risk 30-40%.

### 5. Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE)

Defined as failure of adequate trials of 2 well-tolerated, appropriately chosen ASDs.

Refer to epilepsy surgery centre.

**Resective surgery:** anterior temporal lobectomy + amygdalohippocampectomy (mesial TLE) — 60-70% seizure-free.

**Functional surgery:** corpus callosotomy, hemispherectomy.

**Neuromodulation:** VNS, RNS, DBS (anterior nucleus thalamus).

Ketogenic / modified Atkins diet (children > adults).

### 6. Pregnancy

Levetiracetam, lamotrigine = safest. AVOID valproate (NTD, dysmorphism, autism, IQ; absolute risk 6-10%).

Folate 5 mg/d preconception.

Lamotrigine doses need increasing through pregnancy (oestrogen induces clearance).

### Status epilepticus

Seizure ≥ 5 min OR recurrent without recovery. Stepwise: lorazepam → fosphenytoin/valproate/levetiracetam → midazolam/propofol/pentobarbital infusion (refractory). See Figure 7 below for time-based algorithm.

Fig 7. Status epilepticus — time-based management.

### Prognosis

60-70% achieve seizure freedom on monotherapy.

Mortality 2-3× general population (SUDEP — esp. uncontrolled GTCS).

**Source:** ILAE 2017 Classification; NICE Epilepsy CG137; AAN 2018; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|339.note:
### Definition

Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental disorder characterised by disturbances of thought, perception, affect, volition and social functioning, in a setting of clear consciousness and intact intellect. It is the prototype primary psychotic disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~1% worldwide; M=F.

**Peak onset:** males 15–25 y, females 25–35 y; rare onset <10 y or >50 y.

Heritability ~80%; MZ twin concordance ~50%, sibling risk ~10%, child of one parent ~13%, both parents ~46%.

Higher in lower socio-economic strata (social-drift hypothesis), urban residents, migrants, and winter/spring births.

### Etiology (multifactorial)

**Genetic:** polygenic — DISC1, NRG1, COMT, DRD2, ZNF804A; 22q11.2 deletion.

**Neurodevelopmental:** maternal infection (influenza, toxoplasma) in 2nd trimester, obstetric complications, perinatal hypoxia, advanced paternal age.

**Neurochemical:** mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (positive sx); mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity (negative sx); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin (5-HT2A) dysregulation.

**Neuroanatomic:** ventricular enlargement, ↓ hippocampal & temporal volumes, ↓ prefrontal grey matter.

**Psychosocial:** high expressed emotion in family, urban upbringing, cannabis use in adolescence (dose-related, ↑ risk 2–6 fold).

Pathophysiology — dopamine hypothesis (revised)

Mesolimbic pathway hyperactivity → positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations).

Mesocortical hypoactivity → negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.

Nigrostriatal blockade by typical antipsychotics → extrapyramidal side effects.

Tuberoinfundibular blockade → hyperprolactinaemia.

**Atypicals:** combined D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism — less EPS, better negative-symptom coverage.

Clinical features (Schneider's first-rank symptoms — Kurt Schneider 1959)

Audible thoughts (thought echo) — voice repeats thoughts aloud.

Voices arguing / discussing — third-person auditory hallucinations.

Voices commenting on actions (running commentary).

Thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting.

Made affect, made impulse, made volition (passivity phenomena).

Somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by outside force).

Delusional perception — normal perception with bizarre delusional meaning.

### Positive symptoms

Hallucinations — auditory most common (~70%), then visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory.

Delusions — persecutory (most common), referential, grandiose, religious, somatic, bizarre.

Formal thought disorder — loosening of associations, neologisms, word salad, tangentiality, derailment.

Disorganised behaviour — bizarre dress, posturing, agitation.

Catatonia — stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia/echopraxia.

Negative symptoms (the '5 A's')

Affective flattening — restricted emotional expression.

Alogia — poverty of speech/content.

Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure.

Avolition — loss of motivation/goal-directed behaviour.

Asociality — social withdrawal.

### Cognitive symptoms

Deficits in attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed.

Often pre-morbid and major determinant of long-term functional outcome.

ICD-11 subtypes (subtype-based classification removed in DSM-5 but still asked in Indian exams)

Paranoid — predominant delusions and hallucinations (commonest).

Hebephrenic / disorganised — disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect, thought disorder; early onset, poor prognosis.

Catatonic — motor abnormalities predominate.

Simple — gradual negative-symptom development without positive symptoms.

Residual — past positive symptoms, current chronic negative symptoms.

Undifferentiated — does not fit any category.

### Diagnostic criteria

### DSM-5 schizophrenia

**A. Active-phase symptoms:** ≥2 of: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech, (4) grossly disorganised / catatonic behaviour, (5) negative symptoms. ≥1 must be (1), (2), or (3). Present ≥1 month.

B. Social/occupational dysfunction: Marked impairment in work, interpersonal relations or self-care.

**C. Duration:** Continuous signs ≥6 months (active + prodromal ± residual).

**D. Exclusions:** Schizoaffective + mood disorder with psychotic features excluded; substance / general medical condition excluded.

### ICD-10 schizophrenia (F20)

≥1 'first-rank' (a–d) OR ≥2 'second-rank' (e–h) for ≥1 month:

(a) Thought echo, insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.

(b) Delusions of control, influence or passivity; delusional perception.

(c) 3rd-person auditory hallucinations: voices arguing/discussing or running commentary.

(d) Persistent bizarre delusions (culturally inappropriate).

(e) Persistent hallucinations in any modality with delusions / overvalued ideas.

(f) Breaks / interpolations in train of thought — neologisms, incoherence.

(g) Catatonic behaviour.

(h) Negative symptoms — apathy, paucity of speech, blunted affect.

Differential diagnosis (must exclude)

Investigations (mainly to exclude organic / metabolic causes)

**Bedside:** detailed MSE; cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA); risk assessment (suicide, homicide, vulnerability).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, calcium.

**Infective:** VDRL, HIV serology; CSF if encephalitis suspected.

**Toxicology:** urine drug screen — cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, LSD.

**Imaging:** MRI brain — if first episode, late onset, focal neurological signs, treatment resistance, or atypical course.

**EEG:** if seizures or temporal-lobe epilepsy suspected.

Autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti-NMDA-R) if subacute psychosis with neurological signs.

**Baseline pre-antipsychotic:** ECG (QTc), weight/BMI/waist, fasting lipids, fasting glucose/HbA1c, LFT, prolactin.

### Management

Figure 1. Schizophrenia management — from DSM-5/ICD-10 diagnosis through atypical antipsychotic first-line to clozapine for treatment-resistant disease.

### Acute episode

Ensure safety — assess suicidality, aggression, self-neglect; admit if needed (voluntary / under MHCA 2017).

Address concurrent substance use, malnutrition, infection.

**For agitation:** lorazepam 2–4 mg IM / olanzapine 10 mg IM / haloperidol 5–10 mg IM ± promethazine 25–50 mg IM (rapid tranquillisation per NIMHANS protocol). Avoid IM olanzapine + IM lorazepam together (hypotension, respiratory depression).

### Pharmacotherapy

**First-line:** Atypical (2nd-gen) antipsychotic — start low, titrate weekly to therapeutic range. Risperidone 2–6 mg/d, olanzapine 10–20 mg/d, aripiprazole 10–30 mg/d, quetiapine 300–600 mg/d, ziprasidone 80–160 mg/d, amisulpride 400–800 mg/d. Continue at therapeutic dose ≥4–6 wk before judging response.

**Inadequate response:** Try a 2nd atypical (different agent) or a typical (haloperidol 5–15 mg/d, trifluoperazine 5–20 mg/d, chlorpromazine 300–800 mg/d).

Treatment-resistant (failed ≥2 antipsychotics, ≥6 wk, adequate dose): CLOZAPINE — 12.5 mg → titrate to 300–450 mg/d (max 900 mg). Most effective drug for refractory disease (CATIE, CUtLASS-2). Mandatory monitoring: CBC weekly × 18 wk, then fortnightly to 1 yr, then monthly. Stop if WBC <3,000 or ANC <1,500. Other AEs: myocarditis (esp. 1st month), sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures (dose-related), constipation/ileus, weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia.

Long-acting injectables (LAIs) — for poor adherence: Risperidone LAI 25–50 mg IM q2wk; paliperidone palmitate IM monthly or 3-monthly; aripiprazole LAI monthly; haloperidol decanoate 50–200 mg IM monthly; fluphenazine decanoate 12.5–50 mg IM monthly.

Augmentation in clozapine-resistant: Add ECT, second antipsychotic (amisulpride / aripiprazole), or mood stabiliser (lithium / valproate).

Duration of antipsychotic treatment

**First episode:** continue ≥1–2 years after full remission, then taper slowly.

GENERAL MEDICINE|340.note:
### Definition (ILAE 2014)

Disease of the brain defined by ANY of: (a) at least 2 unprovoked seizures > 24 h apart, or (b) one unprovoked seizure + recurrence risk ≥ 60% over 10 y, or (c) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

### Classification (ILAE 2017)

### By seizure type

FOCAL onset — aware (formerly simple partial) vs impaired awareness (complex partial).

- Motor onset (automatisms, atonic, clonic, epileptic spasms, hyperkinetic, myoclonic, tonic).

- Non-motor onset (autonomic, behaviour arrest, cognitive, emotional, sensory).

- Focal → bilateral tonic-clonic (formerly secondarily generalised).

GENERALIZED onset — motor (tonic-clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, atonic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor (typical absence, atypical absence, myoclonic, eyelid myoclonia).

UNKNOWN onset.

### By epilepsy type

Focal, generalized, combined generalized + focal, unknown.

### By aetiology

Structural (stroke, tumour, trauma, malformation, hippocampal sclerosis).

Genetic (CDKL5, SCN1A — Dravet, GLUT1).

Infectious (neurocysticercosis — commonest in India; TB, HIV, JE, meningitis sequelae).

Metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, mitochondrial).

Immune (NMDA-R encephalitis, LGI-1, GAD).

Unknown.

### Common syndromes

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) — adolescent, morning myoclonic jerks + GTCS + absence; best Rx valproate (males), levetiracetam (women of child-bearing age).

Childhood absence epilepsy — ethosuximide first-line.

Lennox-Gastaut — multiple seizure types, intellectual disability, slow spike-wave.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis — drug-resistant, surgical candidates.

Dravet syndrome — SCN1A, intractable seizures starting in infancy.

### Investigations

EEG — interictal epileptiform discharges (sensitivity ~30% one record; sleep-deprived/prolonged EEG improves to 80%).

MRI brain — protocol with hippocampal cuts (3T preferred); identifies structural cause.

**Biochemistry:** glucose, calcium, sodium, magnesium, urea, LFTs.

Toxicology, ASD levels (if relevant).

ECG to exclude convulsive syncope.

**Specific:** NCC serology + imaging (India), HIV, autoimmune Ab panel, genetic testing.

### Management

### 1. General

**Counselling:** driving (no driving for 1 y after seizure-free in India per AERB; varies by region), swimming alone avoided, height work, alcohol.

Identify and avoid triggers (sleep deprivation, flashing lights, fever, alcohol withdrawal).

Treat aetiology — Rx NCC, control glucose, etc.

- Antiseizure drugs (ASDs)

### 3. Newer drugs

Brivaracetam (SV2A — newer levetiracetam analog, fewer behavioural AEs).

Lacosamide (slow Na-channel inactivation; focal).

Perampanel (AMPA antagonist; focal + GTCS).

Eslicarbazepine (carbamazepine class, OD).

Cannabidiol (Epidiolex — Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut, tuberous sclerosis).

Cenobamate (focal refractory; PRECISE-1).

Fenfluramine (Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut).

Stiripentol (Dravet adjunct).

### 4. Withdrawal of ASD

Consider after 2-5 y seizure-free; taper over 6-12 months. Relapse risk 30-40%.

### 5. Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE)

Defined as failure of adequate trials of 2 well-tolerated, appropriately chosen ASDs.

Refer to epilepsy surgery centre.

**Resective surgery:** anterior temporal lobectomy + amygdalohippocampectomy (mesial TLE) — 60-70% seizure-free.

**Functional surgery:** corpus callosotomy, hemispherectomy.

**Neuromodulation:** VNS, RNS, DBS (anterior nucleus thalamus).

Ketogenic / modified Atkins diet (children > adults).

### 6. Pregnancy

Levetiracetam, lamotrigine = safest. AVOID valproate (NTD, dysmorphism, autism, IQ; absolute risk 6-10%).

Folate 5 mg/d preconception.

Lamotrigine doses need increasing through pregnancy (oestrogen induces clearance).

### Status epilepticus

Seizure ≥ 5 min OR recurrent without recovery. Stepwise: lorazepam → fosphenytoin/valproate/levetiracetam → midazolam/propofol/pentobarbital infusion (refractory). See Figure 7 below for time-based algorithm.

Fig 7. Status epilepticus — time-based management.

### Prognosis

60-70% achieve seizure freedom on monotherapy.

Mortality 2-3× general population (SUDEP — esp. uncontrolled GTCS).

**Source:** ILAE 2017 Classification; NICE Epilepsy CG137; AAN 2018; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|341.note:
### Definition

Sustained intracranial pressure (ICP) > 20 mmHg (normal 5-15 mmHg, < 7 mmHg upright). Monroe-Kellie doctrine: cranial vault is rigid; volumes of brain (80%), CSF (10%) and blood (10%) must remain constant. Increase in one → compensation by others (CSF displacement, venous compression) until exhaustion → ICP rises rapidly.

### Aetiology

Increased brain volume (mass effect)

**Tumours:** primary (glioma, meningioma), metastases.

**Haemorrhage:** ICH, SAH, EDH, SDH, contusion.

Abscess, tuberculoma, cysticercosis.

**Cerebral oedema:** ischaemic stroke (malignant MCA), trauma, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, hypertensive encephalopathy, PRES, hepatic encephalopathy, hyponatraemia.

### Increased CSF volume

Obstructive hydrocephalus (aqueduct stenosis, posterior fossa mass, colloid cyst).

Communicating hydrocephalus (post-SAH, post-meningitis).

CSF overproduction (choroid plexus papilloma — rare).

### Increased blood volume

**Venous:** cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, jugular vein obstruction, IVC obstruction, SVC syndrome.

**Arterial:** hypercapnia (CO₂ retention), hypoxia, hyperthermia, malignant hypertension.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH / pseudotumour cerebri)

Young obese females; secondary IIH — tetracyclines, hypervitaminosis A, OCP, steroid withdrawal, venous sinus stenosis.

### Clinical features — SYMPTOMS

### Triad of raised ICP

Headache — worse mornings, on coughing/sneezing/straining/lying down; later constant.

Vomiting — projectile, often without nausea (especially posterior fossa).

Papilloedema — bilateral; takes 24-48 h to develop.

### Other symptoms

Drowsiness, altered consciousness → coma.

Diplopia (false-localising VI nerve palsy — long course).

Transient visual obscurations (greying-out on bending).

Pulsatile tinnitus (IIH, dural fistula).

Cognitive slowing, behavioural change.

Seizures.

### SIGNS

Cushing's reflex (late, ominous — brainstem compression)

Hypertension (widened pulse pressure) + Bradycardia + Irregular respiration (Cheyne-Stokes / apneustic).

### Papilloedema (fundoscopy)

**Grade I:** blurred disc margins (nasal first).

**Grade II:** full obliteration of disc margin.

**Grade III:** elevation of disc + haemorrhages.

**Grade IV:** above + cotton-wool spots; visual loss.

**Grade V:** above + macular oedema; severe visual loss.

### Cranial nerve palsies

VI nerve palsy (false localising — long course makes it vulnerable to stretch).

III nerve palsy (uncal herniation — fixed dilated pupil, eye 'down and out').

Herniation syndromes (impending coning)

**Uncal (transtentorial):** III palsy → fixed dilated pupil ipsilateral → contralateral hemiparesis (Kernohan's notch — false localising) → coma.

**Subfalcine (cingulate):** contralateral leg weakness (ACA compression).

**Tonsillar (foramen magnum):** neck stiffness, head tilt, apnoea, cardiac arrest.

**Upward (transtentorial):** posterior fossa mass; brainstem compression.

### Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) — track over time

Drop ≥ 2 points → urgent imaging + neurosurgery.

### Investigations

### 1. Imaging

NCCT head — first investigation. Look for: mass, midline shift, effaced sulci, effaced ventricles, loss of basal cisterns.

MRI brain with Gd, MR venogram — better characterisation, CVT.

- Lumbar puncture — CONTRAINDICATED if mass effect or focal signs

Risk of cerebral herniation.

Safe and diagnostic ONLY in IIH (no mass on imaging): opening pressure > 25 cm H₂O (or > 28 in obese).

### 3. ICP monitoring (ICU)

Intraventricular catheter (EVD) — gold standard; also therapeutic.

Intraparenchymal bolt (Codman / Camino).

**Non-invasive:** optic nerve sheath diameter > 5.0-5.5 mm on US; trans-cranial Doppler.

### 4. Cause-specific

MR venography (CVT).

EEG (encephalopathy).

**Bloods:** glucose, electrolytes, ABG, ammonia (hepatic), TSH, LFT.

### Management — General principles

### 1. ABCs

Intubation if GCS ≤ 8.

Avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia (worsen ICP); target PaCO₂ 32-35 mmHg.

Maintain CPP 60-70 mmHg (CPP = MAP - ICP).

### 2. Position

Head-up 30°, midline, avoid tight neck ties.

### 3. Osmotherapy

Mannitol 20% — 0.5-1 g/kg over 15-20 min; repeat q6h. Target serum osm < 320.

Hypertonic saline 3% — 250 mL bolus; ongoing infusion. Target Na 145-155.

### 4. CSF drainage

EVD if hydrocephalus.

- Sedation, analgesia, paralysis

Propofol, midazolam; rocuronium if needed.

- Hyperventilation — transient bridge only

Brief PaCO₂ 30-32 mmHg if impending herniation (causes vasoconstriction; sustained use harmful).

### 7. Steroids

Useful for VASOGENIC oedema (tumour, abscess): dexamethasone 16 mg STAT then 4 mg q6h.

AVOID in TBI and stroke (no benefit/harmful).

- Avoid pyrexia, hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia, seizures

Paracetamol/cooling.

Glucose 140-180.

Na 145-155 in raised ICP.

Levetiracetam if seizures.

### 9. Surgical

Decompressive craniectomy (malignant MCA, refractory TBI).

Tumour resection, evacuation of haematoma.

VP shunt for hydrocephalus.

### 10. Cause-specific

CVT — anticoagulation (heparin/LMWH).

Hyponatraemia — correct slowly.

Hepatic encephalopathy — lactulose, rifaximin, ammonia control.

Hypertensive emergency — IV labetalol/nicardipine.

### 11. IIH-specific

Weight loss (cornerstone), acetazolamide 1-4 g/d, topiramate.

CSF shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration if vision threatened.

Venous sinus stenting for transverse sinus stenosis.

### Prognosis

Depends on cause; sustained ICP > 25 mmHg or impending herniation predicts poor outcome unless reversed quickly.

**Source:** Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines 2017; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental disorder characterised by disturbances of thought, perception, affect, volition and social functioning, in a setting of clear consciousness and intact intellect. It is the prototype primary psychotic disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~1% worldwide; M=F.

**Peak onset:** males 15–25 y, females 25–35 y; rare onset <10 y or >50 y.

Heritability ~80%; MZ twin concordance ~50%, sibling risk ~10%, child of one parent ~13%, both parents ~46%.

Higher in lower socio-economic strata (social-drift hypothesis), urban residents, migrants, and winter/spring births.

### Etiology (multifactorial)

**Genetic:** polygenic — DISC1, NRG1, COMT, DRD2, ZNF804A; 22q11.2 deletion.

**Neurodevelopmental:** maternal infection (influenza, toxoplasma) in 2nd trimester, obstetric complications, perinatal hypoxia, advanced paternal age.

**Neurochemical:** mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (positive sx); mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity (negative sx); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin (5-HT2A) dysregulation.

**Neuroanatomic:** ventricular enlargement, ↓ hippocampal & temporal volumes, ↓ prefrontal grey matter.

**Psychosocial:** high expressed emotion in family, urban upbringing, cannabis use in adolescence (dose-related, ↑ risk 2–6 fold).

Pathophysiology — dopamine hypothesis (revised)

Mesolimbic pathway hyperactivity → positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations).

Mesocortical hypoactivity → negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.

Nigrostriatal blockade by typical antipsychotics → extrapyramidal side effects.

Tuberoinfundibular blockade → hyperprolactinaemia.

**Atypicals:** combined D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism — less EPS, better negative-symptom coverage.

Clinical features (Schneider's first-rank symptoms — Kurt Schneider 1959)

Audible thoughts (thought echo) — voice repeats thoughts aloud.

Voices arguing / discussing — third-person auditory hallucinations.

Voices commenting on actions (running commentary).

Thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting.

Made affect, made impulse, made volition (passivity phenomena).

Somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by outside force).

Delusional perception — normal perception with bizarre delusional meaning.

### Positive symptoms

Hallucinations — auditory most common (~70%), then visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory.

Delusions — persecutory (most common), referential, grandiose, religious, somatic, bizarre.

Formal thought disorder — loosening of associations, neologisms, word salad, tangentiality, derailment.

Disorganised behaviour — bizarre dress, posturing, agitation.

Catatonia — stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia/echopraxia.

Negative symptoms (the '5 A's')

Affective flattening — restricted emotional expression.

Alogia — poverty of speech/content.

Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure.

Avolition — loss of motivation/goal-directed behaviour.

Asociality — social withdrawal.

Deficits in attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed.

Often pre-morbid and major determinant of long-term functional outcome.

Paranoid — predominant delusions and hallucinations (commonest).

Hebephrenic / disorganised — disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect, thought disorder; early onset, poor prognosis.

Catatonic — motor abnormalities predominate.

Simple — gradual negative-symptom development without positive symptoms.

Residual — past positive symptoms, current chronic negative symptoms.

Undifferentiated — does not fit any category.

### DSM-5 schizophrenia

**A. Active-phase symptoms:** ≥2 of: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech, (4) grossly disorganised / catatonic behaviour, (5) negative symptoms. ≥1 must be (1), (2), or (3). Present ≥1 month.

B. Social/occupational dysfunction: Marked impairment in work, interpersonal relations or self-care.

**C. Duration:** Continuous signs ≥6 months (active + prodromal ± residual).

**D. Exclusions:** Schizoaffective + mood disorder with psychotic features excluded; substance / general medical condition excluded.

### ICD-10 schizophrenia (F20)

≥1 'first-rank' (a–d) OR ≥2 'second-rank' (e–h) for ≥1 month:

(a) Thought echo, insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.

(b) Delusions of control, influence or passivity; delusional perception.

(c) 3rd-person auditory hallucinations: voices arguing/discussing or running commentary.

(d) Persistent bizarre delusions (culturally inappropriate).

(e) Persistent hallucinations in any modality with delusions / overvalued ideas.

(f) Breaks / interpolations in train of thought — neologisms, incoherence.

(g) Catatonic behaviour.

(h) Negative symptoms — apathy, paucity of speech, blunted affect.

**Bedside:** detailed MSE; cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA); risk assessment (suicide, homicide, vulnerability).
