GENERAL MEDICINE|344.note:
### Definition

Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental disorder characterised by disturbances of thought, perception, affect, volition and social functioning, in a setting of clear consciousness and intact intellect. It is the prototype primary psychotic disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~1% worldwide; M=F.

**Peak onset:** males 15–25 y, females 25–35 y; rare onset <10 y or >50 y.

Heritability ~80%; MZ twin concordance ~50%, sibling risk ~10%, child of one parent ~13%, both parents ~46%.

Higher in lower socio-economic strata (social-drift hypothesis), urban residents, migrants, and winter/spring births.

### Etiology (multifactorial)

**Genetic:** polygenic — DISC1, NRG1, COMT, DRD2, ZNF804A; 22q11.2 deletion.

**Neurodevelopmental:** maternal infection (influenza, toxoplasma) in 2nd trimester, obstetric complications, perinatal hypoxia, advanced paternal age.

**Neurochemical:** mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (positive sx); mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity (negative sx); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin (5-HT2A) dysregulation.

**Neuroanatomic:** ventricular enlargement, ↓ hippocampal & temporal volumes, ↓ prefrontal grey matter.

**Psychosocial:** high expressed emotion in family, urban upbringing, cannabis use in adolescence (dose-related, ↑ risk 2–6 fold).

Pathophysiology — dopamine hypothesis (revised)

Mesolimbic pathway hyperactivity → positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations).

Mesocortical hypoactivity → negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.

Nigrostriatal blockade by typical antipsychotics → extrapyramidal side effects.

Tuberoinfundibular blockade → hyperprolactinaemia.

**Atypicals:** combined D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism — less EPS, better negative-symptom coverage.

Clinical features (Schneider's first-rank symptoms — Kurt Schneider 1959)

Audible thoughts (thought echo) — voice repeats thoughts aloud.

Voices arguing / discussing — third-person auditory hallucinations.

Voices commenting on actions (running commentary).

Thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting.

Made affect, made impulse, made volition (passivity phenomena).

Somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by outside force).

Delusional perception — normal perception with bizarre delusional meaning.

### Positive symptoms

Hallucinations — auditory most common (~70%), then visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory.

Delusions — persecutory (most common), referential, grandiose, religious, somatic, bizarre.

Formal thought disorder — loosening of associations, neologisms, word salad, tangentiality, derailment.

Disorganised behaviour — bizarre dress, posturing, agitation.

Catatonia — stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia/echopraxia.

Negative symptoms (the '5 A's')

Affective flattening — restricted emotional expression.

Alogia — poverty of speech/content.

Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure.

Avolition — loss of motivation/goal-directed behaviour.

Asociality — social withdrawal.

### Cognitive symptoms

Deficits in attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed.

Often pre-morbid and major determinant of long-term functional outcome.

ICD-11 subtypes (subtype-based classification removed in DSM-5 but still asked in Indian exams)

Paranoid — predominant delusions and hallucinations (commonest).

Hebephrenic / disorganised — disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect, thought disorder; early onset, poor prognosis.

Catatonic — motor abnormalities predominate.

Simple — gradual negative-symptom development without positive symptoms.

Residual — past positive symptoms, current chronic negative symptoms.

Undifferentiated — does not fit any category.

### Diagnostic criteria

### DSM-5 schizophrenia

**A. Active-phase symptoms:** ≥2 of: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech, (4) grossly disorganised / catatonic behaviour, (5) negative symptoms. ≥1 must be (1), (2), or (3). Present ≥1 month.

B. Social/occupational dysfunction: Marked impairment in work, interpersonal relations or self-care.

**C. Duration:** Continuous signs ≥6 months (active + prodromal ± residual).

**D. Exclusions:** Schizoaffective + mood disorder with psychotic features excluded; substance / general medical condition excluded.

### ICD-10 schizophrenia (F20)

≥1 'first-rank' (a–d) OR ≥2 'second-rank' (e–h) for ≥1 month:

(a) Thought echo, insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.

(b) Delusions of control, influence or passivity; delusional perception.

(c) 3rd-person auditory hallucinations: voices arguing/discussing or running commentary.

(d) Persistent bizarre delusions (culturally inappropriate).

(e) Persistent hallucinations in any modality with delusions / overvalued ideas.

(f) Breaks / interpolations in train of thought — neologisms, incoherence.

(g) Catatonic behaviour.

(h) Negative symptoms — apathy, paucity of speech, blunted affect.

Differential diagnosis (must exclude)

Investigations (mainly to exclude organic / metabolic causes)

**Bedside:** detailed MSE; cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA); risk assessment (suicide, homicide, vulnerability).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, calcium.

**Infective:** VDRL, HIV serology; CSF if encephalitis suspected.

**Toxicology:** urine drug screen — cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, LSD.

**Imaging:** MRI brain — if first episode, late onset, focal neurological signs, treatment resistance, or atypical course.

**EEG:** if seizures or temporal-lobe epilepsy suspected.

Autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti-NMDA-R) if subacute psychosis with neurological signs.

**Baseline pre-antipsychotic:** ECG (QTc), weight/BMI/waist, fasting lipids, fasting glucose/HbA1c, LFT, prolactin.

### Management

Figure 1. Schizophrenia management — from DSM-5/ICD-10 diagnosis through atypical antipsychotic first-line to clozapine for treatment-resistant disease.

### Acute episode

Ensure safety — assess suicidality, aggression, self-neglect; admit if needed (voluntary / under MHCA 2017).

Address concurrent substance use, malnutrition, infection.

**For agitation:** lorazepam 2–4 mg IM / olanzapine 10 mg IM / haloperidol 5–10 mg IM ± promethazine 25–50 mg IM (rapid tranquillisation per NIMHANS protocol). Avoid IM olanzapine + IM lorazepam together (hypotension, respiratory depression).

### Pharmacotherapy

**First-line:** Atypical (2nd-gen) antipsychotic — start low, titrate weekly to therapeutic range. Risperidone 2–6 mg/d, olanzapine 10–20 mg/d, aripiprazole 10–30 mg/d, quetiapine 300–600 mg/d, ziprasidone 80–160 mg/d, amisulpride 400–800 mg/d. Continue at therapeutic dose ≥4–6 wk before judging response.

**Inadequate response:** Try a 2nd atypical (different agent) or a typical (haloperidol 5–15 mg/d, trifluoperazine 5–20 mg/d, chlorpromazine 300–800 mg/d).

Treatment-resistant (failed ≥2 antipsychotics, ≥6 wk, adequate dose): CLOZAPINE — 12.5 mg → titrate to 300–450 mg/d (max 900 mg). Most effective drug for refractory disease (CATIE, CUtLASS-2). Mandatory monitoring: CBC weekly × 18 wk, then fortnightly to 1 yr, then monthly. Stop if WBC <3,000 or ANC <1,500. Other AEs: myocarditis (esp. 1st month), sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures (dose-related), constipation/ileus, weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia.

Long-acting injectables (LAIs) — for poor adherence: Risperidone LAI 25–50 mg IM q2wk; paliperidone palmitate IM monthly or 3-monthly; aripiprazole LAI monthly; haloperidol decanoate 50–200 mg IM monthly; fluphenazine decanoate 12.5–50 mg IM monthly.

Augmentation in clozapine-resistant: Add ECT, second antipsychotic (amisulpride / aripiprazole), or mood stabiliser (lithium / valproate).

Duration of antipsychotic treatment

**First episode:** continue ≥1–2 years after full remission, then taper slowly.

**Recurrent / multi-episode:** ≥5 years; many patients need lifelong therapy.

Abrupt discontinuation → 80% relapse within 2 years.

Psychosocial interventions (essential — not optional)

Psychoeducation — patient and family; reduces high expressed emotion.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for psychosis (CBT-p) — reduces residual positive symptoms.

Family therapy — reduces relapse.

Supported employment / Individual Placement & Support (IPS).

Social skills training, assertive community treatment (ACT) for severe persistent disease.

Cognitive remediation for cognitive symptoms.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) — indications

Catatonia (response in 80–90%).

Severe suicidality / homicidality.

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (clozapine augmentation).

Severe positive symptoms not responding to ≥6 wk of antipsychotic.

6–12 sessions, 2–3 times per week; modified (anaesthesia + suxamethonium).

Antipsychotic side effects (sub-question — Boloor A372)

Typical (1st-generation) — high-potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine)

**Extrapyramidal:** acute dystonia (hours–days; oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonus → IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg or promethazine 25–50 mg), parkinsonism (days–weeks; bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor → anticholinergic e.g. trihexyphenidyl 2–10 mg/d), akathisia (motor restlessness → propranolol 30–80 mg/d or BZD), tardive dyskinesia (months–years; orobuccolingual choreoathetosis → switch to clozapine, valbenazine or tetrabenazine).

Hyperprolactinaemia → amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, ↓ libido, osteoporosis (esp. risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride).

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, ↑↑ CK, leucocytosis. STOP drug, ICU, IV fluids/cooling, dantrolene 1–2 mg/kg q6h, bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS. Mortality 10–20%.

Lowered seizure threshold (chlorpromazine > others).

QTc prolongation (haloperidol IV, thioridazine — withdrawn).

Typical low-potency (chlorpromazine, thioridazine)

Anticholinergic — dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, ileus.

Antihistaminic — sedation, weight gain.

α-blockade — postural hypotension.

Photosensitivity, blue-grey skin pigmentation; corneal/lens deposits with prolonged use.

Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice with chlorpromazine).

Atypical (2nd-generation) — overall fewer EPS, more metabolic

Metabolic syndrome — weight gain, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance / diabetes (olanzapine + clozapine highest; ziprasidone + aripiprazole + lurasidone lowest).

Risperidone / paliperidone — dose-related EPS and hyperprolactinaemia.

Clozapine — agranulocytosis, myocarditis, sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures, ileus, weight gain, metabolic syndrome.

Quetiapine — sedation, postural hypotension.

Aripiprazole — akathisia (most common SE), impulse-control problems (gambling, hypersexuality).

Ziprasidone, lurasidone — QTc prolongation; lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal food.

Asenapine — sublingual; oral hypoaesthesia, EPS at high dose.

Drugs causing hallucinations (sub-question — Boloor A363)

**Recreational / drugs of abuse:** cannabis, LSD, psilocybin (magic mushroom), mescaline, MDMA (ecstasy), amphetamines, cocaine, PCP, ketamine, alcohol (in withdrawal — DT).

**Anti-Parkinsonian:** levodopa, dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine), amantadine, selegiline.

**Anticholinergics:** atropine, scopolamine, hyoscine, trihexyphenidyl, benztropine; antihistamines (diphenhydramine); TCAs at toxic doses.

**Steroids:** prednisolone (high-dose), ACTH ('steroid psychosis').

**Antimalarials:** chloroquine, mefloquine, primaquine.

**Antibiotics:** ciprofloxacin (CNS), isoniazid, cycloserine, clarithromycin, voriconazole.

**Antivirals:** aciclovir (renal failure), efavirenz, oseltamivir.

**Anaesthetics:** ketamine, nitrous oxide.

Opioids in overdose; tramadol; pentazocine.

**Withdrawal-induced:** alcohol (DT), benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids.

**Others:** digoxin toxicity, β-blockers (lipophilic — propranolol), interferon-α, baclofen withdrawal, lithium toxicity.

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk 5–10% (highest in young males, early course, after discharge).

Violence (small but real; usually against family, often with substance co-use).

Substance abuse comorbidity — ~50% (nicotine, cannabis, alcohol).

Cardiovascular disease — leading cause of premature mortality; antipsychotic metabolic effects + smoking + sedentary lifestyle.

Polydipsia, hyponatraemia.

Homelessness, unemployment, social isolation.

Reduced life expectancy by 15–20 years (suicide + CV disease + suboptimal medical care).

Prognosis (rule of thirds)

≈1/3 substantial recovery, ≈1/3 partial response with relapses, ≈1/3 chronic disabling course.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, late onset, female, prominent positive symptoms, mood symptoms, married, good pre-morbid function, family history of mood disorder, paranoid subtype, identifiable stressor, short duration of untreated psychosis (DUP).

**Poor prognostic factors:** insidious onset, early onset, male, negative symptoms, social withdrawal, family history of schizophrenia, hebephrenic / simple subtype, no precipitant, long DUP, poor pre-morbid function.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; ICMR/NIMHANS — Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia (Indian Psychiatric Society); DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock — Synopsis of Psychiatry 12e.

### Definition

Sudden focal neurological deficit lasting > 24 h due to focal cerebral ischaemia from arterial occlusion (embolic, thrombotic, or lacunar). 80% of all strokes; remainder are haemorrhagic.

### Aetiology (TOAST classification)

Large artery atherosclerosis (carotid, vertebrobasilar).

Cardioembolic (AF — commonest, valvular, post-MI LV thrombus, infective endocarditis).

Small vessel (lacunar) — hypertensive lipohyalinosis.

**Other determined:** dissection, vasculitis, Moyamoya, thrombophilia, drugs (cocaine).

Cryptogenic / undetermined — 25%.

Clinical syndromes (Bamford / OCSP)

TACS — total anterior circulation (all 3 of): hemiparesis + hemianopia + cortical dysfunction (aphasia/neglect).

**PACS — partial:** any 2 of above.

**LACS — lacunar:** pure motor / pure sensory / sensorimotor / ataxic hemiparesis (no cortical signs).

**POCS — posterior:** cranial nerve palsy + contralateral motor/sensory; cerebellar; bilateral motor; isolated hemianopia.

### Investigations

NCCT head — rules out haemorrhage; early signs (hyperdense MCA, loss of insular ribbon).

MRI DWI — most sensitive (lights up within 30 min); FLAIR for age of infarct.

CTA/MRA — vessel patency; identifies LVO for thrombectomy.

**Aetiology:** ECG, holter, echo, carotid Doppler, lipids, HbA1c, thrombophilia (young).

### Management

**tPA:** tPA: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV within 4.5 h. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus = acceptable.

**Thrombectomy:** Thrombectomy: LVO within 6-24 h (DAWN/DEFUSE-3).

**Aspirin:** Aspirin: 300 mg loading then 75-150 mg/day.

**BP:** BP: Permissive < 220/120; lower to < 185/110 before tPA.

**Glucose:** Glucose: 140-180 mg/dL.

**DVT prophylaxis:** DVT prophylaxis: IPC then LMWH 24-48 h.

**Stroke unit:** Stroke unit: Mortality ↓ 20%.

### tPA contraindications (abridged)

Haemorrhage on CT; BP > 185/110 unresponsive; INR > 1.7; platelets < 100,000.

Active bleeding, recent major surgery < 14 d, recent stroke / head trauma < 3 mo, recent GI bleed < 21 d.

Glucose < 50 or > 400 mg/dL; suspected SAH; intracranial neoplasm/AVM/aneurysm.

### Complications

Haemorrhagic transformation, malignant cerebral oedema (large MCA), seizures, aspiration pneumonia, DVT/PE.

**Source:** AHA/ASA 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|347.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition (ILAE 2014)

Disease of the brain defined by ANY of: (a) at least 2 unprovoked seizures > 24 h apart, or (b) one unprovoked seizure + recurrence risk ≥ 60% over 10 y, or (c) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

### Classification (ILAE 2017)

### By seizure type

FOCAL onset — aware (formerly simple partial) vs impaired awareness (complex partial).

- Motor onset (automatisms, atonic, clonic, epileptic spasms, hyperkinetic, myoclonic, tonic).

- Non-motor onset (autonomic, behaviour arrest, cognitive, emotional, sensory).

- Focal → bilateral tonic-clonic (formerly secondarily generalised).

GENERALIZED onset — motor (tonic-clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, atonic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor (typical absence, atypical absence, myoclonic, eyelid myoclonia).

UNKNOWN onset.

### By epilepsy type

Focal, generalized, combined generalized + focal, unknown.

### By aetiology

Structural (stroke, tumour, trauma, malformation, hippocampal sclerosis).

Genetic (CDKL5, SCN1A — Dravet, GLUT1).

Infectious (neurocysticercosis — commonest in India; TB, HIV, JE, meningitis sequelae).

Metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, mitochondrial).

Immune (NMDA-R encephalitis, LGI-1, GAD).

Unknown.

### Common syndromes

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) — adolescent, morning myoclonic jerks + GTCS + absence; best Rx valproate (males), levetiracetam (women of child-bearing age).

Childhood absence epilepsy — ethosuximide first-line.

Lennox-Gastaut — multiple seizure types, intellectual disability, slow spike-wave.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis — drug-resistant, surgical candidates.

Dravet syndrome — SCN1A, intractable seizures starting in infancy.

### Investigations

EEG — interictal epileptiform discharges (sensitivity ~30% one record; sleep-deprived/prolonged EEG improves to 80%).

MRI brain — protocol with hippocampal cuts (3T preferred); identifies structural cause.

**Biochemistry:** glucose, calcium, sodium, magnesium, urea, LFTs.

Toxicology, ASD levels (if relevant).

ECG to exclude convulsive syncope.

**Specific:** NCC serology + imaging (India), HIV, autoimmune Ab panel, genetic testing.

### Management

### 1. General

**Counselling:** driving (no driving for 1 y after seizure-free in India per AERB; varies by region), swimming alone avoided, height work, alcohol.

Identify and avoid triggers (sleep deprivation, flashing lights, fever, alcohol withdrawal).

Treat aetiology — Rx NCC, control glucose, etc.

- Antiseizure drugs (ASDs)

### 3. Newer drugs

Brivaracetam (SV2A — newer levetiracetam analog, fewer behavioural AEs).

Lacosamide (slow Na-channel inactivation; focal).

Perampanel (AMPA antagonist; focal + GTCS).

Eslicarbazepine (carbamazepine class, OD).

Cannabidiol (Epidiolex — Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut, tuberous sclerosis).

Cenobamate (focal refractory; PRECISE-1).

Fenfluramine (Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut).

Stiripentol (Dravet adjunct).

### 4. Withdrawal of ASD

Consider after 2-5 y seizure-free; taper over 6-12 months. Relapse risk 30-40%.

### 5. Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE)

Defined as failure of adequate trials of 2 well-tolerated, appropriately chosen ASDs.

Refer to epilepsy surgery centre.

**Resective surgery:** anterior temporal lobectomy + amygdalohippocampectomy (mesial TLE) — 60-70% seizure-free.

**Functional surgery:** corpus callosotomy, hemispherectomy.

**Neuromodulation:** VNS, RNS, DBS (anterior nucleus thalamus).

Ketogenic / modified Atkins diet (children > adults).

### 6. Pregnancy

Levetiracetam, lamotrigine = safest. AVOID valproate (NTD, dysmorphism, autism, IQ; absolute risk 6-10%).

Folate 5 mg/d preconception.

Lamotrigine doses need increasing through pregnancy (oestrogen induces clearance).

### Status epilepticus

Seizure ≥ 5 min OR recurrent without recovery. Stepwise: lorazepam → fosphenytoin/valproate/levetiracetam → midazolam/propofol/pentobarbital infusion (refractory). See Figure 7 below for time-based algorithm.

Fig 7. Status epilepticus — time-based management.

### Prognosis

60-70% achieve seizure freedom on monotherapy.

Mortality 2-3× general population (SUDEP — esp. uncontrolled GTCS).

**Source:** ILAE 2017 Classification; NICE Epilepsy CG137; AAN 2018; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition

Disorder of peripheral nervous system, presenting with sensory, motor, autonomic, or mixed symptoms. Most common — distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP).

### Classification

By number of nerves

Mononeuropathy — single nerve (carpal tunnel, foot drop).

Mononeuritis multiplex — multiple non-contiguous nerves (vasculitis classic).

Polyneuropathy — symmetric, distal (length-dependent).

### By fibres

Motor / Sensory / Autonomic / Mixed.

### By pathology

Demyelinating (slow NCV).

Axonal (low amplitude).

Mixed.

### By course

**Acute (< 4 weeks):** GBS, toxic, porphyria.

Subacute (4-8 weeks).

**Chronic (> 8 weeks):** diabetic, CIDP, hereditary.

### AETIOLOGY (DANG THE RAPIST mnemonic / systematic)

### 1. Metabolic / Endocrine

Diabetes mellitus — COMMONEST cause worldwide. Distal symmetric, autonomic, mononeuropathy, femoral amyotrophy. Dependent on glycaemic control.

Hypothyroidism (carpal tunnel, mild DSP).

Chronic kidney disease (uraemic neuropathy).

Liver failure (chronic).

### 2. Nutritional

Vitamin B12 deficiency (SACD + PN).

Folate, vitamin B1 (Wernicke, beriberi — wet/dry).

Vitamin B6 deficiency (INH neuropathy) or EXCESS (pyridoxine megadose neuropathy).

Vitamin E (cerebellar + PN).

Copper deficiency (myeloneuropathy — gastric bypass, zinc overuse).

Strachan syndrome (multinutrient — Cuban / Tanzanian epidemic).

### 3. Toxic

Alcohol (chronic — thiamine + direct toxic).

**Heavy metals:** lead (motor; wrist drop), arsenic (sensorimotor), mercury, thallium.

**Drugs:** vincristine, cisplatin, oxaliplatin, paclitaxel, bortezomib (chemo); isoniazid (without pyridoxine), metronidazole (high dose), nitrofurantoin, dapsone, amiodarone, hydralazine, statins, colchicine.

Organophosphates (delayed neuropathy after acute toxicity).

n-Hexane (glue-sniffing).

Acrylamide.

### 4. Infections

Leprosy (Hansen's) — COMMONEST treatable cause in India. Mononeuritis multiplex; ulnar > median, common peroneal, posterior tibial, sural, supraorbital. Skin patches with sensory loss.

HIV (DSP — late; ART-related neuropathy — d4T, ddI).

Herpes zoster (post-herpetic neuralgia).

Lyme disease.

Diphtheria, botulism (rare in India now).

Hepatitis B/C, syphilis.

### 5. Immune / Inflammatory

GBS / CIDP.

Multifocal motor neuropathy (anti-GM1).

**Vasculitis:** polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA vasculitis (EGPA, GPA, MPA), cryoglobulinaemia, SLE, Sjögren's, RA. Often mononeuritis multiplex.

**Paraproteinaemic:** MGUS, multiple myeloma, Waldenström, POEMS, amyloidosis (AL > AA > hATTR).

Paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, SCLC; subacute sensory neuronopathy).

### 6. Hereditary

Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) types 1 (demyelinating, PMP22) > 2 (axonal). 'Inverted champagne bottle' legs, pes cavus, hammer toes.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSAN).

Familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR — transthyretin).

Refsum disease (phytanic acid).

Porphyria (intermittent acute; motor predominant; abdominal pain).

Fabry disease.

- Trauma / compressive

Carpal tunnel syndrome (median, commonest entrapment).

Ulnar at elbow.

Common peroneal at fibular head.

Meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous).

Saturday night palsy (radial).

### 8. Critical illness

Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) — acquired in ICU; flaccid weakness.

### 9. Idiopathic

30% remain idiopathic ('cryptogenic axonal polyneuropathy').

### Approach / Investigations

Step 1 — characterise

Distribution (length-dependent vs MM vs cranial), onset, fibres involved (sensory > motor / motor > sensory / autonomic).

Family history; drug history; alcohol; occupational exposure; nutrition; recent infection.

Step 2 — first-line bloods

CBC, ESR, glucose, HbA1c, B12, folate, TSH, U+E, LFT, vitamin D.

HIV, VDRL, hepatitis B/C.

Serum protein electrophoresis + immunofixation (paraproteinaemia).

### Step 3 — NCS / EMG

Distinguish axonal vs demyelinating, length-dependent vs MM, focal vs diffuse, severity.

Step 4 — targeted second-line

ANA, ENA, ANCA, RF, cryoglobulins.

Heavy metals (lead, arsenic) if exposure.

GBS panel (anti-GM1, GQ1b).

Anti-MAG, anti-GD1a (paraproteinaemic / motor neuropathy).

Lyme serology.

Slit-skin smear for AFB (leprosy).

Genetic testing (CMT, hATTR).

Fat pad / nerve biopsy (amyloidosis, vasculitis).

CSF (CIDP — albumino-cytological dissociation).

### Management — overview

Treat the underlying cause (glycaemic control, vitamin replacement, MDT for leprosy, IVIG/steroids for CIDP, stop offending drug, treat vasculitis).

**Neuropathic pain:** gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, duloxetine, carbamazepine; topical capsaicin, lidocaine.

Physiotherapy, OT, gait aids, foot care (especially diabetic).

Surgical decompression for entrapment.

**Source:** Davidson Ch.27; Boloor Ch.15; NLEP Operational Manual.

GENERAL MEDICINE|348.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Acute purulent infection of meninges/subarachnoid space, presenting with fever + headache + neck stiffness +/- altered mental status. Medical emergency: untreated >90% mortality, with treatment 15-25%.

Aetiology by age (community-acquired)

**Neonates (0-1 mo):** GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

**1 mo - 50 y:** Streptococcus pneumoniae > Neisseria meningitidis > H. influenzae (now rare with vaccine).

**> 50 y / immunosuppressed:** S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negatives.

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Staph aureus, CoNS, gram-negatives.

**India-specific:** TB meningitis remains common — always consider.

### Clinical features

**Classic triad (only 44%):** fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status.

**≥ 2 of:** fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental → 95% sensitivity.

Kernig (knee extension with hip flexed → pain) and Brudzinski (neck flexion → hip flexion).

**Meningococcal:** petechial / purpuric rash (purpura fulminans = severe).

**Pneumococcal:** associated otitis/sinusitis/pneumonia.

Cranial nerve palsies, seizures, papilloedema, focal deficit.

### Investigations

Blood cultures × 2 BEFORE antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics > 1 h for cultures).

Lumbar puncture — CT first if focal deficit, GCS < 10, papilloedema, new-onset seizure, immunosuppression.

CSF Gram stain (60-90% sens), culture, latex agglutination (S. pneumo, H.influ, Nm, GBS).

**TB:** CSF AFB smear (low sens), GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (rapid + rifampicin resistance), culture.

**PCR:** HSV-1/2 (encephalitis), enterovirus, JC virus.

**Other:** CBC, blood C/S, CRP, procalcitonin, electrolytes (SIADH), HIV test.

### Management

- Resuscitation (within first hour)

**Sepsis bundle:** fluids, vasopressors if shock, oxygen, glucose check.

**Seizure control:** lorazepam, then levetiracetam load.

### 2. Dexamethasone

0.15 mg/kg IV q6h × 4 days, FIRST DOSE before or with first antibiotic.

Reduces mortality in S.pneumo; reduces neuro sequelae (deafness) in H.influenzae.

Stop if non-pneumococcal organism identified.

**TB meningitis:** prednisolone/dex tapered over 6-8 wk (TBM treatment).

- Empirical antibiotics (do NOT delay)

**Adult immunocompetent:** Adult immunocompetent: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h (target trough 15-20).

Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed:Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed: ADD Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria cover).

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Post-neurosurgery / shunt: Vancomycin + Cefepime or Meropenem 2 g q8h.

**Penicillin allergy severe:** Penicillin allergy severe: Vancomycin + Moxifloxacin + TMP-SMX (Listeria).

**Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h:** Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h: If HSV encephalitis suspected (e.g. temporal seizures, behaviour change).

### 4. Pathogen-specific duration

### 5. Adjunctive

Maintain euvolaemia (avoid SIADH).

**ICP management:** head-up 30°, mannitol if raised, ICU monitor.

Audiology test at discharge (especially children — sensorineural deafness).

- Chemoprophylaxis (close contacts)

**Meningococcal:** Rifampicin 600 mg PO BD × 2 d, OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose, OR Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single.

**H. influenzae type b:** Rifampicin 20 mg/kg/d × 4 d for households with child < 4 y unvaccinated.

### 7. Vaccination prevention

Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23 in elderly/asplenic/CKD/HIV).

Meningococcal (MenACWY for hajj pilgrims, students, military, asplenia).

Hib (in National Immunisation Schedule under Pentavalent).

### Complications

Hydrocephalus (communicating > obstructive).

Cerebritis, brain abscess, subdural empyema.

Sensorineural hearing loss (10-30%).

Seizures, epilepsy, cognitive deficits.

Cranial nerve palsies (esp. III, VI, VII, VIII).

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal, adrenal haemorrhage).

SIADH, DIC, septic shock.

### Prognosis

**Treated mortality:** pneumococcal 20-25%, meningococcal 5-10%, H.influ 3-7%.

**Untreated:** > 90% mortality.

10-20% long-term sequelae (deafness, cognitive, epilepsy).

Fig 5. Bacterial meningitis pathway.

**Source:** IDSA Meningitis Guidelines 2017; ICMR Antibiotic Policy 2022; Boloor Ch.15.

### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Combined Notes (22 topics)

### Why it matters

Tobacco smoking is the leading preventable cause of death globally; responsible for COPD, lung cancer, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, PVD, oral and other cancers. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality, slows FEV1 decline in COPD, and is the most effective single intervention in respiratory medicine.

Approach – the '5 A's'

Ask about tobacco use at every visit.

Advise to quit, clearly and personally.

Assess willingness to quit.

Assist – set a quit date, pharmacotherapy, counselling.

Arrange follow-up within 1 week of quit date.

### Behavioural support

Motivational interviewing, brief advice (~5 min) doubles quit rate.

Group or individual cognitive behavioural therapy.

Telephone quit-lines (Indian National Tobacco Quitline 1800-11-2356).

mCessation programme via SMS (India MoHFW).

Identify and avoid triggers; coping strategies.

### Pharmacotherapy (Indian availability)

Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT): patch (24-h, 21/14/7 mg), gum (2/4 mg), lozenge, sublingual tablet, inhaler. Start on quit date; taper over 8–12 weeks. Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) most effective.

Varenicline (Champix) – partial nicotinic α4β2 agonist; 0.5 mg OD × 3 d → 0.5 mg BD × 4 d → 1 mg BD × 11–23 weeks. Highest single-agent efficacy. Monitor for mood change.

Bupropion SR 150 mg OD × 3 d → BD; start 1–2 weeks before quit date; 7–12 weeks. Contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorder.

Cytisine – natural partial nicotinic agonist; emerging option in low-resource settings.

Combination therapy (varenicline + NRT) for heavy smokers.

### Special populations

**Pregnancy:** behavioural support first-line; NRT only if behavioural fails (intermittent forms preferred).

**Adolescents:** behavioural; NRT for ≥10/day smokers.

**Cardiovascular disease:** all therapies safe; bupropion preferred post-MI per some guidelines.

### Indian regulations

Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA) 2003 prohibits advertising, smoking in public places, sale to minors.

85% pictorial warnings on tobacco packages.

Ban on e-cigarettes (PECA 2019).

First-line drugs and hepatotoxicity

**Isoniazid (H):** Hepatotoxic – stop if ALT >5× ULN (or >3× with symptoms).

**Pyrazinamide (Z):** Most hepatotoxic of the first-line drugs; dose-dependent.

**Rifampicin (R):** Hepatotoxic; also causes orange discoloration of secretions.

**Ethambutol (E):** Not hepatotoxic; main risks – optic neuritis (visual acuity), peripheral neuropathy.

Drugs to avoid in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure: H, R, Z.

Modified regimen for hepatitis / hepatic impairment (NTEP, WHO 2024)

If ALT >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN without – stop all hepatotoxic ATT.

Continue with non-hepatotoxic combination: ethambutol + streptomycin/levofloxacin (+ rifampicin if liver enzymes recovering; reintroduce H or Z sequentially).

**Severe hepatitis:** 2 SH(streptomycin + isoniazid)E + 6 HE OR 9–12 RE + levofloxacin / linezolid based regimen.

**Once LFTs return to normal:** gradually reintroduce R first, then H, last Z (if needed).

Other antimicrobials notable for hepatotoxicity in ATT context

Para-amino salicylic acid (PAS) – hepatotoxic.

Ethionamide / prothionamide – hepatotoxic.

Bedaquiline – QT prolongation, mild LFT rise.

Linezolid – BM suppression, neuropathy; mild hepatic.

Monitor LFTs weekly during reintroduction; counsel patient about alcohol cessation, paracetamol limits, no herbal supplements.

Comprehensive TB management (NTEP 2024) flowchart is shown below for reference.

Fig 8. NTEP 2024 – diagnosis and treatment of TB (drug-sensitive and drug-resistant).

Nutritional assessment – methods

**A:** Anthropometry

Weight, height, BMI (kg/m²). Asian-Indian cut-offs (WHO Asia): underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–22.9; overweight 23–24.9; obese ≥25; (general WHO: 25/30).

Waist circumference (Asian male ≥90 cm, female ≥80 cm = abdominal obesity).

Waist–hip ratio (>0.9 M / >0.85 F = abnormal).

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC; <23 cm = malnourished).

Triceps skinfold thickness, calf circumference (sarcopenia).

**B:** Biochemical (Lab)

Serum albumin (<3.5 g/dL = malnutrition; long half-life 20 d).

Pre-albumin / transthyretin (half-life 2 d – more sensitive).

Total lymphocyte count (<1500 = malnutrition).

Haemoglobin, transferrin, retinol-binding protein.

**Specific deficiencies:** vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D, iron, zinc, magnesium.

**C:** Clinical examination

General – muscle wasting (temporal, thenar), loose skin, oedema (kwashiorkor), pallor.

Hair – sparse, depigmented, easily pluckable (kwashiorkor).

Skin – dermatitis, hyperpigmentation (pellagra), petechiae (scurvy), xerosis.

Eyes – Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia, night blindness (vitamin A).

Mouth – angular stomatitis, glossitis (riboflavin, B12), bleeding gums (vitamin C), dental caries.

Nails – koilonychia (iron), pale, brittle.

Neuro – peripheral neuropathy (B1, B6, B12), beriberi (B1), subacute combined degeneration (B12).

Skeletal – rickets/osteomalacia (vitamin D), bowing.

**D:** Dietary assessment

24-h dietary recall.

3-day food diary.

Food-frequency questionnaire.

Compare to recommended dietary allowance (RDA – ICMR for Indians).

### Composite tools:

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA) – history (weight loss, intake, GI symptoms, functional capacity) + physical exam → A (well), B (moderate malnutrition), C (severe malnutrition).

Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) – elderly.

Nutrition Risk Screening (NRS-2002) – hospitalised adults.

GLIM criteria (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) – phenotypic (weight loss, low BMI, low muscle mass) + etiological (reduced intake/assimilation, inflammation).

Hazards of obesity (medical complications)

### Cardiovascular:

Hypertension, IHD, MI, heart failure (HFpEF), atrial fibrillation, stroke, VTE, varicose veins.

### Metabolic:

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (3-fold risk), insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidaemia (↑LDL, ↑TG, ↓HDL), hyperuricaemia and gout.

### Respiratory:

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), restrictive lung disease, asthma worsening.

### Hepatic:

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) → steatohepatitis (NASH) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma; cholelithiasis.

### Endocrine / reproductive:

PCOS, infertility (anovulation), male hypogonadism, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia.

### Musculoskeletal:

Osteoarthritis (knees, hips), back pain, gout.

### Cancers:

Colon, oesophageal (adeno), breast (post-menopausal), endometrial, ovarian, pancreatic, renal, liver, gall-bladder.

### Other:

Depression, social stigma, surgical risk, intertrigo, lymphoedema, stress incontinence, idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

(See Q2 above for the comprehensive list of obesity hazards. The key categories are repeated here for completeness, with a brief note on management.)

### Complications by system

**Cardiovascular:** HTN, IHD, HF, AF, stroke, VTE.

**Metabolic:** T2DM, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome, gout.

**Respiratory:** OSA, OHS, restrictive lung disease.

**Hepatic / GI:** NAFLD → NASH → cirrhosis, GERD, gallstones.

**Endocrine / reproductive:** PCOS, infertility, hypogonadism, gestational DM.

**Musculoskeletal:** OA (knees, hips), low back pain.

**Cancers:** colon, breast (post-menopausal), endometrial, oesophageal adeno, renal, pancreatic, hepatocellular, GB.

**Psychosocial:** depression, anxiety, social stigma, low quality of life.

**Surgical:** poor wound healing, anaesthetic risk, VTE.

**Skin:** acanthosis nigricans, intertrigo, hidradenitis.

Management of obesity (brief)

**Lifestyle:** ICMR-recommended balanced diet (500 kcal deficit/day), 150 min/wk moderate aerobic + resistance training, behavioural therapy.

Pharmacotherapy (BMI ≥27 with comorbidity or ≥30 alone): orlistat 120 mg TDS; liraglutide 3 mg SC daily; semaglutide (Wegovy) 2.4 mg SC weekly; tirzepatide 5–15 mg SC weekly; naltrexone-bupropion; phentermine-topiramate.

Bariatric surgery (BMI ≥35 with comorbidity or ≥40): sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, OAGB; Indian indication BMI ≥32.5 with comorbidity.

(See Q2 and Q3 for comprehensive list of obesity hazards. The key obesity-related medical disorders are organised here by system.)

### Cardiovascular

Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure with preserved EF, atrial fibrillation, ventricular hypertrophy, stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), VTE, varicose veins.

### Metabolic

Type 2 diabetes mellitus and pre-diabetes.

**Metabolic syndrome (≥3 of:** abdominal obesity, ↑TG, ↓HDL, ↑BP, ↑FPG).

Dyslipidaemia.

Hyperuricaemia and gout.

Hepatic – NAFLD, NASH, cirrhosis, HCC.

### Endocrine / reproductive

PCOS, anovulatory infertility.

Hypogonadism in males.

Gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia.

Increased risk of macrosomia, congenital anomalies in offspring.

### Respiratory

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA).

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS – Pickwickian).

Restrictive lung function, exertional dyspnoea.

Worsening asthma control.

### Cancers

Endometrial, breast (post-menopausal), colorectal, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, renal cell, pancreatic, hepatocellular, gall-bladder, ovarian, thyroid (papillary), multiple myeloma.

### Musculoskeletal

Osteoarthritis (knees, hips, hands).

Low-back pain.

Gout.

### GI / hepatobiliary

GERD, hiatal hernia.

Cholelithiasis.

NAFLD / NASH / cirrhosis / HCC.

Pancreatitis.

### Renal / urogenital

CKD, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (obesity-related).

Stress urinary incontinence.

Erectile dysfunction.

### Skin

Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance marker), intertrigo, hidradenitis suppurativa, stretch marks, lymphoedema, cellulitis.

### Neurological / psychiatric

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Depression, anxiety, eating disorders, low quality of life, stigma, social isolation.

Cognitive impairment, dementia (long-term).

### Surgical / perioperative

Increased anaesthetic risk, difficult intubation, prolonged recovery, wound infection, VTE.

### Definition

Toxic syndrome caused by ingestion / inhalation / dermal exposure to organophosphate compounds (parathion, malathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, fenthion, monocrotophos, dimethoate, dichlorvos, etc., and chemical warfare nerve agents — sarin, tabun, VX). Most common cause of poisoning mortality in rural India (deliberate self-poisoning).

### Mechanism

OP compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active serine residue, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses. 'Ageing' (loss of an R-group) makes the enzyme inhibition permanent — hence early use of oximes is critical.

Clinical features (cholinergic crisis)

### Muscarinic (DUMBELS / SLUDGEM):

Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.

Pulmonary oedema – the major cause of death.

Nicotinic (Days of the Week — MTWThF):

Muscle fasciculation, Tachycardia, Weakness/paralysis (including respiratory), Hypertension, Hyperglycaemia.

### CNS:

Anxiety, headache, confusion, seizures, coma.

### Distinct syndromes:

Intermediate syndrome (24–96 h after acute phase): proximal muscle, neck flexor, and respiratory muscle weakness; cranial nerve deficits; lasts 2–3 weeks; needs prolonged ventilation.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN, 1–3 weeks after exposure): distal sensorimotor neuropathy.

### Diagnosis

History of exposure, characteristic odour (garlic/kerosene), DUMBELS toxidrome.

Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (BChE / pseudocholinesterase) – rapid, available – severely depressed.

RBC acetylcholinesterase – more accurate, slower turnaround.

Atropine challenge test – minimal response to therapeutic dose supports diagnosis.

Ancillary – ABG, CK, troponin, ECG (QT prolongation, AV block), CXR (pulmonary oedema), serum amylase (pancreatitis).

### Treatment

### Resuscitation and decontamination

**ABC:** secure airway (suction copious secretions), 100% O₂.

**Decontamination:** remove all clothing, wash skin with soap and water (rescuers wear PPE — secondary contamination risk).

Gastric lavage – only if presentation <1 h, large amount ingested, and airway protected; NOT recommended routinely (aspiration risk).

Activated charcoal – consider within 1 h; do not give if drowsy without intubation.

### Atropinisation

Atropine 1.8–3 mg IV bolus; double dose every 5 min until atropinisation achieved.

### End-points (must achieve ALL):

(i) Chest clear of crepitations (dry secretions).

(ii) HR >80 bpm.

(iii) Systolic BP >80 mm Hg.

(iv) Pupil dilation.

**Maintenance:** atropine infusion 10–20% of the cumulative atropinising dose per hour; titrate to keep target signs.

Watch for atropine toxicity – hyperthermia, agitation, ileus, urinary retention; lower infusion accordingly.

### Oxime (pralidoxime / 2-PAM)

Reactivates AChE if given before ageing.

**Dose:** 30 mg/kg IV bolus over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h infusion × 48–72 h. Alternatively: 1 g IV q4-6h.

Most effective in first 24 h, but should be given even later (prolonged release from fat).

Particularly effective against nicotinic (muscle) signs.

### Supportive care

ICU monitoring. Mechanical ventilation often needed for days–weeks. Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (prolonged paralysis – use rocuronium or vecuronium).

Seizures – diazepam 5–10 mg IV (does not interact with AChE).

Aggressive electrolyte (K, Mg) replacement; cardiac monitoring.

Treat aspiration pneumonia, ARDS.

Surveillance for intermediate syndrome (FVC, NIF monitoring).

Avoid β-blockers (worsen bronchospasm), morphine, theophylline, phenothiazines.

### Psychiatric and social

Most cases are deliberate self-poisoning – mandatory psychiatric evaluation; suicide-risk assessment; family counselling; safe-storage advice; pesticide bans (e.g. WHO Class I OP withdrawn in India 2020).

Fig 3. Organophosphate poisoning – emergency management.

### Definition

Envenomation by elapid snakes (Cobra — Naja naja, King cobra — Ophiophagus hannah, Common krait — Bungarus caeruleus) produces a neurotoxic syndrome through α- and β-neurotoxins that block post-synaptic and pre-synaptic neuromuscular transmission respectively, leading to flaccid paralysis. India: cobra and krait are two of the 'Big Four' deadly Indian snakes.

Local features (cobra > krait)

Two fang punctures (krait bite often painless and at night).

Local pain, swelling, blistering, sometimes necrosis (cobra).

Krait – minimal local signs; pain disproportionate to swelling; often patient awakes with abdominal pain at 4–6 a.m.

Systemic features – progressive descending paralysis

Early (30 min – 2 h)

Heaviness of eyelids (ptosis – earliest and commonest sign), external ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, blurred vision.

Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia.

Hypersalivation, profuse sweating, paraesthesiae.

Established neurotoxicity (2–6 h)

Bulbar palsy – pooled secretions, tongue weakness, broken neck sign (cannot lift head off pillow).

Limb weakness – proximal first; progressive descending paralysis.

Respiratory muscle paralysis – the most life-threatening complication; intercostal and diaphragmatic weakness leading to respiratory failure.

Patient is conscious throughout (locked-in pattern unless hypoxic).

### Autonomic features

Cobra – bradycardia, hypotension; krait – sometimes mild hypertension, abdominal pain.

### Krait-specific

Bite often at night while sleeping on the floor; little or no local reaction; severe abdominal pain.

Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia may accompany.

Response to neostigmine usually poor (β-neurotoxin pre-synaptic action — already-released ACh is depleted).

### Investigations and monitoring

20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20-WBCT) – usually normal in pure neurotoxic bite (distinguishes from haemotoxic).

FVC (vital capacity) — if <1 L or falling — intubate.

ABG, electrolytes (krait — hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia).

ECG (arrhythmia).

Edrophonium / neostigmine test (improvement supports diagnosis and helps in management).

### Management (Indian National Snakebite Protocol 2017)

**First aid:** reassure, immobilise limb at heart level, remove rings/tight items, pressure-immobilisation bandage; rapid transport to a centre with ASV and ventilator. AVOID tourniquet/cut/suck/ice/electric shock.

Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV): initial 10 vials (100 mL) in 100–200 mL normal saline IV over 1 hour. Repeat every 6 hours up to maximum 30 vials, based on clinical/lab response.

Adjuvant — Neostigmine 0.5 mg + atropine 0.6 mg IV every 30 min × 5 doses (then 1–2 hourly as needed) — useful especially for cobra envenomation.

Early intubation and mechanical ventilation if FVC <1 L, tidal volume <5 mL/kg, or any respiratory distress.

**Treat ASV reactions:** stop infusion, adrenaline 0.5 mg IM, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV, chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV; resume ASV at slower rate.

Tetanus toxoid, antibiotics if cellulitis or wound necrosis.

Supportive — fluids, vasopressors if hypotensive; psychological support.

Fig 5. Snakebite — Indian National Protocol.

### Definition

Sudden focal neurological deficit lasting > 24 h due to focal cerebral ischaemia from arterial occlusion (embolic, thrombotic, or lacunar). 80% of all strokes; remainder are haemorrhagic.

### Aetiology (TOAST classification)

Large artery atherosclerosis (carotid, vertebrobasilar).

Cardioembolic (AF — commonest, valvular, post-MI LV thrombus, infective endocarditis).

Small vessel (lacunar) — hypertensive lipohyalinosis.

**Other determined:** dissection, vasculitis, Moyamoya, thrombophilia, drugs (cocaine).

Cryptogenic / undetermined — 25%.

Clinical syndromes (Bamford / OCSP)

TACS — total anterior circulation (all 3 of): hemiparesis + hemianopia + cortical dysfunction (aphasia/neglect).

**PACS — partial:** any 2 of above.

**LACS — lacunar:** pure motor / pure sensory / sensorimotor / ataxic hemiparesis (no cortical signs).

**POCS — posterior:** cranial nerve palsy + contralateral motor/sensory; cerebellar; bilateral motor; isolated hemianopia.

### Investigations

NCCT head — rules out haemorrhage; early signs (hyperdense MCA, loss of insular ribbon).

MRI DWI — most sensitive (lights up within 30 min); FLAIR for age of infarct.

CTA/MRA — vessel patency; identifies LVO for thrombectomy.

**Aetiology:** ECG, holter, echo, carotid Doppler, lipids, HbA1c, thrombophilia (young).

### Management

**tPA:** tPA: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV within 4.5 h. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus = acceptable.

**Thrombectomy:** Thrombectomy: LVO within 6-24 h (DAWN/DEFUSE-3).

**Aspirin:** Aspirin: 300 mg loading then 75-150 mg/day.

**BP:** BP: Permissive < 220/120; lower to < 185/110 before tPA.

**Glucose:** Glucose: 140-180 mg/dL.

**DVT prophylaxis:** DVT prophylaxis: IPC then LMWH 24-48 h.

**Stroke unit:** Stroke unit: Mortality ↓ 20%.

### tPA contraindications (abridged)

Haemorrhage on CT; BP > 185/110 unresponsive; INR > 1.7; platelets < 100,000.

Active bleeding, recent major surgery < 14 d, recent stroke / head trauma < 3 mo, recent GI bleed < 21 d.

Glucose < 50 or > 400 mg/dL; suspected SAH; intracranial neoplasm/AVM/aneurysm.

### Complications

Haemorrhagic transformation, malignant cerebral oedema (large MCA), seizures, aspiration pneumonia, DVT/PE.

**Source:** AHA/ASA 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

### Definition (Tetrad)

Heavy proteinuria > 3.5 g/d (or PCR > 3.5 g/g; in children > 40 mg/m²/h).

Hypoalbuminaemia < 3 g/dL (often < 2.5).

Generalised oedema (peri-orbital morning, peripheral evening, anasarca, ascites, pleural effusion).

Hyperlipidaemia (↑ cholesterol > 250, triglycerides).

**Pathology:** damage to glomerular filtration barrier → loss of selectivity for protein. Lipiduria (oval fat bodies / Maltese cross under polarised light) is associated.

### Aetiology — Primary vs Secondary

### Primary (Idiopathic) Glomerular Diseases

**Minimal Change Disease (MCD):** Minimal Change Disease (MCD): Commonest in CHILDREN (~90% paediatric NS). Normal LM; foot process effacement on EM. Selective proteinuria (albumin > IgG). Highly steroid-responsive. T-cell / cytokine-mediated. Adult MCD ~10% of adult NS.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS):Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Commonest in ADULTS (especially African descent — APOL1 risk allele). Primary or secondary (HIV — collapsing variant, heroin, obesity, reflux nephropathy, sickle cell). Variable steroid response. Anti-suPAR Ab in some.

**Membranous Nephropathy:** Membranous Nephropathy: Common cause in adults. Anti-PLA2R autoantibody (70–80% — diagnostic). THSD7A (5%). Secondary causes: SLE (Class V), Hep B, malignancy (solid tumours — lung, breast, colon — esp > 65 yr), drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs). Spike + dome on EM.

Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN):Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN): Immune-complex (Type I) or C3 glomerulopathy. Mixed nephritic-nephrotic features. Hep C, monoclonal gammopathy.

**IgA nephropathy:** IgA nephropathy: Usually nephritic but can present as NS.

### Secondary

**Diabetic nephropathy:** Diabetic nephropathy: Commonest cause overall in adults (commoner than primary GN in older diabetic). See Q5 for details.

**Amyloidosis:** Amyloidosis: AL (light chain — myeloma association) or AA (chronic inflammation — RA, TB, IBD, Indian context). Congo red apple-green birefringence. SAP scan, biopsy.

**Lupus nephritis Class V:** Lupus nephritis Class V: Membranous pattern; SLE features.

**Viral:** Viral: Hep B → membranous (children); Hep C → MPGN / cryoglobulinaemia; HIV → collapsing FSGS (HIVAN).

**Drugs:** Drugs: NSAIDs (MCD + AIN), gold, penicillamine, captopril, lithium (FSGS), bisphosphonates (collapsing).

**Malignancy:** Malignancy: Solid tumour membranous (esp > 65 yr), lymphoma → MCD.

**Congenital:** Congenital: Finnish-type CNS (NPHS1 mutation), denys-Drash (WT1).

### Clinical Features

Oedema — onset peri-orbital (morning), progresses to pitting peripheral, ascites, pleural effusion, anasarca; weight gain.

Froamy urine (proteinuria).

Lethargy, malabsorption (oedematous bowel), poor appetite.

Hypotension if severe hypoalbuminaemia (rare).

**Complications-related:** VTE (DVT, renal vein thrombosis — flank pain, AKI), infection (peritonitis pneumococcal in children, encapsulated organisms), AKI.

Secondary cause features (DM control, weight, joints, skin).

**Underlying examination:** BP, fundoscopy, lymph nodes, breast, prostate.

### Investigations

### Confirm Nephrotic Syndrome

**Urinalysis:** dipstick proteinuria 3+/4+; microscopy: oval fat bodies, Maltese cross.

24-h urine protein OR spot PCR / ACR — PCR > 3500 mg/g diagnostic.

Serum albumin, total protein.

Lipid profile.

Creatinine, urea, electrolytes, eGFR.

### Identify Cause

HbA1c, fasting glucose (DM).

ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement (lupus).

Anti-PLA2R antibody (membranous — diagnostic if high).

HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV.

SPEP/UPEP, free light chains, serum IFE, immunoglobulins (amyloid, myeloma).

Cryoglobulins (HCV, MPGN).

Age-appropriate malignancy screen (CXR, mammogram, PSA, colonoscopy, CECT abd) in adults > 65 with membranous.

Renal biopsy (essential in adults with NS; in children empirical steroid if typical MCD; biopsy if atypical features — see below).

### Indications for Biopsy

All adults with new NS.

Children with atypical features: age < 1 or > 12 yr, haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment, low complement, steroid resistance.

Steroid-dependent / frequently relapsing NS.

### Management

### 1. General Supportive Measures

**Oedema:** Oedema: Salt restrict (< 5g/d), fluid 1–1.5 L/d. Loop diuretic — furosemide 40–250 mg/d (often IV in severe; high doses needed due to albumin binding). Combination with thiazide / metolazone if refractory.

**Anasarca / albumin < 2:** Anasarca / albumin < 2: Cautious IV albumin (20% 100 ml) + furosemide if severe respiratory compromise. Routine albumin NOT recommended — short-lived effect.

**BP + proteinuria reduction:** BP + proteinuria reduction: ACEi (ramipril 10 mg) or ARB (losartan 100 mg, telmisartan 80 mg). Target BP < 130/80, proteinuria < 1 g/d.

**Dyslipidaemia:** Dyslipidaemia: Atorvastatin 20–40 mg or rosuvastatin 10–20 mg.

**Diet:** Diet: Protein 0.8–1.0 g/kg/d (NOT high protein — accelerates progression). Low salt, low fat, low cholesterol.

**VTE prophylaxis:** VTE prophylaxis: LMWH if albumin < 2.5 + other risk (immobility, history of thrombosis, PE/DVT/RVT). Long-term anticoagulation if RVT (warfarin 6 mo INR 2–3).

**Infection prophylaxis:** Infection prophylaxis: Pneumococcal vaccination (PCV13 + PPSV23); annual influenza; treat infections promptly.

**Vit D + Ca supplementation:** Vit D + Ca supplementation: Vitamin D-binding protein loss.

**Iron:** Iron: Transferrin loss → IDA.

**Treat secondary cause:** Treat secondary cause: DM control, BP, treat underlying.

### 2. Disease-Specific Treatment

**MCD (children):** MCD (children): Empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60 mg) × 4 wk → 40 mg/m² alternate days × 4 wk → taper over 12 wk (ISKDC). 90% respond within 2 wk. Frequent relapse → cyclophosphamide / mycophenolate / cyclosporine / rituximab.

**MCD (adults):** MCD (adults): Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d (max 80) × 4–16 wk till remission → taper. Slower response. Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) for steroid-resistant.

**FSGS:** FSGS: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/d × 12 wk → taper if response. Steroid-resistant: cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/d × 6 mo (KDIGO 2021). Rituximab for selected. APOL1 gene-related considerations.

**Membranous nephropathy:** Membranous nephropathy: First 6 months: conservative (ACEi/ARB, monitor anti-PLA2R, GFR). If persistent NS / progressive: rituximab 1 g × 2 doses (preferred — MENTOR 2019) OR Ponticelli regimen (alternating monthly methylpred + oral chlorambucil/cyclophosphamide × 6 mo) OR cyclosporine + low-dose steroid.

**Lupus Class V:** Lupus Class V: Steroid + MMF / CNI (similar to Class III/IV but milder). Hydroxychloroquine.

**Diabetic nephropathy:** Diabetic nephropathy: See Q5 — strict glycaemic control, ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA.

**Amyloidosis:** Amyloidosis: AL: chemotherapy directed at clonal plasma cells (bortezomib + dex; autologous SCT in fit). AA: treat underlying inflammation (RA → biologics, TB → ATT). Specific anti-amyloid: tafamidis (TTR), patisiran.

**HBV / HCV / HIV-related:** HBV / HCV / HIV-related: Antivirals — HBV (TDF/entecavir), HCV (DAA), HIV (ART) — often resolves GN.

**NSAID / drug-induced:** NSAID / drug-induced: Stop offending agent → usually resolves.

Fig 4. Nephrotic syndrome — diagnostic and management pathway.

### Complications

Venous thromboembolism (DVT 25%, renal vein thrombosis 30% in membranous, PE) — loss of antithrombin III; high ATIII deficiency risk.

Infection — encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae peritonitis in children); loss of immunoglobulins.

AKI — pre-renal from over-diuresis, or renal vein thrombosis.

Hyperlipidaemia → CV disease.

Malnutrition — protein loss, oedematous bowel malabsorption.

Vitamin D deficiency, calcium deficiency.

Anaemia (transferrin loss + EPO loss).

Hypothyroidism (TBG loss).

Steroid SE — osteoporosis, DM, infection, cushingoid, growth retardation in children.

### Prognosis

Highly variable by aetiology. MCD: > 90% remission with steroids; 70% relapse but generally good long-term renal function. FSGS: ESRD in 30–50% over 10 yr (worse if steroid-resistant). Membranous: ~30% spontaneous remission, 30% partial remission, 30% progressive; anti-PLA2R titre predicts treatment response. Lupus V: depends on activity + chronicity.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.371; KDIGO Glomerular Diseases 2021; ISKDC; MENTOR 2019; Davidson Ch.17.
