### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

COPD is a heterogeneous, preventable and treatable lung condition characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by noxious particles/gases. Diagnosis confirmed by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70.

### Etiology

Tobacco smoking (cigarettes, bidis, hookah) – commonest cause worldwide.

Biomass fuel exposure (wood, dung, coal in poorly ventilated kitchens) – major Indian cause, especially in women.

Occupational dusts and chemicals (coal mining, silica, cotton, isocyanates).

Air pollution (outdoor PM2.5, indoor cooking smoke).

**Genetic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency (early-onset, basal emphysema).

Childhood respiratory infections, low birth weight, asthma.

### Pathogenesis

Chronic exposure → neutrophil + macrophage recruitment → proteases (elastase, MMP-9) overwhelm antiproteases (α1-AT) → elastin destruction → emphysema; goblet-cell hyperplasia + mucus hypersecretion → chronic bronchitis; small-airway fibrosis and remodelling → fixed obstruction. Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation drive comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, lung cancer, cachexia).

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Chronic productive cough (≥3 months in 2 consecutive years – chronic bronchitis), progressive exertional dyspnoea, recurrent exacerbations.

**Signs:** Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, barrel chest, prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, polyphonic rhonchi, hyper-resonance.

**Late:** Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema) in advanced disease.

**Phenotypes:** 'Pink puffer' (emphysema – thin, hyperventilating, less hypoxic/hypercapnic); 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis – cyanosed, obese, hypoxic, fluid-overloaded).

### Investigations

**Spirometry:** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms diagnosis. GOLD grade by FEV1% predicted (1 ≥80, 2 50–79, 3 30–49, 4 <30).

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray (hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, narrow cardiac silhouette, bullae); HRCT for emphysema phenotype, bronchiectasis, exclude lung cancer.

**ABG:** ABG in advanced disease – type 1 → type 2 respiratory failure.

**Labs:** CBC (polycythaemia if chronic hypoxia), α1-antitrypsin level, ECG/echo (cor pulmonale), CAT/mMRC for symptom assessment.

**Microbiology:** Sputum culture in exacerbations.

### Management

### Stable COPD (GOLD ABE classification):

Group A (low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): bronchodilator (SABA/SAMA PRN or LABA/LAMA).

Group B (high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation): LABA + LAMA dual bronchodilator.

Group E (frequent exacerbations ≥2 or ≥1 hospitalisation): LABA + LAMA; add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 or history of asthma.

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if persistent exacerbations on dual therapy + eosinophils ≥100.

Add roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) if chronic bronchitis with FEV1<50% + exacerbations.

Azithromycin 250 mg 3×/wk for 12 months to reduce exacerbations in selected ex-smokers.

### Non-pharmacological (mandatory):

Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention to slow FEV1 decline. Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion + counselling.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation:** exercise training, education, nutrition support, breathing techniques.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg or SaO₂ ≤88% (or PaO₂ 56–59 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia); ≥15 h/day, improves survival.

**Vaccinations:** annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), COVID-19, RSV (adults ≥60).

Lung volume reduction surgery, endobronchial valves, lung transplantation in selected.

### Acute exacerbation:

Controlled O₂ (28% Venturi, target SpO₂ 88–92%).

Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium.

Prednisolone 40 mg PO × 5 days.

Antibiotic (amoxicillin/doxycycline 5–7 days) if purulent sputum + ≥1 of: increased sputum, increased dyspnoea, fever.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 + PaCO₂ rising – reduces intubation and mortality.

Invasive ventilation if NIV fails or contraindicated.

Fig 3. GOLD 2023 ABE pharmacotherapy framework for COPD.

### Complications

Acute exacerbations (often viral or bacterial), pneumonia, pneumothorax, secondary polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, lung cancer, cachexia, osteoporosis, depression.

### Prognosis

FEV1 declines ~30 mL/year (normal ~20–25). Smoking cessation halves the decline. BODE index (BMI, Obstruction FEV1, Dyspnoea mMRC, Exercise 6MWT) predicts mortality. 5-year mortality ~50% if BODE 7–10.

### Definition

Single, well-defined, rounded opacity ≤3 cm in diameter, surrounded by normal lung, without associated atelectasis or lymphadenopathy. Important because malignancy must be excluded.

### Differential diagnosis

### Malignant (40%):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (adenocarcinoma commonest in non-smokers).

Carcinoid tumour.

Solitary metastasis (colon, breast, renal, sarcoma, melanoma).

Lymphoma (rare).

### Benign (60%):

Infectious granuloma (tuberculoma – India's commonest), histoplasmoma, cryptococcoma, aspergilloma.

Hamartoma (popcorn calcification).

Lung abscess (early).

Pulmonary AVM.

Round atelectasis.

Rheumatoid nodule.

Wegener's granulomatous nodule.

Bronchogenic cyst, sequestration.

Pulmonary infarct.

### Features suggesting malignancy

Age >50, smoker, size >2 cm, spiculated margin, irregular shape, growth on serial imaging, lack of calcification (or eccentric calcification), upper lobe location, PET-avid (SUV >2.5).

### Features suggesting benignity

Age <40, never-smoker, well-defined smooth margin, central/diffuse/popcorn/laminated calcification, stability >2 years, small (<1 cm), fat density (hamartoma).

### Approach (Fleischner Society 2017)

Compare with previous imaging.

**<6 mm low-risk:** no follow-up; high-risk: optional CT at 12 months.

**6–8 mm:** CT at 6–12 m, then 18–24 m.

**>8 mm:** CT at 3 months and/or PET-CT, biopsy as needed.

Biopsy via CT-guided transthoracic, bronchoscopy (EBUS, navigational), or VATS.

### Spirometry – measurements

FVC – forced vital capacity.

FEV1 – forced expiratory volume in 1st second.

FEV1/FVC ratio (key diagnostic).

PEFR – peak expiratory flow rate.

FEF 25–75% – sensitive to small airway disease.

Flow-volume loop – shape diagnostic (e.g. scalloped in obstruction).

### Patterns

**Obstructive:** FEV1/FVC <0.70; FEV1 reduced; FVC normal or reduced. Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, CF. Reversibility (≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator) supports asthma.

**Restrictive:** FEV1/FVC normal or increased (>0.70); FEV1 and FVC reduced; TLC reduced. ILD, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular, obesity.

**Mixed:** both reduced. Sarcoidosis, advanced bronchiectasis.

### Full PFT (lung volumes, DLCO)

Body plethysmography or helium dilution – TLC, RV, FRC.

DLCO (diffusion capacity) – decreased in emphysema, ILD, anaemia, PE; increased in alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, asthma.

### Indications

Diagnose asthma, COPD, restrictive lung disease.

Monitor disease progression and treatment response.

Pre-operative assessment for thoracic or upper-abdominal surgery.

Occupational lung disease assessment.

Disability evaluation.

### Contraindications (relative)

Recent MI (<1 month), unstable angina, recent eye/abdominal/thoracic surgery, pneumothorax, haemoptysis, severe respiratory distress.

### Definition

Acute occlusion of pulmonary arterial circulation by embolus, most commonly thrombus dislodged from a deep venous thrombus, less commonly air, fat, amniotic fluid, or tumour. Together with DVT, constitutes venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Risk factors (Virchow's triad)

**Stasis:** Recent surgery (especially orthopaedic), prolonged immobilisation, long-haul travel, paralysis, plaster cast.

**Endothelial injury:** Trauma, central venous catheter, pelvic surgery, IBD, vasculitis.

**Hypercoagulability:** Pregnancy and puerperium, OCP/HRT, malignancy (Trousseau), inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin III, prothrombin G20210A), antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, dehydration, nephrotic syndrome.

### Clinical features

Sudden dyspnoea (commonest – >80%), pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis (classic triad in <20%).

**Massive PE:** syncope, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, sudden death.

Tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia, low-grade fever, gallop rhythm, loud P2, raised JVP; pleural rub if infarction.

Signs of DVT in lower limbs – unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness.

### Investigations

Pulse oximetry, ABG (Type 1 RF, A-a gradient widened, respiratory alkalosis).

ECG – sinus tachycardia commonest; S1Q3T3 classical but uncommon; T wave inversion V1–V4; RBBB.

CXR – often normal; Hampton's hump (peripheral wedge), Westermark's sign (oligaemia), Fleischner sign (enlarged PA).

D-dimer – sensitive (>500 ng/mL), not specific; used to exclude PE in low-Wells probability.

CT pulmonary angiogram – investigation of choice.

V/Q scan – if CTPA contraindicated (renal failure, pregnancy).

Echocardiography – RV dilatation/dysfunction (McConnell's sign), pulmonary hypertension; risk-stratifies PE.

Lower-limb compression USS for DVT.

Troponin, BNP – risk stratification.

Thrombophilia screen if unprovoked or recurrent.

### Management

**Risk-stratify:** PESI / sPESI score; haemodynamic stability; RV dysfunction; troponin elevation.

High-risk (massive PE, hypotensive): IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 h, followed by heparin. Surgical or catheter-directed embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated.

Intermediate-risk (sub-massive, RV dysfunction): anticoagulation with LMWH/UFH; consider thrombolysis if deterioration.

**Low-risk:** anticoagulation – LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD), then DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or warfarin INR 2–3. DOACs are first-line (except active cancer – LMWH preferred, or pregnancy – LMWH only).

**Duration:** provoked 3 months; unprovoked ≥6 months or indefinite if low bleeding risk; cancer-associated for as long as cancer active.

IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE on anticoagulation.

**Supportive:** O₂, IV fluids, vasopressors (noradrenaline) if hypotensive.

**Prevention:** VTE risk-assess all medical inpatients; mechanical (compression stockings, IPC) + pharmacological (LMWH 40 mg OD, fondaparinux) prophylaxis.

Fig 7. Acute pulmonary embolism – diagnostic and management algorithm.

(See Q24 above for the comprehensive answer on acute PE. The essence summarised here for this SN.)

### Risk factors

Recent surgery, immobilisation, malignancy, OCP/HRT, pregnancy and puerperium, prior VTE, inherited thrombophilias, antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, smoking, indwelling catheter, long-haul travel, IBD, nephrotic syndrome.

### Investigations

Wells score / Geneva score to estimate probability.

D-dimer for low-probability (rule-out).

CT pulmonary angiogram (first-line).

V/Q scan – pregnancy, renal failure.

Echocardiogram – RV strain, risk-stratify.

Compression USS legs, ECG, troponin, BNP.

### Management

Anticoagulation – LMWH then DOAC or warfarin INR 2-3.

Thrombolysis (alteplase) – haemodynamically unstable.

Surgical / catheter embolectomy – thrombolysis contraindicated.

IVC filter – anticoagulation contraindicated.

**Duration:** 3 months provoked; ≥6 months unprovoked; indefinite if cancer or recurrent.

GENERAL MEDICINE|351.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

Dyspnoea may result from metabolic abnormalities driving respiration without primary lung or cardiac disease – usually stimulating central or peripheral chemoreceptors.

### Acidosis

Diabetic ketoacidosis – Kussmaul breathing (deep, sighing, compensatory).

Lactic acidosis – sepsis, shock, metformin toxicity, severe exercise.

Uremic acidosis (CKD).

Toxic alcohols – methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates.

### Anaemia

Severe anaemia (any cause) – decreased O₂ delivery → tachypnoea.

### Hypoxaemia (any cause)

Cyanide/carbon-monoxide poisoning – tissue hypoxia.

Methaemoglobinaemia.

### Thyrotoxicosis

Increased metabolic demand.

### Pregnancy

Progesterone stimulates respiratory centre.

### Hypoglycaemia

Sympathetic surge + tachypnoea.

### Drugs/toxins

Salicylates (early respiratory alkalosis), beta-2 agonists, theophylline toxicity.

### Approach

ABG (acid-base status), CBC, glucose, electrolytes, lactate, creatinine, urinalysis, drug screen, TSH, blood gas methaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin.

### Definition

An acid-base disturbance characterised by reduction in blood pH (<7.35) and primary decrease in serum bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L) due to either gain of fixed acid, loss of base, or impaired renal acid excretion. The respiratory compensation (reduced PaCO₂) typically follows Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2.

### Approach – Anion gap

Anion gap (AG) = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO₃-]); normal 8–12 mmol/L. Albumin-corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4 – albumin).

High anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) — 'MUDPILES' or 'KULT-GOLD-MARS'

M – Methanol (formic acid)

### U – Uremia (CKD)

D – Diabetic ketoacidosis / alcoholic / starvation ketoacidosis

P – Paraldehyde, propylene glycol

### I – Isoniazid, iron

L – Lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock, metformin, hypoxia)

### E – Ethylene glycol

### S – Salicylates

Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA / hyperchloraemic):

Diarrhoea (loss of HCO₃).

Renal tubular acidosis (type 1 distal, type 2 proximal, type 4 hyporeninaemic).

Ureteric diversion (uretero-sigmoidostomy).

Pancreatic/biliary fistula.

**Drugs:** acetazolamide, topiramate, cholestyramine.

Saline infusion (dilutional).

Early renal failure.

### Clinical features

Underlying cause-related (DKA – hyperglycaemia, ketones).

Kussmaul respiration (deep, sighing).

Decreased myocardial contractility, hypotension, arrhythmias.

Increased catecholamines + insulin resistance + hyperkalaemia.

Bone demineralisation (chronic).

**CNS:** lethargy, confusion, coma.

### Investigations

### 1. Confirm acidosis

ABG (arterial pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃).

Venous bicarbonate, base excess.

- Calculate anion gap

Serum Na, K, Cl, HCO₃. Calculate AG and corrected AG (for albumin).

- Look for cause (HAGMA)

Glucose + ketones (DKA, alcoholic ketosis).

Serum lactate (lactic acidosis).

Renal function – urea, creatinine, eGFR (uremia).

Osmolar gap >10 mOsm/kg suggests toxic alcohol (methanol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol).

Toxicology screen – salicylate, methanol/ethylene glycol levels, isoniazid.

### 4. NAGMA workup

Urine pH, urine anion gap (UAG = UNa + UK − UCl).

Urine ammonium (low in RTA).

Stool electrolytes / osmolality if diarrhoea.

Renal ultrasound, urine for calcium/citrate.

### Management principles

Treat underlying cause (insulin for DKA, dialysis for uremia, fomepizole/dialysis for toxic alcohols, glucose+B1 for ketoacidosis).

**Sodium bicarbonate:** usually only if pH<7.1 in DKA; <7.2 in lactic acidosis; or in hyperkalaemic acidosis. Routine HCO₃ in DKA is controversial (paradoxical CSF acidosis).

Correct K+; haemodialysis for uremic acidosis, toxic alcohols, severe lactic acidosis with metformin.

GENERAL MEDICINE|352.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Inability of respiratory system to meet metabolic needs, defined by ABG: PaO₂ <60 mmHg (8 kPa) breathing room air at sea level, with or without PaCO₂ >50 mmHg (6.5 kPa).

### Classification (gas exchange)

**Type 1 (Hypoxaemic):** PaO₂ <60, PaCO₂ normal or low. Caused by V/Q mismatch or shunt – pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, PE, COPD, asthma early.

Type 2 (Hypercapnic / ventilatory failure): PaO₂ <60, PaCO₂ >50. Caused by alveolar hypoventilation – COPD (commonest), neuromuscular (GBS, MG, MND, polio), chest-wall (kyphoscoliosis, obesity), CNS depression (opiates, stroke), OSA.

Type 3 (Perioperative / atelectasis) – form of type 1, post-operative atelectasis.

Type 4 (Shock) – peri-arrest, low cardiac output.

### Classification (onset)

Acute (hours) – ARDS, asthma, GBS.

Chronic (months/years) – COPD, ILD, neuromuscular.

Acute-on-chronic – COPD exacerbation.

### Clinical Features

**Hypoxia:** dyspnoea, tachypnoea, cyanosis, restlessness, confusion, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias.

**Hypercapnia:** warm peripheries, bounding pulse, headache, flap, drowsy, papilloedema, CO₂ retention narcosis.

### Investigations

ABG (essential), pulse oximetry.

CXR, CT chest as indicated.

Spirometry/PEFR if obstructive disease suspected.

ECG, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, blood sugar.

### Management

Treat underlying cause.

**Type 1:** high-flow O₂ (target SpO₂ 94–98%), HFNC, NIV (CPAP) in pulmonary oedema, invasive ventilation if PaO₂ remains <60 on FiO₂>0.6.

**Type 2 (especially COPD):** controlled O₂ 24–28% Venturi mask, target SpO₂ 88–92%; NIV (BiPAP) if pH<7.35 and PaCO₂ rising; intubate if NIV fails or contraindicated (vomiting, copious secretions, haemodynamic instability, low GCS).

**Supportive:** fluids, nutrition, VTE/stress-ulcer prophylaxis.

Fig 5. Respiratory failure – ABG-based classification and management.

Cardiovascular causes (mostly Type 1)

Acute pulmonary oedema (LVF, valvular crisis, hypertensive emergency).

Acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock.

Cardiac tamponade.

Severe valvular disease – critical AS, acute MR (papillary rupture).

Massive pulmonary embolism (RV failure + hypoxaemia).

High-output failure – severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, sepsis.

Pulmonary hypertension crisis.

### Respiratory causes

### Type 1 (Hypoxaemic):

Pneumonia (bacterial, viral – including COVID-19).

ARDS (sepsis, pancreatitis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion-related TRALI).

Asthma (severe acute).

Pulmonary embolism.

Pneumothorax.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.

### Type 2 (Hypercapnic):

COPD exacerbation (commonest).

Severe asthma (late).

Neuromuscular – GBS, MG crisis, MND, polio, botulism.

CNS depression – opioid overdose, sedatives, brainstem stroke.

Chest-wall – flail chest, kyphoscoliosis, severe obesity (OHS).

Obstructive sleep apnoea.

GENERAL MEDICINE|353.note:
Indications for oxygen therapy

Acute hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <94% or PaO₂ <60 mmHg) – pneumonia, asthma, COPD exacerbation, PE, ARDS, MI, sepsis.

**Critical care:** shock, post-arrest, peri-intubation, anaesthesia.

Chronic hypoxia – LTOT in COPD with PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg, or 56–59 with cor pulmonale / polycythaemia; ILD.

Cluster headache, carbon-monoxide poisoning (high-flow O₂ to wash out CO).

Palliative – relieve dyspnoea in terminal illness (clinical judgement; not all dyspnoea improves with O₂).

### Targets (BTS 2017, Indian Pulmonology guidelines)

**Most acute illness:** SpO₂ 94–98%.

Type 2 respiratory failure / COPD: SpO₂ 88–92% (avoid CO₂ narcosis).

### Low-flow devices (variable FiO₂)

Nasal cannula – 1–6 L/min, FiO₂ ~24–44%. Comfortable; first-line for mild hypoxia.

Simple face mask – 5–10 L/min, FiO₂ ~40–60%. Risk of CO₂ rebreathing if <5 L/min.

Partial rebreather mask (reservoir bag) – 6–10 L/min, FiO₂ ~60–80%.

Non-rebreather mask (one-way valves) – 10–15 L/min, FiO₂ ~80–95%. Used for severe acute hypoxia.

High-flow / fixed-FiO₂ devices

Venturi mask – delivers precise FiO₂ (24, 28, 31, 35, 40, 60%) – preferred in COPD when controlled O₂ needed.

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC, Optiflow/AIRVO) – up to 60 L/min humidified gas at FiO₂ 21–100%. Generates low PEEP, washes out CO₂, improves oxygenation; used in type 1 RF, post-extubation.

### Non-invasive ventilation

CPAP – cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, OSA.

BiPAP – COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis, OHS, neuromuscular respiratory failure.

### Invasive (mechanical) ventilation

**Endotracheal intubation:** failed NIV, depressed consciousness, haemodynamic instability, copious secretions, severe ARDS, exhaustion.

### Hazards of oxygen

CO₂ retention/narcosis in COPD.

Absorption atelectasis (high FiO₂).

Oxygen toxicity (free-radical lung damage with FiO₂>0.6 prolonged).

Retinopathy of prematurity in neonates.

Fire hazard (combustion).

Drying of mucosa – humidify if >2 L/min for prolonged use.

GENERAL MEDICINE|356.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Organs anatomically anchored to or in close apposition with the diaphragm, or held within the retroperitoneal/peritoneal compartments that descend with diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration. Useful for distinguishing them from fixed retroperitoneal masses on examination.

### Organs That MOVE with Respiration

### Organs That DO NOT MOVE Significantly with Respiration

Pancreas — retroperitoneal, deep, doesn't move with breathing; pancreatic masses (pseudocyst, tumour) are typically fixed.

Aortic aneurysm — pulsatile, expansile but fixed; differentiates from transmitted aortic pulsation.

Lymph nodes (retroperitoneal / paraaortic) — fixed; para-aortic lymphadenopathy in lymphoma.

Adrenal glands — small, retroperitoneal, normally not palpable.

Inferior vena cava — fixed.

Vertebral column / bony pelvis — fixed.

### Clinical Significance

Moving with respiration → likely intraperitoneal (liver, spleen) or perirenal (kidney) origin.

Fixed on palpation → retroperitoneal mass (pancreatic tumour, aneurysm, lymph nodes).

Bimanual ballotability + moving = kidney typically.

**Spleen:** moves with respiration, dull to percussion, notched on medial border, cannot get above it (vs renal — can get above).

Distinguishing splenomegaly from left renal mass: spleen has notch, dull percussion, cannot get above; kidney is ballotable, has resonant area above, may have flank dullness with lateral position.

### Method of Palpation

**Position:** supine, knees flexed, abdomen relaxed.

Examiner's warm hand placed flat on abdomen, fingers gently flexed.

Patient takes a deep breath in through mouth; examiner feels for organ edge moving down to meet fingertips.

Start in RIF for liver/spleen (avoid missing massive organ), move up to costal margin.

Spleen — palpate from RIF towards left costal margin; turn patient to right lateral decubitus to bring spleen forward.

Kidney — bimanual ballottement; one hand in renal angle posteriorly, other on anterior abdomen.

**Source:** Boloor Clinical Examination Ch.; Hutchison's Clinical Methods 24e.

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) — Sharp's syndrome

### Definition

MCTD is an overlap connective tissue disorder with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis (SSc) and polymyositis, characterised by very high titre antibodies to U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP). It evolves from Raynaud's + puffy hands → established multisystem disease. Some patients eventually 'differentiate' into definite SLE, SSc or RA.

### Clinical features

Raynaud's phenomenon (≥90%) — usually first feature

Puffy hands, sausage fingers

### Arthralgia/arthritis — non-erosive, RA-like

Myositis — proximal weakness, ↑ CK, EMG myopathic

Oesophageal dysmotility — dysphagia, reflux

Pulmonary hypertension — leading cause of death

### ILD (NSIP pattern), pleurisy

Sicca symptoms, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly

Renal involvement uncommon (<5%, milder than lupus nephritis)

### CNS involvement rare

### Investigations

ANA positive (speckled), high titre

Anti-U1 RNP — hallmark, very high titre (≥1:1600)

Anti-Sm negative (helps distinguish from SLE)

CK if myositis suspected; EMG, muscle biopsy

Pulmonary function tests, HRCT chest, echocardiography (PAH screen)

Nailfold capillaroscopy — SSc-pattern changes

### Management

Hydroxychloroquine — for skin, joints, fatigue

Low-dose steroid + steroid-sparing (MTX, AZA, MMF) for inflammatory features

CCB / PDE5 inhibitor / prostacyclin for Raynaud and PAH

### PPI for reflux

Specific PAH therapy (endothelin antagonist, PDE5, sGC stimulator, prostacyclin) — major prognostic intervention

Systemic sclerosis (SSc, scleroderma)

### Definition

SSc is a multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by autoimmune vasculopathy and progressive fibrosis of skin and internal organs. F:M ≈ 4:1; peak onset 30–50 yrs.

### Subsets

Sine scleroderma — internal organ disease without skin involvement

Localised scleroderma (morphoea, en coup de sabre) — skin only, no systemic

### Pathogenesis (brief)

Vascular injury → endothelial dysfunction → capillary loss

T-cell and B-cell autoimmunity → autoantibodies → fibroblast activation

TGF-β, PDGF, CTGF drive collagen overproduction → fibrosis

Clinical features — by system

Raynaud's (>95%) → digital pits, ulcers, gangrene

**Skin — three phases:** oedematous (puffy hands) → indurative (sclerotic, thickened) → atrophic (tight, hidebound). Use Modified Rodnan Skin Score (MRSS) for severity

**CREST features:** Calcinosis, Raynaud, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia

**Face:** mask-like facies, microstomia, perioral furrows, beaked nose, telangiectasia

Pulmonary — ILD (NSIP > UIP; commonest cause of death now), PAH (commonest in limited), aspiration pneumonitis

GI — dysphagia, reflux, watermelon stomach (GAVE), small-bowel dysmotility, bacterial overgrowth, pseudo-obstruction, malabsorption, faecal incontinence

Renal — scleroderma renal crisis (SRC): malignant hypertension, AKI, MAHA, thrombocytopenia; risk factors — early dcSSc, anti-RNA polymerase III, high-dose steroids (>15 mg/d)

Cardiac — pericardial effusion, myocardial fibrosis, conduction defects, arrhythmias

Musculoskeletal — arthralgia, tendon friction rubs, contractures, myopathy

### Endocrine — hypothyroidism

### Investigations

**Antibodies:** ANA (>95%, nucleolar in dcSSc, centromere in lcSSc), anti-Scl-70 (topo I) in 30% dcSSc, anti-centromere in 60% lcSSc, anti-RNA polymerase III (renal crisis risk), anti-U3 RNP (PAH/myositis)

Nailfold capillaroscopy — early/active/late SSc pattern

PFT with DLCO — annual; ↓ FVC + ↓ DLCO = ILD; isolated ↓ DLCO = PAH

HRCT chest — ground-glass, reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycomb

Echocardiography — estimated pulmonary artery pressure; right heart catheter if elevated (mPAP ≥20 confirms PH)

Endoscopy / barium swallow — dysmotility, GAVE

Hand X-ray — resorption of distal phalanges, calcinosis

Management — disease-modifying and organ-directed

### Skin and Raynaud's

Methotrexate, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide for early dcSSc with active skin

Rituximab, tocilizumab — emerging evidence

Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation — selected severe early dcSSc

Raynaud's — CCB, PDE5 inhibitor, iloprost, bosentan (digital ulcers)

### ILD

Mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/d — first-line (Scleroderma Lung Study II)

Cyclophosphamide IV monthly × 6 — historical first-line, equivalent to MMF

Nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) — SENSCIS trial; combined with MMF or alone for progressive SSc-ILD

Tocilizumab — focuSSced and faSScinate trials; preserves FVC

### Rituximab — refractory

### PAH

Endothelin receptor antagonist — bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan

PDE5 inhibitor — sildenafil, tadalafil

Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator — riociguat

Prostacyclin — IV epoprostenol (severe), SC treprostinil, oral selexipag

Combination therapy from diagnosis (AMBITION trial)

### Renal crisis

ACE inhibitor (captopril) — first-line, urgent, life-saving. Start low and titrate every 12 h to BP control

Dialysis often required acutely; ~50% can come off after 6–18 months

AVOID high-dose steroids in dcSSc

### GI

PPI for reflux (lifelong)

Prokinetics — metoclopramide, domperidone, prucalopride

Antibiotics rotated for small-bowel overgrowth — rifaximin, ciprofloxacin, doxycycline

Octreotide for severe dysmotility

Argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency for GAVE

### Calcinosis, contractures

No proven medical therapy — colchicine, diltiazem, minocycline tried

Surgical excision for symptomatic deposits

### Physiotherapy for contractures

### Complications (across MCTD/SSc spectrum)

Progressive ILD with respiratory failure

### Pulmonary hypertension

### Scleroderma renal crisis

Digital ulcers, gangrene, amputation

### Malnutrition (oesophageal/intestinal dysmotility)

Cancer — increased risk; lung in ILD, bladder in cyclophosphamide-treated

### Prognosis

MCTD better than SLE/SSc overall, but pulmonary hypertension drives later mortality. SSc — diffuse cutaneous subset and ILD/PAH/SRC involvement predict worst outcomes. With modern therapy 10-yr survival approaches 70–80% in limited and 50–60% in diffuse SSc. Early aggressive treatment of active inflammation and organ-specific therapy at diagnosis are key.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 + EULAR/EUSTAR 2017 SSc treatment update + Sharp 1972 original MCTD description (criteria) + ACR/EULAR 2013 SSc classification.

GENERAL MEDICINE|357.note:
### Definition

Air in the pleural cavity, causing lung collapse. Classified as spontaneous (primary/secondary), traumatic (penetrating/blunt), or iatrogenic; and by severity as simple, tension, or open.

Risk factors and causes

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP – no underlying lung disease):

Tall, thin young males (apical sub-pleural blebs).

Smoking (×20 risk).

Family history (Marfan syndrome, Birt-Hogg-Dubé).

Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, homocystinuria.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP – with lung disease):

COPD/emphysema (bullae rupture) – commonest in adults.

Asthma exacerbation.

Tuberculosis (cavitary disease, India).

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (HIV/AIDS).

Cystic fibrosis, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM – women), Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers), Birt-Hogg-Dubé.

Bronchogenic carcinoma, metastatic disease.

Necrotising pneumonia (Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Catamenial pneumothorax – endometriosis (around menstruation).

### Traumatic pneumothorax:

**Penetrating:** stab, gunshot.

**Blunt:** rib fracture, deceleration injury.

### Iatrogenic:

Central venous catheterisation (especially subclavian).

Thoracentesis, pleural biopsy.

Transbronchial / transthoracic lung biopsy.

Barotrauma from mechanical ventilation, NIV.

Acupuncture, intercostal nerve block.

**Tension pneumothorax:** any of above with continued air entry through a one-way valve mechanism → mediastinal shift, cardiovascular collapse – emergency.

### Clinical features (brief)

Sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, dry cough.

Decreased breath sounds, hyper-resonance, decreased vocal fremitus on the affected side.

**Tension:** tachycardia, hypotension, tracheal deviation away, raised JVP – needle decompression in 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line immediately, then chest tube.

### Management (brief)

PSP <2 cm rim, no breathlessness: observe + O₂.

**PSP ≥2 cm or breathless:** needle aspiration; if fails, chest tube.

**SSP ≥1 cm or breathless:** chest tube (most cases).

**Recurrent:** VATS pleurodesis or pleurectomy.

Stop smoking, avoid scuba diving and flying (until resolved).

GENERAL MEDICINE|358.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Acute purulent infection of meninges/subarachnoid space, presenting with fever + headache + neck stiffness +/- altered mental status. Medical emergency: untreated >90% mortality, with treatment 15-25%.

Aetiology by age (community-acquired)

**Neonates (0-1 mo):** GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

**1 mo - 50 y:** Streptococcus pneumoniae > Neisseria meningitidis > H. influenzae (now rare with vaccine).

**> 50 y / immunosuppressed:** S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negatives.

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Staph aureus, CoNS, gram-negatives.

**India-specific:** TB meningitis remains common — always consider.

### Clinical features

**Classic triad (only 44%):** fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status.

**≥ 2 of:** fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental → 95% sensitivity.

Kernig (knee extension with hip flexed → pain) and Brudzinski (neck flexion → hip flexion).

**Meningococcal:** petechial / purpuric rash (purpura fulminans = severe).

**Pneumococcal:** associated otitis/sinusitis/pneumonia.

Cranial nerve palsies, seizures, papilloedema, focal deficit.

### Investigations

Blood cultures × 2 BEFORE antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics > 1 h for cultures).

Lumbar puncture — CT first if focal deficit, GCS < 10, papilloedema, new-onset seizure, immunosuppression.

CSF Gram stain (60-90% sens), culture, latex agglutination (S. pneumo, H.influ, Nm, GBS).

**TB:** CSF AFB smear (low sens), GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (rapid + rifampicin resistance), culture.

**PCR:** HSV-1/2 (encephalitis), enterovirus, JC virus.

**Other:** CBC, blood C/S, CRP, procalcitonin, electrolytes (SIADH), HIV test.

### Management

- Resuscitation (within first hour)

**Sepsis bundle:** fluids, vasopressors if shock, oxygen, glucose check.

**Seizure control:** lorazepam, then levetiracetam load.

### 2. Dexamethasone

0.15 mg/kg IV q6h × 4 days, FIRST DOSE before or with first antibiotic.

Reduces mortality in S.pneumo; reduces neuro sequelae (deafness) in H.influenzae.

Stop if non-pneumococcal organism identified.

**TB meningitis:** prednisolone/dex tapered over 6-8 wk (TBM treatment).

- Empirical antibiotics (do NOT delay)

**Adult immunocompetent:** Adult immunocompetent: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h (target trough 15-20).

Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed:Age > 50 / pregnant / alcoholic / immunosuppressed: ADD Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria cover).

**Post-neurosurgery / shunt:** Post-neurosurgery / shunt: Vancomycin + Cefepime or Meropenem 2 g q8h.

**Penicillin allergy severe:** Penicillin allergy severe: Vancomycin + Moxifloxacin + TMP-SMX (Listeria).

**Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h:** Add Acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h: If HSV encephalitis suspected (e.g. temporal seizures, behaviour change).

### 4. Pathogen-specific duration

### 5. Adjunctive

Maintain euvolaemia (avoid SIADH).

**ICP management:** head-up 30°, mannitol if raised, ICU monitor.

Audiology test at discharge (especially children — sensorineural deafness).

- Chemoprophylaxis (close contacts)

**Meningococcal:** Rifampicin 600 mg PO BD × 2 d, OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose, OR Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single.

**H. influenzae type b:** Rifampicin 20 mg/kg/d × 4 d for households with child < 4 y unvaccinated.

Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23 in elderly/asplenic/CKD/HIV).

Meningococcal (MenACWY for hajj pilgrims, students, military, asplenia).

Hib (in National Immunisation Schedule under Pentavalent).

Hydrocephalus (communicating > obstructive).

Cerebritis, brain abscess, subdural empyema.

Sensorineural hearing loss (10-30%).

Seizures, epilepsy, cognitive deficits.

Cranial nerve palsies (esp. III, VI, VII, VIII).

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal, adrenal haemorrhage).

SIADH, DIC, septic shock.

### Prognosis

**Treated mortality:** pneumococcal 20-25%, meningococcal 5-10%, H.influ 3-7%.

**Untreated:** > 90% mortality.

10-20% long-term sequelae (deafness, cognitive, epilepsy).

Fig 5. Bacterial meningitis pathway.

**Source:** IDSA Meningitis Guidelines 2017; ICMR Antibiotic Policy 2022; Boloor Ch.15.

### Background

TBM accounts for 10-15% of all extrapulmonary TB in India. Diagnosis is challenging — CSF is the cornerstone.

### CSF findings in TBM

### Microbiological tests

**Ziehl-Neelsen smear:** low sensitivity (10-20%) but high specificity; needs minimum 5-10 mL CSF, repeated × 3.

Culture (Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT): gold standard but 4-6 weeks; sensitivity 30-60%.

**GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra:** 70-85% sensitivity, 1-2 h turnaround, detects rifampicin resistance — recommended FIRST by WHO/RNTCP.

**TB-LAMP:** alternative molecular test.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 10 U/L: supportive but non-specific (also elevated in lymphoma, bacterial, brucellosis).

### Imaging correlation

**CT/MRI with contrast:** basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, tuberculomas, infarcts (basal ganglia).

### Stages (BMRC / Modified MRC)

**Stage I:** Conscious, no neurological deficit.

**Stage II:** GCS 11-14 OR focal deficit OR cranial nerve palsy.

**Stage III:** GCS ≤ 10 OR severe deficit.

Outcome correlates with stage at start of therapy — Stage I mortality < 10%, Stage III > 50%.

Treatment overview (links to NTEP regimen)

**Intensive 2 mo:** Intensive 2 mo: HRZE (isoniazid 5 mg/kg + rifampicin 10 mg/kg + pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg + ethambutol 15 mg/kg).

**Continuation 7-10 mo:** Continuation 7-10 mo: HR. Total duration 9-12 months.

**Steroids:** Steroids: Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/d IV × 1 wk → 0.3 → 0.2 → 0.1 → oral 4-3-2-1 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks. Reduces mortality, esp. Stage II/III.

**Pyridoxine:** Pyridoxine: 10-25 mg/d to prevent INH neuropathy.

**Hydrocephalus:** Hydrocephalus: VP shunt if communicating; ETV/EVD if obstructive.

**Drug-resistant TBM:** Drug-resistant TBM: Refer to programmatic MDR-TB regimen (BPaL/BPaLM not yet validated for TBM — older bedaquiline-linezolid-clofazimine regimens used cautiously).

Differentiate TBM from other meningitides

**Source:** WHO TB Guidelines 2022; NTEP 2024; Indian Academy of Neurology TBM Consensus 2019; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|359.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterised by reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness, and clinically by recurrent episodes of wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough – typically worse at night or early morning.

### Etiology and Risk Factors

**Host:** Atopic individuals; family history of asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, ORMDL3, IL-13.

**Environmental:** Allergens (house dust mite, animal dander, pollen, moulds, cockroach), respiratory infections (RSV, rhinovirus), tobacco smoke, indoor/outdoor air pollution, occupational exposures (isocyanates, flour, latex), exercise, cold air.

**Drugs:** β-blockers, aspirin/NSAIDs (AERD/Samter's triad – asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity).

**Triggers:** Emotion, GERD, obesity, OSA, pregnancy.

**Indian context:** Urban air pollution, biomass fuel exposure, and undiagnosed allergic rhinitis are particularly relevant.

### Pathophysiology

Antigen exposure → IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation → release of histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4), prostaglandins → early-phase bronchoconstriction (15–30 min). Cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes → late-phase response (4–8 h) with mucosal oedema, mucus plugging and ongoing inflammation. Chronic inflammation leads to airway remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia) and fixed obstruction. Result: airway hyper-responsiveness, variable airflow limitation, and reversibility with bronchodilators or steroids.

### Clinical Features

**Symptoms:** Episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, dry cough, chest tightness – often nocturnal / early morning; symptom-free intervals.

**Pattern:** Diurnal variation; triggers (cold, exercise, allergen, URTI); personal/family atopy.

**Signs:** Tachypnoea, prolonged expiration, bilateral polyphonic wheeze, hyperinflation; eczema, allergic rhinitis. In severe attacks: tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, accessory-muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences.

### Asthma severity in acute attack (BTS/GINA)

**Mild:** PEFR >75%, talking in sentences.

**Moderate:** PEFR 50–75%.

**Acute severe:** PEFR 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, cannot complete sentences.

**Life-threatening:** PEFR <33%, SpO₂ <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, hypotension, exhaustion, altered consciousness, normal/raised PaCO₂.

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) – diurnal variation >20%, drop during attack.

**Spirometry:** Obstructive pattern – FEV1/FVC <0.70, reversibility with bronchodilator (FEV1 ↑≥12% AND ≥200 mL).

**Bronchial provocation:** If spirometry normal but symptoms suggestive – methacholine or histamine challenge (PC20 < 8 mg/mL = positive).

**Labs:** Eosinophil count, total IgE, specific allergen IgE; sputum eosinophil count >2%; fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) >25 ppb in eosinophilic asthma.

**Imaging:** Chest X-ray – usually normal; hyperinflation in exacerbation; rules out pneumothorax, infection.

**ABG:** ABG in acute severe attack (normal/rising PaCO₂ is a warning sign).

**Other:** Skin prick test, RAST for specific allergens; ENT review for nasal polyps.

### Management (GINA 2023 + Indian context)

**Goals:** control symptoms, prevent exacerbations, maintain normal lung function, avoid medication side-effects.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA tracks 1 & 2):

**Step 1:** As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred Track 1) or SABA + low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA used.

**Step 2:** Daily low-dose ICS (budesonide 200–400 µg, fluticasone 100–250 µg) + SABA PRN.

**Step 3:** Low-dose ICS-LABA (budesonide/formoterol) + PRN.

**Step 4:** Medium-dose ICS-LABA + PRN.

**Step 5:** High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on: tiotropium (LAMA), biologics (omalizumab anti-IgE; mepolizumab/reslizumab anti-IL-5; dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast); low-dose oral corticosteroid (last resort).

Acute severe asthma (Indian ICU practice + BTS/GINA):

Sit patient up, high-flow O₂ via mask, target SpO₂ 94–98%.

Salbutamol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebuliser (back-to-back q15min × 3).

Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (or Methylprednisolone 60–125 mg IV) → continue Prednisolone 40–50 mg PO daily × 5 days.

Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min in severe attack.

IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg loading, 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion) only if above measures fail; monitor levels.

Antibiotics only if clear infection (CXR consolidation, purulent sputum, fever).

ICU admission if life-threatening / not improving; intubation for exhaustion, falling PEFR, rising PaCO₂.

### Non-pharmacological:

Trigger avoidance (allergens, smoke, occupational), weight reduction, GERD treatment, treat allergic rhinitis (nasal steroid).

Patient education, written action plan (green-yellow-red zones), inhaler technique (MDI + spacer for children/elderly; turbohaler/DPI for adults).

Annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination for severe.

Allergen immunotherapy in selected cases.

Fig 1. GINA 2023 stepwise management of asthma (Track 1, preferred path with ICS-formoterol reliever).

Fig 2. Acute severe asthma – emergency management algorithm.

### Complications

Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

Aspergillosis (ABPA – worsening asthma + central bronchiectasis + peripheral eosinophilia + raised IgE).

Long-term airway remodelling, fixed obstruction.

**Side-effects of treatment:** oral candidiasis, dysphonia (ICS), osteoporosis, cushingoid features (oral steroids), tremor (β-agonists).

### Prognosis

Most patients have well-controlled disease with modern therapy. Asthma mortality is low but preventable; under-treatment with ICS, over-reliance on SABA, and poor adherence/inhaler technique are the key contributors to fatal asthma.

Bronchial breath sounds are produced in the trachea and large airways; they are heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is consolidated or replaced by a sound-conducting medium.

### Characteristics

**Normal site:** Heard over manubrium, trachea normally.

**Components:** Inspiration = expiration in duration; expiration is louder than inspiration; clear gap between them.

**Quality:** High-pitched, harsh.

### Types

Tubular bronchial breathing – classical, heard over consolidation (lobar pneumonia – S. pneumoniae), and over a tense pleural effusion (compressed lung above effusion).

Cavernous breathing – low-pitched, hollow, with reverberating quality (over large lung cavity ≥6 cm communicating with bronchus – TB cavity, lung abscess).

Amphoric breathing – high-pitched, metallic, hollow (like blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle); heard over a smooth-walled cavity (>4 cm) communicating with a bronchus, or over an open pneumothorax. Often associated with metallic tinkling.

Associated signs of consolidation

Increased vocal fremitus, dull percussion note, increased vocal resonance with whispering pectoriloquy and aegophony, fine crackles and bronchial breathing.

Bronchial breathing is heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is more uniform / conducting than normal aerated lung. Causes:

Lobar pneumonia (commonest – S. pneumoniae causing red hepatisation).

Compressed lung above a large pleural effusion (top edge).

Lung abscess opened to bronchus (cavernous, amphoric variants).

Tuberculous cavity (cavernous or amphoric).

Collapse with patent bronchus (paradoxically – consolidation-like transmission).

Mass lesion compressing airway open to large bronchus.

Pulmonary infarction (rare).

Associated signs of consolidation: increased vocal fremitus and resonance, whispering pectoriloquy, aegophony, dull percussion, fine end-inspiratory crackles.

GENERAL MEDICINE|361.note:
Indications for oxygen therapy

Acute hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <94% or PaO₂ <60 mmHg) – pneumonia, asthma, COPD exacerbation, PE, ARDS, MI, sepsis.

**Critical care:** shock, post-arrest, peri-intubation, anaesthesia.

Chronic hypoxia – LTOT in COPD with PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg, or 56–59 with cor pulmonale / polycythaemia; ILD.

Cluster headache, carbon-monoxide poisoning (high-flow O₂ to wash out CO).

Palliative – relieve dyspnoea in terminal illness (clinical judgement; not all dyspnoea improves with O₂).

### Targets (BTS 2017, Indian Pulmonology guidelines)

**Most acute illness:** SpO₂ 94–98%.

Type 2 respiratory failure / COPD: SpO₂ 88–92% (avoid CO₂ narcosis).

### Low-flow devices (variable FiO₂)

Nasal cannula – 1–6 L/min, FiO₂ ~24–44%. Comfortable; first-line for mild hypoxia.

Simple face mask – 5–10 L/min, FiO₂ ~40–60%. Risk of CO₂ rebreathing if <5 L/min.

Partial rebreather mask (reservoir bag) – 6–10 L/min, FiO₂ ~60–80%.

Non-rebreather mask (one-way valves) – 10–15 L/min, FiO₂ ~80–95%. Used for severe acute hypoxia.

High-flow / fixed-FiO₂ devices

Venturi mask – delivers precise FiO₂ (24, 28, 31, 35, 40, 60%) – preferred in COPD when controlled O₂ needed.

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC, Optiflow/AIRVO) – up to 60 L/min humidified gas at FiO₂ 21–100%. Generates low PEEP, washes out CO₂, improves oxygenation; used in type 1 RF, post-extubation.

### Non-invasive ventilation

CPAP – cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, OSA.

BiPAP – COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis, OHS, neuromuscular respiratory failure.

### Invasive (mechanical) ventilation

**Endotracheal intubation:** failed NIV, depressed consciousness, haemodynamic instability, copious secretions, severe ARDS, exhaustion.

### Hazards of oxygen

CO₂ retention/narcosis in COPD.

Absorption atelectasis (high FiO₂).

Oxygen toxicity (free-radical lung damage with FiO₂>0.6 prolonged).

Retinopathy of prematurity in neonates.

Fire hazard (combustion).

Drying of mucosa – humidify if >2 L/min for prolonged use.

GENERAL MEDICINE|362.note:
### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Pneumonia acquired outside healthcare settings (or within first 48 h of admission). Major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.

### Etiology

### Typical bacterial:

Streptococcus pneumoniae – the leading cause (50–60%); lobar pneumonia, rusty sputum.

Haemophilus influenzae (especially COPD).

Moraxella catarrhalis (COPD).

Staphylococcus aureus – post-influenza, IV drug users, necrotising.

Klebsiella pneumoniae – alcoholics, diabetics; currant-jelly sputum, bulging fissure sign, upper-lobe.

### Atypical:

Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii.

### Viral:

Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, hMPV, adenovirus.

### Special host groups:

Alcoholics – Klebsiella, anaerobes, S. pneumoniae, TB.

Diabetics – Klebsiella, S. aureus, fungi (mucormycosis).

HIV – Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, fungal.

Aspiration – oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus).

Indian context – TB always differential.

### Clinical features

Sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, rusty/blood-stained sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

**Atypical pneumonia:** dry cough, headache, myalgia, GI upset, subacute course.

**Signs of consolidation:** tachypnoea, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, fine crackles.

Sepsis features – tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness.

### Severity (CURB-65)

C – Confusion (AMT ≤8 or new disorientation).

U – Urea > 7 mmol/L (>20 mg/dL).

R – Respiratory rate ≥ 30.

B – BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic.

65 – Age ≥65 years.

**0–1:** home; 2: ward; 3–5: ICU (consider).

Empirical therapy (ICMR 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2019)

**Outpatient:** amoxicillin 1 g TDS 5–7 d (± macrolide if atypical suspected) or doxycycline.

**Ward (CURB-65 = 2):** IV amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ceftriaxone + macrolide.

**ICU (CURB-65 ≥3):** IV ceftriaxone + macrolide OR levofloxacin; add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; add antipseudomonal cover if structural lung disease.

De-escalate based on cultures.

**Supportive:** O₂, fluids, antipyretic, VTE prophylaxis.

**Step 4:** Medium-dose ICS-LABA + PRN.

**Step 5:** High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on: tiotropium (LAMA), biologics (omalizumab anti-IgE; mepolizumab/reslizumab anti-IL-5; dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast); low-dose oral corticosteroid (last resort).

Acute severe asthma (Indian ICU practice + BTS/GINA):

Sit patient up, high-flow O₂ via mask, target SpO₂ 94–98%.

Salbutamol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebuliser (back-to-back q15min × 3).

Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV stat (or Methylprednisolone 60–125 mg IV) → continue Prednisolone 40–50 mg PO daily × 5 days.

Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min in severe attack.

IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg loading, 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion) only if above measures fail; monitor levels.

Antibiotics only if clear infection (CXR consolidation, purulent sputum, fever).

ICU admission if life-threatening / not improving; intubation for exhaustion, falling PEFR, rising PaCO₂.

### Non-pharmacological:

Trigger avoidance (allergens, smoke, occupational), weight reduction, GERD treatment, treat allergic rhinitis (nasal steroid).

Patient education, written action plan (green-yellow-red zones), inhaler technique (MDI + spacer for children/elderly; turbohaler/DPI for adults).

Annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination for severe.

Allergen immunotherapy in selected cases.

Fig 1. GINA 2023 stepwise management of asthma (Track 1, preferred path with ICS-formoterol reliever).

Fig 2. Acute severe asthma – emergency management algorithm.

### Complications

Status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

Aspergillosis (ABPA – worsening asthma + central bronchiectasis + peripheral eosinophilia + raised IgE).

Long-term airway remodelling, fixed obstruction.

**Side-effects of treatment:** oral candidiasis, dysphonia (ICS), osteoporosis, cushingoid features (oral steroids), tremor (β-agonists).

### Prognosis

Most patients have well-controlled disease with modern therapy. Asthma mortality is low but preventable; under-treatment with ICS, over-reliance on SABA, and poor adherence/inhaler technique are the key contributors to fatal asthma.

Bronchial breath sounds are produced in the trachea and large airways; they are heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is consolidated or replaced by a sound-conducting medium.

### Characteristics

**Normal site:** Heard over manubrium, trachea normally.

**Components:** Inspiration = expiration in duration; expiration is louder than inspiration; clear gap between them.

**Quality:** High-pitched, harsh.

### Types

Tubular bronchial breathing – classical, heard over consolidation (lobar pneumonia – S. pneumoniae), and over a tense pleural effusion (compressed lung above effusion).

Cavernous breathing – low-pitched, hollow, with reverberating quality (over large lung cavity ≥6 cm communicating with bronchus – TB cavity, lung abscess).

Amphoric breathing – high-pitched, metallic, hollow (like blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle); heard over a smooth-walled cavity (>4 cm) communicating with a bronchus, or over an open pneumothorax. Often associated with metallic tinkling.

Associated signs of consolidation

Increased vocal fremitus, dull percussion note, increased vocal resonance with whispering pectoriloquy and aegophony, fine crackles and bronchial breathing.

Bronchial breathing is heard over peripheral lung fields only when the lung is more uniform / conducting than normal aerated lung. Causes:

Lobar pneumonia (commonest – S. pneumoniae causing red hepatisation).

Compressed lung above a large pleural effusion (top edge).

Lung abscess opened to bronchus (cavernous, amphoric variants).

Tuberculous cavity (cavernous or amphoric).

Collapse with patent bronchus (paradoxically – consolidation-like transmission).

Mass lesion compressing airway open to large bronchus.

Pulmonary infarction (rare).

Associated signs of consolidation: increased vocal fremitus and resonance, whispering pectoriloquy, aegophony, dull percussion, fine end-inspiratory crackles.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

ILDs are a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases characterised by varying degrees of inflammation and fibrosis of the alveolar walls and interstitium, producing restrictive lung disease and impaired gas exchange.

Examples by category (four key examples + classification)

### Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias:

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – usual interstitial pneumonia pattern; older adults; honeycombing.

Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP).

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP).

Acute interstitial pneumonia.

ILD due to known cause:

Connective tissue disease–associated ILD: RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, dermatomyositis (anti-Jo1), Sjögren's, MCTD.

**Drug-induced:** amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin, busulfan, gold, statins.

Radiation pneumonitis.

### Pneumoconioses (occupational):

Silicosis (silica – stone-cutters, quartz miners – egg-shell calcification of hilar nodes).

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis (coal dust – Caplan's syndrome with RA).

Asbestosis (asbestos – pleural plaques, mesothelioma risk).

Berylliosis (aerospace industry).

Byssinosis (cotton dust – Monday-morning chest tightness).

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (organic dusts) – Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay), Bird-fancier's lung (avian proteins).

### Granulomatous ILDs:

Sarcoidosis – multisystem; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + interstitial infiltrates.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

### Other:

Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers).

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women of reproductive age).

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

### Clinical features

Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, fatigue, clubbing (especially IPF and asbestosis).

Velcro-like end-inspiratory crackles at lung bases.

Extra-pulmonary features (rash, arthritis, eye involvement) point to connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis.

### Investigations

HRCT chest is the cornerstone – pattern (UIP, NSIP, OP, HP) often diagnostic.

**Spirometry:** restrictive (FEV1/FVC ≥0.70, ↓TLC, ↓DLCO).

6-minute walk test – desaturation, exercise tolerance.

**Serology:** ANA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Scl70, anti-Jo1, ANCA, IgG precipitins for HP.

BAL (cell differential), transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy if diagnosis unclear.

### Treatment principles

Remove inciting agent (drugs, occupational exposure).

Corticosteroids ± immunosuppressants (azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide) for inflammatory ILDs (NSIP, COP, HP, CTD-ILD).

Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) for IPF and progressive fibrosing ILDs – slow FVC decline.

Long-term O₂ therapy in chronic hypoxia.

Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations.

Lung transplantation in eligible.

### Definition

Localised collection of pus within the lung parenchyma due to microbial infection, leading to tissue necrosis and cavitation.

### Etiology

**Primary (aspiration):** Aspiration (commonest) – alcoholics, post-anaesthesia, stroke, epilepsy, GERD. Anaerobic flora from oral cavity.

**Secondary:** Bronchial obstruction (carcinoma, foreign body), septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided endocarditis, IV drug use), spread from subphrenic/hepatic abscess.

**Organisms:** Anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides), Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza), Streptococcus milleri, gram-negative bacilli, fungi (immunocompromised).

### Clinical Features

Insidious – fever, malaise, weight loss, night sweats over weeks.

Productive cough with copious foul-smelling sputum (anaerobes); may be blood-stained.

Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

Halitosis.

**Signs:** clubbing (chronic), dull percussion, bronchial/amphoric breathing, post-tussive crackles, signs of consolidation.

### Investigations

CXR – cavity with air-fluid level, surrounding consolidation; usual site posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe (gravity-dependent in supine aspiration).

CT chest – delineates cavity, exclude underlying mass.

Sputum gram stain, AFB, culture (aerobic and anaerobic), cytology.

Bronchoscopy – exclude obstruction, obtain protected specimen, facilitate drainage.

Blood culture (especially in septic embolism, IE).

Echo if right-sided endocarditis suspected.

### Management

Empirical antibiotic with anaerobic cover: IV clindamycin 600 mg q8h, OR β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam), OR metronidazole + ceftriaxone.

Add vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA suspected; add fluconazole/voriconazole if fungal.

**Duration:** 4–6 weeks, IV until clinical improvement then PO (oral amoxicillin-clavulanate + metronidazole).

Postural drainage and physiotherapy to facilitate sputum clearance.

Bronchoscopic drainage if poor response (large cavity >6 cm, obstructing lesion).

Percutaneous catheter drainage in selected (refractory abscess).

Surgical resection (lobectomy/segmentectomy) – rarely needed; indications: persistent abscess despite 6–8 wk antibiotic, massive haemoptysis, suspected malignancy, bronchopleural fistula.

**Treat underlying cause:** dental hygiene, anti-seizure medication, swallow assessment, GERD therapy, treat malignancy if present.

### Complications

Empyema, bronchopleural fistula, massive haemoptysis, septicaemia, metastatic abscess (brain, etc.), amyloidosis (chronic), respiratory failure.

### Pneumoconioses (inorganic dusts)

Silicosis – stone-cutting, quartz, sand-blasting.

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis – coal mining.

Asbestosis – insulation, ship-breaking, construction; pleural plaques, mesothelioma.

Berylliosis – aerospace, ceramics.

Stannosis (tin), siderosis (iron), baritosis (barium).

Organic-dust diseases (hypersensitivity pneumonitis)

Farmer's lung – mouldy hay (thermophilic actinomycetes).

Bird-fancier's lung – avian proteins.

Bagassosis – sugarcane waste.

Mushroom-worker's lung.

Humidifier lung.

### Occupational asthma (cause-and-effect)

Isocyanates (paint, polyurethane).

Flour dust (bakers).

Latex (healthcare workers).

Wood dust (cedar – plicatic acid).

Animal proteins (laboratory workers).

### Other

Byssinosis – cotton, flax dust.

Metal-fume fever (zinc oxide fumes, welding).

Occupational malignancies – mesothelioma (asbestos), lung carcinoma (asbestos, silica, radon, chromates).

Toxic gases – chlorine, ammonia, phosgene (acute injury, RADS).

GENERAL MEDICINE|366.note:
### Light's criteria

Effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met:

Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5.

Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Causes (mnemonic:** 'Pus, blood, fluid from inflammation')

### Infective:

Parapneumonic effusion / empyema (Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Tuberculous pleural effusion (the commonest cause of exudative effusion in young adults in India – lymphocytic, ADA >40 U/L, biopsy shows granulomas).

Fungal (rare), parasitic (amoebic, hydatid).

Malignancy (commonest cause of exudate in elderly):

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Breast carcinoma.

Lymphoma, leukaemia.

Mesothelioma (asbestos-related).

Ovarian carcinoma (Meigs syndrome with ascites).

Connective tissue / autoimmune:

Rheumatoid arthritis (low glucose, low pH, low complement, RF positive).

SLE.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Pulmonary embolism / infarction.

### Gastrointestinal / abdominal:

Pancreatitis (left-sided, high amylase).

Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave's – high amylase from saliva, low pH).

Subdiaphragmatic abscess.

Post-CABG.

### Drugs:

Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine.

### Other:

Radiation therapy.

Chylothorax (lymphoma, trauma, thoracic-duct obstruction – triglycerides >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons).

Haemothorax (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation).

Yellow nail syndrome.

Fig 6. Pleural effusion – diagnostic algorithm using Light's criteria.

GENERAL MEDICINE|368.note:
### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Pneumonia acquired outside healthcare settings (or within first 48 h of admission). Major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.

### Etiology

### Typical bacterial:

Streptococcus pneumoniae – the leading cause (50–60%); lobar pneumonia, rusty sputum.

Haemophilus influenzae (especially COPD).

Moraxella catarrhalis (COPD).

Staphylococcus aureus – post-influenza, IV drug users, necrotising.

Klebsiella pneumoniae – alcoholics, diabetics; currant-jelly sputum, bulging fissure sign, upper-lobe.

### Atypical:

Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii.

### Viral:

Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, hMPV, adenovirus.

### Special host groups:

Alcoholics – Klebsiella, anaerobes, S. pneumoniae, TB.

Diabetics – Klebsiella, S. aureus, fungi (mucormycosis).

HIV – Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, fungal.

Aspiration – oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus).

Indian context – TB always differential.

### Clinical features

Sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, rusty/blood-stained sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

**Atypical pneumonia:** dry cough, headache, myalgia, GI upset, subacute course.

**Signs of consolidation:** tachypnoea, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, fine crackles.

Sepsis features – tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness.

### Severity (CURB-65)

C – Confusion (AMT ≤8 or new disorientation).

U – Urea > 7 mmol/L (>20 mg/dL).

R – Respiratory rate ≥ 30.

B – BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic.

65 – Age ≥65 years.

**0–1:** home; 2: ward; 3–5: ICU (consider).

Empirical therapy (ICMR 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2019)

**Outpatient:** amoxicillin 1 g TDS 5–7 d (± macrolide if atypical suspected) or doxycycline.

**Ward (CURB-65 = 2):** IV amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ceftriaxone + macrolide.

**ICU (CURB-65 ≥3):** IV ceftriaxone + macrolide OR levofloxacin; add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; add antipseudomonal cover if structural lung disease.

De-escalate based on cultures.

**Supportive:** O₂, fluids, antipyretic, VTE prophylaxis.

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis (coal dust – Caplan's syndrome with RA).

Asbestosis (asbestos – pleural plaques, mesothelioma risk).

Berylliosis (aerospace industry).

Byssinosis (cotton dust – Monday-morning chest tightness).

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (organic dusts) – Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay), Bird-fancier's lung (avian proteins).

### Granulomatous ILDs:

Sarcoidosis – multisystem; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + interstitial infiltrates.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

### Other:

Langerhans-cell histiocytosis (smokers).

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women of reproductive age).

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

### Clinical features

Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, fatigue, clubbing (especially IPF and asbestosis).

Velcro-like end-inspiratory crackles at lung bases.

Extra-pulmonary features (rash, arthritis, eye involvement) point to connective tissue disease or sarcoidosis.

### Investigations

HRCT chest is the cornerstone – pattern (UIP, NSIP, OP, HP) often diagnostic.

**Spirometry:** restrictive (FEV1/FVC ≥0.70, ↓TLC, ↓DLCO).

6-minute walk test – desaturation, exercise tolerance.

**Serology:** ANA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Scl70, anti-Jo1, ANCA, IgG precipitins for HP.

BAL (cell differential), transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy if diagnosis unclear.

### Treatment principles

Remove inciting agent (drugs, occupational exposure).

Corticosteroids ± immunosuppressants (azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide) for inflammatory ILDs (NSIP, COP, HP, CTD-ILD).

Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) for IPF and progressive fibrosing ILDs – slow FVC decline.

Long-term O₂ therapy in chronic hypoxia.

Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations.

Lung transplantation in eligible.

### Definition

Localised collection of pus within the lung parenchyma due to microbial infection, leading to tissue necrosis and cavitation.

### Etiology

**Primary (aspiration):** Aspiration (commonest) – alcoholics, post-anaesthesia, stroke, epilepsy, GERD. Anaerobic flora from oral cavity.

**Secondary:** Bronchial obstruction (carcinoma, foreign body), septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided endocarditis, IV drug use), spread from subphrenic/hepatic abscess.

**Organisms:** Anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides), Klebsiella, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza), Streptococcus milleri, gram-negative bacilli, fungi (immunocompromised).

### Clinical Features

Insidious – fever, malaise, weight loss, night sweats over weeks.

Productive cough with copious foul-smelling sputum (anaerobes); may be blood-stained.

Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

Halitosis.

**Signs:** clubbing (chronic), dull percussion, bronchial/amphoric breathing, post-tussive crackles, signs of consolidation.

### Investigations

CXR – cavity with air-fluid level, surrounding consolidation; usual site posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe (gravity-dependent in supine aspiration).

CT chest – delineates cavity, exclude underlying mass.

Sputum gram stain, AFB, culture (aerobic and anaerobic), cytology.
