Bronchoscopy – exclude obstruction, obtain protected specimen, facilitate drainage.

Blood culture (especially in septic embolism, IE).

Echo if right-sided endocarditis suspected.

### Management

Empirical antibiotic with anaerobic cover: IV clindamycin 600 mg q8h, OR β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam), OR metronidazole + ceftriaxone.

Add vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA suspected; add fluconazole/voriconazole if fungal.

**Duration:** 4–6 weeks, IV until clinical improvement then PO (oral amoxicillin-clavulanate + metronidazole).

Postural drainage and physiotherapy to facilitate sputum clearance.

Bronchoscopic drainage if poor response (large cavity >6 cm, obstructing lesion).

Percutaneous catheter drainage in selected (refractory abscess).

Surgical resection (lobectomy/segmentectomy) – rarely needed; indications: persistent abscess despite 6–8 wk antibiotic, massive haemoptysis, suspected malignancy, bronchopleural fistula.

**Treat underlying cause:** dental hygiene, anti-seizure medication, swallow assessment, GERD therapy, treat malignancy if present.

### Complications

Empyema, bronchopleural fistula, massive haemoptysis, septicaemia, metastatic abscess (brain, etc.), amyloidosis (chronic), respiratory failure.

### Pneumoconioses (inorganic dusts)

Silicosis – stone-cutting, quartz, sand-blasting.

Coal worker's pneumoconiosis – coal mining.

Asbestosis – insulation, ship-breaking, construction; pleural plaques, mesothelioma.

Berylliosis – aerospace, ceramics.

Stannosis (tin), siderosis (iron), baritosis (barium).

Organic-dust diseases (hypersensitivity pneumonitis)

Farmer's lung – mouldy hay (thermophilic actinomycetes).

Bird-fancier's lung – avian proteins.

Bagassosis – sugarcane waste.

Mushroom-worker's lung.

Humidifier lung.

### Occupational asthma (cause-and-effect)

Isocyanates (paint, polyurethane).

Flour dust (bakers).

Latex (healthcare workers).

Wood dust (cedar – plicatic acid).

Animal proteins (laboratory workers).

### Other

Byssinosis – cotton, flax dust.

Metal-fume fever (zinc oxide fumes, welding).

Occupational malignancies – mesothelioma (asbestos), lung carcinoma (asbestos, silica, radon, chromates).

Toxic gases – chlorine, ammonia, phosgene (acute injury, RADS).

GENERAL MEDICINE|370.note:
### Light's criteria

Effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met:

Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5.

Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.

Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Causes (mnemonic:** 'Pus, blood, fluid from inflammation')

### Infective:

Parapneumonic effusion / empyema (Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Klebsiella).

Tuberculous pleural effusion (the commonest cause of exudative effusion in young adults in India – lymphocytic, ADA >40 U/L, biopsy shows granulomas).

Fungal (rare), parasitic (amoebic, hydatid).

Malignancy (commonest cause of exudate in elderly):

Bronchogenic carcinoma.

Breast carcinoma.

Lymphoma, leukaemia.

Mesothelioma (asbestos-related).

Ovarian carcinoma (Meigs syndrome with ascites).

Connective tissue / autoimmune:

Rheumatoid arthritis (low glucose, low pH, low complement, RF positive).

SLE.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Pulmonary embolism / infarction.

### Gastrointestinal / abdominal:

Pancreatitis (left-sided, high amylase).

Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave's – high amylase from saliva, low pH).

Subdiaphragmatic abscess.

Post-CABG.

### Drugs:

Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine.

### Other:

Radiation therapy.

Chylothorax (lymphoma, trauma, thoracic-duct obstruction – triglycerides >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons).

Haemothorax (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation).

Yellow nail syndrome.

Fig 6. Pleural effusion – diagnostic algorithm using Light's criteria.

GENERAL MEDICINE|371.note:
### Definition

Chronic kidney disease attributable to diabetes mellitus. Diagnosed clinically by presence of albuminuria and/or reduced GFR in a known diabetic, WITHOUT signs of another primary cause. Histologically: diabetic glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), mesangial expansion, basement membrane thickening, afferent + efferent arteriolar hyalinosis.

COMMONEST CAUSE of CKD and ESRD in India and worldwide (40–50%).

### Risk Factors

**Duration of diabetes (T1DM:** rare before 5 yr; T2DM: may present at diagnosis).

Poor glycaemic control (HbA1c > 7%).

Hypertension.

Genetic susceptibility (family history of DN).

Smoking, obesity, dyslipidaemia.

Asian (Indian) ethnicity — higher risk and earlier onset.

Concomitant diabetic retinopathy + neuropathy (microvascular triad).

### Pathogenesis

Chronic hyperglycaemia → advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), oxidative stress, PKC activation, polyol pathway, hexosamine pathway.

Glomerular hyperfiltration (early) — efferent arteriolar constriction (angiotensin II) → ↑ intraglomerular pressure → mechanical injury.

Mesangial expansion + nodular sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson).

Podocyte loss → proteinuria.

Tubulointerstitial fibrosis.

Stages (Mogensen — historical but clinically useful)

Use KDIGO 'G-A' classification for current staging (G1–G5, A1–A3).

### Clinical Features

Often asymptomatic till advanced (microalbuminuria detected on screening).

Hypertension (early; often coexistent).

Frothy urine, peripheral / pedal oedema (overt proteinuria).

Nephrotic syndrome features (full-blown in 30% — see Q4).

Concomitant features of diabetic microvascular disease: retinopathy (95% in T1, 60% in T2), neuropathy; macrovascular: CAD, stroke, PVD.

ESRD features (anaemia, uraemia, electrolyte disturbance).

### Investigations

### Screening (essential — KDIGO and ADA)

Annual urine ACR + serum creatinine for eGFR — from diagnosis in T2DM, from 5 years in T1DM.

Confirm albuminuria with 2 of 3 samples (variability — exercise, fever, UTI exclude).

Fundoscopy (correlate with retinopathy — absence makes DN less likely).

### Routine

HbA1c, lipid profile, blood pressure.

Serum K, HCO₃, Ca, phosphate, PTH (advanced CKD).

CBC (anaemia of CKD).

When to suspect non-diabetic kidney disease (consider biopsy)

Absence of diabetic retinopathy (T1DM > T2DM).

Rapid decline of GFR.

Active urinary sediment (RBC casts).

Nephrotic-range proteinuria onset < 5 yr from T1DM.

Sudden onset of NS.

Systemic features (rash, joints).

### Management

### 1. Glycaemic Control

HbA1c target 6.5–7% (KDIGO 2022 individualises — 6.5–8% in advanced CKD; avoid hypoglycaemia in G4–G5).

Metformin — safe till eGFR 30 (stop below 30, reduce dose 30–45).

SGLT2 inhibitors (FIRST-LINE in DKD — see below).

GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) — weight + CV benefit.

DPP-4 inhibitors safe in CKD (linagliptin no dose adjustment).

Insulin — dose reduction in advanced CKD (clearance prolonged).

**AVOID:** sulphonylureas (hypoglycaemia in advanced CKD), pioglitazone (oedema, HF).

### 2. Blood Pressure Control

Target BP < 130/80 (< 120/80 if tolerated — KDIGO 2021).

**FIRST-LINE:** ACEi (e.g., ramipril 10 mg) or ARB (losartan 100 mg, telmisartan 80 mg) — renoprotective beyond BP effect; reduces albuminuria 30–50%.

**Add:** CCB (amlodipine), thiazide (chlorthalidone — preferred over HCTZ), spironolactone (consider in resistant).

Avoid combination ACEi + ARB (ONTARGET, ALTITUDE harm — hyperK, AKI).

### 3. SGLT2 Inhibitors (game-changers)

Dapagliflozin 10 mg OD or empagliflozin 10 mg OD or canagliflozin 100 mg OD.

Renal benefit demonstrated in:

CREDENCE 2019 (canagliflozin) — reduced CKD progression, ESRD, CV death by 30%.

DAPA-CKD 2020 (dapagliflozin) — including non-diabetic CKD.

EMPA-KIDNEY 2022 (empagliflozin) — even broader eGFR range.

**Indication:** T2DM + eGFR ≥ 20 + ACR ≥ 200 (any albuminuria) — now recommend for non-diabetic CKD with proteinuria too.

Stop when patient is on dialysis. Caution: euglycaemic DKA, genital mycotic infection, Fournier's gangrene (rare).

### 4. Non-Steroidal Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist

Finerenone 10–20 mg OD — FIDELIO-DKD + FIGARO-DKD trials demonstrated renal + CV benefit when added to ACEi/ARB + SGLT2i.

**Indication:** T2DM + eGFR > 25 + ACR ≥ 30; less hyperK than spironolactone.

Monitor K — stop if > 5.5.

### 5. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

Semaglutide 1 mg/wk SC, dulaglutide 1.5 mg/wk SC, liraglutide 1.8 mg/d SC.

Renal benefit (FLOW trial 2024 — semaglutide reduced kidney composite endpoint).

### 6. Lifestyle

Smoking cessation.

Weight loss (BMI < 25).

Salt < 5g/d.

Protein 0.8 g/kg/d (NOT < 0.6 — malnutrition).

Physical activity 30 min × 5 d/wk.

### 7. Statins + Lipid Control

Atorvastatin 20–40 mg / rosuvastatin 10–20 mg — for ALL diabetic CKD.

LDL target < 70 (very high risk).

### 8. CKD-MBD, Anaemia, Acidosis

As per CKD general management (see Q2).

### 9. ESRD

Refer for RRT preparation at G4. Transplant — best outcome (combined kidney-pancreas in T1DM).

### Prognosis

**Without intervention:** T1DM → microalbuminuria 30% by 20 yr → ESRD 50% by 25 yr. T2DM: 30% develop CKD; 40% of these progress to ESRD. With aggressive RAS blockade + SGLT2i + glycaemic control, progression slowed by 40–70%. CV mortality remains the major cause of death.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.378; KDIGO DKD 2022; ADA 2023; CREDENCE; DAPA-CKD; EMPA-KIDNEY; FIDELIO; FLOW.

GENERAL MEDICINE|372.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

### DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 → prolong endogenous GLP-1 and GIP → glucose-dependent insulin secretion, glucagon suppression.

**Available agents:** Sitagliptin 100 mg OD (adjust in CKD), vildagliptin 50 mg BD, linagliptin 5 mg OD (no renal adjustment), saxagliptin 5 mg OD, alogliptin 25 mg OD, teneligliptin 20 mg OD (Indian-favoured, cheap).

**Advantages:** Weight-neutral, no hypoglycaemia (when used alone), well tolerated, safe in elderly and CKD (linagliptin).

**Adverse:** Nasopharyngitis, headache, pancreatitis (rare), arthralgia, hypersensitivity. Saxagliptin and alogliptin – HF hospitalisation signal.

**Use:** Add-on to metformin when modest reduction in HbA1c (0.5–0.8%) needed; preferred in elderly with renal impairment.

### SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins)

**Mechanism:** Inhibit sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in renal proximal tubule → ~50–80 g/day urinary glucose loss; mild diuresis, weight loss, BP reduction; pleotropic cardiovascular and renal benefits.

**Available agents:** Empagliflozin 10–25 mg OD, dapagliflozin 10 mg OD, canagliflozin 100–300 mg OD, ertugliflozin 5–15 mg OD.

**Benefits beyond glycaemia:** ↓ Cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation (EMPA-REG, CANVAS, DECLARE, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR); ↓ CKD progression (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD); approved for HFrEF/HFpEF and CKD regardless of diabetes.

**Indications:** Indicated in T2DM with established/high-risk ASCVD, HF, or CKD; modest HbA1c reduction (0.6–1.0%); 2–3 kg weight loss; ↓ systolic BP 3–5 mmHg.

**Adverse:** Genital mycotic infection (candida, women > men), UTI, volume depletion (especially elderly, on diuretics), euglycaemic DKA (omit pre-op, in fasting/illness), Fournier's gangrene, lower-limb amputation (canagliflozin), bone fractures (canagliflozin).

**Contra-/cautions:** Severe renal failure (eGFR <20–25), volume depletion, hypotension, type 1 DM, recurrent UTI, history of euglycaemic DKA.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (covered briefly)

Liraglutide 1.8–3.0 mg SC OD (also for obesity), exenatide BD or weekly XR, dulaglutide 1.5–4.5 mg SC weekly, semaglutide 0.25–2 mg SC weekly (or oral 14 mg OD).

Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) 5–15 mg SC weekly – superior HbA1c and weight reduction.

**Benefits:** HbA1c reduction 1–1.5%, weight loss 3–10 kg, CV and renal benefit.

**Adverse:** nausea/vomiting (titrate dose), pancreatitis (rare), gallstones, thyroid C-cell tumour (rodent, theoretical).

Diagnosis (ADA / RSSDI 2024 – any one)

FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL (after 8-h fast) – confirmed by repeat.

2-h plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during 75 g OGTT.

HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (NGSP/IFCC-aligned method).

Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss).

### Pre-diabetes:

**Impaired fasting glucose:** FPG 100–125 mg/dL.

**Impaired glucose tolerance:** 2-h OGTT 140–199 mg/dL.

HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

### Management

### Lifestyle (always first):

Diet – ICMR-recommended balanced Indian diet, complex carbs 55–60%, protein 12–15%, fat 25–30%, fibre 25–40 g/day, limit saturated fat and refined sugar.

Exercise – 150 min/week moderate aerobic + 2 sessions resistance training.

Weight reduction 5–10% if BMI ≥23 (Asian threshold).

Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation.

Sleep 7–9 h; stress management.

### Pharmacotherapy:

Metformin first-line.

Add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA if ASCVD/HF/CKD/obesity present.

Add DPP-4i, SU, pioglitazone if no specific indications.

Insulin (basal) when HbA1c >9% or symptomatic.

Targets – HbA1c <7% (relax to 7.5–8% in elderly/frail/short life expectancy); BP <130/80; LDL <70 (or <55 with established ASCVD).

### Adjunctive:

Statin – moderate-intensity for all >40 yrs; high-intensity if ASCVD risk >20%.

ACEi/ARB for albuminuria.

Aspirin only for secondary prevention (or primary with high ASCVD risk + low bleeding).

Annual screening – eye (fundus), feet, urine ACR, eGFR, lipids, BP, dental.

Vaccines – influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, hepatitis B.

### Complications of T2DM

### Acute:

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) – elderly, glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, no significant ketosis.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (less common than T1DM).

Hypoglycaemia (drug-induced).

### Microvascular:

Retinopathy – non-proliferative, proliferative; diabetic macular oedema. Leading cause of acquired blindness; annual screening essential.

Nephropathy – albuminuria → progressive eGFR loss → ESRD. ACEi/ARB and SGLT2i slow progression.

Neuropathy – distal symmetric polyneuropathy ('stocking-glove'), autonomic neuropathy (orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction), mononeuropathy.

### Macrovascular:

Ischaemic heart disease (#1 cause of death in T2DM).

Stroke.

Peripheral vascular disease, lower-limb amputation.

### Other:

Diabetic foot – ulcer, infection, Charcot arthropathy.

Increased infection risk (UTI, candida, mucormycosis, TB).

NAFLD/NASH, cataracts, sleep apnoea.

Cognitive impairment, depression.

### Definition

Disorder of water balance characterised by polyuria (>3 L/day) and polydipsia due to deficient secretion (central / cranial DI) or renal action (nephrogenic DI) of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin, AVP).

### Causes

### Central (cranial) DI:

Idiopathic / autoimmune.

Post-surgery, head injury, pituitary apoplexy.

Pituitary/hypothalamic tumour (craniopharyngioma, metastases).

Infiltration – sarcoidosis, Langerhans-cell histiocytosis, lymphocytic hypophysitis, TB.

Vascular – Sheehan's syndrome, AVM.

Genetic (autosomal dominant AVP gene mutations).

### Nephrogenic DI:

Drugs – lithium (commonest acquired), demeclocycline, amphotericin, foscarnet, cidofovir.

Hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia.

CKD, sickle-cell disease, multiple myeloma, amyloidosis, obstructive uropathy.

Pregnancy (placental vasopressinase – gestational DI).

Genetic (X-linked AVPR2 gene, AQP2).

### Clinical features

Polyuria (5–20 L/day), nocturia, polydipsia (especially craving cold water).

Dehydration if no access to water, hypernatraemia, lethargy, confusion, seizures.

In children – enuresis, sleep disturbance, irritability, growth failure.

### Investigations

24-h urine volume (>3 L confirms polyuria).

Serum sodium and osmolality (high-normal/raised), urine osmolality (low – <300 mOsm/kg; usually <200).

Water deprivation test – 8 h fluid restriction; serial urine and plasma osmolality. DI: urine fails to concentrate. Then give desmopressin 2 µg IM/IV:

**- Central DI:** urine osmolality rises >50% (responsive).

**- Nephrogenic DI:** urine osmolality rises <10% (unresponsive).

**- Primary polydipsia:** urine concentrates with deprivation; no further rise with desmopressin.

Plasma copeptin (surrogate for AVP) – stimulated test increasingly used.

MRI pituitary (loss of normal bright spot of posterior pituitary; any mass).

Rule out drugs, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia.

### Management

### Central DI:

Desmopressin (DDAVP) – intranasal 10–40 µg/day in divided doses; oral 100–800 µg/day; SC 1–2 µg/day.

Monitor serum sodium (avoid hyponatraemia from over-treatment).

### Nephrogenic DI:

Treat underlying cause (stop lithium if possible; correct calcium/potassium).

Low-sodium, low-protein diet.

Thiazide diuretic + amiloride (paradoxical antidiuretic effect; induce mild volume contraction → proximal Na/water reabsorption).

NSAIDs (indomethacin) reduce urine output (caution in renal impairment).

### Acute hypernatraemia:

Free water replacement (oral or IV 5% dextrose / 0.45% NaCl); correct slowly (<10 mmol/L/24 h) to avoid cerebral oedema.

### Background

Newer insulin analogues have been engineered for tighter, more physiological glycaemic control and reduced hypoglycaemia risk compared with regular human insulin and NPH. They are classified by their pharmacokinetic profile.

### Rapid-acting analogues (prandial)

Lispro – onset 5–15 min, peak 30–60 min, duration 3–4 h.

Aspart – similar profile.

Glulisine.

Faster aspart (Fiasp) – even faster onset (~2 min via niacinamide); post-meal glucose control.

Inhaled human insulin (Afrezza) – very rapid onset.

### Long-acting analogues (basal)

Glargine U-100 (Lantus) – onset 1–2 h, no peak, duration 20–24 h.

Glargine U-300 (Toujeo) – flatter, more reproducible, 24–36 h duration.

Detemir – duration 14–20 h (often twice daily).

Degludec (Tresiba) – ultra-long, duration >42 h, very stable; lower hypoglycaemia risk.

Icodec (once-weekly) – emerging, approved in 2024.

### Pre-mix and biphasic

Pre-mix 70/30 (NPH/regular), 75/25 (lispro protamine/lispro), 70/30 aspart protamine/aspart, 50/50 mixes.

**Co-formulations:** degludec + aspart (Ryzodeg).

### Combined GLP-1/insulin

iGlarLixi (insulin glargine + lixisenatide) – simplifies regimen, better weight profile.

iDegLira (insulin degludec + liraglutide).

### Indications and choice

**T1DM:** basal-bolus regimen (long-acting analogue + rapid-acting with meals) OR insulin pump (continuous SC infusion of rapid-acting).

**T2DM:** basal insulin added when oral therapy insufficient (HbA1c >9% / symptomatic / contraindications). Add prandial later (basal-plus → basal-bolus).

**Pregnancy:** lispro, aspart, detemir; glargine acceptable; degludec limited data.

Newer agents reduce nocturnal hypoglycaemia and weight gain.

### Adverse effects

Hypoglycaemia (commonest), weight gain, injection site reactions (lipohypertrophy/atrophy), allergic reactions (rare), insulin antibodies.

### Indian context

RSSDI emphasises individualised regimens; cost is a major factor; biosimilar insulin analogues (glargine, lispro, aspart) widely available; NPH and regular human insulin remain affordable backup; continuous glucose monitoring increasingly used in T1DM.

GENERAL MEDICINE|373.note:
### Definition

Renal replacement therapy in which blood is circulated through an extracorporeal circuit and passes through a semi-permeable dialyser membrane against a counter-current dialysate flow. Solutes (urea, K, creatinine, drugs, toxins) move by DIFFUSION down concentration gradient. Water is removed by ULTRAFILTRATION (hydrostatic pressure).

**Modalities:** intermittent haemodialysis (IHD; 4 h × 3/wk standard), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT — CVVH, CVVHD, CVVHDF), sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED), home daily / nocturnal HD, hybrid (CRRT-IHD).

### Principles

- Diffusion (solute removal)

Concentration gradient drives small/middle MW solutes (urea 60, Cr 113, K 39) across membrane. Efficiency depends on: blood/dialysate flow rate, surface area, molecular size + pore size.

- Ultrafiltration (water removal)

Hydrostatic pressure gradient → bulk fluid movement; removes ~ 0.5–1 L/hr.

### 3. Convection

Solvent drag — water carries dissolved solutes. Main mechanism in CRRT (haemofiltration); better removal of middle-MW solutes (β2-microglobulin).

### 4. Adsorption

Some membranes (polysulphone) adsorb protein-bound toxins.

### Components of HD Circuit

Vascular access (see below).

Blood pump (200–400 ml/min flow).

Heparin / citrate anticoagulation.

Dialyser (artificial kidney — hollow-fibre, surface area 1.0–2.0 m²; biocompatible polysulphone / cellulose triacetate).

Dialysate (purified water + electrolytes — Na 138, K 1–3, Ca 1.25, Mg 0.5, HCO₃ 30–35, glucose; counter-current flow 500 ml/min).

Pressure monitors, air detector, blood leak detector.

Reverse osmosis water plant.

### Vascular Access

### Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF) — GOLD STANDARD

Native vessels — radio-cephalic at wrist (preferred), brachio-cephalic at elbow, brachio-basilic transposition.

Patient's own artery and vein anastomosed → vein arterialises (matures) over 6 weeks.

**PLAN AHEAD:** create when eGFR 15–25 (G4 → G5 transition).

Best long-term patency (5-yr 70%); lowest infection.

**Examination:** bruit + thrill on auscultation/palpation.

### Arteriovenous Graft (AVG)

Synthetic (PTFE) graft when veins inadequate.

Used in 2 weeks; lower patency (5-yr 30%); more infections.

### Central Venous Catheter (CVC)

Internal jugular (preferred), femoral, subclavian (avoid — stenosis).

Temporary (non-tunnelled) — acute settings.

Permanent (tunnelled cuffed — Permcath) — bridge to AVF or bridging.

Highest infection (bacteraemia), thrombosis, stenosis.

**Most common reason:** emergent dialysis when AVF not ready.

### Indications for Initiating Dialysis

### Acute (AKI) — AEIOU mnemonic

Acidosis — refractory pH < 7.1.

Electrolytes — K > 6.5 refractory, severe hyperNa/hypoNa, hypercalcaemia.

Intoxication — lithium, salicylate, ethylene glycol, methanol, valproate, metformin.

Overload — refractory pulmonary oedema.

Uraemia — pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding.

### Chronic (ESRD)

**Symptomatic uraemia:** anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, pruritus.

Volume overload despite diuretics.

Hyperkalaemia / acidosis not controlled medically.

Pericarditis, encephalopathy.

Malnutrition.

eGFR 5–10 ml/min/1.73 m² typically (NOT a fixed number; IDEAL trial showed early start ≥ 10 ml/min NO benefit vs late start 5–7).

### Prescription

### Complications

### Intradialytic

Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%):Hypotension (commonest, 20–30%): Causes: excessive UF, hypovolaemia, antihypertensives, cardiac dysfunction, sepsis, Mg/Ca shift. Treat: stop UF, head down, 100–250 ml NS bolus, midodrine pre-HD, reduce dry weight target.

**Cramps:** Cramps: Volume / Na depletion. NS bolus, quinine, vit E.

**Nausea, vomiting:** Nausea, vomiting: Hypotension, dialysate issues. Antiemetics.

**Headache:** Headache: Disequilibrium (rapid urea shifts; cerebral oedema), HTN, caffeine withdrawal.

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome:Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: Rapid initial dialysis → cerebral oedema (urea shifts). Headache, nausea, seizure, coma. Prevention: shorter, gentler first sessions, mannitol.

**First-use syndrome:** First-use syndrome: Type A (anaphylactoid — ethylene oxide sterilant): immediate (stop dialysis, epinephrine, steroids, antihistamine). Type B (chest/back pain): mild, continue.

**Air embolism:** Air embolism: Rare — clamp lines, left lateral Trendelenburg, 100% O₂.

**Haemolysis:** Haemolysis: Mechanical, hypotonic dialysate. Pink plasma. Stop HD.

**Cardiac:** Cardiac: Arrhythmia, ischaemia (electrolyte shifts, hypotension).

**Bleeding:** Bleeding: Heparin-related. Protamine if severe.

### Long-term

**Vascular access:** Vascular access: Thrombosis, stenosis, infection (bacteraemia esp. catheter), aneurysm, steal syndrome, high-output cardiac failure (AVF > 2 L/min).

**Cardiovascular:** Cardiovascular: Major cause of mortality. Accelerated atherosclerosis, LVH, vascular calcification, uraemic cardiomyopathy.

**Anaemia:** Anaemia: Erythropoietin deficiency, iron deficiency, blood loss in circuit, uraemic platelet dysfunction.

**Bone disease (CKD-MBD):** Bone disease (CKD-MBD): 2° hyperparathyroidism, osteitis fibrosa, adynamic bone, β2-microglobulin amyloid (carpal tunnel).

**Infection:** Infection: CRBSI (catheter — Staph aureus, MRSA, MRSE), HBV/HCV transmission (rare in modern era), TB, fungal.

**Malnutrition / protein wasting:** Malnutrition / protein wasting: Anorexia, restrictions, inflammation, protein loss in HD.

**Encephalopathy:** Encephalopathy: Uraemic, aluminium (older — minimal now), thiamine deficiency.

**Psychosocial:** Psychosocial: Depression, sexual dysfunction, financial burden — high suicide risk.

**Other:** Other: Acquired cystic kidney → RCC, gout/pseudogout, restless legs, dementia.

### Comparison with Peritoneal Dialysis (PD)

### Adequacy Assessment

Kt/V (Daugirdas formula) — single-pool > 1.4 per session.

Urea Reduction Ratio (URR) — > 65%.

Weekly Kt/V > 2.0.

**Clinical:** BP control, dry weight, nutrition, symptom resolution.

### Outcomes (India)

1-yr survival on HD ~ 80% (worse than transplant 95%). 5-yr survival ~ 35–40%. Major cause of death: CV disease (45%), infection (20%), withdrawal (5–10%). PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat) and many state schemes (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) cover HD costs. PMNDP (Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme) since 2016 provides free HD across India.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.392; KDIGO Dialysis Initiation 2015; KDOQI; PMNDP 2016; ISN Global Kidney Health Atlas; IDEAL trial.

GENERAL MEDICINE|374.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Overview

**Renal function tests assess:** (1) GFR, (2) tubular function, (3) glomerular permeability (proteinuria), (4) urinary sediment, (5) renal anatomy. Used for screening, diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of kidney disease.

### 1. Assessment of GFR

Direct (Exogenous Markers — gold standard, research)

Inulin clearance — gold standard; cumbersome.

Iohexol, iothalamate, EDTA clearance — used clinically when accurate GFR needed (transplant donor, chemotherapy dosing).

### Endogenous Markers

**Serum Creatinine (Cr):** Serum Creatinine (Cr): Normal 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (M), 0.6–1.1 (F). Easy, cheap. Limitations:

Affected by muscle mass (low in elderly, women, vegetarians, amputees, sarcopenia).

Insensitive in early CKD ('creatinine-blind range' — GFR can drop to 50% before Cr rises).

Affected by drugs blocking tubular secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine).

Diet — cooked meat ↑ Cr.

**Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas:** Estimated GFR (eGFR) Formulas: Calculated from serum Cr + age + sex (± race, removed 2021).

CKD-EPI 2021 (PREFERRED — race-free) — most accurate across all ranges.

MDRD — older; less accurate at normal/high GFR.

Cockcroft-Gault — older; uses weight; used for drug dosing.

Schwartz (children) — eGFR = k × height/Cr.

**Creatinine Clearance (24-h):** Creatinine Clearance (24-h): Cr clearance = (Urine Cr × Urine volume) / Plasma Cr. Limitations: incomplete urine collection, overestimates GFR (tubular secretion of Cr 10–15%, more with low GFR). Less used now than eGFR. Adequate collection: Cr × 1.5 (males) / 1.2 (females) g/kg/d.

**Cystatin C:** Cystatin C: Constant cellular production; freely filtered; not reabsorbed; not secreted. Independent of muscle mass. Useful in elderly, sarcopenic, paediatric. CKD-EPI Cr-cystatin C combined — most accurate. Expensive.

**Blood urea / BUN:** Blood urea / BUN: Normal 7–25 mg/dL. Affected by protein intake, GI bleeding (↑), liver disease (↓), hydration. Urea:Cr ratio > 100 → pre-renal / GI bleed.

### 2. Glomerular Permeability — Proteinuria

### Quantification

Dipstick — semi-quantitative; detects albumin > 30 mg/dL. Negative in non-albumin proteinuria (myeloma — light chain).

24-h urine protein — gold standard. Normal < 150 mg/d.

**Spot UACR (urine albumin:** creatinine ratio):

< 30 mg/g — normal

30–300 mg/g — moderately increased (microalbuminuria)

> 300 mg/g — severely increased (macroalbuminuria)

**Spot UPCR (urine protein:** creatinine ratio) — total proteinuria. PCR > 3500 mg/g = nephrotic range.

Urinary protein electrophoresis (UPEP) + immunofixation — myeloma (Bence-Jones).

Sulphosalicylic acid (SSA) test — detects total protein (incl. light chains; dipstick misses).

### Selectivity

**Selective proteinuria:** predominantly albumin (smaller MW) — MCD.

**Non-selective:** albumin + IgG + larger proteins — advanced glomerular disease.

Selectivity index = clearance of IgG / clearance of transferrin; < 0.2 = highly selective.

### 3. Tubular Function Tests

### Concentration / Dilution

Urine osmolality (random) — normal 50–1200 mOsm/kg.

Urine specific gravity — 1.005–1.030.

Water deprivation test — for diabetes insipidus (Uosm < 300 after deprivation).

ADH (DDAVP) challenge — central vs nephrogenic DI.

### Acidification

Urine pH (random) — 5–6.5 normal.

Ammonium chloride loading test — RTA diagnosis (urine pH should fall < 5.5 if normal).

Serum bicarbonate, anion gap, urinary anion gap.

### Tubular Reabsorption / Secretion

Fractional excretion of Na (FENa) — pre-renal vs ATN.

Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) — pre-renal if < 35% (use if on diuretics).

Fractional excretion of phosphate (FEPO₄) — TmP/GFR (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / GFR) — Fanconi syndrome (< 80%).

Glucosuria with normal serum glucose — proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi).

Aminoaciduria — Fanconi syndrome.

**Tubular markers:** NGAL, KIM-1, IL-18 (research; early AKI biomarkers).

### 4. Urinary Sediment Examination

### 5. Imaging

**Ultrasound (USG) — first-line:** size (10–14 cm normal; < 9 cm = chronic), echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, masses, Doppler (renal artery flow, RVT).

KUB X-ray — radio-opaque stones (calcium, struvite). Cystine = semi-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent.

CT (CECT, KUB) — masses, complex cysts, stones (gold standard for nephrolithiasis).

MRI / MRA — RAS, masses (avoid gadolinium if eGFR < 30 — NSF risk).

DTPA scan — split function (each kidney's contribution).

DMSA scan — cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy).

MAG-3 scan — obstruction.

Renal biopsy — definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.

### 6. Other / Specialised

Complement (C3, C4) — see Q3.

Autoantibodies — ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM.

Anti-PLA2R — membranous.

SPEP / UPEP / IFE — myeloma.

Cryoglobulins.

### Approach to Interpretation

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.353; KDIGO CKD 2012; CKD-EPI 2021 race-free.

### Indications

ESRD (eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.73 m²) or imminent ESRD.

Pre-emptive (before dialysis starts) — best survival outcomes.

Failed dialysis (HD / PD) — life expectancy + quality of life improved by transplant.

### Donor Types

### Living Donor

Living related — first-degree relatives (parent, sibling, child).

Living unrelated — spouse, friend (Indian Transplant of Human Organs Act 1994 + Rules 2014 — Authorisation Committee approval mandatory; commercial transplant illegal).

Paired exchange (kidney swap) — incompatible donor-recipient pairs swap.

**Advantages:** best outcomes (5-yr graft survival 90%), shorter waiting, scheduled, less rejection (better HLA match).

**Donor evaluation:** thorough — medical, psychological, social, ethical clearance.

### Deceased Donor (DDKT)

Brain-death donors (donation after brain death — DBD) — standard.

Circulatory death donors (DCD) — newer.

Allocation through state / national registry (NOTTO — National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation, India).

Long waiting list — Indian average wait > 5 years (severe organ shortage).

5-yr graft survival 80%.

### Recipient Pre-transplant Workup

### Comprehensive Assessment

Detailed history + examination, cause of ESRD.

**Cardiac:** ECG, echo, stress test, cardiology consult (CAD risk).

**Infectious:** HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV, CMV, EBV, TB (CXR + IGRA / Mantoux), syphilis, screening for endemic infections (malaria, dengue), dental clearance.

**Malignancy screen:** PSA, mammogram, PAP smear, colonoscopy (age-appropriate).

**Immunology:** ABO blood group, HLA typing (A, B, DR loci), HLA antibody screening (panel reactive antibody — PRA), cross-match.

**Urinary:** USG, MCU (if reflux), urodynamics if indicated.

Psychiatric and social assessment.

**Vaccinations:** pneumococcal, influenza, HBV (40 µg × 4), HZV, COVID-19 — BEFORE transplant.

### Contraindications

### Absolute

Active malignancy (< 2 yr remission usually required).

Active uncontrolled infection.

Severe cardiac disease (uncorrected).

Severe pulmonary disease.

Severe psychiatric disease with poor adherence.

Active substance abuse.

Untreated HIV with non-suppressed viral load.

Short life expectancy < 2 yr from other comorbidity.

### Relative

Age > 70 yr (case-by-case).

Severe peripheral vascular disease.

Obesity BMI > 35.

HBV / HCV (now mostly treatable — DAA).

Recurrent kidney disease risk (FSGS, MPGN, primary oxaluria).

### Surgical Procedure

Kidney placed in extraperitoneal iliac fossa (right preferred — iliac vessels superficial).

Renal artery anastomosed to external iliac (or internal iliac in living donor).

Renal vein to external iliac vein.

Ureter to bladder (Lich-Gregoir extravesical anastomosis with stent).

Native kidneys usually LEFT in place (unless symptomatic — ADPKD, infection, RCC).

Duration 2–4 h; recipient hospital stay 7–14 d.

### Immunosuppression

### Induction (at transplant)

Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R) — standard low-risk.

Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG, rabbit) — high-risk (high PRA, deceased donor, retransplant).

Methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g pulse.

### Maintenance (lifelong)

**Triple therapy:** Calcineurin inhibitor + Antiproliferative + Steroid.

**Calcineurin inhibitor:** Calcineurin inhibitor: Tacrolimus (preferred, trough 5–10 ng/ml) OR cyclosporine 100–200 ng/ml. Side effects: nephrotoxic, neurotoxic (tremor), DM, HTN, gingival hyperplasia (CsA), hirsutism (CsA), alopecia (Tac).

**Antiproliferative:** Antiproliferative: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 1–2 g/d OR mycophenolic acid (MPA). Side effects: diarrhoea, leucopenia, infection. Azathioprine alternative (cheaper India).

**Steroid:** Steroid: Prednisolone 10–20 mg/d tapered to 5 mg/d maintenance. Side effects: DM, osteoporosis, infection, weight, cushingoid, cataracts.

Alternative — mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus, everolimus) — replaces CNI in nephrotoxicity.

Belatacept — costimulation blocker; less nephrotoxic.

### Complications

### Surgical (early)

Bleeding, haematoma, lymphocoele.

Renal artery / vein thrombosis (graft loss).

Ureteric leak / obstruction.

Wound infection, dehiscence.

Delayed graft function (need post-transplant dialysis).

### Rejection

**Hyperacute:** Hyperacute: Minutes-hours; pre-formed antibodies (ABO / HLA); thrombosis; graft loss (prevent by cross-match).

Acute cellular (T-cell mediated):Acute cellular (T-cell mediated): Days-weeks. Rising Cr, oliguria, fever. Biopsy: tubulitis, lymphocyte infiltration. Treat: pulse methylpred 500 mg × 3 d → tacrolimus boost; severe: ATG.

**Acute antibody-mediated (AMR):** Acute antibody-mediated (AMR): Donor-specific antibodies. C4d on biopsy, peritubular capillaritis. Treat: plasmapheresis + IVIG + rituximab.

Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA):Chronic rejection / Interstitial fibrosis + tubular atrophy (IF/TA): Months-years. Gradual Cr rise, proteinuria. Mostly irreversible — optimise immunosuppression, manage as CKD.

Infection (commonest cause of death; from immunosuppression)

**Early (< 1 mo):** nosocomial — wound, UTI, line, surgical site.

**1–6 mo:** opportunistic — CMV (commonest viral), BK polyomavirus (nephropathy), Pneumocystis jirovecii, Aspergillus, mycobacteria.

**Late > 6 mo:** community-acquired + late opportunistic (PML, CMV reactivation).

**Prophylaxis:** cotrimoxazole (PCP) × 6 mo; valganciclovir × 3 mo (CMV mismatch); INH 9 mo (latent TB).

### Malignancy (chronic immunosuppression)

Skin cancers (SCC, BCC) — 100× general population.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD — EBV-driven).

Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

**Solid tumours:** lung, breast, prostate, cervix, GI — moderately ↑ risk.

### Metabolic

New-onset diabetes (NODAT) — tacrolimus, steroid (15–30%).

Hypertension (CNI, steroid).

Hyperlipidaemia (CNI, sirolimus, steroid).

Osteoporosis, avascular necrosis (steroid).

Hyperuricaemia, gout.

### Disease Recurrence in Graft

FSGS (30%), MPGN, IgA, lupus, primary oxaluria — variable.

### Long-term Care

Lifelong immunosuppression + adherence.

Regular monitoring — Cr, eGFR, drug levels, urine ACR.

Vaccinations (avoid live — MMR, varicella, yellow fever; OK inactivated).

Sun protection, skin cancer screening annually.

BP < 130/80, lipid control, glucose control.

Pregnancy possible after 1 yr stable function — switch MMF to AZA pre-conception.

### Outcomes (India)

**Living donor:** 5-yr graft survival 90%; deceased donor: 80%. Patient survival transplant > dialysis at 5 yr (95% vs 35%). Cost (India): initial ₹5–10 lakhs + lifelong immunosuppression ₹15–25k/month. Many state schemes and PMJAY cover transplant. Best modality but limited by organ availability.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.398; THOTA 1994 + Rules 2014; NOTTO India; KDIGO Care of Transplant 2009.

### Principles

Nutrition therapy is foundational in CKD — slows progression, controls complications (electrolyte disturbances, oedema, malnutrition, MBD), and improves quality of life. Individualised by CKD stage, modality (conservative / dialysis / transplant), and comorbidity (DM, HTN, obesity).

### Macronutrients

### Protein

**CKD G3–G5 (non-dialysis):** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (KDOQI 2020). Lower protein slows progression but risks malnutrition; do not go below 0.6 g/kg/d.

**Diabetic CKD:** 0.6–0.8 g/kg/d (lower in non-diabetic, slightly higher in DKD).

**Maintenance HD:** 1.0–1.2 g/kg/d (replace protein lost in HD).

**Peritoneal dialysis:** 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d (protein lost in dialysate).

**Post-transplant:** 1.0 g/kg/d.

Acute illness / hospitalised CKD: 1.0–1.3 g/kg/d.

50% from high biological value (animal — egg, fish, chicken).

**Indian sources:** dal, paneer, dahi, soya — moderate amounts.

### Calories

25–35 kcal/kg/d (sufficient to prevent protein catabolism).

Lower if BMI > 30; higher if BMI < 22 or muscle wasting.

Adequate carbohydrate to spare protein.

### Fat

30–35% of total calories.

Limit saturated; favour MUFA / PUFA (olive oil, fish oil, nuts in moderation).

Restrict cholesterol < 200 mg/d (atherogenic).

### Electrolytes / Minerals

### Sodium

< 5 g salt/d (= 2 g sodium); ideally < 4 g.

**Avoid:** pickles, papad, namkeen, processed foods, canned, fast food.

Cook with less salt; use spices (cumin, coriander, mint, lime).

Avoid salt substitutes (KCl — hyperK risk in CKD).

### Potassium

Restrict in CKD G4–G5 or hyperK: 2–3 g/d (50–80 mEq).

### AVOID / LIMIT (high K):

**Fruits:** banana, orange, sweet lime, citrus, kiwi, melon, mango, papaya, coconut water, dried fruits (raisin, dates, apricot).

**Vegetables:** tomato, spinach, leafy greens, potato, sweet potato, beans, drumstick, mushroom.

**Other:** salt substitutes, instant coffee, chocolate, nuts.

**ALLOWED (low K):** apple, pear, papaya (small), pineapple, grapes, watermelon (small), guava, cauliflower, cabbage, capsicum, brinjal, lauki, tinda, parwal.

DOUBLE BOIL / LEACH vegetables (peel, cut, soak in warm water 2 h, drain, boil with excess water, discard water) — reduces K by 30–50%.

### Phosphate

**Restrict in CKD G4–G5:** 800–1000 mg/d.

**AVOID:** dairy excess (milk > 250 ml/d, cheese), egg yolk excess, organ meats, nuts, seeds, whole grains (wheat bran, oats), cola drinks, processed food (phosphate additives — well-absorbed).

USE phosphate binders with meals (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum).

Refined cereals (white rice, white bread) lower phosphate than whole grain.

### Calcium

1000–1500 mg/d total (from diet + binders).

Avoid Ca-rich foods + Ca binders + Vit D simultaneously (hypercalcaemia).

### Other Minerals

Magnesium — limit if hyperMg (CKD G4–G5).

Iron — adequate (anaemia); often supplement.

Zinc — supplement if dialysis (loss).

### Fluid

**Pre-dialysis CKD:** 1.5–2 L/d unless oliguric.

**Oliguric:** previous day's urine output + 500 ml insensible.

**On HD:** 500 ml + previous day's urine output; restrict interdialytic weight gain < 5% body weight (~ 1 kg/d).

**PD:** usually liberal (continuous fluid removal).

Include ALL fluids — tea, coffee, soup, milk, fruit juice, ice cream, jelly.

### Vitamins

Water-soluble — supplement on dialysis (lost in dialysate): B1 1.5 mg, B6 5 mg, B12 1 µg, folate 1 mg, C 75 mg, niacin.

Avoid high-dose vitamin C (> 250 mg/d — oxalate nephropathy).

Vitamin D — active form (calcitriol / alfacalcidol) as needed.

AVOID vitamin A (retinol — accumulates).

### Indian Diet Practical Tips

Rice over chapatti for low phosphate (preferred in South India).

Roti / chapati from refined flour preferred over whole wheat.

Egg WHITE (low phosphate, good protein).

**Pulses (dal):** boil in excess water, discard, then cook — reduces K, P.

Limit dahi to 1 small bowl/d (75 g).

Limit fruits to 1 small portion of low-K fruits.

Avoid namkeen, biscuits, instant noodles, papad, pickle, chutney.

**Beverages:** lime water (no salt), weak tea, coconut water AVOID, packaged juice AVOID.

**Eating out:** avoid; if must, choose plain rice + vegetable curry.

### Special Situations

### Diabetic CKD

Restrict refined carbs (white rice, sugar).

Whole grains tolerable in earlier CKD; restrict in advanced (phosphate).

Time meals with insulin/SGLT2i/GLP-1.

### Nephrotic Syndrome

Protein 0.8 g/kg/d (NOT high — accelerates loss).

Strict low salt (oedema).

Low cholesterol, low fat.

Adequate calories.

### Renal Stones (prevention)

High fluid > 2.5 L/d.

Low salt < 5 g/d.

Adequate dietary calcium (NOT supplemental).

Low oxalate (avoid spinach, beetroot, tea, chocolate, nuts, soy, rhubarb) — Ca oxalate stones.

Low purine (uric acid stones).

Low animal protein (Ca oxalate, uric acid).

Citrate (lemon, orange — for non-CKD; risk vs benefit in CKD).

### Monitoring

Weight (dry weight in dialysis).

Serum albumin (> 3.5 — good nutrition), pre-albumin.

Electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, phosphate), Mg.

BP, oedema.

Anthropometry (MUAC, BMI).

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA — gold standard for CKD nutrition).

Dietitian review every 3–6 months.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.10 p.408; KDOQI Nutrition CKD 2020; ISN Nutrition; ISN India Renal Diet guidelines.

GENERAL MEDICINE|375.note:
### Indications

**Absolute:** Apnoea or impending respiratory arrest.

**Oxygenation failure:** Failure of oxygenation – severe Type 1 RF; PaO₂ <60 on FiO₂>0.6 / P/F ratio <200.

**Ventilatory failure:** Type 2 RF with pH <7.25; CO₂ narcosis; failed NIV.

**Airway protection:** GCS ≤8, brainstem injury, intracranial hypertension, status epilepticus.

**Circulatory failure:** Shock, post-arrest, sepsis with respiratory exhaustion.

**Neuromuscular:** GBS with decreasing VC (<15 mL/kg), MG crisis, MND with respiratory muscle failure.

Chest-wall – flail chest, severe burns.

Peri-operative – major surgery, anaesthesia.

Therapeutic hyperventilation in raised ICP (controlled, short-term).

### Modes

Volume-controlled (VCV), pressure-controlled (PCV), assist-control (AC), SIMV (synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation), pressure support, PEEP, BiPAP, CPAP.

Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS: tidal volume 6 mL/kg ideal body weight, plateau pressure <30 cm H₂O, permissive hypercapnia.

### Complications

### Endotracheal tube–related:

Failed/oesophageal intubation, displacement, blocked tube, cuff leak, tracheal stenosis, subglottic injury, vocal-cord damage, tracheomalacia, tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

### Ventilator-induced:

Barotrauma – pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, surgical emphysema.

Volutrauma – over-distension injury.

Atelectrauma – cyclic alveolar collapse and re-opening.

Biotrauma – release of inflammatory mediators.

Oxygen toxicity (prolonged FiO₂>0.6).

### Infections:

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) – 10–30% of mechanically ventilated patients.

Sinusitis (nasal intubation).

### Haemodynamic:

Hypotension from positive intrathoracic pressure (reduced venous return), especially with high PEEP.

### Other:

ICU-acquired weakness, deconditioning, delirium.

DVT, stress ulcer.

Critical illness polyneuropathy / myopathy.

Failure to wean.

### Weaning

Daily spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) with pressure support / T-piece for 30 min when underlying cause improving, haemodynamic stable, adequate oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂ >200, PEEP ≤5–8), acceptable secretions, and patient cooperative.

Extubate if SBT tolerated; reintubate if respiratory distress, haemodynamic instability, hypoxia, hypercapnia, or altered mental status.

GENERAL MEDICINE|376.note:
### Combined Notes (5 topics)

### Definition

Pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after hospital admission, not incubating at admission. VAP = HAP developing ≥48 h after endotracheal intubation.

### Common Organisms

Gram-negative bacilli (commonest): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL/CRE), E. coli, Enterobacter.

**Gram-positive:** Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

**Less common:** Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae (early HAP <5 d).

**Fungi:** Aspergillus, Candida (especially in immunocompromised).

### Risk Factors for MDR Pathogens

Antibiotic therapy in previous 90 d, ≥5 days hospital stay before HAP, septic shock at presentation, ARDS, acute renal replacement before HAP, immunosuppression, ICU stay, chronic dialysis, prior MDR colonisation.

### Clinical Features

New/progressive infiltrate on CXR + 2 of: fever (>38°C) or hypothermia (<36°C), leukocytosis (>10,000) or leukopenia (<4,000), purulent secretions.

### Investigations

CXR (new infiltrate), CBC, CRP, procalcitonin (helps de-escalate), ABG.

Lower-respiratory cultures – endotracheal aspirate, BAL, protected specimen brush (before starting antibiotics where possible).

Blood cultures × 2, urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella).

Consider HIV/COVID/influenza testing.

Management (ICMR antibiotic policy 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2016)

### Empirical antibiotic therapy:

Early HAP (<5 d), no MDR risk: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Late HAP (≥5 d) or MDR risk: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime OR meropenem; cover MRSA with vancomycin or linezolid if local prevalence high.

Suspected Pseudomonas (structural lung disease, prior antibiotics, ICU): dual antipseudomonal cover until cultures back – β-lactam (pip-tazo/cefepime/meropenem) + aminoglycoside (amikacin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).

De-escalate based on culture and sensitivity.

**Duration:** 7 days for most HAP/VAP; longer for non-fermenting GNB (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) and immunocompromised. Use clinical response + procalcitonin to guide stopping.

### Supportive:

O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥92%; NIV/HFNC; mechanical ventilation if indicated.

IV fluids cautiously; vasopressors if septic shock.

VTE prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, enteral nutrition, physiotherapy, daily sedation hold and spontaneous-breathing trial in ventilated patients.

### Prevention:

Hand hygiene, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral chlorhexidine in ICU, subglottic suction ETT, daily review of intubation need, selective digestive decontamination in selected ICUs.

Fig 4. Pneumonia – CAP vs HAP empirical management algorithm.

### Causative viruses

Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B – most common viral pneumonia in adults; complicated by bacterial superinfection.

SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) – bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities; ARDS in severe cases.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – children <2 y; elderly and immunocompromised.

Parainfluenza virus 1–4.

Adenovirus.

Human metapneumovirus.

Rhinovirus (mostly upper RTI but can cause LRTI in elderly/immunocompromised).

Varicella-zoster (severe primary varicella in adults, especially pregnant, smokers).

Measles (in unimmunised; ARDS, Hecht's giant-cell pneumonia).

Hantavirus (rare; hantavirus pulmonary syndrome).

CMV, HSV (especially in immunocompromised).

### Diagnosis

Multiplex PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) – influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 panel.

Rapid antigen tests (influenza, COVID).

Serology for VZV, measles, hantavirus.

Bronchoalveolar lavage for cytology + PCR in severe/immunocompromised.

### Treatment

**Influenza:** oseltamivir 75 mg BD × 5 days within 48 h.

**COVID-19:** supportive O₂/NIV; remdesivir, dexamethasone 6 mg/d × 10 days if O₂-requiring; tocilizumab/baricitinib for severe.

**RSV:** supportive; nirsevimab/palivizumab prophylaxis in high-risk infants.

**VZV pneumonia:** IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h.

**Measles pneumonia:** vitamin A, supportive.

**CMV:** ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

Empirical antibiotic cover for bacterial superinfection in severe viral pneumonia.

### Classification

**By setting:** Community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated (VAP), aspiration, immunocompromised host.

**By pattern:** Lobar (anatomical lobe), bronchopneumonia (patchy multi-lobar), interstitial, necrotising/abscess.

**By organism:** Bacterial (typical and atypical), viral, fungal, parasitic.

### Lobar pneumonia

**Etiology:** Affects an entire lobe; classic of S. pneumoniae (also Klebsiella – upper-lobe, 'bulging fissure' sign, Friedländer's pneumonia).

**Pathology:** Four stages – Congestion (day 1), Red hepatisation (days 2–3), Grey hepatisation (days 4–6), Resolution (days 7+).

**C/F:** Sudden fever with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with rusty sputum, herpes labialis. Signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing, vocal resonance increased, fine crackles).

**Mx:** IV ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± macrolide, escalate based on CURB-65; oxygen, supportive.

### Atypical pneumonia

**Organisms:** Mycoplasma pneumoniae (young adults, cold agglutinin, AIHA, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson), Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (bird exposure – psittacosis), Legionella pneumophila (water-source, hyponatraemia, GI symptoms, urinary antigen), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever – farm animals).

**C/F:** Insidious onset – dry cough, headache, myalgia, low-grade fever, GI symptoms; CXR worse than examination findings ('walking pneumonia').

**Mx:** Macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline, fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for Legionella.

### Viral pneumonia

Influenza A/B (oseltamivir within 48 h), SARS-CoV-2 (remdesivir, dexamethasone), RSV (supportive), parainfluenza, adenovirus, VZV (acyclovir), measles, hMPV.

Diffuse bilateral interstitial / ground-glass infiltrates on CT.

Bacterial superinfection common; cover empirically if severe.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae – young adults; bullous myringitis, cold agglutinin AIHA, erythema multiforme.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (Chlamydophila pneumoniae) – pharyngitis, long-course macrolide.

Chlamydia psittaci (Chlamydophila psittaci) – birds/poultry exposure (psittacosis).

Legionella pneumophila – water systems (air-conditioning, hotel, fountains); hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes, GI symptoms; urinary antigen for L. pneumophila serogroup 1.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) – farm animals (sheep, cattle), abattoir workers; serology.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in any subacute respiratory illness in India.

Viral pneumonias (influenza, COVID, RSV, adenovirus, hMPV) – often classified separately but share atypical clinical features.

**Empirical therapy:** macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD) or doxycycline 100 mg BD; fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg OD) for Legionella.

### Definition

Pneumonia acquired outside healthcare settings (or within first 48 h of admission). Major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.

### Etiology

### Typical bacterial:

Streptococcus pneumoniae – the leading cause (50–60%); lobar pneumonia, rusty sputum.

Haemophilus influenzae (especially COPD).

Moraxella catarrhalis (COPD).

Staphylococcus aureus – post-influenza, IV drug users, necrotising.

Klebsiella pneumoniae – alcoholics, diabetics; currant-jelly sputum, bulging fissure sign, upper-lobe.

### Atypical:

Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii.

### Viral:

Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, hMPV, adenovirus.

### Special host groups:

Alcoholics – Klebsiella, anaerobes, S. pneumoniae, TB.

Diabetics – Klebsiella, S. aureus, fungi (mucormycosis).

HIV – Pneumocystis jirovecii, TB, fungal.

Aspiration – oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus).

Indian context – TB always differential.

### Clinical features

Sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, rusty/blood-stained sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea.

**Atypical pneumonia:** dry cough, headache, myalgia, GI upset, subacute course.

**Signs of consolidation:** tachypnoea, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, fine crackles.

Sepsis features – tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness.

### Severity (CURB-65)

C – Confusion (AMT ≤8 or new disorientation).

U – Urea > 7 mmol/L (>20 mg/dL).

R – Respiratory rate ≥ 30.

B – BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic.

65 – Age ≥65 years.

**0–1:** home; 2: ward; 3–5: ICU (consider).

Empirical therapy (ICMR 2022 + IDSA/ATS 2019)

**Outpatient:** amoxicillin 1 g TDS 5–7 d (± macrolide if atypical suspected) or doxycycline.

**Ward (CURB-65 = 2):** IV amoxicillin-clavulanate OR ceftriaxone + macrolide.

**ICU (CURB-65 ≥3):** IV ceftriaxone + macrolide OR levofloxacin; add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; add antipseudomonal cover if structural lung disease.

De-escalate based on cultures.

**Supportive:** O₂, fluids, antipyretic, VTE prophylaxis.

GENERAL MEDICINE|377.note:
### Definition

Bulbous enlargement of distal phalanges with increased curvature of the nail – a sign of underlying systemic disease (rarely congenital).

Grades / stages (Lovibond)

**Stage 1:** increased fluctuation of nail bed ('boggy', fluctuant), softening of nail-bed.

**Stage 2:** loss of normal Lovibond angle (>180°) – nail-bed angle between nail and proximal nail-fold flattens or becomes obtuse. Schamroth's window (formed by opposing dorsal aspects of distal phalanges of corresponding fingers of the two hands) is obliterated.

**Stage 3:** bulbous swelling and increased curvature of nail with parrot-beak/'drumstick' appearance.

**Stage 4:** hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) – periostitis, painful swelling of wrists, ankles, knees; subperiosteal new bone formation on X-ray.

### Causes

### Pulmonary (commonest):

Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially adenocarcinoma, squamous; small-cell less commonly).

Mesothelioma.

Bronchiectasis.

Lung abscess.

Empyema.

Cystic fibrosis.

Pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

Pulmonary AV malformation.

Asbestosis.

### Cardiac:

Cyanotic congenital heart disease (Tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger).

Subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Atrial myxoma.

### Gastrointestinal:

Cirrhosis (especially with hepatopulmonary syndrome).

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, UC).

Coeliac disease.

GI lymphoma.

Tropical sprue.

### Other:

Thyroid acropachy (Graves' disease).

Familial / congenital (autosomal dominant) – pachydermoperiostosis.

Unilateral – aortic aneurysm, axillary tumour, Pancoast tumour.

Pseudoclubbing – hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis.

**(Note:** COPD per se does NOT cause clubbing – its presence in COPD should prompt a search for lung cancer or another cause.)

GENERAL MEDICINE|379.note:
### Combined Notes (3 topics)

Nutritional assessment – methods

**A:** Anthropometry

Weight, height, BMI (kg/m²). Asian-Indian cut-offs (WHO Asia): underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–22.9; overweight 23–24.9; obese ≥25; (general WHO: 25/30).

Waist circumference (Asian male ≥90 cm, female ≥80 cm = abdominal obesity).

Waist–hip ratio (>0.9 M / >0.85 F = abnormal).

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC; <23 cm = malnourished).

Triceps skinfold thickness, calf circumference (sarcopenia).

**B:** Biochemical (Lab)

Serum albumin (<3.5 g/dL = malnutrition; long half-life 20 d).

Pre-albumin / transthyretin (half-life 2 d – more sensitive).

Total lymphocyte count (<1500 = malnutrition).

Haemoglobin, transferrin, retinol-binding protein.

**Specific deficiencies:** vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D, iron, zinc, magnesium.

**C:** Clinical examination

General – muscle wasting (temporal, thenar), loose skin, oedema (kwashiorkor), pallor.

Hair – sparse, depigmented, easily pluckable (kwashiorkor).

Skin – dermatitis, hyperpigmentation (pellagra), petechiae (scurvy), xerosis.

Eyes – Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia, night blindness (vitamin A).

Mouth – angular stomatitis, glossitis (riboflavin, B12), bleeding gums (vitamin C), dental caries.

Nails – koilonychia (iron), pale, brittle.

Neuro – peripheral neuropathy (B1, B6, B12), beriberi (B1), subacute combined degeneration (B12).

Skeletal – rickets/osteomalacia (vitamin D), bowing.

**D:** Dietary assessment

24-h dietary recall.

3-day food diary.

Food-frequency questionnaire.

Compare to recommended dietary allowance (RDA – ICMR for Indians).

### Composite tools:

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA) – history (weight loss, intake, GI symptoms, functional capacity) + physical exam → A (well), B (moderate malnutrition), C (severe malnutrition).

Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) – elderly.

Nutrition Risk Screening (NRS-2002) – hospitalised adults.

GLIM criteria (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) – phenotypic (weight loss, low BMI, low muscle mass) + etiological (reduced intake/assimilation, inflammation).

Hazards of obesity (medical complications)

### Cardiovascular:

Hypertension, IHD, MI, heart failure (HFpEF), atrial fibrillation, stroke, VTE, varicose veins.

### Metabolic:

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (3-fold risk), insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidaemia (↑LDL, ↑TG, ↓HDL), hyperuricaemia and gout.

### Respiratory:

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), restrictive lung disease, asthma worsening.

### Hepatic:

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) → steatohepatitis (NASH) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma; cholelithiasis.

### Endocrine / reproductive:

PCOS, infertility (anovulation), male hypogonadism, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia.

### Musculoskeletal:

Osteoarthritis (knees, hips), back pain, gout.

### Cancers:

Colon, oesophageal (adeno), breast (post-menopausal), endometrial, ovarian, pancreatic, renal, liver, gall-bladder.

### Other:

Depression, social stigma, surgical risk, intertrigo, lymphoedema, stress incontinence, idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

(See Q2 above for the comprehensive list of obesity hazards. The key categories are repeated here for completeness, with a brief note on management.)

### Complications by system

**Cardiovascular:** HTN, IHD, HF, AF, stroke, VTE.

**Metabolic:** T2DM, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome, gout.

**Respiratory:** OSA, OHS, restrictive lung disease.

**Hepatic / GI:** NAFLD → NASH → cirrhosis, GERD, gallstones.

**Endocrine / reproductive:** PCOS, infertility, hypogonadism, gestational DM.

**Musculoskeletal:** OA (knees, hips), low back pain.

**Cancers:** colon, breast (post-menopausal), endometrial, oesophageal adeno, renal, pancreatic, hepatocellular, GB.

**Psychosocial:** depression, anxiety, social stigma, low quality of life.

**Surgical:** poor wound healing, anaesthetic risk, VTE.

**Skin:** acanthosis nigricans, intertrigo, hidradenitis.

Management of obesity (brief)

**Lifestyle:** ICMR-recommended balanced diet (500 kcal deficit/day), 150 min/wk moderate aerobic + resistance training, behavioural therapy.

Pharmacotherapy (BMI ≥27 with comorbidity or ≥30 alone): orlistat 120 mg TDS; liraglutide 3 mg SC daily; semaglutide (Wegovy) 2.4 mg SC weekly; tirzepatide 5–15 mg SC weekly; naltrexone-bupropion; phentermine-topiramate.

Bariatric surgery (BMI ≥35 with comorbidity or ≥40): sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, OAGB; Indian indication BMI ≥32.5 with comorbidity.

(See Q2 and Q3 for comprehensive list of obesity hazards. The key obesity-related medical disorders are organised here by system.)

### Cardiovascular

Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure with preserved EF, atrial fibrillation, ventricular hypertrophy, stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), VTE, varicose veins.

### Metabolic

Type 2 diabetes mellitus and pre-diabetes.

**Metabolic syndrome (≥3 of:** abdominal obesity, ↑TG, ↓HDL, ↑BP, ↑FPG).

Dyslipidaemia.

Hyperuricaemia and gout.

Hepatic – NAFLD, NASH, cirrhosis, HCC.

### Endocrine / reproductive

PCOS, anovulatory infertility.

Hypogonadism in males.

Gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia.

Increased risk of macrosomia, congenital anomalies in offspring.

### Respiratory

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA).

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS – Pickwickian).

Restrictive lung function, exertional dyspnoea.

Worsening asthma control.

### Cancers

Endometrial, breast (post-menopausal), colorectal, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, renal cell, pancreatic, hepatocellular, gall-bladder, ovarian, thyroid (papillary), multiple myeloma.

### Musculoskeletal

Osteoarthritis (knees, hips, hands).

Low-back pain.

Gout.

### GI / hepatobiliary

GERD, hiatal hernia.

Cholelithiasis.

NAFLD / NASH / cirrhosis / HCC.

Pancreatitis.

### Renal / urogenital

CKD, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (obesity-related).

Stress urinary incontinence.

Erectile dysfunction.

### Skin

Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance marker), intertrigo, hidradenitis suppurativa, stretch marks, lymphoedema, cellulitis.

### Neurological / psychiatric

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Depression, anxiety, eating disorders, low quality of life, stigma, social isolation.

Cognitive impairment, dementia (long-term).

### Surgical / perioperative

Increased anaesthetic risk, difficult intubation, prolonged recovery, wound infection, VTE.

GENERAL MEDICINE|380.note:
### Definition

Chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis) affecting skin, peripheral nerves, mucous membranes, eyes, testes, and reticulo-endothelial system. India carries ~60% of global new case burden; leprosy is a notifiable disease (NLEP).

### Classification (WHO operational)

Paucibacillary (PB) – 1–5 skin lesions, smear-negative.

Multibacillary (MB) – >5 lesions or smear-positive.

Single skin lesion – ROM regimen (Rifampicin + Ofloxacin + Minocycline single dose) – discontinued by NLEP 2022 in favour of standard MDT.

### Multi-Drug Therapy (NLEP / WHO 2018)

MB regimen (>5 lesions or smear+): 12 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily (self-administered).

Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered).

PB regimen (1–5 lesions, smear-negative): 6 months

Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised).

Clofazimine added since 2018 — 300 mg monthly + 50 mg daily.

Dapsone 100 mg daily.

### Paediatric (10–14 yrs)

Rifampicin 450 mg monthly; Clofazimine 150 mg monthly + 50 mg alternate day; Dapsone 50 mg daily.

Children <10 yrs / <40 kg – body-weight-based dosing.

### Treatment of reactions

Type 1 (reversal reaction – upgrade or downgrade)

Continue MDT.

Prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, taper over 12–20 weeks; treat neuritis aggressively (preserve nerve function).

Rest, splinting, analgesia.

Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL)

Continue MDT.

**Mild:** NSAIDs.

**Moderate-severe:** Prednisolone 40 mg/day, taper over 8–12 weeks.

Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (refractory ENL; contraindicated in women of childbearing age – teratogenic).

Clofazimine — high dose 300 mg/day × 12 weeks then taper.

Supportive care and rehabilitation

Education on disease, transmission, course.

Wound care, footwear, protective gloves to prevent injuries to insensate areas.

Physiotherapy, splinting for clawed hands, dropped foot.

Reconstructive surgery for established deformities (lagophthalmos, claw hand, foot drop, plantar ulcer).

Eye care – artificial tears, protective glasses, surgery for lagophthalmos.

Social rehabilitation – combating stigma, vocational training, monthly disability allowance for permanent disability ≥40% under NLEP.

Contact tracing and single-dose rifampicin chemoprophylaxis (SDR-PEP – NLEP 2017).

GENERAL MEDICINE|382.note:
### Definition

OCD is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterised by intrusive, unwanted, recurrent thoughts, images or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) performed to neutralise distress, that are time-consuming (>1 hour/day) or cause marked distress / functional impairment. Reclassified in DSM-5 into 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders' (separate from anxiety disorders).

### Epidemiology

Lifetime prevalence ~2–3%; current ~1%.

M=F overall; childhood onset M>F, adult onset F>M.

**Bimodal onset:** 8–12 years and late adolescence / early adulthood (mean ~20 y).

Heritability ~50%; first-degree relative risk 4×.

High comorbidity with depression (40–60%), anxiety, tic disorders / Tourette's, ADHD, autism spectrum, eating disorders.

### Etiology

Genetic — polygenic (SLITRK1, glutamate genes); familial clustering.

Neurochemical — serotonergic dysregulation (basis for high-dose SSRI efficacy); glutamatergic hyperactivity in cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop.

Neuroanatomic — hyperactivity in orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, caudate; CSTC circuit dysfunction.

PANDAS / PANS — sudden-onset OCD with tics in children after streptococcal / autoimmune trigger.

Psychological — behavioural model: obsession → anxiety → compulsion → relief (negative reinforcement). Cognitive model: thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

### Clinical features

Obsessions — common themes

Contamination — germs, dirt, body fluids.

Doubts — gas left on, door unlocked, hit someone while driving.

Symmetry / ordering — things must be 'just right'.

Aggressive / sexual / blasphemous intrusive thoughts (ego-dystonic — patient horrified).

Religious / scrupulosity.

Hoarding (now a separate DSM-5 disorder but historically grouped).

Compulsions — common forms

Washing / cleaning (paired with contamination obsessions).

Checking (paired with doubts).

Counting, repeating, ordering / arranging.

Mental compulsions — silent prayer, counting in head, neutralising thoughts.

Reassurance-seeking.

Key clinical features (boards-style)

Recognised by the patient as own (insight may be variable — 'good/fair/poor/absent insight' specifier in DSM-5).

Ego-dystonic — distressing, unwanted.

Resisted (at least initially).

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) or marked distress / impairment.

**Average delay to treatment:** 7–10 years (shame, lack of awareness).

### DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria

Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both.

Time-consuming (>1 h/d) OR clinically significant distress / impairment.

Not due to substance / medical condition.

Not better explained by another mental disorder.

**Specify:** with good/fair insight, with poor insight, with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related (current/past).

### OCD spectrum (DSM-5 'Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders')

Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with perceived defect in appearance.

Hoarding disorder.

Trichotillomania (hair-pulling).

Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder.

### Severity assessment

Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) — 10-item, clinician-rated; gold standard. 0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme.

Children's Y-BOCS (CY-BOCS) for paediatric.

Floyd-Padua, Maudsley scales — self-report alternatives.

### Differential diagnosis

### Investigations

**Bedside:** Y-BOCS / CY-BOCS; PHQ-9, GAD-7 for comorbidity.

**Routine:** rule out organic — CBC, TSH, ASO titre (PANDAS in children), B12.

MRI brain if late onset, focal signs, or atypical presentation.

**Pre-treatment baseline:** ECG (QTc) if planning high-dose SSRI / clomipramine; LFT for clomipramine.

### Management

Figure 5. OCD management — Y-BOCS severity triage, high-dose SSRI + ERP, ladder to clomipramine, antipsychotic augmentation and DBS.

### First-line — pharmacotherapy

SSRIs — must use HIGH dose, allow LONG trial: Fluoxetine 40–80 mg/d, sertraline 150–200 mg/d, paroxetine 40–60 mg/d, fluvoxamine 200–300 mg/d, escitalopram 20–40 mg/d, citalopram 40 mg max. Start at standard dose, titrate every 2 wk; allow 10–12 wk trial at maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure.

### First-line — psychotherapy

CBT with ERP (Exposure & Response Prevention): Gold standard; 13–20 sessions. Patient exposed in hierarchy to feared stimulus while being prevented from performing compulsion → habituation + extinction of anxiety. Equally effective as SSRI; combination superior to either alone in moderate–severe.

Cognitive therapy — challenge thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility, intolerance of uncertainty.

Inadequate response after 10–12 wk

Step 1 — switch SSRI (different agent at maximum dose × 10–12 wk).

Step 2 — clomipramine (TCA, potent serotonergic) 100–250 mg/d. Highly effective but ECG monitoring (QTc, AV block), sedation, anticholinergic, weight gain, sexual SE, seizure risk; AVOID combining with SSRI without specialist (serotonin syndrome). Often most effective single agent.

Step 3 — augmentation with atypical antipsychotic: risperidone 0.5–3 mg/d, aripiprazole 5–15 mg/d, low-dose haloperidol (esp. with comorbid tics).

Step 4 — intensive ERP / residential programme; combine SSRI + clomipramine (specialist + serial ECG).

Severe refractory OCD (failed ≥3 SSRIs + clomipramine + augmentation + ERP)

Repetitive TMS (rTMS) over orbitofrontal cortex / supplementary motor area.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of ventral capsule / ventral striatum or subthalamic nucleus — FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption.

Ablative neurosurgery (anterior capsulotomy, cingulotomy) — last resort, specialist centres only.

Trial of glutamate modulators (memantine, riluzole, N-acetylcysteine, lamotrigine, ketamine) — experimental.

### Special situations

Paediatric OCD — sertraline / fluoxetine / fluvoxamine licensed; CBT-ERP first line for mild-moderate; combine for severe.

PANDAS / PANS — antibiotics (penicillin, azithromycin); IVIG / plasmapheresis in severe.

Pregnancy — CBT preferred; sertraline / fluoxetine if pharmacotherapy essential.

### Duration

Maintain effective drug ≥1–2 years after response; relapse rate ~50% on stopping. Many patients need lifelong treatment.

Gradual taper over months; monitor for return of symptoms.

### Complications

Functional impairment — work, education, relationships, self-care.

Comorbid depression (40–60%), suicide risk elevated.

Substance abuse — self-medication.

Dermatological — chronic hand-washing → eczema, fissures.

Financial — checking compulsions, hoarding effects.

### Prognosis

Chronic fluctuating course; ~10–20% recover completely, ~50% partial response, ~30% chronic.

**Better prognosis:** shorter duration before treatment, good insight, no comorbidity, family support.

**Worse:** early onset, severe symptoms, hoarding subtype, comorbid tics / autism, poor insight, comorbid depression.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for OCD; NICE-CG31; APA Practice Guideline 2007 (with updates); WFSBP 2008/2012; DSM-5; ICD-11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|383.note:
### Definition

Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental disorder characterised by disturbances of thought, perception, affect, volition and social functioning, in a setting of clear consciousness and intact intellect. It is the prototype primary psychotic disorder.

### Epidemiology

**Lifetime prevalence:** ~1% worldwide; M=F.

**Peak onset:** males 15–25 y, females 25–35 y; rare onset <10 y or >50 y.

Heritability ~80%; MZ twin concordance ~50%, sibling risk ~10%, child of one parent ~13%, both parents ~46%.

Higher in lower socio-economic strata (social-drift hypothesis), urban residents, migrants, and winter/spring births.

### Etiology (multifactorial)

**Genetic:** polygenic — DISC1, NRG1, COMT, DRD2, ZNF804A; 22q11.2 deletion.

**Neurodevelopmental:** maternal infection (influenza, toxoplasma) in 2nd trimester, obstetric complications, perinatal hypoxia, advanced paternal age.

**Neurochemical:** mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (positive sx); mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity (negative sx); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin (5-HT2A) dysregulation.

**Neuroanatomic:** ventricular enlargement, ↓ hippocampal & temporal volumes, ↓ prefrontal grey matter.

**Psychosocial:** high expressed emotion in family, urban upbringing, cannabis use in adolescence (dose-related, ↑ risk 2–6 fold).

Pathophysiology — dopamine hypothesis (revised)

Mesolimbic pathway hyperactivity → positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations).

Mesocortical hypoactivity → negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.

Nigrostriatal blockade by typical antipsychotics → extrapyramidal side effects.

Tuberoinfundibular blockade → hyperprolactinaemia.

**Atypicals:** combined D2 + 5-HT2A antagonism — less EPS, better negative-symptom coverage.

Clinical features (Schneider's first-rank symptoms — Kurt Schneider 1959)

Audible thoughts (thought echo) — voice repeats thoughts aloud.

Voices arguing / discussing — third-person auditory hallucinations.

Voices commenting on actions (running commentary).

Thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting.

Made affect, made impulse, made volition (passivity phenomena).

Somatic passivity (bodily sensations imposed by outside force).

Delusional perception — normal perception with bizarre delusional meaning.

### Positive symptoms

Hallucinations — auditory most common (~70%), then visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory.

Delusions — persecutory (most common), referential, grandiose, religious, somatic, bizarre.

Formal thought disorder — loosening of associations, neologisms, word salad, tangentiality, derailment.

Disorganised behaviour — bizarre dress, posturing, agitation.

Catatonia — stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia/echopraxia.

Negative symptoms (the '5 A's')

Affective flattening — restricted emotional expression.

Alogia — poverty of speech/content.

Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure.

Avolition — loss of motivation/goal-directed behaviour.

Asociality — social withdrawal.

### Cognitive symptoms

Deficits in attention, working memory, executive function, processing speed.

Often pre-morbid and major determinant of long-term functional outcome.

ICD-11 subtypes (subtype-based classification removed in DSM-5 but still asked in Indian exams)

Paranoid — predominant delusions and hallucinations (commonest).

Hebephrenic / disorganised — disorganised behaviour, inappropriate affect, thought disorder; early onset, poor prognosis.

Catatonic — motor abnormalities predominate.

Simple — gradual negative-symptom development without positive symptoms.

Residual — past positive symptoms, current chronic negative symptoms.

Undifferentiated — does not fit any category.

### Diagnostic criteria

### DSM-5 schizophrenia

**A. Active-phase symptoms:** ≥2 of: (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganised speech, (4) grossly disorganised / catatonic behaviour, (5) negative symptoms. ≥1 must be (1), (2), or (3). Present ≥1 month.

B. Social/occupational dysfunction: Marked impairment in work, interpersonal relations or self-care.

**C. Duration:** Continuous signs ≥6 months (active + prodromal ± residual).

**D. Exclusions:** Schizoaffective + mood disorder with psychotic features excluded; substance / general medical condition excluded.

### ICD-10 schizophrenia (F20)

≥1 'first-rank' (a–d) OR ≥2 'second-rank' (e–h) for ≥1 month:

(a) Thought echo, insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.

(b) Delusions of control, influence or passivity; delusional perception.

(c) 3rd-person auditory hallucinations: voices arguing/discussing or running commentary.

(d) Persistent bizarre delusions (culturally inappropriate).

(e) Persistent hallucinations in any modality with delusions / overvalued ideas.

(f) Breaks / interpolations in train of thought — neologisms, incoherence.

(g) Catatonic behaviour.

(h) Negative symptoms — apathy, paucity of speech, blunted affect.

Differential diagnosis (must exclude)

Investigations (mainly to exclude organic / metabolic causes)

**Bedside:** detailed MSE; cognitive screen (MMSE / MoCA); risk assessment (suicide, homicide, vulnerability).

**Routine:** CBC, FBS, LFT, RFT, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, calcium.

**Infective:** VDRL, HIV serology; CSF if encephalitis suspected.

**Toxicology:** urine drug screen — cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, LSD.

**Imaging:** MRI brain — if first episode, late onset, focal neurological signs, treatment resistance, or atypical course.

**EEG:** if seizures or temporal-lobe epilepsy suspected.

Autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti-NMDA-R) if subacute psychosis with neurological signs.

**Baseline pre-antipsychotic:** ECG (QTc), weight/BMI/waist, fasting lipids, fasting glucose/HbA1c, LFT, prolactin.

### Management

Figure 1. Schizophrenia management — from DSM-5/ICD-10 diagnosis through atypical antipsychotic first-line to clozapine for treatment-resistant disease.

### Acute episode

Ensure safety — assess suicidality, aggression, self-neglect; admit if needed (voluntary / under MHCA 2017).

Address concurrent substance use, malnutrition, infection.

**For agitation:** lorazepam 2–4 mg IM / olanzapine 10 mg IM / haloperidol 5–10 mg IM ± promethazine 25–50 mg IM (rapid tranquillisation per NIMHANS protocol). Avoid IM olanzapine + IM lorazepam together (hypotension, respiratory depression).

### Pharmacotherapy

**First-line:** Atypical (2nd-gen) antipsychotic — start low, titrate weekly to therapeutic range. Risperidone 2–6 mg/d, olanzapine 10–20 mg/d, aripiprazole 10–30 mg/d, quetiapine 300–600 mg/d, ziprasidone 80–160 mg/d, amisulpride 400–800 mg/d. Continue at therapeutic dose ≥4–6 wk before judging response.

**Inadequate response:** Try a 2nd atypical (different agent) or a typical (haloperidol 5–15 mg/d, trifluoperazine 5–20 mg/d, chlorpromazine 300–800 mg/d).

Treatment-resistant (failed ≥2 antipsychotics, ≥6 wk, adequate dose): CLOZAPINE — 12.5 mg → titrate to 300–450 mg/d (max 900 mg). Most effective drug for refractory disease (CATIE, CUtLASS-2). Mandatory monitoring: CBC weekly × 18 wk, then fortnightly to 1 yr, then monthly. Stop if WBC <3,000 or ANC <1,500. Other AEs: myocarditis (esp. 1st month), sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures (dose-related), constipation/ileus, weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia.

Long-acting injectables (LAIs) — for poor adherence: Risperidone LAI 25–50 mg IM q2wk; paliperidone palmitate IM monthly or 3-monthly; aripiprazole LAI monthly; haloperidol decanoate 50–200 mg IM monthly; fluphenazine decanoate 12.5–50 mg IM monthly.

Augmentation in clozapine-resistant: Add ECT, second antipsychotic (amisulpride / aripiprazole), or mood stabiliser (lithium / valproate).

Duration of antipsychotic treatment

**First episode:** continue ≥1–2 years after full remission, then taper slowly.

**Recurrent / multi-episode:** ≥5 years; many patients need lifelong therapy.

Abrupt discontinuation → 80% relapse within 2 years.

Psychosocial interventions (essential — not optional)

Psychoeducation — patient and family; reduces high expressed emotion.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for psychosis (CBT-p) — reduces residual positive symptoms.

Family therapy — reduces relapse.
