Supported employment / Individual Placement & Support (IPS).

Social skills training, assertive community treatment (ACT) for severe persistent disease.

Cognitive remediation for cognitive symptoms.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) — indications

Catatonia (response in 80–90%).

Severe suicidality / homicidality.

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (clozapine augmentation).

Severe positive symptoms not responding to ≥6 wk of antipsychotic.

6–12 sessions, 2–3 times per week; modified (anaesthesia + suxamethonium).

Antipsychotic side effects (sub-question — Boloor A372)

Typical (1st-generation) — high-potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine)

**Extrapyramidal:** acute dystonia (hours–days; oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonus → IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg or promethazine 25–50 mg), parkinsonism (days–weeks; bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor → anticholinergic e.g. trihexyphenidyl 2–10 mg/d), akathisia (motor restlessness → propranolol 30–80 mg/d or BZD), tardive dyskinesia (months–years; orobuccolingual choreoathetosis → switch to clozapine, valbenazine or tetrabenazine).

Hyperprolactinaemia → amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, ↓ libido, osteoporosis (esp. risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride).

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, ↑↑ CK, leucocytosis. STOP drug, ICU, IV fluids/cooling, dantrolene 1–2 mg/kg q6h, bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS. Mortality 10–20%.

Lowered seizure threshold (chlorpromazine > others).

QTc prolongation (haloperidol IV, thioridazine — withdrawn).

Typical low-potency (chlorpromazine, thioridazine)

Anticholinergic — dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, ileus.

Antihistaminic — sedation, weight gain.

α-blockade — postural hypotension.

Photosensitivity, blue-grey skin pigmentation; corneal/lens deposits with prolonged use.

Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice with chlorpromazine).

Atypical (2nd-generation) — overall fewer EPS, more metabolic

Metabolic syndrome — weight gain, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance / diabetes (olanzapine + clozapine highest; ziprasidone + aripiprazole + lurasidone lowest).

Risperidone / paliperidone — dose-related EPS and hyperprolactinaemia.

Clozapine — agranulocytosis, myocarditis, sialorrhoea, sedation, seizures, ileus, weight gain, metabolic syndrome.

Quetiapine — sedation, postural hypotension.

Aripiprazole — akathisia (most common SE), impulse-control problems (gambling, hypersexuality).

Ziprasidone, lurasidone — QTc prolongation; lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal food.

Asenapine — sublingual; oral hypoaesthesia, EPS at high dose.

Drugs causing hallucinations (sub-question — Boloor A363)

**Recreational / drugs of abuse:** cannabis, LSD, psilocybin (magic mushroom), mescaline, MDMA (ecstasy), amphetamines, cocaine, PCP, ketamine, alcohol (in withdrawal — DT).

**Anti-Parkinsonian:** levodopa, dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine), amantadine, selegiline.

**Anticholinergics:** atropine, scopolamine, hyoscine, trihexyphenidyl, benztropine; antihistamines (diphenhydramine); TCAs at toxic doses.

**Steroids:** prednisolone (high-dose), ACTH ('steroid psychosis').

**Antimalarials:** chloroquine, mefloquine, primaquine.

**Antibiotics:** ciprofloxacin (CNS), isoniazid, cycloserine, clarithromycin, voriconazole.

**Antivirals:** aciclovir (renal failure), efavirenz, oseltamivir.

**Anaesthetics:** ketamine, nitrous oxide.

Opioids in overdose; tramadol; pentazocine.

**Withdrawal-induced:** alcohol (DT), benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids.

**Others:** digoxin toxicity, β-blockers (lipophilic — propranolol), interferon-α, baclofen withdrawal, lithium toxicity.

### Complications

Suicide — lifetime risk 5–10% (highest in young males, early course, after discharge).

Violence (small but real; usually against family, often with substance co-use).

Substance abuse comorbidity — ~50% (nicotine, cannabis, alcohol).

Cardiovascular disease — leading cause of premature mortality; antipsychotic metabolic effects + smoking + sedentary lifestyle.

Polydipsia, hyponatraemia.

Homelessness, unemployment, social isolation.

Reduced life expectancy by 15–20 years (suicide + CV disease + suboptimal medical care).

Prognosis (rule of thirds)

≈1/3 substantial recovery, ≈1/3 partial response with relapses, ≈1/3 chronic disabling course.

**Good prognostic factors:** acute onset, late onset, female, prominent positive symptoms, mood symptoms, married, good pre-morbid function, family history of mood disorder, paranoid subtype, identifiable stressor, short duration of untreated psychosis (DUP).

**Poor prognostic factors:** insidious onset, early onset, male, negative symptoms, social withdrawal, family history of schizophrenia, hebephrenic / simple subtype, no precipitant, long DUP, poor pre-morbid function.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18; ICMR/NIMHANS — Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia (Indian Psychiatric Society); DSM-5; ICD-10/11; Sadock & Sadock — Synopsis of Psychiatry 12e.

GENERAL MEDICINE|384.note:
### Definition

Alcohol Use Disorder (DSM-5) is a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment / distress, manifested by ≥2 of 11 criteria in a 12-month period (replacing DSM-IV abuse + dependence). ICD-10 retains alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria) and harmful use. India has the largest population of male alcohol users in Asia; NMHS 2016 estimates prevalence of any alcohol-use disorder at 4.6% in adults (9% in men).

Hazards of alcohol (Boloor A365)

### Neurological

Acute — intoxication, blackouts, traffic accidents, traumatic brain injury, alcohol-induced psychotic disorder.

Withdrawal — tremor, seizures, delirium tremens (see below).

Chronic — Wernicke encephalopathy / Korsakoff psychosis, cerebellar degeneration (truncal ataxia, gait), peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor, painful), optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia), central pontine myelinolysis (with rapid sodium correction), Marchiafava–Bignami disease (corpus callosum demyelination), alcohol-related dementia.

### Gastrointestinal / hepatic

Acute / chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, Mallory–Weiss tear, Boerhaave syndrome.

Pancreatitis — acute and chronic (alcohol is the #1 cause of chronic pancreatitis in India after gallstones).

Alcoholic liver disease — fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >32 → steroids/pentoxifylline) → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Oesophageal varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal / hepatopulmonary syndromes.

Malabsorption — folate, thiamine, B6, B12, Mg, Zn.

### Cardiovascular

Dilated cardiomyopathy (alcoholic), holiday heart (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke, sudden cardiac death.

### Haematological

Macrocytic anaemia (folate deficiency, direct marrow toxicity), megaloblastic, sideroblastic, haemolysis (Zieve syndrome with hepatitis + hyperlipidaemia), thrombocytopenia, leucopenia.

### Endocrine / metabolic

Hypoglycaemia (gluconeogenesis blocked), ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia / gout, hyperlipidaemia, pseudo-Cushing's.

Hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, infertility, erectile dysfunction.

### Cancer (Group I carcinogen — IARC)

Oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver (HCC), breast, colorectum.

### Obstetric

Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder — microcephaly, growth retardation, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, intellectual disability.

Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm birth.

### Psychiatric

Depression, anxiety, suicide (alcohol present in ~40% of completed suicides in India), insomnia.

Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, pathological jealousy (Othello syndrome).

### Social

Domestic violence, marital breakdown, child neglect, occupational accidents, road traffic accidents, financial ruin, legal issues.

Diagnosis — DSM-5 AUD criteria (≥2 of 11 in 12 months)

**Severity:** 2–3 mild; 4–5 moderate; ≥6 severe.

Larger amounts / longer than intended.

Persistent desire / unsuccessful attempts to cut down.

Great time spent obtaining / using / recovering.

Craving.

Failure to fulfil role obligations.

Continued use despite social / interpersonal problems.

Important activities given up.

Use in physically hazardous situations.

Continued use despite physical / psychological problems.

Tolerance.

Withdrawal.

ICD-10 alcohol dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross criteria — ≥3 of 6 in past year)

Strong desire / compulsion to drink.

Impaired control over use (onset, level, termination).

Withdrawal state on abstinence.

Tolerance.

Neglect of alternative interests.

Persistence despite clearly harmful consequences.

### Screening

**CAGE:** Cut down, Annoyed by criticism, Guilty, Eye-opener. ≥2 = significant.

**AUDIT (WHO, 10 items):** 0–7 low risk, 8–15 hazardous, 16–19 harmful, ≥20 dependence.

AUDIT-C — 3-item screening tool.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (Boloor A373 ★2026)

Figure 6. Alcohol use disorder — withdrawal triage by CIWA-Ar, thiamine-first inpatient protocol, methanol-poisoning pathway and maintenance pharmacotherapy.

Time course (after last drink)

**6–12 h:** Minor withdrawal — tremor, anxiety, nausea, sweating, palpitations, insomnia, headache.

**12–24 h:** Alcoholic hallucinosis — visual / tactile / auditory hallucinations with clear sensorium and orientation (key DDx from DT).

**24–48 h:** Withdrawal seizures — generalised tonic-clonic, brief, 1–6 episodes; usually self-limited; 3% progress to status.

**48–96 h (peak 72 h):** Delirium tremens (DT) — clouded sensorium, disorientation, agitation, fluctuating consciousness, fever, autonomic storm (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis), vivid visual / tactile (formication — 'bugs crawling') hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% untreated; 1–2% with modern care.

Risk stratification — CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised)

10 items, scored 0–7 each (orientation 0–4); total 0–67.

<8 — mild, no intervention.

8–15 — moderate, BZD treatment.

16–20 — severe.

>20 — very severe, ICU.

Management of withdrawal — Indian protocol (NIMHANS / AIIMS de-addiction)

**Inpatient if:** CIWA-Ar ≥10, history of DT / withdrawal seizures, severe medical / psychiatric comorbidity, poor support.

Thiamine FIRST, before any glucose (Wernicke prevention) — 100 mg IV/IM TDS × 3 days, then 100 mg PO OD long-term.

Wernicke / Korsakoff treatment dose: thiamine 500 mg IV TDS × 2–3 days → 250 mg IV/IM daily × 3–5 days → 100 mg PO long-term. Also IV Mg replacement (thiamine requires Mg cofactor).

**Benzodiazepines — first-line:** chlordiazepoxide 25–50 mg PO q4–6h symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar guided), tapered over 5–7 days. Diazepam 10–20 mg PO/IV q1–2h for severe.

Lorazepam preferred in hepatic dysfunction, elderly (no active metabolites): 2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h.

Phenobarbital — for refractory / BZD-resistant DT.

IV fluids (NS + 5%D), electrolyte correction — Mg 1–2 g IV q12h, K, PO4.

Multivitamin, folate 5 mg/d.

AVOID antipsychotics as monotherapy (↓ seizure threshold); use only haloperidol low dose if psychosis / agitation persists despite adequate BZD.

AVOID alcohol substitution.

Monitor vital signs q1–2h initially; CIWA-Ar q1–4h.

Treat fever, sepsis, pneumonia (high risk in DT), dehydration, rhabdomyolysis.

### Withdrawal seizures

**Treat acute seizure:** IV lorazepam 2–4 mg or diazepam 10 mg.

**Prevention:** adequate BZD coverage during detox.

Long-term anti-epileptics not needed unless underlying epilepsy.

Maintenance — relapse prevention (anti-craving)

**Naltrexone:** 50 mg PO OD (or 380 mg IM monthly). μ-opioid antagonist; ↓ craving and pleasure of drinking (COMBINE trial). Avoid in liver failure, opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); LFT monitoring.

**Acamprosate:** 666 mg PO TDS (2 g/d in <60 kg). NMDA modulator; ↓ relapse rate (PROJECT MATCH). Safe in liver disease; needs adequate renal function.

**Disulfiram:** 250 mg PO OD (max 500 mg). Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor; causes aversive reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, hypotension) on alcohol ingestion. Supervised dosing (family member). Avoid in CAD, severe psychiatric illness, pregnancy, peripheral neuropathy. Warn re: hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrups, perfumes).

Baclofen (off-label, useful in liver disease): 10–30 mg TDS; GABA-B agonist; reduces craving especially in cirrhotics where naltrexone and disulfiram unsafe (ANRS-BACLOVILLE).

**Topiramate, gabapentin:** Off-label adjuncts.

Psychosocial interventions (cornerstone — often dominate outcome)

Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MI / MET) — stage-of-change-based.

CBT — relapse prevention, coping skills.

12-step facilitation / Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) — Indian chapters widespread.

Family therapy, community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT).

Residential rehabilitation for severe / relapsing.

Treat comorbid depression / anxiety / PTSD.

Indian de-addiction infrastructure: AIIMS NDDTC, NIMHANS Centre for Addiction Medicine, Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP — MoHFW), state-level Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs).

Methyl alcohol (methanol) poisoning — Boloor A367

Methanol is a toxic alcohol found in adulterated illicit liquor ('hooch'), industrial solvents, anti-freeze, windshield-washer fluid and formalin. Toxic dose ~10 ml; fatal 30 ml.

### Toxicokinetics

Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → FORMALDEHYDE → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → FORMIC ACID — the principal toxin (causes optic neuritis, metabolic acidosis).

### Clinical features

Latent period 12–24 h (longer if co-ingested ethanol).

Phase 1 — CNS depression (mild intoxication / inebriation).

Phase 2 (12–24 h) — N/V, abdominal pain, headache, vertigo.

Phase 3 — visual disturbance ('snowstorm', blurring, blindness), optic disc hyperaemia / oedema → permanent blindness.

Phase 4 — severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) with ↑ osmolar gap, Kussmaul respiration, seizures, coma, parkinsonism (putaminal necrosis), death.

### Investigations

ABG — severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2, HCO3 <10).

Anion gap — high (>20).

Osmolar gap — high (>10 mOsm/kg) early, falls as methanol is metabolised.

Serum methanol level — confirmatory (toxic >20 mg/dL; severe >50).

Fundus — optic disc hyperaemia / oedema.

MRI brain — putaminal haemorrhage / necrosis (classic).

### Management

ABC, IV access, gastric lavage (if <1 h), activated charcoal NOT effective (poorly adsorbed).

Block ADH (prevent toxic metabolite formation):

- FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole) — drug of choice if available; 15 mg/kg IV load → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 4 doses → 15 mg/kg q12h thereafter (induces own metabolism). Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL + acidosis resolved + asymptomatic.

- ETHANOL (alternative if no fomepizole) — IV loading 10 ml/kg of 10% ethanol over 30 min → 1.5 ml/kg/h infusion. Target blood ethanol 100 mg/dL. Cheaper and widely available in India.

FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1 mg/kg IV q4–6h (max 50 mg) × 6 doses — accelerates formate metabolism. Folic acid acceptable if folinic unavailable.

Correct acidosis — IV sodium bicarbonate to keep pH >7.2.

HAEMODIALYSIS — definitive removal of methanol and formate. Indications: serum methanol ≥50 mg/dL, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2), visual / mental status changes, electrolyte imbalance refractory, renal failure.

Supportive — ICU, mechanical ventilation, treat seizures.

Complications of alcohol use (summary)

Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis (irreversible amnesia, confabulation).

Delirium tremens — mortality 5–15% untreated.

Cirrhosis, HCC, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy.

Suicide, accidental injuries, road traffic accidents.

Family disruption, economic loss, occupational impairment.

### Prognosis

Without treatment — progressive decline, premature mortality.

With comprehensive treatment (pharmacotherapy + psychosocial) — 30–50% achieve sustained remission at 1 year.

Better with stable social support, employment, no comorbid psychiatric illness, motivation for change.

Worse with antisocial personality, depression / suicide history, polysubstance use.

**Source:** Boloor 10e Ch.18 + Ch.16 (toxicology); Indian Psychiatric Society — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Alcohol Use Disorders; NIMHANS / AIIMS NDDTC protocols; COMBINE 2006; PROJECT MATCH; American Academy of Clinical Toxicology — methanol/fomepizole; DSM-5; ICD-10/11.

GENERAL MEDICINE|385.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Recurrent primary headache disorder characterised by attacks of moderate-severe unilateral pulsating headache lasting 4-72 h, with associated nausea/vomiting and photo/phonophobia, +/- aura. Prevalence 12-15%; F:M = 3:1.

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Trigeminovascular activation → CGRP, substance P release → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, central sensitisation.

Cortical spreading depression underlies aura.

Genetic predisposition (familial hemiplegic migraine — CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

### Triggers (CHOCOLATE mnemonic)

Chocolate, Cheese (tyramine), Caffeine withdrawal.

Hormones (menstrual), Hunger (skipped meals).

OCPs / Oestrogens.

Alcohol (red wine).

Lifestyle (sleep deprivation / oversleeping).

Travel / Tobacco.

Exercise / Exertion.

### ICHD-3 criteria

Migraine without aura (≥ 5 attacks)

Duration 4-72 h untreated.

**≥ 2 of:** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by movement.

**≥ 1 of:** nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia.

Migraine with aura (≥ 2 attacks)

Fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor or brainstem aura.

≥ 1 aura over ≥ 5 min; each lasts 5-60 min.

Followed by headache within 60 min (or accompanied).

### Phases of attack

**Prodrome (24-48 h):** yawning, fatigue, mood change, food cravings.

**Aura (5-60 min):** visual scintillations/scotoma > sensory > speech.

Headache (4-72 h).

**Postdrome ('hangover'):** fatigue, cognitive slowing.

### Investigations

Clinical diagnosis — no routine tests.

MRI brain if red flags (SNNOOP10): new headache > 50 y, change in pattern, focal deficit, papilloedema, thunderclap, posttraumatic, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

### Management

### 1. Acute (abortive)

**Mild-moderate:** Mild-moderate: NSAID — naproxen 500-750 mg or ibuprofen 400-800 mg or aspirin 900 mg. Paracetamol 1 g.

**Moderate-severe:** Moderate-severe: Triptan — sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO / 6 mg SC / 20 mg intranasal; rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan. Take early.

**Antiemetic:** Antiemetic: Metoclopramide 10 mg / domperidone 10 mg (also enhances absorption).

**Refractory:** Refractory: DHE-45 (dihydroergotamine), CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant (gepants).

**5-HT1F agonist:** 5-HT1F agonist: Lasmiditan — useful in cardiovascular contraindication to triptans.

**Avoid:** Avoid: Opioids and barbiturates (medication overuse headache).

- Preventive — indicated if ≥ 4 attacks/month, prolonged > 72 h, severe disability, or contraindication to abortive

**Beta-blocker:** Beta-blocker: Propranolol 80-240 mg/d. Metoprolol 50-200 mg.

**Antiepileptic:** Antiepileptic: Topiramate 50-100 mg/d (avoid in pregnancy). Valproate 500-1500 mg.

**Tricyclic:** Tricyclic: Amitriptyline 10-75 mg HS (useful if comorbid TTH, depression, insomnia).

**Ca-channel blocker:** Ca-channel blocker: Flunarizine 5-10 mg HS (effective in Indian practice).

**Anti-CGRP mAb:** Anti-CGRP mAb: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab — monthly SC. India: erenumab launched 2023.

**Botulinum toxin A:** Botulinum toxin A: 155 U for chronic migraine (≥ 15 d/mo).

- Status migrainosus (> 72 h)

IV fluids, prochlorperazine 10 mg IV, sumatriptan 6 mg SC, dexamethasone 4-10 mg IV, magnesium 1 g IV.

### 4. Lifestyle (SEEDS)

Sleep regularity, Exercise (aerobic 30 min ≥ 3×/wk), Eating regularly, Diary, Stress management.

### Special situations

**Menstrual migraine:** short course NSAID/triptan perimenstrually; estradiol patch.

**Pregnancy:** paracetamol; metoclopramide; avoid triptans/ergots/valproate/topiramate.

**Aura + smoker + OCP:** STOP OCP — stroke risk.

**Source:** ICHD-3; AAN/AHS 2021; Indian Migraine Practice Guidelines (IAN); Boloor Ch.15.

### Approach

ICHD-3 classifies > 200 headache types. First task = exclude secondary (dangerous) headache using SNNOOP10 red flags; then classify primary headache.

SNNOOP10 — red flags for secondary headache

S — Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats).

N — Neoplasm (cancer history).

N — Neurological deficit (focal signs, altered consciousness, papilloedema).

O — Onset sudden (thunderclap, peak < 1 min) — SAH until proven otherwise.

O — Older > 50 with new headache (GCA, mass).

P — Pattern change / Progressive.

P — Positional / Precipitated by Valsalva / Cough (raised ICT, Chiari).

P — Papilloedema / Vision change.

P — Pregnancy / Postpartum (CVT, eclampsia, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy).

P — Painful eye + autonomic (cluster, acute angle-closure glaucoma).

P — Posttraumatic.

P — Painkiller overuse / Pathology of immune system (HIV, immunosuppressed).

### PRIMARY headaches (ICHD-3)

### Migraine — see Q6

### Tension-type headache (TTH)

Most common primary headache; 30-78% lifetime.

Bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-moderate, not aggravated by routine activity.

Episodic (< 15 d/mo) or chronic (≥ 15 d/mo).

**Rx:** NSAID; amitriptyline for prevention; lifestyle, stress management.

### Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias

**Cluster headache:** M > F (3:1); strictly unilateral periorbital/temporal; 15-180 min; ipsilateral autonomic (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, ptosis, miosis); agitation/restlessness (vs migraine quiet). Acute: 100% O2 12 L/min × 15 min + sumatriptan 6 mg SC. Prevention: verapamil 240-480 mg, prednisolone bridging, lithium, galcanezumab.

Paroxysmal hemicrania — shorter (2-30 min), more frequent (5-40/d), absolute response to indomethacin.

SUNCT / SUNA — very short (1-600 s), very frequent.

Hemicrania continua — continuous unilateral, indomethacin-responsive.

### Other primary

Primary cough / exertional / sexual headache.

Stabbing headache.

Hypnic headache ('alarm-clock', wakes from sleep, elderly).

New daily persistent headache (NDPH).

### SECONDARY headache causes

### Vascular — thunderclap

SAH (NCCT + LP).

RCVS (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction — pregnancy, vasoactive drugs).

CVT (D-dimer, MR venography — pregnancy, OCP, dehydration, thrombophilia).

Carotid/vertebral dissection.

Pituitary apoplexy.

Hypertensive emergency / PRES.

### Infection

Meningitis (bacterial, TB, viral, fungal).

Encephalitis (HSV — temporal lobe seizures).

Brain abscess (HIV, post-otitis).

Systemic infection (dengue, malaria, enteric fever, COVID-19).

Neurocysticercosis (Indian context — seizure + headache + cyst on imaging).

### Raised ICT

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (young obese F; papilloedema; LP pressure > 25 cm H₂O; Rx weight loss + acetazolamide; CSF diversion if severe).

Brain tumour (worse mornings/Valsalva; progressive).

Hydrocephalus, ventriculitis.

### Inflammatory / autoimmune

Giant cell arteritis (> 50, temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, ESR > 50, biopsy; Rx prednisolone 60 mg/d IMMEDIATELY).

CNS vasculitis.

Tolosa-Hunt (painful ophthalmoplegia).

### Medication / substance

Medication overuse headache (MOH) — analgesics ≥ 15 d/mo, triptans/opioids ≥ 10 d/mo.

Nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors, calcium-channel blockers.

Caffeine withdrawal.

Sinus / facial / dental

Sinusitis (frontal headache + nasal discharge + fever; CT sinuses).

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (red painful eye + halos + nausea — emergency).

Dental, TMJ disorders.

### Cervicogenic

Occipital pain referred from upper cervical joints; aggravated by neck movement.

### Posttraumatic

Post-concussion, subdural haematoma (elderly, alcoholic, anticoagulant).

Investigations (selectively, based on red flags)

NCCT head — first if thunderclap, posttraumatic, focal deficit, altered mental.

LP — if SAH suspected and CT normal, or meningitis.

MRI brain ± MRA/MRV — chronic progressive, atypical features.

ESR, CRP — GCA suspected.

Tonometry — angle-closure glaucoma.

**Other:** HIV, dengue NS1, malaria smear, autoimmune panel.

Fig 8. Headache — red flags and DD.

**Source:** ICHD-3; Do TG et al, BMJ 2019 (SNNOOP10); Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|386.note:
### Definition

Dorsiflexion (extension) of the great toe with fanning of other toes on stroking the lateral plantar surface from heel to forefoot, then medially across metatarsal heads — performed with blunt object. Normal in infants < 1 year (myelination immature). After 1 year = UMN sign.

Neurological causes (UMN lesion anywhere along corticospinal tract)

### Brain

Stroke (ischaemic / haemorrhagic) — commonest cause in elderly.

Brain tumour (primary or metastatic).

Traumatic brain injury, intracranial haemorrhage.

Cerebral palsy.

Multiple sclerosis (cerebral plaque).

Encephalitis, brain abscess, neurocysticercosis.

Hydrocephalus.

Hypoxic-ischaemic injury (post-cardiac arrest).

### Spinal cord

**Cord compression:** Pott's spine, disc prolapse, tumour, abscess, haematoma.

Transverse myelitis.

MS / NMO / MOGAD (cord plaque).

Subacute combined degeneration (SACD, B12).

HTLV-1 tropical spastic paraparesis.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.

Anterior spinal artery syndrome.

Syringomyelia (late).

Tabes dorsalis / neurosyphilis.

Friedreich's ataxia (despite areflexia — characteristic combination).

Conus medullaris lesions.

### Combined UMN + LMN

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS / MND) — UMN + LMN signs together.

Transient extensor plantar (reversible — non-structural)

Postictal (after seizure — Todd's paralysis).

Deep coma from any cause.

**Drug intoxication:** barbiturates, opioids, alcohol, anaesthesia (rocuronium, sevoflurane).

Hypoglycaemia.

Hepatic / uraemic encephalopathy.

Hypothermia.

Migraine aura with hemiparesis.

Special pearls — exam differential

Absent ankle jerks + extensor plantar — classical for: SACD, Friedreich's ataxia, tabes dorsalis, MND (early), diabetic neuropathy + concurrent cerebral lesion, conus + cauda equina lesion.

Unilateral Babinski with contralateral hemiparesis — usually stroke.

Bilateral Babinski + spastic paraparesis + sensory level — cord compression / myelopathy.

Other 'pyramidal' signs equivalent to Babinski

Chaddock — stroking lateral malleolus.

Oppenheim — pressure down the shin.

Gordon — squeezing calf.

Schaeffer — squeezing Achilles tendon.

Gonda — pulling down 4th toe.

Bing — pricking dorsum of foot.

**Source:** Davidson Ch.27; Bickerstaff's Neurological Examination; Boloor Ch.15.

GENERAL MEDICINE|387.note:
### Combined Notes (2 topics)

### Definition

Narrowing of aortic valve area producing obstruction to LV outflow. Severe when valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4.0 m/s.

### Etiology

**Calcific (degenerative):** >70 yr, most common cause in developed countries.

**Bicuspid aortic valve:** presents 40–60 yr; commonest congenital cause.

**Rheumatic:** commonest cause in India in younger adults; usually with associated MS.

Subvalvular (HOCM, membrane) or supravalvular (Williams syndrome).

### Pathophysiology

Narrow valve → ↑ LV pressure to maintain stroke volume → concentric LV hypertrophy → compliance ↓ → diastolic dysfunction → ↑ LVEDP → pulmonary congestion. Hypertrophied myocardium also has ↑ O₂ demand and impaired subendocardial perfusion → angina. Fixed cardiac output during exertion + reflex vasodilation → syncope. Eventually LV decompensation → systolic failure.

### Clinical Features

Asymptomatic for decades; triad (SAD) of Syncope (exertional), Angina, Dyspnoea heralds critical AS – mean survival without surgery: 5/3/2 years respectively. Sudden cardiac death possible.

### Signs

**Pulse:** slow-rising, low-volume (pulsus parvus et tardus).

Narrow pulse pressure.

**Apex:** heaving, sustained, not displaced (pressure overload).

Systolic thrill at aortic area radiating to carotids.

**Auscultation:** ejection systolic murmur, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo, maximal at aortic area, radiating to carotids; in elderly, harsh murmur may radiate to apex (Gallavardin phenomenon).

S1 normal; S2 softens/absent (calcified valve); paradoxical splitting; S4 (LVH); ejection click in bicuspid valve.

**Severity pointers:** longer murmur peaking later, soft/absent A2, presence of S4, narrow pulse pressure, slow-rising pulse, signs of LVH.

### Investigations

**ECG:** LVH, strain pattern, LBBB late.

**Echocardiography (key):** valve morphology, AVA (planimetry/continuity equation), peak/mean gradient, LV function, LVH.

**CXR:** cardiomegaly, post-stenotic dilatation of aorta, calcified valve.

**Cardiac catheterisation:** gradient, coronary anatomy before surgery.

**Exercise testing:** only if asymptomatic to unmask symptoms.

**Cardiac CT:** TAVR work-up (annulus size, peripheral vascular access).

Natriuretic peptides (BNP) for risk stratification.

### Management

Pharmacotherapy does not alter prognosis; valve replacement is the only definitive treatment.

**Mild–moderate, asymptomatic:** review yearly with echo. Treat HTN cautiously (ACEi/ARB); avoid vasodilators (GTN) and aggressive diuresis in severe AS.

**Severe symptomatic AS:** aortic valve replacement (AVR). Indicated also if asymptomatic with LVEF <50% or undergoing other cardiac surgery.

SAVR (mechanical/bioprosthetic) for younger, lower-risk patients.

TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement) for elderly/high-surgical-risk patients; now extending into intermediate-risk groups.

**Balloon aortic valvuloplasty:** palliative or bridge to surgery, especially in children/young adults with congenital AS.

Endocarditis prophylaxis if history of IE or prosthetic valve.

Fig 4. Aortic stenosis – management decision tree.

Loud S1 (palpable as 'tapping' apex), reflects increased force of MV closure with elevated LA pressure.

**Opening snap (OS):** high-pitched, follows A2, best heard at apex, occurs 0.06–0.12 s after A2; shorter interval = more severe MS.

**Mid-diastolic murmur (MDM):** low-pitched rumble, best heard with bell at apex in left lateral decubitus position after exercise, in expiration; duration correlates with severity.

Pre-systolic accentuation (in sinus rhythm, due to atrial contraction) – absent in AF.

**Pulmonary hypertension signs:** loud P2, parasternal heave (RV hypertrophy), pansystolic murmur of TR.

**Associated:** Graham Steell murmur (early-diastolic murmur of functional PR), Carey-Coombs murmur of acute rheumatic mitral valvulitis (transient MDM, soft S1).

**Severity pointers:** short A2-OS interval, long MDM, signs of pulmonary hypertension, S3 (suggests associated MR), AF.

### Definition

Non-invasive ultrasound imaging of the heart (2–4 MHz) used to assess cardiac structure and function. The single most useful first-line cardiac investigation after ECG.

### Modalities

**TTE (Transthoracic):** standard outpatient examination.

**TOE/TEE (Transoesophageal):** better imaging of LA, MV, aorta, prosthetic valves, vegetations, atrial thrombus – guided cardioversion.

**Stress echo:** dobutamine or exercise – inducible ischaemia, viability assessment.

3-D, contrast, strain (speckle-tracking) – advanced techniques.

### Information obtained

**Structure:** Chamber dimensions, wall thickness, mass.

**LV systolic function:** EF (M-mode/Simpson's), regional wall motion (ischaemia), diastolic function (E/A, e′).

**Valves:** Stenosis (planimetry, pressure gradients), regurgitation (colour Doppler jet, vena contracta, PISA), prosthetic valve.

**Pericardium:** Effusion, tamponade physiology, constriction.

**Congenital lesions:** ASD/VSD/PDA, Tetralogy of Fallot, etc.

**Pulmonary haemodynamics:** PA pressure (via TR jet), pulmonary regurgitation.

**Masses:** Vegetations, intracardiac thrombi, masses (tumours).

### Common indications

Suspected heart failure, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, cardiomyopathy, pericardial disease, infective endocarditis, source of embolism, pulmonary hypertension, screening before chemotherapy, peri-operative risk.

GENERAL MEDICINE|389.note:
### Combined Notes (4 topics)

Common inhaled corticosteroids (Indian availability)

Budesonide (Budecort, Pulmicort) – MDI 100/200 µg; DPI 200/400 µg; neb 0.5/1 mg.

Fluticasone propionate (Flohale, Flixotide) – MDI 50/125/250 µg; DPI 100/250/500 µg.

Fluticasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg (once-daily).

Beclomethasone dipropionate (Beclate) – MDI 50/100/250 µg.

Ciclesonide (Alvesco) – MDI 80/160 µg.

Mometasone furoate – DPI 100/200 µg.

Combination ICS-LABA inhalers (most prescribed)

Budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort, Foracort) – preferred Track 1 GINA reliever-controller.

Fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide).

Fluticasone furoate + vilanterol (Relvar Ellipta).

Beclomethasone + formoterol.

### Triple-therapy inhalers (ICS-LABA-LAMA)

Fluticasone + umeclidinium + vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta).

Budesonide + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

Beclomethasone + glycopyrrolate + formoterol.

### Adverse effects

**Local:** oral candidiasis (Candida albicans – use spacer + rinse mouth), dysphonia, throat irritation.

Systemic (with high dose / long-term): osteoporosis, skin thinning, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, adrenal suppression, increased pneumonia risk in COPD.

### Indications

Asthma – mainstay of controller therapy from GINA Step 1 onwards.

COPD – with LABA in patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥100/300.

Other obstructive airways disease (some forms of bronchiectasis with asthma overlap).

### Definition

Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. Confirmed by gastric scintigraphy showing > 10% retention at 4 h. Commonest cause is diabetic autonomic neuropathy (especially long-standing T1DM/T2DM); idiopathic, post-viral, post-surgical (vagotomy, fundoplication), drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 agonists), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), Parkinson's.

### Symptoms

Early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting (often undigested food hours after meal), upper abdominal pain, weight loss, poor glycaemic control in diabetics (mismatch with insulin).

### Pharmacological Management

### 1. Prokinetics (first-line)

**Metoclopramide:** Metoclopramide: 5–10 mg PO/IV TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. MOA: D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist + acetylcholine release. Black-box warning: tardive dyskinesia (limit to ≤ 12 weeks); extrapyramidal SE, hyperprolactinaemia.

**Domperidone:** Domperidone: 10 mg PO TDS, 30 min before meals + bedtime. Peripheral D2 antagonist — does NOT cross BBB → fewer EPS. Caution: QT prolongation (avoid in cardiac disease, electrolyte abnormalities); lower dose in elderly; not available in USA but widely used in India.

**Erythromycin:** Erythromycin: 50–250 mg PO TDS (lower dose for prokinesis) or 3 mg/kg IV; motilin receptor agonist. Tachyphylaxis (loss of effect after 2–4 wk) — limit use. Useful as IV in acute settings (e.g. pre-OGD for blood clearance).

**Cisapride:** Cisapride: Withdrawn in most countries (QT prolongation, torsades).

**Prucalopride:** Prucalopride: 1–2 mg OD — 5-HT4 agonist; emerging evidence for refractory gastroparesis.

### 2. Antiemetics (symptomatic)

Ondansetron 4–8 mg PO/IV TDS — 5-HT3 antagonist; first-line for symptom control.

Prochlorperazine, promethazine — alternatives; sedation, EPS.

Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist, for refractory.

### 3. Other / Emerging

Mirtazapine 15 mg HS — TCA-related; appetite + nausea relief.

Botulinum toxin pyloric injection — only short-term (no longer recommended in guidelines).

Ghrelin agonists (relamorelin) — in trials.

### Non-Pharmacological

**Dietary:** small frequent meals (5–6/day), low-fat, low-fibre, soft/liquid consistency.

Strict glycaemic control in diabetics (hyperglycaemia worsens emptying).

Avoid carbonated drinks, alcohol, smoking.

Stop / reduce offending drugs (opioids, GLP-1 agonists if possible, anticholinergics).

Vitamin / micronutrient supplementation (chronic malnutrition risk).

### Refractory Cases

Gastric electrical stimulation (Enterra device) — FDA HUD; selected refractory cases.

Pyloroplasty / G-POEM (gastric per-oral endoscopic myotomy).

**Surgical:** subtotal gastrectomy, jejunostomy feeding tube.

TPN in severe cachexia.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ACG Gastroparesis 2022; AGA 2022.

### Overview

IBD (UC, Crohn's) treatment uses a step-up or top-down approach based on severity, location, and prognostic factors. Goals: induce + maintain remission, achieve mucosal healing, prevent complications, avoid surgery.

### Classification of IBD Drugs

### 1. Aminosalicylates (5-ASA / Mesalamine)

**Sulfasalazine:** Sulfasalazine: 1–2 g BD-QID. Sulfapyridine + 5-ASA. Cleaved by colonic bacteria. SE: nausea, headache, hypersensitivity, oligospermia (reversible).

**Mesalamine:** Mesalamine: 2.4–4.8 g/d divided. pH-dependent or time-released formulations (Asacol, Pentasa, Salofalk). For colonic and ileal disease.

**Olsalazine, Balsalazide:** Olsalazine, Balsalazide: 5-ASA dimers / azo-bonded; site-specific colonic release.

**Topical 5-ASA:** Topical 5-ASA: Suppositories (proctitis), enemas (left-sided UC) — adjunct or monotherapy.

**Indications:** Indications: Mild-moderate UC (induction + maintenance); less effective in Crohn's (some role in colonic CD).

### 2. Corticosteroids

**Prednisolone:** Prednisolone: 40–60 mg/d PO, taper over 8–12 weeks. Severe UC: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg q6h or methylprednisolone 60 mg/d. Induction only — NOT maintenance.

**Budesonide:** Budesonide: 9 mg/d × 8 wk for mild-moderate ileal/right colonic Crohn's. Topically active; high first-pass metabolism → fewer systemic SE.

**Topical (PR foam/enema):** Topical (PR foam/enema): Hydrocortisone, budesonide foam for distal UC.

Steroid dependence (cannot taper) or refractoriness (failure of high dose for 7–10 d) → step up to immunomodulators or biologics.

Long-term steroid avoidance — bone protection (Ca/Vit D, DEXA), DM/HTN screening, infection.

### 3. Immunomodulators (steroid-sparing)

Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine:Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine: AZA 2–2.5 mg/kg/d (6-MP 1–1.5 mg/kg/d). Check TPMT activity before starting (deficiency → severe myelosuppression). Onset 6–12 wk. Maintenance.

**Methotrexate:** Methotrexate: 25 mg/wk IM/SC × 16 wk → 15 mg/wk maintenance (Crohn's). Folic acid 5 mg/wk. Less effective in UC.

**Cyclosporine:** Cyclosporine: 2 mg/kg/d IV (or 4 mg/kg/d PO) for steroid-refractory severe UC — rescue therapy. Bridge to AZA/biologics. Trough 200–400 ng/mL.

**Tacrolimus:** Tacrolimus: Alternative calcineurin inhibitor.

**Monitoring:** CBC, LFT every 2 wk × first month, then 3-monthly.

**Risks:** bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis (AZA), lymphoma (slightly raised), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (rare in young men on AZA + anti-TNF).

- Biologics (anti-TNF and others)

**Infliximab (anti-TNF):** Infliximab (anti-TNF): 5 mg/kg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk maintenance. Can escalate to 10 mg/kg or every 6 wk if loss of response.

**Adalimumab (anti-TNF):** Adalimumab (anti-TNF): 160 mg SC week 0 → 80 mg week 2 → 40 mg every 2 wk maintenance.

**Golimumab:** Golimumab: 200 mg SC week 0 → 100 mg week 2 → 50–100 mg every 4 wk (UC).

**Certolizumab pegol:** Certolizumab pegol: 400 mg SC at 0, 2, 4 wk → every 4 wk (Crohn's).

**Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7):** Vedolizumab (anti-α4β7): 300 mg IV at 0, 2, 6 wk → every 8 wk. Gut-selective; lower infection risk.

**Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40):** Ustekinumab (anti-IL12/23 p40): Weight-based loading IV → 90 mg SC every 8–12 wk maintenance. Crohn's + UC.

**Risankizumab (anti-IL23):** Risankizumab (anti-IL23): 600 mg IV at 0, 4, 8 wk → 360 mg SC every 8 wk (Crohn's).

### Pre-biologic screening (essential)

**TB screening:** chest X-ray + Mantoux/IGRA (especially Indian context — high TB burden, anti-TNF reactivates latent TB).

Hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV.

Vaccinate live attenuated BEFORE starting (yellow fever, varicella).

CBC, LFT, albumin baseline.

### 5. Small Molecule Drugs (new class)

**Tofacitinib:** Tofacitinib: Pan-JAK inhibitor; 10 mg BD × 8 wk → 5 mg BD maintenance. Moderate-severe UC. Caution: VTE risk (especially with risk factors), shingles.

**Upadacitinib:** Upadacitinib: JAK1 selective; 45 mg/d × 8 wk → 15 mg/d (or 30 mg/d) maintenance. UC + Crohn's.

**Ozanimod:** Ozanimod: S1P modulator; UC.

**Etrasimod:** Etrasimod: S1P modulator; newer.

### 6. Antibiotics

**Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin:** Metronidazole + Ciprofloxacin: For perianal Crohn's, fistulae, abscess, pouchitis. 400 mg TDS + 500 mg BD for 4–8 wk.

**Vancomycin PO:** Vancomycin PO: For C. difficile co-infection.

### 7. Adjunctive / Supportive

Iron supplementation (oral or IV; IV preferred in moderate-severe).

B12 (terminal ileitis / resection).

Vitamin D, calcium (osteoporosis prevention).

Probiotics (some evidence for pouchitis; mild UC).

Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) — emerging in UC, very promising in pouchitis.

### Indication-Based Algorithm

### Ulcerative Colitis

**Mild proctitis/distal:** topical 5-ASA, topical steroid.

**Mild-moderate extensive:** PO + topical 5-ASA, PO steroids if needed.

**Moderate-severe:** PO steroids → AZA → biologic (anti-TNF, vedo, ustek) or tofacitinib.

**Severe:** IV hydrocortisone; day-3 response (Travis criteria — > 8 stools or 3–8 + CRP > 45 = high colectomy risk); rescue infliximab 5 mg/kg or cyclosporine 2 mg/kg/d IV.

**Refractory:** colectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (curative).

### Crohn's Disease

**Mild ileal:** budesonide 9 mg/d.

**Moderate:** PO prednisolone → AZA / methotrexate maintenance.

Severe / fistulating / perianal: anti-TNF ± AZA ('top-down'); anti-TNF + seton for perianal fistulae; metronidazole.

**Stricture:** balloon dilatation; surgery (stricturoplasty, segmental resection).

**Goal:** deep remission (clinical + endoscopic mucosal healing).

**Source:** Boloor Ch.11; ECCO 2022 UC + Crohn's guidelines; ACG 2019; ISG IBD India consensus.

### Definition

Portal hypertension = pathological elevation of pressure in the portal venous system, diagnosed clinically (varices, splenomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy) or by hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) > 5 mm Hg (clinically significant > 10 mm Hg; variceal threshold > 12).

### Classification by Site of Obstruction

**Pre-hepatic:** portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein thrombosis (post-pancreatitis), schistosomiasis (Indian).

**Intra-hepatic:** cirrhosis (commonest), idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal HTN (NCIPH/INCPH — important in India), nodular regenerative hyperplasia, primary biliary cholangitis.

**Post-hepatic:** Budd-Chiari, IVC obstruction, constrictive pericarditis, right heart failure.

### Drug Classes

### 1. Non-Selective Beta-Blockers (NSBB) — first-line

**Propranolol:** Propranolol: Start 20–40 mg BD → titrate to HR 55–60 bpm (or 25% reduction from baseline). Max 320 mg/d. β1 + β2 blockade → reduced cardiac output + splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal flow + pressure.

**Nadolol:** Nadolol: 20–80 mg/d. Longer half-life, once-daily dosing; preferred over propranolol in some patients (less compliance issues).

**Carvedilol:** Carvedilol: 6.25 mg BD → titrate to 12.5 BD (or 25 mg/d in some). Non-selective β + α1 antagonism → further reduces portal pressure via intrahepatic vasodilation. Preferred in compensated cirrhosis (Baveno VII).

**Goals:** Goals: ↓ HVPG > 20% from baseline OR ≤ 12 mm Hg → reduces variceal bleed and mortality.

**Contraindications:** Contraindications: Severe asthma/COPD, bradycardia (HR < 55), AV block, decompensated heart failure, refractory ascites (caution — may worsen).

**Indications:** Indications: Primary prophylaxis (medium/large varices, or small varices with high-risk features), secondary prophylaxis after first variceal bleed.

### 2. Vasoactive Drugs for Acute Variceal Bleed

Terlipressin (1st-line in India):Terlipressin (1st-line in India): 2 mg IV bolus q4h × 24–48 h → 1 mg q4h × 5 d total. Vasopressin analogue → V1 receptor → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure. Indian context: cheap, widely available, DOC for acute variceal bleed + HRS.

**Octreotide:** Octreotide: 50 µg IV bolus → 50 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Somatostatin analogue → inhibits splanchnic vasodilator release (glucagon, VIP) → ↓ portal flow. Useful when terlipressin unavailable.

**Somatostatin:** Somatostatin: 250 µg IV bolus → 250 µg/h infusion × 5 d. Less commonly used in India.

**Vasopressin:** Vasopressin: Largely replaced — significant systemic vasoconstriction (coronary, mesenteric, peripheral) → ischaemic complications.

### 3. Antibiotics in Variceal Bleed

**Ceftriaxone:** Ceftriaxone: 1 g IV/d × 5–7 d. Reduces SBP, rebleed risk, and mortality (Garcia-Tsao). Norfloxacin 400 mg BD PO as alternative in countries with low quinolone resistance.

### 4. Diuretics for Ascites

**Spironolactone:** Spironolactone: 100 mg/d → titrate to 400 mg/d (in 100 mg increments). First-line; competitive aldosterone antagonist. SE: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia.

**Furosemide:** Furosemide: Add 40 mg/d → titrate to 160 mg/d. Combined with spironolactone in 100:40 ratio. Loop diuretic; SE: hypokalaemia, AKI, hyponatraemia.

**Amiloride:** Amiloride: Alternative to spironolactone; no gynaecomastia. Less potent.

**Goals:** Goals: Daily weight loss ≤ 0.5 kg (no oedema) / ≤ 1 kg (with oedema). Daily Na restriction 88 mmol (2 g sodium).

**Caution:** Caution: Watch for HRS, encephalopathy (over-diuresis), hyponatraemia (Na < 125 → stop diuretics).

### 5. Albumin

**Indicated for:** large-volume paracentesis (8 g per L removed > 5 L); SBP (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 — reduces HRS, mortality); HRS (1 g/kg day 1 then 20–40 g/d); spontaneous decompensation with hypoalbuminaemia.

### 6. HRS-Specific

**Terlipressin + Albumin:** Terlipressin + Albumin: Terlipressin 1 mg q4–6 h IV (titrate to 2 mg q4h) + albumin 1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/d × 5–14 d. Reverses HRS in 30–50%.

**Noradrenaline + Albumin:** Noradrenaline + Albumin: 0.5–3 mg/h infusion (target MAP rise 10 mm Hg) — alternative in ICU.

Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin:Midodrine + Octreotide + Albumin: Less effective; outpatient alternative.

### 7. Hepatic Encephalopathy

Lactulose 30–45 ml TDS → titrate to 2–3 soft stools/d.

Rifaximin 550 mg BD — maintenance / recurrent.

See Q14 for full details.

- Statins (emerging in compensated cirrhosis)

Simvastatin 20–40 mg/d — improves liver microcirculation, reduces portal pressure, may improve survival (Abraldes 2016, EASL 2018). Caution in decompensated.

### Comprehensive Algorithm

Primary Prophylaxis (no bleed yet)

Small varices + high-risk (Child B/C, red wale marks) → NSBB or carvedilol.

Medium/large varices → NSBB / carvedilol OR EVL.

**Combined NSBB + EVL:** NOT recommended primarily.

Acute Bleed (within 12 h)

Resuscitate (restrictive Hb 7), terlipressin + ceftriaxone + IV PPI; urgent OGD with EVL.

Secondary Prophylaxis (after first bleed)

NSBB / carvedilol + EVL every 2–4 wk till varices eradicated.

**Refractory:** TIPS / liver transplant evaluation.

### Combined Notes (3 topics)

### Definition

Microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to depleted body iron stores, with ferritin <30 ng/mL. Commonest anaemia in the world; >50% of Indian women and >70% of pre-school children (NFHS-5) are anaemic, predominantly IDA.

### Etiology

**Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet (vegetarian, infants, adolescents).

**Decreased absorption:** Achlorhydria (PPI, atrophic gastritis, post-gastrectomy), coeliac disease, bariatric surgery.

**Increased demand:** Adolescence, pregnancy, lactation, growth spurts.

**Increased loss:** Menstrual loss, GI bleed (PUD, hookworm, haemorrhoids, malignancy), recurrent haematuria, haemoglobinuria (PNH, mechanical valve), repeated blood donation.

### Clinical features

### Symptoms of anaemia

Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, irritability, syncope.

Pica – craving for ice (pagophagia), clay, starch.

Restless legs syndrome.

### Signs

Pallor (palms, conjunctiva, tongue), tachycardia, haemic murmur (ejection systolic at base).

Glossitis (atrophic, smooth, red tongue).

Angular cheilitis (cracking at the corners of mouth).

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails – late sign).

Brittle hair, dry skin.

Dysphagia + post-cricoid web = Plummer-Vinson syndrome (pre-malignant).

### Investigations

CBC – low Hb, low MCV (<80 fL), low MCH (<27 pg), low MCHC, ↑RDW.

Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells, anisocytosis, target cells.

Reticulocyte count – low or normal.

Iron profile – serum iron ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation <15%, serum ferritin <30 ng/mL (most specific; >100 in inflammation can mask deficiency).

Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) – ↑ in IDA, normal in ACD (helpful when ferritin is unreliable).

Hb electrophoresis if microcytic anaemia not improving on iron (thalassaemia screen).

Stool occult blood, endoscopy, colonoscopy in adult males and post-menopausal women.

Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), urinalysis, gynaecologic evaluation.

### Management

- Treat underlying cause

Treat GI source (PUD, hookworm – albendazole 400 mg single), menorrhagia, coeliac disease, optimise diet.

### 2. Oral iron

Ferrous sulphate 200 mg TDS (60 mg elemental iron TDS).

**Alternatives:** ferrous fumarate 200 mg TDS (65 mg elemental), ferrous gluconate, iron polymaltose.

Take on empty stomach with vitamin C; avoid tea/coffee/milk within 1 h.

Continue for 3 months after Hb normalisation (replenish stores).

**Side effects:** nausea, constipation, dark stools, metallic taste – switch to lower-dose / alternate-day dosing if intolerant.

### 3. Parenteral iron (IV)

**Indications:** oral intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia requiring rapid response, advanced CKD on EPO, IBD, pregnancy 2nd-3rd trimester, peri-operative.

Iron sucrose 100–200 mg per dose IV, repeated to total calculated dose (Ganzoni formula: deficit mg = wt × (target Hb – actual Hb) × 2.4 + 500).

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – up to 1000 mg in single infusion (Indian: 'Encicarb', 'Ferinject').

Iron isomaltoside (Monofer), iron dextran (rarely used – anaphylaxis risk; test dose required).

Watch for hypersensitivity; phosphate may fall with FCM.

### 4. Blood transfusion

Only if Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms, or active bleeding, or <8 g/dL with cardiac compromise.

### 5. Follow-up

Reticulocyte rise within 1 week.

Hb rise ~2 g/dL by 3 weeks; full correction in 6–8 weeks.

If non-response – revisit diagnosis, check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption, mixed deficiency.

### 6. Prevention

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) – age-appropriate IFA supplementation: children 6–59 mo, school children, adolescents (WIFS), pregnant women (180 IFA + 360 calcium), lactating mothers.

Iron + folic acid fortification of staples (atta, rice, salt – DD iron).

Fig 2. Iron-deficiency anaemia — workup and management.

### Indications

Intolerance to oral iron (GI side effects despite dose modification).

Malabsorption – coeliac disease, gastric surgery, IBD.

Non-compliance.

Continued blood loss exceeding capacity of oral iron.

Pregnancy with severe anaemia in 2nd/3rd trimester or intolerance.

CKD anaemia, especially on EPO therapy.

Heart failure with iron deficiency (functional or absolute).

Need for rapid replenishment (pre-operative).

Anaemia of chronic disease where oral inefficient (hepcidin-mediated block).

### Preparations and doses

Iron sucrose – 100–200 mg slow IV, max 600 mg/week; multiple doses needed; safe in pregnancy.

Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM, e.g. Ferinject, Encicarb) – single dose up to 1000 mg over 15 min IV infusion; preferred for rapid correction; weekly if larger doses needed; widely used in India.

Iron isomaltoside / derisomaltose – up to 20 mg/kg in single infusion.

Ferumoxytol – 510 mg IV.

Iron dextran – high dose possible (total dose infusion) but anaphylaxis risk; test dose mandatory; rarely used.

Total iron deficit (Ganzoni formula)

Total iron required (mg) = Weight (kg) × (Target Hb − Actual Hb) × 2.4 + iron stores (500 mg adults / 15 mg/kg <35 kg).

Target Hb typically 15 g/dL (men), 14 g/dL (women); 11 g/dL in pregnancy.

### Adverse effects

**Infusion reaction:** fever, flushing, myalgia, hypotension (usually mild).

Anaphylaxis – rare with newer formulations (~1:200,000 FCM); higher with dextran.

Hypophosphataemia – particularly with FCM and iron isomaltoside (repeated doses).

Extravasation – skin staining (administer in proximal vein, stop if pain at site).

Iron overload – haemochromatosis-like with prolonged unmonitored use.

### Administration precautions

Resuscitation facility available (anaphylaxis).

Monitor BP/pulse/SpO₂.

Avoid in 1st trimester of pregnancy and active infection (except life-threatening anaemia).

Reassess Hb / ferritin / TSAT in 4–8 weeks post-infusion.

### Common preparations

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (60 mg elemental).

Ferrous fumarate 200 mg (65 mg elemental).

Ferrous gluconate 300 mg (35 mg elemental).

Ferrous ascorbate 100 mg (33 mg elemental) — improved tolerance.

Iron polymaltose (ferric) — slower release, better tolerated.

Carbonyl iron — less GI toxicity.

GI adverse effects (most common, 20–40%)

Nausea, vomiting.

Epigastric pain / discomfort.

Constipation (commonest).

Diarrhoea (less common).

Metallic taste.

Black tarry stools – may be mistaken for melaena, but occult-blood-negative.

Heartburn, oesophagitis (especially extended-release tablets).

### Other AEs

Teeth staining with liquid formulations (use straw, rinse mouth).

Allergic reaction – rare with oral.

Iron overload with prolonged unmonitored use in haemochromatosis carriers, thalassaemia.

**Reduced absorption of:** levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, methyldopa, mycophenolate (separate by 2 h).

Drug interactions / absorption inhibitors

**Reduce absorption:** antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, calcium, tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, whole-grain (phytates), oxalates, food in general.

**Enhance absorption:** vitamin C (100 mg with each dose), fasting, gastric acid.

Iron poisoning (acute overdose)

**Stage 1 (0.5–6 h):** GI – vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain.

**Stage 2 (6–24 h):** quiescent phase.

**Stage 3 (12–48 h):** systemic toxicity – metabolic acidosis, shock, AKI, hepatic failure, coagulopathy.

**Stage 4 (2–4 d):** hepatic failure peak.

**Stage 5 (2–6 wk):** gastric scarring, pyloric stenosis.

**Toxic dose:** >20 mg/kg elemental iron; lethal >60 mg/kg.

**Antidote:** desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (vin-rose urine indicates chelation).

Strategies to improve tolerance

Take with food (less absorption but less GI upset).

Start at lower dose, gradually escalate.

Alternate-day dosing — equally effective, better tolerated (recent evidence).

Switch to ferrous ascorbate, polymaltose, carbonyl iron.

Add stool softener for constipation.

Take with vitamin C (orange juice).

Avoid concurrent tea/coffee/calcium.

Switch to parenteral if intolerant (see Q18).

### Definition

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetric, erosive, inflammatory polyarthritis predominantly affecting peripheral synovial joints, associated with systemic features and extra-articular manifestations. Prevalence ~0.75% in India; female:male ≈ 3:1; peak onset 30–55 yrs.

### Etiology / Risk factors

**Genetic:** HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (DR4, DR1) — strongest in seropositive RA; PTPN22, STAT4

### Female sex, postpartum

Smoking — major modifiable risk; interacts with shared epitope to drive anti-CCP production

Periodontal disease (Porphyromonas gingivalis citrullination)

Obesity, low birth weight

### Silica dust exposure

### Pathophysiology (brief)

Citrullination of self-proteins → anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) in genetically susceptible host

Synovial hyperplasia (pannus) infiltrated by T cells, B cells, plasma cells, macrophages

**Pro-inflammatory cytokines:** TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1, IL-17

Osteoclast activation (RANKL) → bone erosion; matrix metalloproteinases → cartilage destruction

### Clinical features

### Articular

Insidious onset symmetric polyarthritis — MCPs, PIPs, MTPs, wrists, knees, ankles, cervical spine; DIPs and lumbar spine spared

Morning stiffness >30–60 min, improves with activity

Swelling, warmth, tenderness; reduced grip strength

**Late deformities:** ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, hammer toes, hallux valgus

Atlanto-axial subluxation — neck pain, neurological deficit (caution at intubation)

### Systemic

Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anorexia

Extra-articular manifestations (~40%; more in seropositive RA, high anti-CCP, smokers)

**Cutaneous:** rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces — olecranon, Achilles)

**Pulmonary:** ILD (UIP/NSIP), pleural effusion (exudative, low glucose, low pH), Caplan syndrome, bronchiectasis, rheumatoid lung nodules

**Cardiac:** pericarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis, ↑ MI risk (1.5×), cardiomyopathy

**Ocular:** keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren), episcleritis, scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, scleromalacia perforans

**Haematological:** anaemia of chronic disease, Felty's syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), large granular lymphocyte syndrome

**Neurological:** carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitic), atlanto-axial myelopathy

**Vasculitis:** small/medium vessel — digital gangrene, leg ulcers, mononeuritis

**Renal:** AA amyloidosis (long-standing disease), drug nephropathy

**Lymphoma:** 2–4× increased risk, especially DLBCL

**Bone:** peri-articular osteoporosis, systemic osteoporosis

Diagnostic criteria — ACR/EULAR 2010

Score ≥6/10 classifies as definite RA (in a patient with synovitis in ≥1 joint without alternative explanation):

### Investigations

### Inflammatory and serology

RF (IgM-RF) — sensitivity 60–80%, specificity 60–80%

Anti-CCP — sensitivity 60–70%, specificity >95%; prognostic for erosive disease

ESR, CRP — disease activity

### General workup

CBC (ACD, leukopenia in Felty), comprehensive metabolic, LFT, urinalysis

ANA — screen for overlap

HBsAg, anti-HCV, latent TB (Mantoux/IGRA) — pre-biologic

HIV (Indian context, before biologics)

### Imaging

X-ray hands and feet — soft-tissue swelling, juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, deformities, subluxation; cervical spine for atlanto-axial subluxation

Ultrasound joints — synovitis, power Doppler signal, erosions earlier than X-ray

MRI — most sensitive for early synovitis, erosions, bone marrow oedema

### Disease activity

DAS28-ESR or DAS28-CRP (tender + swollen joint count + global + ESR/CRP)

### CDAI, SDAI — alternatives

**Targets:** DAS28 <2.6 = remission; ≤3.2 low; 3.2–5.1 moderate; >5.1 high activity

### Management — treat-to-target

### General

Smoking cessation; weight reduction; physiotherapy and occupational therapy

Patient education; vaccination pre-immunosuppression (influenza, pneumococcal, HBV, HPV); avoid live vaccines on biologics

CV risk assessment and treatment (statin, BP control)

### Symptom relief

NSAIDs at lowest effective dose for short periods

Prednisolone 5–10 mg/d as 'bridge' until DMARD effective; intra-articular steroid for active joints

Avoid long-term steroids — osteoporosis, infection, diabetes

csDMARDs (conventional synthetic) — start within 3 months of diagnosis

**Methotrexate:** Anchor drug. Start 7.5–10 mg/week, titrate to 20–25 mg/week. Co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg/wk (not on MTX day). AE: nausea, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, pneumonitis, teratogenicity. Stop 3 months before conception (M and F). Avoid alcohol. Reduce dose in CKD; contraindicated in eGFR <30.

**Sulfasalazine:** 1 g BD–TDS. AE: GI upset, rash, hepatitis, agranulocytosis, G6PD-related haemolysis, oligospermia.

**Hydroxychloroquine:** 200–400 mg/d (≤5 mg/kg). AE: retinal toxicity — eye check baseline + annual after 5 yrs.

**Leflunomide:** 10–20 mg/d (loading 100 mg × 3 days then maintenance — most centres skip loading). AE: hepatotoxicity, diarrhoea, hypertension, teratogenicity (very long half-life; cholestyramine washout needed before pregnancy).

**Combination 'triple therapy':** MTX + SSZ + HCQ — Indian-favoured cost-effective combination, comparable efficacy to early biologic in many patients

Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) — after inadequate response to ≥2 csDMARDs

**TNF inhibitors:** etanercept (50 mg SC weekly), adalimumab (40 mg SC q2wk), infliximab (3–10 mg/kg IV q8wk + MTX), golimumab (50 mg SC monthly), certolizumab

**IL-6 inhibitor:** tocilizumab 162 mg SC weekly OR 4–8 mg/kg IV q4wk

**B-cell depletion:** rituximab 1 g IV × 2 (day 0 and 14), every 6 months — RF/anti-CCP-positive; safer in latent TB

**T-cell co-stimulation:** abatacept 125 mg SC weekly OR weight-based IV monthly

**IL-1 inhibitor:** anakinra (rarely used in RA)

Always combine with MTX where tolerated for synergy and reduced anti-drug antibodies

Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) — JAK inhibitors

Tofacitinib 5 mg BD, baricitinib 4 mg OD, upadacitinib 15 mg OD

**ORAL Surveillance trial (2022):** increased major CV events, malignancy, VTE with tofacitinib vs TNFi in older patients with CV risk

**EMA/FDA:** use only if no TNFi alternative in patients ≥65 yr, smokers, malignancy, CV risk

Pre-biologic screening (essential — viva point)

**TB:** Mantoux/IGRA, CXR; if positive — INH 300 mg/d × 9 months started ≥1 month before biologic

### HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV

### CBC, LFT, RFT

Pregnancy test; contraception counselling

### Surgical

### Synovectomy (rare today)

Arthrodesis, arthroplasty (hip/knee/shoulder) for end-stage joint damage

C1–C2 fixation for atlanto-axial instability

### Carpal tunnel release

Fig 5. Rheumatoid arthritis — treat-to-target DMARD ladder

### Complications

Joint destruction, deformity, functional disability

Premature CV death (leading cause)

### ILD, pulmonary fibrosis

### Cervical myelopathy (atlanto-axial)

### Infections (immunosuppression)

### Lymphoma, skin cancers

### Osteoporosis, fragility fractures

### AA amyloidosis

### Prognosis

Modern treat-to-target therapy achieves remission/low disease activity in 50–80%. Adverse prognostic factors: female, smoking, high titre RF/anti-CCP, early erosions, multiple joint involvement, extra-articular features, high inflammatory markers. Untreated RA shortens life expectancy by 5–10 years, mostly from CV disease.

**Source:** Boloor Ch.9 RA + ACR 2021 guideline for RA + EULAR 2022 RA management recommendations + Indian Rheumatology Association RA position paper.

### Combined Notes (7 topics)

First-line drugs and hepatotoxicity

**Isoniazid (H):** Hepatotoxic – stop if ALT >5× ULN (or >3× with symptoms).

**Pyrazinamide (Z):** Most hepatotoxic of the first-line drugs; dose-dependent.

**Rifampicin (R):** Hepatotoxic; also causes orange discoloration of secretions.

**Ethambutol (E):** Not hepatotoxic; main risks – optic neuritis (visual acuity), peripheral neuropathy.

Drugs to avoid in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure: H, R, Z.

Modified regimen for hepatitis / hepatic impairment (NTEP, WHO 2024)

If ALT >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN without – stop all hepatotoxic ATT.

Continue with non-hepatotoxic combination: ethambutol + streptomycin/levofloxacin (+ rifampicin if liver enzymes recovering; reintroduce H or Z sequentially).

**Severe hepatitis:** 2 SH(streptomycin + isoniazid)E + 6 HE OR 9–12 RE + levofloxacin / linezolid based regimen.

**Once LFTs return to normal:** gradually reintroduce R first, then H, last Z (if needed).

Other antimicrobials notable for hepatotoxicity in ATT context

Para-amino salicylic acid (PAS) – hepatotoxic.

Ethionamide / prothionamide – hepatotoxic.

Bedaquiline – QT prolongation, mild LFT rise.

Linezolid – BM suppression, neuropathy; mild hepatic.

Monitor LFTs weekly during reintroduction; counsel patient about alcohol cessation, paracetamol limits, no herbal supplements.
